summary: Only his location survives for this day: Cambridge, at college.

headline: Rain and gloomy thoughts
summary: Kept indoors all day by rain, Roosevelt broods over the family's loss.

headline: Sizing up his Sunday school boys
summary: Roosevelt calls his grief selfish but still painful. He sketches each boy in his Sunday school class, from eager Watson to troublesome Phillipot, and takes comfort that his father approved of his teaching. He also writes Bamie.

headline: A day without an entry
summary: Roosevelt is a Harvard student in Cambridge; the record is silent otherwise.

headline: Night boat home with Harry Chapin
summary: Two months to the day after his father's death, Roosevelt sets out for New York on the overnight boat with his friend Harry Chapin.

headline: A joyful welcome home
summary: Roosevelt's family greets him warmly in New York; only Bamie is missing, away in Denver.

headline: Harder to be home than expected
summary: The memories at home hit Roosevelt hard, and he writes that his days of pure happiness are over. He still counts his blessings and enjoys an evening meal with his Gracie aunt and uncle.

headline: Sweet Conie, warming to Emlen
summary: Roosevelt delights in his sister Conie's company and finds his opinion of cousin Emlen improving.

headline: Visiting Cassin, a bedridden man
summary: Roosevelt calls on Cassin, a poor man confined to bed, one of many who will feel his father's absence keenly.

headline: Choosing his mottoes
summary: After a talk with the boys, Roosevelt adopts two Bible verses as personal mottoes.

headline: Three days at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt goes out to Oyster Bay with his mother and Conie. Everything there reminds them of his father, which makes the start of the stay painful.

headline: Rowing Centre Island, hunting muskrats
summary: Roosevelt rows his skiff around Centre Island, kills an oldsquaw duck and shoots two muskrats in a brackish pond.

headline: One more muskrat, then the city
summary: Roosevelt bags a muskrat in a tiny brook before returning to New York, where Bamie is just back from Denver.

headline: A hymn from Conie, thoughts of a wife
summary: Conie copies out a hymn of consolation for Roosevelt. He writes that he has lost the one person he told everything, and wonders who the wife will be who might one day fill that place.

headline: Home in New York, nothing noted
summary: Roosevelt is home in New York City; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Unrecorded day in New York
summary: The chronology places Roosevelt in New York and notes no events.

headline: Quiet day in the city
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City with his family; the day has no entry.

headline: Mother sees him off to Boston
summary: Roosevelt boards the overnight boat for Boston, with his mother coming down to say goodbye. On board he is homesick and grieving for his father.

headline: Back in his snug room
summary: Roosevelt settles back into his small room in Cambridge, and his friends give him a hearty welcome.

headline: Four weeks of grinding left
summary: Roosevelt notes that a month of hard study stands between him and the end of term.

headline: Easier at college than at home
summary: Roosevelt writes that the sharpest grief is passing, though nights are still hard. College holds fewer reminders than home, and the Bible chapters his father loved bring him both joy and sadness.

headline: Quiet day at Harvard
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard in Cambridge; the record notes nothing else for the day.

headline: Unrecorded day in Cambridge
summary: The chronology places Roosevelt in Cambridge and logs no letters or events.

headline: Last Sunday school until fall
summary: Roosevelt teaches what he expects to be his final Sunday school class until October.

headline: Strong grades, a proud father remembered
summary: Roosevelt's marks are excellent, and he recalls how proud his father was of his progress.

headline: Clean-shaven and teased for it
summary: Roosevelt shaves off his whiskers and takes no end of ribbing from his friends. He also takes up lawn tennis.

headline: Memories that bring pleasure
summary: Kept indoors by gloomy weather, Roosevelt thinks about his father at length, and for once the memories bring him only happiness.

headline: Hal Minot leaves Harvard
summary: Roosevelt is sorry to learn that his friend Hal Minot has left college, remembering how kind Minot was during his worst days of grief.

headline: Off to Minot Weld's for the weekend
summary: Roosevelt heads to Minot Weld's home for the evening, planning to stay until Monday.

headline: Cows, chickens and a drive
summary: Roosevelt and Minot Weld poke around the farmyard in the morning, then drive over to visit Dick Saltonstall.

headline: A short, practical sermon
summary: Roosevelt hears a brief sermon he likes and reflects on how widely his father was loved.

headline: An early return to college
summary: Roosevelt gets back to Cambridge early in the day.

headline: Grades mean less without Father
summary: Roosevelt keeps working hard but admits his marks matter less now, since he valued them most for his father's pride in them.

headline: Club table photographed
summary: Roosevelt and the friends who share his club dining table have their picture taken.

headline: Three months on, a boat to New York
summary: Three months after his father's death, Roosevelt and Harry Chapin catch the evening Fall River line boat to New York.

headline: Spring warblers at Oyster Bay
summary: Arriving in New York at dawn, Roosevelt takes a morning train to Oyster Bay to join his mother. He finds the countryside lovely, collects a warbler and spends the night.

headline: Family gathering at Orange
summary: After noting plenty of warblers at Oyster Bay and shooting two squirrels, Roosevelt goes into the city and straight out to Uncle Corneil's place in Orange, New Jersey, where the whole family and the Gracies make a fuss over him.

headline: A lonely Sunday at Orange
summary: Roosevelt spends a quiet Sunday in Orange, New Jersey, where he last stayed years ago with his father. Being with the family lifts his spirits.

headline: Night boat back to Boston
summary: Roosevelt goes into the city early and takes the overnight boat to Boston.

headline: Back in Cambridge at dawn
summary: Roosevelt reaches Cambridge early in the morning.

headline: Studying like a Trojan
summary: Roosevelt is deep in exam preparation.

headline: Missing Father's advice on his future
summary: On a walk into town with Jack Tebbetts, whom he calls a rough diamond, Roosevelt is moved by his friend's words about his father. He writes how lost he feels without his father's guidance on what to do after college.

headline: Unrecorded day in Cambridge
summary: The chronology places Roosevelt in Cambridge and logs no letters or events.

headline: No entry for the day at college
summary: Roosevelt is at college in Cambridge, with no activity written down.

headline: Sunday with the Minot family
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday with the George Minot family, hears a sermon on finishing whatever one starts, and takes a long afternoon walk.

headline: Battling French
summary: Back in Cambridge, Roosevelt is putting extra effort into French, which he despises, amid poor weather.

headline: Tennis and rowing for exercise
summary: Roosevelt is keeping fit with lawn tennis and the occasional row on the river in a racing shell.

headline: DKE theatricals
summary: Dick Saltonstall comes to the Delta Kappa Epsilon theatricals, and Roosevelt is pleased he will join their table next year. Several students, Pellew among them, drink far too much.

headline: Feverish, dreaming of Father
summary: Feeling ill and feverish, Roosevelt has a vivid dream about his father that leaves him sad and lonely.

headline: Bob Bacon flies at Beacon Park
summary: At the Harvard Athletic Association's foot races at Beacon Park, Robert Bacon turns in an impressive time.

headline: French exam, a loss to Yale
summary: Roosevelt sits his French midyear exam, and the Harvard baseball team is badly beaten by Yale.

headline: Breaking his Sunday rule
summary: With his exams piling up, Roosevelt studies on a Sunday and feels ashamed of it.

headline: Anatomy final
summary: Roosevelt takes his year-end anatomy exam.

headline: Coaching classmates for an exam
summary: Roosevelt helps about six classmates prepare for the next day's exam.

headline: Rhetoric final
summary: Roosevelt sits his annual rhetoric exam.

headline: German final
summary: Roosevelt takes his year-end German exam.

headline: Sophomore year by the numbers
summary: Cool weather helps Roosevelt study. His sophomore marks average 89, from a 96 in German I down to a 51 in French, and the year at Harvard cost him $2,049.

headline: French final, freshmen beat Yale
summary: Roosevelt takes his annual French exam after a week of feeling poorly. Harvard's freshman nine trounces Yale's class of 1881.

headline: 'How pleased Father will be!'
summary: With the spring's hard work behind him, Roosevelt catches himself still imagining his father's pleasure at each success.

headline: Boston hospitality and summer invitations
summary: Roosevelt credits his Boston friends' hospitality with brightening college life. Jack Tebbetts invites him to Schooner Head for a month and Harry Shaw for a Sunday. With his club table disbanded, he now eats at Memorial Hall beside Gorham Peters.

headline: Quiet day at Harvard
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard in Cambridge; the record notes nothing else for the day.

headline: Botany exam, then off for summer
summary: Roosevelt finishes his botany final and leaves Cambridge that evening, heading for Oyster Bay as the term ends.

headline: Oyster Bay full of Father
summary: Roosevelt reaches Oyster Bay around noon and finds every corner of the house tied to memories of his father.

headline: Warblers, a ride and a cry for Father
summary: Roosevelt collects a parula warbler and a grasshopper sparrow in Fleets Woods and takes a fine ride on Lightfoot. Annie Murray is visiting Conie, the Gracies are in town, and his grief breaks through again.

headline: Varnishing his boat
summary: Roosevelt sands and varnishes his boat. He is grateful for his family's affection but wishes his mother and Bamie would stop quarreling.

headline: Seeing Father in the pew
summary: Four months after his father's death, Roosevelt spends the sermon picturing him in his familiar corner of the family pew.

headline: Dawn tramp, then a boathouse
summary: Roosevelt is up with the sun for a long hike, back by nine, and spends the rest of the day building his boathouse.

headline: Rainy day of chores, a petted son
summary: On a wet day Roosevelt divides his time among the boathouse, his gun and his rowboat, and worries that his doting family will spoil him.

headline: Riding with Annie Murray
summary: Roosevelt and Annie Murray ride out to Syosset and back through Laurel Hollow, then takes her rowing. He finds her sweet, pretty and clever; she leaves the next day.

headline: Pine Island and the season's first swim
summary: Roosevelt rows to Pine Island, collects a pine warbler and takes his first swim of the year. He notes that all the Roosevelt young men but him are now in business.

headline: Fanny Smith arrives; West smitten
summary: Fanny Smith has come to visit, and cousin West Roosevelt, who has loved her for three years, comes for tea. Roosevelt rows her to Cooper Bluff, where they race down the slope like children.

headline: Picnic at Yellow Banks
summary: Roosevelt picnics at Yellow Banks with Fanny, Conie and West, and in the afternoon takes Fanny on a long ride. The Gracies arrive for a stay of several weeks.

headline: A gloomy stop at West 57th
summary: After church Roosevelt sets out for Harvard to take his last two exams, stopping for tea at the family's New York house, which feels empty and desolate.

headline: Asthma sank his French exam
summary: After a botany exam, Roosevelt explains that he did badly on French three weeks earlier because asthma kept him awake the night before. He shrugs it off.

headline: Elected to the A.D. Club
summary: After his final German exam, Roosevelt is surprised to be elected to the A.D. Club. He judges his second Harvard year happy and useful, and boards the night boat for New York.

headline: Remembering Father's nights of care
summary: Roosevelt visits Cassin in New York before going out to Oyster Bay. He recalls his father pacing the floor for hours carrying him through childhood asthma attacks.

headline: Bad shooting, rowing and riding
summary: Roosevelt shoots poorly with the rifle, rows to Plum Point and goes riding.

headline: A happy outdoor summer
summary: Roosevelt describes his days of riding, tramping after specimens and rowing or sailing, gun in hand. He resolves not to be gloomy, since his father was always cheerful, and gallops twenty miles on Lightfoot.

headline: Sailing to Lloyd Neck with Alfred
summary: Roosevelt rows to Plum Point and back, then sails with Alfred to Lloyd Neck for lunch and some shooting. In the afternoon he rides with two girls; the day's bag is two herons and two sandsnipe.

headline: Quiet Sunday at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: A chickadee nest and a sunburn
summary: Roosevelt finds a chickadee nest on Pine Island and takes Nellie Beekman riding. His sunburned face, he jokes, looks like an undercooked lobster, and he frets about Elliott's friends.

headline: Rough water around Centre Island
summary: Roosevelt rows around Centre Island in two hours, shooting along the way and taking on water in a heavy sea. A long gallop on the flat Long Island roads follows; he bags two sandpipers.

headline: Water lilies and a supper sail
summary: Roosevelt rides to Brookville and Glen Cove, walks Fleets Woods with his mother, drives Conie to Cold Spring for water lilies, rows to the marsh, and sails with Elliott at dusk, eating dinner aboard.

headline: At New London for the boat race
summary: Roosevelt travels to New London for the Harvard-Yale race, staying at Harry Chapin's with Minot Weld and Jackson.

headline: Harvard wins; hoarse from cheering
summary: Harvard wins the race handily and Roosevelt shouts himself hoarse. He takes the night boat to New York that evening.

headline: A new Sharps rifle
summary: Back at Oyster Bay, Roosevelt buys a Sharps rifle, and Harvard takes the baseball championship.

headline: 'Rest in trouble, not from trouble'
summary: A sermon line strikes Roosevelt, who credits his faith with carrying him through his grief; the family spends the evening singing hymns. Meanwhile President Hayes removes Chester A. Arthur and puts Edwin A. Merritt in charge of New York's customhouse.

headline: Target practice and a tan at Tranquility
summary: Summering at the family's Oyster Bay house, Roosevelt tests a new rifle and scores 67 of 100, calling himself a poor marksman. Rowing has bronzed his upper body, his horse has gone slightly lame, and the swimming is a delight.

headline: Rifle practice, then a farewell visit in town
summary: Roosevelt improves to 71 of 100 at the rifle, then heads into New York City to see Annie Murray, who leaves for Europe the next day, and spends a pleasant evening calling on her.

headline: Seeing Annie off, then a night sail
summary: At seven in the morning Roosevelt boards the steamer Russia to bid Annie Murray goodbye, finding her pretty but a touch cross. He accompanies Aunt Susie on the trip to Oyster Bay, and that night he and his brother Elliott sail Elliott's 21-foot Daphne across to Rye Harbor, dropping anchor at 1:30 a.m.

headline: Fourth of July sail home from Rye
summary: Roosevelt and Elliott pass the morning and have dinner at the Bulkleys' near Rye, then set off for home at 4:15 p.m., not reaching their Oyster Bay mooring until eleven. The long sail calls up memories of the brothers' many earlier cruises together.

headline: A tender talk with his mother
summary: Roosevelt and his mother Mittie talk at length, sweetly and sadly, about his late father. Uncle Jimmie Gracie stays over from the city, and he and Roosevelt spend time sailing and rowing.

headline: Timed row around Centre Island
summary: Roosevelt rows eight miles around Centre Island, logging each landmark against the clock, though low tide forces a half-mile detour and the portage eats 14 minutes. In the afternoon he outshoots Alfred at the rifle, 54 to 18.

headline: Missing Father at Sunday prayers
summary: Roosevelt writes that he is heartsick for his father. At evening singing the family cannot get through a hymn they last sang together on the Sunday he died, and Roosevelt reads Isaiah 55, one of his father's favorites, at prayers.

headline: Winning a rifle match on Mittie's birthday
summary: On his mother's 43rd birthday, Roosevelt wins a shooting match against his cousins West and Emlen, 57 to their 48 and 49. His horse has nearly recovered from its lameness.

headline: Five months without his father
summary: Marking five months since his father's death, Roosevelt reflects that he feels much older and must now solve his own problems instead of bringing them to his father, whose words and gestures he still recalls with startling clarity.

headline: Stuck in the mud at Lloyd Neck
summary: Rowing around Lloyd Neck, Roosevelt bogs down in the mud flats while carrying his boat across the isthmus and struggles to free himself. On the way home a thunder squall catches him in a stiff southwest wind. Fifteen miles, two plover and two gulls.

headline: Sailing with cousins, doubting himself
summary: Roosevelt sails with West and Alfred, picnic lunch aboard, and splits the rest of the day between riding and rowing. In his diary he frets that so remarkable a father deserved a worthier son.

headline: Rained in, sizing up his friends
summary: Rain keeps Roosevelt indoors for the first time all summer. He takes stock of his five closest friends: Elliott and Jack Elliott think too well of him, West and Emlen too little, and Alfred judges him about right.

headline: A daily run through the woods
summary: Roosevelt runs a mile flat out through the woods and plans to make it a daily habit.

headline: Pascal and doubts at Communion Sunday
summary: On Communion Sunday Roosevelt copies out a line from Pascal warning against both excluding and relying only on reason, and writes that he finds materialism and superstition equally distasteful. During church he broods on feeling less useful than his father, yet ends on a note of faith.

headline: Hot row and a long gallop
summary: In dead calm and fierce heat at high tide, Roosevelt rows around Centre Island again, the portage this time taking only five minutes. Later he and Emlen gallop out beyond Wheatley and around it.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Riding to Lake Ronkonkoma
summary: Roosevelt and West ride out on a cool, cloudy morning, reach Smithtown by 10:45, push on to Lake Ronkonkoma for supper, and return to Smithtown to sleep. About 35 miles, and his horse finishes as fresh as it began.

headline: Back from Smithtown in the heat
summary: Roosevelt rides home from Smithtown to Oyster Bay in two and a half hours on a very hot day.

headline: Twenty-five miles by oar to Rye
summary: Leaving at 5:15 a.m., Roosevelt rows across to Rye Beach by way of Rocky Point and Oak Bluff, then rows home that evening, a round trip of more than 25 miles in calm, heavy heat. He spots a stormy petrel.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: A one-line Sunday prayer
summary: Roosevelt's diary for this Sunday holds a single line of scripture, a plea from the Gospel of Mark.

headline: Woodcock in the woods
summary: Roosevelt hikes far through woods and fields with his shotgun and brings back four woodcock and two doves.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Visiting the sick, then the Dickeys
summary: In New York City Roosevelt calls on his ailing friend Cassin, then spends the evening with the Dickey family, whose warmth he loves. Young Charles Dickey will enter Harvard next year, and Roosevelt promises himself to help him.

headline: Home again to Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt heads back out to Oyster Bay from his stay near the city.

headline: Rigging a sail on his skiff
summary: Roosevelt fits his small outrigger skiff with a leg-of-mutton sail on a seven-foot mast and takes her out. She points poorly into the wind but holds steady and moves briskly downwind.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Marsh shooting on Alice Lee's birthday
summary: On the day Alice Lee, his future wife, turns 17, Roosevelt rows to Lloyd Neck and paddles the winding marsh channels at high tide, taking shots at herons and snipe. A southerly breeze lets him sail several miles out into the Sound. Elliott leaves on a three-week holiday.

headline: Rainy woods, then a fine ride
summary: Despite rain, Roosevelt roams the woods with his gun in the morning, bagging a dove and a wild pigeon, and enjoys a splendid ride in the afternoon.

headline: Quick row around Centre Island
summary: Roosevelt borrows Alfred's boat and circles Centre Island in an hour and 24 minutes.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Timed circuit of Lloyd Neck
summary: Starting at ten, Roosevelt rows around Lloyd Neck past the Huntington Harbor lighthouse and is home by 1:45. A dead-high tide trims the portage to four minutes.

headline: Aiming for Greenwich, landing in Darien
summary: Roosevelt and Emlen sail across the Sound meaning to reach Greenwich but misjudge which side of Shippan Point to pass and end up at Darien. Roosevelt notes he has ridden his horse every day he has been home this season.

headline: Doers of the word
summary: Roosevelt admires the scripture carved over his church door and writes that he puts no stock in faith without deeds. He has been reading the published memorial to his father and resolves to live as his father would have hoped.

headline: Woodcock in thick cover
summary: Roosevelt hunts woodcock over some 25 miles of rough country, where the birds now hide in dense brush. He misses more than half his shots and comes home with seven, he and the dog both worn out by the heat.

headline: A birthday gift for Edith Carow
summary: For Edith Carow's 17th birthday, Roosevelt sends her a bonbonniere. His sister Corinne also writes Edith an affectionate letter about her future.

headline: Jack Elliott comes to stay
summary: Roosevelt's good friend Jack Elliott arrives at Oyster Bay for a visit of five or six weeks.

headline: Sail, oar and paddle to Lloyd Neck
summary: With a following wind, Roosevelt and Jack Elliott make good time to Lloyd Neck using sail, oars and paddle together. They hunt the lagoons, lunch, fight their way out of the marsh at dead low tide and row home into a headwind, with two yellowlegs and two herons.

headline: Six months gone, a glorious sail
summary: Roosevelt and Jack sail in a near-reefing breeze without shortening canvas. He calls Oyster Bay the ideal place for young men and wonders if anyone could be happier, while noting it has been six months since his father died.

headline: Harvard grades arrive
summary: Roosevelt's Harvard rank list comes, showing an average near 85, a ten-point gain over the year before, with his best marks in German and natural history. He is pleased and thinks his father would have been too, though he is laid up with cholera morbus.

headline: Missing church, thinking of Father
summary: Still ill, Roosevelt misses church for nearly the first time that year. With idle hours, a rarity for him, his thoughts keep returning to his father.

headline: Mosquito portage and a note from Edith
summary: Roosevelt and Jack row to Plum Point, haul the boat 200 yards over miserable, mosquito-thick ground into the big marsh behind Centre Island, then hunt, lunch and sail home. Edith Carow has sent a sweet thank-you for her birthday gift.

headline: Riding the tide through Lloyd Neck marsh
summary: Roosevelt and Jack row to Lloyd Neck, going into the marsh as the tide rises and coming out as it falls. A stiff southerly holds them out until late afternoon. One yellowlegs, one sand snipe.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Nine hours after woodcock
summary: Roosevelt hunts woodcock from eight to five without stopping to eat or rest, testing new knickerbockers, gaiters and hunting shoes. The cover is so thick he misses two shots in three, yet he takes six birds and feels completely fresh.

headline: Edith visits; caught in a squall
summary: Edith Carow arrives for a two-week stay with Corinne. Roosevelt, Emlen and Jack sail to the Connecticut shore and run into a heavy rainstorm on the way back.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Picnic sail and boxing lessons
summary: Roosevelt, Edith, Corinne, Jack and Emlen sail out for a picnic lunch at Yellowbanks. He starts teaching Jack to box, gets the better of Emlen in a bout, and loses to him at the rifle.

headline: Rowing Edith; West's confession
summary: Roosevelt rows Edith out toward Lloyd Neck and spars with Jack and West. Riding with West, he hears all about his cousin's devotion to a young woman named Fanny and is touched by how smitten West is.

headline: Water lilies with Edith
summary: Roosevelt drives Edith to Cold Spring to gather water lilies, a lovely morning together. In the afternoon Elliott sails in on the Waterwitch with cousin Jack Roosevelt after a three-week cruise.

headline: Family sail and tea at West's
summary: Roosevelt, Elliott and Jack take their mother, Edith and Corinne sailing. That evening a large family party has tea at West's, after which Roosevelt and Edith walk up to the summer house. He worries his hard ride that day may have hurt his horse.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Shooting a troublesome dog
summary: Having warned a dog's owner after the animal harassed him on horseback, Roosevelt carries out the threat while riding with West, killing it with his revolver as it runs beside his horse.

headline: Sunday family prayers
summary: Roosevelt notes how much he values the family habit of morning and evening prayers on Sundays.

headline: A dawn gallop, then off on the Addie
summary: On a crisp, clear morning Roosevelt rides twenty miles at a gallop with Emlen. Around noon he, Emlen, West and Jack board the Addie for a short cruise, reaching New Haven about ten that night in light air.

headline: Lazy day under sail to New London
summary: Light winds keep the Addie under way until 8 p.m. before she reaches New London. The young men swim, read the New Symposium, climb the rigging and play whist.

headline: Revolver practice off Greenport
summary: The party sails on to Greenport in fitful breezes. With hundreds of cartridges aboard, they fire their revolvers at anything that surfaces, from bottles and buoys to sharks and porpoises.

headline: Along the Long Island shore
summary: In a steady breeze the Addie sails all day along Long Island's low, sandy shoreline. Roosevelt spends long stretches up in the crosstrees; the rest goes to whist and arguments about materialism and politics.

headline: Cruise ends at Oyster Bay
summary: The Addie reaches Oyster Bay at 1 a.m. and the crew comes ashore for breakfast. Roosevelt has loved the cruise, and in the afternoon he goes sailing again with Jack and Alfred. Corinne writes Edith that her visit was worth another painful goodbye.

headline: Hunting sea coots in vain
summary: Roosevelt and Jack row nearly twenty miles after sea coots without seeing a single one. George Minot arrives for a few days' visit.

headline: Uncertain about the future
summary: Roosevelt talks with Uncle Jim about what he will do with his life and admits he has no idea what follows college. Missing his father's guidance keenly, he decides his job for the next two years is plain: study hard and live as a brave Christian gentleman.

headline: Racing to Rye and back
summary: A strong westerly sends two boats across to Rye and back: Roosevelt and Alfred in the Meteor, with Elliott, Jack and George Minot crewing the Daphne. They lunch with the Bulkleys, where Roosevelt meets Miss Lee Berry.

headline: Racing a squall to Rocky Point
summary: Roosevelt and Jack plan a night out in the skiff, but heavy rain sends them home. After lunch at Matinecock Point a fierce northwest squall hits off Oak Bluff, and they run before it under sail to Rocky Point, taking on a lot of water.

headline: Grim news about Hal Minot
summary: George Minot tells Roosevelt that his brother Hal, a close friend, has lost his reason and been placed in an asylum. Roosevelt grieves for the gentle, bright young man and his family. Later Uncle Hill and Aunt Susie come to stay.

headline: Sad news, then dinner at the Union League
summary: Overnighting in New York, Roosevelt visits Cassin, who is slowly dying, and learns that Cousin Sam Roosevelt has died. Still low about Hal Minot, he dines that evening at the Union League Club with Jack Roosevelt and Emlen.

headline: Northbound for the Maine woods
summary: Roosevelt, West and Emlen board an early-morning train to Boston, bound for three weeks in the Maine woods. Writing of Hal Minot, he says his father's death has dulled his ability to grieve.

headline: Arriving at Island Falls
summary: After an overnight train to Mattawamkeag, the party rides a buckboard to Island Falls, arriving at 8 p.m. Roosevelt is suffering a bad bout of asthma and misses his horse.

headline: Psalm 19 and a Methodist meeting
summary: Roosevelt walks, reads his Bible and memorizes Psalm 19. With no church in Island Falls, he attends a Methodist meeting in the schoolhouse. Thoughts of Hal Minot bring back his grief for his father.

headline: Partridge hunt, seven months on
summary: Seven months after his father's death, Roosevelt spends the whole day after partridges without seeing one.

headline: Paddling down to Mattawamkeag Lake
summary: The party heads downstream to camp at the foot of Mattawamkeag Lake, the others in a bateau with guide Sewall while Roosevelt goes ahead by canoe with guide Dow. He enjoys the paddling and woods walking but misses every shot at pigeons and ducks.

headline: A loon at long range and a quiet ramble
summary: Roosevelt and Emlen canoe the lake; Roosevelt fires at a loon over a hundred yards away and nearly hits it. In the afternoon they hike about ten miles after partridge, taking one ruffed grouse, and he praises Emlen as a loyal companion.

headline: Rainy day in camp
summary: Rain keeps the party under canvas with books, cards and gun cleaning, eating duck, partridge, trout and pickerel. Roosevelt and Emlen sit three hours in the wet waiting for ducks and come back empty-handed.

headline: Still raining at camp
summary: Another wet day of reading, euchre, whist and rifle practice in camp. Roosevelt waits for ducks again with one long miss, and kills a bat and a nighthawk.

headline: Missing foxes across the river
summary: When the rain stops at noon, Roosevelt hikes fifteen miles with Sewall and comes back with nothing. He misses two foxes at about sixty yards and is fed up with his week of poor shooting.

headline: Bible, guns and specimens
summary: Roosevelt reads his Bible in the morning, then fills the afternoon cleaning guns and labeling specimens before a swim in the mill race.

headline: Thirty miles along the Mattawamkeag
summary: After a frosty night, Roosevelt and Sewall hike thirty miles near the Mattawamkeag River, on the move from eight to seven save a half-hour lunch. He gets only four shots, bagging a rabbit, a merganser and two grouse, but loves the walk.

headline: A night in a wigwam
summary: Roosevelt, West and guide Dow paddle to the head of the lake and hunt the sloughs and bogs with middling luck, taking two ducks. The three camp overnight in a wigwam on a meager supper.

headline: Up at four for ducks
summary: Up before dawn, the three hunt ducks and see none. Back at the main camp, Roosevelt walks about ten miles with Will Dow for four shots, a merganser and three grouse, and decides moccasins are the best footwear for the woods.

headline: Through alder and cedar swamps
summary: Roosevelt hikes about fifteen miles, three of them through some of the hardest swamp walking he has known. He takes a spruce partridge among the cedars and a ruffed grouse up on a hemlock ridge.

headline: Fooled by a decoy duck
summary: On a ten-mile walk with Sewall, Roosevelt stalks and kills a duck on a small lake. The others then trick him with a dead duck propped up to look alive in a pond. He has bathed in the mill race daily.

headline: Autumn color in the Maine woods
summary: Roosevelt and Emlen hunt in the afternoon; Emlen never fires, and Roosevelt misses a duck but drops a partridge. The leaves are turning, and he counts the trip a real success.

headline: Quiet Sunday in camp
summary: Roosevelt passes Sunday much as he did the week before.

headline: Breaking camp by bateau
summary: The party breaks camp and heads back to Island Falls in the clumsy bateau: Sewall paddling, Roosevelt and Dow at the oars, Thompson trolling, and West and Emlen in the bow watching for game. Roosevelt spends the afternoon in the woods with West.

headline: Twenty-five miles with Dow
summary: Roosevelt hikes 25 miles with Dow, taking a woodcock and two partridges. Game has been scarce all trip, but he has loved it, and the party has not had one quarrel.

headline: Hunting from a buckboard
summary: Roosevelt rides around all day in a buckboard, Will Dow at his side, climbing down each time they spot a partridge. He gets five grouse and sees a fox.

headline: Leaving Maine
summary: The party drives by wagon to Mattawamkeag and boards the night train for Boston. His companions will continue to New York; Roosevelt is bound back to Harvard.

headline: Back at Harvard, a surprise invitation
summary: Roosevelt returns to Cambridge for his junior year to a warm welcome. To his astonishment the Porcellian Club asks him to join, and he feels he must decline because he belongs to the A.D. Club, though he wishes otherwise. His sister Corinne turns 17.

headline: Settling into the junior-year routine
summary: Roosevelt finds his classes and lab work will fill about twenty hours a week, with an 8 a.m. recitation daily, Saturdays included. Harry Shaw and Dick Saltonstall each invite him for Sunday, and his club table at Mrs. Wilson's serves excellent meals.

headline: Sunday church in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt goes to church and plans to resume teaching Sunday school in a week or two.

headline: Down to work and the rifle club
summary: Roosevelt starts studying in earnest and joins the rifle club, meaning to shoot regularly this year. In New York the cables for the Brooklyn Bridge are finished.

headline: Into the Glee Club
summary: Roosevelt is voted into the Harvard Glee Club.

headline: At the D.K.E., but not drinking
summary: Roosevelt attends the first D.K.E. meeting of the year. He finds its drinking tiresome as a steady diet, though fun now and then; he does not drink there, drinks very little anyway, and will not smoke before he is 21.

headline: First meeting of the Art Club
summary: Roosevelt goes to the opening meeting of the Art Club and enjoys it.

headline: Favorite courses: philosophy and economics
summary: Roosevelt ranks his courses: philosophy and political economy come first, natural history is engaging if less so than last year, and the rest interest him little.

headline: Morning at the rifle range
summary: Roosevelt spends the morning shooting at the range.

headline: Communion Sunday at Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt marks Communion Sunday.

headline: Hard work, with holidays ahead
summary: Roosevelt is studying hard, but his strong average last year earns him optional recitations, so he expects some three weeks of winter holidays.

headline: Boxing lessons resume
summary: Roosevelt starts up again with his boxing teacher and writes his mother an affectionate letter saying his studies take six or seven hours a day.

headline: Caught between two clubs
summary: After two drunk club men argue about him and reveal his preference for the Porcellian, the A.D. members vote to let Roosevelt choose between the clubs, since he never formally joined theirs. Knowing either choice will hurt someone, he spends a miserable day weighing what honor requires.

headline: At Harvard
summary: Roosevelt is at Cambridge; no activities are recorded.

headline: Choosing the Porcellian
summary: Roosevelt settles it and joins the Porcellian, listing classmates on each side: Weld, Shaw, Trimble, Morgan and Griswold among the Porcellian men; Bob Bacon, Billy Hooper and others in the A.D.

headline: Notes on classmates
summary: Roosevelt records that Arthur Hooper has left Harvard and that Brooks and Peters have been dropped. He has warmed to Charley Ware and Harry Shaw, and calls Harry Chapin a perfect trump.

headline: Charley Dickey under the same roof
summary: Roosevelt is glad to have Charley Dickey living in his house and feels he has helped him. He writes Bamie that more than half his college career is behind him.

headline: Lab work eats the hours
summary: One of Roosevelt's natural history courses demands heavy laboratory work, which he enjoys though it devours his time.

headline: Sparring and gratitude to the A.D.
summary: Roosevelt has been boxing with several classmates and writes that the A.D. men have handled the club episode very decently.

headline: Who sits at his table
summary: Roosevelt lists his dining-table companions: Weld, Chapin, Ware, Washburn, Ellis, Peters and Saltonstall.

headline: Dinner with the Hoopers
summary: Roosevelt enjoys dinner at the Hoopers' and is pleased to meet Miss Jeannie once more.

headline: Off to Chestnut Hill with Dick Saltonstall
summary: After boxing Tucker Burr to a standstill, Roosevelt rides in Dick Saltonstall's buggy to the Saltonstall home at Chestnut Hill, where the family's kindness makes him feel completely at home.

headline: Meeting Alice Lee
summary: Roosevelt rambles through the woods alongside Dick, Dick's sister Rose and their cousin Alice Lee, whom he finds sweet and pretty. The group dines and takes tea at the Whitneys', dancing and singing until they drive home around eleven. He would marry Alice in 1880.

headline: Chestnutting with Alice Lee
summary: After church, Roosevelt spends the afternoon gathering chestnuts with Alice Lee.

headline: Back to Cambridge and the Glee Club
summary: Roosevelt returns by carriage to Cambridge early in the day and that evening hears some lovely singing at the Glee Club.

headline: Town and gown scuffle
summary: A political meeting for Benjamin Butler and Denis Kearney sets off a brawl between students and townspeople, and Roosevelt enjoys watching the crew pile in.

headline: Arguing with Mill, tiring of Ferrier
summary: Roosevelt finds political economy absorbing even though he does not fully accept John Stuart Mill, and is losing patience with Ferrier's philosophy.

headline: A long walk and a family scandal
summary: Roosevelt hikes with Jack Tebbetts, who has grown on him. Then a letter brings word that his cousin Cornelius has married a French actress, which Roosevelt condemns harshly in his diary.

headline: Evening boat to New York
summary: Roosevelt takes the night boat to New York for a break, admitting he has not studied as hard as he should in some subjects and vowing to buckle down on his return.

headline: Home with family at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts with West, who is upset over Cornelius's marriage, visits Aunt Annie, lunches with West and Alfred, and reaches Oyster Bay in the afternoon, happy to be with his family. All look well except Elliott.

headline: Turning twenty
summary: Roosevelt marks his 20th birthday at Oyster Bay with his mother and sisters, but the day is shadowed by longing for his father. He also shoots two gray squirrels.

headline: Rough water around Centre Island
summary: In a stiff north wind Roosevelt rows around Centre Island through seas that half-fill his boat, then sails home fast from Pine Island. An afternoon walk with his gun turns up nothing.

headline: Coots and a checker-back loon
summary: Sailing for ducks in light, shifting wind, Roosevelt finds few birds but plenty of fun: he drops two coots from a flock, runs down a loon after a lengthy pursuit, and misses an old squaw.

headline: Drenched and empty-handed
summary: A southeaster with steady rain squalls soaks Roosevelt on a duck-hunting sail, and he comes home with nothing after missing a grebe.

headline: Bad luck with the weather
summary: Rain again. Roosevelt grumbles that his whole break has been spoiled by weather: too rough one day, too calm the next, then two days of rain.

headline: Back to Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt returns from Oyster Bay to Harvard.

headline: Porcellian initiation night
summary: Roosevelt serves as a steward at the athletic association's field meeting, and that evening is initiated into the Porcellian Club. He admits the wine left him tipsier than ever before, vows it won't happen again, and notes that drink makes him combative.

headline: Morning after, back to Sunday school
summary: Feeling the effects of the previous night, Roosevelt nonetheless resumes teaching his Sunday school class, whose pupils are delighted to have him back.

headline: A sample day, hour by hour
summary: Roosevelt begins logging a typical week: chapel at 7:45, study nearly all day, a walk before dinner, then an evening with the University crew and a couple of hours lounging at his club after midnight.

headline: A surprise visit from Mother and Elliott
summary: Between chapel and study, Roosevelt is astonished when his brother Elliott and their mother arrive for the day. He shows Elliott his club and lunches in Boston with Mittie, then studies, boxes, plays whist and works until eleven.

headline: Study, then a walk with friends
summary: Roosevelt studies from 8:30 to 4, goes walking alongside Dick Saltonstall and Jack Tebbetts, spends the evening at the club and studies again until eleven.

headline: Study, boxing and billiards
summary: Another full study day, broken up by boxing and a game of billiards.

headline: Partridge and burgundy at the club
summary: After a day of study, Roosevelt joins eight or ten friends for a late supper of partridges and burgundy at the club, not getting to bed until nearly 2 a.m.

headline: Football, then a weekend at Minot Weld's
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts late at the club, drives with Harry Chapin to watch a football game, and in the afternoon heads to Minot Weld's home to stay through Monday.

headline: Moonlit drive home from the Saltonstalls'
summary: Staying with Minot Weld in Jamaica Plain, Roosevelt attends church and walks home with Miss Wheelwright, then rides in Minot's tilbury to the Saltonstalls' for tea, where Alice Lee is as lovely as ever. He writes to Corinne and Bamie, telling Bamie how much he enjoys the Porcellian.

summary: Roosevelt is at Cambridge; no activities are recorded.

headline: Boxing Billy Gaston
summary: Roosevelt spars with classmate Billy Gaston.

headline: At Harvard
summary: Roosevelt is at Cambridge; no activities are recorded.

summary: Roosevelt is at Cambridge; no activities are recorded.

headline: At Harvard
summary: Roosevelt is at Cambridge; no activities are recorded.

headline: Economics exam and a night at George Minot's
summary: Roosevelt sits his political economy exam and in the afternoon goes out to George Minot's to stay the night.

headline: Back in time for Sunday school
summary: After Sunday dinner Roosevelt drives back to Cambridge to teach his Sunday school class.

headline: Three exams ahead
summary: Facing three exams this week, Roosevelt has been studying flat out.

summary: Roosevelt travels to New York for Christmas break. Much as he loves college, he is always glad to be home, and he calls these his golden years.

headline: Sweetness overtaking sorrow
summary: Though cheerful, the family cannot help thinking of his father. Roosevelt senses the sweet now outweighing the bitter in their memories, and finds he has been very happy these past six months despite his loss.

headline: Mission school visit and cousins in love
summary: Roosevelt visits his former mission school pupils and learns that his friend Cassin has died. Among his cousins, romance is everywhere: Emlen confesses his love for Miss Parish, West is devoted to Fanny, and Alfred is courting Miss Tuckerman.

headline: Jack Elliott arrives, a touch of fever
summary: Jack Elliott comes from Philadelphia, as delightfully absent-minded as ever, and Roosevelt is relieved to find one friend not in love. He is slightly unwell with what West calls an 'ephemeral fever.'

headline: First Christmas without Father
summary: Christmas is a sad one for Roosevelt, the first without his father, whom he remembers as the heart of every family celebration. His gifts are mostly books.

headline: Leaning toward a naturalist's life
summary: Kept indoors by fever, Roosevelt writes that he seems headed for a career as a naturalist, which would mean three years of study abroad, a prospect that depresses him.

headline: Cheering on Emlen
summary: Still housebound, Roosevelt listens to Emlen's heartfelt talk about Grace Parish and wishes him well. Elliott is doing well, and Roosevelt marvels at his relatives.

headline: A rare Ipswich sparrow
summary: Roosevelt heads out to Oyster Bay, Jack Elliott along with him, for a long cold tramp. Amid redpolls and crossbills he shoots an Ipswich sparrow, a rarity, and the evening goes to philosophy talk and double-dummy whist.

headline: Winter rambles at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt goes to church, then takes a long walk with Jack, whom he calls the best partner for such outings. He loves these winter trips: thin shooting but a warm supper and roaring fire at day's end. Snow falls overnight.

headline: Swamped in the winter surf
summary: In snow and wind, Roosevelt and Jack smash through shore ice in the rowboat, sail to Plum Point and lunch on Pine Island. Finding West Harbor frozen, they are swamped twice launching through heavy surf, soaked in icy water, then fight their way to Rocky Point before racing home under sail.

headline: Twelve hours afield on New Year's Eve
summary: Setting out at 7:30 with a local gunner and no dog in four inches of snow, Roosevelt covers about 25 miles without food or rest, home twelve hours later. He calls it one of his best days ever, shooting six quail, five rabbits and a squirrel.

headline: New Year's at Oyster Bay
summary: The family, joined by Uncle Jimmie and Aunt Annie Gracie, has come out to Oyster Bay for a merry New Year's. After they leave in the afternoon, Roosevelt and Jack Elliott take their guns into the snowy woods.

headline: Rabbit tracks lost in the snow
summary: Roosevelt hunts through a heavy snowfall, taking three rabbits before fresh snow buries the tracks. In the afternoon he returns to New York City.

headline: Usher twice over, confidant to cousins
summary: Tom Ludlow and cousin Jack Roosevelt both ask Roosevelt to usher at their weddings, to his puzzlement. West, Emlen and Alfred all confide their romances to him, and Elliott brings two friends to dinner, one named Russell whom Roosevelt likes.

headline: Sorry to leave home
summary: Roosevelt dreads leaving his family even though Cambridge suits him so well. He calls on Annie Murray and praises his brother Elliott.

headline: Tea with Hal Chapin, a talk with Bamie
summary: Hal Chapin comes to tea, and Roosevelt has a heartfelt talk with his sister Bamie, wondering whether any man has two better sisters. That evening he leaves for Harvard.

headline: Back to the books

headline: Bound for Island Falls
summary: Roosevelt boards an evening train north toward Island Falls, Maine, planning a two-week stay.

headline: A winter sleigh ride to Island Falls
summary: Bill Sewall meets Roosevelt's train at Mattawamkeag with a sleigh, and the two travel 36 miles over half-broken roads, reaching Island Falls near ten at night. The air is bitter but still, and well bundled, Roosevelt loves the ride. Elliott turns 19. His notes on Oyster Bay birds are dated to this period.

headline: First try on snowshoes in Maine
summary: Roosevelt straps on snowshoes for the first time and covers about six miles checking lynx traps with Will Dow. The traps are empty, but he marvels at the snow-heavy evergreens and drops a porcupine from a hemlock with his rifle.

headline: Bible reading and a winter tramp
summary: A quiet Sunday: Roosevelt reads his Bible in the morning, then walks the snowy pine and spruce woods in the afternoon. He finds the cold easy to bear among the trees but harsh in the wind, and notes how little life stirs in the forest.

headline: Eight hours in the woods with Dow
summary: With Will Dow, Roosevelt hikes to Dyer Brook and then strikes off cross-country through hardwoods and tangled spruce and cedar swamps. Over an eight-hour tramp he logs an arctic woodpecker, chickadees, two gray jays at lunch, and the tracks of hare, lynx and spruce grouse.

headline: A ruffed grouse after a long hunt
summary: Roosevelt spends the day in the woods with Bill Sewall. Tracks of a dozen kinds of animals are everywhere, yet they see only chickadees and a woodpecker until they trail a partridge, flush it from a fallen birch and Roosevelt brings it down.

headline: Asthma at night, grouse by day
summary: Another day of snowshoeing with little game to show for it, though Roosevelt is having the time of his life. Asthma keeps him awake at night. After lunch at a logging camp he shoots a partridge from a spruce top and a porcupine; the traps have so far yielded a lynx and a fox.

headline: Thirty miles by pung to a logging camp
summary: Roosevelt, Sewall and Dow set out with a box sleigh and a scrawny horse for a logging camp thirty miles off, arriving after dark. It is ten below at the start and the roads are terrible. Along the way he spots a red crossbill, flocks of snow buntings and some unusually tame grosbeaks.

headline: On the trail of a caribou
summary: Through a heavy snowstorm Roosevelt and Dow hunt all day, finally jumping a caribou in thick spruce. He glimpses it at under thirty yards but cannot shoot, and they track it until dark, then spend a cold, hungry night by a big fire with no blankets.

headline: Caribou chase ends without a shot
summary: Before sunrise, in subzero cold, the hunters take up the caribou's trail again through swamps, ledges and open cranberry bogs. Roosevelt studies how the animal trots and bounds in snow over three feet deep. By midday they quit and are back at the logging camp at sunset.

headline: Resting among the lumbermen
summary: Worn out from two days after the caribou, Roosevelt rests. His asthma has not troubled him since reaching camp, and he warms to the rough, generous lumbermen, especially one named Charley Brown. Rain followed by frost has coated every tree in ice.

headline: A buck, rabbits and a venison feast
summary: Roosevelt and Sewall find a small deer yard. He trips and misses his first shot at the buck, then runs it down over a mile and kills it with his rifle. After an afternoon of rabbit hunting, venison replaces the usual pork and beans. He writes his mother that he has stored up health enough to last into summer.

headline: Dragging the sleigh back to Island Falls
summary: The return trip is miserable: sleet and rain, wretched roads, and a horse that keeps floundering into drifts until the men unhitch it and haul the sleigh themselves. Wet, chilled and hungry after walking the whole way, Roosevelt still notes snow buntings singing, and reaches Island Falls by teatime.

headline: A raccoon and a camp on Mattawamkeag Lake
summary: After another empty seven-mile trap round, Roosevelt follows a raccoon's track and shoots it from a dead tree. The party then snowshoes to Mattawamkeag Lake and camps at its foot, picking up two spruce grouse on the way in the best snow conditions of his stay.

headline: Long-range rifle practice on the ice
summary: The party breaks camp and returns to Island Falls by dinner, traveling over the frozen lake and river. Seeing no game, they pass the time shooting at targets 300 to 500 yards off, and all three do well with a Sharps rifle.

headline: Counting trophies from two happy weeks
summary: A last morning hunt turns up no partridges and empty traps, but Roosevelt is content. He sums up the trip as his pleasantest two weeks ever, with skins of fox, lynx, raccoon and buck to take home, plenty of game eaten and many specimens collected.

headline: Leaving Maine to catch up on studies
summary: Roosevelt leaves by sleigh at five in the morning for Mattawamkeag and boards the night train to Boston. He resolves to work double time until Easter to make up for the holiday.

headline: Back at Harvard, too late for church
summary: After a train held up six hours, Roosevelt reaches Cambridge late Sunday morning and writes his mother from the Porcellian Club that he arrived too late for church.

headline: Overnight with the Saltonstalls
summary: Roosevelt goes out to Chestnut Hill to dine and sleep at the Saltonstalls', who make him feel like family. He spends the evening at the Lees' with Alice Lee and plans to give Alice and Rose Saltonstall rugs made from his Maine fox and lynx skins.

headline: D.K.E. theatricals
summary: Roosevelt takes in the Delta Kappa Epsilon club's theatricals, which he rates as very good, followed by a convivial night.

headline: Hasty Pudding show and a gift of poems
summary: Roosevelt calls the Hasty Pudding theatricals the best he has seen, and enjoys the singing that follows in the club room and the Yard. He mails his sister Corinne a little volume of verse, Charles Fletcher Lummis's Birch Bark Poems.

headline: Skipping supper to see Alice
summary: Roosevelt ducks out of the start of a Porcellian supper to join Jack Tebbetts' party with Alice Lee, Rose Saltonstall and other young women, then returns around eleven for the rowdy end of the club evening, where a tipsy Otho Williams asks him to be his second in a mock duel with Charley Sprague.

headline: Eastern photographs for Sunday school
summary: At his Sunday school class Roosevelt shows the boys a batch of photographs from the East, which makes for an unusually lively session. In the evening he calls on Jeannie Hooper and Mrs. Jude.

headline: Private theatricals at Minot Weld's
summary: Roosevelt drives to Minot Weld's for amateur theatricals, sitting beside Alice Lee and later spending much of the evening with Nana Rotch. Back around one, he stays up singing and talking at the Porcellian until three.

headline: Game supper at the Porcellian
summary: Roosevelt shares a game supper at the Porcellian Club with Otho Williams, Jim Wright and Charley Sprague.

headline: A lunch party and gifts of fur rugs
summary: Roosevelt hosts a luncheon in his rooms, with Mrs. Saltonstall as chaperone, for Alice Lee, Rose Saltonstall and a dozen friends, then shows them the Porcellian and Pudding clubs. He gives Alice the lynx rug and Rose the fox; Alice is making him slippers. That night he sails for New York with Minot Weld and Dick Saltonstall.

headline: Shaving off the whiskers
summary: Home in New York for vacation, Roosevelt shows Minot Weld and Dick Saltonstall the city. At Aunt Annie's that evening he sees Fanny Smith, Margie Tuckerman and Edith Carow. He announces to his sister Corinne that his side-whiskers are gone.

headline: Worry over a sick mother
summary: Christine and Lucy Kean come to lunch, and Roosevelt likes them both. His mother has fallen ill, which leaves him feeling wretched.

headline: Elliott's dinner at the Jockey Club
summary: Elliott hosts a dinner at the Jockey Club. Roosevelt travels in Harold Haddon's dog cart while the rest of the party, including Grove Porter and Ike Iselin, comes by drag, and he takes a strong liking to Haddon.

headline: Consoling cousin Emlen
summary: Roosevelt's cousin Emlen has been turned down by Grace Parish, and the two have a long talk. His mother is still unwell.

headline: Lunch downtown, dinner at West's
summary: Emlen treats the group to a successful lunch at the Down Town Club, and they dine at cousin West's before an evening at the theater.

headline: Dog show, then the night train north
summary: Roosevelt visits the dog show, lunches with Lizzie Moran and escorts Annie Murray to a rehearsal for the Fancy Dress Ball before catching the night train to Boston. His guests loved the holiday, and his mother is nearly recovered.

headline: Exams done and a horse arrives
summary: After two examinations and a week of hard study, Roosevelt welcomes his horse to Cambridge, stabling it at Pike's for the spring. He heads to Chestnut Hill for the weekend and dines at the Lees'.

headline: A snowy walk with Alice
summary: Snow falls all day at Chestnut Hill, but Roosevelt takes a long walk with Alice Lee anyway. He spends much of the day showing the young women how to dance the five-step, plus a newer step called the knickerbocker, and the evening goes to whist and ghost stories.

headline: Church and a walk at Chestnut Hill
summary: After church the party visits the Francises, and in the afternoon Roosevelt walks out with Codman, Rose Saltonstall and Alice Lee. He writes his sister Bamie an account of the day.

headline: First ride on the new horse
summary: Roosevelt returns reluctantly to Cambridge after two days of rest. That afternoon he rides his horse for the first time; it goes well and is full of spirit, which he enjoys.

headline: Riding and the Jeffries collections
summary: Roosevelt rides again, calling the horse the one thing missing from his happiness this spring. He visits the Jeffries family to look over their collections, stays for dinner and plays whist.

headline: Early study, free afternoons
summary: With spring in full swing, Roosevelt rises early to study before breakfast and keeps the rest of the day for himself, his heavy work for the year done. He loves riding out to Milton, Jamaica Plain, Forest Hills and Chestnut Hill and staying for a meal.

headline: A drive with Alice, then a conversazione
summary: Roosevelt rides to Chestnut Hill early and takes an afternoon drive with Alice, Rose and Endicott. After dinner he hurries back to Cambridge for a conversazione at Laughlin's, where he meets a lively Miss Longfellow.

headline: Theater in town, night at Jamaica Plain
summary: Roosevelt gallops out past Watertown to work off his horse's winter coat. He dines in Boston with Harry Chapin at Young's Hotel, catches a play with Weld and Dick Saltonstall, and goes home with Weld to Jamaica Plain for the night.

headline: A flirtation he regrets
summary: Roosevelt tours Minot Weld's livestock, then drives to Chestnut Hill, where he spends the afternoon with Nana Rotch and later wishes he had not flirted with her. At a Porcellian dinner, Van Rensselaer confides his feelings for Lulu Lane.

headline: Last Sunday school class of the year
summary: Roosevelt teaches his Sunday school class for the last time before summer, handing every boy a present and praising their good behavior.

headline: Riding to Chestnut Hill and Jamaica Plain
summary: Roosevelt rides out to Chestnut Hill and on to Jamaica Plain.

headline: An exam and an evening at the Rotches'
summary: Roosevelt sits an hour-long exam and spends the evening with the Rotch family. He writes his mother asking her to send along some suits and hoping she is well and resting.

headline: Theater party with Alice
summary: Roosevelt and Harry Shaw take Mr. and Mrs. Saltonstall, Rose and Alice to the theater after dining together. He and Alice sit a row behind the others.

headline: Calling on the Welds
summary: Roosevelt rides to Jamaica Plain to pay a call on the Weld family.

headline: A rifle match, won and lost
summary: In a shooting match Roosevelt outscores Sam Skinner but falls to Fred Sharon.

headline: Lunch with the Lees, a ride with George Minot
summary: Roosevelt rides to Chestnut Hill for lunch at the Lees' and drives Alice and Rose into Boston to see the Rotches. George Minot arrives on horseback at four; the pair ride a long way and then go to Minot's home at Forest Hills for the night.

headline: Six hours' walk with Alice
summary: After church with the Minots, Roosevelt sees Julia Bacon home, then drives to Chestnut Hill. A walking party sets out, but he and Alice Lee drift off alone and are not back until nearly six. He takes tea at the Lees' and rides to Cambridge late.

headline: Weekend news for Corinne
summary: Roosevelt writes his sister Corinne about his weekend at Forest Hills and Chestnut Hill.

headline: A ride with Rose and a D.K.E. election
summary: Roosevelt rides with Rose Saltonstall, dines at her family's home and passes the evening dancing and talking with Alice and Frank Lee. He returns past ten for the D.K.E. meeting, which names Woodbury Kane and Charles Dickey first and second of the class of '82's first ten.

headline: A long day at the Whitneys' in Milton
summary: Roosevelt rides to Milton right after breakfast, stopping briefly at Chestnut Hill. At the Whitneys' he spends six hours before a late dinner rambling the woods and farm with Bessie Whitney, then rides home at dusk in high spirits.

headline: Lawn tennis at the Bacons'
summary: Dining at the Bacons', Roosevelt is surprised to find Rose and Alice there, and they spend the afternoon at lawn tennis. He likes Julia Bacon, and rides back in time for tea at the Tudors'.

headline: Photographs and a bicycle meet
summary: Roosevelt meets Rose and Alice in Boston, where the three sit for photographs, then goes with them to Chestnut Hill for the weekend. They watch the Suffolk Club's bicycle meet among many friends, dance in the evening, and he walks out with Alice after tea.

headline: Church, a drive and a call on the Lowells
summary: Roosevelt again walks with Alice after church at Chestnut Hill. The group goes for a drive in the afternoon and in the evening visits the Lowells, who have a houseful of young people.

headline: His longest ride yet
summary: Roosevelt takes his longest ride so far, through the country beyond Waverley, and spends the evening at the O.K. society. His horse, now in summer coat, looks splendid; bringing it to Cambridge, he says, was his best move. He also writes to his mother.

headline: A fall in the dark
summary: Roosevelt rides hard to and from an evening at the Lees'. Coming home at about a quarter past ten in pitch darkness, he and the horse go down while galloping downhill, a spill he admits he fully earned.

headline: A lame horse and regrets
summary: His horse is lame after the previous night's gallop, so Roosevelt has to skip dinner at the Saltonstalls'. He spends the evening at the D.K.E., scolding himself for pushing the animal too hard.

headline: Class races, then a weekend in Milton
summary: Roosevelt watches the class boat races in the morning, in the company of the Lee family. Later he heads to Milton for a Sunday stay with the Whitneys, where the evening is given to singing and dancing.

headline: Through the Blue Hills to Punkapoag
summary: The Whitney party drives through the Blue Hills to Lake Punkapoag, and Roosevelt finds the springtime country perfect. In the afternoon he walks a long way through the woods with Bessie Whitney.

headline: Tea with the Lanes
summary: Roosevelt returns early from Milton to Cambridge and spends a pleasant evening taking tea with the Lane family, whose daughters he admires.

headline: Charms for the girls; a horse laid up
summary: Roosevelt and Dick Saltonstall drive a buggy to Chestnut Hill, where he presents the young women with gold and silver charms. He fears his horse is lamed for good but is glad of the three and a half weeks of riding he had. He urges Corinne to come up for Class Day.

headline: The photographs are a hit
summary: Roosevelt dines at the Lees' and walks with Alice in the evening. The photographs taken earlier in the month have turned out well. John Tebbetts walks back to Cambridge with him.

headline: Judging the athletic games
summary: Roosevelt serves as a judge at the Harvard Athletic Association meet. In the evening he calls on the Lanes, finds Alice and Rose there, and dances most of the night.

headline: Glee Club and waltzes in Memorial Hall
summary: Roosevelt sits beside Miss Bacon at the Glee Club concert, then waltzes in Memorial Hall with Alice, Rose, Lulu Lane and Miss Francis.

headline: Sending the lame horse home
summary: Roosevelt and Van Rensselaer show Mrs. Lane and her daughters Lulu and Kitty their college rooms, play lawn tennis and stay to dance into the night. With the horse hopelessly lame, he decides to ship it back to New York and misses it badly.

headline: Sunday walk at Chestnut Hill
summary: Roosevelt takes a buggy to Chestnut Hill in the afternoon and walks out with the young women there.

headline: At Harvard in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard in Cambridge; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Chestnut Hill, then tea with Bessie
summary: Roosevelt spends the afternoon at Chestnut Hill with Alice and Rose, then drives on to the Whitneys' for tea and an evening with Bessie, with whom he is now close. The drive home is very dark.

headline: At Harvard in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard in Cambridge; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: On foot to Chestnut Hill
summary: Roosevelt walks out to Chestnut Hill, spends the afternoon with Rose and Alice, dines at the Saltonstalls' and walks back that evening.

headline: A circus party with Alice
summary: Roosevelt, Harry Shaw and Dick Saltonstall head into Boston for a theater and circus party hosted by Charley Codman. He escorts Alice both ways and sits beside her.

headline: Junior year ends 13th in his class
summary: Roosevelt drives to the Bacons' for tea with Nellie and Julia Bacon and George Minot, then visits the Frothinghams. His junior-year results put him 13th of 166, averaging 87, with top marks of 97 in zoology and 92 in geology. He spent $4,113 at college this year.

headline: No entry for the day
summary: The record gives no place or activity for Roosevelt today; he is presumably still at Harvard ahead of exams.

headline: First of the annual examinations
summary: Roosevelt sits his first annual exam. Looking back over two weeks of cramming, he tallies early rising at six and seven to ten hours of study a day. His horse is much better, and he exercises it a little daily.

headline: No entry for the day
summary: The record gives no place or activity for Roosevelt today; exams are under way at Harvard.

headline: Evening at the Whitneys'
summary: Roosevelt and Dick Saltonstall drive out to the Whitneys' for tea and a lively evening.

headline: At Harvard in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard in Cambridge; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: At Harvard in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard in Cambridge; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Hardest exam passed, horse sound again
summary: Having passed his third and toughest exam, Roosevelt takes the afternoon off. The horse is healthy and frisky, and he struggles to keep it from straining its leg on the ride to Chestnut Hill. He walks with Alice, dines at the Lees' and rides home at ten.

headline: Evening with the Lanes
summary: Roosevelt and Van Rensselaer spend a pleasant evening with the Lane family.

headline: At Harvard in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard in Cambridge; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Afternoon at the Saltonstalls'
summary: Roosevelt rides to Chestnut Hill and passes the afternoon with the Saltonstall family.

headline: At Harvard in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard in Cambridge; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: At Harvard in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard in Cambridge; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Last exam of the year
summary: Roosevelt finishes his final examination, then rides to the Saltonstalls', walks with Rose in the afternoon, dines there and goes walking with Alice afterward.

headline: Looking after a drunken clubmate
summary: After a late Porcellian breakfast, Roosevelt rides to the Bacons' for lunch with Nellie and Julia. At the club dinner that night, Charley Morgan, on a weeklong binge, nearly goes into delirium tremens; Roosevelt sleeps in his room and, heading home next morning in evening clothes, almost collides with a proctor.

headline: Caught in a downpour
summary: Roosevelt and Van Rensselaer drive to the Saltonstalls' for tea. A rainstorm drenches them during a walk with Alice and Rose, and on the dark drive home Roosevelt barely avoids crashing into a wagon.

headline: A life of luxurious ease
summary: With exams behind him, Roosevelt describes his routine: breakfast at the club around ten, his horse waiting at the door, a ride out to lunch with friends, and if not dining out, a champagne supper at the club. Pleasant, he admits, but probably not healthy for long.

headline: Fans for Rose's birthday
summary: It is Rose Saltonstall's birthday, and Roosevelt rides to Chestnut Hill with fans for her and Alice, spending the day there. He tallies that the two have cost him more than $150 so far. That night he attends to the O.K. society's strawberry night.

headline: Three strawberry parties
summary: Roosevelt calls on the Guilds at Forest Hills, dines at the Lees', and escorts Alice to the Lowells' strawberry festival before the Hasty Pudding's own strawberry night.

headline: Called a flirt, then a fistfight
summary: At the Whitneys' in Milton, Roosevelt teases Bessie for calling him a flirt; it seems she and Nana Rotch traded impressions of him. That evening, at a D.K.E. strawberry party, he brawls with a rough and knocks him down, cutting his knuckles on the man's teeth.

headline: Class Day, and a moment with Alice in Hollis
summary: As a junior usher, Roosevelt works Class Day from Saunders to the tree exercises, dances with some twenty young women at Van Rensselaer's spread, then sits with Alice Lee in a Hollis Hall window watching the lit Yard and hearing the Glee Club. Historians think he may have first proposed to her there and been gently refused.

headline: Visit to the Lowells
summary: Roosevelt rides out for a pleasant visit with the Lowells and attends a Porcellian supper that evening.

headline: Sunday tea and a group walk
summary: Harry Shaw drives Roosevelt to the Saltonstalls' for tea, where callers stream in all afternoon. In the evening three couples go walking, Roosevelt paired with Alice.

headline: A day at the Lees'
summary: After breakfast with Harry Shaw at the club, Roosevelt rides to the Lees' for a day of walking and dancing with Alice, returning late. He plans to send the horse, now in fine form, home at week's end.

headline: Grateful to the Saltonstalls
summary: Roosevelt calls on Susie Wheelwright in Jamaica Plain, then settles in at the Saltonstalls' until Thursday. He talks with Rose, teaches young Phil to shoot and plays with Getty. He writes that the Saltonstalls and the Lees have added so much to his year that leaving Chestnut Hill will hurt more than leaving Harvard.

headline: Ushering at Commencement; Harvard beats Yale
summary: Roosevelt rides to Cambridge early to usher at Commencement, lunches with the Lanes alongside Alice, Rose, Lulu and Kitty, and spends the afternoon at the club and the baseball game, which Harvard wins over Yale. He is back at the Saltonstalls' for tea.

headline: Goodbye to Chestnut Hill
summary: With deep regret Roosevelt takes leave of Chestnut Hill after breakfast and rides to Cambridge. In the afternoon he goes to the Whitneys' for a couple of days, joined by the Lane sisters and Nana Rotch.

headline: Cheering Harvard at the Yale race
summary: A large party boards a special car to watch the Harvard-Yale boat race, which Harvard wins handily. They sing most of the way home, reaching it at 2 a.m.; Roosevelt has shouted himself hoarse and spent much of the day with Alice.

headline: Junior year comes to an end
summary: Roosevelt says goodbye to the Whitneys and heads to New York. Looking back on the year, he credits his studies, the club, his horse and above all the young women of Chestnut Hill, and doubts he will ever enjoy himself as much again.

headline: Home to Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt goes out to Oyster Bay, overjoyed to see his family; his mother and his two sisters welcome him warmly. Weekend guests include Russell, Haddon, Betts, Maud Elliott and the Kane sisters, and all the Roosevelt cousins are on hand.

headline: Back to the old Oyster Bay life
summary: Roosevelt fixes up his rowboat, builds a boathouse, rows to Plum Point and sails with Uncle Jimmie, who is summering there with Aunt Annie. He relishes the outdoor life of horse, gun and boat. Edith Carow's aunt dies this day, and the Carows move to East 36th Street.

headline: Summer at Tranquility
summary: Roosevelt is at Tranquility, the family's summer house at Oyster Bay; no other details are recorded.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Thrown in a jumping spill
summary: Roosevelt has been rowing himself into shape, including a trip to Lloyd's Neck. Trying his horse over fences, he takes a hard fall when it rolls on top of him. That evening he sails with Emlen, West and Alfred to Matinecock Point to meet Elliott's boat carrying the Haddons, Douglas Robinson and Percy King.

headline: Independence Day with the crowd
summary: Roosevelt spends the Fourth with his friends and cousins, sailing, playing lawn tennis and jumping horses.

headline: A moonlight sail
summary: A morning ride with Emlen schooling the horses over jumps is followed by a row around Hog Island with West and lawn tennis with the group. At night about twenty people take a moonlight sail and come home to dance, sing and swap stories.

headline: Communion Sunday
summary: On Communion Sunday Roosevelt reflects that the plain Presbyterian service always sets him thinking, something he admits he rarely does on serious matters.

headline: Overnight with the Dodges
summary: Roosevelt goes to stay a night with the Dodge family, whose sons Earl and Cleve he admires. They drive past the family's old summer places at Mosholu and Riverdale, and he sees the two Oyne boys.

headline: His mother turns 44
summary: Roosevelt's mother, Mittie, celebrates her 44th birthday while the family summers at Oyster Bay.

headline: Sixteen miles around Lloyd's Neck
summary: Roosevelt rows sixteen miles around Lloyd's Neck and reports that he is tanned to the waist and in top shape. Afternoons, once Elliott is up from the city, the brothers play tennis, wrestle and swim, and he sleeps soundly every night.

headline: Training the horse to harness
summary: Cousin Alfred spends the day, and they row around Centre Island, play tennis and ride. Roosevelt begins teaching his horse to pull in harness. In the evening he dances at West's, where Gerty, Tiny and Virginia Roosevelt are guests.

headline: The carefree charm of Oyster Bay
summary: Emlen takes a holiday to spend with Roosevelt, and they row around Centre Island. He writes that the mix of active outdoor life and freedom from care is what he loves most about Oyster Bay.

headline: A day with Elliott
summary: Elliott takes a day off, and the brothers sail and play tennis together. Roosevelt is teaching his horse to trot, thinking of hitching it to a tilbury next winter.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Rowing thirty miles across the Sound
summary: Roosevelt rows across Long Island Sound to Sheffield Island light and back, about thirty miles. With the tide and no wind, the outward leg takes under three hours; the return, into a stiff headwind, takes four and a half and ships plenty of water. Charades and dancing follow at the crowded house.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.
