headline: Setting out on the Meteor
summary: Roosevelt, Alfred and West set off for a week aboard the Meteor, an open 24-foot sloop, stocked with hardtack, canned meat and coffee. The breeze dies by evening and they anchor off the Saugatuck River, sleeping in sailors' hammocks slung in the cockpit.

headline: Sheltering at the Thimble Islands
summary: The Meteor weighs anchor at 5:30 into light headwinds. Roosevelt notes terns, gulls, coots and a storm petrel. Becalmed in the afternoon, they anchor off the Thimble Islands, then run for shelter behind one when a southerly wind kicks up at night.

headline: A rough beat to New London
summary: Low on water, the crew sails on Sunday despite Roosevelt's misgivings. Beating into a strengthening northeaster and a heavy sea, they struggle off Bartlett's Reef to keep the boat upright, taking on much water, and reach New London at 4 p.m.

headline: Dinner with the Chapins, revolvers at sea
summary: The sailors call at the Chapins' house for dinner, then turn back into a strong southwesterly and put into Saybrook at sunset. Sharks and porpoises along the way serve as revolver targets.

headline: Fighting out of Saybrook
summary: Leaving at 5 a.m., the Meteor battles over the shoals and tide rips at Saybrook's harbor mouth in a strong wind and big sea. Rain falls all morning, the breeze dies at noon, and they anchor in the lee of Charles Island at 7:30.

headline: Rowing home in a dead calm
summary: Light, shifting winds give way to a flat calm from nine to six, and the crew labors at the long oars, not reaching Oyster Bay until 11:15 that night. Roosevelt judges the cruise a great success and his cousins fine company.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Friends worth having
summary: Roosevelt describes his days of riding, rowing, sailing, swimming and shooting, with one of his four cousin-companions staying over most days. He wishes John Elliott were there too. Evenings mean reading, whist or dancing, and he often takes Miss Hale of Philadelphia, a guest of Aunt Lizzie's, out rowing.

headline: Against too much slaughter
summary: Roosevelt writes to fellow naturalist Henry Minot that he has collected little this summer because he disapproves of killing too many specimens.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Alice Lee turns 18
summary: While Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay, Alice Lee marks her 18th birthday at Chestnut Hill.

headline: Racing Elliott around Lloyd's
summary: Elliott stays out from town and the brothers row fifteen miles around Lloyd's Neck, racing nearly all the way. Roosevelt sizes them up as evenly matched athletes: Elliott the better rower, sailor, swimmer and shotgun hand; he the better runner, wrestler, boxer and rifle shot.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Twelve hours after woodcock
summary: Roosevelt hunts woodcock with young Pendleton Cruger from seven in the morning to seven at night through brutal cover in the heat, wading waist-deep in mud holes and swamps. Cruger shoots well; Roosevelt says he does not. They bag seven birds.

headline: A big woodcock bag near Locust Valley
summary: Hunting with Cruger again, Roosevelt works Fleet's swamp, Townsend's and the Beekman place, then a string of boggy spots near Locust Valley. For once, he notes, he shoots very well.

headline: Rowing and riding with Emily Swan
summary: Roosevelt counts Emily Swan among the prettiest and most charming young women in Oyster Bay, and has enjoyed several rows and rides with her.

headline: A birthday book for Edith
summary: For Edith Carow's 18th birthday, Roosevelt gives her a copy of the verse novel Lucile, signing it as her sincere friend.

headline: Snipe hunting by skiff
summary: Roosevelt and Cruger take a skiff after snipe, rowing the beaches, poling through shallow lagoons and twisting marsh creeks, sailing when the wind allows and carrying the boat over several portages. The fast ebb sweeps them out of Lloyd's Neck so they need only steer and shoot.

headline: Rowing, tennis and walks with Mother
summary: Roosevelt rows nearly every day, plays tennis with whichever cousins stay over, walks with his mother and takes his sisters Bamie and Corinne rowing. He is also giving Emily Swan tennis lessons.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay

headline: A poor day for woodcock
summary: Roosevelt and Cruger hunt woodcock all day, but the molting birds are scattered and both shoot badly, so they come home with just three.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is spending the summer at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Junior grades top the class in zoology
summary: Roosevelt's junior-year marks arrive: an average above 87 percent, his best yet, and first in the class in zoology and political economy. Afternoons bring tennis and a swim with Elliott, and the horse is getting used to harness.

headline: A happy home
summary: Roosevelt notes the family's Sunday morning and evening prayers and wishes they were daily. He writes warmly of his mother, his sisters Bamie and Corinne, and Elliott, his best friend, who together make as happy a home as anyone could ask for.

headline: Weighing science or law
summary: On the eve of leaving for Maine, Roosevelt reflects on a fine, sunburned summer. He is thinking hard about life after college and expects either to pursue science or to read law as a path into public life.

headline: Dinner at the University Club
summary: In New York Roosevelt praises his guardians, Uncle Jim Roosevelt and Uncle Jimmie Gracie, as the best he could have. That evening Douglas Robinson joins him for dinner at the University Club, along with Haddon, Stratton, Sedgwick and Kingsford.

headline: Warm welcome at Chestnut Hill
summary: Roosevelt travels to Boston and on to Chestnut Hill, where Dick Saltonstall greets him heartily. After dining with Mrs. Lee they drive to the Whitneys', where Bessie, Rose, Rosy Lee and Alice are staying, and plan a picnic for Ell Whitney's birthday.

headline: Picnic day at the Whitneys'
summary: Roosevelt and Dick Saltonstall drive to the Whitneys' at nine and stay past midnight, sailing, walking, dancing and playing tennis. He is especially glad to see Rose and Alice again.

headline: Turning down Alice to keep a promise
summary: Roosevelt visits Rose, Rosy Lee and Alice in town as they leave for the Slades', and they press him to come along. Alice is so lovely that refusing is hard, but he keeps his promise to meet Emlen and takes the night train for Mattawamkeag after dinner with Frank Lee at the Union Club. On the train he writes Bamie about his Boston stay.

headline: Back in the Maine woods
summary: Roosevelt reaches Mattawamkeag at 10 a.m. and drives to Island Falls with Dave Sewall. Emlen and Arthur Cutler are there, and he plans a short trip with them to Mount Katahdin.

headline: Packing for Katahdin
summary: Roosevelt spends the day getting ready, listing his kit: two changes of clothes, wool socks, a flannel shirt, duck trousers, a blanket and thick jacket, plus rifle and shotgun.

headline: Paddling the lake with Emlen
summary: Roosevelt and Emlen paddle about 25 miles to their former campsite at the lake's lower end and back. No partridges turn up, but he picks up wood ducks along the channels and praises Emlen and Arthur as good-natured trail partners.

headline: Starting for Katahdin with a 45-pound pack
summary: Roosevelt, Emlen, Arthur Cutler, Will Dow and Bill Sewall set out for Mount Katahdin, driving 23 miles and then backpacking about ten before camping. He carries roughly 45 pounds and loses a shoe in a stream crossing, luckily having moccasins tied to his pack.

headline: Campfire at Katahdin Lake
summary: The party walks to the upper end of Katahdin Lake and makes camp. Roosevelt stalks and kills four ducks, adds two grouse, and they land some trout. By day the black flies are fierce, but evenings around the blazing fire feel like old times.

headline: Lost after dark
summary: After a morning partridge hunt the group heads for Katahdin, catching about a hundred trout at Sandy Brook. Then they lose their way, push through terrible ground into the night, and camp beside a small water hole, soaked, worn out and hungry yet happy. Fresh bear and caribou tracks are everywhere.

headline: Climbing Mount Katahdin
summary: Starting before dawn, Roosevelt climbs Mount Katahdin through hard terrain; Emlen and Arthur give out before the top, but he reaches the summit and its fine view. He finds he can bear fatigue nearly as well as the woodsmen. Back at Katahdin Lake by dark, in rain, with about 60 trout.

headline: Scarce game around the lake
summary: Roosevelt circles half the lake in the morning without seeing anything, then walks down Sandy Brook in the afternoon and takes a black duck on Moose Pond. Small trout are plentiful, but game is sparse or out of reach.

headline: A lazy Sunday in camp
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday around camp cleaning guns, mending clothes and bathing in the lake. The black flies torment his companions but hardly trouble him, and though game is scarce he is having a grand time.

headline: Breaking camp for Island Falls
summary: Up before sunrise, Roosevelt hunts the bogs around a barrens pond and wounds a duck that escapes into the rushes. In the afternoon the party shoulders packs and heads for Island Falls, camping after crossing the Wassataquoik. He says he can now walk, wrestle and shoot with most of the lumbermen.

headline: Katahdin trip ends at Island Falls
summary: The party hikes to the Penobscot's East Branch, fords it and rides on to Island Falls. Roosevelt calls the trip a delight and his companions excellent company.

headline: Buckboard hunt comes up empty
summary: Roosevelt spends the afternoon riding around in a buckboard in search of partridges, without seeing a single bird.

headline: Outfitting a canoe trip with Sewall
summary: Roosevelt prepares for a trip to the Munsungan waters, just he and Bill Sewall in a canoe. He packs tea, pork, hardtack and flour, a shelter tent, two blankets, spare underclothes and plenty of ammunition, and plans to wear only moccasins. He writes Bamie that moccasins served his feet well on Katahdin.

headline: Forty-five miles to the Aroostook Oxbow
summary: Setting off before dawn by farm wagon, Roosevelt and Sewall cover 45 miles of thinly settled forest and some burned-over land to reach the Oxbow of the Aroostook by 6 p.m. They lodge in a bare-bones backwoods house. From the wagon he shoots a spruce grouse and a red-tailed hawk.

headline: Poling up the Aroostook in a dugout
summary: In a dugout that handles rough going better than birchbark, the pair works some twenty miles upriver on the Aroostook, mostly poling. The country is wild and lovely, with no sign of people or game, though trout abound. They camp before dark to cook bread, trout and partridge.

headline: Wading the Munsungan in the rain
summary: They push on despite the Sabbath, though Roosevelt neither shoots nor fishes. After poling to the Munsungan's mouth by lunchtime, they wade upstream hauling the boat, sometimes hip-deep, in heavy rain, and camp at dusk soaked and spent.

headline: Beaver dams, falls and a lovely time
summary: In steady rain they drag the heavy dugout through rapids, cut through beaver dams and logjams, unload it to climb past falls, then paddle across the lower Munsungan Lake and halfway up the middle one to camp. Roosevelt is cold, wet and hungry but still enjoying himself, though there is no sign of game.

headline: Turning back for lack of game
summary: Through more rain they paddle up the middle lake and slog over brutal terrain to the top of the upper lake. Roosevelt finds only old moose sign, a fresh bear track, a few grouse, loons and mergansers, so he decides to head back to Island Falls rather than stay as planned.

headline: Running the rapids downstream
summary: Starting before sunrise, Roosevelt and Sewall paddle out of the lakes, run the falls, wade the quick water and then pole swiftly downstream, reaching Saturday's campsite by early afternoon. He treasures the evenings by the fire under their small tent.

headline: Living off the land
summary: They paddle down to the Oxbow, where Roosevelt shoots a wood duck, then walk about 15 miles, partly overland, to a crude farmhouse in the woods. Food is plain but there is good milk, and with a rabbit and a partridge taken on the way they supply their own meat.

headline: Twenty miles to a cranberry-bog pond
summary: Roosevelt walks over 20 miles round trip through the woods to a bog pond ringed with cranberries, shooting a duck there and picking up two grouse and a hawk along the way.

headline: Footsore return to Island Falls
summary: A 25-mile walk through the forest brings Roosevelt back to Island Falls, past waterfalls in deep ravines, with five grouse shot on the way. One moccasin is nearly worn through and his feet are sore.

headline: Admiring the Yankee backwoodsmen
summary: Roosevelt attends church, reads his Bible and spends the day shaving, bathing and readying for another expedition. He praises the backwoods meeting houses and the hunters, lumbermen and farmers of the region. To Bamie he writes that the Katahdin outing was luxury next to this second trip.

headline: Rained in
summary: Steady rain keeps Roosevelt from starting out.

headline: Rough road, rougher cabin
summary: Roosevelt and Bill Sewall set out by wagon behind an unruly horse over bad roads, stopping after about 30 miles at a very crude cabin.

headline: A welcome at Littlefield's clearing
summary: Roosevelt walks about 25 miles through the woods to a backwoods homestead run by a settler named Littlefield, who looks after them well. He shoots spruce grouse in a spruce thicket and a tamarack swamp.

headline: Tough as a pine knot
summary: Walking back to the horse, Roosevelt kills four grouse, then drives to Island Falls and shoots a pigeon from the wagon. Two weeks of foul weather have not dampened him; he feels superbly healthy.

headline: To the foot of Mattawamkeag Lake
summary: Roosevelt walks through the woods to the lower end of Mattawamkeag Lake, where he camps.

headline: Seven grouse from one flock
summary: On a 20-mile walk Roosevelt takes two partridges on a hemlock ridge and then seven from a flock of eight in a river meadow. At rifle practice that afternoon he shoots well, though Dow and Sewall shoot better.

headline: Luxury and hardship, both enjoyed
summary: Roosevelt paddles to Island Falls for the night and packs to leave. A porcupine that wanders into camp is chased off with a tin dipper. He marvels at the swings of his year between high living and hard toil, both of which he loves.

headline: Down the Mattawamkeag by birchbark
summary: Roosevelt, Sewall and Dow start down the Mattawamkeag in a birch canoe, covering about ten miles below the lake. He and Dow circle through the woods to ambush a flock of mergansers, and he misses some long rifle shots at loons and cranes. He will hate to end the trip but is eager to get back to Harvard.

headline: Camp below Wytopitlock
summary: The canoe party paddles past Wytopitlock and camps. Dow shoots well at ducks and pigeons while Roosevelt misses most, but he redeems himself with rifle shots at hawks and owls. Muskrat and merganser both prove good eating.

headline: Leaving Maine strong as a bull
summary: Roosevelt paddles about 12 miles of still water to Kingman and takes the train to Boston, sorry to part from Sewall and Dow after a superb month. He feels immensely strong and almost fears his happiness is too great to last.

headline: Senior year begins with a stylish rig
summary: Back in Cambridge, Roosevelt is greeted by his friends with noisy delight. He boards his horse and a new dogcart at Pike's Stable and expects a fine winter.

headline: Feeling at home at Chestnut Hill
summary: Roosevelt drives Dick Saltonstall to Chestnut Hill, where the welcome is so warm he feels he has come home.

headline: Tennis at Minot Weld's and gifts for the Saltonstalls
summary: Roosevelt drives Harry Chapin to a tennis party at Minot Weld's with Rose, Rosy Lee, Alice and others, then goes to the Saltonstalls' for Sunday, bringing a gun for Phil, toy soldiers for Cotty and pins for Rose and Mrs. Saltonstall. It is also Corinne's 18th birthday.

headline: Sunday with the Saltonstalls
summary: Roosevelt enjoys his Sunday at Chestnut Hill with the Saltonstalls and takes Rose for a walk in the afternoon.

headline: Italian and political economy
summary: Roosevelt begins logging his study hours: Italian prep and recitation in the morning, then political economy, six hours in all. He is thrilled with his horse and cart, and tells Bamie he came back from Maine tough as a pine knot.

headline: Zoology at the Museum, geology in the field
summary: Roosevelt puts in eight hours: zoology at the Museum through the morning, geology fieldwork in the afternoon and political economy at night. After dark he pays a call on the Lane sisters.

headline: Naming his closest friends
summary: After six hours of Italian, political economy and a geology lecture, Roosevelt takes his cart out as he does most afternoons. He ranks Dick Saltonstall as his closest friend at Harvard, ahead of Harry Shaw, Minot Weld, Harry Chapin and John Tebbetts, and as dear to him as his Roosevelt cousins.

headline: Moonlit drive from the Whitneys'
summary: After zoology and political economy, Roosevelt and Dick Saltonstall drive his cart to the Whitneys' for the evening and return under a full moon.

headline: Dinner with new acquaintances
summary: Following his usual six hours of classes, Roosevelt dines at the Saltonstalls', where Rosy Lee, Mary Tuckerman and the delightful Harriet Lawrence are guests.

headline: Thirty-six hours a week
summary: Roosevelt tallies his schedule at about 36 hours of study a week. He takes Minot Weld on a long cart ride and ends the night with a boisterous party at the club.

headline: Porcellian breakfasts resume
summary: The Porcellian's Sunday morning breakfasts start up again, and in the afternoon Roosevelt and Harry Chapin walk into Boston to call on the Hoopers.

headline: At Harvard in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard in Cambridge; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: At Harvard in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard in Cambridge; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Training to run
summary: Roosevelt drives out every afternoon and finds his horse a quick trotter. He is also training as a runner, covering about a mile a day at roughly a 5:15 pace.

headline: A quick call, then the theater
summary: Roosevelt and Dick Saltonstall drive to Chestnut Hill, but he cuts the visit short to make the theater with Harry Shaw.

headline: Officer of half the clubs on campus
summary: Roosevelt complains of too many club duties: he keeps the Porcellian's library, serves as Pudding secretary, treasurer of the O.K., second in command at the Natural History Society, head of the A.D.G. club and an editor of the Advocate. Evenings go to whist, billiards and late suppers at the club.

headline: A rowdy roommate for the night
summary: After a big Porcellian supper, Dick Saltonstall and Jack Tebbetts come to the club, and a tipsy Dick sleeps in Roosevelt's room, to its considerable damage.

headline: Nursing Dick, walking with Rosy and Rose
summary: With Dick feeling the effects of the night before, Roosevelt drives him to Chestnut Hill after a late club breakfast. He has tea at the Saltonstalls' and takes walks with Rosy Lee and then Rose.

headline: Nineteenth in the class
summary: Roosevelt drives Jack Tebbetts to call on the Bacon sisters, pleased that his cart rides smooth as a cradle. He tells Bamie he ranks 19th in his class and sends Corinne an outline of his schedule.

headline: A missing diary page
summary: The diary page for this day and the next was torn out. A later letter to his mother indicates that sometime in these two days Roosevelt dined at the Lees'.

headline: An evening at the Lees'
summary: Per a letter to his mother written five days later, Roosevelt dined at the Lees' around this time and had a wonderful evening with Rosy Lee, Alice and Rose.

headline: Visiting the Chinese professor
summary: Roosevelt and Dick Saltonstall bring the Lane sisters along for a visit with the Chinese professor, an outing he found highly entertaining. His later letter home also refers to an evening at the opera with Alice.

headline: A birthday fan chain for Mrs. Saltonstall
summary: Roosevelt drives Minot Weld home, calls on George Minot, and stops briefly at the Saltonstalls' to wish Mrs. Saltonstall a happy birthday, giving her a small silver fan chain.

headline: Tennis and a weekend with the Guilds
summary: Roosevelt plays tennis all morning with the Lane sisters, then drives Harry Guild to his family's home for Sunday. He likes the Guilds, who he notes are Harry Shaw's cousins.

headline: Church with the Bacons, tea at the Whitneys'
summary: Roosevelt walks the Bacon sisters home from church and drives to the Whitneys' for tea in the afternoon.

headline: A perfect morning drive
summary: Roosevelt drives home from the Guilds' on a glorious morning, the horse flying. That afternoon he and Van Rensselaer walk with Rose and Alice. He writes his mother a full account of his busy week and tells Henry Minot he can likely get to the White Mountains for a weekend in October.

headline: Edison's light bulb
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard; his own day goes unrecorded. Meanwhile, at Menlo Park, New Jersey, Thomas Edison achieves a working electric light bulb.

headline: Thrown from the cart after the opera
summary: Roosevelt and Harry Shaw take the Saltonstall parents, Rose and Alice to the opera after dining at the Saltonstalls'. Leaving near midnight, the restless horse rears and falls, spilling both young men from the cart, but no one is hurt.

headline: Whist and late suppers
summary: Roosevelt takes Charley Morgan out for a drive. Most evenings he plays whist at the club or joins a theater party, and a habitual late supper keeps him up past bedtime.

headline: Night boat to New York
summary: Roosevelt drives Minot Weld home, noting that his horse goes well apart from rearing at the start and occasional shying. He then takes the overnight boat to New York.

headline: Home to the family
summary: In New York Roosevelt has breakfast and lunch at Aunt Lizzie's, then goes out to Oyster Bay, where Aunt Annie is staying. He is delighted to be with the family again.

headline: A classic Oyster Bay Sunday
summary: Roosevelt enjoys the familiar Oyster Bay Sunday routine: family prayers, a late breakfast, church, a long afternoon walk and an evening of hymn singing.

headline: Turning 21, thinking of Father
summary: Roosevelt celebrates his 21st birthday at Oyster Bay surrounded by his uncle James A. Roosevelt, Aunt Annie, Aunt Lizzie and cousins West, Emlen and Alfred; Emily Swan and other young women come for tea, charades and dancing. Amid the joy he thinks sadly of his late father and prays to live as he would have wished.

headline: Tennis, walking and rowing
summary: Roosevelt fills the day at Oyster Bay with tennis, walks and rowing.

headline: Bloodied in the catbrier
summary: Roosevelt spends twelve hours out with dog and gun. The morning brings rabbits and woodcock; in the afternoon he chases a wild covey of quail through catbrier so dense it soaks his shirt with blood, staying out past moonrise but shooting only two.

headline: Ducking on the Sound
summary: Roosevelt sails into Long Island Sound after ducks, but the few birds are wary and the wind is so strong he can barely handle the old fishing boat under a reefed sail. Back in the bay he finally downs a lone loon after many wasted shots.

headline: Quail hunting and a Halloween party
summary: Roosevelt drives with an old gunner named Ramson to a farmhouse eight miles away and spends six or seven hours in woods and stubble, whistling scattered quail back together. That evening he enjoys a Halloween party at the Swans', complete with the customary rituals and dancing.

headline: A last day of autumn shooting at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt spends the whole day hunting the woods and fields around Oyster Bay, bagging squirrels, rabbits and quail despite poor aim. He caps a fine week of crisp fall weather with evenings of reading and whist with his mother and sisters, and his brother Elliott arrives that night.

headline: Leaving Oyster Bay for New York
summary: Reluctantly leaving Oyster Bay, Roosevelt heads into New York and stays the night at his Uncle Jim's. That evening he calls on the visiting Lee family, whom his mother and sisters are entertaining with a round of outings all week.

headline: On to Boston
summary: Roosevelt leaves New York and returns to Boston, heading back to college.

headline: Back to the books at Harvard
summary: Back in Cambridge, Roosevelt throws himself into his studies, determined to catch up on everything he missed within the week.

headline: Driving out with Harry Shaw
summary: Roosevelt takes his friend Harry Shaw on a drive to the Lyman home, then has dinner with the Saltonstall family.

headline: A quiet day in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard in Cambridge; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: A quiet day in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is in Cambridge at college, with no other details for the day.

headline: Dinner at the Whitneys, night at the Minots
summary: Roosevelt makes a round of calls by carriage, from the Saltonstalls to the Whitneys, where he enjoys dinner and finds himself growing fonder of Bessie Whitney. He ends at Harry Minot's house for the night, with whist and billiards among the young men of several families.

headline: Sunday school, and a talk on machine politics
summary: Roosevelt hurries back to Cambridge to teach his Sunday school class and spends the evening with Lulu Lane. At an O.K. Society meeting he speaks about political machines, drawing on New York's recent election, and classmate Frederick Almy notes in his own diary that the talk sparked a lively discussion.

headline: Evening at the Lees
summary: Roosevelt drives out to the Lee family's home, stays for dinner and a long evening, and doesn't get back until after eleven. He is pleased with how well his new horse and cart are running.

headline: A rueful note to Bamie
summary: Roosevelt writes to his sister Bamie, grumbling about how fickle women can be, as he senses that Alice Lee is turning him away.

headline: Club life and late nights at Harvard
summary: After taking Minot Weld on a drive to the Saltonstalls and a walk with Rose Lee and Rose Saltonstall, Roosevelt reflects in his diary on his college routine: free hours at his club and the A.D., many outings, hard study and late nights, all carried on the strength of his summer conditioning.

headline: A quiet day in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is at college in Cambridge; the day has no other entry.

headline: To New York for the Princeton game
summary: Roosevelt travels to New York to watch Harvard's football team take on Princeton. Classmates Jack Tebbets and Harry Chapin come along as his guests, planning to return to Boston on Monday with Bamie and Conie, who are bound for a week at Chestnut Hill.

headline: Harvard loses; a night on the town
summary: Harvard's football team goes down to defeat. Roosevelt calls on Grace Potter, has Fanny Smith to dinner, then takes in the theater, supper at Delmonico's and a long, song-filled night at the Harvard Club.

headline: A Sunday visit with Edith Carow
summary: Roosevelt enjoys a familiar family Sunday in New York; the family takes warmly to his friend Jack Tebbets. He lunches with Aunt Annie and pays a delightful call on his childhood friend Edith Carow, whom he calls the best-read girl he knows.

headline: Back to Boston with his sisters
summary: Roosevelt returns to Boston with Bamie and Conie and attends a class meeting that night. His sisters settle in at Chestnut Hill, where the Saltonstalls host a dinner in their honor.

headline: A runaway ride home from the Lees
summary: On a rainy day Roosevelt and Dick Saltonstall drive a buggy to dinner with the Lees, followed by an evening of dancing and talk with friends. On the way home a brandy-fueled Dick gallops the horse, which bolts several times, leaving Roosevelt helpless with laughter.

headline: Another evening at the Lees
summary: Roosevelt brings Jack Tebbets to dinner at the Lees, and the evening passes in dancing and games.

headline: Through the snow to the Saltonstalls
summary: In a heavy snowfall, Roosevelt and Dick Saltonstall drive over to the Saltonstall home for dinner.

headline: Dinner with the Lawrences
summary: Roosevelt has dinner with the Lawrence family and enjoys a pleasant evening.

headline: A 34-guest luncheon at the Porcellian
summary: Roosevelt hosts a grand lunch for 34 at the Porcellian Club in honor of Bamie and Corinne, with the Lees, Saltonstalls, Whitneys and many classmates at the table. Flowers, food, wine and witty toasts all land well. He finishes the day at a small party at the Minots.

headline: Sisters' last day in Boston
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts at his club, makes a trip out to Chestnut Hill, and returns to teach Sunday school. His sisters, who have loved their stay, head home the next day.

headline: A quiet day in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard; no other details survive for the day.

headline: A quiet day in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is in Cambridge at college; the record is blank otherwise.

headline: Settling in with the Saltonstalls
summary: Roosevelt lunches with the Lees, drives Rose Lee to the Lawrences' for tennis and takes her on a long drive afterward. He then moves in with the Saltonstalls through Sunday, feeling completely at home with the whole family, and plays whist in the evening.

headline: Thanksgiving dinner with the Lees
summary: Roosevelt takes Rose Saltonstall out in the dog cart and goes skating with young Phil before heading to the Lees at four for Thanksgiving dinner. The evening dissolves into games, dancing and charades.

headline: Rain, candy and late-night theology
summary: Caught in the rain on a long cart ride with Alice Lee, Roosevelt must beg an umbrella at a stranger's door. Later he walks with Alice and Rose, who tease him into buying candy, and stays up talking poetry and theology with Mr. Saltonstall long after Mrs. Saltonstall dozes off.

headline: A rainy day of stories and dancing
summary: Kept indoors by rain, Roosevelt reads, dances with Mamie and Hattie and tells stories to the younger children. After lunch he walks out with Ell Whitney, Rose and Alice, calls on Julia Bacon, and spends the evening at the Lees.

headline: Five lovely days end
summary: After church, Roosevelt sadly leaves Chestnut Hill and drives back to Cambridge, teaching Sunday school and spending the evening at the Whitneys. Privately he has lost hope of winning Alice Lee, and friends find him roaming the wintry Cambridge woods without purpose.

headline: A quiet day in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard; nothing more is noted for the day.

headline: Alice and Rose make their debut
summary: Roosevelt attends a party at the Wares that marks the society debut of Alice Lee and Rose Saltonstall, and enjoys watching the crowd of debutantes. He resolves to go out into society this winter.

headline: Supper at the Porc
summary: Roosevelt has a small supper at the Porcellian Club.

headline: Overnight at Minot Weld's
summary: Roosevelt drives Jack Tebbets and Minot Weld to the Weld home, where they stay the night, and goes on to an enjoyable party at the Grays after dinner.

headline: Dinner at the Lees, a drive to Boston
summary: Roosevelt returns to Cambridge in the morning, drives out to the Lees for dinner, and then takes Frank Lee into Boston.

headline: Seven-fifteen every morning
summary: Roosevelt spends most of the day at Minot Weld's, dines with Harry Shaw in Boston and passes the evening at a commerce party with Miss Silsbee. He notes his growing pleasure in his horse and cart and worries that society life may wear him down, since he rises at 7:15 every weekday no matter how late he stays out.

headline: Sunday school is thriving
summary: Roosevelt reports that his Sunday school class is doing well, then takes tea with the Lane sisters and enjoys the evening.

headline: Nightly whist and a spree
summary: Roosevelt plays his regular evening whist at the club with Jack, Dick and Minot, a nightly habit, and then the four go out on a lively spree.

headline: A grand party at the Amorys
summary: Roosevelt dines with Emmons Blaine at Harry Shaw's and then goes on to a large party given by the Amory family.

headline: Dinner with the Lanes
summary: Roosevelt dines with the Lane family, who have been kind to him; he is especially fond of Lulu Lane.

headline: Dancing at the first Harvard Assembly
summary: At the season's first Harvard Assembly Roosevelt dances happily with Rose Lee. Back in Cambridge afterward, he and friends hold a small 'Symposium'.

headline: A quiet day in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is in Cambridge; no other entry exists for the day.

headline: A three-mile run and a night at the theater
summary: Roosevelt runs three miles in the morning, at an easy 21 minutes. He drives Jack and Dick to Chestnut Hill after lunch, then heads into town with Harry Chapin for dinner at Young's and a play.

headline: Tea at Minot's
summary: After his customary breakfast at the Porcellian and his Sunday school class, Roosevelt drives Harry Chapin to the Minots for tea; Howard Townsend is also spending Sunday there.

headline: Lulu Lane is engaged
summary: Roosevelt calls on Mrs. Shaw and Mrs. Whitney in Boston with Jack Tebbets and dances with Nana Rotch at the first Papanti Hall party of the season. He is delighted to learn that his friend Van Rensselaer is engaged to Lulu Lane.

headline: A comic play at the Gaiety
summary: After dinner at the Amorys, Roosevelt goes with Harry Chapin and Jack Tebbets to see a comedy at the Gaiety that has them laughing.

headline: Hasty Pudding theatricals
summary: Roosevelt drives Tom Lee to the Saltonstalls and spends the evening at the Hasty Pudding Club's theatricals, which he rates very good.

headline: Champagne supper and D.K.E. theatricals
summary: Roosevelt takes Dick for a drive and calls on the Lanes and Rotches. That night brings a champagne dinner, a D.K.E. stage show he ranks above any he has seen, and a nightcap of punch at the club.

headline: Night boat to New York
summary: Roosevelt and Harry Chapin board the overnight boat bound for New York at the start of the holidays.

headline: Home for the holidays
summary: Roosevelt arrives in New York and is overjoyed to be reunited with his family.

headline: Sunday with the Roosevelt cousins
summary: After church Roosevelt spends the day with his Roosevelt relatives, and his cousin West, known as Doc, stays the night.

headline: Ike Iselin's dinner
summary: Ike Iselin hosts a dinner for Roosevelt, with Elliott, Harold Haddon, Douglas Robinson, Archie Russell, Sydney Stratton and Bob Sedgwick at the table. Roosevelt pronounces them all good company.

headline: Sleighing to Jerome Park
summary: After a heavy snow, Roosevelt and Elliott take a cutter up to Jerome Park for a cozy dinner and ride home under the moon around ten. Then he heads to the University Club where the Harvard Glee Club is hosting a supper.

headline: Christmas Eve calls
summary: Roosevelt spends Christmas Eve making the rounds of New York friends, including Annie Murray, Emily Post, Edith Carow, Fanny Smith and the Kane and Potter sisters.

headline: Christmas and the newsboys' dinner
summary: Roosevelt enjoys a happy Christmas with fine presents. He and Elliott oversee the holiday dinner for the city's newsboys, and every Roosevelt turns out for the family's traditional Christmas dinner.

headline: Chestnut Hill friends arrive
summary: Roosevelt has lunch with Edith Carow. That evening Alice Lee, Rose Lee, Rose Saltonstall, Dick Saltonstall, Harry Shaw and Ell Whitney arrive from Boston to stay with the family for a week.

headline: Showing the boys the city
summary: Roosevelt shows his visiting college friends around New York and goes to a small party at Aunt Annie's in the afternoon.

headline: Afternoon at the Newsboys' Lodging House
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday afternoon at the Newsboys' Lodging House and delights in having the Chestnut Hill visitors under the family roof.

headline: A rowdy theater party
summary: Roosevelt, Jack Kingsford and Ell Whitney escort the three Chestnut Hill girls around the city, lunch at West and Hilly Roosevelt's, and end with an uproarious theater party hosted by Aunt Lizzie.

headline: Music hall and a dinner at Mrs. Haddon's
summary: The whole party takes in an afternoon show at the music hall, and Roosevelt dines at Mrs. Haddon's in the evening, seated between his hostess and Rose Lee.

headline: Dancing out the old year
summary: Roosevelt gives Rose a buggy ride around the park and takes Alice for a walk. Alfred treats him and the visiting men to lunch at a downtown club, and the night ends with a small party that dances out 1879. He also closes his diary year with a page of accounts.

headline: New Year's sleigh party at Jerome Park
summary: Elliott throws a lavish New Year's lunch at Jerome Park, with couples riding out in cutters and the rest piled into a great sleigh. The group dances waltzes, polka redowas and the Virginia Reel, and that evening Roosevelt and Dick pay a comical visit to Fanny Smith.

headline: The Boston visitors head home
summary: Roosevelt drives Alice Lee in the park after breakfast; at 11 the Boston guests leave after a much-enjoyed stay. That night he joins Elliott and the members of their whist club for a theater party and supper.

headline: A day of calls
summary: Roosevelt spends the day visiting friends young and old across New York.

headline: Newsboys, then the night train
summary: Roosevelt spends a last afternoon at the Newsboys' Lodging House and boards the overnight train for Boston.

headline: Back at work in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt resumes his studies, working until three, then takes Jack Tebbets for a drive behind his now-steady horse. His new cutter has arrived, but snow is still too thin for sleighing, so he passes the evening reading and playing whist at the club.

headline: A quiet day in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard, with no further entry for the day.

headline: Reception at the Homers
summary: Roosevelt and Jack Tebbets drive into Boston in the evening for a large reception given by the Homer family.

headline: Meeting the Rathbone sisters
summary: At the Harvard Assembly Roosevelt leads the german with Julia Bacon and meets two charming young women from Albany, the Rathbone sisters.

headline: A rainy afternoon at the Saltonstalls
summary: With rain falling, Roosevelt hires a buggy instead of using his cart and spends the afternoon and evening with the Saltonstall family.

headline: A drive with Grace Rathbone
summary: Roosevelt drives his cart to the Brunswick Hotel and takes Grace Rathbone on a long outing. He dines with the Whitneys and finishes at an enjoyable party at the Amorys.

headline: Asked to give up his Sunday school class
summary: After three and a half years of teaching, Roosevelt is asked to resign his Sunday school class because he is a Presbyterian unwilling to become an Episcopalian, and he finds it unfair. He spends the afternoon and evening at the Saltonstalls and writes home asking his mother to send his silk hat.

headline: The Papanti parties
summary: Roosevelt goes to the Papanti party, his favorite of the season's dances, and notes that dancing is the amusement he loves most after riding.

headline: First sleigh ride and the Great Assembly
summary: Roosevelt hitches his horse to the new sleigh for the first time and it performs perfectly. That evening he goes to the Great Assembly ball in Horticultural Hall, the biggest ball he has seen in Boston.

headline: Party at Mrs. Parkman Shaw's
summary: Roosevelt and Minot Weld dine in Boston with Harry Shaw before going on to a lovely small party at Mrs. Parkman Shaw's.

headline: Sleighing to a Saltonstall dinner
summary: Roosevelt takes Jack Tebbets in his cutter to a small, pleasant dinner with the Saltonstalls, where he sits between his hostess and Kitty Lane.

headline: A quiet day in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard; the day has no further record.

headline: Single-stick, vaulting and sparring
summary: Roosevelt attends a lunch given by Van Rensselaer for the Rathbone sisters and an afternoon reception at the Minots, where he admires Grace Minot. He notes that he works out steadily in the gym, fencing with single-sticks, vaulting, boxing and running three or four miles daily.

headline: Bamie turns 25
summary: On his sister Bamie's 25th birthday, Roosevelt writes to her from the Porcellian Club with news of sleighing and his regular workouts, and spends a pleasant evening with the Rotch family.

headline: A party at the Dexters
summary: Roosevelt takes Minot Weld on a long afternoon drive and goes to an enjoyable party at the Dexters that night. With Dick Saltonstall's ankle on the mend, he feels free to invite other friends driving.

headline: A birthday gift for Rosy
summary: For Rose Lee's birthday Roosevelt drives to Chestnut Hill with a present, spending the afternoon and dinner with the Lees.

headline: A dull dinner party
summary: Roosevelt attends a dinner at the Wales home that he finds rather dull.

headline: A.D. Club dinner for a hundred
summary: Roosevelt joins more than 100 men at a big A.D. Club dinner in Boston, leaves around eleven, and moves on to the Sears home for a party that lasts until about two.

headline: Off to old Salem
summary: Roosevelt travels to Salem with Alice, Rose, Mrs. Lee and Mrs. Saltonstall, lodging in a curious old house owned by Miss Saltonstall, and enjoys a lively party at Hamilton Hall.

headline: Back from Salem
summary: Roosevelt returns from Salem, dines at Theodore Lyman's and finishes with a small spree at the Porcellian.

headline: Alice Lee says yes
summary: Nearly eight months after his first proposal, Roosevelt drives to the Lees determined to settle things, and after long pleading Alice Lee agrees to marry him. In a rapturous diary entry he vows to devote his life to her happiness and gives thanks to God.

headline: Semiannual exams begin
summary: Roosevelt sits the first of his midyear examinations, then dances at the Papanti Hall party, where Alice is the belle of the room and gives him her favor.

headline: Afraid it won't last
summary: Only now beginning to grasp his engagement, Roosevelt confesses a lingering fear that Alice may change her mind, as she has before.

headline: Hinting at big news
summary: Roosevelt looks in on a little gathering at the Parkman Shaws', though parties have lost their appeal this winter. He writes Bamie that he has important news to share, promising to reveal it when he comes home at week's end.

headline: A day with his sweetheart
summary: Roosevelt lunches with the Saltonstalls, spends the afternoon with Alice, dines with Frank Lee at the Union Club and closes the evening at the Horticultural Assembly, where Alice looks lovelier than ever.

headline: Looking back on months of torment
summary: Roosevelt reflects on the four months of anguish behind him, sleepless nights over Alice that no one else suspected. He admits it was love at first sight and his first love.

headline: Telling the family
summary: Roosevelt travels to New York to break the news of his engagement; the family is thrilled and very surprised. His mother writes to Alice Lee.

headline: Sharing the news with uncles and aunts
summary: Roosevelt tells his uncles and aunts about the engagement and they are delighted. He still feels he must be dreaming.

headline: Choosing a diamond ring
summary: Roosevelt selects a diamond engagement ring for Alice and returns to Boston that afternoon.

headline: Upset in a snowdrift
summary: In heavy snow Roosevelt sleighs to Chestnut Hill, his horse sinking to its belly in drifts, to see Alice. On the way home the sleigh overturns and he is dragged some 300 yards clinging to the reins. Alice writes his mother that she loves him deeply.

headline: Keeping the secret
summary: Roosevelt and Dick go for a long sleigh ride in perfect sleighing weather. The engagement won't be made public until a week from Monday, and staying away from Alice is hard.

headline: Harvard Assembly with Lulu Lowell
summary: Roosevelt dances with Lulu Lowell at the Harvard Assembly.

headline: Almost too happy
summary: Roosevelt sleighs over to the Saltonstalls, dines there and spends the evening with Alice.

headline: A great Porcellian supper
summary: Roosevelt drives Minot Weld home and back, and attends a big supper at the Porcellian in the evening.

headline: A new mission school and a tribute to friends
summary: Roosevelt begins teaching at a mission school in East Cambridge. In his diary he praises his circle of friends, led by Elliott, as plucky, honorable and sensible, and declares his happiness complete now that Alice is his. He ends the day with tea at the Whitneys.

headline: A below-zero sleigh ride
summary: Roosevelt dines at Jim Parker's and dances with Nana Rotch at the Papanti party. Afterward he and Dick ride out to Chestnut Hill in Dick's cutter with the thermometer below zero, so bundled up they hardly notice.

headline: Nothing to hide from Alice
summary: Roosevelt drives back to Cambridge and goes to a party at the Winthrops. In his diary he gives thanks that he has nothing in his past he could not tell Alice.

headline: Sleighing to the Lowells for leap year
summary: Seven friends pile into a sleigh bound for the Lowells' leap year gathering, where Alice is among the guests.

headline: Presiding at an A.D. dinner
summary: Roosevelt presides over an A.D. Club dinner for 25 in Boston and counts it among the best he has attended, full of good songs, stories and speeches.

headline: Storm-bound with his 'Little Sunshine'
summary: Roosevelt drives through hard rain to dine with the Lees and, thanks to the storm, stays the night. He fills his diary with devotion to Alice, his 'Little Sunshine', and writes Henry Minot to announce the engagement.

headline: Champagne for the club
summary: On Valentine's Day Roosevelt returns to Cambridge, tells his club about the engagement and buys champagne for all. He spends the evening at the Fish family's leap year dance.

headline: A snowy drive with Alice
summary: After Sunday school Roosevelt drives to the Lees and takes Alice for a long ride as snow begins to fall, then spends the evening and night there.

headline: A boxing benefit
summary: Roosevelt returns to Cambridge early and goes into Boston in the evening for a boxing benefit.

headline: The family comes to meet Alice
summary: Roosevelt goes into Boston to greet his family, who have come to see Alice, and brings Elliott back to stay the night with him.

headline: Forty-two bouquets
summary: Roosevelt drives Elliott to lunch at the Saltonstalls, where his whole family gathers. He spends the afternoon with Alice, dines at the Lees and stays late at the Porcellian. Alice has received 42 bouquets.

headline: Theater party for Bamie and Conie
summary: Roosevelt drives Elliott into Boston, dines with his family at the Brunswick and joins a theater party that Frank and Tom Lee give for his sisters, with Alice acting as chaperone. He also accepts Henry Minot's invitation to dinner for himself and Alice on March 1.

headline: Up all night after the Pudding
summary: After a family day and a big family dinner at the Lees, Roosevelt drives home by moonlight and joins a rowdy night at the Hasty Pudding Club. He stays up until a quarter to six and plays billiards at the club until breakfast.

headline: Forty-four hours without sleep
summary: Roosevelt and Jack Tebbets see the family off in Boston. He makes calls with Alice, dines with 'Uncle' Bill Lee and returns for the annual Porcellian dinner, finally going to bed at midnight after 44 hours awake.

headline: A drive toward Milton
summary: After teaching at the mission school, Roosevelt takes Alice on a long drive to Forest Hills and out toward Milton on a beautiful day.

headline: A stormy day with Alice
summary: With rain and snow all day, Roosevelt happily spends nearly every hour with Alice, and his diary overflows with affection for her.

headline: Surprise party for Danny Peabody
summary: Roosevelt returns to Cambridge early and that evening joins a surprise gathering at the Rogers home in honor of Danny Peabody.

headline: A day without Chestnut Hill
summary: For once Roosevelt stays away from Chestnut Hill, driving his dogcart in the afternoon and spending the evening at the club. He writes to his uncle John Roosevelt in praise of Alice.

headline: Dinner at the Bartletts
summary: Roosevelt lunches at Chestnut Hill and takes Alice for a cart ride. In the evening he escorts Alice and Rose to dine with the Bartletts, sitting between Miss Whitney and Miss Sears and spending the rest of the night with Miss Perkins.

headline: Overnight in Salem with Alice
summary: Roosevelt returns to Cambridge early, then travels to Salem with Alice to stay with the Lees there. He is charmed by the old town and by her company.

headline: Lunch for two at Parker's
summary: Roosevelt and Alice return to Boston and share a cozy lunch for two at Parker's. That evening Colonel Russell is his host for dinner at the Somerset Club. It is also Elliott's 20th birthday.

headline: Leap Day drive through Milton
summary: After Sunday school Roosevelt drives to Chestnut Hill as usual and takes Alice on a long cart ride through Forest Hills and Milton, staying the night at the Lees. In New York, the Second Avenue elevated railway opens the same day.

headline: Calls in Boston, and plans for an autumn wedding
summary: Roosevelt drives Alice into Boston in his high cart behind his horse Lightfoot to pay calls and lunch, and the Minots host a dinner for the couple that evening. He writes Bamie that his first two exams earned 94 and 98, and that Alice hopes to marry next fall.

headline: A lecture to the Natural History Society
summary: Roosevelt drives back to Cambridge and gives a lecture to the college's Natural History Society.

headline: The bowling parties begin
summary: Roosevelt attends the first in a series of bowling parties, which he enjoys.

headline: Dinner at the Lees with Dick
summary: Roosevelt drives Dick Saltonstall in his cart to a pleasant dinner with the Lees, with Fanny Peabody and Mrs. Jack Peabody on either side.

headline: An afternoon drive with Alice
summary: Roosevelt heads to the Lees in the afternoon, takes Alice for a drive and stays the evening and the night.

headline: Dinner with the Whitneys
summary: Roosevelt returns to Cambridge that morning and dines with the Whitneys.

headline: A headache cancels the drive
summary: After Sunday school Roosevelt goes to the Lees as usual, but Alice has a headache and their drive is called off.

headline: Mr. Lee agrees to a fall wedding
summary: Back in Cambridge, Roosevelt writes Conie that he will bring Alice to live at the family home on West 57th Street after they marry. That promise has won George Lee's consent to an autumn wedding.

headline: Danny Peabody's dinner for Alice
summary: Roosevelt goes into town for a pleasant dinner that Danny Peabody gives in Alice's honor.

headline: Bowling and a stag dinner
summary: Roosevelt bowls in the afternoon and attends a men's dinner in the evening. The bowling series will run to six parties, hosted in turn by Alice, Rose, Rosy, the Lee brothers and himself, and Dick, Ralph Ellis and Peters keep the stag dinner laughing.

headline: Planning the wedding party
summary: Roosevelt drives to Chestnut Hill after breakfast and spends a snowy day with Alice. He writes his mother that he will bring home a Boston bride, and tells Bamie that Alice, her sisters and Mrs. Lee have chosen his ushers, with Elliott as best man and four bridesmaids including Corinne.

headline: A failed sleigh outing
summary: With snow on the ground, Roosevelt tries to take Rose out in the Lees' cutter and makes a sorry mess of it. A big dinner follows that evening.

headline: Sparring and wrestling in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt goes over to Cambridge to watch the sparring and wrestling matches, then returns and escorts Alice to a dinner at the Amorys in Boston.

headline: Sunday school and back
summary: Roosevelt drives to Cambridge to teach Sunday school and returns to Chestnut Hill.

headline: Visiting Alice's grandparents in New Bedford
summary: Mrs. Lee takes Roosevelt and Alice to visit her own parents in New Bedford, and the couple travel home on their own. He enjoys the day in the quaint old house and its even quainter household.

headline: Rained in at Chestnut Hill
summary: Rain keeps Roosevelt from returning to Cambridge, so he spends the whole day with Alice.

headline: Back for bowling
summary: Roosevelt drives back to Cambridge and attends an afternoon bowling party.

headline: Cousin West's heartbreak
summary: His cousin West Roosevelt arrives, and Roosevelt brings him to Chestnut Hill for dinner and then to the Porcellian. West has been turned down by Fanny, whom Roosevelt thinks has treated him shamefully, but West plans to try again.

headline: Dinner at the Minots
summary: West heads back to New York. Roosevelt goes to Chestnut Hill and takes Alice, Rosy and Rose to dinner with the Minot family.

headline: Athletic sports and dinner at the Shaws
summary: Roosevelt returns to Cambridge for the college athletic games and dines that evening at the Shaws.

headline: Tea with Alice at the Cabots
summary: With Alice staying at the Cabot home in Boston, Roosevelt goes to see her for tea after Sunday school.

headline: Overnight at the Saltonstalls
summary: Roosevelt and Dick drive over for a pleasant dinner at the Saltonstall home and stay the night.

headline: Dinner at the Lowells
summary: Roosevelt and Dick head back to Cambridge early. Later he walks to the Lees to stay the night, and dines with the Lowells that evening.

headline: D.K.E. theatricals
summary: Roosevelt returns on foot to Cambridge early and watches the D.K.E. theatricals that evening.

headline: Writing his economics thesis
summary: Roosevelt spends the day in the library working on his political economy thesis. He admits he has barely studied since his engagement and skips most recitations, reasoning that good grades have earned him a last holiday before law school.

headline: Defying a doctor's warning
summary: Roosevelt walks to Chestnut Hill and spends the evening with Alice, writing that they have no secrets between them. Dr. Dudley Sargent warns him that his heart is weak and that he must avoid strain, even running up stairs; Roosevelt answers that he intends to do the very opposite.

headline: More sparring and wrestling
summary: Roosevelt returns to Cambridge to watch the boxing and wrestling. He writes Conie that he took Alice driving on both Thursday and Friday afternoons.

headline: A snowy Sunday buggy ride
summary: Snow is falling, so after Sunday school Roosevelt takes a buggy to Chestnut Hill to spend the night.

headline: Back and forth to Chestnut Hill
summary: Roosevelt drives to Cambridge for the day and returns to Chestnut Hill in the evening for another night.

headline: Party at the Bryants
summary: Roosevelt drives back to Cambridge and goes to an evening party given by the Bryants.

headline: Dinner for the 'Big Six'
summary: After an afternoon of bowling, Roosevelt dines at Young's with his close circle, Dick Saltonstall, Jack Tebbets, Minot Weld, Harry Chapin and Harry Shaw, and they finish at the theater with a comic play. Around this time he steps down from many posts and gives less time to his studies.

headline: Specimen hunting at Nahant
summary: Roosevelt sets out early with fellow advanced zoology students on a specimen-collecting trip to Nahant. In the afternoon he takes Alice, whom he calls Birdie, for a drive, and at night escorts her to the Harvard Assembly, where she is the belle. The same day, New York's new Metropolitan Museum of Art welcomes its first visitors.

headline: No mortal happier
summary: Roosevelt goes to Cambridge for recitations, returns to Chestnut Hill, drives Alice out and spends the evening with her, so happy he wonders if it is a dream.

headline: A dinner from the Rotches
summary: After a trip to Cambridge, Roosevelt takes Alice on a long afternoon drive, and in the evening the couple ride into town for a dinner the Rotches give in their honor.

headline: Last Sunday school class of the year
summary: Roosevelt drives to Cambridge for his final Sunday school class of the year, then returns to spend the evening with Alice.

headline: Calls in town and a Papanti party
summary: Roosevelt drives Alice into Boston to make calls, including one on Fanny Peabody, his favorite Boston girl after Rose and Rosy. That night he dances with Rose Saltonstall at the Papanti party.

headline: A day of driving friends
summary: Roosevelt drives to Dick Saltonstall's, takes him on to the Minots, dines at Jack Tebbets' and then drives Jack out to Cambridge.

headline: Bringing Alice to New York
summary: Roosevelt, Alice and Mrs. Lee travel to New York for a ten-day visit, where his mother, Bamie, Conie and Elliott welcome them warmly.

headline: Introducing Alice to the family
summary: Roosevelt spends most of the day on his thesis, and in the evening the family holds a party to introduce Alice.

headline: Aunt Laura's dinner
summary: Roosevelt's Aunt Laura Roosevelt gives Alice a large family dinner.

headline: Dinner at home
summary: Roosevelt dines at home, with Miss Prince and Miss Moran beside him.

headline: Everyone rallies around Alice
summary: Roosevelt is touched by the warm attention his cousins, friends, mother and sisters give Alice, and especially by Elliott's flowers and kindness.

headline: Harvard theatricals in New York
summary: After an afternoon tea, Roosevelt takes Alice and Bamie to see the Harvard theatricals.

headline: A big party for Alice
summary: The Roosevelt family hosts a large party in Alice's honor.

headline: Emlen's stag dinner
summary: Cousin Emlen Roosevelt throws Roosevelt a stag dinner.

headline: A drive past Jerome Park
summary: Roosevelt drives Alice far out past Jerome Park in the morning, and Aunt Annie gives a party for her.

headline: Last day in New York
summary: On the final day of the visit, Roosevelt reflects that everyone has gone out of their way for Alice.

headline: A dream of happiness
summary: Roosevelt, Alice and Mrs. Lee take the 11 a.m. train to Boston, and he attends a Porcellian supper for Charley Dickey's initiation. Looking back on three blissful months, he describes days of light work, frequent drives, and most nights at Chestnut Hill with Alice.

headline: Back to Cambridge with Dick
summary: Roosevelt drives Dick Saltonstall back to Cambridge.

headline: A quiet day in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is in Cambridge; no other entry survives for the day.

headline: Funeral of Alice's grandmother
summary: Alice's grandmother, Mrs. Haskell, has died, and Roosevelt travels to New Bedford for the funeral.

headline: Packed for a long stay
summary: Roosevelt drives to Chestnut Hill in the afternoon with a bag tucked under the seat, planning to stay several days, and takes Alice out driving.

headline: Evenings of whist and music
summary: Roosevelt drives to Cambridge and back. He describes the Lee household's evenings of whist, reading and piano, with an hour or two alone with Alice.

headline: A drive through Milton and Forest Hills
summary: Roosevelt spends the morning with Mamie Saltonstall and little Bella, then drives Alice for hours by way of Milton, Forest Hills and Longwood.

headline: Church and a drive past the Charles
summary: Roosevelt attends the small Chestnut Hill church and takes Alice on a long afternoon drive beyond the Charles River. He writes that he has never been as happy as in these last three months.

headline: A sample day at Chestnut Hill
summary: Roosevelt describes a typical day: studying while Alice practices music, tennis, reading Prescott's Conquest of Peru aloud as she sews, a three-hour drive out past Dedham to the Blue Hills, stories and games with the children, whist, and an hour alone with Alice.

headline: Return to Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt returns to Cambridge early.

headline: Tennis and the Pudding theatricals
summary: Roosevelt plays tennis with Harry Chapin and enjoys the Hasty Pudding theatricals at night. He admits he has hardly studied since getting engaged, working only about three days a week, since his earlier marks give him room to coast.

headline: A quiet day in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard; no other details are recorded.

headline: A drive with 'Baby'
summary: Roosevelt drives to Chestnut Hill and takes Alice, his 'Baby', out driving.

headline: Tennis weather
summary: Roosevelt romps with the children Georgie and Bella, plays tennis with Rose Saltonstall and takes Alice on a long drive in glorious spring weather.

headline: An ideal Sunday at Chestnut Hill
summary: Roosevelt goes to the little church in the morning and drives Alice in the afternoon, calling Chestnut Hill an ideal place and the Lee home a joy to stay in.

headline: Tennis all day
summary: Roosevelt plays tennis with Rose and Rosy in the morning and with Alice in the afternoon, drives her into Boston and back, and spends the evening at the Saltonstalls.

headline: Return to Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt returns to Cambridge early.

headline: Living like a prince
summary: Roosevelt drives Minot Weld 12 miles to Frank Codman's farm in Lincoln for a day of fun. In his diary he sums up his last two college years: ample money, the Porcellian, hunting trips, a good horse, true friends, light work and, above all, Alice.

headline: A quiet day in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is in Cambridge; nothing else is noted.

headline: The Rotch sisters visit
summary: Roosevelt drives to Chestnut Hill, where the Rotch sisters are guests of the Lees.

headline: Tennis all day and a Porcellian dinner
summary: With the Rotch sisters and Miss Reynolds visiting, Jack Tebbets, Frank Codman and Tom Lee drive over and everyone plays tennis all day. Roosevelt then drives Jack to a Porcellian dinner that he, Harry Shaw and Dick give for some older honorary members.

headline: Sunday at Chestnut Hill
summary: After breakfast at the Porcellian, Roosevelt drives Dick to Chestnut Hill and takes Alice out in the cart that afternoon.

headline: An evening drive in the heat
summary: The day is so hot that Roosevelt waits until after dinner to take Alice for a pleasant drive.

headline: Early return to Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt drives back to Cambridge early in the morning.

headline: A quiet day in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard; the day is otherwise blank.

headline: A quiet day in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is in Cambridge, with no further record for the day.

headline: Tennis after tea
summary: Roosevelt drives to Chestnut Hill in the afternoon and plays tennis after tea.

headline: Class races and a drive down Beacon Street
summary: Roosevelt takes Alice to the Union Boat Club in Boston to watch the class races, which his class loses. Driving her home along Beacon Street, he feels very grand in his smart rig beside her.

headline: A walk in the woods with the children
summary: After church Roosevelt takes Cotty, Georgie and Bella walking in the woods, and in the afternoon drives Alice through Waverley and Belmont.

headline: Back with Dick
summary: Roosevelt brings Dick Saltonstall back to Cambridge early.

headline: A quiet day in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard; no entry exists for the day.

headline: A call on Joe Whitney's fiancée
summary: Roosevelt and Dick pay a comical call on Georgie Heyward, Joe Whitney's fiancée, then he attends an O.K. dinner and the D.K.E. He sends Bamie a 'Rollo' piece from the Harvard Lampoon and reports his horse Lightfoot looking thin and the cart a bit worn.

headline: A few days at the Lees
summary: Roosevelt drives to the Lees for a stay of several days and plays tennis in the afternoon.

headline: A moonlight drive
summary: Roosevelt walks to Cambridge and back for his recitations, and after dinner takes Alice on a long drive by moonlight.

headline: Athletic games and a garden party
summary: Roosevelt takes Tom Lee to the college athletic games, which he rates very good, then on to the Dixwells' garden party, and drives Alice home under the moon.

headline: A drive around Auburndale
summary: Fanny Peabody and Cotty are guests at the Saltonstalls, and after church the group takes a woodland walk. Later Roosevelt takes Alice on a long drive through the countryside near Auburndale.

headline: Reading aloud and tea at the Whitneys
summary: Roosevelt spends the whole day with Alice, reading to her while she sews. In the afternoon they make calls in the cart, end up having tea and fun at the Whitneys, and drive home by moonlight around ten.

headline: Return to Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt drives back to Cambridge.

headline: A quiet day in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard; nothing more is recorded.

headline: A quiet day in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is in Cambridge; the day has no other entry.

headline: Off to Chestnut Hill
summary: Roosevelt drives over to Chestnut Hill.

headline: Their longest drive yet
summary: Roosevelt reads Thackeray's Pendennis aloud to Alice as she sews, then takes her on their longest drive so far, through Dedham and Needham nearly to Wellesley and back by Grantville. In New York, the family closes the 57th Street house and his mother leaves for Oyster Bay.

headline: A rainy Sunday indoors
summary: Rain keeps everyone inside after church, and Roosevelt spends the day spinning tales for the children or sitting with Alice.

headline: Senior thesis on equal rights
summary: Roosevelt reads Pendennis to Alice in the morning and drives her out at night. He completes his senior thesis, on whether men and women can practically be given equal rights, and his grades include 91 and 89 in natural history.

headline: Early return to Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt heads back to Cambridge at an early hour.

headline: A quiet day in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is at Harvard; no further record exists.

headline: Tea and tennis
summary: Roosevelt reaches Chestnut Hill by teatime and plays tennis afterward.

headline: A darling of a sweetheart
summary: Roosevelt takes Alice for a cart ride and marvels in his diary at his good fortune.

headline: A day of reading and driving
summary: Roosevelt spends the day with Alice, reading aloud and taking her on a long, lovely cart drive.

headline: A rainy Sunday walk
summary: It rains, so after church Roosevelt walks by himself, and when the weather clears he walks again with Alice.

headline: Cramming for finals
summary: Roosevelt returns to Cambridge for his first final exam and resolves to stay there for ten days of hard study to make up for months of loafing, not returning to Chestnut Hill until his last exam on the 16th.

headline: Exam season in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is in Cambridge studying for his finals; no other entry is recorded.

headline: Exam season in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt remains in Cambridge during finals, with no other details recorded.

headline: A call on the Lanes
summary: Roosevelt visits the Lane sisters and remarks that his friend Van Rensselaer, Lulu Lane's fiancé, is a lucky man.

headline: Exam season in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is in Cambridge during his final examinations; nothing more is noted.

headline: Exam season in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt stays in Cambridge studying; the day is otherwise blank.

headline: Nine hours a day at the books
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts at his club and dines with the Lanes. He reports studying nine or ten hours daily, with only a walk or tennis and an hour of whist for relief, and misses Alice terribly.

headline: Exam season in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is in Cambridge with finals under way; no other entry survives.

headline: Exam season in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt is in Cambridge on the eve of his last exam; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Last exam, and back to Alice
summary: Roosevelt passes his final examination after ten days of real effort, then drives his cart to the Lees, delighted to be back among the family and above all with Alice.

headline: Games, a drive and tennis
summary: Roosevelt spends the morning playing with the children Georgie and Bella, drives Alice in the afternoon, and plays tennis until dark.

headline: The finest drive of the season
summary: Roosevelt takes Alice on an evening drive from about 6:30 to 9:30 through the wooded hills north of Wellesley, returning in clear moonlight. To him it is the best drive of the whole season.

headline: Elliott arrives
summary: Roosevelt drives to Cambridge for a Porcellian supper, then meets Elliott's late train in Boston and takes him to the club.

headline: Two families together
summary: Roosevelt and Elliott idle at the club until four, then drive to the Lees, where their mother and sisters are staying. He is pleased that the two families get along so well.

headline: Tennis and singing at the Lees
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts with Elliott and brings him to the Lees for a day of tennis, walks and songs.

headline: Garden party at the Winthrops
summary: Roosevelt brings Elliott to dinner at the Lees, escorts Alice to the Winthrops' garden party and back under a bright moon, and then drives Elliott home.

headline: Charades and hide-and-seek in Salem
summary: A big party of Roosevelts, Lees, Saltonstalls and Peabodys has lunch at the Lee home in Salem, then drives over to the Peabodys to spend the night with dancing, charades and hide-and-seek.

headline: Ike Iselin comes to visit
summary: The party is back in Boston by morning, and Ike Iselin arrives to stay a few days, and Roosevelt takes him and Elliott to the D.K.E. theatricals and then to the club.

headline: Class Day in Hollis Hall
summary: On Class Day Roosevelt marches with his class in dress suits and silk hats, helps run the class spread in the gym and joins the exercises around the tree. That night he sits with Alice for nearly two hours in his old Hollis Hall room, looking down on the lantern-lit Yard, and gets to bed at four.

headline: Garden party at the Lowells
summary: After breakfast at the club, Roosevelt drives Jack Kingsford, Ike Iselin and Elliott to dinner at the Lees, followed by the Lowells' garden party.

headline: A stroll in the woods with Alice
summary: Roosevelt takes his visitors to Chestnut Hill by a roundabout route to show off the countryside. Iselin and Kingsford return to New York, and in the evening he and Alice take a lovely walk in the woods.

headline: A summer evening walk
summary: After a late breakfast Roosevelt brings Elliott to the Lees for the day, and in the evening he and Alice walk out in the cool summer air.

headline: Packing up four years
summary: While the others go to Nahant, Roosevelt stays behind to pack and settle his bills. He marvels that college is over but feels no gloom, with Alice beside him and only four months until their wedding.

headline: Harvard graduate, magna cum laude
summary: Roosevelt receives his B.A. from Harvard magna cum laude, finishing 21st among 177 classmates, with John D. Long giving the main address. He spends the day at the club, attends the Dexters' garden party and drives Alice back to Chestnut Hill. Meanwhile Douglas Robinson is courting Conie and Elliott works at Uncle James Gracie's bank.

headline: Alice and friends come to Oyster Bay
summary: Fresh from Harvard, Roosevelt brings his fiancée Alice Lee, her sister Rosy and Rose Saltonstall out to Oyster Bay, where they arrive after dark. His new cart and horse turn up safely, and he pauses to look back on his college years with real satisfaction.

headline: Drives and tennis with his 'Queen'
summary: Roosevelt revels in having Alice at Oyster Bay. He takes her on a carriage ride to Laurelton and Syosset with Rose and Ike Iselin riding behind, plays tennis after lunch, and passes the evening alone with her in the garden summer house.

headline: A full house at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt takes Alice on a morning drive through the Long Island countryside, goes sailing with the group after lunch, and visits Uncle Jim's in the evening. Houseguests Douglas Robinson and Romy Colgate swell the party at home.

headline: A Fourth of July vow of love
summary: After church, Roosevelt walks Alice through Fleets woods and down to the dock in the evening. In his diary he pours out his devotion, writing that no hardship could shake her loyalty and that his love will only deepen with time.

headline: Pond lilies and a condolence letter
summary: Roosevelt drives Alice to Cold Spring to gather pond lilies and that evening watches some amateur acting at the Weeks home. He also writes his Harvard friend Henry Minot, whose mother has died, confessing that Alice has consumed his last two college years.

headline: Tea at Aunt Annie's
summary: Roosevelt takes Alice for a morning drive, then goes to tea at Aunt Annie Gracie's in the evening. He tells his diary he spends most of every day with her and has never been happier.

headline: Rowing Alice to Yellow Banks
summary: Roosevelt rows Alice across to Yellow Banks and back in time for lunch. The afternoon brings tennis, and the evening a lively tea with the Beekman family.

headline: A long drive past Glen Cove
summary: On his mother's 45th birthday, Roosevelt rows in the morning and later takes Alice on a lengthy carriage outing by way of 'Old Kentuck' and around behind Glen Cove and Norwich, ending the day with her in the summer house.

headline: Sailing, then a drive over the plains
summary: Roosevelt sails in the morning. After lunch he drives Alice out across the open plains country and again spends the evening at her side in the summer house.

headline: Seeing Alice off to Chestnut Hill
summary: Alice, Rosy and Rose Saltonstall head home to Chestnut Hill, and Roosevelt rides into the city to see them off. Even a week apart feels too long to him.

headline: A quiet Sunday at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: At Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt remains at Oyster Bay with no entry in the record for the day.

headline: Another day at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is still at Oyster Bay; the record notes nothing more.

headline: Summer games feel flat without Alice
summary: Roosevelt keeps up his usual round of Oyster Bay sport, from tennis and rowing to swimming and sailing, but admits that with Alice away none of it holds the old appeal.

headline: At Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.

headline: Last day before the trip north
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay, with nothing further noted, the day before he sets off to rejoin Alice.

headline: Reunited with Alice at Chestnut Hill
summary: Roosevelt travels from Oyster Bay to Chestnut Hill and is overjoyed to see Alice again, delighted by how pretty she looks and how warmly she welcomes him.

headline: A whole Sunday with Alice
summary: Roosevelt spends the entire day at Chestnut Hill with Alice and fills his diary with praise for her, calling her the noblest of women.

headline: Blackberrying at Chestnut Hill
summary: Most of the day again goes to Alice, but Roosevelt also spends about three hours leading George, Cottie and Bella out to pick blackberries.

headline: Overnight train to Mount Desert
summary: Roosevelt, Alice, Rose Saltonstall and her brother Richard board the night train for Mount Desert, Maine, transferring to the boat at 11 p.m. The same day Commander Henry Gorringe delivers the ancient obelisk known as Cleopatra's Needle to New York, bound for Central Park.

headline: Settling in on Mount Desert
summary: The party lands on Mount Desert after midday. Alice and Rose lodge with the Weld family at Bar Harbor, while Roosevelt and Dick Saltonstall are put up by Jack Tebbets at Schooner Head, about three and a half miles off.

headline: Two rides into Bar Harbor
summary: From his base at Schooner Head, Roosevelt rides over to Bar Harbor twice, and fits in tennis and bowling besides.

headline: Taking in the Maine coast
summary: Roosevelt plays tennis through the morning and spends the afternoon walking around to the local sights, marveling at the grandeur of the Maine scenery.

headline: Laid up with cholera morbus
summary: A stomach illness keeps Roosevelt indoors. He writes his sister Corinne to ask after Douglas Robinson and jokes about how awkward it is for a suitor to be sick.

headline: Up and about again
summary: Recovered enough to get around, Roosevelt is driven by Jack Tebbets over to Otter Creek in the afternoon.

headline: Moving in with the Welds
summary: Roosevelt and Dick Saltonstall leave Schooner Head and take rooms with the Weld family in Bar Harbor, under the same roof as Alice and Rose.

headline: Tennis, woods and rocky shores
summary: Roosevelt plays tennis all morning, then spends the rest of the day with Alice exploring the Bar Harbor woods and the rugged shoreline.

headline: A buggy ride and a party
summary: Roosevelt takes Alice for an afternoon spin in a buggy and goes to an enjoyable party that evening.

headline: Alice turns nineteen
summary: On Alice's 19th birthday, Roosevelt marvels in his diary at his luck in winning her, promising to repay her love with lifelong care and tenderness.

headline: Sick, and nursed by Alice
summary: Roosevelt falls ill again. His 'Big Six' friends rally around him, and Alice gives up her own fun to look after him, which leaves him more devoted to her than ever.

headline: Alice wins the ladies' tennis prize
summary: Roosevelt is on the mend, and Alice carries off first prize in the women's tennis tournament.

headline: Sunday sermon at Bar Harbor
summary: Roosevelt attends church and hears what he judges an excellent sermon.

headline: Evenings in the Welds' kitchen
summary: Roosevelt praises the Welds' kindness. When rough weather keeps them off the rocks at night, he and Alice slip away to the kitchen to be alone.

headline: Climbing Newport Mountain
summary: Roosevelt hikes up Newport Mountain in the morning.

headline: Rain, Alice and a dance
summary: Wet weather does not stop Roosevelt from spending most of the day beside Alice, and there is a dance in the evening.

headline: Dinner at Schooner Head
summary: Roosevelt drives Alice over to Schooner Head for dinner.

headline: Leaving Maine for Chestnut Hill
summary: The Mount Desert party breaks up. Roosevelt and Alice travel with Shaw, Chapin and the Saltonstalls and reach Chestnut Hill late at night. It is also Edith Carow's 19th birthday.

headline: Glad to be among the Lees
