summary: Rain falls again as the delegates receive women's suffrage petitions and hear William McKinley present the party platform. Sixteen nominating speeches fill the evening, and the hall doesn't empty until 1:45 in the morning.

headline: Blaine wins on the fourth ballot
summary: Voting starts and Blaine gains ground on every roll call. After the third ballot Joseph Foraker moves to recess and Roosevelt leaps up shouting in support, but the motion fails in the uproar. Blaine takes the nomination on the fourth ballot with 541 votes.

headline: Off to the Badlands after defeat
summary: Beaten at the convention, Roosevelt leaves Chicago and heads west for Dakota, and the papers note his retreat to the wilds.

headline: A gloomy letter from St. Paul
summary: Traveling west, Roosevelt writes his sister Bamie from St. Paul that the reformers have been crushed, and he judges Blaine the worst choice of anyone the convention weighed.

headline: Back at the Little Missouri
summary: Roosevelt steps off the train in Medora, where Joe and Sylvane Ferris and Bill Merrifield greet him and talk over the convention at the newspaper office. A St. Paul Pioneer Press interview quotes him saying he will stay with the party ticket.

headline: Riding out to the Maltese Cross
summary: Roosevelt saddles up and rides from town to his Maltese Cross Ranch.

headline: A day at the Maltese Cross
summary: Roosevelt is at his Maltese Cross Ranch; no other activity is recorded.

headline: 1,000 more cattle for $26,000
summary: Roosevelt signs a second deal with Sylvane Ferris and Bill Merrifield, paying $26,000 for a thousand head of cattle. Back East, his refusal to bolt Blaine has made the news, and New York's Union League Club blackballs him for it.

headline: Fitted for a buckskin suit
summary: Staying at Gregor Lang's, Roosevelt bags a jackrabbit and a curlew with his heavy express rifle and is itching to go after antelope. Mrs. Maddox takes his measurements for a buckskin outfit.

headline: Two curlew with the rifle
summary: At the Maltese Cross, Roosevelt drops two curlew with his rifle, one in flight, and is pleased with the shooting. Harper's Weekly declares against Blaine.

headline: Setting out after antelope
summary: Roosevelt prepares to leave the Maltese Cross on a four-day antelope hunt.

headline: A badger run down on horseback
summary: Roosevelt spots a badger far from its burrow, gallops up and kills it with his revolver, then watches a cattle roundup.

headline: Ranching becomes his business
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie the St. Paul interview was made up, delights in the June weather after thirteen hours on horseback, and says ranching will be his real business. He means to bring Bill Sewall and Wilmot Dow out from Maine. To Lodge he admits he has heard no news since the convention.

headline: A fine buck antelope at full gallop
summary: Riding alone on the prairie, Roosevelt races his pony across the path of a small band of antelope, jumps down and drops a big-horned buck. From a cattleman's shack he writes Lodge asking to see him soon and insisting they cannot bolt the party.

headline: Out on the antelope hunt
summary: Roosevelt is away hunting; no details survive for the day.

headline: Still hunting on the prairie
summary: Another day afield for Roosevelt, with nothing further recorded.

headline: His best rifle shot yet
summary: Rounding a knoll, Roosevelt sees two antelope watching from far off. He gets down, aims high and breaks one's neck at a measured 300 yards, the longest shot he has ever made. He spends the night in the trees.

headline: Return to the Maltese Cross
summary: Roosevelt comes back to the Maltese Cross Ranch from his hunting trip.

headline: Playing frontier hunter in earnest
summary: After shooting two plover for the cook pot, Roosevelt tells Bamie he has spent a week alone on the plains, sleeping out under the sky, and has two antelope and a deer to show for it.

headline: Visitors crowd out the writing
summary: The Maltese Cross sits right on the main trail, so cowboys drop by every day to visit, and Roosevelt manages little writing.

headline: Finding the Elkhorn site
summary: After a mallard for the pot, Roosevelt scouts the river north of Medora for a new ranch site. He buys a squatter's claim for $400, and a pair of locked elk antlers found on the ground gives the place its name: the Elkhorn.

headline: Turned away by Montana vigilantes
summary: Roosevelt travels by rail with the Marquis de Mores and a man named Jameson, to Mills City in Montana, hoping to join a vigilance group formed to stamp out horse stealing. The vigilantes turn all three down because they come from prominent families.

headline: A pintail grouse for supper
summary: Back at the Maltese Cross, Roosevelt shoots a sharp-tailed grouse cock with his rifle for the table.

headline: At the Maltese Cross
summary: Roosevelt is at his ranch; the day has no further record.

headline: Quiet Sunday at the ranch
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday at the Maltese Cross; nothing else is noted.

headline: Heading back East
summary: Roosevelt boards an eastbound train at Medora for New York.

headline: On the rails eastward
summary: Roosevelt is on the train, making his way from Dakota toward New York.

headline: Another day on the train
summary: Roosevelt's eastbound journey to New York continues.

headline: Home to Bamie's house
summary: Roosevelt reaches New York and settles in with his sister Bamie at her home on Madison Avenue.

headline: A Dakota paper on his reform work
summary: Roosevelt is in New York as the Mandan Pioneer, back in Dakota, runs a piece on him and the reform fight in New York City politics.

headline: Reformers shun Blaine
summary: Roosevelt meets with Republican leaders in New York and finds that every prominent reformer wants no part of Blaine.

headline: In New York
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; the record notes nothing more.

headline: Still in New York
summary: Another unrecorded day for Roosevelt in New York City.

headline: Inviting Sewall and Dow west
summary: Roosevelt writes his old Maine guides Bill Sewall and Wilmot Dow, asking them to join his Dakota ranching venture, and encloses a $3,000 check to clear a mortgage.

headline: A New York day
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; no events are noted.

headline: Unrecorded day in the city
summary: Roosevelt remains in New York City with nothing further on record.

headline: Democrats pick Cleveland and Hendricks
summary: The Democrats name New York's governor, Grover Cleveland, as their presidential candidate, with Thomas A. Hendricks as his running mate. Roosevelt loathes Hendricks as a Copperhead, a Northerner who sided with the South during the Civil War.

headline: Visiting Conie in Orange
summary: Roosevelt goes to Orange, New Jersey, to see his younger sister Corinne.

headline: Sunday in Orange
summary: Roosevelt stays on in Orange, New Jersey.

headline: Baby Lee meets her grandparents
summary: Roosevelt takes his baby daughter Alice to Chestnut Hill to visit her mother's parents. Old college friends in Boston give him the cold shoulder, since many reform Republicans, the Mugwumps, have broken away to back Cleveland, along with a long list of major newspapers.

headline: At Chestnut Hill
summary: Roosevelt is staying at Chestnut Hill; nothing more is recorded.

headline: Chestnut Hill visit continues
summary: Another quiet day for Roosevelt at Chestnut Hill.

headline: Still with the Lees
summary: Roosevelt remains at Chestnut Hill with no other details noted.

headline: A porch talk with Lodge at Nahant
summary: Roosevelt visits Henry Cabot Lodge's summer place at Nahant, and the two talk late on the porch. Lodge, who took the brunt of the Blaine backlash alone while Roosevelt was out West, is feeling low.

headline: Declaring for the Republican ticket
summary: From Chestnut Hill, Roosevelt writes the Boston Herald to say publicly that he will vote for the Republican presidential ticket.

headline: Running amuck among the Mugwumps
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge's wife, Nannie, joking that he has been tangling with Boston's Mugwumps.

headline: Bad press and a Cleveland scandal
summary: Newspapers criticize Roosevelt and Lodge for sticking with Blaine, and the story of Grover Cleveland's child born out of wedlock breaks.

headline: Back in New York
summary: Roosevelt is back in New York City; no details survive.

headline: A New York day
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City with nothing else on record.

headline: Talking ranch life with the Tribune
summary: At Bamie's Madison Avenue home, Roosevelt gives an interview to a New York Tribune reporter and speaks warmly of the West and cattle ranching.

headline: In the city
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; no events are noted.

headline: Unrecorded Saturday
summary: Roosevelt spends a quiet, unrecorded day in New York City.

headline: Sunday in New York
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing more is known.

headline: Westward with Sewall and Dow
summary: Roosevelt meets Bill Sewall and Wilmot Dow in New York and the three set off for Medora. He tells Lodge that friends seem startled he has not sprouted hooves and horns.

headline: An Englishman joins the party
summary: On the way to Dakota, Roosevelt, Sewall and Dow pick up a traveling companion at Harrisburg, an Englishman named Messiter, whom Roosevelt judges no great thinker but a gentleman.

headline: Rolling toward Dakota
summary: Roosevelt and his party are still on the train heading west.

headline: Interview in St. Paul
summary: Passing through St. Paul on the trip west, Roosevelt sits for a newspaper interview.

headline: Two ranches, 4,500 cattle
summary: Roosevelt's cattle operation now runs on two spreads: the Maltese Cross, seven miles south of Medora and run by Merrifield and Sylvane Ferris, and the new Elkhorn, thirty miles north, placed under Sewall and Dow. Together they carry about 4,500 head.

headline: Sewall sizes up the Badlands
summary: Roosevelt pulls into Medora with his Maine men. Bill Sewall takes one look around and is unimpressed by the place as cattle country.

headline: Sending cattle north to Elkhorn
summary: Roosevelt dispatches Sewall and Dow downriver to the Elkhorn with a hundred head. While he was away, Merrifield and Sylvane Ferris had driven in a thousand cattle from Iowa.

headline: Out to Gregor Lang's
summary: Roosevelt rides to Gregor Lang's ranch, with the Englishman Messiter along. Lang's wife has just come over from Ireland to join him.

headline: Staying with the Langs
summary: Roosevelt remains a guest at Gregor Lang's ranch.

headline: Edith Carow turns 23
summary: Roosevelt is at the Maltese Cross on the 23rd birthday of Edith Carow, his childhood friend and future wife.

headline: Checking on the Elkhorn
summary: Roosevelt rides north from the Maltese Cross to look in on Sewall and Dow and their progress at the Elkhorn.

headline: Congressman Roosevelt of Dakota?
summary: While Roosevelt is at the Elkhorn, the Mandan Pioneer muses that he could win a seat in Congress the moment Dakota becomes a state.

headline: Grouse hunting at Elkhorn
summary: Roosevelt spends the day after grouse near the Elkhorn.

headline: A tribute to Alice Lee
summary: At the Maltese Cross, Roosevelt completes his written memorial to his late wife Alice and mails it East to the Putnam firm to be printed.

headline: Fond of the grim Badlands
summary: At the Maltese Cross, Roosevelt writes of his growing affection for the stark Badlands landscape.

headline: Sombrero and a house under way
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge that he would laugh to see him in his wide sombrero. To Bamie he recounts traveling out with his Maine friends and asks her to keep the builders moving on Leeholm, the new house she is overseeing at Oyster Bay.

headline: Facing down a gunman in Mingusville
summary: This is the likeliest date for Roosevelt's run-in at Nolan's Hotel in Mingusville. A drunk waving two pistols mocks him as a bespectacled dude; Roosevelt knocks him down, the shots go wild, and the man hits his head on the bar. The tale races across the Badlands.

headline: Backing a Tribune letter
summary: Roosevelt writes W. L. Hubbell confirming the facts in a Tribune letter concerning the state legislature.

headline: On the Little Missouri
summary: Roosevelt is on the Little Missouri; no details are recorded.

headline: Outfitting for the Bighorns
summary: Roosevelt plans a two-month overland hunt to Wyoming's Bighorn Mountains with Bill Merrifield as hunting partner and a seasoned plainsman named Lebo as teamster and cook. His diary lists ponies, clothes, food and an arsenal of guns. That day he covers 72 miles in the saddle.

headline: A thousand-mile hunt ahead
summary: From Chimney Butte, Roosevelt tells Bamie about the coming hunting expedition and how much he has come to love the place.

headline: Hailstorm on the first day out
summary: The Bighorn trip gets a slow start. Roosevelt and Merrifield leave the wagon and ride to Lang's for the night, ducking into a washout when a hailstorm hits so hard the ponies won't face it. Their slickers keep them dry, and his new Winchester performs well.

headline: Rain all day, roast duck at night
summary: In a steady downpour Roosevelt leaves Lang's, shoots ducks and grouse in the sloughs and skips lunch, then catches up with the wagon at Lake Station on the old Keogh Trail. They burn the old station's logs for a fire, eat fried duck and sleep in the wagon.

headline: A whitetail buck in velvet
summary: Under gray skies the wagon struggles through soaked ground. Roosevelt drops a whitetail buck at a hundred yards and two sage grouse, all with his Winchester. They make only twelve miles and camp early at a muddy pool to dry out, crossing from prairie into rough Badlands.

headline: Cowboys singing to the herd
summary: After a frosty night, a big herd of beef steers that had bedded nearby passes the camp; all night Roosevelt heard the riders singing around it. The party's greyhound dies, and they make 25 miles past countless buffalo skulls. He sketches his companions Lebo and Merrifield in his diary.

headline: Storm-soaked on the Keogh Trail
summary: A fierce night storm drenches the tentless party. Following a cattle trail southwest about twenty miles, Roosevelt misses two good shots at blacktail bucks. They camp beside a lovely natural park dotted with pine-topped sandstone pillars.

headline: Cattle where buffalo once roamed
summary: The party crosses the Little Beaver onto wide brown-grass plains, where Roosevelt notes that cattle herds have replaced the buffalo. He misses a doe, shoots two young sage grouse through the head for the evening meal, and they camp in the Powder River Badlands to the howl of coyotes.

headline: Letters written on a water keg
summary: The party follows a creek down to the Powder River and pushes on through sagebrush bottoms to a dry camp. Using an upturned keg as a desk, Roosevelt writes Bamie and Lodge and hands the letters to a passing cowboy. To Lodge he mixes trail news with talk of Cornwallis and the Puritans.

headline: A pony tumbles down a cliff
summary: Moving up the Powder to where the Little Powder joins it, Roosevelt shoots grouse, doves and teal for the pot. Merrifield misses a cougar, the pair nearly bog down in a swamp, and Merrifield's pony somersaults twice down a thirty-foot sandy bank.

headline: Night with the N Bar outfit
summary: A short day's travel. Roosevelt shoots eight prairie chickens and buys a fine young horse from a cowboy for $100. They stop at the N Bar Ranch, where thirty men and some three hundred horses are gearing up for the beef roundup, and he admires the cowboys' style.

headline: A yearling buck in the swamp
summary: The Powder valley narrows between bold, pine-dotted bluffs. Roosevelt fills the bag with sage hens and prairie chickens, and at dusk, kneeling in a marsh, he shoots a young whitetail buck through the heart at fifty yards.

headline: Nine crossings of the Powder
summary: Heading up the Powder, the party fords the river nine times, the wagon nearly sinking in quicksand once, and camps just short of Clear Creek.

headline: Two bucks with one bullet
summary: Climbing Clear Creek over barren sagebrush country, the wagon sticks three times and the team nearly gives out. In the afternoon Roosevelt breaks the backs of two blacktail bucks with a single shot at 431 paces and keeps the bullet.

headline: Into Wyoming
summary: The party makes about twenty miles up Clear Creek and crosses from Montana into Wyoming, passing many cattle and a Cheyenne camp. Roosevelt notes that he has been bathing in the river daily.

headline: Bighorns in sight, marksmanship match
summary: Camped a few miles from Buffalo with the snowy Bighorns in view, Roosevelt nearly halves a jackrabbit at 75 yards. Near a Cheyenne village, Merrifield proposes a shooting match, and the two hunters easily beat the Cheyenne marksmen.

headline: Rolling into Buffalo, Wyoming
summary: The hunting party reaches Buffalo, which Roosevelt sizes up as a genuine frontier settlement.

headline: Trading the wagon for pack ponies
summary: At a Crazy Woman Creek sawmill the party leaves its wagon behind and sets up a pack string of seven horses, with the wagon cover doubling as a tent, for the climb into the mountains.

headline: Up onto the Bighorn plateau
summary: Balky ponies and a faint trail delay the start until ten. The party grinds up the steep climb to the Bighorn plateau, camps on Willow Creek, and Roosevelt shoots two blue grouse out of a tree for supper. Ice forms overnight.

headline: First elk in the high country
summary: The party works up to about 8,000 feet into green park country of glades, lakes and clear streams and camps by a rushing creek. Hunting on foot, Roosevelt trails a band of elk and kills a cow and a calf; Merrifield takes two more.

headline: Chasing a bugling bull
summary: With the ponies worn out, they stay put to dry meat and stretch hides. A bull elk calling near camp the night before lures Roosevelt out alone all day, but he never sees it, coming home with only a rabbit and a grouse.

headline: Snowbound beside the fire
summary: Snow covers the camp by morning and rain and sleet fall all day, so the men stay in the tent before a roaring log fire. In the afternoon Roosevelt takes a brisk three-hour ride on his horse California through the mist.

headline: Helter-skelter after three bulls
summary: Roosevelt and Merrifield ride out at dawn on Blackie and Splitear and hunt until dusk over rough burned timber. They find three bull elk and wound all of them, give chase on foot, and bring down two; Roosevelt also kills a blacktail doe. He is fascinated by the bulls' bugling in the rut.

headline: Merrifield trees a black bear
summary: Out alone, Roosevelt lets a doe and two fawns pass since camp has plenty of meat, then shoots a dozen blue grouse for variety. Meanwhile Merrifield chases a black bear up a tree and kills it, to Roosevelt's regret at missing it.

headline: Snow, moonlight and bear meat
summary: The party moves camp about six miles to a fork of the Ten Sleep. Snow falls off and on, and Roosevelt finds the scene lovely by moonlight. He reports the bear meat tasty and his health never better.

headline: Woods that recall Maine
summary: A long, fruitless still-hunt with Merrifield turns up only a few deer tracks amid snow and frozen ponds. The silent pine and spruce forest reminds Roosevelt of the woods of Maine and the Adirondacks.

headline: Fifty trout and a weary hike
summary: Roosevelt and Merrifield ride and hike most of the day to reach a mountain lake, catch about fifty trout, and return exhausted to a trout feast in camp.

headline: A great bull elk at 75 yards
summary: Finding no game, they move camp six miles toward the foothills. Hunting on foot that afternoon, Roosevelt kills a big bull elk with a superb rack facing him at 75 yards, and picks off two grouse for supper.

headline: His first grizzly
summary: Roosevelt shoots a spike blacktail in the morning, wearing moccasins for silence. That afternoon he and Merrifield trail a grizzly through thick forest to its bed, and Roosevelt kills it with one shot to the brain from 25 feet. He is very proud of his first bear.

headline: A sow grizzly and her cub
summary: After skinning yesterday's grizzly, Roosevelt rides to a scenic canyon and needs six shots to kill a blacktail buck. While skinning it at dusk, he and Merrifield spot a mother grizzly and a big cub, chase them a mile on foot, and kill both.

headline: A grizzly for Merrifield
summary: The men haul the bears into camp. That afternoon they find a big grizzly feeding on the bull elk carcass, and Roosevelt has Merrifield take the shot, since he has yet to kill one on his own. Four blue grouse make supper.

headline: An elk on the run
summary: All three men beat the woods for bear all day with no luck. When Lebo misses a bull elk, it crosses Roosevelt's path; he wounds it, sprints after it in his moccasins, and drops it with a second shot.

headline: Leaving the mountains
summary: The party breaks camp and starts down, three pack ponies loaded with hides and antlers, and camps again on the creek they used coming up.

headline: Back to the wagon
summary: The party reaches the Crazy Woman Creek sawmill where the wagon waited. Roosevelt's horse California is worn out after falling into a creek.

headline: Dinner at Fort McKinney
summary: With the wagon back in service, the party rolls to Fort McKinney, where Roosevelt dines at the post. He jots down a Dr. Tyrell's account of two 8th Cavalry soldiers killed by a grizzly in New Mexico in 1872.

headline: Starting the 300-mile trip home
summary: The party makes a decent day's travel, camping above Piney Fork, and Roosevelt bags a jackrabbit and two ducks. He writes Bamie about his bears and elk as they head home.

headline: Camp under the balm tree
summary: A long day on the trail brings the party back to its August 30 lunch spot beneath a big balm tree, where they camp.

headline: Saving the bear skins
summary: The party follows Clear Creek to within six miles of the Powder, then stops under two big cottonwoods so the spoiling bear hides can be scraped and dried. The horses are in poor shape.

headline: Waiting on the hides
summary: The bear skins are still drying, so the party stays put. Roosevelt hunts the north side of the creek and sees nothing.

headline: Teal and chickens by the river
summary: With the hides still damp, Roosevelt hunts south of the creek without luck, then takes the shotgun along the river and bags two teal and five sharptail grouse.

headline: An off day with the rifle
summary: After a long day's travel the party camps where the Powder curves. Short of fresh meat, Roosevelt goes hunting but misses three whitetail shots, and Merrifield misses two.

headline: Wet night, whitetail doe
summary: Rain soaks the men overnight despite the wagon cover. They travel well and camp a few miles upriver from the N Bar Ranch, and Merrifield brings down a whitetail doe.

headline: Camp by the S H ranch
summary: The party pastures its horses near the S H ranch, and it rains again overnight. Back East, Roosevelt's sister Corinne turns 23.

headline: A dozen ducks near Powderville
summary: Traveling down the Powder, the party camps near Powderville. Roosevelt shoots two blue-winged teal with the rifle and ten more ducks with a right-and-left from the shotgun.

headline: Cold rain and muddy water
summary: Cold rain falls through the night and all the next day. The party travels until dark and camps near White Clay Buttes with poor grass and muddy water, the team nearly spent.

headline: Pitch-pine fire at the Medicine Buttes
summary: After a hard frost, Roosevelt shoots seven sharptail grouse. On a cold, windy day one team horse gives out and Splitear goes into harness. They camp after dark among the Medicine Buttes beside a blazing pitch-pine fire under a sandstone cliff.

headline: Pinned in camp by a gale
summary: On the trail back from his Wyoming hunt, Roosevelt and his party sit out a day of howling wind and rain squalls rather than risk the open prairie.

headline: Strayed horses and a mare in the mud
summary: Wet bedding, wandering horses and a team mare stuck in a mud hole cost Roosevelt's party the day; it takes two hours to haul her out, and she is too weak to travel.

headline: Out of meat, he shoots supper
summary: After two days without meat, Roosevelt takes his shotgun out from camp on the big sand and brings back three teal and two sharp-tailed grouse.

headline: A fifty-mile moonlight ride
summary: Roosevelt drives to Muddy Creek, shooting a jackrabbit and two grouse along the way. Then he and Bill Merrifield ride all night under the moon, 9 p.m. to 6 a.m., covering fifty miles to the Chimney Butte ranch. He later recalled the hoofbeats and coyote cries of that ride in print.

headline: Home from Wyoming with a big bag
summary: Back at Chimney Butte from the Bighorn country, Roosevelt tallies a season's take of more than a hundred birds and small animals, plus three grizzly bears, six elk and seven deer.

headline: Facing down the Marquis's gunman
summary: At Elkhorn, Sewall and Dow tell Roosevelt of threats against him and his men, of lynchings while he was away, and of the Marquis de Morès's hired gunmen stopping in for a meal. As the story was later told, Roosevelt rode to E. C. Paddock's cabin, told him that if there was to be killing it could start now, and warned him off his men and his claim.

headline: Leaving Medora for the East
summary: Roosevelt departs Medora for New York City.

headline: On the rails east
summary: Roosevelt is on the way to New York City.

headline: Arrives at Bamie's
summary: Roosevelt reaches New York City and goes to his sister Bamie's house on Madison Avenue.

headline: Friday in New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Backing Blaine; a niece named Eleanor
summary: At 422 Madison Avenue, Roosevelt tells reporters he will support Blaine in November and voices anger that Governor Cleveland never removed Sheriff Davidson. His brother Elliott and Elliott's wife, Anna, welcome a daughter, Anna Eleanor.

headline: Catching up on mail
summary: Roosevelt works through a pile of letters in New York City.

headline: Says no to Congress
summary: Roosevelt is offered the Republican nomination for Congress in New York's First District, which includes Oyster Bay, and turns it down.

headline: Tuesday in New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; no events are noted.

headline: Wednesday in New York
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City with nothing logged.

headline: Thursday in New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing further appears.

headline: Friday in the city
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; no events are recorded.

headline: Stumping for Blaine in Brooklyn
summary: Speaking to Brooklyn's Young Republicans, Roosevelt campaigns for Blaine and lands a stinging line on the Democratic running mate, Thomas A. Hendricks.

headline: Sunday in New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing is noted.

headline: Campaigning for Lodge in Malden
summary: In Malden, Massachusetts, Roosevelt rallies Republicans for Henry Cabot Lodge's congressional race, arguing Blaine won the nomination honestly and the party will keep him in check. He also writes William Clapp of Boston denying a remark newspapers pinned on him after Chicago.

headline: Melrose speech for Lodge
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Melrose, Massachusetts, on Lodge's behalf.

headline: A warm crowd at Chickering Hall
summary: Roosevelt gives a strong speech at Chickering Hall in New York City, and the partisan audience receives it well.

headline: Thursday in New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; no events are listed.

headline: Newark speech; a letter to the Globe
summary: Roosevelt speaks at the Grand Opera House in Newark, New Jersey, and writes the Boston Globe's editor to deny that on June 6 he vowed not to support Blaine.

headline: Saturday in New York
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing more is noted.

headline: Sunday in New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City with no recorded events.

headline: A literary birthday dinner in Boston
summary: Roosevelt turns 26 in Boston and dines at Henry Cabot Lodge's home with three celebrated writers: the novelist William Dean Howells, the poet Thomas Bailey Aldrich, and Dr. Oliver Wendell Holmes.

headline: Winchester speech for Lodge
summary: Roosevelt campaigns for Lodge in Winchester, Massachusetts.

headline: Blaine's campaign stumbles
summary: While Roosevelt is in Boston, Blaine's campaign blunders in New York: a minister brands the Democrats the party of "rum, Romanism and Rebellion," Blaine fails to disown the insult to Catholics, and a showy dinner with wealthy backers at Delmonico's after a big parade sours voters further.

headline: Praise for a Grace supporter
summary: From Boston, Roosevelt writes Francis Scott to commend him for supporting William R. Grace in the New York mayoral race.

headline: Rebutting a duplicity charge
summary: Roosevelt answers Richard R. Bowker of Publishers Weekly, who had accused him in the Brooklyn Eagle of double-dealing over Blaine, and tells Charles H. Knox he is backing Grace for mayor.

headline: Elmira speech for Van Duzer
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Elmira, New York, for Jonas Van Duzer.

headline: Sunday in New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; no events listed.

headline: Monday in New York
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing noted on the eve of the election.

headline: Cleveland beats Blaine
summary: Roosevelt casts his vote in New York City as Democrat Grover Cleveland narrowly defeats Republican James G. Blaine for President. The race is so tight that Blaine waits two weeks to concede.

headline: Help for Hubbell's Speakership bid
summary: Roosevelt promises Walter Hubbell his help in the race for Speaker of the State Assembly.

headline: Thursday in New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing is recorded.

headline: Consoling a defeated Lodge
summary: Writing Lodge, who has lost his race for Congress, Roosevelt reports that New York is in turmoil after the election.

headline: Saturday in New York
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; no events noted.

headline: Sunday in New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City with nothing logged.

headline: Monday in the city
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; the day has no entries.

headline: Cheering Lodge; a talk at the Nineteenth Century Club
summary: Roosevelt writes again to Lodge, beaten by fewer than 300 votes, trying to lift his spirits and inviting him and his wife Nannie for a visit in midwinter. He also gives a talk at the Nineteenth Century Club about what the campaign revealed of Republican principles; he had seen Blaine as the lesser evil.

headline: Wednesday in New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing more is recorded.

headline: Heading back to Dakota
summary: Roosevelt sets out for Dakota Territory.

headline: Westbound
summary: Roosevelt is still on the way to Dakota.

headline: Still on the train
summary: A third day of travel toward Dakota.

headline: Back on the Little Missouri
summary: Roosevelt reaches the Little Missouri and heads out to his Chimney Butte ranch.

headline: A cold night alone on the way to Elkhorn
summary: Roosevelt helps Sylvane Ferris and Merrifield move a small beef herd, then sets out mid-afternoon from Medora for Elkhorn as the Badlands turn wintry. Darkness and cold stop him; he shelters in an empty shack with nothing but tea for supper.

headline: Felling logs for the Elkhorn house
summary: Roosevelt shoots grouse from the trees for breakfast and joins Sewall and Dow, who are cutting logs for the Elkhorn ranch house. In ten-below cold, Sewall drops 53 trees, Dow 49, and Roosevelt 17. Final returns show that a shift of just 575 votes in the city would have made Blaine President.

headline: Siting the Elkhorn ranch house
summary: Roosevelt picks the spot for the Elkhorn ranch house and pitches in on construction.

headline: Riding the range with Captain Robbins
summary: Roosevelt rides his range with Captain Robbins and shoots seven grouse. Back East, his childhood friend Edith Carow has dinner with a Mr. Stratton at his Aunt Annie Gracie's. Roosevelt is weighed down by his political setbacks and family losses.

headline: Through snow at twenty below

summary: Roosevelt joins the crowd at the Republican State Committee meeting in New York City and tells a Tribune reporter he is ready for orders. By chance he meets Edith Carow at Bamie's, begins calling at her 36th Street home, and asks her to Leeholm's Hunt Ball. The house is now renamed Sagamore Hill for the Sagamore Mohannis, who signed the land away two centuries before.

headline: Riding to hounds at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt joins the Oyster Bay hunt and comes away delighted with his old horse, which carried him up close enough to finish second at the kill.

summary: The hunt gathers at Sagamore Hill, and Roosevelt, mounted on Frank, takes a hard fall that badly breaks his left arm. Bloodied, the arm dangling, he rides on to the finish, then chases little Alice around the house and hosts the Hunt Ball that night. Edith Carow is at the ball.

summary: In Medora Roosevelt meets Joe Ferris's new bride, then drives down the valley to his Elkhorn Ranch.

summary: At Elkhorn, Roosevelt shoots four sharp-tailed grouse for supper and finds the ranch in better shape than he feared. An ice jam has formed on the Little Missouri right in front of the house, as he tells Bamie in a letter.

headline: A muddy hike to Tomkins Ranch
summary: Roosevelt walks across the hay plateau to the Tomkins ranch through deep mud.

summary: Roosevelt hikes out to collect four deer carcasses that Sewall and Dow had hung in a tree, only to find that cougars have eaten them.

summary: Roosevelt's diary notes four prairie chickens shot at Elkhorn.

headline: The boat is stolen
summary: Roosevelt discovers that thieves have made off with the ranch boat. Sewall and Dow set to work building a new one so the three can chase them down the river.

headline: Boat building on a swollen river
summary: Work on the new boat goes on while Roosevelt hunts deer without luck. The river runs high, with ice heaped several feet up its banks.

summary: The diary for the day is two words: boat building.

headline: Boat done, Benton begun
summary: The new boat is finished, but it is too cold to set out. Roosevelt shoots four chickens, completes the first chapter of his Benton book, and tells Lodge that writing comes very hard for him.

headline: Bitter cold and steady work
summary: In bitter cold, Roosevelt writes to Bamie that life at the ranch has fallen back into its usual routine. He is reading and pressing on with his Benton biography.

headline: Blizzard at Elkhorn; news of the Carows
summary: A furious blizzard sweeps the ranch. Back east, Roosevelt's sister Corinne writes Bamie that the Carow family has sold its house and will go abroad in late April for perhaps a year and a half.

headline: Downriver after the thieves
summary: With milder weather, Roosevelt, Sewall and Dow push off in the new boat to hunt down the men who stole theirs. They camp below Eaton's and shoot three prairie chickens.

headline: Below zero on the chase
summary: Temperatures drop below zero as the pursuit of the boat thieves goes on. Roosevelt bags four prairie chickens.

headline: Capturing the boat thieves
summary: Far downriver, north of Elkhorn, Roosevelt, Sewall and Dow find their stolen boat and catch the three thieves completely off guard. Rifles leveled, Roosevelt orders hands up, and the men surrender without a shot. Earlier he brings down a whitetail doe at 75 yards.

headline: Guarding prisoners on an icy river
summary: With the captives aboard both boats, Roosevelt, Sewall and Dow start the slow trip back toward Medora until an ice jam stops them. The prisoners cannot be tied up for fear of frostbite, and supplies dwindle until only flour is left. To pass the long watches, Roosevelt reads Anna Karenina cover to cover.

headline: Stuck in the ice
summary: The boats are held fast by river ice, Roosevelt's diary reports.

headline: Still frozen in
summary: For a second day, ice keeps Roosevelt's party and its prisoners from moving.

headline: Two miles, then ice again
summary: The boats inch a couple of miles downstream before ice stops them once more.

headline: To the tail of the jam
summary: Another couple of miles brings the party to the lower end of the ice jam.

headline: Reaching the C Ranch
summary: The boats make it to the C Ranch, and Roosevelt shoots two prairie chickens.

headline: Hiring a wagon at Killdeer
summary: On a borrowed horse, Roosevelt rides to the Killdeer Mountains and hires a wagon and driver, and lays in supplies for the overland leg.

headline: Forty-five miles on foot behind the wagon
summary: While Sewall and Dow carry on downriver with the boats, Roosevelt marches the prisoners overland to the Killdeer Mountains. The captives ride in the wagon; he trudges behind through sticky gumbo mud, Winchester in hand, and goes without sleep.

headline: On to Captain Brown's ranch
summary: Roosevelt drives his captives by wagon to Captain Brown's ranch.

headline: Handing the thieves to the sheriff
summary: Roosevelt delivers the three prisoners to the sheriff in Dickinson, about 40 miles east of Medora, ending the chase. While in town he has Dr. Victor Hugo Stickney treat his blistered feet.

headline: Back to Medora, letters home
summary: Roosevelt returns from Dickinson to Medora and writes his sisters. To Bamie he tells the boat-thief story and shares his verdict on Anna Karenina; to Corinne he asks, pretending not to know, when Edith leaves for Europe. Local elections also fill county offices.

headline: Chairing the stockmen
summary: Roosevelt chairs the Little Missouri Stockmen's Association at its spring session in Medora, keeping strict parliamentary order. The members pick him to represent them at the Montana stockmen's gathering in Miles City.

headline: Riding to Elkhorn with Merrifield
summary: Roosevelt and Bill Merrifield ride down the valley to Elkhorn Ranch.

headline: Flowers for Edith's sailing
summary: On a rainy day at Elkhorn, Roosevelt writes Corinne about political campaigns and arranges for a card to go with flowers for Edith when she sails.

headline: Telling Lodge about the chase
summary: Roosevelt rides up to Medora and sends Henry Cabot Lodge an account of how he ran down the boat thieves.

headline: Out to Chimney Butte
summary: Roosevelt rides out to his Chimney Butte ranch.

headline: Off to Miles City
summary: Roosevelt and Sylvane Ferris travel to Miles City to represent the local ranchers at the Montana Stock Growers meeting, taking rooms at the MacQueen House.

headline: Parade of cowmen in Miles City
summary: The stock growers' meeting opens in Miles City with a morning parade from the MacQueen House: the 5th Infantry band, mounted cowboys and some 150 cattlemen marching four abreast.

headline: Named to the executive committee

headline: Executive committee meets
summary: Roosevelt attends a session of the stock growers' executive committee in Miles City.

headline: Edith sails for Europe
