summary: Roosevelt tells Corinne his life keeps getting more sedentary and that he is selling his polo ponies. He tells Lodge that Washington Post editor Frank Hatton, a foe of reform, has accused him in print of winning his job through machine politicians. Two visitors, W. H. Russell and a Charles A. Ul, sign the Sagamore Hill guest book.

headline: Monday in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is at work in Washington; nothing more is recorded.

headline: More to Swift
summary: Roosevelt writes Swift on civil service business.

headline: Answering Hatton; a job for Shidy
summary: Roosevelt publicly rebuts what he calls falsehoods in Hatton's editorial and writes Brander Matthews on civil service. Through Roosevelt, Hamilton Shidy lands a post at the Census Bureau. Washington is hot and drowsy, with most officials away.

headline: Hatton strikes again; Harrison won't budge
summary: A second Hatton editorial insults Roosevelt. A chance encounter with President Harrison goes badly: the President declines to act against Paul. Roosevelt files a report on the western trip with the Commission and writes Lodge.

headline: Blaming a Cabinet officer
summary: Roosevelt charges that an unnamed Cabinet member has been dragging his feet on the Paul case.

headline: Hatton's 'silver plated' jab
summary: Frank Hatton attacks Roosevelt yet again, mocking him as a reformer with only a thin coat of virtue.

headline: Sunday in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.

headline: Paul resigns, but isn't fired
summary: Summoned to the White House, Roosevelt learns that Harrison has let Paul resign rather than removing him. Roosevelt takes it as a defeat.

headline: Edith turns 28
summary: Edith marks her twenty-eighth birthday; Roosevelt is in Washington.

headline: Westward for a Rockies holiday
summary: Roosevelt sets off for a vacation in the Rocky Mountains and writes William Clapp about civil service reform.

headline: Politics from St. Paul
summary: Passing through St. Paul, Roosevelt writes Lodge about politics.

headline: In St. Paul
summary: Roosevelt is in St. Paul on his way west.

headline: Elkhorn plans, and a grizzly
summary: At Elkhorn Ranch, Roosevelt writes Bamie that next year he means to bring the whole family out to Elkhorn. On this trip he survives a fierce fight with a grizzly, which becomes his most prized hunting trophy.

headline: Edith begs him to be careful
summary: Edith writes Roosevelt that she is trying not to worry while he is in the wilds, but finds it hard.

headline: Vincent Rowe visits
summary: Vincent Rowe signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.

headline: Homeward from Helena, feeling fine
summary: From Helena, Montana, Roosevelt tells Lodge his month off is over, he is headed home, and he feels terrific.

headline: Missing him; Elliott hurt; a big bag
summary: Edith, expecting a baby, writes that she misses Roosevelt terribly and counts the weeks. Elliott breaks an ankle that is misdiagnosed, then rebroken and reset. Roosevelt reports a haul of two moose, a mountain bison, two bears and a cougar, one bear charging him.

headline: Healthy and homesick
summary: Roosevelt writes Edith that he has never felt fitter, misses her badly, hopes to be home before the 20th, and wants her with him at Yellowstone next year.

headline: Ted turns two
summary: Roosevelt's son Ted celebrates his second birthday.

headline: Back to Washington
summary: Roosevelt returns to Washington.

headline: A reviewer cries collaborator
summary: A New York Sun review of The Winning of the West claims Roosevelt had help writing it. Suspecting James R. Gilmore wrote the review, Roosevelt fires back a long, cutting reply to him and the paper.

headline: Good luck to Merrifield
summary: Roosevelt wishes Bill Merrifield success in his race for the North Dakota legislature, and writes Charles A. Dana and the editor of the New York Sun.

headline: Thursday at the Commission
summary: Roosevelt is at work in Washington; nothing more is recorded.

headline: Cheering Lodge's platform
summary: Roosevelt congratulates Lodge on the planks adopted at the Massachusetts Republican convention. Corinne turns 28.

headline: A nephew is born
summary: Elliott and Anna Roosevelt welcome a son, Elliott Roosevelt Jr.

headline: No entry
summary: Nothing is recorded beyond a stray word carried over from the day before.

headline: Plagiarism charge answered
summary: Gilmore replies by accusing Roosevelt of plagiarism, and Roosevelt's second rebuttal cuts him down even further.

headline: Monday in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is at work in Washington; nothing more is recorded.

headline: Knights Templar in town
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge about the Knights Templar reunion filling Washington.

headline: Wednesday at the Commission
summary: Roosevelt is at work in Washington; nothing more is recorded.

headline: Kermit arrives early
summary: Roosevelt fires a last shot at Gilmore, saying he takes no joy in beating down a weakling. Then a telegram from Sagamore Hill brings news that his son Kermit has been born prematurely, with Bamie helping at the birth.

headline: A midnight dash home
summary: Arriving at Long Island City after the last train has gone, Roosevelt hires an engine of his own and pulls in at home around 4 a.m. It is also niece Eleanor's fifth birthday.

headline: With the new baby
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with Edith and the new baby; nothing more is recorded.

headline: Money worries, and thanks to Bamie
summary: Roosevelt confides to Bamie his worries about money and job security, and passes on Edith's heartfelt thanks for Bamie's help at the birth.

headline: Quiet days with Kermit
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with Edith and the new baby; nothing more is recorded.

headline: At home with the family
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with Edith and the new baby; nothing more is recorded.

headline: Mid-October at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with Edith and the new baby; nothing more is recorded.

headline: Take on the Mugwumps
summary: Roosevelt urges Lodge to make a speech going after the Mugwumps.

headline: Drafting the annual report
summary: At Sagamore Hill Roosevelt writes the Commission's annual report to President Harrison.

headline: Sizing up politicians
summary: Roosevelt gives Lodge his frank views of the strengths and flaws of various politicians.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with Edith and the new baby; nothing more is recorded.

headline: Autumn at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with Edith and the new baby; nothing more is recorded.

headline: Another home day
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with Edith and the new baby; nothing more is recorded.

headline: Midweek at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with Edith and the new baby; nothing more is recorded.

headline: Family time on Long Island
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with Edith and the new baby; nothing more is recorded.

headline: Late October at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with Edith and the new baby; nothing more is recorded.

headline: Saturday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with Edith and the new baby; nothing more is recorded.

headline: Roosevelt turns 31
summary: Roosevelt marks his thirty-first birthday at Sagamore Hill and writes Carl Ernst on civil service matters.

headline: Monday at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with Edith and the new baby; nothing more is recorded.

headline: Dinner with the Crugers
summary: Roosevelt dines with the Cruger family and Frank Hiscock.

headline: Dinner with Warner Miller
summary: Roosevelt dines with former Senator Warner Miller and writes Lodge.

headline: Back to Washington
summary: Roosevelt returns to Washington, to quarters off Connecticut Avenue.

headline: Kermit is christened
summary: Baby Kermit is baptized at home, in Edith's sitting room at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Election Day
summary: It is Election Day.

headline: Report draft done
summary: Roosevelt tells Swift he has finished a rough draft of the Commission's annual report.

headline: Frontier warfare with Poole
summary: Roosevelt sends historian William Poole a long letter on military affairs on the western frontier in the 1700s.

headline: Report goes to the President
summary: The Commission's annual report is delivered to the White House. The same day, New York World reporter Nellie Bly leaves New York to race around the globe.

headline: Backing Reed; the budget grows; Edith arrives
summary: Roosevelt sides with Thomas B. Reed over William McKinley in the contest for Speaker. Harrison signs off on the Commission's yearly report and asks Congress to give it more money. Edith sets up the Washington household and explores the city while the children stay at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Anniversary, and Reed wins
summary: Roosevelt and Edith mark three years of marriage, and Thomas B. Reed, the man Roosevelt backed, becomes Speaker of the House.

headline: Writing to Godkin
summary: Roosevelt writes editor Edwin Godkin on civil service matters.

headline: No help for a San Francisco examiner
summary: Roosevelt tells J. G. Underwood, an examiner at the San Francisco customs house, that the Commission cannot assist him, and writes Charles Fingard on civil service.

headline: Paperwork for job seekers
summary: Roosevelt writes William Merville about the papers applicants need for federal jobs.

headline: About Chicago's postmaster
summary: Roosevelt writes James Sexton, the postmaster of Chicago.

headline: Philadelphia customs and a special commission
summary: Roosevelt reports to the Commission on Collector Cadwalader and the Philadelphia Custom House, and writes Charles Bonaparte about setting up a special panel.

headline: Christmas with Edie and the bunnies
summary: The Roosevelts spend Christmas at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt's 'Blessed Bunnies' (the children) all together with Edith.

headline: Historians hear Roosevelt
summary: Roosevelt reads a paper on the westward movement during the Revolution to the American Historical Association.

headline: Elliott heads south
summary: Elliott, still in pain from his foot, goes south, taking laudanum and morphine and drinking hard. Edith's household budget for the year shows clothes, groceries, a staff of ten and fuel.

headline: New Year's at the White House
summary: Roosevelt and Edith go to a White House reception to welcome 1890.

headline: Back to work
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.

headline: Theater and supper with John Hay
summary: Roosevelt takes in the theater and has supper with John Hay, and writes Curtis Guild Jr. to endorse his platform.

headline: Settling in; Sternberg to tea
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie, who has the grippe, that the new house is coming together, and that Germany's Baron Speck von Sternberg came for tea.

headline: Bamie bound for London
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie about her coming move to London.

headline: Asking Congress for staff money
summary: Roosevelt asks Charles Collins for more Congressional funding for Commission staff, writes George Putnam about Volumes III and IV of The Winning of the West and the New York book, and sends civil service letters to James Warner, William Lyall and Brander Matthews.

headline: Bamie turns 35
summary: Roosevelt's sister Bamie has her thirty-fifth birthday.

headline: Calling for his own investigation
summary: Roosevelt wants Congress to look into the Commission itself, apart from the Lyman inquiry, so the agency can be cleared of the accusations against it.

headline: Nellie Bly beats Phileas Fogg
summary: Nellie Bly completes her trip around the world, nearly 25,000 miles covered in just 72 days, outpacing Jules Verne's fictional traveler; the New York World tells her story.

headline: The House opens an inquiry
summary: The House opens a full inquiry into Roosevelt's Commission, chaired by Representative Hamilton Steward of South Carolina with Frank Hatton assisting.

headline: Feasting at the Mortons'
summary: Roosevelt describes for Bamie a banquet at Vice President Levi P. Morton's mansion.

headline: Out five nights a week
summary: The Washington social season keeps Roosevelt and Edith out five evenings a week. The Century publishes his article on the merit system versus patronage.

headline: A quarter through New York
summary: Roosevelt tells Brander Matthews he has written about a fourth of his New York City history.

headline: Alice turns six
summary: Roosevelt's daughter Alice celebrates her sixth birthday.

headline: Edith loves Washington dinners
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie that Washington hostesses balance their guest lists with care, mixing power, intellect and pedigree, and that Edith is enjoying society more than ever.

headline: Hearings begin
summary: House hearings on the Commission open with twelve charges. One accuses Roosevelt of placing Hamilton Shidy at the Census Bureau though Shidy broke his oath at the post office.

headline: Shidy's damaging testimony
summary: On Elliott's thirtieth birthday, Shidy takes the stand and concedes he would falsify records again. Around this time Roosevelt's Washington circle includes John La Farge, Clarence King, the Chanlers, Speaker Reed, Spring-Rice, the Lodges, John Hay, Henry Adams, Augustus Saint-Gaudens and the Camerons.

headline: Headlines skewer Shidy
summary: Newspapers savage Shidy's testimony, branding him both dishonest and foolish.

headline: Holding his own at the hearings
summary: Census Superintendent Robert Porter testifies at the House hearings, and Roosevelt defends himself skillfully.

headline: Hearings week in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.

headline: Too busy to speak
summary: Roosevelt tells Isaac Sharpless he is buried in work and cannot come speak for him.

headline: Taking Paul apart
summary: At the House hearings Roosevelt demolishes George H. Paul under questioning.

headline: Round two with Paul
summary: Roosevelt and Paul clash again at the hearings.

headline: Hearings close
summary: The House hearings wrap up after a final day of Roosevelt against Paul.

headline: Speaking in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt delivers a speech in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

headline: Pitching the grizzly story
summary: Roosevelt writes Century editor Richard Watson Gilder about articles by himself and Lodge and offers a piece on his grizzly fight.

headline: Riis recalls a Chicago speech
summary: Jacob Riis's Theodore Roosevelt, the Citizen tells of a speech Roosevelt gave at Chicago's Madison Street Theater; the date of that speech is not given.

headline: Hard words to Bamie about Anna Hall Roosevelt
summary: Roosevelt writes his sister Bamie a blunt judgment of his sister-in-law Anna, saying a life given over to frivolity has worn away her character.

headline: Veterans' preference in the new bill
summary: Writing from Washington, Roosevelt explains to Lucius Swift that the pending Civil Service bill would favor former soldiers when filling government jobs.

headline: Missing Bamie in quiet Washington
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie that he and Edith miss her badly and that their evenings have grown quiet without her.

headline: Letters on reform and copyright
summary: Roosevelt writes William Potts about Civil Service matters and sends Brander Matthews a letter on copyright law.

headline: Business trip to New York
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City tending to business.

headline: Good news about Ted
summary: In a note to Bamie from Washington, Roosevelt reports that young Ted has recovered.

headline: Trouble at the New York Customshouse
summary: Roosevelt writes John Comstock about irregular practices at the New York City Customshouse.

headline: Corinne's eighth anniversary
summary: Roosevelt's sister Corinne marks eight years of marriage to Douglas Robinson.

headline: Writing New York, shelving the West
summary: Roosevelt pushes ahead on his overdue New York City history yet cannot find time for The Winning of the West. Captain Alfred Thayer Mahan's sea power book appears this season, and Edith's butcher bill comes to $119.

headline: No half measures on Elliott
summary: Roosevelt urges Bamie to act firmly on their brother Elliott's drinking, warning that delay only deepens the danger and the risk of scandal. The same day, Oklahoma land opens to settlers.

headline: Copyright bill goes down
summary: Roosevelt writes A. W. Greely about Civil Service matters and commiserates with Brander Matthews over the copyright bill's defeat.

headline: A pause in the press attacks
summary: Hatton's stinging editorials against Roosevelt go quiet while a House committee prepares its verdict on the Civil Service Commission. Roosevelt writes Swift on reform and William Miller about the New York customs service.

headline: Calling on a 'colorless' President
summary: Roosevelt meets with President Benjamin Harrison, whom he finds colorless, then dines with the Davises.

headline: Lodge hears about the Dudley case
summary: Roosevelt writes Henry Cabot Lodge about the Dudley case and Civil Service affairs.

headline: Reading Mahan on sea power
summary: Roosevelt picks up Alfred Thayer Mahan's new study of sea power and history.

headline: Can't put Mahan's book down
summary: Roosevelt tells Mahan he has given half of two busy days to his book and read it from cover to cover.

headline: Answering a critic of his West
summary: Roosevelt asks historian Lyman Draper for material to rebut Butterfield, whose book on Simon Girty faults The Winning of the West.

headline: Edith takes the children to Sagamore
summary: Edith brings Alice, Ted and Kermit to Sagamore Hill for the summer.

headline: Pushing back at General Greely
summary: Roosevelt firmly rejects A. W. Greely's claim that the reform commission had wrecked the Signal Corps.

headline: Ferguson and Spring Rice at Sagamore
summary: Roosevelt tells Swift that the merit rules govern only six or eight percent of yearly federal hires and firings. Bob Ferguson and Cecil Spring-Rice sign the guest book.

headline: Commission cleared by the House
summary: A House committee files its report clearing Roosevelt's Civil Service Commission of the charges against it.

headline: Greely did nothing wrong
summary: Roosevelt assures A. W. Greely that he does not think him guilty of wrongdoing.

headline: Standing up for the Commission
summary: Roosevelt writes Herman Lehlbach defending the Civil Service Commission as fair and honest.

headline: Elliott sails to Europe for a cure
summary: Roosevelt's brother Elliott leaves for Europe to sober up, taking his wife Anna, daughter Eleanor and son Elliott Jr.

headline: Idaho joins the Union
summary: Idaho enters the Union as the 43rd state.

headline: Wyoming becomes the 44th state
summary: Wyoming enters the Union as the country's 44th state.

headline: E. Willard Reby signs the guest book
summary: A visitor named E. Willard Reby is recorded in the Roosevelt guest book.

headline: Promising Gilder an essay on reform
summary: Roosevelt tells Century editor Richard Watson Gilder that his reform article for the magazine should be done within a few days.

headline: Nellie Tyler visits
summary: Nellie Tyler's name appears in the guest book.

headline: Iselin and Dickey come calling
summary: Isaac Iselin and Charles P. Dickey Jr. sign the guest book.

headline: Reviewing Mahan for the Atlantic
summary: Roosevelt mails Horace Scudder of the Atlantic Monthly his review of Mahan's book on sea power.

headline: New York history is done
summary: Roosevelt completes his book on the history of New York City.

headline: Talking shop with Brander Matthews
summary: From Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt writes Brander Matthews about the work of writing his New York history.

headline: Edith turns 29
summary: Roosevelt's wife Edith celebrates her 29th birthday.

headline: Three guests at the house
summary: Rachel Sherman, H. Marquand and Frank Roosevelt are entered in the guest book.

headline: Clearing the desk at the Commission
summary: Back in Washington, Roosevelt works through his pile of Civil Service Commission business and writes Lodge about reform and a visit from Bryce.

headline: Nothing left of Grosvenor
summary: Writing Lodge from Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt boasts that he has thoroughly demolished his critic Grosvenor.

headline: Family party heads for the Badlands
summary: Roosevelt, Edith, Bamie, Conie, Douglas Robinson, Bob Ferguson and Lodge's 16-year-old son Bay set off for a week at Medora and Elkhorn and two weeks in Yellowstone. His essay on college graduates in public life runs in the Atlantic Monthly.

headline: Westbound as Elliott slips
summary: Roosevelt's party rolls west by train while, far off in Vienna, his brother Elliott falls back into drinking. Edith's meat bill comes to $29.

headline: Back to Elkhorn with the family
summary: Roosevelt's party steps off the train at Medora at 4:30 in a hard rain and rides 33 roadless miles to Elkhorn, fording the river 23 times, the women jolting along in a springless wagon. By noon they are at the ranch, where Roosevelt shows them around and a prairie dog town.

headline: Edith sketches the Elkhorn cabin
summary: Edith writes her sister Emily Carow and includes her own drawing of the Elkhorn cabin.

headline: Ranch life agrees with Edith
summary: Edith now weighs 131 pounds, six above her usual.

headline: On to Livingston
summary: Roosevelt's party leaves the Badlands and heads west by rail to Livingston, Montana.

headline: Ted turns three
summary: Roosevelt's son Ted celebrates his third birthday.

headline: No record for the day
summary: The chronology lists this date with no legible entry.

headline: Yellowstone tour wraps up
summary: A letter to Emily Carow reports that the party has finished seeing Yellowstone: frosty nights, geysers, and a fall from a horse that left Edith bruised.

headline: Back in Medora
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge twice from Medora, announcing that he has just arrived.

headline: Sequoia National Park created
summary: Congress sets aside Sequoia, the nation's third national park.

headline: Corinne turns 29
summary: Roosevelt's sister Corinne celebrates her 29th birthday.

headline: Home to the children
summary: Roosevelt and Edith return to Washington and rejoin the family.

headline: Yosemite and General Grant parks created
summary: Congress creates Yosemite and General Grant national parks in California.

headline: Fighting a prairie fire
summary: Roosevelt pitches in to battle a prairie fire.

headline: Hunting with Bob Ferguson
summary: Roosevelt goes hunting with his friend Bob Ferguson.

headline: Harrison cools on reform
summary: Writing from Elkhorn, Roosevelt tells Lodge that President Harrison has lost all interest in Civil Service reform. He also writes Bamie.

headline: Kermit's first birthday
summary: Roosevelt's son Kermit turns one.

headline: Eleanor turns six
summary: Roosevelt's niece Eleanor, Elliott's daughter, celebrates her sixth birthday.

headline: Edith loved the ranch
summary: Roosevelt tells his mother-in-law Gertrude Carow how much Edith enjoyed her days at Elkhorn and shares news of the three growing children.

headline: A chilly meeting with the President
summary: Roosevelt reports to Lodge that his interview with President Harrison was brief and frosty.

headline: A note to Rufus Dawes
summary: Roosevelt writes Rufus Dawes on Civil Service business.

headline: Roosevelt turns 32
summary: Roosevelt marks his 32nd birthday.

headline: Whistling to work, branding toy cattle
summary: Roosevelt walks to the office in grey trousers and a boyish hat, whistling. At home he heats hairpins into tiny branding irons and marks the children's toy herds: the Elkhorn brand for Ted, the Maltese Cross for Kermit, a triangle for Alice. Elliott's family is in Venice.

headline: Democrats sweep the House
summary: Midterm elections hand Democrats a commanding majority in the House, 255 seats to 88.

headline: Low spirits after the election
summary: Roosevelt confesses to Lodge that the election results left him too gloomy to write.

headline: Hal Minot killed
summary: Roosevelt's college friend Henry (Hal) Minot dies in a train wreck near New Florence, Pennsylvania. Minot headed the Eastern Railroad of Minnesota.

headline: Minot item continued
summary: The chronology continues the account of Hal Minot's death, placing the wreck near New Florence, Pennsylvania.

headline: Minot item concluded
summary: The chronology finishes its note on Hal Minot, president of a Minnesota railroad.

headline: Fourth anniversary
summary: Roosevelt and Edith mark four years of marriage.

headline: Sitting Bull killed
summary: Sitting Bull is shot dead by Indian police.

headline: Stockings at Jefferson Place
summary: Christmas morning at 1820 Jefferson Place: the children dive into their stockings and cheer each new find.

headline: Christmas wishes to Bamie
summary: Roosevelt sends Bamie holiday greetings and insists she spend next Christmas with them.

headline: Massacre at Wounded Knee
summary: Troops of the 7th Cavalry kill more than 300 Sioux at Wounded Knee.

headline: Boone and Crockett rallies for Yellowstone
summary: Roosevelt plays host to his Boone and Crockett friends over dinner at the Metropolitan Club, where members agree to back laws shielding Yellowstone from exploitation. Edith, pleased, is expecting again; the year's grocery bills total $550.

headline: Yellowstone resolution, continued
summary: The chronology completes its note on the Boone and Crockett Club's pledge to defend Yellowstone.

headline: Washington gossip about Edith
summary: Elizabeth Cameron is startled that Edith is pregnant again and frets about the Roosevelts' modest income.

headline: Bamie turns 36
summary: Roosevelt's sister Bamie celebrates her 36th birthday.

headline: Blessing Bamie's rescue trip
summary: Roosevelt agrees that Bamie should travel to Europe to help Elliott.

headline: Elliott committed; scandal looms
summary: Bamie takes Elliott to a sanitarium at Graz in the Austrian Alps. In New York a servant, Katy Mann, is carrying a child she says is Elliott's, and an angry Roosevelt resolves to pay to keep it quiet.

headline: Proud of his work, grieving for Bamie
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie he is glad to serve as Civil Service Commissioner and believes he has done good work, and says he and Edith wish they could stand beside her through her ordeal with Elliott.

headline: Free silver dominates Congress
summary: Roosevelt reports to Bamie that the main battle in Congress is now over free silver.

headline: Reform for the Indian Bureau?
summary: Roosevelt replies to Joseph Thorp's proposal to bring the Indian Bureau under Civil Service rules.

headline: Alice turns seven as Grosvenor strikes
summary: On his daughter Alice's seventh birthday, Congressman Grosvenor goes after the Civil Service Commission's funding.

headline: Staying put for the fight
summary: With the Commission's budget under attack, Roosevelt tells William Potts he will not leave Washington.

headline: Commission funding survives
summary: A compromise amendment passes, keeping money flowing to the Civil Service Commission.

headline: Speaking in New Haven
summary: Roosevelt gives a speech in New Haven, Connecticut.

headline: A nightmare letter from Elliott
summary: After a letter arrives from Elliott, Roosevelt writes Bamie that the situation is horrible, like a nightmare that will not lift.

headline: Bear games and fairy tales
summary: Edith reads Grimm and the Arabian Nights to Alice, who is surprised to learn Edith is not her father's sister; only Bamie speaks to her of her mother, Alice Lee. Roosevelt romps with Ted and Kermit, playing bear. A forest reserve law, pushed by the Boone and Crockett Club, passes.

headline: Taking a senator to task
summary: Roosevelt writes Senator Arthur Gorman to rebuke him for attacking Civil Service reform.

headline: Congress goes home
summary: Congress adjourns.

headline: Off to New York with the Lodges and Reed
summary: Roosevelt and Edith travel to New York City together with Tom Reed and the Lodges, Cabot and Nannie.

headline: Federal Club speech, then Carmencita
summary: Roosevelt and Tom Reed both give speeches at a Federal Club dinner and afterward go to Chase's studio to watch the dancer Carmencita.

headline: Lunch with Douglas Robinson
summary: Roosevelt lunches with his brother-in-law Douglas Robinson.

headline: Back to Washington
summary: The party returns to Washington.

headline: Letter to Bamie
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie from Washington; the chronology gives no details.

headline: Dinner with the Camerons
summary: Roosevelt and Edith dine at the Camerons' with a group of Italian diplomats.

headline: Itching to return to the West
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie he is eager to resume The Winning of the West and is mapping out its next two volumes.

headline: A tip from Baltimore
summary: John C. Rose of Baltimore brings Roosevelt evidence of Civil Service abuses; Roosevelt asks him to keep it quiet for now.

headline: Wanamaker won't act
summary: Rose hands over his findings on vote buying, and Roosevelt takes them to John Wanamaker, who declines to do anything.

headline: Surprise visit to Baltimore's polls
summary: On election day Roosevelt turns up unannounced in Baltimore, walks the wards, and sees open lawbreaking at the polls.

headline: Dinner with a new Justice
summary: At dinner at the Pellews', Roosevelt meets Judge Brown, newly named to the Supreme Court.

headline: Bad press over Baltimore
summary: Newspapers turn on Roosevelt for his Baltimore foray.

headline: Spoilsmen want him fired
summary: Patronage politicians call on President Harrison to demand Roosevelt's removal.

headline: Bob Ferguson laid up
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie that Bob Ferguson has been very ill and is recovering at Mrs. Cameron's.

headline: Back to Baltimore to build his report
summary: Roosevelt returns to Baltimore while drafting his election report, and writes old Albany friend Frederick Kruse about his books and Lucius Swift about Commission business.

headline: Deep in the Baltimore inquiry
summary: Roosevelt tells Lucius Swift he is hard at work investigating matters in Baltimore.

headline: Bonaparte joins the Baltimore probe
summary: Back in Baltimore, Roosevelt gets help from local lawyer Charles J. Bonaparte, later a member of his Cabinet. He also tells W. T. Huff that public ownership of railroads and telegraphs could not work here.

headline: Bay Lodge sweeps the jumps
summary: At a riding academy jumping contest, Lodge's son Bay wins every weight class aboard Toronto.

headline: Another Baltimore visit
summary: Roosevelt is back in Baltimore pursuing his election inquiry.

headline: London likes his New York
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie that English reviewers have welcomed his New York history, and sends love to Elliott and Anna.

headline: Rock Creek runs and a question from Ted
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie that he takes walks and runs through Rock Creek Park, and that young Ted has asked whether God is a fairy.

headline: Corinne's ninth anniversary
summary: Roosevelt's sister Corinne and Douglas Robinson mark nine years of marriage.

headline: Elliott denies it; the book appears
summary: Still in Europe, Elliott writes Roosevelt denying he fathered Katy Mann's child, and Roosevelt takes him at his word. Roosevelt's New York history comes out to mixed notices.

headline: The Baltimore report goes public
summary: Roosevelt's 146-page report on the Baltimore elections is released.

headline: Ever closer to Edith and the children
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie his ties to Edith and the children grow stronger every day.

headline: Bachelor days with Spring-Rice
summary: With the Lodges and his own family gone for the summer, Roosevelt and Cecil Spring-Rice move into Lodge's house. Roosevelt writes Charles Peters about a faulty appointment letter.

headline: A ride with Speck von Sternberg
summary: Roosevelt and Spring-Rice dine in, and he rides out with Speck von Sternberg. He writes Theodore Babcock about New York customs exams, and tells Bamie he is leaving for Indianapolis and St. Louis.

headline: Trip to Indianapolis and St. Louis
summary: The chronology finishes its note that Roosevelt is setting out for Indianapolis and St. Louis.

headline: On the Republican Party
summary: Roosevelt writes G. Garbet about the Republican Party.

headline: Elliott a horror
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie that Elliott's troubles have become a waking nightmare for him.

headline: Running the Commission solo
summary: With two fellow commissioners away, Roosevelt writes Bamie that he is enjoying handling the Commission's work by himself.

headline: Writing the letter carriers
summary: Roosevelt writes John F. Victory about the Letter Carriers Association.

headline: Partisanship at the Custom House
summary: Roosevelt writes John Clarke about party politics inside the New York Custom House. Speck von Sternberg stays at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Elliott's fall in Paris
summary: Edith takes the children to Sagamore Hill, where Bob Ferguson visits, while Roosevelt and Spring-Rice share bachelor rooms in Washington. In Europe, Elliott drags his wife, children and Bamie off to Paris and takes a mistress.

headline: Letting Elliott go
summary: In a painful letter, Roosevelt tells Bamie that for the sake of Anna and the children, Elliott must be left to destroy himself with drink.

headline: Thoughts on immigration
summary: From Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt writes Lodge about restricting immigration.

headline: Robinson's polo team loses
summary: Douglas Robinson's Orange, New Jersey, polo team falls to Meadowbrook of Long Island.

headline: Hoping Katy Mann is lying
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie he still wants to believe Katy Mann's claim about Elliott is false.

headline: Word of Elliott's D.T.'s
summary: A letter from Bamie tells Roosevelt that Elliott is suffering delirium tremens. Roosevelt writes Clarke and praises Lodge's Boston history, built on the same plan as his New York book.

headline: Elliott 'a maniac morally'
summary: Roosevelt judges his brother as unbalanced in morals as in mind. That evening he hosts the British Minister and the Secretary of War for dinner.

headline: Dinner for the Navy Secretary
summary: Roosevelt hosts the British Minister and the Secretary of the Navy at dinner.

headline: Spring-Rice reads Lodge's Boston
summary: Roosevelt tells Lodge that Spring-Rice has read his history of Boston.

headline: Hot nights with Springy
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie that he and Spring-Rice are enjoying their time together in the heat, though Elliott's troubles have him at his wits' end.

headline: Writing to Elliott
summary: Roosevelt sends a letter to his brother Elliott.

headline: Creaky boots and wild chicken
summary: Spring-Rice reports to Elizabeth Cameron on his housemate's quirks: pacing in creaking boots while he thinks, and attacking chicken like a wild animal. Roosevelt urges Lodge to come for polo week at Oyster Bay.

headline: A nephew born in Paris
summary: Elliott and Anna Roosevelt's son Hall is born in Paris.

headline: Lodge loses at Harvard
summary: Roosevelt consoles Lodge on his defeat for Harvard Overseer and praises Carl Schurz's Atlantic article on Lincoln.

headline: Moving house, and Alice's orchard
summary: Roosevelt and Spring-Rice move to 1721, where Springy, lost in the dark, climbs to the third floor, finds a bare bed and calls out in alarm. At Sagamore Hill, Bob Ferguson and Gertrude and Emily Carow visit, and Alice rents out trees in her orchard to her siblings.

headline: An unpleasant hour with Harrison
summary: Roosevelt meets President Harrison about the Civil Service and finds him disagreeable from start to finish. He tells Lodge he is busy on the Commission's annual report.

headline: Terms for Elliott's marriage
summary: Roosevelt advises Bamie that Anna should keep her distance from Elliott as a husband until he has proven himself through three years of abstinence, given his affair with Katy Mann and others.

headline: Fireworks for the children
summary: Roosevelt rides the train to New York and stages a fireworks display for the children.

headline: Burying cousin Alfred
summary: Roosevelt crosses Long Island Sound to bury his cousin Alfred, killed beneath the wheels of a train.

headline: Katy Mann wants $10,000
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie that Katy Mann is demanding $10,000 to stay quiet, and no settlement looks close.

headline: Another letter to Bamie
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie; no details survive in the chronology.

headline: Spring-Rice visits
summary: Cecil Spring-Rice is recorded in the guest book.

headline: The baby looks like Elliott
summary: Roosevelt reports to Bamie that an investigator, judging by the baby's looks, believes Katy Mann. Bamie writes that Elliott is confined in a Paris asylum for inebriates and that Anna will sail home without him.

headline: Seeing the child for himself
summary: Roosevelt and Douglas Robinson go to see Katy Mann's infant. She receives a payment and drops from the record.

headline: Writing Bamie again
summary: Roosevelt sends Bamie a letter; its contents are not described.

headline: Anna and the children come home
summary: Bamie returns to America with Anna and her three children.

headline: Edith turns 30
summary: Roosevelt's wife Edith celebrates her 30th birthday.

headline: Ethel is born
summary: After a long, hard labor at Sagamore Hill, Edith gives birth to a daughter, Ethel, with Dr. West Roosevelt in attendance. The baby is so big that her father dubs her Elephant Johnnie.

headline: Spring-Rice on Emily Carow
summary: Spring-Rice complains to Elizabeth Cameron that Edith's sister Emily Carow bores him with endless tales of romance in Rome.

headline: Baltimore report makes front pages
summary: Roosevelt's Baltimore report goes to the newspapers and lands on page one.

headline: Lunacy petition makes headlines
summary: Newspapers report that Roosevelt has sought a court ruling declaring his brother Elliott insane.

headline: Writing Taft on choosing civil servants
summary: Roosevelt writes Charles Wilby on Civil Service and Solicitor General William Howard Taft on how to select government workers.

headline: Dinner with Taft
summary: William Howard Taft dines with Roosevelt.

headline: Pressing on through the horror
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie that the ordeal is beyond belief but the only course is forward. Elliott, quoted in the Paris Herald, insists he is sane.

headline: Sane but without morals
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie that Elliott's letters read as perfectly rational yet utterly lacking in conscience.

headline: Genealogy and letter carriers
summary: Roosevelt writes E. B. Livingston about family history and life in Southern California, and Joseph Mulvey about the Letter Carriers Association.

headline: New house, closed ranch
summary: Roosevelt rents a house at 1215 19th Street in Washington. Out west the Merrifields leave for Montana and Roosevelt shuts up the Elkhorn ranch house.

headline: Wilmot Dow dies; west to Medora
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie that his old Maine guide and ranch partner Wilmot Dow has died, and sets out for Medora.

headline: Ted turns four
summary: Roosevelt's son Ted celebrates his fourth birthday.

headline: Nine elk in four weeks
summary: Roosevelt's hunting tally reaches nine elk in four weeks.

headline: Hunting Two Ocean Pass
summary: Roosevelt hunts with Bob Ferguson at Two Ocean Pass in the Shoshone Mountains of northwest Wyoming.

headline: Still in the Shoshones
summary: The chronology completes the location of the hunt: Two Ocean Pass in the Shoshones of northwest Wyoming.

headline: Corinne turns 30
summary: Roosevelt's sister Corinne celebrates her 30th birthday.

headline: Trouble brewing with Chile
summary: Revolution grips Chile. An American minister shelters the ousted president, enraging Chileans, and the U.S. seizes the rebel steamer Itata. Nellie Tyler is staying at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Rumors of his firing, again
summary: At Sagamore Hill on Kermit's second birthday, Roosevelt tells Lodge he has come home once more to talk of his own removal.

headline: Eleanor turns seven
summary: Roosevelt's niece Eleanor celebrates her seventh birthday.

headline: Sailors attacked in Valparaiso
summary: A mob in Valparaiso, Chile, assaults sailors from the cruiser Baltimore on shore leave, killing two; Chile later pays the U.S. $75,000 in reparations.

headline: Note to Lucius Swift
summary: Roosevelt writes Lucius Swift about the Civil Service system.

headline: A form for the railway mail
summary: Roosevelt sends James White a sample form for the railway mail service.

headline: Violations of the merit rules
summary: Roosevelt writes Daniel Griffin about the Commission's handling of Civil Service violations.

headline: Typed praise for Lodge
summary: Roosevelt sends Lodge a typewritten letter applauding one of his speeches.

headline: Headed to New York to dig into abuses
summary: Roosevelt tells Lucius Swift he is going to New York to look into abuses.

headline: The Carows head back to Europe
summary: After five months in America, Edith's mother and sister sail for Europe, and Edith is glad enough to have them gone.

headline: Election Day
summary: Americans vote in the 1891 off-year elections.

headline: Reform and Indian affairs
summary: Roosevelt writes Herbert Welsh about the Civil Service and Indian matters.

headline: New York, Bamie and tea
summary: Roosevelt goes to New York City, planning to see Bamie at Sagamore Hill, and takes tea with Mrs. Jones and the Greens.

headline: A literary breakfast
summary: Roosevelt hosts a ten o'clock breakfast for a table of writers and editors: Charles Dudley Warner, William Dean Howells, Richard Watson Gilder, Brander Matthews, Green and Lodge.

headline: Edith promises a European visit
summary: Edith writes her mother that she will come to Europe for about a week once their investments recover.

headline: Down with bronchitis
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie that a bad case of bronchitis has left him very ill.

headline: Worn out and sent to bed
summary: Roosevelt rallies for a time, but exhausted in body and spirit he breaks down in December, and Edith confines him to bed for eight days.

headline: Fifth anniversary
summary: Roosevelt and Edith mark five years of marriage.

headline: Letter to Bamie
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie; the chronology gives no details.

headline: Bamie and Herbert Welsh
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie and sends Herbert Welsh a letter on Civil Service matters.

headline: Reform in Philadelphia
summary: Roosevelt writes Stuart Wood about Civil Service reform in Philadelphia.

headline: Three magazines into one
summary: Roosevelt writes Richard Henry Dana about merging three Civil Service reform magazines into a single publication.

headline: Ready for war with Chile
summary: Angry over the two American sailors killed in Valparaiso, Roosevelt wants the United States to go to war with Chile.

headline: Ellis Island opens
summary: The federal immigration station on Ellis Island opens its doors.

headline: Letter to Bamie
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie; no details are given.

headline: Note to George Jolley
summary: Roosevelt sends George W. Jolley a letter about the merit system.

headline: Sailing to confront Elliott
summary: Roosevelt leaves New York by ship for Europe to face his brother Elliott.

headline: Bamie turns 37
summary: Roosevelt's sister Bamie celebrates her 37th birthday.

headline: Elliott gives in
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie in triumph: Elliott has accepted his terms, signing over two-thirds of his property, including a $60,000 trust, to a fund for his wife and children, and agreeing to two years' probation away from his family.

headline: Missing Springy
summary: Roosevelt writes Spring-Rice that he and Edith miss him very much.

headline: Homeward from Le Havre
summary: Roosevelt sails from Le Havre for home.

headline: Elliott sails separately
summary: Elliott boards a different steamer for America, leaving his mistress, Mrs. Evans, in France.

headline: Home again
summary: Roosevelt arrives home from Europe.

headline: No petitions for a federal officer
summary: Roosevelt tells Joseph Mulvey he cannot sign a petition while holding a government post.

headline: Alice turns eight
summary: Roosevelt's daughter Alice celebrates her eighth birthday.

headline: Letter to Bamie
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie; no details are given.

headline: Firings at the Cincinnati post office
summary: Roosevelt writes Charles Wilby about removals at the Cincinnati post office.

headline: Elliott turns 32
summary: Roosevelt's brother Elliott turns 32.

headline: Elliott takes the Keeley cure
summary: Elliott spends five weeks in Dwight, Illinois, taking Dr. Keeley's gold cure for alcoholism.

headline: Blaming Wanamaker
summary: With 25 tainted officials still drawing federal pay in Baltimore despite his findings, Roosevelt goes to a New York Civil Service Reform Association meeting and blasts John Wanamaker as the root of many abuses.

headline: In New York
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City.

headline: Still in New York
summary: Roosevelt remains in New York City.

headline: Elkhorn Stock Company formed
summary: Roosevelt joins Archibald D. Russell, Bob Ferguson and Douglas Robinson in organizing the Elkhorn Stock Company.

headline: Baltimore probe and a Texas hunt
summary: Roosevelt asks the House to investigate the Baltimore affair. He then takes Elliott south, stopping at Owensboro, Kentucky, before going on to a Texas ranch on the Nueces River, where he brings down a sow and a boar.

headline: Note to John Clarke
summary: Roosevelt writes John Clarke about Civil Service matters.

headline: Investigating in Chicago
summary: Roosevelt is in Chicago looking into Civil Service abuses reported by Oliver T. Morton.

headline: House orders a Baltimore inquiry
summary: The House votes to have its Civil Service Reform Committee investigate the Baltimore affair.

headline: An inheritance for Edith
summary: Edith tells her mother that their uncle John Carow, who had no children, has left her and her sister Emily $32,000 apiece.

headline: Wanamaker explains it all away
summary: At a special hearing before the Postmaster General, which Roosevelt does not attend, Wanamaker has an excuse for every charge. Roosevelt writes Oliver T. Morton about the Civil Service.

headline: Reporting on Chicago
summary: Roosevelt writes his fellow Civil Service commissioners about his Chicago investigation.

headline: Back to Chaucer
summary: Roosevelt tells Thomas Lounsbury he enjoyed his Chaucer study and has reread the Canterbury Tales.

headline: Corinne's tenth anniversary
summary: Corinne and Douglas Robinson mark ten years of marriage.

headline: Testifying on Baltimore
summary: Roosevelt goes before the House committee looking into corruption in Baltimore.

headline: A gift and a peccary hunt
summary: Roosevelt thanks Spring-Rice for a present and describes the peccary he hunted in Texas not long ago.

headline: Dinner with Henry Adams
summary: Roosevelt and Edith are Henry Adams's dinner guests.

headline: Chicago report finished
summary: Roosevelt tells Oliver T. Morton the Chicago report is complete, and writes Osborne Howes about Americanizing immigrants.

headline: New York Customs House report
summary: Roosevelt writes Lucius Swift about a report on wrongdoing at the New York customs office.

headline: Baltimore and Wanamaker
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge about the Baltimore investigations and Wanamaker.

headline: A registered letter to Wanamaker
summary: Roosevelt sends Wanamaker a registered letter holding him responsible for the abuses, with a copy to President Harrison.

headline: Explaining himself to Harrison
summary: Sending Harrison a copy of his Wanamaker letter, Roosevelt says he never sought a fight with the Post Office Department but was drawn into one by pressing for the inquiry.

headline: Thanking Francis Parkman
summary: Roosevelt thanks historian Francis Parkman for two books.

headline: Facts against Wanamaker's
summary: With no answer from Wanamaker, Roosevelt attends the House committee's last session and sets the facts beside Wanamaker's account.

headline: Praise for his testimony
summary: Roosevelt is applauded for his House testimony.

headline: Striking hard
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie that once forced to fight, he chose to hit hard. He also writes Horace Johnson that he stands behind his report.

headline: Recounting the Wanamaker history
summary: Roosevelt writes John Andrew reviewing the history of the Wanamaker matter back to March 23, 1891, and learns that Brander Matthews has the measles.

headline: Missouri irregularities
summary: Roosevelt writes James T. Beach about irregular Civil Service appointments in Missouri, and tells N. B. Pearce why his son was not hired.

headline: Gertrude Carow's relief
summary: Gertrude Carow writes Edith that she is deeply grateful her daughters received such a generous inheritance.

headline: Vindicated against Wanamaker
summary: The investigating committee's majority report calls Wanamaker's testimony evasive and garbled, a clear win for Roosevelt.

headline: Cleveland nominated
summary: The Democratic Party names Grover Cleveland as its presidential nominee.

headline: Reform and literature
summary: Roosevelt writes Brander Matthews about Civil Service and books.

headline: Note to W. C. Kenyon
summary: Roosevelt writes W. C. Kenyon about the Civil Service.

headline: Elliott sobers up in Virginia
summary: Elliott takes a job with the Robinson family's holdings near Abingdon, Virginia, and stops drinking.

headline: Thorndikes and Lodge visit
summary: Dr. and Mrs. Paul Thorndike and Henry Cabot Lodge sign the guest book.

headline: Bloodshed at Homestead
summary: The Homestead strike erupts in Pennsylvania; 13 die in the fighting and mobs control the town for five days.

headline: Troops reach Homestead
summary: Militia arrive at Homestead, Pennsylvania. Governor Hugh S. Thompson and his wife sign the Roosevelt guest book.

headline: J. Hallett visits
summary: J. Hallett is entered in the guest book.

headline: Ruby and Winthrop call
summary: E. Willard Ruby and Bronson Winthrop sign the guest book.

headline: Hallett returns
summary: J. Hallett again appears in the guest book.

headline: A strong-willed baby
summary: Edith writes her sister Emily that baby Ethel is sturdy and headstrong.

headline: Roosevelt on the polo field
summary: Harper's Weekly describes Roosevelt as a polo player.

headline: Saving for the boys' schooling
summary: Edith tells Emily she has set aside her shares in the Elevated Railroad to pay for the boys' schooling.

headline: No fan of either candidate
summary: Roosevelt tells Lodge that both Cleveland and Harrison have poor records. Most afternoons he plays tennis with Wharton at the Legation.

headline: Edith turns 31
summary: Roosevelt's wife Edith celebrates her 31st birthday.

headline: West Roosevelt and family visit
summary: Dr. West Roosevelt and his wife are recorded in the guest book, along with a Laura Roosevelt.

headline: A lonely Elkhorn
summary: At Elkhorn, Roosevelt writes Bamie that he finds little to hunt and the deserted cabin weighs on him. The Independent publishes his article on President Harrison's foreign policy.

headline: Ethel's first birthday
summary: Roosevelt's daughter Ethel turns one.

headline: Riding south to Deadwood
summary: Roosevelt rides south alongside Sylvane Ferris and Hell-Roaring Bill Jones, swapping cowboy talk, and reaches Deadwood. Edith writes Emily that Kermit would rather sit with her in a dim room than go walking with anyone else.

headline: Opening the Harrison campaign in Deadwood
summary: At the Deadwood Opera House, Roosevelt kicks off the Republican campaign for Harrison. He tells Bamie he has shot pronghorn and prairie fowl.

headline: Touring Pine Ridge and Crow Creek
summary: Roosevelt visits two Sioux reservations, Pine Ridge and Crow Creek. A speech he gave on Indian affairs is reprinted in a later biography.

headline: Ted turns five
summary: Roosevelt's son Ted celebrates his fifth birthday.

headline: Mocking party assessments
summary: At a Sioux City press conference, Roosevelt ridicules the South Dakota Republican Central Committee's assessments on officeholders.

headline: Lodge for Senator
summary: From Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt tells Lodge he has a good shot at the Senate. He and Edith go riding on polo ponies.

headline: Corinne turns 31
summary: Roosevelt's sister Corinne celebrates her 31st birthday.

headline: Election outlook
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge and Seth Low about the coming elections.

headline: In Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington.

headline: A mother's longing
summary: Gertrude Carow writes Edith that she sometimes weeps for her when unwell, and that her life would be empty without Edith, the children and Theodore.

headline: Family portrait for Gertrude
summary: Roosevelt sends his mother-in-law a lively report: he rides Pickle and Edith rides Diamond; Edith walks him to the office each day and reads Marbot's memoirs by the fire while he writes; Alice dotes on Edith and the little ones; Ethel is a handful; and Ted totes a tin sword everywhere.

headline: Elliott writes Eleanor
summary: From Virginia, Elliott sends his daughter Eleanor a birthday message.

headline: Kermit turns three
summary: Roosevelt's son Kermit celebrates his third birthday.

headline: Cosmopolitan shake-up
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge about a new editor at the Cosmopolitan and shifts among Republicans before the election. Niece Eleanor turns eight.

headline: Back from Lake Mohonk
summary: Roosevelt tells Lodge he has just returned from an Indian conference at Lake Mohonk that he found ridiculous yet worthwhile.

headline: Harrison versus Cleveland
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge about the Harrison-Cleveland race.

headline: Back to Washington
summary: Roosevelt returns to Washington.

headline: Letter to Bamie
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie; no details are given.

headline: Solicitation in Indianapolis
summary: Roosevelt offers Lucius B. Swift his help proving that federal workers in Indianapolis were pressed for political money.

headline: Lyman heads to Indianapolis
summary: Roosevelt tells Swift that Commissioner Lyman will reach Indianapolis on Wednesday.

headline: Death of Caroline Harrison
summary: First Lady Caroline Harrison, wife of President Benjamin Harrison, dies.

headline: Roosevelt turns 34
summary: Roosevelt celebrates his 34th birthday.

headline: Building a case against Gowdy
summary: Roosevelt tells Swift his papers will help prosecute John K. Gowdy, chairman of the Indiana Republican committee. Anna Roosevelt has surgery and asks Elliott to stay in Virginia.

headline: Coon hunting with Ted at home
summary: Roosevelt and his son Ted track a raccoon to a hollow tree near Sagamore Hill and take it.

headline: Cleveland wins back the White House
summary: Election Day: Grover Cleveland beats President Benjamin Harrison, returning to the presidency after four years out, the only president to serve two terms that do not follow one another.

headline: Taking the election loss in stride
summary: Writing to Lodge from Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt admits the Republican defeat disappoints him but did not catch him off guard; only the scale of the New York margin surprised him. Nellie Tyler signs the guest book.

headline: Back to the capital
summary: Roosevelt travels to Washington, D.C.

headline: Lodge called the election right
summary: From Washington, Roosevelt tells Lodge that every one of his election forecasts proved accurate.

headline: No activity recorded
summary: The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.

headline: Asking Swift about a blue book
summary: In Washington Roosevelt writes to Lucius Swift about obtaining a "blue book," the federal register of government employees. The same day, the long Homestead steel strike against Carnegie and Frick collapses.

headline: An essay on Parkman in print
summary: The Independent runs Roosevelt's essay on the historical writings of Francis Parkman.

headline: A letter to Foulke
summary: Roosevelt writes to William Dudley Foulke; the subject is not recorded.

headline: A move toward annexing Hawaii
summary: The United States begins taking steps to annex the Hawaiian Islands.

headline: Off to Washington with Edith
summary: Roosevelt and his wife Edith travel together to Washington, D.C.

headline: Anniversary, and a cool first meeting
summary: Roosevelt and Edith mark six years of marriage. He also meets the celebrated war correspondent Richard Harding Davis, and the two do not hit it off at first.

headline: Proud of four years enforcing the law
summary: Roosevelt tells William Dudley Foulke about meeting Richard Harding Davis over dinner at the British Legation, and that he did not care for him. Expecting to leave office in March, he says he can at least claim he never backed away from enforcing the law.

headline: Advice for a cowboy story
summary: Roosevelt sends Brander Matthews tips on a cowboy tale Matthews is writing. Meanwhile his brother Elliott pleads by letter with Mrs. Hall to know why he is kept from seeing his wife Anna.

headline: Elliott's wife Anna dies
summary: Anna Hall Roosevelt, wife of Roosevelt's brother Elliott, dies of diphtheria at 29. A telegram to Elliott in Virginia tells him to stay away; he comes anyway.

headline: Reporting party misconduct in Indianapolis
summary: Roosevelt sends the Civil Service Commission a report on improper conduct by the Democratic Committee in Indianapolis.

headline: Christmas greetings, and spectacles for Ted
summary: Roosevelt sends holiday wishes to Cecil Spring-Rice, reporting that young Ted now wears glasses and that Henry Adams is back in town, hosting his usual pleasant dinners.

headline: Urging Schurz to write on Lincoln
summary: Roosevelt asks Carl Schurz for a talk in New York about civil service matters and says he wishes Schurz would take on a life of Lincoln for the American Statesmen series.

headline: No activity recorded
summary: No events are recorded for this day; the source page holds only bibliography notes.

headline: Reaching the President-elect through Schurz
summary: Roosevelt asks Carl Schurz to serve as his go-between with President-elect Cleveland on civil service questions.

headline: Sledding with the children
summary: Roosevelt takes the children out sledding,, joined by Ted and several Black boys.

headline: Dinner at Blair Lee's; eyeing Remingtons
summary: Roosevelt dines at Blair Lee's and asks his sister Bamie to find out what two Frederic Remington paintings would cost. Edith writes her sister Emily that Elliott was merry and singing comic songs at his late wife's sister's home barely two weeks after the funeral.

headline: Inspecting the Philadelphia post office
summary: Roosevelt travels to Philadelphia to look into the workings of the post office there.

headline: Lunch with Corinne; Boone and Crockett dinner
summary: In New York Roosevelt has lunch with his sister Corinne and her husband Douglas Robinson, then joins 28 members at a Boone and Crockett Club dinner.

headline: Writing, then dinner at the Players
summary: Roosevelt puts in time writing, then dines with Brander Matthews at the Players club in New York.

headline: Back in Washington, dinner at Mrs. Slater's
summary: Roosevelt returns to Washington and has dinner at the home of Mrs. Slater.

headline: Rides with Cabot, romps with the children
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie he rides with Lodge whenever he can and that Willie Phillips joined him that morning for a rough-and-tumble outing with the children. He is weighing parting with most of the Sagamore Hill land, keeping just 20 acres, with Uncle Jim or Bamie as possible buyers.

headline: No activity recorded
summary: The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.

headline: No activity recorded
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is noted for the day.

headline: Bamie turns 38
summary: Roosevelt's older sister Bamie celebrates her 38th birthday.

headline: Bound for Chicago
summary: Roosevelt sets out for Chicago.

headline: Speaking in Buffalo
summary: Roosevelt gives a speech in Buffalo, New York.

headline: A Boone and Crockett book appears
summary: The Boone and Crockett Club publishes American Big-Game Hunting, edited by Roosevelt and George Bird Grinnell. His own contribution is a story titled "Coursing the Prongbuck."

headline: Giving up on reforming Elliott
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie of Elliott's latest misadventure in Abingdon, where he knocked over a lamp and burned himself badly, and says he sees no point in trying further to steer his brother onto a better path.

headline: Letters on books
summary: Roosevelt writes Brander Matthews about literary matters.

headline: Battle of Mobile Bay in the sickroom
summary: With every child in the house sick with measles, Roosevelt builds model warships, an ironclad ram and a monitor, and refights the Battle of Mobile Bay alongside Ted and Alice.

headline: Dinner with the Navy Secretary
summary: Roosevelt dines at the home of Secretary of the Navy Benjamin Tracy.

headline: Alice turns nine
summary: Alice celebrates her ninth birthday in leg braces doctors thought she needed; years later she believed her legs had been fine all along. Roosevelt dines at Cochrane's and writes Bamie about Edith's and Lodge's love of belles lettres.

headline: Seeking more money for the Commission
summary: Roosevelt presses Senator Edward Wolcott for bigger appropriations for the Civil Service Commission, which now oversees 43,447 federal jobs.

headline: The Atlantic turns down a review
summary: Roosevelt tells Brander Matthews that the Atlantic has rejected his review of books by Matthews and Lodge.

headline: Elliott's birthday brings worrying news
summary: On Elliott's 33rd birthday, with his brother back in Virginia, word reaches Roosevelt of new bouts of hard living.

headline: Writing up the Boone and Crockett Club
summary: Harper's Weekly publishes Roosevelt's article about the Boone and Crockett Club.

headline: Resigning as Cleveland takes office
summary: On Inauguration Day for Democrat Grover Cleveland, Roosevelt submits his formal resignation from the Civil Service Commission, assuming the new President will want his own party's man in the seat.

headline: In Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Cleveland asks him to stay
summary: In a talk with President Cleveland, Roosevelt learns, to his astonishment, that the new President wants him to remain as Civil Service Commissioner.

headline: Edith glad to stay in Washington
summary: Edith writes her sister Emily that she is happy Roosevelt will keep his post and spare them from leaving their Washington life.

headline: No new activity recorded
summary: Nothing new is recorded; the entry finishes Edith's letter from the day before.

headline: Writing to the Pine Ridge agent
summary: Roosevelt writes to George Brown, the Indian agent at Pine Ridge in South Dakota; the contents are not recorded.

headline: Subscribing to the Chronicle; staying on
summary: Roosevelt mails Lucius Swift a dollar for a subscription to the Civil Service Chronicle along with reform business, and tells Carl Schurz about his decision to remain on the Commission.

headline: Thanks for a wildflower book
summary: Roosevelt writes his childhood friend Fanny Dana, who has sent him her popular field guide to wildflowers, about plants as they turn up in literature.

headline: Named a Harvard overseer
summary: Roosevelt is appointed to Harvard's Board of Overseers and placed on a three-member committee to review the zoology department and suggest improvements. He visits Cambridge during the month.

headline: Pitching articles to the Century
summary: Roosevelt proposes to Richard Watson Gilder a joint article with Lodge on immigration drawing on the 1890 census, plus one on Lincoln's speeches.

headline: Local boards in Indiana
summary: Roosevelt and William Dudley Foulke trade views on Indiana's local civil service boards.

headline: Reporting on Harvard zoology
summary: Roosevelt writes ornithologist William Brewster about his report to the Harvard Overseers on the zoology department.

headline: No new activity recorded
summary: Nothing new is recorded; the entry finishes the note on the previous day's letter to William Brewster.

headline: Civil service letter to Foulke
summary: Roosevelt writes William Dudley Foulke on civil service business.

headline: No activity recorded
summary: The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.

headline: No activity recorded
summary: The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.

headline: No activity recorded
summary: The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.

headline: No activity recorded
summary: The record is silent for this day; no events, letters or guests are noted.

headline: A believer in manifest destiny
summary: Roosevelt tells James Clarkson he favors a bigger navy and hopes one day to see every European power pushed off the American continent.

headline: Cleveland wants him a while longer
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie that President Cleveland recently asked him to remain another year or two. His letter covers the Boone and Crockett Club's log cabin exhibit too, planned at Chicago's world's fair, where Bamie sits on the organizing commission.

headline: Corinne's anniversary; note to Swift
summary: Corinne marks 11 years of marriage. In Washington, Roosevelt writes Lucius Swift on civil service.

headline: A council of war on the Navy
summary: Roosevelt, Lodge, Henry Davis and Admiral Stephen Luce gather for what they call a "council of war" on the U.S. Navy and why it must grow.

headline: At Sagamore Hill; loss in Elliott's family
summary: Roosevelt's record places him at Sagamore Hill. The entry also notes that Elliott's young son, "Little Ellie," will die of scarlet fever before May is out.

headline: World's fair opens; writing Mahan
summary: Chicago throws open the gates of the World's Columbian Exposition, marking 400 years since Columbus reached the Americas. In Washington, Roosevelt writes Alfred Thayer Mahan about the Navy and expansion.

headline: Fighting a stall on free delivery
summary: Roosevelt writes William Dudley Foulke about Senator Daniel Voorhees's charges, aimed at holding up civil service classification of the free postal delivery service. He also writes Lucius Swift on reform business.

headline: Visiting Bamie in New York
summary: Roosevelt calls on Bamie in New York and writes Brander Matthews about the American Revolution.

headline: A political dinner in New York
summary: Roosevelt attends a political dinner in New York.

headline: Heading west to Chicago
summary: Roosevelt is on the train to Chicago.

headline: At the fair with family and the Lodges
summary: Roosevelt reaches Chicago accompanied by Edith, Senator Lodge and his wife Nannie, and they join Bamie, who helps manage the world's fair.

headline: In Chicago for the fair
summary: Roosevelt is in Chicago during his visit to the world's fair.

headline: In Chicago for the fair
summary: Roosevelt is in Chicago during his visit to the world's fair.

headline: In Chicago for the fair
summary: Roosevelt is in Chicago during his visit to the world's fair.

summary: Roosevelt meets Seth Bullock in the West.

summary: Roosevelt tells William Dudley Foulke the Interior Department has not improved and that Josiah Quincy has outdone everyone as a dispenser of patronage.

summary: Roosevelt marks his 35th birthday in Washington and writes Lucius Swift about Indiana post offices.

headline: Uncle Jimmy visits

summary: Roosevelt writes Carl Schurz on civil service business.

summary: Roosevelt's book The Wilderness Hunter is published.

summary: From New York Roosevelt tells Bamie of plans to host Commission representatives at dinner at 689 Madison Avenue. Bamie, having nursed Bob Ferguson through scarlet fever, is leaving for London to run the household of their widowed cousin James "Rosy" Roosevelt, the embassy's First Secretary, and his two children. Roosevelt then returns to Washington.

summary: Edith tells Bamie that Roosevelt fears they are headed for the poorhouse.

summary: Roosevelt takes Alice, Ted and Kermit to Rock Creek Park and the zoo, and that evening he and Edith are Henry Adams's dinner guests. He tells Bamie his spending outruns his income by $2,500 and he may have to give up Sagamore Hill.

summary: Roosevelt exercises in Rock Creek Park. He sends Bamie a note from Alice and admits The Winning of the West is going slowly; he praises Brander Matthews's article on Andrew Lang. Elliott has sent him a coachman's fur collar for Christmas, and he is baffled that Edith's sister Emily has become a Catholic.

summary: Edith describes the White House dinner to Bamie: as the only Republicans at the table, she and Roosevelt felt like outsiders and watched every word.

summary: Roosevelt and Lodge ride for three hours across fields and along the Potomac. He tells Bamie that Uncle Jim wants to buy a ten-acre parcel of his Sagamore Hill land.

summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie, newly presented at the English court, and grumbles that Cleveland and the Democrats have made a mess of governing.

summary: Roosevelt's wife Edith celebrates her 33rd birthday.

headline: Edith worries about Elliott's troubles
summary: Edith writes to her sister Emily that she lives in fear of Elliott's behavior bringing scandal down on Roosevelt. To her mother Gertrude she adds that she is glad her husband never went into business, where worry would have driven him wild.

headline: A note of praise to J. W. Fox
summary: Working in Washington, Roosevelt writes J. W. Fox to say he enjoyed Fox's latest book.

headline: Tennis, talk, and worry over Elliott
summary: Roosevelt writes his sister Bamie from Washington about his busy days with Lodge: tennis, shared dinners, long political conversations. He also tells her that their brother Elliott has started drinking again.

headline: Ethel turns 3 as bad news arrives
summary: Daughter Ethel celebrates her third birthday; she is a strong-willed little girl who bosses her mother. The same day a telegram reports that Elliott is gravely ill in New York City, where he lives with Mrs. Evans on West 102nd Street. Fanny Sturgis visits.

headline: Elliott Roosevelt dies in New York
summary: Roosevelt's younger brother Elliott, after trying to leap from a window of his apartment, suffers a last seizure and dies. Roosevelt is crushed by grief. Mrs. Evans, the woman Elliott lived with, receives $1,250 to stay silent. Roosevelt also sends a civil service letter to Lucius Swift.

headline: Conie mourns Elliott in a letter
summary: Roosevelt's sister Conie writes Bamie about seeing Elliott after his death, describing how the swelling had left his face and the gentle look that brought her to tears.

headline: Elliott laid to rest in Brooklyn
summary: Roosevelt weeps at his brother Elliott's funeral; Elliott is buried at Green-Wood Cemetery in Brooklyn. Writing to Bamie, Roosevelt likens his brother in his last days to a hunted animal.

headline: Commission business with Senator Gorman
summary: Back at work in Washington, Roosevelt writes Senator Arthur Gorman about the Civil Service Commission and a congressional committee, and sends Lucius Swift a letter on commission affairs.

headline: Another letter on commission affairs
summary: From Washington, Roosevelt writes the Swifts again on civil service business.

headline: Remembering Elliott at his best
summary: Writing to his sister Conie, Roosevelt says he now wants to hold only happy memories of Elliott, recalling the boy who explored hotels with them and went to dancing class.

headline: Turning down a run for mayor
summary: New York City reformers urge Roosevelt to run for mayor. Edith objects, preferring their settled life and his steady post in Washington, and Roosevelt, against his own wishes, says no.

headline: A gift for a pony cart

headline: Heading west to Medora

headline: Ted turns 7
summary: Roosevelt's son Ted turns seven. He reads all the time, but he squints and his eyesight is poor.

headline: Robinsons and Uncle Jimmy visit
summary: Douglas and Corinne Robinson, Teresa Houghton, Mr. Peel, Mr. Morris, and Uncle James K. Gracie all appear in the guest book.

headline: Conie turns 33
summary: Roosevelt's sister Corinne celebrates her 33rd birthday.

headline: Edith regrets the mayoral decision
summary: Edith is upset to learn how much Roosevelt had wanted to run for mayor and how readily he treated her objection as final. She writes Bamie that she had not understood his feelings at all.

headline: Back from the West
summary: Roosevelt returns home from his trip to the Dakota ranch country.

headline: Five antelope in two weeks
summary: Home at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt tells Lodge that his ranch visit lasted just two weeks and that he shot five antelope.

headline: Promising Lodge the mayoralty story
summary: From Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt tells Lodge he will explain his side of the mayoral episode in person.

headline: Back to Washington; family to Vermont
summary: Roosevelt returns to Washington. Meanwhile his sister Bamie carries Edith and the youngsters off to Vermont for a two-week holiday.

headline: Kermit turns 5; plans for a Bronx zoo
summary: Son Kermit turns five, a self-contained boy with a curious mind who does little schoolwork. In Washington, Roosevelt writes Swift on the civil service and tells Madison Grant about plans he and others are making to found the Bronx Zoo.

headline: Election talk and feeling against Platt
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge from Washington about the coming elections and the mood against New York party boss Thomas C. Platt. The record also notes a birthday for his niece Eleanor.

headline: Itching to speak his mind
summary: Roosevelt confides to Swift that he wishes he could leave office briefly just to say some things publicly. He also writes T. T. Hudson about resisting anti-Catholic societies.

headline: Civil service letter to Swift
summary: In Washington, Roosevelt sends Swift another letter about the civil service.

headline: In Washington, nothing more recorded
summary: The chronology places Roosevelt in Washington but notes nothing else for the day.

headline: Reassuring Bishop Keane
summary: Roosevelt writes Bishop John Keane to assure him the Republican party holds no prejudice against Catholics.

headline: Looking ahead to the elections
summary: From Washington, Roosevelt writes Swift about the approaching elections.

headline: More civil service mail
summary: Roosevelt writes Swift from Washington about the civil service.

headline: No money to run for mayor
summary: Writing Bamie, Roosevelt explains that he lacked the money for a mayoral campaign. He also writes Swift about post offices in Indiana.

headline: A letter on Scottish history
summary: Roosevelt writes J. W. Fox from Washington about the history of Scotland.

headline: "I would have given my right arm"
summary: Roosevelt pours out his regret to Lodge over the mayoral race he passed up, calling it a chance that would not come again. He takes the blame himself rather than putting it on Edith, and says the matter is best left behind.
