summary: New York's Mayor William L. Strong offers Roosevelt the job of Street Cleaning Commissioner, and Roosevelt declines. He also writes Henry Merwin about Harvard and athletics.

headline: Christmas jumping horses
summary: On Christmas Day, Roosevelt takes his horses over jumps.

headline: Saying no to street cleaning
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie he has, after long wavering, refused the street cleaning post in New York. He also writes Carl Schurz turning the job down.

headline: No entry for this day
summary: The chronology records nothing for this day beyond a stray page mark.

headline: Starting the fourth volume
summary: In bitter cold Washington weather, Roosevelt tells Bamie he is trying to get Volume IV of his frontier history, The Winning of the West, under way.

headline: Braces, weaning, and migraines
summary: At year's end the household has its share of troubles: Kermit and Alice both wear leg braces, baby Archie is being weaned, and Edith suffers from migraines.

headline: Edith reports the job refusal
summary: From Washington, Edith tells her sister Emily that Roosevelt has turned down New York's street cleaning commissionership.

headline: Riis as the mayor's adviser
summary: Roosevelt writes Jacob Riis that he ought to become an adviser to Mayor William L. Strong.

headline: Literary letter to Horace Scudder
summary: From Washington, Roosevelt writes editor Horace Scudder about literary matters.

headline: Bamie turns 40
summary: Roosevelt's older sister Bamie celebrates her 40th birthday.

headline: Worried about Edith
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie that he is anxious about Edith, who will not look after her own health no matter what he tries.

headline: Edith's rest in New Jersey
summary: Edith writes her sister Emily that a fortnight at Corinne's home in Orange, New Jersey, gave her a needed break from family cares.

headline: Comparing civil services
summary: Roosevelt writes Edward Porritt comparing the American civil service with Britain's.

headline: Minding four children in Washington
summary: With Edith in Orange to have Alice's ankle braces adjusted, Roosevelt tells Bamie he is caring for the four younger children at home in Washington.

headline: Cleveland warns of Treasury drain
summary: President Grover Cleveland sends Congress a message about a $45 million drain on the Treasury.

headline: Gold crisis
summary: The nation's gold crisis deepens.

headline: A Boone and Crockett book appears
summary: The Boone and Crockett Club publishes Hunting in Many Lands, edited by George Bird Grinnell, with Roosevelt's piece "Hunting in the Cattle Country" among its stories.

headline: Letter to Bamie
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie from Washington.

headline: Mounted officers and exams
summary: Roosevelt writes William Fitch, customs collector at the Texas border town of Eagle Pass, about having mounted officers draw up civil service examinations.

headline: Cleveland and Morgan confer on gold
summary: At the White House, President Cleveland meets J. Pierpont Morgan to deal with the gold crisis. Roosevelt is in Washington.

headline: In Washington, nothing more recorded
summary: The chronology places Roosevelt in Washington but notes nothing else for the day.

headline: Defending the Civil Service Law
summary: Roosevelt writes F. Doremus standing up for the civil service statute.

headline: Dinner with the Chanlers
summary: Winthrop Chanler and his wife join Roosevelt for dinner in Washington.

headline: In Washington, nothing more recorded
summary: The chronology places Roosevelt in Washington but notes nothing else for the day.

headline: Alice turns 11
summary: Alice celebrates her 11th birthday in Washington with her grandfather George Lee visiting. Edith calls her a right hand and companion, and of the children Alice is closest to Ted.

headline: The commission secretary's pay
summary: Roosevelt writes Senator Francis Cockrell about a proposed pay cut for the Civil Service Commission's secretary.

headline: Skiing in the snow
summary: Snow covers Washington, and Roosevelt tells Bamie he has been trying out Norwegian snowshoes, as skis were then called, and riding with Lodge.

headline: Stray page header
summary: Nothing is recorded for this day beyond a page heading.

headline: Standing up for civil service
summary: Roosevelt writes Hugh McKittrick defending civil service reform.

headline: Revolt breaks out in Cuba
summary: Cuban rebels launch an uprising against Spanish rule.

headline: Guests at the dinner table
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie that Henry White and his wife came to dinner, along with the young architect Grant LaFarge, son of artist John LaFarge.

headline: Fed up with Bissell
summary: Writing Lucius Swift, Roosevelt says he is disgusted with Postmaster General Bissell.

headline: Skis, appropriations, and Hero Tales
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge about Doyle's appropriation, keeps teaching himself to ski, and works alongside Lodge on their book of Hero Tales for young Americans.

headline: A good word for O'Beirne
summary: Roosevelt tells General James R. O'Beirne he has written Mayor Strong on his behalf.

headline: Inspecting Cincinnati; Taft introduces him
summary: Roosevelt travels to Cincinnati to inspect the city's post office and federal revenue office. He gives a speech, with William Howard Taft making the introduction.

headline: In Cincinnati
summary: Roosevelt remains in Cincinnati.

headline: Still in Cincinnati
summary: Roosevelt is still in Cincinnati.

headline: Edith writes her mother
summary: Edith sends a letter to her mother, Gertrude Carow.

headline: Sparring with Kipling
summary: Roosevelt meets Rudyard Kipling again, and the two argue over a great many things, America above all.

headline: New York politics and Joe Murray
summary: Edith visits the Tylers. Roosevelt writes Charles Parkhurst about Joe Murray and city politics, writes Murray about politics and obeying civil service rules, and dines at the Shoreham.

headline: A sketch of Kipling for Bamie
summary: Roosevelt sends Bamie an account of his week, including a less than flattering description of Kipling's face.

headline: Why football matters
summary: Roosevelt writes Walter Camp about a book of football facts and figures. He argues Americans need sport and exercise, names football his favorite, scorns critics who call it too rough, and notes he boxed and wrestled at college but was too nearsighted for football.

headline: Hero Tales for young readers
summary: Roosevelt writes Joseph Sears, who edits Harper's Young People, the magazine where portions of his Hero Tales book were appearing.

headline: School reform, Murray, and Cuba
summary: Roosevelt sends a flurry of letters: to Parkhurst vouching for Joe Murray's character, to Lemuel Quigg and Governor Levi Morton backing New York school reform that Platt opposes, and to Brander Matthews about Kipling. He tells Morton he would want a commission if troops went to Cuba, though he expects no war.

headline: The school bill report
summary: Roosevelt writes Lemuel Quigg about a subcommittee's report on the school bill.

headline: Surprised by a police board push
summary: Roosevelt tells Lemuel Quigg he had not expected Quigg to actually urge the mayor to name him a Police Commissioner.

headline: Lodge to meet Quigg about the police job
summary: Roosevelt wires Lemuel Quigg that Lodge will see him in New York, a meeting meant to arrange Roosevelt's appointment to the city's Police Board.

headline: Writing to an anonymous reviewer
summary: Roosevelt writes to the unnamed critic who reviewed the third volume of his frontier history; the reviewer turns out to be historian Frederick Jackson Turner.

headline: Yes to the New York Police Board
summary: Roosevelt agrees to become one of New York City's four police commissioners, at $6,000 a year, and wires Quigg his acceptance. To Lodge he admits he still feels unsure about the job and what lies ahead.

headline: A dinner full of writers and diplomats
summary: Roosevelt hosts a dinner for a lively company: novelist Owen Wister, Kipling, Tom Page, John Hay, and Austin Wadsworth, along with Merriam, Procter, and Rockhill.

headline: Coming around on Kipling
summary: Roosevelt tells Brander Matthews he now shares Matthews's view of Kipling, and mentions dining with the Brooks Adamses.

headline: Spring in Rock Creek
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie that spring has arrived and takes the children out to Rock Creek.

headline: Archie turns 1
summary: Baby Archie celebrates his first birthday.

headline: Turner unmasked; Edith on a bicycle
summary: Roosevelt writes Frederick Jackson Turner, now known to be his reviewer, about western history. Edith tells her sister Emily she has taken up bicycle lessons and finds them hard going.

headline: Rock Creek scramble and police news
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie about the family's regular Sunday afternoon romp in Rock Creek and shares news of his New York police appointment.

headline: Police appointment confirmed
summary: Roosevelt's appointment as a New York police commissioner is confirmed for a six-year term. He writes Quigg about the post.

headline: Setting a start date
summary: Roosevelt informs Mayor William L. Strong that he will take up his police duties on May 1, 1895.

headline: In Washington, nothing more recorded
summary: The chronology places Roosevelt in Washington but notes nothing else for the day.

headline: Suggesting his successors
summary: Roosevelt writes President Grover Cleveland proposing two candidates for his Civil Service Commission seat: Bellamy Storer and William Wharton.

headline: Sad to leave Washington
summary: With Corinne and Douglas Robinson visiting, Roosevelt writes Bamie that he is sorry to be leaving Washington after six years.

headline: Mary Leiter weds Lord Curzon
summary: In Washington, Mary Leiter, whose parents are friends of Roosevelt's family, weds Lord Curzon.

headline: In Washington, nothing more recorded
summary: The chronology places Roosevelt in Washington but notes nothing else for the day.

headline: Word of a death in the family
summary: Edith's aunt Mary Moore writes to tell her that her mother has died.

headline: Resigning from the commission
summary: Roosevelt sends President Cleveland his resignation from the Civil Service Commission and writes fellow police commissioner Avery Andrews about the New York force.

headline: Questions about the Police Board's powers
summary: Roosevelt asks Quigg to clarify the laws governing the Police Board, and tells Frederick Jackson Turner their views on western history line up.

headline: Edith's mother dies abroad
summary: A telegram brings word that Edith's mother, Gertrude Carow, has died abroad at 59 after a mix of illnesses; she had been dependent on morphine. Roosevelt writes Bamie about beach rights at Sagamore Hill and thanks Lucius Swift for a letter.

headline: In Washington, nothing more recorded
summary: The chronology places Roosevelt in Washington but notes nothing else for the day.

headline: Exam letter; the Robinsons' anniversary
summary: Corinne and Douglas Robinson mark 13 years of marriage. Roosevelt writes Judson Grenell about civil service examinations.

headline: The police world Roosevelt is entering
summary: On the eve of the move, the chronology sketches New York's police: headquarters on Mulberry Street, reporters Lincoln Steffens and Jacob Riis keeping watch from across the street, board meetings twice a week, a powerful and wealthy chief in Thomas Byrnes, and corruption throughout the ranks.

headline: In Washington, nothing more recorded
summary: The chronology places Roosevelt in Washington but notes nothing else for the day.

headline: A goodbye lunch with Henry Adams
summary: Roosevelt is honored at a goodbye lunch in Washington, with Henry Adams among those present.

headline: Civil service resignation takes effect
summary: Roosevelt's six years on the U.S. Civil Service Commission formally come to an end as his resignation takes effect.

headline: Sworn in as police commissioner
summary: At City Hall, Roosevelt takes the oath as a New York police commissioner, then walks north to Mulberry Street, where his fellow commissioners Frederick D. Grant, Avery Andrews, and Andrew Parker choose him board president. Hurrying into his new office with reporters Steffens and Riis, he asks what they should do first.

headline: In New York, nothing more recorded
summary: The chronology places Roosevelt in New York City but notes nothing else for the day.

headline: Albany trims the board president's power
summary: The State Legislature passes a bill that reduces the authority of the Police Board's president, the post Roosevelt now holds.

headline: In New York, nothing more recorded
summary: The chronology places Roosevelt in New York City but notes nothing else for the day.

headline: Corruption trials make news
summary: Roosevelt lands in the headlines as patrolmen accused of corruption go on trial. He writes Charles Saxton about the veto of the Ainsworth bill.

headline: A woman secretary at headquarters
summary: Roosevelt hires Minnie Gertrude Kelly, the first woman to serve as a secretary at police headquarters.

headline: Long days on Mulberry Street
summary: Roosevelt's routine: at headquarters by 8:30, striding fast and taking the stairs at a bound, and gone at 6:00. He writes Lodge about the new job.

headline: Never worked harder
summary: Roosevelt rents his sister Bamie's house at 689 Madison Avenue and writes her in London that his first six days were the hardest work of his life.

headline: At 689 Madison Avenue
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; the page cites a source on his move from the civil service to the police.

summary: The New York World runs a portrait of Roosevelt. He writes Quigg about Police Chief Thomas Byrnes.

headline: Ready to move on Byrnes
summary: Roosevelt tells Lodge he plans to act against Chief Byrnes right away and does not trust him at all.

headline: The city's most corrupt department
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie that he now runs the most important and most corrupt department in New York.

headline: In New York, nothing more recorded
summary: The chronology places Roosevelt in New York City but notes nothing else for the day.

summary: At Lincoln Steffens's urging, Roosevelt pushes the notoriously brutal Inspector Alexander "Clubber" Williams into resigning.

headline: Sagamore Hill opened for summer
summary: Edith records in the guest book that the house was opened for the season on May 25.

headline: Chief Byrnes steps down
summary: Facing an investigation, with a generous pension waiting, Chief Thomas Byrnes resigns. Peter Conlin becomes the new chief.

headline: Byrnes had to go
summary: Roosevelt writes Seth Low that removing Byrnes was essential.

headline: In New York, nothing more recorded
summary: The chronology places Roosevelt in New York City but notes nothing else for the day.

headline: Decoration Day with the children
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill for Decoration Day and delights in the children. Edith's sister Emily Carow arrives to stay for six months; the two sisters are mourning their mother.

headline: In charge of the Police Board
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie he spends the work week alone in New York City and now has the Police Board firmly under his control.

headline: Henry White and M. Maxwell visit
summary: Henry White and M. Maxwell are guests at the house.

headline: Politics with Lodge
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge about politics.

headline: The first midnight ramble
summary: At 2 a.m. Roosevelt and Jacob Riis set out from the Union League Club and walk to Third Avenue and 27th Street without meeting a single policeman. Second Avenue proves a bit better. Roosevelt tracks down the missing men and sends them back to their beats, though he punishes no one. Every paper headlines the patrol.

headline: Bicycling to the station
summary: From Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt tells Bamie he rides a bicycle between the station and 689 Madison Avenue.

headline: Grant LaFarge and Dr. Morris visit
summary: Grant LaFarge and Dr. Morris appear in the guest book.

headline: Order to close saloons on Sunday
summary: Roosevelt directs the police captains to enforce the law keeping the city's saloons shut for the full 24 hours of Sunday, beginning at midnight Saturday.

summary: Roosevelt goes out again by night with writer Richard Harding Davis and Commissioner Avery Andrews. He praises a sergeant on the well-covered Lower East Side, catches Patrolman Rath, eats steak at Mike Lyons's all-night place on the Bowery at 3 a.m., then finds the West Side poorly patrolled.

headline: At 689 Madison Avenue
summary: Roosevelt is at his New York City house on Madison Avenue.

headline: Missing the children
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie he has little time to write and misses the children during the work week; at home he romps with Archie in the evening and plays with baby Ethel at her crib. He also writes Lodge about Jessie the dog.

headline: A patrolman stands up to "King" Callahan
summary: The closing law is enforced in New York: Patrolman Bourke makes saloonkeeper Pat "King" Callahan shut his bar and is assaulted for it. Roosevelt writes Bamie that he relishes his late-night walks for the force.

headline: Bourke cleared in court
summary: Patrolman Bourke is vindicated at the Tombs Police Court in the Callahan case.

headline: No entry for this day
summary: The chronology records nothing for this day beyond a stray page mark.

headline: Harvard class dinner; elected Overseer
summary: Roosevelt attends his Harvard class dinner, 15 years after graduating, the only one he ever went to. He is elected a Harvard Overseer, leading the poll.

headline: Marshal at Harvard, then to Nahant
summary: Roosevelt serves as a marshal under Roger Wolcott, then goes with Lodge to Lodge's home at Nahant.

headline: Back to New York
summary: Roosevelt returns to New York City.

headline: A remarkably dry Sunday
summary: Sunday closing is enforced again, and the papers call it the driest Sunday in years. Roosevelt sends Bamie a letter from Alice with a joke about Edith's efforts to get it written. His review of Benjamin Kidd's Social Evolution appears in the North American Review.

headline: Chanlers and Spring-Rice visit
summary: Winthrop Chanler, William Astor Chanler, Cecil Spring-Rice, and Lt. Von Hornell sign the guest book.

headline: Bamie is engaged
summary: A cable reaches Sagamore Hill: Bamie, 40, is engaged to William Sheffield Cowles, 49, a Navy commander serving as naval attaché at the American embassy in London. One snag is that New York does not recognize his divorce.

headline: Dumbfounded, and glad
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie that the news of her engagement stunned the family, but that they are truly happy for her.

headline: No entry for this day
summary: The chronology records nothing for this day beyond a stray page mark.

headline: Cousin John Elliott visits
summary: John Elliott appears in the Sagamore Hill guest book.

headline: Bars find back doors; Ethel's narrow escape
summary: Saloonkeepers dodge the Sunday law with side doors and hidden liquor. Roosevelt writes Bamie that her engagement is the family's main topic and that he approves her choice, and reports that Ethel swallowed a bottle of nitre and a toadstool without harm.

headline: Keeping the peace at a parade
summary: Roosevelt tells Lodge he turned out the police to guarantee order at a New York parade of Protestant Irish.

headline: Winning over German-Americans
summary: Speaking at the Good Government Club on East 115th Street, Roosevelt persuades German-Americans, angered by the closing law, that his intentions are good.

headline: Reporting to Schurz
summary: Roosevelt writes Carl Schurz about events in the city and his Good Government Club speech.

headline: Saloons' weekend losses
summary: The New York Times puts the saloons' average weekend loss from the closing crackdown at $20,000.

headline: Legal advice on Cowles's divorce
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie he has asked New York lawyers about Will Cowles's divorce problem; Cowles could seek relief in court or settle in a more tolerant state.

headline: Trials of the liquor law
summary: Roosevelt gives Lodge a full account of his struggles enforcing the liquor law.

headline: Thirsty New Yorkers leave town
summary: On Sunday, at least half a million New Yorkers head to saloons in New Jersey and on Long Island to escape the closings.

headline: W. Hallett Phillips visits

headline: Indian words for Dana
summary: Roosevelt writes editor Charles A. Dana on the subject of Indian words. Avery Andrews, Grant LaFarge, and Mr. Smalley are guests at Sagamore Hill.

headline: A bomb in the mail
summary: A bomb mailed to Roosevelt is opened by a wary post office clerk; it fails to go off.

headline: Edith turns 34
summary: On Edith's 34th birthday, Roosevelt writes Horace Scudder introducing Lincoln Steffens to the Atlantic, and writes Carl Schurz about false stories in the German press.

headline: Sunday and the family wage
summary: At Carnegie Hall, Roosevelt addresses the national convention of the Catholic Total Abstinence Union. Mayor Strong, Archbishop Corrigan, Commissioner Parker, and State Senator "Big Tim" Sullivan share the stage. He argues that no man's Sunday pleasures should cost his family his week's pay.

headline: Thanks to Lodge in Europe
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge, who is traveling in Europe, that he enjoyed his letter.

summary: Dan Tyler Moore appears in the Sagamore Hill guest book.

summary: Roosevelt tells Lodge he has quarreled with Lemuel Quigg. His wife Edith wishes her husband had held back his jab that the good-government reformers had turned foolish.

summary: The day after the election, Roosevelt summons the police captains and makes clear the Board expects the laws to be enforced as strictly as ever.

summary: Back at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt rides, chops wood and walks with Edith and the children. He also writes Lemuel Quigg that plenty of people are hoping the two of them will split.

summary: Roosevelt is in New York City, where his fight at the Police Board goes on. Nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Honored by the Naval Reserve
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie he was guest of honor at a Naval Reserve dinner, and sends Mayor Strong a statement on how disorderly houses are being closed.

summary: Roosevelt is in New York City, where his fight at the Police Board goes on. Nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Lunch aboard the Montgomery
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie he has met Earl Spencer, complains of petty quarrels with Fitch and Parker, and describes lunch on Harry Davis' ship Montgomery off Staten Island. The guest book notes the house opened for the season.

headline: Grant joins Parker's boycott
summary: Parker has won over Commissioner Frederick Grant, who now stays away from board meetings too.

headline: Evidence of Parker's graft
summary: Roosevelt uncovers graft by Parker and takes it to Mayor Strong, who writes Parker. Parker will not step down.

headline: Kermit in overalls
summary: Roosevelt paints Bamie a picture of the boys' outfits, above all Kermit in blue overalls Edith sewed to look just like the hired man's, plus a cap, battered tennis shoes and gloves over poisoned hands, tumbling head over heels.

headline: No entry for the day
summary: Nothing is recorded for this day.

headline: Dinner at the Claremont
summary: Roosevelt dines at the Hotel Claremont.

headline: Two thousand police on parade
summary: Roosevelt reviews the yearly police parade from Fifth Avenue at 40th Street as some 2,000 officers march. Word reaches the papers that Parker was told to quit.

headline: Doubts about Parker
summary: In New York Roosevelt tells Bamie he cannot vouch for Commissioner Parker's honesty with money.

summary: Roosevelt attends the regular meeting of the Police Board.

summary: Mrs. Clifford Richardson signs the guest book.

headline: Guest: Commander Davis
summary: Commander Davis is recorded in the guest book.

headline: Formal charges against Parker
summary: Roosevelt prepares formal charges against Commissioner Parker.

headline: Parker goes on trial
summary: The trial of Commissioner Parker opens, with Elihu Root prosecuting, General Benjamin Tracy for the defense, and Mayor Strong sitting as judge.

headline: The Parker trial goes on
summary: Proceedings continue in New York City in the case against Commissioner Andrew Parker.

headline: No entry for the day
summary: Nothing is recorded for this day.

headline: Edith stayed in town for him
summary: Roosevelt heads out to Sagamore Hill only to learn that Edith had remained in the city to keep him company. He confides to Bamie his worries about national politics and his distrust of McKinley's backbone.

headline: Republicans gather in St. Louis
summary: Republicans open their national convention in St. Louis, with William McKinley, Tom Reed and Governor Levi Morton in the running.

headline: McKinley wins on the first ballot
summary: In St. Louis the Republicans make McKinley their nominee in a single ballot, with 661½ votes. Roosevelt is in New York City.

headline: The Parker trial goes on
summary: Proceedings continue in New York City in the case against Commissioner Andrew Parker.

headline: First swim of the summer
summary: At Sagamore Hill the family takes its first swim of the season, and Alice trots and canters on her horse Diamond. Roosevelt writes Will Cowles.

headline: Content with St. Louis
summary: Grace Potter is a guest at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt tells Bamie he is fairly pleased with how the convention turned out.

headline: The Parker trial goes on
summary: Proceedings continue in New York City in the case against Commissioner Andrew Parker.

headline: Guest: Bertha Potter
summary: Bertha Potter visits Sagamore Hill.

headline: Warming to McKinley
summary: Roosevelt writes Bellamy Storer that the party platform is excellent and that McKinley will make both a strong candidate and a good President.

headline: Children in the hired man's garb
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie how hard his job has become, then turns to the children: Ted and Kermit dressed like farmhands and happily dirty, Ethel chubby, Archie sweet, and Alice the best of big sisters.

headline: A tedious trial
summary: The Parker trial continues, and Roosevelt finds it deadly boring.

headline: Out of shape in Geneseo
summary: Roosevelt and Edith travel to Austin Wadsworth's in Geneseo, New York, where riding leaves him aching all over.

headline: A tumble over a fence
summary: Riding at Geneseo, Roosevelt goes over a fence and falls.

headline: The Parker trial goes on
summary: Proceedings continue in New York City in the case against Commissioner Andrew Parker.

headline: The Parker trial ends
summary: The case against Commissioner Parker comes to a close.

headline: Bryan nominated; TR on his nerves
summary: The Democrats in Chicago nominate William Jennings Bryan for President. Roosevelt writes Fanny Parsons about the nervousness she, Edith and Corinne noticed in him before the Mayor's committee and in Albany.

headline: Guest: Nellie Tyler
summary: Nellie Tyler signs the guest book.

headline: Still waiting on the mayor
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie that Mayor Strong has not yet ruled on Parker, and that Strong hopes Parker has learned from the episode.

headline: Guest: Grant La Farge
summary: Architect Grant La Farge appears in the guest book.

headline: "Parker is still in"
summary: Roosevelt tells Lodge Parker keeps his seat, and scoffs at the wild scene at the Democrats' Chicago convention.

headline: Correcting the Daily Mail
summary: Roosevelt writes S. J. Pryor to correct a false London Daily Mail story about New York police and visitors to the city. Bob Ferguson is a guest.

headline: Fireworks a little late
summary: Jacob Riis visits Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt rows Edith out on the bay, and the family throws a delayed Fourth of July party with the children and fireworks.

headline: Riis stays the weekend
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie that their friend Riis is passing Sunday with the family at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Phillips and young Corinne visit
summary: Hallett Phillips and Roosevelt's niece Corinne Robinson are listed as guests.

headline: Dinner with Riis and Stephen Crane
summary: Colonel Andrews is a guest at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt tells Bamie he had dinner the week before with Stephen Crane and Jacob Riis, and sizes up the McKinley-Bryan race.

headline: Meeting Mark Hanna
summary: Roosevelt calls on Mark Hanna, McKinley's campaign manager, at the Waldorf, and that evening has a private dinner with Hanna and two executive committee members.

headline: Politics and books
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge about politics and literature.

headline: Handling Hanna
summary: Roosevelt advises Lodge that Hanna needs careful handling, and hopes Lodge's son Bay will publish "The Wave."

headline: Wishing Reed were the nominee
summary: Roosevelt tells Tom Reed he wishes Reed, not McKinley, were heading the ticket.

headline: The Storers come to Sagamore Hill
summary: Bellamy and Maria Storer, friends of Roosevelt's from his Washington years, arrive as houseguests at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Rowing the Storers around Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt takes his guests out on the water and confides to Maria Storer, a well-connected Washington lobbyist close to McKinley and Mark Hanna, that he wants the Navy's number-two job. He also writes Bamie about meeting Hanna.

headline: Storers still visiting
summary: The Storers remain at Sagamore Hill. The record notes that William McKinley owes the couple $10,000.

headline: Family news for Spring-Rice
summary: From the city, Roosevelt sends Cecil Spring-Rice a long letter: Ted is picking up shooting, Alice has grown as tall as Edith, Kermit is out of his brace and squabbling with Ethel. He also muses at length on race and nationality.

headline: Edith turns 35
summary: Roosevelt's wife Edith celebrates her 35th birthday.

headline: John Elliott visits
summary: John Elliott signs in as a guest at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Gordon Cummings visits
summary: A Mr. Gordon Cummings is the day's guest at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Ready to take the Navy post
summary: Roosevelt writes both Bellamy and Maria Storer that, if the Navy's assistant secretaryship comes his way, he should take it.

headline: Bryan's Garden rally goes badly for police
summary: William Jennings Bryan launches his presidential bid at Madison Square Garden, and the city police, Roosevelt's department, handle the crowd poorly.

headline: Ethel turns 5
summary: Roosevelt's daughter Ethel celebrates her fifth birthday.

headline: Heat wave and plans to head west
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie he is going west while Edith and the children summer at Lake Champlain. The city is sweltering, horses are dying in the streets, and police are handing out ice to the poor.

headline: Cockran's gold speech, police redeemed
summary: At Madison Square Garden, Bourke Cockran argues for gold, and this time the police manage the crowd well after the Bryan fiasco. Roosevelt writes Lodge about the anti-Platt Republicans.

headline: Shouting match with Parker
summary: A police board session turns into an open clash, with Roosevelt and fellow commissioner Andrew Parker yelling at each other.

headline: Off to Medora with a new rifle
summary: Roosevelt heads west for the Badlands, carrying a new Winchester that fires smokeless powder.

headline: On the western trip
summary: Roosevelt is away in the West; the record gives no details for the day.

summary: While Roosevelt is still out west, the Chinese statesman Li Hung-chang visits New York and is greeted by Police Commissioner Frederick Grant.

summary: Roosevelt writes Kermit from the prairie: six hours out after pronghorn, dinner eaten in the wagon's shade, his gun cleaned, a bath in a pool nearby, and nights spent fully dressed inside a buffalo-hide sleeping bag.

headline: On the western trip
summary: Roosevelt is in the West; the record has nothing more for the day.

headline: Ted starts at the Cove School
summary: Back home, nine-year-old Ted enrolls at Oyster Bay's single-room Cove School, where most classmates are children of local gardeners, groundskeepers and valets.

headline: Hunting in Dakota
summary: Roosevelt is hunting in the Dakota country.

headline: Home from the ranch
summary: Roosevelt gets back to New York City after his time at his Dakota ranch.

headline: Speech to the Sound Money League
summary: Roosevelt addresses the Sound Money League and, in a letter to publisher George Haven Putnam, wishes people would see him more broadly as a historian.

headline: Ted's ninth birthday and first gun
summary: For Ted's ninth birthday, Roosevelt presents the boy with a Flobert rifle, his first firearm, and tries it out by shooting into the ceiling. He tells Bamie the western cattle are struggling and that he bagged five antelope.

headline: Platt men and British critics
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge that the Republican nominee for governor, Frank Black, belongs to Platt, and describes his battles with Parker and the Grand Army veterans. British reviewers, he adds, have bristled at his remarks about Britain in volume four of his Winning of the West.

headline: Send-off dinner for Emlen and Christine
summary: Uncle Jim and Aunt Lizzie host a farewell dinner for their son Emlen Roosevelt and his wife Christine.

headline: Campaign notes from the barn
summary: Roosevelt sends Bamie a campaign update, noting McKinley is running his race from his Ohio front porch, and reports romps with the children in the old barn.

headline: Corinne turns 35
summary: Roosevelt's sister Corinne marks her 35th birthday. He writes Bamie, who is in Scotland.

headline: Stumping for McKinley upstate
summary: Roosevelt campaigns for McKinley across upstate New York, from Utica to Buffalo.

headline: Calling on McKinley in Canton
summary: Roosevelt and Lodge travel to Canton, Ohio, to see McKinley at his home.

headline: Packed halls and a cool reception
summary: Roosevelt boasts to Bamie that his upstate rallies overflowed, but admits McKinley, though friendly, does not count him and Lodge among his favorites.

headline: Political letter to Henry White
summary: Roosevelt writes diplomat Henry White on political matters.

headline: Bryan and free silver
summary: Roosevelt writes Spring-Rice about Bryan and the silver question that splits the 1896 race, with Bryan for silver and McKinley for gold.

headline: Kermit turns 7
summary: Roosevelt's son Kermit celebrates his seventh birthday.

headline: Eleanor turns 12
summary: Roosevelt's niece Eleanor has her 12th birthday, and he writes to Bamie.

headline: Full house at the Chicago Coliseum
summary: Roosevelt fills the Chicago Coliseum with a speech for McKinley and sound money, part of a swing across the Midwest.

headline: First color comics in the Journal
summary: The New York Journal runs the first color comic strips. Nothing is recorded for Roosevelt himself.

headline: Morristown rally and an election forecast
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Morristown, New Jersey, then back in New York writes Lodge about how the election looks.

headline: Confident of a Republican win
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie he expects the Republicans to carry the election.

headline: Wilmington speech in a busy week
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Wilmington, Delaware, one stop in a week of McKinley rallies across Maryland, Pennsylvania and New Jersey.

headline: The Lamberts visit
summary: Dr. Alexander Lambert and his wife are guests at Sagamore Hill, and Roosevelt writes Bamie.

headline: Roosevelt turns 38
summary: Roosevelt marks his 38th birthday.

headline: Bread, coins and a copycat speech
summary: Roosevelt makes the case for gold using loaves of varying size plus gold and silver coins to make his point. At Sagamore Hill, Ted copies his father with an unplanned speech to the household staff on the back porch.

headline: James K. Gracie visits
summary: Roosevelt's uncle James K. Gracie is a guest at Sagamore Hill.

headline: McKinley wins; Alice waits up
summary: McKinley takes the White House by more than 600,000 votes, and Republicans capture both houses of Congress. With no telephone at Sagamore Hill, the news comes by carriage, while Alice creeps out of bed to listen from the stair landing.

headline: Thanking Frederick Jackson Turner
summary: Roosevelt tells historian Frederick Jackson Turner he enjoyed Turner's review of his Winning of the West, while standing by the book's criticism of Jefferson. He also writes editor Albert Shaw of the Review of Reviews.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Glad the election is won
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie of his relief at the Republican victory.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: Another quiet day at Sagamore Hill with nothing further noted.

headline: Victory party with the money men
summary: Roosevelt joins Mark Hanna and wealthy Republicans to celebrate the win, though he is disgusted by how McKinley was marketed to voters.

headline: Gracie visits again
summary: James K. Gracie is once more a guest.

headline: Write more often, Bamie
summary: Roosevelt chides Bamie for sending so few letters and urges her to come home to the United States before long.

headline: Should he go to Canton?
summary: Bertha Potter is a guest. Roosevelt asks Bellamy Storer whether he ought to visit President-elect McKinley in Canton.

headline: Bob Ferguson arrives
summary: Roosevelt's friend Bob Ferguson is a guest.

headline: Jacob Riis and family friends visit
summary: Jacob Riis and his wife are guests, along with Morton Procter.

headline: Bamie's first anniversary
summary: Roosevelt's sister Bamie marks one year of marriage.

headline: Thanksgiving trail clearing
summary: On Thanksgiving, Roosevelt, Bob Ferguson and Ted shoulder axes for a ten-mile tramp, cutting the bridle path clear as they go.

headline: Lodge pleads his case in Ohio
summary: Roosevelt reports to Bamie that Lodge has met McKinley in Ohio to push for him, and that McKinley hopes Roosevelt has no fixed ideas about appointments.

headline: Checking up on Little Egypt
summary: Roosevelt and Jacob Riis look into a burlesque show by the dancer known as Little Egypt at Clarendon Hall, which had drawn many complaints over her skimpy costume.

headline: Ten years married
summary: Roosevelt and Edith celebrate their tenth wedding anniversary. Edith tells Spring-Rice that Ted is thriving among his Cove School classmates and will miss them once Alice's governess takes over in town.

headline: Lunch with Dana; Hawaii and Cuba
summary: Roosevelt lunches with General Wilson and editor Charles A. Dana, and writes Lodge hoping McKinley will act firmly on Hawaii and Cuba.

headline: The Navy job again
summary: Roosevelt writes Maria Storer about the assistant secretaryship of the Navy.

headline: Maceo killed; help for an honest officer
summary: Spanish forces kill the Cuban rebel general Antonio Maceo, and Americans clamor for intervention. Roosevelt asks Dr. Matthew Beattie to testify for an honest policeman facing trial.

headline: Platt asks to see him
summary: Roosevelt tells Elihu Root that Boss Platt wants a meeting.

headline: A polite note from McKinley
summary: President-elect McKinley sends Roosevelt a courteous reply acknowledging Storer's visit on his behalf, and Roosevelt thanks Lodge for working to land him the Navy post.

headline: Staying away from Canton
summary: Roosevelt tells Maria Storer he has decided against a visit to McKinley in Canton.

headline: Board meetings and Edith's Christmas letter
summary: Roosevelt attends a meeting with the mayor and a police board session. A letter from Edith to Bamie paints the family's Christmas morning: Archie bundled in her blue shawl, Bob in a sofa blanket, Theodore in his old brocade robe, and big presents opened in the Gun Room.

headline: Talking Cuba with Lodge
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge about an interview on Cuba.

headline: Last police board session of 1896
summary: The police board holds its final meeting of the year.

headline: No day record, only bibliography
summary: The source page for this date holds bibliography and editorial notes rather than any account of Roosevelt's day.

headline: A Review of Reviews essay and a book review
summary: Roosevelt's article "How Not to Better Social Conditions" runs in the Review of Reviews, and he reviews Brooks Adams's The Law of Civilization and Decay. Meanwhile newspapers fault the reform police board as powerless.

headline: A Cuba Libre man
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie he backs Cuban independence and would like to see Spain driven out. A thaw at Sagamore Hill has ended the skiing.

headline: Defending his stand against Platt
summary: Roosevelt writes Albert Shaw defending his opposition to Platt and praising departing Governor Levi Morton.

headline: Done with board squabbles
summary: Roosevelt declares he will stop joining the police board's quarrels, and sends Bamie his frank views of diplomat Henry White.

headline: Police at the cab strike
summary: During a city cab strike, Roosevelt tells Jacob Baucsh that peaceful strikers have nothing to fear from police. He also hears via Lodge that Cornelius Bliss would take him as assistant if Bliss gets the Navy.

headline: Platt wins the Senate caucus
summary: New York Republicans nominate Thomas Platt for the U.S. Senate by 147 votes to 7. Platt asks who backed Joseph Choate and later makes those men pay; Roosevelt had stayed in Platt's camp.

headline: In town at Madison Avenue
summary: The family is at 689 Madison Avenue in New York; nothing more is noted.

headline: Tea with Mahan and Lounsbury
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie that Thomas Lounsbury and Alfred Thayer Mahan came to tea, and that he dislikes John Sherman as McKinley's pick for Secretary of State.

headline: Bamie turns 42
summary: Roosevelt's sister Bamie has her 42nd birthday.

headline: Platt goes to the Senate
summary: The legislature sends Thomas Platt to Washington as New York's U.S. Senator.

headline: Speaking at Annapolis
summary: Roosevelt gives an address at the U.S. Naval Academy.

headline: Letter to Bamie
summary: Roosevelt writes his sister Bamie.

headline: Correcting the Sun on immigration
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge that he has set the New York Sun straight after it claimed he favors open immigration.

headline: Dancing class, Selous, and a campfire story
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie the children are taking dancing lessons in the city, Ted is staying with Corinne, and Kermit dreads his father ending up a street sweeper. A letter has come from the hunter Frederick Selous, and a Boone and Crockett Club volume edited by George Bird Grinnell appears with Roosevelt's piece "On the Little Missouri."

headline: Defending police hiring in print
summary: Roosevelt's letter to William Sanger defending the board's hiring and other practices is printed in the New York Sun.

headline: Alice turns 13
summary: Roosevelt's daughter Alice has her 13th birthday.

headline: Yes to the Navy, no to London
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie he would take the Navy post if offered, and that a visit to her in London is impossible.

headline: Work near intolerable
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie that John Hay will be ambassador to Britain and that his own police work has grown almost unbearable amid new fights, corruption flare-ups and resignation threats. His board record includes tougher fitness standards for recruits, a lower age limit, civil-service exams, a standard .32 Colt revolver, and required courtesy from officers.

headline: Strong regrets Parker
summary: Mayor Strong now regrets putting Parker on the board but has no authority to remove him. Roosevelt sends Thomas Lounsbury a letter on spelling and books.

headline: McKinley inaugurated
summary: William McKinley takes the oath as the 25th President in Washington.

headline: Letter to Bamie
summary: Roosevelt writes his sister Bamie.

headline: Too busy to think of the Navy
summary: Roosevelt tells Henry White that board fights consume him and leave scant time to dwell on the Navy job.

headline: A barbed line about Grant
summary: Roosevelt vents to Lounsbury about fellow commissioner Frederick Grant, likening his mind to some tree-dwelling forebear.

headline: Board at a standstill
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge that Parker and Grant have stalled all board business, and he sees no hope for the Navy appointment.

headline: Thanks to Henry White
summary: Roosevelt thanks Henry White for helping his bid for the Navy post.

headline: Blaming the machine
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie he thinks Grant and Parker are tangling police business on orders from the Republican machine.

headline: Strong fires Parker
summary: Mayor Strong removes Commissioner Parker for neglect of duty, based on charges from the previous summer, pending the governor's approval.

headline: Socialists and anarchists
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge about socialists and anarchists.

headline: Platt won't block him
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie he doubts the appointment will happen, plans to leave 689 Madison by late April, and wants her home. He reports to Lodge that Platt will not stand in his way.

headline: Writing to Secretary Long
summary: Roosevelt tells Lodge he will write John D. Long, McKinley's choice to run the Navy, about the assistant's job.

headline: A way to get him out of New York
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge that machine politicians see the Navy job mainly as a means of removing him from New York.

headline: Worried for the police board
summary: Roosevelt shares his worries about the police board's future with Lodge.

headline: Who will replace him?
summary: Roosevelt tells Lodge he has discussed his own successor on the police board with Mayor Strong.

headline: Platt gives way
summary: Lodge and others press Roosevelt's case in Washington. Platt drops his resistance, reasoning Roosevelt will do less harm there than in New York, while McKinley, anxious to avoid war, worries about Roosevelt's hawkish talk on Cuba.

headline: Nominated to the Navy Department
summary: McKinley picks Roosevelt to be the Navy's assistant secretary, at a salary of $4,500, and sends the nomination to the Senate. Roosevelt crows to Lodge with a line from the Arabian Nights.

headline: Senate confirms him
summary: The Senate approves Roosevelt for the Navy post. Parker laughs long over what he calls Roosevelt's retreat. Roosevelt writes Lodge about remarks linking him with John Altgeld printed in the Sun.

headline: Archie turns 3
summary: Roosevelt's son Archie celebrates his third birthday.

headline: Happy, but no London trip
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie that he is delighted by the appointment, though sorry it means he cannot join her in London.

headline: Japan sends a cruiser to Hawaii
summary: Japan dispatches a cruiser toward Hawaii, a hedge against the United States moving to annex them.

headline: Stockmen re-elect their chairman
summary: Roosevelt is chosen again to chair the Little Missouri Stockmen's Association.

headline: Glad to be leaving
summary: Roosevelt writes Henry White that he is relieved to leave the police board, having done all he could. Frank Moss becomes board president. Parker was never removed and later resigned, the one opponent Roosevelt never bested.

headline: A quiet last board meeting
summary: At Roosevelt's final police board meeting, Parker and Grant stay away, so there is no quorum and no vote of thanks; Chief Conlin leaves without a farewell. Roosevelt sends Mayor Strong his formal resignation.

headline: Thanks to Jacob Riis
summary: Roosevelt writes Jacob Riis a warm thank-you for two years of support.

headline: First day at the Navy Department
summary: Roosevelt starts work as the Navy's second-in-command under Secretary John D. Long, 58, and moves in with Lodge in Washington. He thanks Captain Bowman McCalla for his congratulations.

headline: Thank-you notes all round
summary: Roosevelt answers well-wishers William Mantius, Governor Hugh Thompson and William Fitch, and lets William Trent know he has gone through Trent's study of Southern leaders.

headline: At work in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington at his new Navy post; nothing specific is recorded.

headline: Briefing McKinley on Hawaii
summary: Roosevelt alerts President McKinley that Japan has sent a cruiser to Hawaii and lists the American warships nearby.

headline: At work in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington at his new Navy post; nothing specific is recorded.

headline: Fleet readiness memo
summary: Roosevelt writes a memorandum on fleet preparedness that tucks in four warnings about trouble over Cuba, and writes both McKinley and Long about sending ships to the Mediterranean.

headline: A summer away from the family
summary: Roosevelt writes Spring-Rice, now posted with the British diplomats in Germany, lamenting that he will see little of Edith and the children this summer.

headline: Sagamore Hill reopens
summary: The guest book marks the opening of Sagamore Hill for the season. In Washington, Roosevelt writes Lincoln Steffens about the police board, Speck von Sternberg about his new job, and Frank Moss praising his early work as board president.

headline: Corinne's 15th anniversary
summary: In Washington, Roosevelt notes his sister Corinne's 15th wedding anniversary.

headline: Settling in among the expansionists
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie, Hamlin Garland, Henry White and Francis Lowell; Will Cowles has a berth on the cruiser Topeka through his help. His article on scientific naming appears in Science. With the old Henry Adams circle scattered, he starts dining nearly every day at the Metropolitan Club with Mahan, Dewey, Wood and other expansionists.

headline: Claiming Gustavus Fox's old desk
summary: Roosevelt digs up the Civil War desk of an earlier assistant secretary, Gustavus Fox, carved with Monitors, warships and flags, and has it moved into his office. Bamie's ship arrives in New York.

headline: A day at the Navy Department
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; no particular business is recorded for the day.

headline: Annex Hawaii tomorrow
summary: Roosevelt tells Alfred Thayer Mahan he would take Hawaii at once if it were up to him. He also writes John Hay that he misses him and is waiting for Lodge to come by for a walk.

headline: A day at the Navy Department
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; no particular business is recorded for the day.

summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; no particular business is recorded for the day.

summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; no particular business is recorded for the day.

headline: Missing home
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie he enjoys Will's letters and longs for Sagamore Hill, Edith and the children. Mrs. Hilborne Roosevelt and Miss Dorothy Roosevelt are recorded as guests.

headline: Sparring with Merriam over species
summary: At the Biological Society of Washington, Roosevelt debates C. Hart Merriam of the Biological Survey over how to classify species and subspecies. He writes Richard Henry Dana opposing stacked turrets on new battleships and tells General James Wilson he won't raise Wilson's case with McKinley today, having pestered the President enough lately.

headline: A day at the Navy Department
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; no particular business is recorded for the day.

headline: Torpedo boat trip and a baby on the way
summary: Roosevelt rides a torpedo boat and writes Taft that Willie Phillips died in a boating accident. Edith tells her sister Emily to expect a new niece or nephew in early December.

summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; no particular business is recorded for the day.

summary: Roosevelt offers John Merritt ideas for new stamp designs, writes Chanler again on Hawaii, writes Richard Wainwright about a picture of himself, and tells C. Whitney Tillinghast he is ready to fight Spain.

headline: Sails give way to steam
summary: On Christmas Eve Roosevelt writes Captain Charles Sigsbee about the Navy giving up sail power for good, and Carl Schurz on civil service. He again tells General Tillinghast he will go to war if it comes.

headline: Christmas dinner with the Lodges
summary: Roosevelt and Edith bring Alice, Ted and Kermit to Christmas dinner at the home of Henry Cabot Lodge.

headline: Praise for Remington's West
summary: Roosevelt compliments Frederic Remington on his writing about the West.

headline: Thanks to Secretary Long
summary: Roosevelt thanks Navy Secretary John D. Long for a supportive note and covers Navy business.

headline: Writing on American game animals
summary: The year-end record notes Roosevelt's eleven articles on American game animals for a British sporting encyclopedia, on subjects ranging from the bison and wapiti to the puma, peccary, pronghorn and wolf.

headline: New Year's thanks to Bamie
summary: Roosevelt thanks Bamie for a gift book that was just what he wanted, reports that Edith is starting to look well again, and tucks in notes from Ted and Kermit.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Promising to behave
summary: Roosevelt assures Secretary Long that he means to be 'good' and avoid saying or doing anything embarrassing.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: A long letter to Kipling
summary: Roosevelt discusses the Navy personnel legislation with Edwin Godkin and Senator Eugene Hale on Navy matters, and sends Rudyard Kipling news of the New York police, politics, the Navy and the family.

headline: Edith sick again
summary: Edith falls ill with the grippe once more. The younger children are sent to stay with friends, and a trained nurse comes into the house.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Missing the Boone and Crockett dinner
summary: Because Edith is ill with neuralgia pains, Roosevelt tells Grant La Farge he must miss the yearly dinner of the Boone and Crockett Club.

headline: A letter to Bamie
summary: Roosevelt writes his sister Bamie.

headline: Advice for the new police chief
summary: Roosevelt discusses the pending Navy personnel legislation with Ira Hollis and offers guidance to John McCullagh, newly named chief of the city's police force.

headline: Naval retirement
summary: Roosevelt writes Francis Higginson about the Personnel Bill and retirement rules for naval officers.

headline: Maine ordered toward Cuba
summary: Rioting erupts in Havana, and the battleship U.S.S. Maine is sent from Key West toward Cuba. Roosevelt writes Admiral William Kirkland about admirals and tells Captain Caspar Goodrich he gives his weekends to the children.

headline: Seeking an Army commission
summary: Secretary Long brushes off Roosevelt's warnings about war with Spain. With Edith still ill, possibly with typhoid, Roosevelt writes Francis Greene and Adjutant General Tillinghast about getting a commission if war comes.

headline: Concentrate the fleet
summary: Roosevelt urges Secretary Long to get ready for war with Spain by pulling the battle fleet together, and Long goes along.

headline: Trouble with Boutelle
summary: Roosevelt tells Captain Bowman McCalla that Charles Boutelle, who chairs the House Naval Affairs Committee, dislikes him.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Ted worn down; dreaming of the hunt
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie that Ted has broken down from nervous strain and that he cannot attend the Boone and Crockett dinner. He writes Speck von Sternberg on Cuba, confesses to Selous he longs to slip away after big game, and discusses naval moves against Spain with Charles Davis.

headline: Bamie's birthday
summary: Roosevelt's sister Bamie turns 43.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: A sick household and a tax tangle
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie that Ted and Edith are worse and Kermit is sick too. He writes Emlen Roosevelt, C. Rockland Tyng and Douglas Robinson about his taxes: a steep Oyster Bay assessment pushed him to claim New York City residence, where the bill came in even higher. By evening Edith is better, though Ted is not.

headline: Planning more Winning of the West
summary: Roosevelt writes George Haven Putnam about adding two more volumes to his frontier history.

headline: Worried about Cuba policy
summary: Roosevelt confides to Captain Robley Evans his fear that the McKinley administration is following the previous one's line on Cuba.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: The Maine reaches Havana
summary: The U.S.S. Maine steams into Havana harbor on an official 'courtesy call'; no welcome is offered, but the rioting has ended. Roosevelt writes Bamie that Edith is so ill she must wean the baby.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: A letter to Bamie
summary: Roosevelt writes his sister Bamie.

headline: Breakfast with the Lamberts
summary: Roosevelt has breakfast with the Lamberts and Avery Andrews.

headline: Oyster Bay taxes
summary: Roosevelt writes Franklin Hall about his tax bill at Oyster Bay.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Edith's fever holds at 101
summary: Edith's temperature stays at 101 degrees and Ted is too sick to be moved. Lodge warns that Cuba could blow up any day. Roosevelt writes his cousin James Roosevelt about his taxes and the illnesses at home.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Learning to ski
summary: Roosevelt tells Frederick Selous about the cold snap in Washington and confesses he has taken up skiing, which he finds great sport.

headline: Setting the bar for club membership
summary: Roosevelt writes the London firm Rowland Ward about hunting books, and spells out for William Wadsworth what it takes to join the Boone and Crockett Club.

headline: Wary of Germany
summary: In a letter to Frank Moore, Roosevelt names Germany as the European power most hostile to the United States, with France and England not far behind.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: College men in politics
summary: Roosevelt writes Thomas R. Woodrow about why educated college graduates belong in public life.

headline: Torpedo tubes and monitors
summary: Roosevelt writes Secretary Long about fitting battleships with torpedo tubes, and Robert Johnson about ironclads and monitors.

headline: The de Lôme letter sets him off
summary: Hearst's New York Journal prints a private letter from Spanish minister Enrique Dupuy de Lôme that mocks President McKinley as weak. Roosevelt is furious and eager for war. At a dinner party he lectures Mark Hanna and a Miss Adler so energetically that one sweeping gesture tears her dress.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Alice turns 14
summary: Roosevelt's daughter Alice celebrates her 14th birthday in Washington.

headline: Alice goes to Bamie's
summary: Alice is sent off to New York City to live with her aunt Bamie.

headline: A warning about Germany
summary: Roosevelt writes Charles Moore about possible alliances with Russia, England or Germany, cautioning especially against Germany.

headline: The Maine explodes in Havana
summary: At 9:40 that night the battleship Maine explodes in Havana harbor; 260 of her crew die at once and six more later. The sensational papers clamor for war while much of the country seems unmoved. Roosevelt calls it treachery. He also writes Selous, wishing he could get away, and Edith writes her sister Emily Carow.

headline: Where to send the ships
summary: The day after the Maine disaster, Roosevelt writes Secretary Long about deploying American warships, and writes Benjamin Diblee about Harvard's Porcellian Club.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Torpedo boats
summary: Roosevelt writes Secretary Long about torpedo boats.

headline: A father's regret
summary: Doctors find that Ted's nervous exhaustion comes from being pushed too hard by his father. Roosevelt tells Bamie that Edith is still very ill and vows not to press Ted again. He also writes Long about the Maine inquiry and calls for more battleships.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Defending the Navy's existence
summary: Roosevelt fires back at J. E. Myers, who had argued that the country should do away with its Navy altogether.

headline: A worrying swelling
summary: Edith notices a swelling low in her abdomen.

headline: Piano and bicycle for Alice?
summary: Roosevelt writes his brother-in-law Will Cowles about the Maine and Edith's illness, discusses books with William Trent, and asks Bamie whether he should ship Alice's piano and bicycle to New York.

headline: A bogus interview
summary: Roosevelt writes Assistant Secretary of State William R. Day about a made-up 'interview' with him printed in New York newspapers.

headline: The cable to Dewey
summary: With Secretary Long away for the afternoon, Roosevelt runs the Navy Department and cables Commodore Dewey to gather his squadron at Hong Kong, keep coaling, and be ready to strike the Spanish in the Philippines if war comes. He orders ships everywhere to fill their bunkers. He also brings in Dr. William Osler to examine Edith.

headline: Long returns to the office
summary: Secretary Long comes back to work, grumbling in his diary that Roosevelt nearly set off a bigger blast than the Maine in his absence. Still, Long cancels none of the orders Roosevelt sent.

headline: Osler urges surgery
summary: Dr. Osler finds Edith critically ill with an abscess in the psoas muscle and advises operating at once, but Roosevelt wants further opinions first.

headline: Alice and the boys of Washington
summary: Roosevelt writes Charles O'Neil about the Maine inquiry. Alice, who had been leading a crowd of admiring boys around Washington, frets at first at Bamie's in New York, then takes to the city's social life so well she refuses to come back.

headline: How Germans become Americans
summary: Roosevelt compliments Ernest Bruncken on his pamphlet How Germans Become Americans.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Edith still very ill
summary: Roosevelt tells Douglas Robinson that Edith remains seriously sick, and goes over his tax troubles.

headline: Lessons of the Maine
summary: Roosevelt writes naval historian William Clowes, then in Switzerland, about the Maine disaster and readiness for war.

headline: A second opinion on Edith
summary: A gynecologist examines Edith and agrees with Dr. Osler's diagnosis.

headline: Drifting toward war
summary: Roosevelt tells Douglas Robinson the country is moving toward war, though McKinley will try to avoid it. He writes Bamie about Edith's planned operation and Bradley Johnson about the Navy.

headline: Edith's operation succeeds
summary: Roosevelt at last agrees to surgery, and doctors successfully remove the abscess near Edith's hip.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Fifty million for defense
summary: At McKinley's request Congress votes $50 million to build up the armed forces. Roosevelt writes John Roosevelt about moving his legal residence to Washington for tax reasons, tells Charles Davis he will fight if war comes, asks Tillinghast about raising a regiment, and writes Henry White about the Maine.

headline: A slow recovery
summary: Edith's surgical wound is left open to drain, and she stays very sick for weeks. Roosevelt writes Mahan about Hawaii.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: The Navy budget
summary: Roosevelt writes Secretary Long about the Navy Department's budget.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Fake photos and a hunting invitation
summary: Roosevelt tells Bradley Johnson he hopes to join him for some hunting, writes Mahan on war preparations, and writes wildlife photographer A. G. Wallihan about faked pictures.

headline: Aching for the front
summary: Roosevelt tells Senator William Chandler he will be miserable if kept at a desk while others fight, and writes General Francis Greene that he hopes to see combat.

headline: A war plan for Mahan
summary: Roosevelt fears to Bamie that McKinley is set on peace. He writes Robley Evans on the Navy and lays out a plan of campaign against Spain for Mahan.

headline: Proctor's Cuba speech
summary: Back from Cuba, Senator Redfield Proctor of Vermont tells the Senate what he saw and calls for American armed intervention. Roosevelt writes journalist Walter Wellman about Robert Peary's Arctic plans.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Sabotage finding expected
summary: President McKinley learns that the Maine inquiry will conclude the ship was destroyed from outside.

headline: Sworn a Washington resident
summary: Roosevelt signs an affidavit that he is a Washington resident to escape New York City taxes. He tells Brooks Adams that Edith is slowly recovering and that it is not too late to intervene in Cuba, and sends Mahan ideas on war with Spain.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: White hulls turn gray
summary: The Navy orders its ships repainted from peacetime white to battle gray. Roosevelt writes Mahan about warships.

headline: Langley's flying machine
summary: Spain's minister is told his country's rule in Cuba can no longer be tolerated. Roosevelt asks Long about resigning, and tells him of Professor Samuel Langley's flying experiments on the Potomac, which fascinate him.

headline: Challenging Hanna at the Gridiron Club
summary: Speaking after dinner at Washington's Gridiron Club, Roosevelt openly takes on Senator Mark Hanna's caution about Spain. He asks William Chanler if he can raise a regiment, and tells Tillinghast that trouble with Spain is near.

headline: Walking and plotting with Wood
summary: Roosevelt writes Ted, now with Bamie and Alice in New York, about a hard walk with Dr. Leonard Wood spent figuring out how they might both join the army bound for Cuba.

headline: The Maine report goes public
summary: The Maine report is made public. Roosevelt objects to Paul Dana about false stories in the Journal, tells his sister Conie he is worked to the limit, and writes William Tudor that America's inaction since the explosion is humiliating.

headline: Weighing what war would mean
summary: In a reflective letter to William Sturgis Bigelow, Roosevelt considers the consequences of war. He tells Will Cowles he is disgusted with foreign policy and hopes the Senate, led by men like Lodge, will demand Cuban independence. He also writes Dr. Alexander Lambert about not pressing Ted.

headline: Telling the President to his face
summary: Spain accepts every point of McKinley's ultimatum except an armistice. Roosevelt reports to Will Cowles that he urged armed intervention in front of the President and Cabinet. He writes Henry White and Douglas Robinson on Cuba, and Long about Langley's flying machine.

headline: Spain out of the hemisphere
summary: Roosevelt applauds Senator William Frye of Maine for his work on Cuba, writes John Roosevelt about his legal residence, and tells James Bryce that Spain should be pushed out of the Western Hemisphere.

headline: Two days in command
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie he would give anything for two days in full charge, and tells Dr. Alexander Lambert, Ted's physician, that he must fight if war comes.

headline: Resisting Douglas Robinson's advice
summary: Douglas Robinson has urged Roosevelt not to join the fighting, but Roosevelt answers that duty tells him to go. He also tells P. Lee Phillips he will not need maps and writes Long about men seeking to return to service.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Edith surprises him at the club
summary: McKinley drafts a war message. Roosevelt writes William Wadsworth about getting into a regiment and General Benjamin Tracy on why war must come. Edith, much improved, hires a carriage to the Metropolitan Club and has Leonard Wood call him outside; Roosevelt is overjoyed to see her up.

headline: Against 'peace at any price'
summary: Roosevelt writes Robert Bacon, William Tudor and Elihu Root about the looming war, scorning those who want peace at any cost.

headline: Diplomacy has run out
summary: Roosevelt tells Dr. Henry Jackson that diplomacy has done all it can and rejects Jackson's call for peace at any cost.

headline: McKinley warns off the powers
summary: Roosevelt wants Cuba freed from harsh Spanish rule. McKinley meets envoys of six major powers and makes clear he will not accept interference over Cuba. Roosevelt writes Wadsworth about a volunteer regiment.

headline: Fight for a free Cuba
summary: Roosevelt urges Robert Bacon to support a fight for Cuban independence that would drive Spain from the Americas.

headline: Archie turns four
summary: Fitzhugh Lee, the American consul general in Cuba, is called home. In Washington, Archie celebrates his fourth birthday.

headline: Easter in Washington
summary: Roosevelt spends Easter in Washington.

headline: McKinley asks Congress to act
summary: President McKinley sends Congress his message on Cuba, calling for American intervention.

headline: A Yale clipping
summary: Roosevelt writes Robert W. de Forest about a Yale newspaper clipping de Forest had sent him.

headline: Congress should declare it
summary: Roosevelt tells Lodge that a resolution for war ought to come from Congress.

headline: Forces begin to mobilize
summary: The first orders go out to mobilize America's army and navy.

headline: 'The army is awful'
summary: In his diary Roosevelt mocks McKinley's continued efforts for peace, credits himself with having the Navy ready, and despairs of the Army and the War Department. He presses Long for a blockade of Cuba before Spain can mobilize.

headline: Sizing up Alger and Miles
summary: Roosevelt's diary is unimpressed by Secretary of War Russell Alger and the Army's commanding general, Nelson Miles.

headline: Congress votes to intervene
summary: After long debate Congress passes the intervention resolution in the small hours of April 19. Roosevelt explains to Paul Dana why he wants to fight, writes General Tracy on the Navy, and scoffs in his diary at Alger and Miles's boast of 100,000 men in Tampa within a day.

headline: Cuba declared free
summary: Roosevelt's diary accuses Speaker Thomas Reed, with Joseph Cannon and Charles Boutelle, of blocking war preparations. Congress adopts joint resolutions recognizing Cuban independence and telling Spain to get out.

headline: Envoys depart
summary: McKinley signs the Cuba resolution. Spain's minister leaves Washington and U.S. minister Stewart Woodford leaves Madrid. Roosevelt writes Captain Robley Evans about the Marines, confident of beating Spain even with damaged battleships.

headline: Relations with Spain cut
summary: The United States formally breaks diplomatic relations with Spain. Roosevelt's diary praises the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. He tells General Tracy the country must strike now, and writes William Chanler about Army volunteers.

headline: Fleet heads into the Caribbean
summary: The Atlantic Squadron leaves Key West for Caribbean waters.

headline: A volunteer cavalry post in sight
summary: McKinley asks for 125,000 volunteers to bolster a regular army of about 28,000, among them three regiments of frontier horsemen and crack shots. Roosevelt is in line for second in command of the first of these cavalry regiments, under his friend Leonard Wood.

headline: Spain declares war
summary: Spain formally goes to war with the United States. Secretary Long cables Dewey to go after the Philippines. Roosevelt writes his old ranch partner Sylvane Ferris about the cavalry regiment he is raising.

headline: Congress declares war
summary: Congress declares war on Spain, and Dewey gets orders to go after Spain's ships. Roosevelt's commission dates from today; friends think he has lost his mind. He writes Chanler, John Fox, Wadsworth and Will Cowles about the volunteer regiments.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Flood of volunteers
summary: Bags of applications start pouring in for Roosevelt's new regiment; some 23,000 arrive in all. He writes John Moore about horses for the unit.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Corinne's anniversary
summary: Roosevelt's sister Corinne marks her 16th wedding anniversary with Douglas Robinson.

headline: Elkhorn goes to Sylvane Ferris
summary: Roosevelt hands his Elkhorn ranch over to Sylvane Ferris and buys life insurance. Bamie, now expecting, still has Ted and Alice. Wood leaves for San Antonio to build the training camp, and Roosevelt lands Krag carbines with smokeless powder and khaki uniforms for the men. He later said he would have left even a deathbed to answer this call.

headline: Dewey wins at Manila Bay
summary: Commodore Dewey destroys Spain's Pacific squadron in Manila Bay in about seven and a half hours of action, without losing a single American life.

headline: Congratulations to Dewey
summary: Roosevelt wires his congratulations to Dewey. McKinley and Long approve Roosevelt's plan for a combined naval and military attack on Cuba. He wires Guy Murchie to recruit Harvard men and orders a blue cravenette lieutenant colonel's uniform from Brooks Brothers.

headline: A watch and the last cattle
summary: Roosevelt thanks Douglas Robinson for a watch; Douglas is buying up the few cattle Roosevelt still owns.

headline: Dandies and champions enlist
summary: Roosevelt thanks his old Maine guide Bill Sewall for caring about how the new unit fares, and wires Lincoln Steffens about Eastern college men joining up. Among them are polo star Joseph Sampson Stevens, quarterback Dudley Dean, tennis champion Bob Wrenn, Columbia oarsman Hamilton Fish and the fashionable Woodbury Kane.

headline: Untangling red tape
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie he has stayed in Washington to cut through red tape. He has signed up about 40 men from Harvard, Yale and the Knickerbocker Club, Bob Ferguson among them, signing up at the 1814 G Street office. Edith keeps gaining, though worry about him wears on her. He thanks Conie for a watch.

headline: Resigns from the Navy Department
summary: Roosevelt's diary records his commission as lieutenant colonel with Wood as colonel, by his own choice, after he had been offered the top post. He sends to McKinley, by way of Long, his resignation from the Navy's second-ranking post, and writes Bamie, Douglas Robinson and Fitzhugh Lee.

headline: Fuming at the War Department
summary: Roosevelt vents in his diary about delays in the Army's ordnance office and a War Department without leadership.

headline: Edith back on her feet
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie that Edith is well and that the two of them have gone out to dinner a few times. He tells Conie that Douglas Robinson's cousin Kenneth has joined the Rough Riders.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Carbines for Texas
summary: Roosevelt tells Colonel Wood that the Krag carbines he obtained are being shipped to San Antonio.

headline: A spring drive with Edith
summary: Roosevelt takes Edith for a drive through the countryside in bloom.

headline: Leaving for San Antonio
summary: At 10 p.m. Roosevelt boards a train for San Antonio. Kermit, who stayed up to see him off, writes that his father has gone to war. Roosevelt sends Bamie a goodbye note and thanks Conie for a poem.

headline: Heading southwest
summary: Roosevelt is on the train bound for San Antonio.

headline: Still on the rails
summary: Roosevelt's journey to San Antonio continues.

headline: Arrives at Camp Wood
summary: Roosevelt reaches the regiment's camp at San Antonio, about 500 tents holding some 1,000 men.

headline: Life by the bugle
summary: Roosevelt judges Major Alexander Brodie a good man and settles into camp routine: reveille before dawn, watering horses in the river, mounted drill and bronco busting he oversees, skirmish practice, dress parade, officers' school at night, then taps. Afterward he writes letters, while many troopers slip into town.

headline: Drilling the troopers
summary: Kenneth Robinson writes Conie that Roosevelt has been putting the men through drill for several days.

headline: A lesson from Wood
summary: Bob Ferguson tells Douglas Robinson that Roosevelt already has a firm grip on the men. Around now Roosevelt buys the troopers a round of beer; Wood rebukes him for blurring the line between officers and men, and Roosevelt promptly admits the mistake.

headline: Working like beavers
summary: Roosevelt's diary marvels at the regiment's progress under constant drill, and he tells Lodge they are hard at work getting it into shape.

headline: Ivy League meets cow country
summary: Roosevelt notes in his diary that the Harvard and New York recruits are getting along well with the cowboys.

headline: Rifles by slow freight
summary: Roosevelt's diary blasts the Ordnance Bureau for sending what the regiment doesn't need by express and its rifles by slow freight, and he lays the ultimate blame on the President. He writes Robert Bridges about writing an account of the coming campaign.

headline: In camp at San Antonio
