summary: Roosevelt is with the regiment in San Antonio; nothing further is recorded.

headline: Another day in camp
summary: The regiment's training continues at San Antonio, with no other entries.

headline: Camp routine continues
summary: Roosevelt remains at the San Antonio camp; no other events are noted.

headline: The Rough Riders get their name
summary: Roosevelt assures President McKinley the regiment is in fine form and eager for Cuba, and describes for Lodge the 'Rough Riders,' as the newspapers now call them.

headline: Nearly full strength
summary: Roosevelt's diary notes the regiment is almost at full quota and praises Wood's tireless work. The mounted drill is excellent, but restless troopers have taken to shooting up San Antonio on nights in town.

headline: Waiting for orders
summary: Roosevelt is in camp at San Antonio; no other events are recorded.

headline: Orders for Tampa
summary: The regiment is ordered to Tampa, Florida, and sits for its regimental photograph. Edith writes Roosevelt about Ted.

headline: Breaking camp
summary: At 5 a.m. Camp Wood comes down, and loading the horses onto the train takes until midnight. Roosevelt takes charge of the rear four of the train's seven sections.

headline: Rolling toward Florida
summary: The train finally pulls out at 6 a.m. Roosevelt's diary complains of a rail system breaking down, endless delays, and no proper places to unload, water and feed the horses.

headline: Spare spectacles sewn in
summary: The regiment rolls on toward Tampa in a long train of passenger, baggage, box and livestock cars, loading and unloading horses through each night. Roosevelt carries a dozen pairs of spectacles stitched into his clothes and hat.

headline: Rough Riders roll toward Tampa
summary: On a long, sweltering, crowded train ride to Florida, Roosevelt lets his troopers drink but comes down hard on anyone who gets drunk. In spare moments he reads a French book on Anglo-Saxon superiority.

headline: Hot coffee on a hungry train
summary: With no hot meals aboard, Roosevelt arranges hot coffee for his troopers. At station stops along the way, townspeople hand the soldiers watermelons and beer.

headline: Into the chaos at Tampa
summary: The regiment arrives at Tampa to find the railroads in a snarl; the troopers ride the last six miles and Roosevelt and Wood hunt for their campsite after dark in 90-degree heat. Edith has come down to the Tampa Bay Hotel, and he spends the night there with her.

headline: Weary horses, drill on foot
summary: The horses are worn out from the trip, so the regiment drills on foot. Roosevelt rides into Tampa, and Edith writes home to the children.

headline: A diary cry over Tampa's disorder
summary: Roosevelt pours his frustration into his diary, blaming the mess at Tampa on a collapse of both the rail and military systems. Edith writes her sister Emily about her journey to Florida.

headline: Mounted drill and hard news
summary: The Rough Riders show off a sharp mounted drill on the flats, watched by foreign military observers, Richard Harding Davis and Edith. Then word comes that only officers' horses will ship to Cuba, and just eight of the regiment's twelve troops will go.

headline: Edith heads home; orders to embark
summary: Edith starts back to New York. Drinking coffee in the hotel, Roosevelt hears the troops will ship out right away, and he dashes off notes to his sisters brimming with eagerness to go.

headline: Seizing a coal train and a ship
summary: When no train shows up, Roosevelt commandeers a coal train going the wrong way and has it backed down to the docks with his men aboard. Wood grabs the transport Yucatan, meant for two other regiments, and the Rough Riders hold it. Two Vitagraph cameramen come along; the fleet sails but halts on reports of ships in the Gulf.

headline: Packed aboard and going nowhere
summary: The troopers sit crammed aboard the Yucatan in the heat, waiting without complaint while the food goes bad. Roosevelt fumes in his diary about the bungling.

headline: Sharks and swimmers in midstream
summary: The transports move out into the channel. Sharks prowl the water, but some overheated men go swimming anyway. Roosevelt tells Lodge the disorder is beyond words.

headline: Baking in the harbor
summary: Another day stalled in Tampa harbor. Roosevelt notes in his diary that the tropical sun is hard on his men.

headline: Sixth day aboard the sweltering ship
summary: Still stuck in the bay, Roosevelt writes Bamie about a small ship carrying a thousand men, warns Edith the wait is hurting morale, and asks Lodge to carry word of the Tampa mismanagement to the President.

headline: Anchors up, then down again
summary: In the afternoon the transports finally raise anchor, move down the bay and drop anchor once more.

headline: At last, the fleet sails for Cuba
summary: The transports clear the Tampa Bay lighthouse and steam for Cuba that evening, every ship lit up while the bands play the national anthem together. Roosevelt sends Douglas Robinson a quick note.

headline: Lights off Key West
summary: Late in the evening Roosevelt spots the lights of the Tortugas and Key West. The 31-ship convoy stretches 25 miles and straggles, and General Shafter brushes off the Navy's plea to darken the ships at night.

headline: Slow going, school at sea
summary: The convoy crawls along, slowed by a schooner and a scow under tow. By day the officers hold classes and the men drill on deck.

headline: At sea
summary: Another day aboard ship on the way to Cuba; the record notes nothing more.

headline: Sent back to guard a straggler
summary: Shafter orders the Yucatan back to escort a transport towing a schooner. Roosevelt calls the order idiotic: his ship has no towline and only gives the rear gunboat Bancroft one more vessel to watch.

headline: Left behind with the schooner
summary: The Yucatan plods along beside the towed schooner while the rest of the fleet disappears over the horizon.

headline: Santiago is the target
summary: The fleet turns southwest and the destination becomes clear: Santiago. The ships stop some 20 miles to the east of Morro Castle after a day hugging the Cuban shore.

headline: Battle orders and a war dance
summary: Orders for the landing are read out to the troops, and Roosevelt celebrates with a war dance and a rousing Irish-American song.

headline: Ashore in Cuba with a toothbrush
summary: After a 3:30 a.m. reveille and a morning naval bombardment, the landing begins. Officers' horses are pushed overboard to swim; Roosevelt's Rain-in-the-Face drowns while Texas reaches shore. The Yucatan sails off with the baggage, leaving him only a toothbrush and a yellow mackinaw. By midnight 6,000 troops are on the beach.

headline: Marching to Siboney
summary: After General Lawton seizes Siboney that morning, the regiment sets out at 3:45 p.m. under General Joseph Wheeler and cover seven steamy miles by sundown, Roosevelt on foot beside his men. Movie cameras catch pack mules on the trail toward Santiago.

headline: Under fire at Las Guasimas
summary: Before dawn the regiment pushes toward Las Guasimas, and Spanish snipers open up from cover, killing Sergeant Hamilton Fish and Captain Allyn Capron. Roosevelt, splinters in his eyes, leads three troops on a flanking fire that opens the way for the charge. In two hours the Spanish fall back, and he pockets three Mauser cartridges for his children.

headline: A day of rest after the fight
summary: The regiment rests. Roosevelt writes Edith an account of the Las Guasimas fight.

headline: Eleven hundred pounds of beans
summary: The regiment moves three miles. Told the commissary's beans are for officers only, Roosevelt orders 1,100 pounds of them as an officer, feeds his whole regiment, and hauls one sack himself over eight miles of jungle road.

headline: Scouting while the papers cheer
summary: The regiment stays put while Roosevelt goes out scouting. Back home the newspapers praise the Rough Riders and ignore the other units at Las Guasimas. Letters pass between him and Edith, and he writes Lodge about the battle.

headline: Governor talk begins at home
summary: The Rough Riders remain on the Las Guasimas ridge. In New York, people are already talking about making Roosevelt the next governor.

headline: Back to the coast for supplies
summary: Roosevelt heads back to the coast to push ammunition and food forward. General Shafter at last reaches the Las Guasimas ridge.

headline: Night march toward San Juan
summary: Shafter surveys the heights of San Juan from El Pozo and holds a war council; the advance on Santiago begins as Wheeler falls ill with fever. The regiment marches late and camps at 9 p.m. At Sagamore Hill, Edith buys a horse she names Cuba and fills scrapbooks with clippings.

headline: The charge up Kettle and San Juan hills
summary: Roosevelt's 'crowded hour.' With Wood moved up to brigade command, he leads the Rough Riders. After hours pinned down by fire at Bloody Ford, he rides Little Texas up Kettle Hill, takes a graze on the elbow, and finishes on foot. He then rallies the men across to San Juan Hill, where the flag is already up. The regiment suffers the heaviest losses of any unit there.

headline: Holding the ridge under shellfire
summary: Before dawn a shell lands near Roosevelt, who keeps striding the San Juan ridge under rifle and artillery fire. His diary lists officers of the regular cavalry. Bob Ferguson writes Edith that he now believes nothing can kill her husband.

headline: Truce, and the Spanish fleet is gone
summary: A truce takes hold at noon. Off Santiago, the Navy under Sampson and Schley destroys the Spanish squadron as it runs for the open sea. Roosevelt's men dig in through daily rain, and he writes Edith and urges Lodge to get more troops and supplies sent.

headline: A grim Fourth in the trenches
summary: The truce holds, but men in the trenches suffer from wounds, dysentery, malaria and hunger. Army bands play for them, and the Rough Riders ask for 'Fair Harvard.' Across the Pacific, the U.S. takes Wake Island. Roosevelt sends Wood a report on what has happened since the July 1 battle.

headline: Calling Shafter incompetent
summary: Outside Santiago, Roosevelt writes Lodge that General Shafter is criminally incompetent and describes the hardship and disorder of the siege. Bob Ferguson tells Edith her husband is reveling in the fight.

headline: A letter to McKinley
summary: The siege of Santiago continues. In Washington, Congress votes to annex Hawaii. Roosevelt writes to President McKinley.

headline: Hoping for the Medal of Honor
summary: Still in the lines outside Santiago, Roosevelt tells Lodge he believes he has earned both a higher rank and the Medal of Honor, should General Wheeler recommend him.

headline: Siege lines at Santiago
summary: Another day in the trenches outside Santiago; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Siege lines at Santiago
summary: Roosevelt and the regiment remain in the lines outside Santiago; the day passes without other notes.

headline: Bombardment resumes
summary: The guns open again outside Santiago, as the dynamite gun and the Colt guns fire on the Spanish lines. Roosevelt tells Lodge that Shafter ought to be removed from command.

headline: Promoted to full colonel
summary: Roosevelt is formally commissioned colonel. The regiment shifts a mile to the right taking its Gatling gun along to cover the road to El Caney, and the hardest rain yet falls that night. Stephen Crane later praised how hard he worked for his men during the siege.

headline: Rain until noon
summary: The siege goes on outside Santiago, with rain pouring down until midday.

headline: Surrender talks begin
summary: Outside Santiago, American and Spanish officers meet to discuss the city's surrender.

headline: A letter from Edith
summary: The regiment holds its lines outside Santiago, and a letter arrives from Edith.

headline: A face-saving deal; Uncle James dies
summary: Negotiators agree the Santiago garrison will give up within two days, after a token bombardment aimed harmlessly over the houses to preserve Spanish honor. Roosevelt writes Ethel about the endless rain. At home, his uncle James Alfred Roosevelt dies that evening on the Long Island Rail Road near New Hyde Park.

headline: Waiting outside Santiago
summary: Roosevelt and the regiment spend the day in the lines outside Santiago, with the surrender close at hand; nothing more is noted.

headline: Santiago surrenders
summary: At noon the American flag rises over Santiago as 17,000 Spanish troops give up the city.

headline: Half the regiment out of action
summary: Roosevelt shifts his camp across the ridge to the foothills west of El Caney as yellow fever cases mount. He notes that half his men are dead, wounded or sick.

headline: Letters on triumph and breakdown
summary: Roosevelt writes a burst of letters: to Edith on victory and the collapse of transport, food and hospital services; to Douglas Robinson thanking him for supplies; to Lodge describing San Juan; to General Bradley T. Johnson on his pride in the men; and to Bamie with news.

headline: Command of the brigade
summary: With more officers falling sick, Roosevelt takes command of the 2nd Brigade. He reports on bad conditions near Santiago to General Wood and writes Ethel about Cuba's lizards and birds.

headline: In camp in Cuba
summary: The regiment remains in camp near Santiago; no events are recorded.

headline: Feeding the men from his own pocket
summary: Roosevelt tells Douglas Robinson he is paying for the Rough Riders' food himself and that half the regiment is out of action. He writes Lodge about bad organization and fears of yellow fever, though none of his men actually has the disease.

headline: Fresh meat at last
summary: Fresh meat finally reaches the sick-ridden camp. Roosevelt writes Secretary of War Russell Alger asking that his men be sent on to fight in Puerto Rico.

headline: A Sunday service in camp
summary: A service is held in camp, and Roosevelt notes a slight improvement in the men's health.

headline: Diary notes on camp characters
summary: Roosevelt jots down camp anecdotes in his diary, including a lost hat, troopers Pollock and Paunce, and a man who refused to grow his hair long in wartime.

headline: In camp in Cuba
summary: Another day in camp in Cuba with nothing recorded.

headline: Governorship and Harvard men
summary: Roosevelt tells Douglas Robinson he never expected to come through unhurt, discusses a possible run for governor with John Lewis Childs, and praises the young Harvard men serving as troopers in a letter to President Charles W. Eliot.

headline: Red Cross goods from Bamie
summary: Roosevelt records troopers' stories in his diary, including Crockett's wound and the parson who ground coffee. He thanks Bamie for Red Cross supplies she arranged and calls the regiment thoroughly American.

headline: Remembering the bronco busters
summary: Roosevelt's diary names two bronco busters in the regiment, Darnell and Smoky Moore.

headline: Colonel's commission accepted
summary: Roosevelt formally accepts his colonelcy. General Shafter calls all officers together to discuss the army's health crisis. In his diary Roosevelt recalls Happy Jack, a former lightweight boxer sure he could not catch fever.

headline: Pleading to bring the men home
summary: Roosevelt tells Lodge he would much rather take on national politics than New York's sewers and police boards, and he writes Seth Low that his men must leave Cuba before sickness kills them.

headline: In camp in Cuba
summary: The regiment stays in camp in Cuba; the record is blank.

headline: In camp in Cuba
summary: Nothing is recorded for the day in Cuba.

headline: The round robin letter
summary: Roosevelt writes two letters warning that disease will destroy the army unless it leaves Cuba: one under his own name and a 'round robin' signed by many officers around Santiago. Both go to the Associated Press for publication at home.

headline: The letters hit the papers
summary: Roosevelt's warnings appear in American morning newspapers, and both the President and Secretary Alger are furious.

headline: Visitors at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is still in Cuba while Bamie and Winthrop Chanler stay at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Ordered home to Montauk
summary: Washington orders Shafter's army to Montauk on Long Island. It is Edith's 37th birthday.

headline: Last days in Cuba
summary: Roosevelt remains in Cuba while Douglas Robinson signs the guest book at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Leaving Santiago on the Miami
summary: The Rough Riders sail out of Santiago harbor aboard the troopship Miami. Wood stays behind as the city's military governor.

headline: At sea
summary: The Miami steams north toward home.

headline: At sea
summary: Still at sea aboard the Miami. Jacob Riis signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.

headline: At sea
summary: Another day aboard the Miami heading for Long Island.

headline: Peace protocol signed
summary: While Roosevelt is at sea, the United States and Spain sign a peace protocol, and Hawaii is formally annexed.

headline: Manila falls; Ethel turns seven
summary: U.S. forces capture Manila in the Philippines. At home, Ethel celebrates her seventh birthday.

headline: Platt cool on Roosevelt for governor
summary: Boss Thomas Platt pushes back against the talk of nominating Roosevelt for governor. At sea, Roosevelt writes Brander Matthews about an article he hopes to write for Macmillan's.

headline: Home at Montauk, 'disgracefully well'
summary: Tugs bring the Miami in at noon as a big crowd waits on the Montauk shore. Roosevelt, looking fit beside his gaunt troopers, tells reporters he feels ashamed to be so healthy but that it was a bully fight; he will talk only about the regiment. The men go into quarantine at Camp Wikoff, and he slips out to see Edith.

headline: Edith in a Montauk boarding house
summary: Roosevelt is at Montauk, where Edith has taken a room in a grubby boarding house nearby.

headline: An early release from quarantine
summary: Roosevelt wires Lemuel Quigg, Platt's lieutenant in the state Republican organization, that he will be discharged early from quarantine.

headline: Independents come calling
summary: John Jay Chapman, who leads an independent effort to draft Roosevelt for governor, visits him. Roosevelt notes in his diary the tale of Ballard, a former sheriff who broke up the Black Jack gang.

headline: Telling Quigg he wants the job
summary: Lemuel Quigg calls on behalf of the Republican organization, and Roosevelt admits he would like to be their candidate for governor. His diary recalls surf baths with his troopers.

headline: A hero's welcome at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt and Edith leave camp for a five-day family visit at Sagamore Hill, and some 1,500 people turn out in Oyster Bay to greet him. Little Archie, not quite sure who he is, greets him cheerfully as 'Colonel.'

headline: Madeira on the piazza
summary: In the evening Roosevelt puts on a tuxedo and sips madeira on the piazza while guests fill the house, among them Grant La Farge, Corinne and Douglas Robinson, and Speck von Sternberg.

headline: Driving Edith to the Red Cross
summary: Roosevelt takes Edith by carriage to a meeting of the Red Cross.

headline: Delegations, cameras and Lodge
summary: Sagamore Hill hums with visiting delegations and photographers, and Lodge stops by. Roosevelt tells Charles W. Eliot his letter to Alger was written in a spirit of 'calculated imprudence.'

headline: A fallback deal with the independents
summary: Chapman returns alongside Isaac Klein, a Citizens Union leader, and Roosevelt agrees to run as an independent for governor if the Republicans pass him over.

headline: Back to Montauk
summary: Roosevelt returns to camp at Montauk. Bamie signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.

headline: At Montauk
summary: Roosevelt is at Camp Wikoff; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Letting events take their course
summary: Roosevelt tells Seth Low he is 'running' for governor the way Low once did, by letting things unfold. He assures Quigg he has said nothing to reporters.

headline: At Montauk
summary: A quiet day in camp. Dan Tyler Moore appears in the Sagamore Hill guest book.

headline: Funeral in Newport
summary: Roosevelt travels to Newport, Rhode Island, to attend William Tiffany's funeral.

headline: Ready to face the convention
summary: Roosevelt tells Quigg he will go before the Republican convention if the organization wants him, whether or not Governor Black fights back.

headline: Honorary Rough Riders
summary: The record lists honorary Rough Riders: correspondent Richard Harding Davis, British military attaché Arthur Lee, and regular Army artillery Lieutenant Parker.

headline: Platt signals his favor
summary: Platt lets it leak that he backs Roosevelt for the Republican nomination for governor. Alarmed, Chapman and Klein rush to Montauk, and Roosevelt calms them. He also congratulates John Hay on becoming Secretary of State.

headline: At Montauk
summary: A quiet day at the Montauk camp with nothing recorded.

headline: Not bothered 'a particle'
summary: Roosevelt writes Francis E. Leupp that he has not fretted over the nomination at all, and that in party politics one has to work with the machine.

headline: McKinley visits the camp
summary: President McKinley and Secretary Alger visit the troops at Montauk. Roosevelt tugs his glove off with his teeth before he shakes the President's hand. He tells Lodge that Edith is cross with him for not writing and that Alger should go.

headline: At Montauk
summary: Roosevelt is in camp; the day is blank in the record.

headline: The family camps out
summary: Edith brings Alice, Ted, Kermit and Ethel to Montauk for a 24-hour stay. Ted and Kermit bunk in the tent on a cot and an air mattress, and their father sleeps on a table.

headline: At Montauk
summary: Another camp day at Montauk with nothing noted.

headline: Mustering out ahead
summary: Roosevelt tells Quigg the Rough Riders will soon be mustered out.

headline: At Montauk
summary: A quiet day in camp. Bob Ferguson signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.

headline: Will accept, will not seek
summary: Roosevelt says he will accept the Republican nomination for governor but will not go after it. He visits with Colonel L. H. Jerome.

headline: A flag for Edith
summary: Edith tells her sister Emily that the Rough Riders raised a new flag in her honor. Roosevelt wires Quigg that the regiment will muster out Thursday or perhaps Friday.

headline: Yes to the nomination, with reservations
summary: Roosevelt writes both Quigg and Chapman that he wants the nomination, but tells Quigg he does not accept every condition Platt has set.

headline: Farewell gift: The Bronco Buster
summary: On Ted's 11th birthday, bugles call the 900 surviving Rough Riders together one last time. They form a square around a hidden gift, Frederic Remington's bronze The Bronco Buster, and present it to their colonel. Roosevelt, choked up, shakes every man's hand.

headline: Home with an eagle named Teddy
summary: Roosevelt heads to Sagamore Hill with a few Rough Riders, his horse Little Texas, and the regiment's bald eagle mascot, Teddy.

headline: Rough Riders at Sagamore
summary: Several Rough Riders sign the Sagamore Hill guest book, among them Gordon Johnston, Jack Greenway, Bob Ferguson, Hal Sayre, David Goodrich and Charles Ballard.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.

headline: Accepting Platt's backing
summary: Roosevelt goes into New York City for a talk with Senator Platt, held at the Fifth Avenue Hotel, before the convention and accepts the Republican nomination.

headline: Breakfast for riders headed home
summary: Rough Riders Quaid, Kuoblach and McGinty stop at Sagamore Hill for breakfast on their way from Montauk to New York.

headline: 'Dear Jack': turning down the independents
summary: Roosevelt sends John Jay Chapman a 'Dear Jack' letter turning down the independents. Chapman does not think Roosevelt lied but still feels cheated. Roosevelt tells Lodge he cannot leave New York just now.

headline: At the Union League Club
summary: In New York City, Roosevelt confers with Chauncey Depew at the Union League Club along and Benjamin Odell.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home; the record is otherwise blank.

headline: A letter held back three days
summary: Roosevelt writes Chapman a second letter, then sets it aside for three days, and drafts a similar one to Leupp, declining the independent nomination. He tells Chapman his name will likely go before the Republican convention at Saratoga.

headline: Edith hopes he loses the nomination
summary: Edith writes her sister Emily that she would be relieved if her husband were not nominated for governor.

headline: A stormy night and a residency scandal
summary: Chapman storms out to Sagamore Hill and argues hard with Roosevelt, then misses the last train and has to stay the night. Meanwhile the press reports that Roosevelt is legally a resident of Washington, not New York. He offers to withdraw; Platt asks if he is a coward, and Roosevelt vows to run. Elihu Root finds a legal way through.

headline: A quiet Sunday stroll
summary: Chapman catches a morning train back. Roosevelt takes a walk with Edith and has dinner with the children.

headline: Letters on the residency question
summary: Roosevelt writes Platt, Lodge and Nicholas Murray Butler about the residency issue.

headline: Nominated for governor at Saratoga
summary: The Republican convention at Saratoga nominates Roosevelt for governor, 753 votes to 218 for the sitting governor, Frank Black, whose administration was tarnished by Louis Payn's evasion of civil service law and George Aldridge's handling of Erie Canal funds. It is also Corinne's 37th birthday.

headline: Thanking Quigg
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge about his residency trouble and wires Quigg his thanks for helping him win the nomination.

headline: Thanks to Seth Low
summary: Roosevelt goes into New York City in the afternoon and sends Seth Low two letters of thanks for his help with the nomination.

headline: A secretary for a flood of mail
summary: Roosevelt writes Quigg about party unity and tells Butler a tough, aggressive campaign lies ahead. Alice refuses to go to boarding school, so the family must find her a governess. He hires Amy Cheney as secretary, and she, Edith and Alice tackle the mail in the Gun Room.

headline: Strategy session with Odell
summary: Roosevelt meets in New York City with Benjamin Odell, who chairs the state Republican committee, then is home at Sagamore Hill by late afternoon.

headline: Republican Club reception
summary: Roosevelt spends the evening at a Republican Club reception in New York City and writes President McKinley that the shifts in the race look good for their side.

headline: Paying the tax bill
summary: At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt pays his taxes: $995.28.

headline: Official word of the nomination
summary: Leading Republicans travel to Sagamore Hill to formally notify Roosevelt that he is their nominee for governor. His Democratic opponent will be Augustus Van Wyck.

headline: Campaign kickoff at Carnegie Hall
summary: Roosevelt launches his race for governor with a Carnegie Hall address titled 'The Duties of a Great Nation,' telling the crowd the country must meet its destiny with courage. He asks Lodge to come speak in the city.

headline: Odell wants a quieter candidate
summary: President McKinley congratulates Roosevelt on his nomination. Odell, uneasy with the Rough Rider escort and the noise, decides the campaign should be low-key.

headline: Canal scandal shapes the race
summary: The Erie Canal deepening scandal, which ensnares Governor Black, becomes a central campaign issue, and Roosevelt must stand apart as the honest choice. Edith tells her sister Emily that the Carnegie Hall crowd was so excited she forgot to be nervous.

headline: Union League Club in Brooklyn
summary: Roosevelt goes to an evening meeting at Brooklyn's Union League Club.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: A Sunday at home with nothing recorded.

headline: Kermit turns nine
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City on Kermit's ninth birthday.

headline: Speaking at Lyric Hall
summary: Roosevelt gives an evening speech in Manhattan's Lyric Hall and writes Lodge, who liked the Carnegie Hall speech. His niece Eleanor turns 14.

headline: In New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in the city; no events are recorded.

headline: In New York City
summary: Another day in New York City with nothing noted.

headline: A wild goose chase to Troy
summary: Pressed into speaking at the Rensselaer County Fair, Roosevelt rides the train to Albany and on to Troy in a steady drizzle, without Governor Black. Only about 300 people show up, he stays in his carriage, and back at the station his train has left. That night he and Corinne attend a meeting of Black voters in New York City, which also falls flat.

headline: Taking the helm
summary: Still angry over the previous day's fiasco, Roosevelt decides to run his own campaign from now on. That night he addresses a crowd at the Lenox Lyceum.

headline: Courting the Jewish vote
summary: Roosevelt writes Quigg about organizing Jewish voters in New York City and tells Lodge the Republicans are weak statewide this year.

headline: Whistle-stopping up the Hudson
summary: At 10:02 a.m. Roosevelt's train pulls out of Weehawken with six uniformed Rough Riders and six reporters aboard. Along a 212-mile run through the Hudson Valley he makes 17 stops, from West Nyack and Newburgh to Albany, Saratoga and Glens Falls.

headline: North Country attack on Croker
summary: Roosevelt swings north toward the Adirondacks, going after Democratic boss Richard Croker at stops from Whitehall and Plattsburgh to Ogdensburg and Malone. In Oyster Bay, Bamie and Will Cowles welcome a son, William Sheffield Cowles Jr.

headline: Rain-soaked crowds along the St. Lawrence
summary: Moving down the St. Lawrence country, Roosevelt warns that Croker will corrupt the courts. He gives ten-minute talks at Potsdam, Canton, Gouverneur, Carthage, where 3,000 stand in the rain, Lowville and Boonville, then speaks in Brooklyn that evening on state and national issues.

headline: Two evening rallies in Manhattan
summary: Roosevelt speaks in the evening at Durland's Riding Academy and at the Grand Central Opera House.

headline: Seven meetings, then Poughkeepsie
summary: Roosevelt addresses seven big meetings and confers with Republican district leaders before heading to Poughkeepsie for an evening speech and an overnight stay. He urges Quigg to enlist Jacob Riis in the city campaign.

headline: The Roosevelt Special heads west
summary: The 'Roosevelt Special' makes a fast run up the Hudson and Mohawk valleys, with speeches at Little Falls, Johnstown and Gloversville.

headline: In New York City
summary: A Sunday break in the city; nothing recorded.

headline: Southern Tier swing
summary: Roosevelt speaks across the southern edge of the state, from Suffern and Middletown to Port Jervis, Binghamton, Cortland and Elmira.

headline: Sixteen speeches to Buffalo
summary: Touring central and western New York, Roosevelt makes 16 speeches across Steuben, Allegany and Livingston counties, including Corning, Hornellsville and Warsaw, and ends the day in Buffalo.

headline: Nineteen stops and a talk on labor
summary: Roosevelt gives 19 speeches, at Niagara Falls, Lockport, Tonawanda, Medina, Palmyra, Fairport and elsewhere, and in Rochester speaks on the interests of labor.

headline: Turning 40 on the stump
summary: Roosevelt marks his 40th birthday with 14 speeches, among them Canandaigua, Seneca Falls, Geneva, Auburn and Syracuse.

headline: Fifteen speeches to Utica
summary: Roosevelt speaks 15 times, working from Phoenix and Oswego north to Watertown and back down to Rome and Utica.

headline: Making farmers laugh, then Cooper Union
summary: In 11 speeches through the Mohawk Valley, from Herkimer to Schenectady, Roosevelt gets farmers laughing with nothing more than a certain look. That evening he speaks at Cooper Union in New York City.

headline: 102 speeches and counting
summary: Roosevelt wraps up the swing with 15 more speeches and a dozen impromptu talks, 102 in all on the tour, and speaks that evening at Harlem River Park.

headline: Buck Taylor's awkward introduction
summary: Roosevelt speaks at the Lenox Lyceum and stumps Long Island and the southwest of the state. Sergeant Buck Taylor of the Rough Riders introduces him with an unfortunate promise to lead voters 'like sheep to the slaughter.' J. P. Morgan gives $10,000 to the campaign. At home Roosevelt dictates The Rough Riders, which will earn $1,000 per magazine installment.

headline: Three halls and Yonkers
summary: Roosevelt addresses crowds at Cooper Union, Cosmopolitan Hall and Morrisania Hall, then gives an evening speech in Yonkers.

headline: Stumping Long Island
summary: Roosevelt tours Long Island, with stops from Jamaica and Flushing out to Babylon, Islip, Patchogue and Southampton.

headline: Albany and Troy
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Albany and Troy.

headline: Unsure how the fight is going
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Brooklyn and then at Chickering Hall in Manhattan. He admits to Lodge he cannot tell how the race is going and fears 'Blifil and Black George' might come out ahead.

headline: From the Bowery to Wall Street
summary: Roosevelt attends a Cooper Union meeting and speaks on the Bowery and on Wall Street at the Sub-Treasury. His current reading is a German study of Polybius.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt spends the last Sunday before the election at home; nothing else is noted.

headline: Last swing through the Southern Tier
summary: On the eve of the election Roosevelt speaks in Olean, Jamestown, Salamanca, Hornellsville, Wellsville and Kennedy.

headline: Elected governor of New York
summary: Roosevelt wins the governorship by 17,794 votes, 661,715 to Augustus Van Wyck's 643,921, with Timothy Woodruff elected lieutenant governor. He and Alice are reading and Edith is at her needlework when two reporters arrive at Sagamore Hill with the news.

headline: Rebuking anti-Catholic prejudice
summary: Roosevelt writes Andrew Powell, making clear he stands against anti-Catholic bigotry of the kind Powell represents.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: The governor-elect is at Sagamore Hill; nothing is recorded.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: Another quiet day at home after the election.

headline: Conference at party headquarters
summary: Roosevelt confers at Republican headquarters in the Fifth Avenue Hotel.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: A Sunday at home with no entries.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the day is blank.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: No events are recorded at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Off to Boston to lecture
summary: Roosevelt sets out from New York for Boston to lecture at the Lowell Institute.

headline: An evening with Lodge in Boston
summary: In Boston, Roosevelt passes the evening in the company of George Lyman and Lodge.

headline: In New York City
summary: Roosevelt is back in New York City; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Quentin's first birthday
summary: Quentin turns one. In Boston, opponents of overseas expansion form the Anti-Imperialist League, with members such as Senator George F. Hoar, Carl Schurz, Moorfield Storey, Gamaliel Bradford and Edward Atkinson.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: A Sunday at home; nothing recorded.

headline: In New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; the record is blank.

headline: Testifying on conditions in Cuba
summary: Roosevelt appears before the War Department investigating committee to report on conditions the army faced in Cuba.

headline: More testimony on Cuba
summary: Roosevelt gives the committee a second report on what troops endured in Cuba.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing is noted for the day.

headline: 'Bull luck' and English-speaking unity
summary: On Bamie's third wedding anniversary, Roosevelt tells Cecil Spring-Rice of his luck in getting into the war, getting out alive, and winning the governorship. He reviews the year for James Bryce and tells Arthur Lee that Britain and America must stand together.

headline: Snowbound in New London
summary: Bound for Boston, Roosevelt is stopped by snow at New London, Connecticut.

headline: Turning back from New London
summary: Still stuck at New London, Roosevelt gives up on Boston and heads back toward New York City.

headline: Heading back to New York
summary: Roosevelt travels back to New York City.

headline: In New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Lowell lectures and toboggan runs
summary: Before Christmas Roosevelt gives eight Lowell lectures, earning $1,600 in all. Kermit, sick with erysipelas, has to wear a protective face mask; his father takes Alice and Ted tobogganing. Edith makes a trip to Albany, where Mrs. Black shows her the Governor's Mansion.

headline: No to a machine man for Public Works
summary: Roosevelt tells Lodge he does not want machine politician Francis Hendricks as Superintendent of Public Works, and asks about his chances for the Medal of Honor.

headline: Twelfth wedding anniversary
summary: Theodore and Edith mark 12 years of marriage at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Edith takes on new duties
summary: Edith writes her sister Emily in Italy, telling her not to come home and explaining that the new responsibilities of a governor's wife demand all her attention.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: A quiet Sunday at home.

headline: Picking a state team
summary: Roosevelt holds meetings in New York City about state appointments.

headline: 'I want it': the Medal of Honor
summary: Roosevelt continues meetings on state appointments and tells Lodge plainly that he has earned the Medal of Honor and wants it.

headline: Overnight to Boston and back
summary: Roosevelt goes to Boston for an evening Lowell Institute lecture and takes the night train back to New York.

headline: More appointment talks
summary: Roosevelt holds further meetings on state appointments in New York City.

headline: In New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in the city; nothing is recorded.

headline: Peace signed in Paris
summary: The United States and Spain sign the Treaty of Paris. Roosevelt lectures that evening at the Lowell Institute in Boston and tells S. C. Harriott he will appoint only the best people.

headline: In Boston
summary: Roosevelt is in Boston; nothing else is noted.

headline: On women's suffrage
summary: Roosevelt tells Susan B. Anthony he has always favored votes for women, saying the obstacle lies in women's own attitudes rather than in government. He tells Lodge he is unhappy with the peace treaty's terms.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill; the day is blank.

headline: Appointments again
summary: Roosevelt meets in New York City on state appointments.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: Nothing is recorded at Sagamore Hill.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: Another blank day at home.

headline: In New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; no events are noted.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: A Sunday at home.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing is recorded.

headline: In New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in the city; the record is blank.

headline: Medal hopes fade
summary: Roosevelt tells Lodge it now looks unlikely he will receive the Medal of Honor.

headline: Speaking to schoolchildren on Sullivan Street
summary: Roosevelt gives a speech at the Children's Aid Society school on Sullivan Street.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home for the holidays; nothing is recorded.

headline: Christmas gifts at Cove Neck School
summary: At 3 p.m. on Christmas Eve the governor-elect arrives at Cove Neck School with Edith and Alice, hands out presents and gives a short talk. Ted and Kermit are pupils there, and Kermit recites a nursery rhyme.

headline: Christmas guests at Sagamore Hill
summary: Christmas visitors at Sagamore Hill include Speck von Sternberg, Mrs. James B. Leavitt, John Elliott, Grace and Bertha Potter, Helen Cutting, Miss Le Morine and Mrs. Alexander Moore.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: A quiet day after Christmas.

headline: Feeling wronged by the War Department
summary: Roosevelt complains to Lodge that the War Department has not dealt fairly with him over the Medal of Honor.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing is recorded.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: The family's last quiet days at home before Albany.

headline: Moving into the Governor's Mansion
summary: Roosevelt and his family travel to Albany and settle into the Governor's Mansion. Generals Sumner and Wood nominate him for the Medal of Honor.

headline: Sworn in a day early
summary: With New Year's Day on a Sunday, Roosevelt and other state officers take the oath before Secretary of State John Palmer. He and Edith attend a quiet ball at the State Armory. Ted and Kermit start at the Albany Military Academy, Gertrude Young becomes governess to Alice and Ethel, and the first part of The Rough Riders appears in Scribner's.

headline: Locked out of the Governor's Mansion
summary: Roosevelt dines with his old friend Fanny Smith Parsons, now living in Albany, while Edith and the children stay in bed sick. Returning at midnight, he finds himself locked out of the mansion and breaks a window to get in.

headline: Inaugurated in a frozen Albany
summary: In bitter subzero cold, with band instruments frozen silent, Roosevelt is inaugurated governor in the Assembly Chamber and sends lawmakers his yearly message. He is the first governor to serve in the newly finished Capitol, at a salary of $10,000 a year.

headline: Twice-daily press briefings
summary: Roosevelt starts meeting reporters twice a day for 15 minutes, winning them over with an open, friendly manner and plenty of off-the-record talk. He writes Odell about Erie Canal appointments. Edith tells Emily the inauguration so moved her she could barely watch.

headline: The Hendricks fight begins
summary: Roosevelt confers with Odell and with Syracuse politician Francis Hendricks, the machine's pick for Superintendent of Public Works. He writes William Ferguson about appointing Black men to state jobs and asks Max Keyes, a witness, to support his Medal of Honor claim.

headline: A promise to do his duty
summary: Roosevelt assures Herbert Welsh that he intends to act honorably and meet his responsibilities in office.

headline: Twelfth Night at the Century
summary: Roosevelt heads to Manhattan that afternoon for the Century Association's Twelfth Night dinner.

headline: First Saturday breakfast with Platt
summary: Roosevelt meets Platt, Odell and Root about the Public Works post and whether a man named Hill can serve as Erie County district attorney. It is the first of the Saturday morning breakfasts Corinne later described.

headline: Back to Albany
summary: Roosevelt returns to Albany.

headline: Trevelyan, poems and bad beef
summary: Roosevelt praises Trevelyan's American Revolution volumes and young Bay Lodge's poems in a letter to Lodge, writes Captain William Llewellyn about the Medal of Honor, and takes up the army's bad beef with General Nelson Miles.

headline: Women 'not treated as equals'
summary: Roosevelt confers with Elihu Root on the Public Works post and writes Helen Johnson that women are wronged by being denied equal treatment.

headline: Payn, Greene and Wood
summary: Roosevelt confers with Lou Payn, the insurance superintendent. He tells General Francis Greene that Secretary Alger opposes his Medal of Honor and tells Wood he wishes he could come to Albany.

headline: Platt picks from an honest list
summary: Having refused Platt's choice, Hendricks, Roosevelt sends the senator four honest candidates for Superintendent of Public Works. Platt chooses John N. Partridge. Roosevelt also writes Lodge about the medal.

headline: Partridge nominated; boys and gentleness
summary: Roosevelt sends John Partridge's nomination for Public Works to the state Senate. He writes Root about his tax and residency troubles, and tells Edwin Whitehead he wants boys to be tough and athletic yet gentle with the weak.

headline: Labor hearing and army meat
summary: A special commission of the Workingmen's Federation of Labor holds a hearing on pending labor bills. Roosevelt writes Paul Dana and General Miles about spoiled meat fed to soldiers in Cuba, and Seth Low about the Partridge appointment.

headline: In Albany
summary: A Sunday in Albany with nothing recorded.

headline: First cabinet meeting
summary: Roosevelt convenes his cabinet for the first of its weekly meetings. He writes Odell about appointments and tells George Trevelyan how much he admires his American Revolution volumes.

headline: Civil Service Board and Dewey
summary: Roosevelt meets the state's Civil Service Board. He writes Colonel Dibble about the Navy and Dewey at Manila, Odell about appointments, John P. Clarke on legislative matters, and Martha Selmes a chatty letter on how his life has changed in a year.

headline: National Guard speech on Bamie's birthday
summary: Roosevelt addresses the National Guard Association on Bamie's 44th birthday. He writes Winthrop Chanler about the army and politics and Platt about appointments.

headline: First bill signed; 'that infernal medal'
summary: Roosevelt signs the Ellsworth-Allds appropriation, Chapter 1 of the session's laws, covering legislators' contingent expenses. He writes John E. Roosevelt about his residency and asks Lodge to drop the Medal of Honor campaign altogether.

headline: Irish-American historians and the 23rd
summary: In New York, Roosevelt goes to an Irish-American Historical Society reception and a Union League Club dinner, and reviews the 23rd Regiment in Brooklyn.

headline: Boone and Crockett dinner
summary: Roosevelt holds meetings with Riis, Butler, Choate, Sloane, Slicer, Doty and Clarke, then goes to dinner with the Boone and Crockett Club.

headline: In New York City
summary: A Sunday in the city with nothing recorded.

headline: A police bill for the city
summary: Republicans announce they will bring in a bill reshaping the city's police. Roosevelt writes a batch of political letters, including to Riis, Chauncey Depew, Senator Joseph Foraker, Seth Low, and Lodge about Lodge's book on the war.

headline: Special counsel on canal frauds
summary: At a cabinet meeting, Austen Fox is named to probe the canal frauds as special counsel, assisted by Wallace MacFarlane. Roosevelt also confers with Quigg and Hotchkiss on changing the primary law.

headline: Primary law letter to Root
summary: Roosevelt writes Elihu Root about changes to the primary law.

headline: Things going well in Albany
summary: Roosevelt writes Quigg about the primary law and tells Lodge his work in Albany seems to be going smoothly.

headline: Aguinaldo declares a republic
summary: Roosevelt confers with Odell on the police bill. In the Philippines, Emilio Aguinaldo proclaims a Philippine Republic. Roosevelt tells Root that one of Root's jokes has upset the governor's staff.

headline: Primary law talks and a CCNY dinner
summary: In New York, Roosevelt confers with Root and Platt about the primary law and speaks at a City College dinner.

headline: In New York City
summary: A Sunday in the city with no recorded events.

headline: Denying a story about Bryan
summary: Roosevelt tells H. R. Caraway that a claim in the magazine Arena is false: he would never think of using troops to keep William Jennings Bryan from being inaugurated.

headline: A plan for the city police
summary: Roosevelt lays out his plan to overhaul the city's police force in a letter to Frank Moss. He writes William Wharton about Colonel Lay's dismissal and describes his duties as governor to William Howard Taft.

headline: Declining a dinner for Carl Schurz
summary: Governor Roosevelt writes Sherman Rogers from Albany that he will skip a dinner honoring Carl Schurz, citing the political gulf between the two men.

headline: Chosen to lead a war veterans' order
summary: In Albany, Roosevelt is chosen to command the Naval and Military Order, a society of Spanish-American War veterans. He also writes about appointments and the press, and sends Tiffany's a note sharing his thoughts on young Ted.

headline: Letters on state police and a dismissal
summary: From New York City Roosevelt takes up the idea of a state police force with Frank Moss, tells Bellamy Storer how busy he is, and writes former Governor Levi P. Morton about Colonel Lay's removal.

headline: Breakfast with the party bosses
summary: Roosevelt sits down to breakfast with Thomas Platt, Benjamin Odell and Elihu Root at his sister Corinne's house at 422 Madison Avenue.

headline: Sunday in Albany
summary: A quiet Sunday; the record places Roosevelt in Albany with nothing further noted.

headline: Peace treaty with Spain ratified
summary: As the U.S. Senate approves the peace treaty with Spain, the United States takes Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines for $20 million and fighting breaks out with Emilio Aguinaldo's Filipino forces. In Albany, Roosevelt writes Root on politics and Lemuel Quigg on appointments.

headline: On being the best-hated nation
summary: Roosevelt sits in on a hearing on the Ambler dairy bill, writes Lodge about the Philippine treaty, and teases Count von Götzen about which nation the world dislikes most.

headline: Teaching his children to admire courage
summary: Roosevelt thanks General Bradley Johnson for meeting his children, writes Jacob Riis about the condemned Martha Place, and opens a long tug-of-war with Senator Platt over appointments.

headline: Soldiers' Home trustees meet
summary: In the afternoon Roosevelt attends a trustees' meeting for the state home for old soldiers and sailors at Bath.

headline: Missing Medora amid appointment fights
summary: Roosevelt tells his old ranch partner Sylvane Ferris he wishes he could get back to Medora. The rest of the day's mail is politics: appointments, Platt's objections to his picks, police and election bills, and a commission to improve the canals.

headline: A note to a military novelist
summary: Roosevelt writes General Charles King, author of army novels, that he enjoyed Trials of a Staff Officer.

headline: Alice turns fifteen
summary: On his daughter Alice's fifteenth birthday, Roosevelt speaks to the state YMCA gathering in Albany.

headline: Lincoln Day speech on America's role
summary: In New York City Roosevelt gives a Lincoln Day address at the Republican Club on the share of the world's labor that falls to America.

headline: Thinking of Spring-Rice in Persia
summary: Roosevelt writes his friend Cecil Spring-Rice, then in Persia, that he wishes they could meet, and compliments Colonel George Henderson on his Civil War book. He continues to support former slaves of the Roswell plantation that belonged to his mother's family.

headline: Varnum named Surrogate
summary: Roosevelt names James Varnum to be the county's Surrogate in New York and writes about the Civil Service Commission and garment workers. Edith, meanwhile, warns her sister Emily away from an unpromising suitor.

headline: Explaining appointments to a newsman
summary: Roosevelt lays out his appointment choices for Joseph Bucklin Bishop, the newspaperman who would become a close friend, and writes ornithologist Frank Chapman about protecting birds.

headline: Honoring Choate, reviewing the 7th
summary: Roosevelt goes to New York City for a dinner in honor of Ambassador Joseph Choate and reviews the 7th Regiment.

headline: Platt breakfast and a word on police
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts with Platt and Odell, writes explorer Walter Gordon-Cumming about the war and how the U.S. runs its new territories, and tells William Rainsford he will not meddle in police matters.

headline: Edith shares her wardrobe
summary: A Sunday in New York City. Edith writes her sister Emily offering last year's gowns, since a governor's wife shouldn't wear the same clothes two seasons running.

headline: Hearing in the Martha Place case
summary: Roosevelt holds a hearing on Martha Place, a convicted murderer facing execution. No woman had yet been put to death in New York State.

headline: No reprieve for Martha Place
summary: Roosevelt tells Francis Jones he will not halt Martha Place's execution, adding that he could not respect anyone who traded away principle for the hope of higher office.

headline: Speaking to Syracuse businessmen
summary: Roosevelt addresses the Syracuse Chamber of Commerce and writes Frank Moss on politics.

headline: Huddle on the police bills
summary: Roosevelt confers with Root, Odell, Mazet, Stranahan and Raines on the police bills.

headline: In New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; the record notes nothing more.

headline: Off to Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington, D.C.; no details are recorded.

headline: A visit with Lodge
summary: In Washington Roosevelt spends time with his close friend Henry Cabot Lodge.

headline: Hunting books and a mediation board
summary: Roosevelt writes his publisher about book sales and the coming Big Game Hunting, which joins two of his earlier hunting books. He also asks Charles Fairchild to sit on the state Board of Mediation and Arbitration; Fairchild says no.

headline: Settling into the Executive Mansion
summary: Roosevelt writes about the Army beef inquiry, thanks Lodge for his stay, and tells Bellamy Storer he can't sway the choice of an American cardinal. Alice later remembered the Albany mansion as big, shabby and gloomy; Edith becomes a member of the Friday Morning Club and takes botanical walks with Fanny Parsons.

headline: Talking gas franchises with Platt
summary: Roosevelt meets Platt about the Astoria gas bill, corresponds about the British edition of his Naval War of 1812 and other publishing matters, and stands up for Leonard Wood.

headline: Evening with state editors
summary: Roosevelt speaks at an evening dinner of the state's newspaper editors and writes Lodge about what Navy armor plate costs.

headline: Yale men and the war
summary: In New York City Roosevelt speaks at the Yale alumni dinner about Yale's part in the war with Spain.

headline: Sorting out taxes with Emlen
summary: Roosevelt meets his cousin Emlen Roosevelt to go over his personal taxes and property.

headline: Sunday in New York City
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday in New York City; no details survive.

headline: Back in Albany
summary: Roosevelt is in Albany; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Going after a crooked canal man
summary: Roosevelt writes Adam Smith about ousting a dishonest canal superintendent in Herkimer County.

headline: A commission to probe the canals
summary: Roosevelt names a commission to investigate the state canals. He tells Leonard Wood he hopes the Senate will confirm him to a regular Army brigadier generalship, and outlines his canal policy for General Francis Greene.

headline: Frustrated with Congress
summary: Roosevelt complains to Lodge that Congress has been stingy with the Army and Navy, and remarks on General Shafter's coarseness.

headline: Talking good citizenship
summary: Roosevelt speaks on good citizenship to the West Side Republicans in New York City, and writes Nicholas Murray Butler about the school bill.

headline: Conference on Amsterdam Avenue
summary: Roosevelt meets Root, along with Coleman, Clarke and Ford, about the Amsterdam Avenue bill.

headline: Sunday in New York City
summary: A Sunday in New York City with nothing more recorded.

headline: No deal for Armour
summary: Roosevelt turns down a settlement of the state's suits against Armour & Co. over butter-law violations. Pressed by the Storers, he reluctantly writes McKinley about their hope that Archbishop Ireland be made a cardinal, and tells George Gunton his labor bills are a hard sell.

headline: Changing how the city borrows
summary: Roosevelt signs a charter change that pools Greater New York's county funds into one general fund and lets the comptroller borrow against expected revenue. He writes Root about the Astoria gas bill.

headline: Raising the bar for insurers
summary: Roosevelt signs a law requiring new fire and marine insurance companies to start with at least $200,000 in capital, and books a Saturday breakfast with Platt.

headline: Speech at Bleecker Hall
summary: Roosevelt gives a speech at Bleecker Hall and writes about the Place execution and the fight against sweatshops.

headline: Consulting Platt on transit and gas
summary: Roosevelt meets Fallows about the Amsterdam Avenue bill and asks Platt's views on the tunnel, rapid transit and Astoria gas bills.

headline: Pushing a tax on franchises
summary: After breakfast with Platt, Roosevelt backs the Ford bill, sent to the Legislature that day, to tax corporations on the public franchises they hold, then heads back to Albany.

headline: Sunday in Albany
summary: Roosevelt is in Albany; nothing else is noted.

headline: Martha Place is executed
summary: Martha Place is put to death, the first woman executed in New York State. Roosevelt sends Emily Carow a Rough Rider pin and tells her he is enjoying being governor.

headline: Bridges and a dismissal
summary: Roosevelt writes Lucius Littauer about letting an appointee go and Seth Low about the bridge bill.

headline: Birds and a new national park
summary: Roosevelt writes Frank Chapman about saving New York's bird species. The same day Congress creates Mount Rainier National Park, the nation's fifth.

headline: Dairy hearing and the Ireland question
summary: Roosevelt hears more on the Ambler dairy bill and writes Bellamy Storer about Archbishop Ireland, Winthrop Chanler with word for Platt, and Platt about the Greater New York bill.

headline: Speaking to the Citizens Union
summary: Roosevelt addresses the Citizens Union in New York City and writes Stafford Mosher about the canal.

headline: Platt balks at the Ford bill
summary: Over breakfast at his sister Bamie's home, 689 Madison Avenue, Roosevelt learns that Platt opposes the Ford franchise tax bill. Edith tells Spring-Rice the family likes life in the governor's office.

headline: Sunday in New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; the day is otherwise blank.

headline: Yielding to Platt on franchises
summary: Roosevelt gives way to Platt on the Ford bill, asking the Legislature instead for a joint committee to study franchises and corporate taxes. He signs the Ambler dairy law against selling dyed oleomargarine, and Edith turns the mansion's third floor into a gym for him and the children.

headline: Dinner for Platt
summary: Roosevelt attends a dinner held for Senator Platt in Albany.

headline: Help for an old Rough Rider
summary: Roosevelt meets legislative leaders and confers on the Ahearn school bill, and sends former Rough Rider William Proffit $75.

headline: Writing T. Thomas Fortune again
summary: Roosevelt writes T. Thomas Fortune about race relations and internal quarrels in the Black community.

headline: Malolos falls; bills and appraisers
summary: American troops take Malolos and Aguinaldo's forces retreat north. In Albany Roosevelt writes about savings bank, sweatshop and streetcar bills, and recommends Israel Fisher to McKinley for the post of General Appraiser in New York.

headline: A landmark day for labor laws
summary: Roosevelt signs a burst of reform laws: the Costello act policing sweatshop work in tenements, broader powers for factory inspectors with caps on hours for women and minors, canal repair money, and racing revenue for agriculture. He writes Bamie about the dispute over James Roosevelt's will.

headline: Sunday in Albany
summary: Roosevelt is in Albany; no activities are noted.

headline: Grade crossings and a book critic
summary: Roosevelt signs a law helping cities get rid of railroad grade crossings, listens to arguments over the Ahearn school bill, and answers John McBlaine, a critic of The Rough Riders.

headline: No double-dipping for city officials
summary: Roosevelt signs a law barring elected city officials from also holding a city-paid appointed job. A compromise Ahearn school bill goes to the Assembly, and he writes Platt about lengthening the session.

headline: Quiet day in Albany
summary: Roosevelt is in Albany; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Taxing franchises; Osborne for Lunacy
summary: Roosevelt writes John Sleicher about the Ford franchise tax and tells Douglas Robinson he will name Will Osborne to the Lunacy Commission.

headline: Ready to sign the Ford bill
summary: Roosevelt tells Paul Dana he now thinks the Ford franchise bill is sound and will gladly sign it.

headline: Heading west to Chicago
summary: Roosevelt sets out for Chicago, writing Douglas Robinson about the Osborne nomination and complaining to Joe Bishop about Goodman Brown as a Lunacy Commission pick.

headline: Union League dinner on Archie's birthday
summary: In Chicago Roosevelt is the guest at a Union League Club dinner; back home it is his son Archie's fifth birthday.

headline: Preaching the strenuous life
summary: In Chicago Roosevelt speaks at the University of Chicago and the Harvard Club, then delivers his famous call to effort and courage, "The Strenuous Life," at the Hamilton Club's Appomattox Day gathering.

headline: At Ann Arbor, then home
summary: Roosevelt speaks at University Hall in Ann Arbor, Michigan, and starts back to Albany.

headline: Ford bill clears the Senate
summary: The state Senate approves the Ford bill by a vote of 33-11. Roosevelt signs the Raines-Mazet act letting the governor launch election-fraud probes through the attorney general, and vents to Franklin Moulton about the 'goo-goos.'

headline: Bounty for beet sugar
summary: Roosevelt signs a change to the Beet Sugar Act offering a bounty to makers of sugar from New York-grown beets.

headline: Platt buries the Ford bill
summary: Roosevelt says the Ford bill will help the public and urges the Assembly to send it to him quickly, but Platt has it shelved there. He also explains his 'goo-goo' jab to Joe Bishop.

headline: Saturday in Albany
summary: Roosevelt is in Albany; no details recorded.

headline: Another Platt breakfast at Bamie's
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts with Platt at Bamie's home on Madison Avenue and returns to Albany that afternoon.

headline: Pure juice and limited franchises
summary: Roosevelt signs a law against selling adulterated juice as pure, issues a statement favoring limits on rapid transit franchises, and writes about a Rapid Transit Commission and the police bill.

headline: Opening the books of membership groups
summary: Roosevelt signs a law letting Supreme Court officers inspect the accounts of membership corporations, sits through a rapid transit hearing, and writes William Cutting about killings of prisoners in the Philippines.

headline: Civil service reform signed
summary: Roosevelt signs the Civil Service Act overhauling state and local merit systems, Ford and Fallows's Amsterdam Avenue act, and a ban on women and minors working at emery polishing wheels.

headline: In Albany
summary: Roosevelt is in Albany; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Savings banks and local option
summary: Roosevelt signs the Krum act limiting what savings banks may invest in and a revised local-option procedure under the liquor law. He congratulates Bellamy Storer on his new post as U.S. minister to Spain.

headline: Pressing for rapid transit
summary: Roosevelt urges the Legislature to move fast on the rapid transit bill and writes about the savings bank bill and a meeting with labor leaders.

headline: Sunday in Albany
summary: Roosevelt is in Albany; no activities are noted.

headline: Regents and a labor delegation
summary: Roosevelt sits with the Board of Regents and meets labor representatives about rapid transit. He writes Wood about errors in The Rough Riders and Maria Storer about Spain.

headline: School bill signed
summary: Roosevelt signs the Ahearn school act. A committee hears arguments on the Ford franchise tax, and he writes Assembly Speaker S. Fred Nixon about it.

headline: Dinner for Senator Frye
summary: Roosevelt goes down to New York City for the evening to attend the Commerce Commission's dinner for Senator William Frye.

headline: The torn-up message
summary: Roosevelt signs a Poor Law change on relief for Civil War veterans. Having lined up enough Assembly votes for the Ford bill, he sends an emergency message to free it from committee; Speaker Nixon refuses to read it, rips it up, then collapses in an anteroom.

headline: Ford bill forced through
summary: Learning at 7 a.m. that Nixon destroyed his message, Roosevelt writes a second one and threatens to deliver it in person. It is read, and the Assembly approves the Ford franchise tax, 109-35, as the session ends. He also signs carriage and election-registration laws.

headline: Family outing in Rensselaer County
summary: Roosevelt takes the family on a trip into Rensselaer County outside Albany. It is his sister Corinne's seventeenth wedding anniversary.

headline: Picnic by the Hudson
summary: The Roosevelts picnic on the bank of the Hudson. Edith writes Emily that a new Cyrano de Bergerac suffered in translation, and that she has watched Ellen Terry and Henry Irving perform.

headline: Platt fumes over the Ford bill
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie that Platt is angry the Ford bill got through the Assembly, and writes others about the bill, the cardinal question and the primary bill.

headline: Primaries, nature study and commerce
summary: Roosevelt signs an improved primary election law building on Root's 1898 measure, money for more natural history and geography teaching in public schools, and funding to keep the Commerce Commission's inquiry going.

headline: Tax reform note to Odell
summary: Roosevelt writes Odell about the tax reform bill.

headline: Bigger forest preserve, safer food
summary: Roosevelt signs laws outlawing poisonous food coloring, authorizing a Cohoes canal with locks linking the Erie and Champlain canals, and enlarging the forest preserve in four Catskill counties. He invites Odell to Albany to talk taxes.

headline: Keeping police out of politics
summary: Roosevelt signs the Raines-Mazet police act forbidding officers to sway votes, raise political money, or hire and promote for partisan reasons. He also toughens penalties for corrupt practices and lets the governor deputize train conductors and steamboat crews as police.

headline: Helderbergs trip; Platt objects
summary: Roosevelt takes a trip to the Helderberg hills near Albany. Platt writes asking him not to sign the Ford bill, and Roosevelt himself has some doubts about it.

headline: Near Albany
summary: Roosevelt is near Albany; the rest of the entry is unreadable.

headline: Standing firm, and the Buffalo strike
summary: Roosevelt tells Platt the Ford bill must pass this session, promising to recall the Legislature to strip out the objectionable assessment clause. At the Buffalo mayor's request he agrees to send militia into the dock strike.

headline: Evening at the City Club
summary: Roosevelt goes to New York City for an evening speech at the City Club.

headline: News for Bradley Johnson
summary: Roosevelt sends General Bradley Johnson news and his thinking on the franchise bill.

headline: Capping city franchises; special session called
summary: Roosevelt signs a charter amendment holding street franchises in Greater New York to 25 years (tunnels 50) and requiring good service at fair rates, a step toward the Atlantic Avenue tunnel. He wires Odell that he is calling the Legislature back on May 22 for the Ford bill.

headline: Eight-hour day enforcement
summary: Roosevelt signs the Sabine act tightening enforcement of the eight-hour day for state workers at local wages, and a broad reworking of second-class city government. He writes Platt about the Ford bill and the coming session.

headline: Explaining the Ford bill to Garfield
summary: Roosevelt writes Riis that he is rethinking the drug bill, sends Gherardi Davis notes on bills, and lays out the Ford bill for James R. Garfield, a Cleveland lawyer and son of the late President.

headline: Sunday in Albany
summary: Roosevelt is in Albany; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Property and its uses in Buffalo
summary: After meeting Odell about the Ford franchise tax, Roosevelt speaks that evening in Buffalo to the Independent Club about property and the state.

headline: More talks with Odell
summary: Roosevelt again meets Odell about the Ford franchise tax.

headline: Extra session called
summary: Roosevelt formally summons the Legislature into special session and writes Frank Higgins about the Ford bill.

headline: Telegrams on the Ford bill
summary: By telegram Roosevelt tells John Raines he will approve the franchise measure unchanged if the Legislature is withdrawn, and tells Odell some parts are objectionable while others are fine.

headline: Summit with the party leaders
summary: In New York City Roosevelt confers with Platt, Odell, Quigg, Boardman and Cohen, and speaks at the City Club.

headline: Bound for the Adirondacks
summary: Roosevelt leaves New York City for the Adirondacks.

headline: Sunday in the Adirondacks
summary: Roosevelt spends the day in the Adirondacks; no details survive.

headline: Lawmakers return for the special session
summary: Senators and Assemblymen are back in Albany as the special session opens.

headline: Election officers and TB hospitals
summary: Roosevelt signs an election law setting rules for poll officers, especially in New York City, and a law letting large cities build tuberculosis hospitals beyond their limits.

headline: Checking the bill's constitutionality
summary: Roosevelt asks Hobart Krum to examine one part of the franchise bill that may be unconstitutional.

headline: Antitrust law and slot machines
summary: With the Legislature's revisions to the Ford bill done and awaiting his approval, Roosevelt signs bans on slot machines and on monopolies in everyday goods. He tells William Allen White he liked his article.

headline: The Ford franchise tax becomes law
summary: Roosevelt signs the Ford franchise tax, making corporations pay taxes on their public franchises. He also signs a ban on transportation rate-fixing pools and a law keeping state fish hatchery waters clean.

headline: Savoring the Ford victory
summary: Roosevelt opens an inquiry into Insurance Superintendent Louis F. Payn. He tells Bamie and Lodge how pleased he is with the Ford bill win, praises Lodge's new Spanish-American War book, and says he hopes to rest this summer.

headline: In Stockbridge
summary: Roosevelt is in Stockbridge, Massachusetts; no details are recorded.

headline: In New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing more is noted.

headline: Decoration Day with the veterans
summary: Roosevelt joins the Decoration Day parade in New York City and speaks to the Grand Army of the Republic.

headline: Hungarian Republicans
summary: In New York City, Roosevelt addresses the Hungarian Republican Club.

headline: In New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; the record notes nothing more.

headline: Picking tax commissioners over breakfast
summary: Over breakfast Roosevelt talks Tax Commission appointments with Platt and Odell, then spends the night at Cortlandt Park with Andrews and Treadwell, bound for the militia camp at Peekskill. He writes Speaker Nixon about naming Lester Stern a tax commissioner.

headline: On the road to camp
summary: Roosevelt heads for the Peekskill militia camp, with stops at Sing Sing and Nelson Park.

headline: At Peekskill Camp
summary: Roosevelt is at the Peekskill camp; no details are recorded.

headline: At West Point
summary: Roosevelt is at West Point; no details survive.

headline: In New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing more is noted.

headline: An honorary degree from Columbia
summary: Columbia gives Roosevelt an honorary Doctor of Laws. He writes Odell about the city district and tells Kansas editor William Allen White he would very much like to meet him.

headline: New civil service rules
summary: Back in Albany Roosevelt approves new Civil Service Commission rules. He asks Harvard's Charles Eliot whether Leonard Wood will get an honorary degree, and writes McKinley once more for the Storers on the cardinal question.

headline: Honoring Frederick Douglass
summary: In Rochester Roosevelt is on hand as the Frederick Douglass monument is unveiled. Ted and Kermit finish the school year at the Albany Military Academy.

headline: Family heads to Sagamore for summer
summary: Roosevelt travels from Rochester to Peekskill while Edith takes the family home to Oyster Bay for the summer. James K. Gracie visits, and Roosevelt writes Seligman, Straus and Peters about Dreyfus's acquittal in France.

headline: Sunday at Peekskill
summary: Roosevelt is at Peekskill; nothing more is recorded.

headline: Planning a western trip
summary: From Sagamore Hill Roosevelt arranges trains for a trip west with Paul Morton and asks John Hay whether Parker is leaving the Civil Service Commission.

headline: At home at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Summer at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Another day at Sagamore
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: A houseful of friends
summary: Sagamore Hill guests include Nicholas Murray Butler, Colonel Arthur Lee, Captain Andrews and Winthrop Chanler.

headline: Letting the cardinal matter drop
summary: Bob Ferguson visits. Roosevelt tells McKinley he is dropping the cardinal question, writes Hay about resistance to civil service reform, and writes Bruno Hermann about German Americans.

headline: A quiet Sunday at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: In New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; no details survive.

headline: Cornell commencement speaker
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Cornell University's graduation in Ithaca.

headline: Leaving Ithaca for the West
summary: Roosevelt leaves Ithaca, bound west.

headline: Westbound through Chicago
summary: Roosevelt passes through Chicago on his way west.

headline: Rolling toward New Mexico
summary: Roosevelt is on the train to Las Vegas, New Mexico.

headline: First Rough Rider reunion begins
summary: Roosevelt reaches Las Vegas, New Mexico, as the first reunion of the Rough Riders gets under way. Mr. and Mrs. Clifford Richardson are listed as guests.

headline: Reunion parade and memorial
summary: The Rough Rider reunion continues in Las Vegas with memorial services and a parade.

headline: Back toward Chicago
summary: Roosevelt heads east again toward Chicago.

headline: Whistle-stops to Milwaukee
summary: Roosevelt travels from Chicago to Milwaukee, speaking along the way at Fort Madison and Galesburg.

headline: Milwaukee Chamber of Commerce
summary: Roosevelt speaks to the Milwaukee Chamber of Commerce, then starts east.

headline: "Not a candidate" for 1900
summary: With newspapers boosting him for President in 1900, Roosevelt returns to New York City via Albany and declares he is not running. He dines with Generals Wood and Greene, talking over Cuba and the Philippines. Mrs. Regis Post is a guest.

headline: Romps with the children; Lee courts Ruth Moore
summary: Arthur Lee is staying at Sagamore Hill, where he courts Ruth Moore. Roosevelt plays hard with the children: 'stagecoach' on the float, running down Cooper's Bluff, racing through the old barn, and tennis with Alice.

headline: Lodge pushes the vice presidency
summary: Lodge is urging Roosevelt to join McKinley's 1900 ticket, with Vice President Hobart ill. Roosevelt tells Corinne he plans to spend the month writing a life of Oliver Cromwell, and writes about his western trip, his rift with Tom Reed, and worries over U.S. colonial policy.

headline: Cuban fever returns
summary: Roosevelt is down with the fever he picked up in Cuba the summer before, an illness that would return throughout his life.

headline: At home at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Fireworks, grass fires and a giant TR
summary: Firecrackers wake Roosevelt and Edith at 4 a.m. and go on all day; he helps stamp out grass fires on the lawn and gives an Independence Day speech in Oyster Bay. The night ends with a fireworks portrait of him. He invites Admiral Dewey to Sagamore Hill.

headline: Ruling out 1900
summary: Roosevelt thanks John Gansey for a kind letter and says he will seek neither the presidency nor the vice presidency in 1900.

headline: Fourth of July news for Bamie
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie about the Fourth of July fun, the presidential talk swirling around him, and Emlen's lawsuit over James Roosevelt's will.

headline: At home at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: White House talks on a new War Secretary
summary: Roosevelt goes to Washington to confer at the White House with McKinley and others on choosing a Secretary of War, and urges Francis Greene for a Philippine command. He shares with Bill Sewall how hard it is to choose when right and wrong are mixed.

headline: Back to Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt leaves Washington for Oyster Bay.

headline: McKinley sees the Philippines differently
summary: Roosevelt updates Greene on his push to make him military governor of the Philippines, and tells Wood that McKinley disagreed with his view of the islands, calling things there good.

headline: Platt meeting and lunch with Greene
summary: In New York City Roosevelt confers with Platt, then has lunch with Douglas Robinson and General Greene.

headline: A good talk with McKinley
summary: Attorney General Davies visits Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt tells Bamie he had a fine talk with McKinley but little time for vacation, writes General James Wilson about Cuba's troubles, and thanks McKinley for a pleasant White House dinner.

headline: On a district attorney's removal
summary: Roosevelt writes Thomas Slicer about removing Asa Gardiner as New York City's district attorney.

headline: Political callers at Sagamore
summary: Woodruff, Nixon, Bender and Youngs visit Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Robinson cousins come to stay
summary: Corinne's children Corinne and Teddy Robinson arrive as guests. Roosevelt writes James Reynolds about factory inspector appointments.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Teddy Robinson is bored
summary: Roosevelt writes Corinne that her son Teddy, at sixteen, is not enjoying his summer: too old for the children's games and without friends his own age.

headline: At home at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Would refuse the War Department
summary: Roosevelt writes Slicer about removing Fellows and says he would decline the Secretary of War post if offered. He writes Benjamin Shove about removals.

headline: Bamie visits; canal report released
