summary: Bamie and her husband Captain Will Cowles come to Sagamore Hill. The canal investigators, Fox and MacFarlane, publish their findings.

headline: Rowing every day; Root to the War Department
summary: Roosevelt tells Lodge he rows nearly every day, and writes about the Philippines, Cuba and Wood. Alger is out, and Root will become Secretary of War.

headline: Visiting Platt at the shore
summary: At Manhattan Beach Roosevelt calls on Platt, who is staying at the Oriental Hotel, and sends news of New York to General Frederick Funston, serving in the Philippines.

headline: At Manhattan Beach
summary: Roosevelt is at Manhattan Beach; nothing more is noted.

headline: Inspecting the quarantine station
summary: Roosevelt visits the quarantine station on Barren Island.

headline: Cheering Root's appointment
summary: Caspar Whitney and Miss LeMorine visit. Roosevelt praises Root's choice as Secretary of War in letters to Greene and Wilson, and wishes Root luck.

headline: At home at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Edith's homemade toothpaste
summary: Edith tells Emily she mixes her own toothpaste from cuttlefish bone, dragon's blood, alum, orris root and spices. Roosevelt writes Edward Brown about his record on labor as governor.

headline: Senator Higgins calls
summary: Senator Frank Higgins is a guest at Sagamore Hill.

headline: At home at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: A visitor from Australia
summary: C. J. Sage of Melbourne, Australia, visits Sagamore Hill.

headline: Root takes over at War
summary: Russell Alger leaves the War Department and Elihu Root replaces him, while Vice President Hobart signals he means to remain. The Quiggs and General Avery Andrews visit, and Roosevelt sends Bradley Johnson a copy of The Rough Riders with notes on Remington's San Juan painting.

headline: Answering the Tribune on canals
summary: Roosevelt writes Austen Fox and Wallace MacFarlane, the canal investigators, regarding a Tribune editorial on their inquiry.

headline: Cromwell biography finished
summary: Roosevelt completes his life of Oliver Cromwell, sold for magazine serialization at $5,000 plus 15 percent royalties, and writes Robert Bridges about publishing it.

headline: Practical and decent politics
summary: At Asbury Park, New Jersey, Roosevelt speaks at the theological school on practical and decent politics, then spends the night at Norwood Park with Vice President Hobart. He also writes Caspar Whitney on the editorship of Harper's Weekly.

headline: Grant La Farge visits
summary: Grant La Farge is a guest at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Ferguson and Goodrich visit
summary: Bob Ferguson and David Goodrich are at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt writes Lucius Swift about civil service and the effort to keep Proctor, and sends General James Wilson recommendations for government posts.

headline: Edith's birthday
summary: Roosevelt is in Utica on his wife Edith's birthday.

headline: Western trip postponed
summary: Roosevelt tells Hermann Kohlsaat he is putting off his trip west and asks about the Republican position on trusts.

headline: Delegates for the trust conference
summary: Roosevelt writes Harry Newcomb, naming New York's delegates to the Chicago conference on trusts.

headline: At home at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Planning fair visits with Edith
summary: Dr. and Mrs. Alexander Lambert and Colonel Dick visit. Roosevelt writes Charles Scribner about Oliver Cromwell and tells Lodge he lunched with Root and that Edith will join him touring county fairs.

headline: Musings to Spring-Rice
summary: Roosevelt writes Spring-Rice about Irish and German Americans, the Alaska boundary dispute with Canada, Russia, and the waning of the 'old Americans.'

headline: Proofreading Cromwell
summary: Robert Bridges of Scribner's comes to Sagamore Hill to proof Oliver Cromwell. Roosevelt writes Spring-Rice again, and wires McKinley that he will speak in Ohio in October.

headline: Ethel turns eight
summary: Ethel celebrates her eighth birthday at Sagamore. Edith writes Emily she hopes TR wins a second term so Alice can make her debut at the Executive Mansion.

headline: Vouching for Rough Riders
summary: Roosevelt writes Root about particular Rough Riders who served under him.

headline: Wrestling with the trust question
summary: Roosevelt speaks to a firemen's convention in Yonkers, dines with Littauer, Odell and Platt, and leaves for Buffalo that night. He asks Charles Scott for guidance on trusts, admitting he is unsure what stand to take.

headline: To the Niagara County Fair
summary: Roosevelt reaches Olcott by way of Buffalo and sets out for the Niagara County Fair. Edith tells Emily her heart had become 'enlarged' while he was in Cuba, then recovered when he came home safe.

headline: At Niagara Falls
summary: Roosevelt is at Niagara Falls; no details are recorded.

headline: At Silver Lake
summary: Roosevelt is at Silver Lake; nothing more is noted.

headline: At Chautauqua
summary: Roosevelt is at Chautauqua; no details survive.

headline: With McKinley and Hobart at Plattsburgh
summary: At Plattsburgh Roosevelt spends time with McKinley and Hobart, the President and Vice President.

headline: Reporting a successful tour
summary: From Plattsburgh Roosevelt tells Platt his speaking tour has gone well and sends General Wilson ideas for military appointments.

headline: Andrews and Judge Parkhurst visit
summary: Avery Andrews and Judge Parkhurst are guests at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Publisher George Haven Putnam visits
summary: George Haven Putnam is a guest at Sagamore Hill.

headline: At home at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Late summer at Sagamore
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: A Saturday at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Six hours at the oars
summary: Roosevelt spends six straight hours in a rowboat. Baron Speck von Sternberg and Mrs. Rose are guests.

headline: Loeb fills in as secretary
summary: Roosevelt sends Lodge news, tells May Youngs that William Loeb is serving as private secretary, and writes Wood about Cuba.

headline: At home at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Hornellsville fair
summary: Roosevelt speaks at the fair in Hornellsville and stays the night in Olean.

headline: "This Nation" at Little Valley
summary: Bound for Watertown, Roosevelt speaks at Little Valley and stops at Buffalo, continuing his round of county fairs. He writes William Archer about the Germans.

headline: Canals at the Jefferson County Fair
summary: In Watertown Roosevelt talks about canals and how they should be run at the Jefferson County Fair, then leaves for New York City.

headline: Ideas for a better Army
summary: John Fox Jr. visits Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt thanks Root for hearing him out and sends Arthur Lee his thoughts on reorganizing the U.S. Army.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Boosting Wood for brigadier
summary: Roosevelt writes Wood privately about Army matters and urges Root to make him a brigadier general in the Regular Army.

headline: Ogdensburg fair
summary: Roosevelt speaks at the county fair in Ogdensburg.

headline: Fulton County Fair and Philippine geology
summary: Roosevelt addresses fairgoers in Johnstown, Fulton County, and stays the night in Utica. He writes geologist George Becker about his intriguing study of Philippine geology.

headline: Two fairs in one day
summary: Roosevelt addresses fairs in both Norwich and Delhi and spends the night in Syracuse.

headline: Home to Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt travels from Syracuse back to Oyster Bay.

headline: At home at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Sunday at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: All five swimmers
summary: Roosevelt dines in New York City with Odell, Platt and Cohen. He tells Bellamy Storer his five oldest children can all swim, and writes his last letter to Lodge while Lodge is in England.

headline: Orange County Fair; a heckler
summary: Roosevelt speaks at the Orange County Fair in Middletown and writes W. Forbes Murray about a heckler he faced in Hornellsville.

headline: Ted turns twelve
summary: Roosevelt addresses the fair in Walton, Delaware County, on Ted's twelfth birthday. The Chicago conference on trusts opens.

headline: Lewis County Fair
summary: Roosevelt addresses the fair at Lowville in Lewis County and stays in Utica, while the Chicago trust conference goes on. He tells Will Cowles he is swamped with speeches.

headline: Wayne County Fair
summary: Roosevelt addresses the fair at Lyons in Wayne County as the trust conference in Chicago continues.

headline: Brooklyn veterans and a parade outfit
summary: After breakfast with Youngs, Roosevelt speaks to Brooklyn veterans. The Robinsons and Bob Ferguson visit. He writes on political pressure, backs Mazet, asks Avery Andrews what a governor should wear riding in Dewey's parade, and writes Nixon about charges against officials.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Ramapo and canal scandals
summary: Nicholas Murray Butler and Mr. Hollis visit. Roosevelt writes Frank Moss about the Ramapo water scandal, Grant La Farge about the canal scandal, and Samuel Young about the Philippines.

headline: Suffolk County Fair
summary: Roosevelt addresses the fair at Riverhead in Suffolk County and tells Lemuel Quigg he backs Mazet in organization politics.

headline: Reading a life of Forrest
summary: Roosevelt tells Bradley Johnson he is reading Johnson's biography of Nathan Bedford Forrest, and writes George Heins about civil service reform and the Miss Frost complaint.

headline: Cooperstown fair
summary: After stopping in Albany, Roosevelt arrives in Otsego County and speaks at the Cooperstown fair.

headline: Richfield Springs, then Ohio
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Richfield Springs, goes on to Utica, and leaves for Akron, Ohio.

headline: Opening the Ohio campaign
summary: Roosevelt stops in Cleveland to confer with Mark Hanna, then speaks in Akron to launch the Ohio Republican campaign before heading back to New York. He writes Grant La Farge about the canal scandal.

headline: In New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City; nothing more is recorded.

headline: "A fighting man" for the Philippines
summary: Roosevelt tells Root that General Otis is a drag on the American campaign in the islands and that what is needed there is a fighter.

headline: Congratulations to Arthur Lee
summary: Mrs. Alene, Grant La Farge and Mr. McNaughton visit. Roosevelt sends Arthur Lee good wishes on becoming engaged to Ruth Moore.

headline: Dewey's Olympia arrives
summary: Roosevelt addresses the fair in Mineola, Queens County, on his sister Corinne's 38th birthday. Admiral Dewey's flagship Olympia anchors off Staten Island, his first time home since Manila Bay. Roosevelt tells Thomas Slicer he is battling machine politics.

headline: Welcoming Dewey aboard the Olympia
summary: Roosevelt makes an official call on Admiral Dewey aboard the Olympia, while giant letters on the Brooklyn Bridge spell out a welcome. With Admiral Sampson he also tours the Indiana and New Hampshire.

headline: A five-mile flotilla
summary: The Olympia sails up the bay and on into the Hudson River, trailed by hundreds of ships in a line five miles long. General Avery Andrews is a guest.

headline: Leading Dewey's parade on horseback
summary: Roosevelt rides at the head of Admiral Dewey's homecoming parade, 35,000 marchers strong, with McKinley and Hanna also taking part; it passes beneath a victory arch where Fifth Avenue meets 23rd Street. His article on Dewey appears in McClure's, and Bamie and her husband take a new home on N Street in Washington.

headline: Canada's Governor General at Sagamore Hill
summary: Governor Roosevelt plays host at Sagamore Hill to Lord Minto, the Governor General of Canada. Robert C. Pruyn signs the guest book.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more.

headline: Dining in honor of Admiral Dewey
summary: In Washington, Roosevelt joins a dinner honoring Admiral George Dewey, hero of Manila Bay. The guest book lists Lord and Lady Minto, Captain Lascelles, Mrs. Leonard Wood and Colonel Arthur Lee.

headline: Strategy session with Odell
summary: In New York City, Roosevelt sits down with Benjamin Odell, the state Republican chairman.

headline: In Binghamton
summary: Roosevelt is in Binghamton, New York.

headline: Speaking in Elmira and Waverly
summary: Roosevelt addresses crowds in two southern-tier New York towns, Elmira and Waverly.

headline: Back in Albany
summary: Roosevelt is in Albany.

headline: Sunday in Albany
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday in Albany.

headline: Waving off a presidential boom
summary: Roosevelt writes a stack of letters from Albany. He asks H. H. Kohlsaat not to launch a Roosevelt-for-President movement, tells Henry White he is readying for the coming elections, and argues that Leonard Wood has earned a promotion.

headline: Kermit turns ten
summary: Kermit Roosevelt celebrates his tenth birthday. His father writes George Gunton about the franchise tax, Henry Nelson about the Navy, and Martha Selmes a chatty update.

headline: Niece Eleanor turns fifteen
summary: Roosevelt is in Albany on the fifteenth birthday of his niece Eleanor Roosevelt, daughter of his late brother Elliott.

headline: In Albany
summary: Roosevelt is in Albany.

headline: Home to Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is back at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Lodge returns from Europe
summary: At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt's closest political friend, Henry Cabot Lodge, lands back in the United States after a trip to Europe.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Back in Albany
summary: Roosevelt returns to Albany.

headline: A letter on race and crime
summary: From Albany, Roosevelt writes John William Fox about questions of race, including the crime of rape.

headline: Nephew Sheffield's first birthday
summary: Roosevelt is in Albany as his sister Bamie's son, Sheffield Cowles, turns one.

headline: Backing the anti-Tammany ticket
summary: In New York City, Roosevelt speaks in support of the Fusion slate opposing Tammany Hall. He also presses Elihu Root on reorganizing the Army and doubts to William Chandler that Admiral Howell should lead the Asiatic Squadron.

headline: Breakfast with the bosses, then west
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts in New York with Senator Thomas Platt and Benjamin Odell before boarding a train for Cincinnati. He writes Lodge, whose mother is ill.

headline: Talking Philippines at Cincinnati's Music Hall
summary: On the campaign trail in Ohio, Roosevelt speaks at Cincinnati's Music Hall about American policy in the Philippines.

headline: Another Cincinnati speech
summary: Roosevelt gives another campaign address in Cincinnati.

headline: Crediting good timing for the governorship
summary: Back in Albany, Roosevelt admits to Charles Wood that coming home from Cuba just as a governor's race opened had much to do with his election.

headline: Special court term to tackle Tammany
summary: After meeting Platt and Odell in New York, Roosevelt orders an extraordinary term of the Supreme Court to hear cases of lawbreaking tied to Tammany Hall. He then heads for Baltimore.

headline: Whistle-stopping across western Maryland
summary: Roosevelt barnstorms western Maryland for Governor Lloyd Lowndes's re-election, from Barton and Frostburg to Cumberland and Hagerstown, with a stop across the line in Piedmont, West Virginia. He assures Lodge the Presidency holds no interest for him.

headline: Frederick by day, Baltimore by night
summary: Roosevelt keeps up the Maryland swing, speaking in Frederick and stopping at Union Bridge, Westminster and Bruceville before an evening address in Baltimore. Grant La Farge and a Mr. McNaughton appear in the guest book.

headline: A forty-first birthday on the stump
summary: Roosevelt marks his forty-first birthday with a speech at Elkton, Maryland, then catches a train home toward Albany.

headline: Guinea pigs and a special prosecutor
summary: A busy letter day in Albany. Roosevelt tells Philemon Sherman he backs expansion, admires Maria Storer's 'goddess' pictures of Edith, and reports that Ted and Kermit are raising guinea pigs. He also names Ansley Wilcox to prosecute the Gardiner case.

headline: Sunday in Albany
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday in Albany.

headline: A possum for the children
summary: Roosevelt thanks General Bradley T. Johnson for a pet possum sent to the Roosevelt children, takes aim at Carl Schurz in a letter to F. B. Cunz, and writes House Speaker David B. Henderson.

headline: Republican dinner in Boston
summary: Roosevelt speaks to a Republican dinner in Boston. The same day The Century runs his essay on military preparedness.

headline: Home at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with his family.

headline: Home at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with his family.

headline: Home at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with his family.

headline: Home at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with his family.

headline: Home at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with his family.

headline: Home at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with his family.

headline: Election Day at home
summary: Roosevelt spends Election Day at Sagamore Hill.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt remains at Sagamore Hill the day after the election.

headline: Still pushing for Wood's star
summary: From Albany, Roosevelt tells General Leonard Wood he is still working to win him a brigadier general's rank in the Regular Army, and notes that his own expansionist views are drawing fire.

headline: Complaining of newspaper lies
summary: Roosevelt turns down Albert Mills's invitation for his Boston trip to the Harvard-Yale game, and grumbles to John Rose that papers like the Evening Post are printing falsehoods about him.

headline: In Albany
summary: Roosevelt is in Albany.

headline: Sunday in Albany
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday in Albany.

headline: Inviting an editor inside
summary: In two letters, Roosevelt invites Harper's Weekly editor John Finley to Albany to watch state government up close, and hopes Finley can dig up facts on the canal scandal to answer the Evening Post.

headline: In Albany
summary: Roosevelt is in Albany.

headline: Planning a tax commission
summary: Roosevelt meets legislators Stranahan, Frank Higgins and Jotham Allds in Albany to discuss a special commission on taxation.

headline: Odell, and a state police idea
summary: Roosevelt confers with Odell and asks Nicholas Murray Butler to talk over a bill to create a state constabulary.

headline: Bound for Boston
summary: Roosevelt travels to Boston.

headline: Cheering at the Harvard-Yale game
summary: Roosevelt takes in the Harvard-Yale football game in Boston.

headline: Quentin turns two
summary: Roosevelt is in Boston on his youngest son Quentin's second birthday.

headline: Speaking at Yale
summary: Roosevelt addresses students at Yale in New Haven and dines with the university's president, Arthur Twining Hadley.

headline: Vice President Hobart dies
summary: In New York City Roosevelt holds a hearing on charges against District Attorney Gardiner, huddles with Platt, Odell, Quigg, Slicer and Davies, and addresses the Chamber of Commerce. That same day Garret Hobart, the Vice President, dies, leaving open the office that will soon shadow Roosevelt's future.

headline: Breakfast, then home to Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts with Platt and Odell in New York and heads out to Oyster Bay that afternoon.

headline: Thanksgiving week at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Bamie's fourth anniversary
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill on the fourth wedding anniversary of his sister Bamie and William Sheffield Cowles.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Wilcox named; Dewey's bid frowned on
summary: Back in Albany, Roosevelt names Buffalo lawyer Ansley Wilcox to hear the Gardiner charges and meets the Education Commission. He tells Bamie the fuss around Admiral Dewey, who is angling for the Democratic presidential nomination, is beneath dignity.

headline: Mr. Dooley and game wardens
summary: Roosevelt urges the state's conservation commission to hire game wardens and protectors among other reforms. He also writes Finley Peter Dunne, whose Mr. Dooley teased that The Rough Riders should have been titled 'Alone in Cuba,' and invites him to visit.

headline: On raising manly children
summary: Roosevelt hears arguments on a Supreme Court appointment and writes G. Stanley Hall about bringing children up with firmness and manliness.

headline: In Albany
summary: Roosevelt is in Albany.

headline: No appetite for the Vice Presidency
summary: Roosevelt writes Lemuel Quigg about the police bill and says he will talk with him about the Vice Presidency, a job he does not want.

headline: A blue-faced watch for Edith
summary: On their thirteenth anniversary Roosevelt gives Edith a costly watch with a blue face, the gift she liked best of any he had given. He also writes Secretary John D. Long, thanking him on Ted's behalf for a guinea pig named Admiral Dewey that started the boys' brood.

headline: Sunday in Albany
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday in Albany.

headline: Talking taxes and trusts with economists
summary: Roosevelt confers with economists Jeremiah Jenks and Edwin Seligman, along with Senator Stranahan, about taxation and the trusts.

headline: In Albany
summary: Roosevelt is in Albany.

headline: A word for the Storers
summary: Roosevelt asks Secretary of State John Hay to consider moving Bellamy Storer from Madrid to Paris or Rome, and writes Leonard Wood about the men backing his promotion.

headline: Lodge presses the Vice Presidency again
summary: In New York, Henry Cabot Lodge once more urges Roosevelt to go after the Republican vice presidential nomination. Roosevelt tells Hugh Leonard, author of a wrestling book, that he has taken up the sport himself.

headline: Meeting the canal commissioners
summary: In New York City, Roosevelt meets with the state's canal commissioners.

headline: Charter revision and the second spot
summary: Over breakfast with Platt and Odell, Roosevelt talks through naming charter revision commissioners and the question of the vice presidential nomination.

headline: Sunday in Albany
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday in Albany.

headline: Platt backs a second term
summary: Senator Platt tells Roosevelt he officially favors renominating him for governor. Roosevelt's letters range over the Raines liquor law, the Astoria Gas Company, a court vacancy, a breakfast invitation to Butler, and the Vice Presidency.

headline: Planning to drop Payn
summary: Roosevelt resolves to let Insurance Superintendent Louis Payn go when his term ends in February, though Boss Platt wants him kept and Payn vows to stay. He sizes up Francis Hendricks as a replacement.

headline: A breakfast reminder for Platt
summary: Roosevelt reminds Senator Platt of their breakfast on December 23 at Douglas Robinson's house.

headline: Admiring Mr. Dooley's aim
summary: Roosevelt tells Lodge he enjoyed Mr. Dooley's spoof of his book, while marveling at how neatly Dunne finds the weak spots.

headline: Edith misses Washington
summary: Edith writes Cecil Spring-Rice that she misses the old Washington days, and Roosevelt writes Elihu Root about the trusts.

headline: Fielding vice presidential talk
summary: Roosevelt writes Odell about Nicholas Murray Butler and Payn's reappointment, and answers both C. C. Kohlsaat and George Lyman about the vice presidential question.

headline: Saying no to the Vice Presidency
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie he will turn down the vice presidential offer and mourns the war in South Africa between the British and the Boers. In New York, Edith greets her sister Emily Carow, just home from Italy.

headline: Letters to Conie, Platt and Riis
summary: Roosevelt writes his sister Corinne, Senator Platt about Hissock and Payn, and Jacob Riis about a bill on drug clerks.

headline: Annual Message: clean streams, safe birds
summary: Roosevelt meets with Mazet and wraps up his Annual Message, sending a copy to Platt. The message takes a hard line on big corporations and calls for ending pollution of Adirondack streams and protecting birds and deer.

headline: In Albany
summary: Roosevelt is in Albany.

headline: Dinner at Corinne's
summary: Roosevelt goes down to New York City and dines at seven at his sister Corinne's home, 422 Madison Avenue. His essay 'Expansion and Peace' appears in the Independent.

headline: In New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City.

headline: Plotting Payn's removal over breakfast
summary: At Corinne's home, Roosevelt breakfasts with Platt and Odell and they discuss removing Louis Payn.

headline: Christmas Eve in Albany
summary: Roosevelt is in Albany for Christmas Eve.

headline: Stockings and present tables at the Mansion
summary: All six Roosevelt children are at the Governor's Mansion for Christmas, with Emily Carow, Bob Ferguson and Speck von Sternberg as guests. The family keeps its yearly routine: stockings first, then breakfast, then a separate table piled with gifts for each child.

headline: Platt's puzzling support
summary: Roosevelt writes the Land Office about the Astoria grant and Andrew White about pardons. He tells Lodge that Platt still backs his refusal of the vice presidential slot, though he cannot see why.

headline: Thanks for Bamie's gifts
summary: Roosevelt thanks his sister Bamie for her generous Christmas presents, a handsome table and a set of knives.

headline: Another breakfast with Platt and Odell
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts again in New York City with Platt and Odell.

headline: Platt wants no fight over Payn
summary: Roosevelt reports to Lodge that Platt is against a battle over Payn. He also writes Bamie, George Lyman about the Vice Presidency, Platt about Payn and Mazet, and Austen Fox about the canal section of his message.

headline: Platt changes his tune
summary: Roosevelt tells John Williams he must dismiss factory inspector O'Leary, and reports to Lodge that Platt now says he should accept the vice presidential nomination.

headline: Year's end in Albany
summary: Roosevelt closes out 1899 in Albany.

headline: Platt skips the New Year's reception
summary: Roosevelt holds the customary New Year's Day reception in Albany. Senator Platt stays away to show his displeasure with the governor's course.

headline: New Year's notes
summary: Roosevelt writes Platt and Lodge about publisher L. A. Coolidge, and sends New Year's wishes to his friend Cecil Spring-Rice.

headline: Message calls for forest parks and trust curbs
summary: Roosevelt's Annual Message is read to the Legislature. It urges saving the forests, creating preserves in both the Catskills and the Adirondacks, and bold legislation to rein in the trusts. He scolds the Mail and Express for printing the text early.

headline: Regents Commission reports
summary: The Regents Commission releases its report while Roosevelt is in Albany.

headline: Labor law and a leaky newspaper
summary: Roosevelt writes George Gunton about the labor law and asks Frank Mack, an Associated Press man, how to deal with the Mail and Express.

headline: Digging into Payn's past
summary: Roosevelt asks Elihu Root for the testimony from an 1895 trial involving Louis Payn.

headline: Speaking at St. Paul's School
summary: Roosevelt travels to Concord, New Hampshire, to speak at St. Paul's School.

headline: Weighing Pound for insurance chief
summary: Roosevelt tells Cuthbert Pound he would name him Superintendent of Insurance if he were sure the Senate would confirm him.

headline: Eyeing the Kaiser's Germany
summary: In a letter to William Kimball, Roosevelt names Germany, under its current Kaiser, as the likeliest serious rival of the United States.

headline: Choosing Judge Saxton
summary: Roosevelt informs Cuthbert Pound that he has settled on Judge Charles Saxton as his nominee for Superintendent of Insurance.

headline: Investigation ordered; a funeral in Schenectady
summary: Armed with evidence against Louis Payn, Roosevelt directs Adjutant General Avery Andrews to investigate. He goes to Schenectady for the funeral of Samuel Dana Greene and his wife, then on to New York City that night to see Andrews at his hotel on Fifth Avenue.

headline: Near-pick for the trust probe
summary: Roosevelt writes J. P. Clarke that he very nearly named him to investigate the State Trust Company.

headline: The Payn report is in
summary: The investigation of Payn is finished. Roosevelt tells James Sheffield that a successor's name is going to the Senate shortly and writes Lyman Abbott about politics.

headline: Sunday in Albany
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday in Albany.

headline: Thanks for the Payn report
summary: Roosevelt updates Thomas Slicer on the Payn fight, writes George Holls about merging the state's Regents bodies, and thanks Avery Andrews for his report.

headline: A fan of Mr. Dooley on Dreyfus
summary: Roosevelt tells Finley Peter Dunne how much he enjoys some of his pieces, singling out those on the Dreyfus affair.

headline: Senators weigh Payn's successor
summary: State senators confer in Albany over who should follow Payn as insurance chief.

headline: Bamie turns forty-five
summary: Roosevelt is in Albany on his older sister Bamie's forty-fifth birthday.

headline: Toasting the University of the South
summary: That evening Roosevelt speaks in New York City at an alumni dinner for the Sewanee school, the University of the South.

headline: Showdown with Platt over Payn
summary: Over breakfast Roosevelt tells Platt and Odell that Payn must go; Platt rejects Judge Saxton and every name on a list. Roosevelt gives him until January 23 or he will go public. Platt then tells reporters he backs Roosevelt for Vice President. That night Roosevelt speaks at the Union League and Boone and Crockett clubs.

headline: Corinne and Douglas come to Albany
summary: Roosevelt's sister Corinne and her husband Douglas Robinson ride back to Albany with him for a visit.

headline: Ribs caved in by a wrestler
summary: Roosevelt confesses to Will Cowles that he has had too much of the strenuous life lately: a hefty wrestling partner has caved in his ribs. He also writes about the Payn fight, the Vice Presidency, and a scrap young Ted got into at the Albany Academy.

headline: Odell blinks: Hendricks it is
summary: Platt still insists on Payn, so Roosevelt offers Francis Hendricks. Odell holds the bluff to the last moment, then accepts Hendricks. Roosevelt also talks with Robert Bacon about the State Trust Company and tells Bamie he is weighing the Philippines governor-generalship.

headline: Hendricks says yes
summary: Francis Hendricks agrees to become Superintendent of Insurance. Roosevelt writes Platt and Hendricks about the nomination.

headline: Commerce report goes to lawmakers
summary: The New York Commerce Commission's report is sent to the Legislature. Roosevelt writes Seth Low about the Payn affair and George Lyman about his vice presidential chances.

headline: Speak softly and carry a big stick
summary: Roosevelt announces Hendricks's appointment to the press. Writing to Henry Sprague, he quotes the proverb that would become his best-known motto. He also sends Platt good wishes for his ailing wife.

headline: Letters on the Boer War
summary: Roosevelt writes William Sanger about Army reserves, and three correspondents, including Spring-Rice, about the war in South Africa.

headline: Sunday in Albany
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday in Albany.

headline: Claiming victory over Payn
summary: Roosevelt crows to Thomas Slicer about winning the Payn fight, tells Captain Bowman McCalla of his pride in the armed forces, and praises Sanger and Young's Philippine work to President McKinley and Elihu Root.

headline: Weighing the Vice Presidency with Lodge
summary: Roosevelt holds a conference on the Regents Bill, writes Arthur Lee about the Boer War, and lays out for Lodge the arguments for and against the Vice Presidency.

headline: Senate confirms Hendricks
summary: The state Senate confirms Francis Hendricks as Superintendent of Insurance, closing Roosevelt's fight over Payn. He writes General Francis Greene about the canals and sends Platt a report.

headline: Vice presidential rumors in the papers
summary: Stories turn up in the newspapers, from no clear source, claiming Republicans will put Roosevelt on the national ticket. He admits to Platt he has thought hard about the Vice Presidency and tells Odell it looks worse the longer he considers it.

headline: Rather the governor's chair
summary: Roosevelt holds talks on the trusts with Jenks, Higgins, Stranahan and Nixon, and on the Regents Bill with Seth Low. He tells Lodge, the party committee and Butler plainly that he would rather stay governor than run for Vice President.

headline: Insurance men want him kicked upstairs
summary: Furious over Payn's ouster, New York's big insurance firms team up with other corporations to lean on Platt to be rid of Roosevelt, even by promoting him to the Vice Presidency. Roosevelt writes Lodge about the forces lined up against his staying on.

headline: Sunday in Albany
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday in Albany.

headline: 'Harmless there'
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie his opponents want him in the Vice Presidency because they think he can do no harm there, and adds thoughts on the Boer War. He assures L. J. Moore he has no plan to run.

headline: Calling for a stronger Army and Navy
summary: In New York, Roosevelt and Odell meet at the Fifth Avenue Hotel about the Vice Presidency. He then speaks to the state bankers' association and at Carnegie Hall in favor of building up the armed forces, and compliments William Allen White on a Scribner's story.

headline: Professor before Vice President
summary: Roosevelt tells Platt he would sooner teach history at a college than serve as Vice President. He also praises William Howard Taft and writes the hunter Frederick Selous about the Boer War.

headline: Rapid transit for Greater New York
summary: Roosevelt signs the Davis Rapid Transit Act, letting Greater New York's municipal assembly grant franchises for rapid transit lines, and writes about the Backus matter, appointments and city investigations.

headline: Forests, fisheries and franchises
summary: Roosevelt writes Grant La Farge about the Fisheries and Forests commission, Lodge about the Vice Presidency, and George Priest about the franchise tax.

headline: Lunch in the Amen Corner
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Platt and Odell in the Fifth Avenue Hotel's famous 'Amen Corner,' still insisting he wants another term as governor rather than the Vice Presidency.

headline: Against the Nicaraguan canal plan
summary: Roosevelt meets George Holls and Shaw in Yonkers about the Regents Bill and announces his opposition to the proposed Nicaraguan canal arrangement.

headline: 'Under no circumstances'
summary: Roosevelt issues a public statement ruling out the vice presidential nomination. It is also his daughter Alice's sixteenth birthday; she has grown nearly as tall as her father. He tells Lyman Powell he is drafting a bill to regulate trusts.

headline: Advice to Bacon on politics
summary: Roosevelt's letters cover the Philippines, Puerto Rico, Long Island coastal land and his refusal of the Vice Presidency. He also advises Robert Bacon on whether to go into politics.

headline: Doubts about the Hay-Pauncefote Treaty
summary: After meeting Odell, Roosevelt writes Josephine Shaw Lowell about errors he may have made, and tells Captain Alfred Thayer Mahan he considers the Hay-Pauncefote Treaty a mistake.

headline: Back pay for city teachers
summary: Roosevelt signs the Ahearn School Act, which pays New York City teachers and school workers the salaries they are owed. He writes Butler about the Unification Bill and the game commission, and Albert Shaw about his canal treaty statement.

headline: No unfortified canal
summary: Roosevelt objects to Will Cowles and Finley Peter Dunne about the plan, favored by McKinley and Hay, for an isthmian canal left open and unfortified. He also writes about his renomination, a forest commission and the state of New York politics.

headline: Hay signs a canal deal
summary: Roosevelt confers with Limburger, lawyer for the Ramapo water company, and writes Butler. In Washington, Secretary of State John Hay signs an agreement with Nicaragua securing rights for a canal.

headline: Objecting to Hay's treaty
summary: Roosevelt writes John Hay himself, laying out his objections to the Nicaraguan canal treaty.

headline: A landmark forest, fish and game law
summary: Roosevelt signs a sweeping law protecting New York's forests, fish and game, rewriting Chapter 31 of the General Laws. It caps his conservation work as governor. He also meets Greene and Hill on canal funding.

headline: Defending his whole record
summary: Roosevelt confers with Odell about the fish, game and forest preserve boards and speaks to the Foreign Missionary Conference. In a long letter to Josephine Shaw Lowell, he defends his entire term as governor.

headline: Three dinners, three speeches
summary: In New York City, Roosevelt speaks at three dinners: the Harvard Club, the Buyers Association and the Press Club. He writes Quigg about bills and about backing Platt.

headline: Washington's Birthday in Buffalo
summary: In Buffalo, Roosevelt speaks to the Daughters of the American Revolution and then to the Saturn Club on Washington and what is ideal versus practical in politics. He complains to Bamie of fighting the machine on one flank and reformers on the other.

headline: Back to Albany
summary: Roosevelt leaves Buffalo for Albany.

headline: An invitation to Harvard's president
summary: Roosevelt sees Woodruff and invites Harvard president Charles Eliot to stay with him at the Governor's Mansion.

headline: Sunday in Albany
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday in Albany.

headline: Canal bills reach the Legislature
summary: The Canal Commission's bills go to the Legislature. Roosevelt repeats his case against an open Nicaraguan canal to Will Cowles and explains to Maria Storer why he cannot get involved in naming an American cardinal.

headline: 'Better than Cleveland'
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie he believes he has run the governorship better than anyone in his lifetime, Grover Cleveland included. He says sorry to Josephine Shaw Lowell for how sharp his previous letter sounded, and tells Benjamin Ide Wheeler he hopes future historians will also write well.

headline: 'Good Citizenship' in Newburgh
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Odell in Newburgh and speaks on good citizenship at Trinity Episcopal Church. Meanwhile, both McKinley and Senator Hanna are cool to having him as running mate. The six Roosevelt children sit for a group photograph.

headline: Two appointments in question
summary: Roosevelt writes Ray Tompkins about two appointments, those of Van Duzer and O'Neil.

headline: No paying newspapers for support
summary: Roosevelt signs a Penal Code amendment barring anyone from asking a candidate for money in return for a newspaper's or publication's backing. His letters touch city water, the fleet and coastal forts, and the Boer War and Nicaraguan canal.

headline: Speaking to the Ohio Society
summary: Roosevelt goes from Albany to New York City for an evening address to the Ohio Society, and tells William O'Neil his financial dealings have blocked his appointment.

headline: Sunday in New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City.

headline: The Merrimac purchase revisited
summary: Roosevelt writes Elon Brown about quail hunting, General Greene about the canal bill, and John D. Long about the ship Merrimac, which he bought as Assistant Secretary of the Navy and which the press is now criticizing.

headline: A fight over his nominees
summary: Roosevelt warns Grant La Farge of a determined push to defeat his nominees.

headline: Edith sets off to see San Juan Hill
summary: Edith and her sister Emily leave for Cuba; Edith wants to judge for herself how steep San Juan Hill really is. Roosevelt writes Seth Low about the Ramapo water bill and tells La Farge that lumbermen and cold-storage interests are lobbying against him.

headline: Condolences to Lodge
summary: Roosevelt sends Lodge sympathy on the death of his mother, and writes Frederick De Berard about the Ramapo bill, a disputed plan involving upstate land for a New York City reservoir.

headline: West Side Republicans
summary: Roosevelt is the dinner speaker for West Side Republicans at their club in New York and writes A. J. Sage about Australian troops in the Boer War.

headline: Edith lands in Havana
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts with Platt and Odell in New York and tells William O'Neil he will not get the appointment. In Cuba, Edith and Emily arrive by ship at Havana, where Governor General Leonard Wood meets them.

headline: Sunday in New York City
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City.

headline: Edith finds San Juan Hill gentler than expected
summary: Edith writes Ethel that San Juan Hill is less steep and imposing than she imagined. Roosevelt promises General Henry Evans he will help the family of Marshall, his Rough Rider aide, and writes Spring-Rice, James Carter and Lodge.

headline: Asking Woodrow Wilson for help
summary: Roosevelt asks Princeton professor Woodrow Wilson to suggest someone who could assist him with appointments, and writes about Puerto Rican sovereignty and the Ramapo charter.

headline: Opening corporate books to shareholders
summary: Roosevelt signs a change to the Stock Corporation Law requiring companies to keep complete stock books open to shareholders and creditors. He writes George Bird Grinnell about conservation appointments.

headline: Hoping for a state trust bill
summary: Roosevelt tells Henry Lincoln he would like New York to take up legislation on trusts, and compliments J. M'Carthy on his books.

headline: Edith's Cuba in color
summary: From Cuba, Edith writes Spring-Rice about bright flowers and pastel houses. Roosevelt applauds an article by Francis Cabot Lowell about political bosses.

headline: St. Patrick's Day speech
summary: Roosevelt speaks to the Irish-American Friendly Sons society on St. Patrick's Day, and his essay 'The Best and the Good' appears in The Churchman. He writes about objections to his forest bill, volunteer factory inspectors and the Ramapo charter.

headline: Sunday in Albany
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday in Albany.

headline: Why city politics is hard
summary: Roosevelt explains to James C. Carter why New York City politics is so difficult, and writes Frederick Selous about the Boer War and South Africa's troubles.

headline: The Morgan Bill's flaw
summary: Roosevelt tells Butler that the Morgan Bill was not submitted in proper form.

headline: Saving the Palisades
summary: Roosevelt signs the Davis Palisades Act, providing land, money and a managing commission for a park shared with New Jersey along the Hudson's Palisades. He also writes family members after the death of Aunt Laura.

headline: Schooling on the Seneca reservations
summary: Roosevelt signs a law requiring Indian children on the Cattaraugus and Allegany reservations to attend school, and writes Joe Bishop and George Lyman about getting the Ramapo Bill passed.

headline: Canal foes and a book on trusts
summary: Roosevelt writes General Greene about feeling against the canal bill around the state, and tells George Gunton he is interested in his book Trusts and the Public.

headline: The governorship matters more
summary: Roosevelt tells Congressman Lucius Littauer that being governor counts for more than being Vice President, and asks Lyman Abbott to talk over the Ramapo Bill.

headline: Sunday in Albany
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday in Albany.

headline: Military athletes at the Garden
summary: Roosevelt goes down to New York City that evening to review the Military Athletic League's show at Madison Square Garden. He writes Odell about the mortgage tax bill and tells Stephen Thayer he supports the Morgan Bill.

headline: In Albany
summary: Roosevelt is in Albany.

headline: A free hand on the Bath home
summary: Roosevelt thanks Platt for letting him handle the Bath Soldiers' Home question as he sees fit.

headline: Against the Bath Home Bill
summary: Roosevelt tells S. Fred Nixon he opposes the Bath Home Bill, calling it thoroughly vicious.

headline: Enjoying Ironquill's rhymes
summary: Roosevelt tells Eugene Ware he enjoyed his book of verse, Rhymes of Ironquill.

headline: 'Character and Success' in print
summary: Roosevelt's essay 'Character and Success' appears in The Outlook.

headline: Sunday in Albany
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday in Albany.

headline: Prizefighting for profit banned
summary: Roosevelt signs a law outlawing commercial prize fights. In his letters he again declines the vice presidential nomination, discusses the Elsberg bill and the power of Platt and Odell, and complains about the New York Times man in Albany.

headline: Dewey enters the race
summary: Admiral Dewey declares himself a candidate for the Democratic presidential nomination, to the amusement of a doubtful public. Roosevelt invites Seth Low to lunch and writes Mark Hanna about convention tickets.

headline: A commission on tenements
summary: Roosevelt signs the Tenement House Commission Act, letting him name an unpaid panel to study tenement conditions and propose a housing code. He speaks at an Assembly memorial for former Governor Roswell Flower and hurries bills along before adjournment.

headline: Checking the Ramapo water deal
summary: Roosevelt signs the Fallows Anti-Ramapo Act, which bars New York City's water commissioner from signing water contracts without approval from city boards and both the mayor and comptroller.

headline: Legislature adjourns
summary: On the session's last day, Roosevelt signs a cap of six percent a year on loan interest and the General City Act. He writes Interior Secretary Ethan Allen Hitchcock about the Hudson Palisades.

headline: In Albany
summary: Roosevelt is in Albany.

headline: Breakfast and lunch in New York
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts at the Fifth Avenue Hotel with Platt and Odell, then lunches with Seth Low and Hammond at Corinne's house on Madison Avenue.

headline: Archie turns six
summary: It is Archie's sixth birthday. Roosevelt signs another bill to promote sugar beet growing, tells Lodge he has run an honest, efficient administration, and writes Leonard Wood about Dewey, Cuba and Wood's new baby.

headline: Answering charges
summary: Roosevelt writes Truman Backus about charges made against him and tells James H. Wilson he has no wish to be Vice President.

headline: A hospital for crippled children
summary: Roosevelt signs a law creating a state hospital for crippled and deformed children. Angry at Admiral Dewey's switch to the Democrats, he scorns him to Lodge, and writes about corporate danger, appointments and the Vice Presidency.

headline: Surveying the state canals
summary: Roosevelt signs a bill funding surveys and cost estimates for improving three state canals: the Erie, the Oswego and the Champlain. He tells Joe Bishop the machine wants him out as governor.

headline: School bill compromise
summary: Roosevelt hears arguments on a compromise school bill and meets Ellsworth and Nixon. He writes Conie about the meals with Platt and Odell held at her house.

headline: Hours for drug clerks; Cromwell in waiting
summary: Roosevelt signs laws chartering the state medical association and setting hours and working conditions for pharmacists and drug clerks. He asks Robert Bridges when his Cromwell will come out as a book.

headline: Sunday in Albany
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday in Albany.

headline: Strike at the Croton dam
summary: Roosevelt signs a bill letting him appoint a commission to study New York City's government. He writes and wires about a strike by Italian immigrant workers at the Croton dam, and writes Robert De Forest about the Tenement House Commission he chairs.

headline: Delegate-at-large to Philadelphia
summary: The Republican State Convention picks Roosevelt, with Platt, Depew and Odell, as a delegate-at-large to the national convention in Philadelphia. Editor Dana of the Sun advises him to accept if the party wants him. He writes about the Croton riots and strike.

headline: Ending school segregation by race
summary: Roosevelt signs a law that no child may be barred from a New York public school because of race or color, repealing local authority to run separate schools for Black children. He tells Greene that skipping Philadelphia would look like running away.

headline: Seats for working women
summary: Roosevelt signs a Labor Law change requiring employers to provide seats for waitresses and women in factories and let them use them. He writes Lincoln Steffens about his McClure's article on Roosevelt.

headline: An evening in Schenectady
summary: Roosevelt spends the evening in Schenectady and writes Avery Andrews, Seth Low about the street railroad bill, and Elihu Root about the Turks.

headline: At the Ecumenical Mission Conference
summary: Roosevelt holds a hearing on the Remsen bills in Albany, then goes to New York City for an evening at the Ecumenical Mission Conference.

headline: Breakfast with Platt
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts with Senator Platt in New York City.

headline: Wavering on the Vice Presidency
summary: Roosevelt signs a truth-in-labeling law for linen. Flooded with letters urging him to run, he tells Lodge he will accept the vice presidential nomination or the Philippine governorship, yet tells Senator Redfield Proctor the same day he will refuse.

headline: Maple sugar from Bill Sewall
summary: Roosevelt signs a bill letting New York City repair and expand its county courthouse under contract safeguards. He thanks his old Maine guide Bill Sewall for maple sugar and writes about the Boer War and the family.

headline: Bill-signing, then off to Chicago
summary: Roosevelt signs a batch of laws on Fifth Avenue stages, transfer-tax appraisers, pharmacies and municipal civil service, and announces who will serve on the commission to revise New York City's charter. That evening he leaves for Chicago.

headline: Speeches in Chicago
summary: In Chicago Roosevelt gives speeches, saying he can serve the country best by staying governor of New York.

headline: Honoring Grant at Galena
summary: Roosevelt speaks about General Ulysses S. Grant in Grant's hometown of Galena, Illinois.

headline: Homeward from Chicago
summary: Roosevelt travels from Chicago back to Albany.

headline: Ten letters on a Sunday
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie he has no wish for the Vice Presidency despite Lodge's view, and fears to Brander Matthews he may lose the governorship. He contributes $50 to a fund for a soldier who died in the Croton riots and praises Root for upholding the Monroe Doctrine.

headline: Writing for boys; dinner with young Churchill
summary: Roosevelt's essay 'The American Boy' runs in St. Nicholas. He sends John Burroughs a copy of Hunting Trips of a Ranchman and tells Platt he has appointed the Charter Commission. Around this time, Corinne later recalled, he dined at her house with General Joe Wheeler and a young Winston Churchill, talking mostly about the Boer War.

headline: Protecting the state's birds
summary: Roosevelt signs the Hallock Bird Protection Act. His letters cover sweatshops, a pardon he refuses, mistreatment at Elmira prison, and his plan to sign the Soldiers' Home Bill.

headline: Davis school law signed
summary: Roosevelt signs the Davis School Act over New York City's objection, and writes Ansley Wilcox about the Democrats' choice for governor and Bird Coler's chances.

headline: City College and Brooklyn streets
summary: Roosevelt signs the Elsberg City College Act and two Remsen acts to open and improve Bedford and Remsen avenues in Brooklyn. He attends a dinner for the city's Charter Commission.

headline: Ted visits John Burroughs
summary: Roosevelt signs the Platt Act, freeing the veterans' home at Bath from oversight by the State Board of Charities. He tells John Burroughs that Ted is staying with him, and writes Charles Skinner about prison-made furniture for schools.

headline: Sunday in Albany
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday in Albany.

headline: Notes to Dana and Platt
summary: Roosevelt writes Paul Dana about the vice presidential nomination and Platt about the street railroad bill.

headline: Off to Washington with Edith
summary: Roosevelt and Edith head to Washington. Before leaving he writes about sweatshops, hunting, attacks on him, a wildlife bill and the nomination.

headline: Calls on the Cabinet
summary: In Washington, Roosevelt and Edith call on John Hay, John D. Long and Elihu Root, and visit the White House.

headline: Fort Myer and a full dinner table
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Arthur Lee and visits Fort Myer. At dinner he is with the Roots, the Hays, the Cowleses, the Longs, the Thomas Nelson Pages and Mrs. Tuckerman.

headline: Told he is not wanted
summary: Roosevelt tours Congress with Lodge and is guest of honor at a White House dinner given by President McKinley. Talking with Senators Foraker and Chandler, Root, Long and the President, he learns they do not want him as Vice President, which only makes him want it more.

headline: Commandments in politics
summary: Roosevelt's article 'The Eighth and Ninth Commandments in Politics' appears in The Outlook while he is in Washington.

headline: Back to Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt and Edith return home to Oyster Bay.

headline: Henry White at Sagamore Hill
summary: Diplomat Henry White is a guest at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Civil service and the charter
summary: From Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt writes Alford Cooley about civil service appointments and Joe Bishop about the Charter Commission.

headline: Hungarian Republicans' dinner
summary: Roosevelt speaks to the Hungarian Republican Club in New York. He turns down a speaking date in Ottawa and congratulates General Samuel Young on regaining his rank as major general of volunteers.

headline: Back in Albany
summary: Roosevelt is in Albany.

headline: Davis Bill signed; Palisades park
summary: Roosevelt again tells Maria Storer he cannot step into church politics, informs William Allen White he has signed the Davis Bill, and writes George W. Perkins of New York Life about the Palisades Park Commission.

headline: Readying The Strenuous Life
summary: Roosevelt tells Frank Scott he is getting The Strenuous Life ready to publish. Other letters cover civil service exam exemptions, the convention, the attorney generalship, and uniform colors with Speck von Sternberg.

headline: Ted still with Burroughs
summary: Roosevelt is in Albany while Ted continues his stay with naturalist John Burroughs.

headline: Thanks to Burroughs
summary: Roosevelt writes about controversies in Cuba and the Civil Service Act, and thanks John Burroughs for hosting Ted.

headline: In Albany
summary: Roosevelt is in Albany.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Between Oyster Bay and Albany
summary: Roosevelt spends the day between Sagamore Hill and Albany.

headline: Talking municipal finance
summary: In the evening Roosevelt goes to New York City to speak about municipal finance at a Merchants' Association dinner for William King. His letters touch civil service, the Vice Presidency, ranching and the West.

headline: Thirteen letters from home
summary: From Sagamore Hill Roosevelt writes thirteen letters, on topics from citizenship for Indians, Cuba and labor to the Vice Presidency and an honorary degree from Harvard.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday at Sagamore Hill.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Bob Ferguson visits
summary: Rough Rider friend Bob Ferguson is a guest at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt writes William Polk of Louisiana about New York's civil service.

headline: Memorial Day parade
summary: Roosevelt is in New York City for the Memorial Day parade.

headline: Inside the sweatshops
summary: Guided by Jacob Riis and Reynolds, Roosevelt tours New York sweatshops, then joins his old regiment for a Rough Riders reunion dinner held at the Union League Club.

headline: Touring sweatshops with Jacob Riis
summary: Governor Roosevelt spends the day in New York City walking through garment sweatshops alongside his friend Jacob Riis, the reformer and reporter.

headline: Saturday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Major Llewellyn visits
summary: Roosevelt receives Major H. H. Llewellyn as a guest at Sagamore Hill.

headline: A day of letters in Albany
summary: Back at his desk in Albany, Roosevelt sends off a stack of letters ranging from New York tenements and Cuba to Cromwell, civil service, and Spanish cannon taken in the late war.

headline: Going over the Ice Trust case
summary: In Albany, Roosevelt and Attorney General John C. Davies examine the Ice Trust case together, and he writes friends about fish and game law and the men who should run that commission.

headline: Off to Oyster Bay after a busy morning
summary: Roosevelt writes a flurry of letters on civil service, labor and the Philippines, among them one urging Platt to accept Professor Cuthbert Pound for the Civil Service Commission, then heads for Oyster Bay. He also writes his sister Corinne, whose son Ted Robinson is ill with diphtheria.

headline: Speech at St. Paul's School
summary: Roosevelt addresses the students of St. Paul's School in Concord, New Hampshire, then dines in New York City with Senator Platt and Benjamin Odell.

headline: Home at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Sagamore Hill opens for the season
summary: The guest book marks the opening of the house for summer. Roosevelt tells Charles Wheeler he has settled on Professor Pound for the Civil Service Commission and writes Lodge about Platt and the Ice Trust.

headline: Sunday visit from Butler and Holls
summary: Nicholas Murray Butler and George Holls spend Sunday with Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Lunch at the Union League, letters on the vice presidency
summary: Mrs. Dean Sage is a guest at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt lunches in New York with Greene, Butler, Holls and a Mr. Elisberg, then takes the evening train to Albany. His letters weigh the governorship against the vice presidency and pass Lodge some ideas for a labor plank.

headline: "Promise and Performance" in Rochester
summary: After an interview on the Ice Trust in Albany, Roosevelt travels to Rochester and gives an address titled "Promise and Performance" at the university. He tells General Greene the corporate-backed party organization still badly wants him on the ticket.

headline: Dedicating a soldiers' monument
summary: Roosevelt travels from Rochester to Caledonia, New York, to dedicate a monument to the town's soldiers, then returns to Rochester.

headline: Lunch with Odell
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Benjamin Odell at the Union League in New York and goes out to Oyster Bay that afternoon.

headline: Agreeing to run in Philadelphia
summary: Roosevelt and Edith head to the Republican National Convention in Philadelphia and check into the Hotel Walton. Reporters crowd Platt's room asking if he will run. When the Kansas delegation's leader calls on him, Roosevelt gives in and says he will take the nomination.

headline: Courted by delegations
summary: Delegates from Pennsylvania and California seek Roosevelt out in Philadelphia. He warns Hermann Kohlsaat that a fight is ahead.

headline: Mark Hanna arrives angry
summary: Mark Hanna reaches Philadelphia furious that nobody has asked President McKinley about the choice for vice president.

headline: An offer to withdraw
summary: After lunch with Lodge and Edith, Roosevelt offers to pull his name from the vice presidential contest, and Edith approves. He softens the statement, however, and the nomination still looks certain.

headline: A dramatic entrance at the convention
summary: The Republican National Convention opens with Mark Hanna as temporary chairman. Roosevelt, in his black hat, strides slowly into the hall as heads turn. He sits as one of New York's four delegates-at-large with Platt, Odell and Chauncey Depew.

headline: Thucydides after a day of maneuvering
summary: Roosevelt walks Lodge, the newly chosen convention chairman, to the podium. Out of view, Platt's ally Matthew Quay rewrites the rules to clear the way for Roosevelt. That night in his hotel room he reads Thucydides.

headline: Nominated for Vice President
summary: Pressed by the Platt machine and by Roosevelt backers across the country, Hanna yields. McKinley is renominated with 926 votes, and Roosevelt is named his running mate with 925. Roosevelt lunches with General Greene, addresses the convention, and wires the President.

headline: Home, and a visit to Riis
summary: Roosevelt and Edith leave Philadelphia for Oyster Bay. He calls on Jacob Riis, who is sick.

headline: Writing Seth Low about the machine
summary: From Sagamore Hill Roosevelt tells Seth Low he had turned the state machine upside down and made it act against what he wanted.

headline: Asking Platt about Greene
summary: Roosevelt writes Senator Platt to ask whether he is turning his back on General Greene.

headline: "The thing could not be helped"
summary: Roosevelt writes a string of letters on the nomination, telling Bamie he could not have avoided it and is moved by how it came about. In the evening he goes into New York to attend a gathering of the AAAS, the national science association.

headline: Twentieth Harvard reunion
summary: Roosevelt goes to Cambridge for his class's twentieth reunion at Harvard and writes that his campaign is now under way.

headline: "As strong as a bull moose"
summary: Back at Oyster Bay from Cambridge, Roosevelt offers himself to Mark Hanna for the campaign, saying he is fit and ready to be worked hard. Other letters cover the Philippines, the governorship and a pending case.

headline: Lunch, a visit, and dinner
summary: At Sagamore Hill Roosevelt lunches with Seth Low, sees Ansley Wilcox, and dines with Greene and Goddard. He writes John McDonough about Germany.

headline: Planning the Oyster Bay notification
summary: Roosevelt writes Frank Travers to arrange the Oyster Bay committee for his July 12 notification ceremony, then goes to New York for the afternoon.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home; nothing else is noted.

headline: Sunday at home
summary: Roosevelt spends the day at Sagamore Hill; nothing further is recorded.

headline: Whistle-stops on the way to Oklahoma
summary: Heading for Oklahoma City, Roosevelt's train pauses at Newkirk in Oklahoma Territory and at a string of Kansas towns: Newton, Peabody, Florence, Emporia, Osage City, Lawrence and Holliday.

headline: Rough Riders reunite in Oklahoma City
summary: Roosevelt joins his old regiment for the Rough Rider reunion in Oklahoma City.

headline: Reunion ends, train to Chicago
summary: The Rough Rider reunion wraps up in Oklahoma City and Roosevelt boards a train for Chicago. Bob Ferguson is with him.

headline: Speaking in Galesburg
summary: From Chicago Roosevelt goes to Galesburg, Illinois, for an afternoon speech.

headline: Hanna, Canton and dinner with McKinley
summary: Traveling east, Roosevelt confers with Mark Hanna in Cleveland, speaks at Canton, Ohio, and sits down to dinner with President McKinley.

headline: A late Fourth of July
summary: Roosevelt gets back to Sagamore Hill in the afternoon to find the children still waiting to celebrate the Fourth. A thunderstorm holds things up, but at eight o'clock the first rocket climbs, and the fireworks run until ten. His letters plan the notification ceremony and tell Hanna he prefers set speeches to train tours.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: A quiet day at home; nothing more is noted.

headline: The Lamberts visit
summary: Dr. Alexander Lambert and his wife are guests. Roosevelt's letters range over Rough Riders appearing with him in South Dakota, Black regiments in Cuba, the merchant marine, and Bryan.

headline: "The West likes me"
summary: Writing Adelbert Moot about speaking engagements in the West, Roosevelt says he believes the region likes him.

headline: His sisters visit
summary: Roosevelt's sisters, Corinne Robinson and Anna Cowles, come to Sagamore Hill.

headline: Formally notified of the nomination
summary: At Sagamore Hill a committee led by Senator Edward Wolcott officially tells Roosevelt he is the Republican choice for Vice President.

headline: Cornerstone for Nassau County's courthouse
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Mineola as the cornerstone is laid for Nassau County's first courthouse. Lodge is a guest at Sagamore Hill, and Roosevelt promises Leonard Wood he will raise a brigadier general's star with McKinley.

headline: Letters on Gardiner and Harvard
summary: Roosevelt writes Odell and Arthur Cosby about removing Gardiner, tells Harvard's Charles Eliot that his nephew Ted Robinson will enroll, and explains to Silas Burt why he accepted the nomination. He also sends a letter to Alice Lee, cousin to his late first wife.

headline: Overnight train west
summary: Roosevelt leaves Sagamore Hill in the evening, bound for St. Paul, Minnesota.

headline: Rolling toward St. Paul
summary: Roosevelt spends the day on the train to Minnesota.

headline: Addressing Republican clubs in St. Paul
summary: That evening Roosevelt speaks to the convention of the National Republican League in St. Paul.

headline: Milwaukee, then dinner with Hanna
summary: From Milwaukee Roosevelt continues to Chicago and shares dinner with Hanna at the Chicago Club.

headline: Back east to Greene and Odell
summary: Arriving in New York, Roosevelt dines with General Greene and Benjamin Odell at the Union League before heading home to Oyster Bay.

headline: Writing about China and the Boxers
summary: Roosevelt tells Odell he will not campaign in the Northeast, and writes Root, Speck von Sternberg and Spring-Rice about the Boxer uprising in China, the Boers and his candidacy.

headline: Congratulating Rockhill
summary: Roosevelt writes William Rockhill to congratulate him on his new diplomatic post in China.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Speaking to the Jewish Chautauqua
summary: Roosevelt addresses the Jewish Chautauqua Society in Atlantic City, New Jersey, and stays that night at the Union League in New York.

headline: Breakfast with Wood, worries about his voice
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts in New York with Leonard Wood, Alford Cooley and Gherardi Davis, then returns to Oyster Bay. He confides to Odell that his voice may not hold out, and passes on grumbling from Buffalo.

headline: Army shirts and Anglo-American unity
summary: Colonel and Mrs. Alexander Brodie are among the guests. Roosevelt writes Root that the army's blue shirts are impractical, writes Paul Dana about trouble at Elmira prison, and tells Arthur Lee about his hopes for British-American unity.

headline: "Bryan must be defeated"
summary: Austin Wadsworth visits Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt writes Odell about the governorship, tells Winthrop Chanler that Bryan has to lose, and writes William H. Lewis about race relations.

headline: Pushing Wood's promotion
summary: Roosevelt confers with Attorney General Davies about both the Gardiner matter and the Ice Trust. Bellamy Storer offers to rent him his Washington house should he become Vice President, and Roosevelt urges McKinley to make Wood a brigadier general in the regular army.

headline: "Promise and Performance" in print
summary: The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's "Promise and Performance." Walter Goodwin and Bob Ferguson are at Sagamore Hill.

headline: On the Brockway case and a military aide
summary: Roosevelt writes Platt about the Brockway case and Lord Minto about Colonel Kitson as a military aide.

headline: A consulship for Bay Lodge
summary: In New York Roosevelt sees Hanna, has lunch at the Union League with Odell and calls on General Greene before going home. He asks John Hay to name Lodge's son Bay to the consulship at Venice. Butler and William Dudley Foulke visit.

headline: Naval reserve camp, a throat doctor
summary: Roosevelt stops by the camp of Brooklyn's naval reservists on Centre Island. He tells George Holls that all the speaking has worn on his throat, and he is seeing a doctor.

headline: Joseph Bishop visits
summary: Joseph Bucklin Bishop is a guest at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt writes William Byrne about Cuba and sends G. H. Putnam word of Ansley Wilcox's report on the Gardiner case.

headline: Weak spots in the Democratic campaign
summary: Roosevelt points out to Robert Burch where the Democrats' campaign is faltering and writes Ansley Wilcox about his report on Gardiner, the Buffalo district attorney accused of corruption.

headline: Meeting Odell in the city
summary: Roosevelt goes into New York in the afternoon to meet Odell. His letters touch on Cuban marriage law, Platt and the governorship, and his speaking schedule.

headline: Thanking Riis for a profile
summary: Roosevelt writes Jacob Riis to thank him for the piece on him that Riis published in the Review of Reviews.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: A day at home with nothing else on the record.

headline: Edith turns 39
summary: On his wife Edith's 39th birthday, Roosevelt is in New York calling on Hanna and lunching with Odell and Platt. He writes William Howard Taft about the nomination.

headline: Andrew White and Holls call
summary: Andrew D. White and George Holls visit Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill. He shares his political outlook with Alfred Thayer Mahan and tells Lodge he will not speak in Boston.

headline: Fishing with the boys
summary: Roosevelt takes his sons off on a fishing trip and writes Hanna about German-American voters.

headline: Back from fishing, a pick for governor
summary: Home from the fishing trip, Roosevelt suggests Judge Charles Andrews to Platt as Republican candidate for governor and answers false charges made against him in the campaign.

headline: Conferences with Davies and Hanna
summary: In New York Roosevelt confers with Attorney General Davies and with Hanna, then returns to Oyster Bay, where Nicholas Murray Butler is a guest. He tells Odell he will not speak at the State Fair.

headline: Guests at Sagamore Hill
summary: Ferdinand Becker, Bob Ferguson and a Mr. Goodrich visit Sagamore Hill.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home; nothing more is recorded.

headline: Van Wyck charges and a campaign route
summary: On Ethel's ninth birthday, Roosevelt is in New York, going over charges against Augustus Van Wyck with Davies, mapping his campaign tour with Hanna, and lunching with Odell before heading home.

headline: Praising "Unleavened Bread"
summary: Douglas Robinson's son Monroe is a guest. Roosevelt compliments Robert Grant on his novel Unleavened Bread and writes Henry Purroy about the Ice Trust and Van Wyck.

headline: Sizing up the election for Platt
summary: Roosevelt writes Platt about cannon and how the coming election looks.

headline: Defending his war record
summary: Roosevelt speaks at a church fair in Oyster Bay. With opponents attacking his military service, he asks Root for documents on his record and tells Charles Burke he will answer with the letters that recommended him for the Medal of Honor.

headline: Conference with Hanna
summary: Roosevelt meets Mark Hanna in New York.

headline: Bay Lodge's wedding day
summary: Roosevelt goes fishing again. In Boston, Lodge's son Bay marries Matilda Davis. Roosevelt confides to Bamie his worries about the election and party feuds, and tells Henry Payne he must ration his speeches to save his voice.

headline: "I shot him in the left breast"
summary: Answering Democratic charges that he shot a Spanish soldier in the back on San Juan Hill, Roosevelt writes Henry Turner that the man was hit from the front.

headline: A night at the White House
summary: Roosevelt sleeps at the White House in Washington. He writes Platt that either Root or Charles Andrews would make a fine choice for governor, insisting the next governor must be more than an agent of the organization.

headline: Home with Speck and Lambert
summary: Roosevelt returns to Oyster Bay, where Speck von Sternberg and Dr. Alexander Lambert are guests.

headline: Root for governor
summary: Roosevelt spends time with Speck von Sternberg, writes David Sickels backing Root for governor, and tells Wood he has raised the brigadier general question with McKinley.

headline: Quiet day at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.

headline: "Nothing to do save take Odell"
summary: Arthur Lee and his wife visit Sagamore Hill, and Roosevelt spends the afternoon in the city. He tells Butler that Root has refused to run for governor, leaving Odell as the choice.

headline: Vouching for Odell
summary: Mrs. Leonard Wood, her daughter Luisita and Bob Ferguson are guests. Roosevelt assures Whitelaw Reid that Odell is honest and will be a good governor, and writes Seth Low and George Holls in the same vein.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: No activity is recorded beyond a day at home.

headline: Western apathy, Odell for governor
summary: Roosevelt confers in New York with Hanna and Greene. He warns Lodge that voters in the West are indifferent and that Odell will get the nomination for governor.

headline: Letters on Cuba, China and a wedding
summary: Roosevelt writes on Cuba to Indianapolis News editor Charles Williams, turns aside an offered judgeship with Wheeler Peckham, and sends Lodge his thoughts on Bay's wedding and on Odell and Platt.

headline: Gathering his army records
summary: Roosevelt asks Adjutant General Henry Corbin for reports backing up his military record and writes Wood again about Cuban marriage law.

headline: Home at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home; nothing else is noted.

headline: Off to Albany as the campaign takes shape
summary: Roosevelt leaves Sagamore Hill for Albany. The battle lines of 1900 are drawn: Democrats run against imperialism and the trusts, while Republicans point to good times and a full dinner pail.

headline: Gardiner hearing in Albany
summary: The hearing on charges against Buffalo prosecutor Gardiner takes place in Albany. To George Van Ness, Roosevelt writes about expansion and the Philippine question, and answers Louis Viereck's charge that he is hostile to German-Americans.

headline: Bound for Chicago
summary: Roosevelt leaves for Chicago.

headline: Labor Day in Chicago
summary: Roosevelt joins Chicago's Labor Day parade and gives a speech titled "The Labor Question."

headline: Leaving Chicago
summary: Roosevelt departs from Chicago.

headline: At the state convention in Saratoga
summary: Roosevelt addresses the Republican state convention of New York in Saratoga.

headline: Speaking in Detroit
summary: Roosevelt gives a speech in Detroit.

headline: Eleven speeches across Michigan
summary: Roosevelt speaks eleven times in a single day in Michigan, with stops at Lansing, Owosso, Saginaw, Bay City and Grand Rapids among others.

headline: Toward Chicago as Galveston is struck
summary: On his way to Chicago, Roosevelt speaks at Holland, Michigan, and at Madison and South Bend, Indiana, with Bob Ferguson along. That day a hurricane hits Galveston, Texas, killing some 7,000 people.

headline: Chicago speech and lunch with Payne
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Chicago and lunches with Henry Payne.

headline: Speaking in La Crosse
summary: Roosevelt gives speeches at La Crosse, Wisconsin.

headline: Into South Dakota
summary: Roosevelt campaigns across South Dakota, speaking in Yankton and Sioux Falls with shorter stops in Canton, Vermillion, Madison and Flandreau.

headline: Huron and Brookings
summary: Two South Dakota towns, Brookings and Huron, hear Roosevelt speak.

headline: Ted turns 13 while his father campaigns
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Watertown, Redfield and Aberdeen, South Dakota, on his son Ted's 13th birthday.

headline: Into North Dakota; Ted off to Groton
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Ortonville and Wheaton, Minnesota, then at Webster and Fargo, North Dakota. Back east, Edith takes Ted to begin at Groton School in Massachusetts.

headline: Accepting the nomination in writing
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Casselton, Tower City and Bismarck, North Dakota. He writes Senator Edward Wolcott his formal letter accepting the vice presidential nomination, including a history of American expansion.

headline: An afternoon back in Medora
summary: Roosevelt speaks in the North Dakota towns of New Salem and Mandan and in Miles City, Montana, then spends the afternoon in Medora, his old ranching town. That evening he gives a speech in Dickinson.

headline: Across Montana to Helena
summary: Roosevelt makes stops across Montana and speaks that evening in Helena.

headline: Butte and the mining camps
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Butte, Montana, and in the mining towns around it.

headline: Pocatello
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Pocatello, Idaho.

headline: Northern Utah
summary: Roosevelt campaigns in northern Utah, speaking in Ogden, Brigham City and Logan.

headline: Parade in Salt Lake City
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Salt Lake City and rides in a parade there.

headline: Into Wyoming
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Evanston and Green River, Wyoming, and again at Ogden, Utah. James K. Gracie is recorded as a guest.

headline: Cheyenne
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Cheyenne, Wyoming.

headline: Medicine Bow to Laramie
summary: Roosevelt's Wyoming stops include Laramie, Rawlins and Medicine Bow.

headline: Colorado, with the Lodges
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Boulder and Denver. He writes Corinne that Cabot and Nannie Lodge have joined him, with a little horseback riding between the speeches.

headline: Train attacked at Cripple Creek
summary: At Cripple Creek, Colorado, a hired gang of "muckers" attacks Roosevelt's train, and Rough Riders step in to protect him. He goes on to speak at Victor. George Fred Williams later claims Roosevelt was drunk there, a charge without any truth.

headline: Corinne's birthday on the trail
summary: Roosevelt campaigns through Pueblo, Florence, Salida and Granite in Colorado. It is his sister Corinne's 39th birthday.
