headline: Patronage note to Stewart
summary: Roosevelt writes his Colorado friend Philip Stewart about appointments.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; the record lists no activities for the day.

headline: Hay and Wood confer
summary: Roosevelt confers with Secretary of State John Hay and General Leonard Wood.

headline: Butler is a house guest
summary: Nicholas Murray Butler stays at the White House, and Roosevelt confers with Henry C. Payne.

headline: Wood again, then a reception
summary: Roosevelt meets again with General Wood, lunches with Frederick Holls and H. S. New, and hosts a White House reception.

headline: Civil service changes approved
summary: Roosevelt dines with Mrs. Hobson, Mrs. Wolcott, General Young and J. R. Procter, and approves amendments to the civil service rules.

headline: Beet sugar versus Cuba
summary: Roosevelt hears Senator Burrows, beet sugar men and their lawyers on Cuban reciprocity, then confers with Speaker Henderson and Representatives Payne and Dalzell on pending bills. He writes Douglas Robinson about a buildings superintendent.

headline: Navy gunnery on his mind
summary: Roosevelt receives naval officers and senators, reviews the city's police and fire parade, and lunches with George Kennan. He writes Will Cowles about William Sims's reports on poor Navy marksmanship and tells Senator Mitchell he never promised him the Alaska collectorship.

headline: Germany warns on Venezuela
summary: Germany informs Roosevelt that it plans to use force against Venezuela over unpaid debts. He holds a Cabinet meeting and confers with Mark Hanna.

headline: Strategy with senators
summary: Roosevelt confers with Lodge, Hanna, Spooner and Ambassador Choate.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; the record lists no activities for the day.

headline: Senate ratifies the canal treaty
summary: The Senate ratifies the Hay-Pauncefote Treaty, with Britain yielding to America's wish to build an isthmian canal. Roosevelt also receives the court of inquiry's report on the Sampson-Schley dispute over credit for the 1898 victory at Santiago, which leans toward Sampson. He refuses Lyman Abbott's plea to bring the Filipino leader Aguinaldo to America

headline: Readying the Navy near Puerto Rico
summary: Roosevelt orders the Navy to prepare an operating base off Puerto Rico against the chance of sudden war. He names Henry C. Payne Postmaster General, while General Nelson Miles publicly sides with Admiral Schley. Letters go to Edward Everett Hale, Andrew White and Charles Gleed.

headline: Lunch with Carnegie
summary: Roosevelt meets a delegation of the American Asiatic Society and lunches with Andrew Carnegie, Root, J. R. Sheffield and W. N. Cohen.

headline: Congress breaks for the holidays
summary: Roosevelt meets Hay, Beveridge, Foraker and other lawmakers as Congress adjourns for the holidays, and writes William Rainsford about appointments.

headline: Cabinet and Treasury talk
summary: After a Cabinet meeting, Roosevelt confers with Treasury Secretary Gage and Senators Hanna and Penrose.

headline: General Miles rebuked
summary: Roosevelt faces General Nelson Miles over his public comments on the Schley case, and he and Secretary Root reprimand him. He writes Robert Patterson about the episode.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; the record lists no activities for the day.

headline: Defending Payne's appointment
summary: Roosevelt confers with Lodge, Hanna, Senator Warren and Joy, and lunches with Irish reformer Sir Horace Plunkett. He writes Charles R. Miller defending his choice of Henry Payne as Postmaster General.

headline: Christmas Eve with the Cowleses
summary: Bob Ferguson is a White House guest and Chief Justice Fuller calls. Leslie Shaw is named Treasury Secretary. That evening Roosevelt and Edith go to a party at Bamie's and hang the children's stockings on the library mantel.

headline: First White House Christmas
summary: Twenty-six people sit down to Christmas dinner, then everyone dances in the East Room, Bob Ferguson among them. Roosevelt writes John Hay with sympathy on the death of their friend Clarence King.

headline: The children sail on the Dolphin
summary: Edith takes the children down the Potomac for three days on the presidential yacht Dolphin. Roosevelt dines with Root, Admiral Robley Evans and others, and thanks Mark Hanna for a note.

headline: Cheering on William Sims
summary: After lunch with Hay, Root and Knox, Roosevelt thanks Lieutenant William Sims for his counsel and urges him to keep challenging Navy orthodoxy. He also writes Admiral Henry Taylor about better gunnery.

headline: Dinner for two with Bishop
summary: Wayne MacVeagh, Charles Francis Adams, Clarence Bowen and Senators Cullom and Mason call. Roosevelt tells John Hay he is dining alone with editor Joseph Bucklin Bishop and invites Hay to come.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; the record lists no activities for the day.

headline: Lodge and Spooner confer
summary: Roosevelt meets with Senators Lodge and Spooner.

headline: Standing up to Platt
summary: Roosevelt agrees to serve as a trustee of the new Carnegie Institution. He writes Brander Matthews candidly about the Sampson-Schley-Miles-Alger feud, and tells William Allen White that Platt, angry over White's article, asked him to bar White from the White House, and that he refused.

headline: New Year's reception
summary: Roosevelt and Edith come down the grand staircase to Marine Band music and greet diplomats and the public in the Blue Room for the New Year's reception. Edith carries flowers so she can graciously skip the handshakes.

headline: Edith's first Cabinet dinner
summary: A packed day of callers ends with Edith hosting her first Cabinet dinner: fifty guests who follow their hosts through the parlors to dinner. Roosevelt quits the copyright league, writes Foulke on civil service posts, and thanks Joseph Bishop for his help on the Philippines.

headline: Alice makes her debut
summary: Alice's debut ball fills the Blue Room at 10 p.m., with dancing in the East Room until 2 a.m. Beforehand Alice grumbles about the plans and wants to use the $500 the Lees give her to alter them, but Edith says no.

headline: Worried about Ted's football
summary: Roosevelt confers with Hanna and Admiral Dewey and lunches with Leslie Shaw, three Rough Riders and others. He tells Endicott Peabody that Ted is second in his Groton class but worries that rough football, a smashed tooth and a broken collarbone may keep him off the field in college.

headline: Sunday lunch
summary: Hugh Whitney and Constance Gardner join Roosevelt for lunch.

headline: Admiral Schley calls
summary: Roosevelt confers with Admiral Schley and a string of senators, sees August Belmont at six, and dines with the Cowleses, Dr. Presley Rixey and the Redfield Proctors.

headline: Weighing the Sampson-Schley case
summary: Roosevelt studies the Sampson-Schley dispute, lunches with Robert Patterson, and hosts the diplomatic reception that evening.

headline: Hearing from the Panama company
summary: Roosevelt meets Platt, Admiral Walker, and Edouard Lampré, secretary general of the French Panama company, attends the Foraker wedding at noon, lunches with Foulke and James R. Garfield, and hosts a Cabinet dinner honoring Secretary Gage.

headline: Labor leaders at lunch
summary: Henry Payne succeeds Charles Emory Smith as Postmaster General. Roosevelt lunches with Knox and railroad labor leaders including Frank Sargent and E. E. Clark, hosts the diplomatic dinner, and tells Secretary Long he wants Army engineers, not naval officers, manning coastal forts.

headline: Dinner with Hay and Brooks Adams
summary: Roosevelt holds a Cabinet meeting, sees Senators Burrows, O. H. Platt and Wetmore, Commissioner MacFarland and Major Llewellyn, and ends the day dining with Brooks Adams and John Hay.

headline: Straus to The Hague
summary: Roosevelt receives senators and Speaker Henderson, meets the Chinese Exclusion Commission and Samuel Gompers, and dines at the Roots'. He tells Adolph Ochs that Oscar Straus is being named to The Hague tribunal.

headline: Henry Adams comes to dinner
summary: After a midday visit with Regis Post, Roosevelt dines with Henry Adams, the Lodges, Mrs. Selmes and John Hay. Adams later wrote a cutting account of the evening.

headline: Postmaster General Smith hosts
summary: Roosevelt confers with Gage, Crane and Choate, lunches with Horatio King, Moody and Smalley, and he and Edith are guests at a dinner given by Postmaster General Charles Emory Smith.

headline: Judicial reception
summary: A morning of callers, including Senator Charles Fairbanks and Governor Winfield Durbin of Indiana, gives way to the judicial reception that night.

headline: Corcoran visit and a conservation huddle
summary: Roosevelt meets Chief Justice Fuller, Francis Leupp and Platt, visits the Corcoran Gallery with Edith, and spends the evening with Congressman John Lacey, C. Hart Merriam, Dr. Palmer and Gifford Pinchot.

headline: Supreme Court dinner
summary: Roosevelt sees Senator Pettus, Walter Emerson and Governor Bradley, and hosts the Supreme Court dinner. He tells Bellamy Storer that Stanton Sickles's posting to Madrid was a bad appointment and writes Andrew White about the Kaiser and Speck von Sternberg.

headline: Governor Francis calls
summary: Roosevelt's morning caller is former Missouri Governor David R. Francis.

headline: Canal commission swings to Panama
summary: On Bamie's 47th birthday, Roosevelt hears Michigan beet sugar men opposed to Cuban reciprocity and receives the Walker Commission's revised report, now judging Panama the cheaper route. He and Edith dine with the Knoxes, and he jokes to Hay about Alice's words at the Kaiser's yacht christening.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; the record lists no activities for the day.

headline: Canal report goes to Congress
summary: The Isthmian Canal Commission's report goes to Congress, and Roosevelt meets Admiral Robley Evans that evening.

headline: Cleveland backs Cuban reciprocity
summary: Grover Cleveland publicly supports Roosevelt on Cuban reciprocity. After a Cabinet meeting and visits from Senators Clay, Allison, Spooner and Foraker, Roosevelt dines in honor of Senator and Mrs. Depew. He writes Hanna on appointments and the District commissioners about smoke pollution.

headline: Planning a stag dinner for Prince Henry
summary: Roosevelt receives Senator Clapp and others and, in two letters, warns Douglas Robinson against any stake in buying government property and talks over plans for a men's dinner for Prince Henry.

headline: Congressional reception
summary: Roosevelt lunches with John Hay, hosts the congressional reception, and asks George Carter to advise him on Hawaii's tangled politics.

headline: Tea and a Connecticut dinner
summary: After a Cabinet meeting and lunch with Solomon Bethea and others, Edith holds an afternoon tea and the Roosevelts give a dinner for Governor George McLean of Connecticut.

headline: Rangers in fact
summary: Roosevelt confers with Platt, lunches with AP chief Melville Stone, and goes to the Gridiron Club dinner. Hay concludes a pact with Denmark covering the Danish West Indies, and Roosevelt tells Secretary Hitchcock that forest rangers must be real working rangers.

headline: Sunday dinner with Henry Adams
summary: Roosevelt dines with the Lodges, Henry Adams, and Mr. and Mrs. Austin Wadsworth.

headline: Boone and Crockett dinner
summary: Roosevelt attends a Boone and Crockett Club dinner. Edith writes Cecil Spring-Rice a fond sketch of each of the six children, from pretty, level-headed Alice to clever little Quentin.

headline: German ambassador calls
summary: German Ambassador Theodor von Holleben calls in the morning; the evening brings dinner and a musicale. Roosevelt writes George Carter about Hawaii's governorship.

headline: Carnegie trustees at Hay's
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Paul Morton, sees Gifford Pinchot, and dines at John Hay's with Abram Hewitt, William Howard Taft, Andrew Carnegie, Elihu Root and the Carnegie fund trustees.

headline: Portrait sitting and Army-Navy reception
summary: A photographer takes Roosevelt's picture in the morning. He confers with Governor Taft and Senators Quay and Penrose, hosts the Army-Navy reception, and writes Secretary Hitchcock about leases of Indian land in South Dakota.

headline: Gag order on officeholders
summary: Roosevelt issues an executive order barring federal officeholders from lobbying on legislation. He holds a Cabinet meeting on Cuban reciprocity, sees Quay and Penrose and Generals MacArthur and Barry, and welcomes Fanny and Jim Parsons. Prince Henry's goodwill tour of America gets under way.

headline: Shaw takes over the Treasury
summary: Leslie Shaw succeeds Lyman Gage at the Treasury. Roosevelt receives Speaker Henderson, Francis Leupp and a string of other visitors, lunches with Johnstone, and he and Edith are dinner guests of Interior Secretary Hitchcock and his wife.

headline: Worked nearly to the limit
summary: The ransom for missionary Ellen Stone is handed over to her kidnappers in Macedonia. Roosevelt writes Ted that a month of problems large and small has nearly worn him out, describes afternoon rides with Edith, Lodge and Root, and reports Kermit and Archie pelting passersby in the snow.

headline: Naval officers on the Schley case
summary: Roosevelt hears naval officers Wainwright, Evans, Taylor and Clark on the Schley case, meets General Miles and Commissioner Foulke, and lunches with four captains. He asks Seth Low to put Douglas Robinson on Prince Henry's welcome committee and writes Choate about the coming coronation of Edward VII.

headline: Edith's card reception
summary: Roosevelt confers on Cuban reciprocity and on the Schley case, holds a Cabinet meeting, and receives the National Industrial Association while Edith hosts an afternoon card reception. He writes Butler about Georgia patronage and race, and invites Senator Wolcott to the Prince Henry dinner.

headline: Lunch with Richard Harding Davis
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Elihu Root and war correspondent Richard Harding Davis, receives Senators Platt, Clay and McLaurin and Representative Foss, and tells Philip Stewart he has raised the appointments question with Senator Wolcott.

headline: A wedding and a dinner for Taft
summary: Roosevelt attends the wedding of Helen Hay and Payne Whitney, confers with Hanna, Gallinger, Lodge and Gifford Pinchot, and hosts a dinner for William Howard Taft, governor of the Philippines. Richard Harding Davis stays the night.

headline: Civil service classifications
summary: Roosevelt lunches with the Whitelaw Reids, George W. Perkins, Secretary Shaw and the Evanses, meets his Cabinet about how federal jobs are classified, and writes Benjamin Tracy about the Santiago dispute.

headline: Off to Groton
summary: Roosevelt meets Representative Hemenway, lunches with Wynne, Coolidge, West and Barry, and leaves for Groton, Massachusetts. A dinner Agriculture Secretary Wilson had planned for the Roosevelts is put off.

headline: Staying with the Gardiners
summary: Roosevelt is in Groton, Massachusetts, as a guest of the W. H. Gardiner household.

headline: Still at Groton
summary: Roosevelt remains in Groton. He had meant to travel to Charleston, South Carolina, around this time but dropped the trip.

headline: In Groton
summary: Roosevelt is in Groton, Massachusetts; no other activities are noted.

headline: Alice turns 18
summary: On Alice's 18th birthday, Roosevelt, still in Groton, visits with the Reverend Charles H. Parkhurst.

headline: Back to Washington
summary: Roosevelt leaves Groton and returns to Washington.

headline: Cabinet day
summary: Roosevelt confers with Representatives Joy and Bartholdt and meets his Cabinet.

headline: Who escorts whom at the state dinner?
summary: After breakfast with Hanna and Postmaster General Payne and talks with Senate leaders and the Speaker, Roosevelt signs the urgent deficiency appropriation. As Prince Henry sails from Germany, he asks John Hay, half in jest, how to seat everyone without bruising German pride.

headline: Ambassador Holleben calls
summary: German Ambassador Theodor von Holleben calls on Roosevelt early in the afternoon.

headline: Praise for a whaling book
summary: Roosevelt meets General Miles, talks the Schley case with Shaw and Representative Foss and railroad rules with Senator Elkins, and lunches with editor Paul Dana, whose son joins them. He praises Frank Bullen's whaling book and tells Seth Low he wishes he could host Prince Henry his own way, not by protocol.

headline: Sampson gets the credit
summary: Roosevelt upholds the inquiry's verdict that Admiral Sampson, as overall commander, deserves credit for Santiago though Schley directed the fighting. He warns Root that Miles is angling for the Philippine command, threatening to expose Army abuses, and notes Miles led at Wounded Knee, where the treatment of Native Americans was far worse.

headline: Taking on Northern Securities
summary: Roosevelt has Attorney General Knox announce a federal suit to break up the Northern Securities Company, the railroad holding company that Morgan and Kuhn, Loeb money built out of the Harriman and Hill lines; it will be filed at St. Paul in March. The Schley report is published. Ted falls ill with pneumonia at Groton and Edith hurries north to nurse him.

headline: The trust suit hits the papers
summary: Morning newspapers carry the Northern Securities suit. Roosevelt's callers include Attorney General Knox, railroad man James J. Hill himself, Board of Trade delegates, John Hay and Peru's vice president. He dines with David Starr Jordan.

headline: Railroad combinations
summary: After a Cabinet meeting Roosevelt talks railroad combinations with George W. Perkins of the Morgan firm, then lunches with publisher George Haven Putnam and Secretary Root.

headline: Morgan comes calling
summary: J. P. Morgan, William Rockefeller and Pennsylvania Railroad chief A. J. Cassatt are among Roosevelt's callers. He talks Cuban tariff cuts with House members. Ted is better and Edith comes home. Roosevelt refuses a marshal's post to Ben Daniels, once jailed for murder, and writes Long about Sampson at Santiago.

headline: Ellen Stone set free
summary: Roosevelt calls at Secretary Root's home in the afternoon. In Macedonia, brigands release Ellen Stone, Mrs. Tsilka, and the baby Ellena, born to Mrs. Tsilka while they were held and given Miss Stone's name.

headline: Beer steins for the Kaiser's brother
summary: Prince Henry of Prussia, brother of Kaiser Wilhelm II, arrives at the White House. That evening Roosevelt gives him a stag dinner in the East Room, with beer served in steins, one bearing a joke inscription Roosevelt had added. In Cuba, electors choose Tomás Estrada Palma as president. At midnight the family leaves for New Jersey.

headline: Alice christens the Kaiser's yacht
summary: At Shooter's Island off Jersey City, Roosevelt and Edith watch Alice launch the Meteor, the Kaiser's new yacht. Prince Henry presents her with a diamond bracelet from his brother, newspapers giddily pair her with the prince, and the nickname Princess Alice is born. Everyone lunches aboard the Hohenzollern before the Roosevelts head home.

headline: No warning needed
summary: Booker T. Washington, Postmaster General Payne and Secretary Long are among Roosevelt's callers. He answers Herschel Jones's complaint about the surprise Northern Securities suit by saying no advance notice was required.

headline: Dinner at the German Embassy
summary: Roosevelt joins Prince Henry for a small, private dinner at the German Embassy.

headline: Honoring McKinley; Alice stays home
summary: Roosevelt attends Congress's memorial service for McKinley, lunches with Hanna, Fairbanks and others, and dines with Taft, while Edith receives 300 delegates of the Congress of Mothers. Amid press grumbling about American royalty, he tells Whitelaw Reid Alice should skip the coronation; instead she sails for Cuba with Harriet Blaine Beale to stay with the Woods.

headline: Wisconsin lumbermen and a full day
summary: In a crowded day, Roosevelt sees Commissioner Foulke, W. J. Calhoun, John Hay, William Rockhill and thirty Wisconsin lumbermen. He writes Hay about Alfred Moe's post in Honduras and Thomas Nast's in Guayaquil.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: A ride in the rain with the prince
summary: Roosevelt meets a delegation from the Charleston Exposition. He tells Whitelaw Reid he enjoyed Prince Henry's visit, above all a long horseback outing through the rain, and promises former Rough Rider Micah Jenkins a sword at Charleston.

headline: Cuba and the census
summary: The Cabinet takes up Cuba and a bill for a permanent Census Bureau, and Roosevelt lunches with Attorney General Knox.

headline: Miles denied the Philippines
summary: Roosevelt confers with Speaker Henderson and Representatives Payne and Cannon about the Cuban reciprocity bill, and lunches with Irving Scott. He backs Root's refusal to give General Miles command in the Philippines.

headline: A permanent Census Bureau
summary: After consulting Knox, Merriam, Foulke and Senator Proctor, Roosevelt signs the act creating a permanent Census Bureau. He hears California and Michigan lawmakers on tariff cuts, meets Root, and drafts a never-sent letter to Speck von Sternberg on Cuba, polo and Prince Henry.

headline: Miles's old scheme
summary: After a Cabinet meeting, Roosevelt discusses Brooklyn patronage with Platt, lunches with Judge Day and Witherbee, and sees Foulke and Senator Hoar. He tells Root that Miles had once floated a 1900 challenge to McKinley, with Roosevelt on his ticket.

headline: Philippine tariff signed
summary: Roosevelt signs the Philippine Tariff Bill after meeting Speaker Henderson and Payne, sees Hanna and Colombia's minister, who presents his recall, and lunches with Eugene Philbin. Edith goes to see Quality Street. A short note tells Speck von Sternberg that Berlin has given no sign of sending him.

headline: Sunday of appointments
summary: Roosevelt's Sunday is booked: Senator Hoar at one, Senator O. H. Platt, Representative Moody, dinner with Governor Odell, and reformer Josephine Shaw Lowell at nine.

headline: Long resigns from the Navy
summary: Roosevelt talks Cuba with Payne and Grosvenor and gives a dinner for Governor Odell. He accepts Navy Secretary John D. Long's resignation with regret, and sends an Albany Sunday school teacher a favorite verse from Romans.

headline: First veto
summary: Roosevelt sends the Senate his first veto, rejecting a bill to clear a Civil War sailor's record of desertion. Two Boer envoys and a Mr. White call, and he lunches with C. C. Shayne.

headline: An evening musicale
summary: Roosevelt meets Moody, lunches with John G. Milburn, sees Representative Hepburn and Senator Penrose, and hosts a late musicale.

headline: Visitors from Illinois
summary: Roosevelt confers with Secretary Shaw, Payne, Commander Evans, and Illinois Governor Richard Yates and his wife.

headline: Cuban tariff and the Kershner case
summary: After a Cabinet meeting, Roosevelt discusses the Cuban tariff with Payne and Dalzell and the Kershner case with Representative Butler, lunches with John Davis, and dines with editor Albert Shaw.

headline: Russia's ambassador calls
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Senator Beveridge, Edward Everett Hale and Knox, and meets Russian Ambassador Arthur Cassini. In two letters to Root he asks whether three officers can attend German army maneuvers, and says Army surgeons in the Philippines must keep their prostitution reports out of print.

headline: Sunday callers
summary: William Dinwiddie and Israel Putnam call on Roosevelt early in the afternoon.

headline: Colombia's new minister
summary: Colombian Minister José Vicente Concha presents his credentials. Roosevelt lunches with Payne, Root, Leupp and several others.

headline: The Robinsons stay over
summary: Roosevelt goes walking with Count von Arnim, dines with the Storers and General Frederick Funston, and has Douglas and Corinne Robinson as overnight guests. He writes Jacob Riis about the Powderly-McSweeney inquiry and the Danish islands governorship.

headline: Miles goes to the press
summary: A Mr. White photographs Roosevelt in the morning. He meets Senator O. H. Platt on Indian Territory, lunches with Judge Hornblower, and tells Root that Miles has leaked his side of the dispute to the newspapers.

headline: How he makes appointments
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts with James R. Sheffield, lunches with Jacob Gould Schurman and Belford, meets Root, and explains his philosophy of appointments to Lyman Gage.

headline: Should Miles be removed?
summary: The Cabinet weighs removing General Miles. Lawmakers including Foraker and Dalzell call, and Roosevelt lunches with Crimmins, Judge O'Brien and Dr. Dabney.

headline: Fencing, and a Harvard degree
summary: Roosevelt confers with Wood and Root on pulling U.S. troops out of Cuba and on Missouri patronage with Quay, Joy and Bartholdt, then goes to the Fencers' Club. Letters urge peace among Missouri factions, say he wants Miles gone, and tell President Eliot he will be in Cambridge to accept his honorary degree.

headline: Cuba on a Sunday
summary: Roosevelt confers with Payne and Root about Cuba.

headline: Miles is a perfect curse
summary: Roosevelt meets Root, Leonard Wood, Cuba's president-elect Estrada Palma and House members on reciprocity, and lunches with McIlvane. To Hermann Kohlsaat he vents that Miles has hurt the Army for eight years.

headline: Wishing Edward Everett Hale well
summary: Roosevelt meets Estrada Palma and holds a Cabinet meeting on Cuba. He writes Senator George Hoar that he wishes he could attend the celebration of Edward Everett Hale's 80th birthday.

headline: Late meeting with Platt and Aldrich
summary: Roosevelt confers late in the evening with Senators Platt and Aldrich, and praises Donald Dickinson's note about Abram Hewitt.

headline: Cavalry to the Alaska border
summary: Roosevelt sends 800 cavalry troopers to the Alaska-Canada border to hold key towns and ground should arbitration of the boundary dispute collapse. He talks with labor's Frank Morrison about a shorter-workday bill and keeping out Chinese laborers, and again endorses keeping Miles out of the Philippine command.

headline: Withdrawal from Cuba
summary: The Cabinet discusses taking U.S. forces out of Cuba. Roosevelt sees Ridder and Hanna, lunches with Williams, Holls and Torrance, and receives Commander Evans and Colonel Kitson of the British Embassy. He tells Horace White that Lodge and Butler urged him to keep Powderly.

headline: Irrigation with western lawmakers
summary: Roosevelt meets western congressmen about the irrigation bill and writes his old political mentor Joe Murray that he wants him at the New York Custom House.

headline: Checking Murray's record
summary: Roosevelt asks Joe Murray to send any evidence from past investigations or charges, so his record is spotless before the nomination.

headline: The Deer Family published
summary: The Deer Family comes out, the first book published by a sitting president. Roosevelt lunches with Dr. William Everett, receives Michigan teachers and others, and dines with his cousin James W. Roosevelt. The artist Cecilia Beaux paints Edith and Ethel together in the Red Parlor, though he dislikes the result.

headline: A letter on Cecil Rhodes's passing
summary: After a Cabinet meeting and talks with Hay, Beveridge and Knox, Roosevelt lunches with Wilkins, and he and Edith dine at the Hays'. He writes St. Clair McKelway on the Philippine friars and Albert Grey about Cecil Rhodes, who has just died.

headline: Careful with Germany over borax
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts with Joe Murray, meets the Irrigation Commission and Boston schoolteachers, and gives a dinner for Stranahan with New York legislators. He tells Agriculture Secretary Wilson to check with him before saying anything publicly about the borax dispute with Germany.

headline: Paderewski plays Chopin
summary: Roosevelt lunches with banker Jacob Schiff. After dinner, Ignacy Jan Paderewski plays Chopin at a late musicale for the Roosevelts, sculptor Augustus Saint-Gaudens, the Lodges, Mrs. West Roosevelt and Senator Proctor.

headline: Breakfast with Perkins
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts with George W. Perkins and visits with Senator Hanna.

headline: Dinner with Joe Bishop
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts with Williams, lunches with Harry New, Sylvane Ferris of his Dakota days and others, confers with Senators Quay and Penrose, and dines with Joseph Bucklin Bishop.

headline: Lunch with Norton Goddard
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Norton Goddard.

headline: South to Charleston
summary: After morning meetings with Sylvane Ferris and Speaker Henderson, Roosevelt leaves in the afternoon for the Charleston Exposition, stopping at Charlottesville, Virginia.

headline: Touring Charleston harbor
summary: In Charleston, Roosevelt tours the harbor aboard the Algonquin and attends a reception.

headline: Parade and speech in Charleston
summary: Roosevelt rides in a parade and speaks in Charleston, then moves on to Summerville. At home, Archie turns eight.

headline: Rolling home through the Carolinas
summary: Roosevelt heads back to Washington from Summerville, with stops at Branchville and Chester, South Carolina, and Charlotte, North Carolina.

headline: Dinner with Melville Stone
summary: Back at work, Roosevelt meets his Cabinet, sees Senator Burton, and dines with Associated Press chief Melville Stone.

headline: War taxes repealed
summary: Roosevelt signs the repeal of the Spanish-American War revenue taxes. Callers include Senator Quarles, General Sickles and Mooswa author W. A. Fraser. He dines with Cassatt, Spooner and Knox, and tells George von Lengerke Meyer that King Edward will not read The Winning of the West, though he was given a copy.

headline: Hawaii's governor calls
summary: Hawaii's Governor Sanford Dole and George Carter call on Roosevelt in the evening.

headline: Helen Keller visits
summary: Helen Keller and Alexander Graham Bell are among Roosevelt's callers. He lunches with Root, Villard, Leupp and Colonel Mills, talks Iowa patronage with Allison and Dolliver, and dines with John A. McCall. Historian James Ford Rhodes is an overnight guest.

headline: Kill and burn
summary: Word reaches Washington that General Jacob Smith ordered troops in the Philippines to kill and burn. General Chaffee is told to investigate the atrocity reports and Roosevelt orders a court of inquiry. The Cabinet also takes up Indian Territory posts, and he writes Hitchcock about a forest reserve in Alaska.

headline: Lunch with Knox and Riis
summary: Roosevelt has a full calendar of appointments and has Jacob Riis and the Attorney General to lunch.

headline: Gompers and Riis call
summary: Roosevelt confers with five senators: Hoar, Hale, Platt, McComas and Allison. Jacob Riis, Samuel Gompers and Francis Leupp call, and he dines with Marvin Hughitt and Payne.

headline: To New York with Edith
summary: After a Cabinet meeting and visits from the Sons of the Revolution, University of Michigan students and Senator Kean, Roosevelt leaves with Edith for New York City.

headline: Butler becomes Columbia's president
summary: In New York, Roosevelt breakfasts with Nicholas Murray Butler, sees the Robinsons, cousin Emlen Roosevelt and architect Charles McKim, and with Edith attends Butler's installation as president of Columbia University, followed by a dinner at Sherry's. Then it is back to Washington.

headline: Angry at a leaked dinner talk
summary: Roosevelt meets W. C. Sanger and tells him he is reluctant to launch a campaign against the Moros. He writes George Eggleston in anger that his White House dinner remarks appeared in the New York Herald as an interview.

headline: Dinner with Taft
summary: Senators and congressmen including Beveridge, Warren and Aldrich call. Roosevelt lunches with McKim, the Newbolds and Mr. Knott, and dines with Taft.

headline: Sims and the gunnery problem
summary: After a Cabinet meeting and talks with Littauer and Senator Foraker, Roosevelt lunches with Constance Lodge. He writes Admiral Henry Taylor about poor Navy gunnery as shown in William Sims's letters, and E. I. Bonner about Indian agents.

headline: A circuit judgeship
summary: Roosevelt discusses a circuit judgeship with Platt and the customs service with Stranahan, lunches with Roche, Stranahan and George Peck, and thanks Joseph Bishop for an editorial.

headline: Edith is expecting
summary: Roosevelt meets Platt, lunches with railroad man Charles S. Mellen, and he and Edith are dinner guests of Navy Secretary Long and his wife. Edith writes her sister Emily that she is pregnant again.

headline: Weighing canal routes
summary: The Cabinet weighs Colombian against Nicaraguan canal routes. General Corbin and Sanger call, and Roosevelt lunches with Taft, John Hay, Burlingame and Cecil Spring-Rice. He asks Stranahan to talk with Braun of the Hungarian Republican Club on New York's East Side.

headline: Charleston's mayor at lunch
summary: Representative Joseph Cannon calls. Roosevelt lunches with Charleston Mayor J. Adger Smyth, John C. Rose and Captain Crozier, and sees Senators Quarles and Spooner at nine.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Shopping for a second horse
summary: Roosevelt signs the Legislative Appropriation Act, lunches with editor Richard Watson Gilder, and he and Edith dine with Agriculture Secretary Wilson and his wife. He asks Trumbull Cary about buying a second horse, The Philosopher, and tells Hanna that Bob liked the cartoon.

headline: Chinese Exclusion Act signed
summary: On Corinne's 20th wedding anniversary, the Senate confirms William H. Moody as Navy Secretary. The Cabinet discusses illegal fencing of public land, and Roosevelt signs the Chinese Exclusion bill. He tells Moody that Subic Bay is too sprawling for the Navy to hold as a base.

headline: Money to remake the White House
summary: Congress votes over half a million dollars to renovate the White House under architect Charles McKim: a new office wing, guest rooms upstairs, a larger State Dining Room, Arthur's Tiffany screen gone, the greenhouses down. Roosevelt also meets Hanna and Payne, lunches with Root, and his article on blacktail deer appears in Outing.

headline: Moody takes the Navy
summary: William H. Moody succeeds John D. Long as Navy Secretary. Roosevelt breakfasts with Curtis, talks with Hitchcock and Land Commissioner Binger Hermann about monopolies on public land, and confers with Allison, Littauer and Fairbanks.

headline: This nation must win
summary: Roosevelt hands out diplomas and speaks at the Naval Academy commencement in Annapolis, telling the graduates that if war ever comes the country must win and the Navy will decide it, so every patriotic American should want the fleet built up. He returns to Washington.

headline: A photo on a jumping horse
summary: The Cabinet meets on illegal fencing of public land, and at noon Roosevelt is photographed on a jumping horse. He lunches with Smalley and Waller, meets the French ambassador, and dines with Henry Clay Frick and Knox. He assures Josephine Shaw Lowell he will work as hard as anyone to end cruelties in the Philippines.

headline: Evening with the Roots and Taft
summary: Secretary Root, Mrs. Root, their daughter and Judge Taft visit Roosevelt in the evening.

headline: Cuba's flag rises
summary: Cuba's Congress opens and Cuban flags fly for the first time. On a busy day, Roosevelt names labor leader Frank Sargent to head the immigration service, sits for photographer Strohmeyer, and lunches with Curtis Guild. He warns James Clarkson about civil service law and writes Hamlin Garland on homesteading and fenced western land.

headline: Lunch with Grinnell and Merriam
summary: After a Cabinet meeting and visits from Payne, Speaker Henderson and western lawmakers, Roosevelt lunches with naturalists George Bird Grinnell and C. Hart Merriam, then rides with General Young. He introduces London Times correspondent Smalley to Knox.

headline: No sheep in Yellowstone
summary: Roosevelt meets Gifford Pinchot and lunches with Root and Taft. He tells Secretary Hitchcock to keep sheep out of Yellowstone while letting cattle and horses graze, and argues with William Austin Wadsworth about Philippine atrocities.

headline: Dinner with Moody and Garfield
summary: Roosevelt receives a Maryland congressional delegation and Commander Evans, then dines with Lodge, James R. Garfield, Senator Kean, Secretary Moody and Ware.

headline: Sampson's funeral; Edith falls ill
summary: Roosevelt attends Admiral William Sampson's funeral and lunches with Governor Taft. Overnight Edith suffers another miscarriage and is confined to bed for twelve days. In letters he answers Massachusetts church protests over Philippine atrocities, asks Wood to show Bryan courtesy in Havana, and asks Root about an investigating commission.

headline: Beef trust suit and a deadline for McKim
summary: Attorney General Knox opens the government's case against the beef trust. Roosevelt talks over the Rathbone case with Senator Hanna, receives a visiting English textile commission, and has Owen Wister and John Hay to lunch. He tells architect Charles McKim that speed comes first: the new offices and the family's rooms must be ready by October 1. Word is spreading of the eruption of Mount Pelée, which wiped out Saint-Pierre on Martinique two days earlier.

headline: Colonel Sawyer calls
summary: Roosevelt has an appointment with Colonel Sawyer.

headline: Anthracite miners strike
summary: Some 140,000 anthracite miners in eastern Pennsylvania walk out; John Mitchell's union seeks recognition, while George Baer of the Reading railroad speaks for the owners. Roosevelt asks Congress for aid to Martinique, meets Root and the Speaker, and dines at the Lodges'. He notes that captions in The Deer Family got switched.

headline: Edith on the Sylph
summary: Roosevelt confers with Platt and lunches with Bishop James Thoburn, while Edith passes a few hours on the presidential yacht Sylph. He writes supporter John Shafter about politics.

headline: A cornerstone at Tenleytown
summary: Senators Platt, Hanna, Penrose and Foraker call. In the afternoon Roosevelt travels to Tenleytown to lay the cornerstone of the McKinley Memorial Ohio College of Government.

headline: Sargent should paint a President
summary: Roosevelt watches the high school cadets' annual drill and receives Charles Francis Adams. He writes Leonard Wood upholding Estes Rathbone's Cuban conviction despite Rathbone's friendship with Hanna, and tells Henry White that John Singer Sargent is the artist to paint a president.

headline: Meeting Ellen Stone
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Charles Francis Adams and Commissioner Foulke and in the afternoon meets Ellen Stone, recently freed by her Macedonian captors. He dines with Senator Allison.

headline: Reburying General Rosecrans
summary: Roosevelt goes to Arlington Cemetery to speak at the reburial of Civil War General William Rosecrans, then lunches with Charles Bonaparte, the Civil Service Commissioners and Knox.

headline: A quiet day in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; no activities are recorded.

headline: A playful note to Hay
summary: Roosevelt writes John Hay a humorous letter about an appointment at Fort Erie.

headline: Carnegie Hall speech on Cuba
summary: After a Cabinet meeting Roosevelt takes the Pennsylvania Railroad to New York and speaks about Cuba at Carnegie Hall during a Central Presbyterian Church celebration of home missions, then returns to Washington.

headline: Monument to the war of 1898
summary: Roosevelt sees a string of senators, discusses a Court of Claims vacancy with Littauer, and lunches with Henry Chapman. At Arlington he speaks as a new monument to the war with Spain is unveiled and dines with Dana, Root, Knox, Lodge and Spooner. Edith is up and feeling much better.

headline: Crater Lake becomes a national park
summary: Crater Lake National Park is established. A treaty with Mexico sets up a five-member panel, with members drawn from both nations and The Hague list, to settle the Pious Fund claims of California's Catholic Church. Roosevelt meets lawmakers on Indian appropriations and attends a dinner honoring Count Rochambeau.

headline: Aboard the French cruiser Gaulois
summary: Roosevelt spends the day at Annapolis aboard the French cruiser Gaulois, lunching on board, then dines at the French Embassy in Washington with Secretary Moody and Admiral Dewey.

headline: Rochambeau statue; a dog that won't vote Democratic
summary: Roosevelt watches the new Rochambeau statue unveiled across from the White House, with Alice standing in as hostess while Edith recovers. He tells Hermann Kohlsaat about Bozzie, a Milwaukee collie who barked Kermit's age, counted the crowd and made clear she would sooner die than vote for a Democrat.

headline: Trinity Church centennial
summary: Roosevelt attends Trinity Church's 100th anniversary observance.

headline: Reviewing the Knights Templars
summary: On a busy day Roosevelt lunches with R. W. Patterson, reviews Washington's Knights Templars from the White House North Portico, and dines with Senator Allison. Whitelaw Reid stays the night.

headline: Defending his policies to Butler
summary: Roosevelt meets Senators Aldrich, Scott and Beveridge, and writes Nicholas Murray Butler a defense of his course on reciprocity, tariffs and the Philippines.

headline: Farewell to Lord Pauncefote
summary: Leonard Wood calls. At noon Roosevelt attends the funeral of British Ambassador Lord Pauncefote. His old friend Sir Michael Herbert, whom he called Mungo, is named the new ambassador.

headline: Personnel bill and tariffs
summary: Senator Platt calls, and Roosevelt writes Eugene Hale on the Navy personnel bill and John C. Rose about lowering tariffs.

headline: Memorial Day at Arlington
summary: On Memorial Day at Arlington, Roosevelt addresses Philippine policy, promising to root out every act of brutality by American troops. He also condemns lynching of Black Americans in the South, angering many Southerners as the Washington dinner had.

headline: Saving the buffalo
summary: Roosevelt meets Senators Aldrich, Dolliver and Allison. Congress funds protection of the American bison, and a government herd is started in Yellowstone. The White House menagerie now counts a terrier, a Chesapeake Bay dog, the macaw Eli Yale, a spotted rat named Jonathan, two kangaroo rats, a flying squirrel and Archie's pony Algonquin.

headline: Sunday evening with four senators
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday evening at the White House talking with four senators: Stewart, Clapp, Millard and Dietrich.

headline: Rallying senators for Cuban reciprocity
summary: Roosevelt gathers a large group of Republican leaders from both houses at night to push for a trade deal with Cuba, and writes Root to introduce Bishop Bienk of Puerto Rico.

headline: Cabinet talks naval maneuvers
summary: The Cabinet takes up planned naval exercises and the needs of the consular service. Roosevelt lunches with Senator Aldrich and dines with Leonard Wood and Lodge, then answers critics in a run of letters, including one standing by his Memorial Day comparison of Southern lynchings with abuses in the Philippines.

headline: Planning Kermit's path to Groton
summary: Governor Van Sant of Minnesota is among the day's callers. Roosevelt writes Groton headmaster Endicott Peabody that Kermit will enter the school, with master Walter Hinchman coaching him at Sagamore Hill over the summer.

headline: Locomotive engineers and military surgeons
summary: Roosevelt receives a delegation of railroad engineers in the morning and addresses the convention of the nation's military surgeons.

headline: Public buildings on the Cabinet agenda
summary: The Cabinet discusses the Public Buildings Bill, C. S. Francis calls, and Roosevelt writes his old Rough Rider Alexander Brodie, now governor of Arizona Territory, about Treasury business and patronage.

headline: A Kipling portrait comes to the White House
summary: Roosevelt goes over Army appointments with Secretary Root, lunches with Commander Ware and Leonard Wood, and in the afternoon views a portrait of Rudyard Kipling delivered to the White House.

headline: Jasmine and honeysuckle on the South Portico
summary: Roosevelt confers with Wright about the anthracite coal strike. After dark he and Edith sit out on the South Portico, looking toward the Washington Monument with the scent of jasmine and honeysuckle in the air.

headline: White House renovation begins
summary: Work starts on rebuilding the White House. Edith takes Ethel, Kermit, Archie and Quentin aboard the Dolphin down the Potomac, bound for Sagamore Hill, while Roosevelt moves into a temporary home on Jackson Place and hosts senators and Leonard Wood for dinner. He tells Joel Chandler Harris the children have heard every one of his stories.

headline: Cabinet, dinner, then off to West Point
summary: After a Cabinet meeting and dinner with Knox, Payne, Moody and Hanna, Roosevelt heads for West Point. His letters say General Miles should have been removed long before, discuss an embassy for Bellamy Storer, push Cuban reciprocity with Spooner, and ask Root for capable Army chaplains.

headline: Speaking at West Point as Sagamore opens
summary: Roosevelt gives a speech at West Point. On Long Island, Edith notes in the guest book that she has opened Sagamore Hill for the season; the season's first visitors are Mrs. Clifford Richardson and John R. Procter.

headline: Back to Washington from West Point
summary: Roosevelt returns to the capital in the afternoon and takes up with Senator Platt the charge that Leonard Wood spent Cuban money to circulate pro-reciprocity literature.

headline: Special message on Cuban reciprocity
summary: Roosevelt sends Congress a special message urging a trade bill for Cuba right away. He talks with Hepburn about a new Department of Commerce, dines with George Perkins, and asks Joe Cannon not to fight the irrigation bill in the House.

headline: Breakfast at Hanna's, dinner with McKim
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts at Senator Hanna's with Root and Payne, meets again with Hepburn, and dines with architect Charles McKim, Root and Littauer. He writes Dewey that the admiral will lead the fleet exercises in the fall.

headline: Sunday in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: General Smith retired after inquiry
summary: A court of inquiry has found General Jacob Smith guilty over his conduct in the Philippines, and Roosevelt orders him retired. He meets Booker T. Washington at noon about appointments in the South, receives Cuban Minister Quesada, and cheers Woodrow Wilson's election as Princeton's president in a letter to Cleveland Dodge.

headline: Signing the Reclamation Act
summary: Roosevelt signs the Newlands Act, which puts money from public land sales in 16 Western states into a fund for irrigating the dry West. He dines with Lodge, Root and Colonel Johnson, and writes Grover Cleveland in praise of Woodrow Wilson.

headline: Visits from the French ambassador and Butler
summary: Leonard Wood is staying with Roosevelt. He sees the French ambassador in the morning and has Nicholas Murray Butler, John Hay and Hill to dinner; Butler stays overnight.

headline: Senate picks Panama for the canal
summary: The Senate votes for a Panama route and authorizes buying the canal rights from Colombia, which then held the isthmus. Roosevelt sits for photographer Prince in the morning, lunches with architect McKim, and has Moody, Hale, Lodge, Spooner and Knox to dinner.

headline: Reciprocity stalls in the Senate
summary: Over breakfast with William Williams and in two letters to Joe Bishop, Roosevelt takes stock: senators are fighting Cuban reciprocity hard, and if it fails now he will bring it back next session.

headline: Canal talk with Hepburn
summary: Roosevelt goes over canal business with Congressman Hepburn and receives the Swiss minister. His Dakota friend Bob Ferguson signs the guest book.

headline: Lunch with Hay, canal talk with Morgan
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Secretary of State John Hay and spends the evening talking canal matters with Senator John T. Morgan.

headline: Maryland feuds and canal bills
summary: Roosevelt hears Representative Mudd on Republican quarrels in Maryland, talks canal legislation again with Morgan, and dines with Navy Secretary Moody. Letters go to Hitchcock about rations being cut off on Indian reservations and to Governor Odell about the concessionaires removed from Ellis Island.

headline: Senators call, then north to Harvard
summary: After a Cabinet meeting and visits from seven senators, among them Platt, Beveridge and Spooner, Roosevelt leaves late in the afternoon for Boston and Cambridge.

headline: An honorary degree from Harvard
summary: Harvard gives Roosevelt an honorary Doctor of Laws at Commencement. At the alumni dinner he tells graduates a college education confers no special rank, only a heavier duty to live well, and he credits Leonard Wood, Root and Taft. He then leaves for New London.

headline: Watching Harvard row against Yale
summary: Roosevelt takes in the Harvard-Yale boat race at New London, then heads back to Washington.

headline: The friars' lands question
summary: The Cabinet takes up the lands held by religious orders in the Philippines, and Roosevelt dines with the Lodges. Miss Alice Harder signs the guest book.

headline: Spooner Act signed for a Panama canal
summary: Roosevelt meets Admiral Walker and signs the Spooner Act, letting him buy canal rights across Panama from the French company and Colombia for no more than $40 million. He tells Senator Platt the coming Caribbean fleet maneuvers, the Navy's first, were his own idea.

headline: Unveiling a McKinley tablet
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts and dines at Senator Hanna's house, attends the late-morning unveiling of a memorial tablet to McKinley, and lunches with Senator Beveridge and Philip Stewart.

headline: A full day as the canal news breaks
summary: Roosevelt meets Admiral Walker while newspapers report his signing of the canal bill, then has Knox, Garfield, Lodge and Spooner to dinner. In Oyster Bay, Kermit's tutor Walter Hinchman settles in for the summer.

headline: Congress adjourns with a flurry of signatures
summary: Roosevelt signs a stack of bills, among them the Philippine Civil Government Act and the naval budget, as Congress goes home. He lays a church cornerstone in the afternoon and writes Hay that the canal will be the greatest achievement of his presidency.

headline: Sulphur Springs becomes a national monument
summary: Roosevelt proclaims Sulphur Springs in Indian Territory, today's Oklahoma, a national monument. He works on a Philippine amnesty with Root, lunches with a group of cabinet members and senators, and tells Hitchcock the irrigation program is of the first importance.

headline: Off to Pittsburgh with Knox
summary: After lunch with Root, Butler, Spooner and McLaurin, Roosevelt leaves for Pittsburgh with Attorney General Knox. Bob Ferguson is again in the guest book.

headline: Fourth of July in Pittsburgh
summary: Roosevelt gives an Independence Day speech in Schenley Park, lunches with Henry Clay Frick, joins a dinner in Knox's honor at the Schenley Hotel, and boards a train for Oyster Bay.

headline: Home to Oyster Bay for the summer
summary: Roosevelt's train pulls into Oyster Bay in the rain. Waiting are his secretaries Loeb and Cortelyou, Ted on horseback, and three more children, Ethel, Kermit and Archie, riding in the surrey.

headline: Oyster Bay turns into the Summer White House
summary: Reporters pour into Oyster Bay as Sagamore Hill takes on its role as the Summer White House, complete with a telephone, number 67, that Edith did not want. The family goes to Christ Church with Aunt Emily and Bob Ferguson. Archie's Boston bull pup Bozzie dies and is laid to rest in the family pet graveyard; his brother is sent for from Chicago.

headline: A morning on the bumpy home tennis court
summary: Cortelyou and Loeb set up the executive office in two rooms over the Oyster Bay Bank. Roosevelt plays tennis with the children all morning on the bumpy dirt court in the hollow below the house, where burrowing animals and low branches call for house rules. The Secret Service turns away its first crank, and fireworks light up the evening.

headline: Lunch with Montague White
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Montague White and writes Governor Odell about a Brooklyn Navy Yard job, adding that he would like a meeting with E. H. Harriman. He also complains to Payne about newspaper falsehoods.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Holding firm on the Alaska boundary
summary: Roosevelt writes Hay that Canada's bid to send the Alaska boundary dispute to The Hague comes close to blackmail, that Britain must be held firmly to account, and that the United States will give up no territory.

headline: Church estates in the Philippines
summary: Stranahan, W. B. Parsons and Senator McLaurin call at Sagamore Hill, and Roosevelt discusses the Philippine friars' estates with Father Malone.

headline: Root and Father Donovan on church lands
summary: Root visits Sagamore Hill to discuss the friars' lands with Father Donovan, and Dr. Alexander Lambert is a guest. Roosevelt tells Root he wants turned-down collars, not stand-up ones, on Army field uniforms.

headline: Canal and church lands with Root and Spooner
summary: Roosevelt continues the friars' lands talks with Root and reviews the canal plans with Root and Spooner.

headline: Inspecting the Mayflower
summary: Roosevelt looks over the presidential yacht Mayflower, one of three government vessels at his disposal, with Root and Dr. Lambert. Architect Charles McKim, who is directing the White House rebuilding, comes for lunch.

headline: Dinner with St. Clair McKelway
summary: Roosevelt dines with Brooklyn Eagle editor St. Clair McKelway, who is entered in the guest book.

headline: Troops for Alaskan border towns
summary: Robert Munn stays overnight at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt writes Hay about posting soldiers to towns along the Alaska border for police work, and writes Eugene Philbin about Catholic representation on the Philippine Commission and the church lands.

headline: Urging Hay to take a real rest
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Hawley, Colonel Bingham, Charles Carroll, Regis Post and Caspar Whitney, and talks Cuban reciprocity with Hawley. Nellie Tyler and Lucius Littauer sign the guest book. He tells John Hay, for heaven's sake, to get some genuine rest.

headline: A family picnic
summary: The Roosevelts go on a picnic together. Edith's secretary, Belle Hagner, is a guest.

headline: Lunch with Seth Low and New Yorkers
summary: Roosevelt has New York Mayor Seth Low to lunch along with Crimmins, Elsberg, Kean and more. He writes Baron Speck von Sternberg about the Indian army, the Philippines and General Smith, and thanks Wilbur Wakeman for backing reciprocity.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Bamie and Will Cowles come to stay
summary: Roosevelt talks with Hepburn about the canal and about who should replace Tichenor as general appraiser in New York, and sees H. S. Bliss late that evening. His sister Bamie and her husband Will Cowles arrive, along with Miss Helen Roosevelt.

headline: Praising Hay's life of Lincoln
summary: Roosevelt meets Frederick Gibbs about state elections over lunch, and Mrs. Clifford Richardson visits again. He writes Simon Wolf about Jews in Romania and Russia, and tells Hay he has been reading the Lincoln biography Hay wrote with John Nicolay and admires it.

headline: Trusts and tariffs with Schurman
summary: Nicholas Murray Butler and G. E. Graham call. Roosevelt goes over trusts and island tariff rates with Jacob Gould Schurman, lunches with Captain Goddard, Schurman, Graham and Butler, and dines with Leonard Wood and Butler.

headline: Speaking at the Sea Girt encampment
summary: Roosevelt travels to Sea Girt, New Jersey, to address the 2nd Regiment at its camp, is received by Governor Murphy, and spends time on Senator Kean's yacht.

headline: Holmes chosen for the Supreme Court
summary: Justice Gray has resigned, and Roosevelt writes Senator Hoar that he will name Oliver Wendell Holmes of Massachusetts in his place. Visitors include Meyer and Albert Shaw; Dr. Lambert, Treasury Secretary Shaw, painter Cecilia Beaux and Grace Potter are guests. He tells Speaker Reed he can only pass through Maine, not stay.

headline: A day of New York callers
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Knox, Spooner, William Byrne and New York's attorney general, Davies, dines with Eugene Philbin, Father Belford and F. C. Travis, and at nine sees Commodore Swan and Colonel Vrooman.

headline: Moody comes calling
summary: Navy Secretary Moody calls and is listed as a guest; Roosevelt has Mr. Perkins and Cushing Stetson to lunch.

headline: Lunch aboard the Mayflower
summary: Roosevelt lunches on the Mayflower and sees Colonel Hood at nine that evening.

headline: Rowing the Sound with Edith
summary: Roosevelt spends the whole day with Edith on a long row and picnic down Long Island Sound and back. Sheffield, Garfield, Butler and Dr. Alderman come to dinner and stay the night.

headline: New York politics with Platt
summary: Roosevelt discusses New York State politics with Senator Platt and Colonel George Dunn while his overnight guests are still in the house. He writes Hoar again about Holmes and complains to Paul Dana that the Sun's man at Oyster Bay is making up stories about the family.

headline: Edith dodges a Grand Duke
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Governor William Hunt of Puerto Rico, Adolph Ochs, Postmaster General Payne and others; Winthrop Chanler visits. He warns Taft that Catholic critics are stirring trouble over his mission to Rome and reports that the boys fill their days with rifle practice, tennis, riding, rowing and swimming. When Russian Grand Duke Boris visits, Edith arranges a lunch elsewhere to avoid receiving a man of notorious reputation.

headline: Working on tariff revision
summary: Roosevelt spends the day at Sagamore Hill on tariff revision.

headline: A crowded lunch table
summary: Roosevelt's lunch guests include editor George Harvey, Silas McBee, Edward Kent, Wakeman, a Mr. Cowles, Charles Nugel and Bishop Duducy.

headline: Joe Bishop visits
summary: Joseph Bucklin Bishop is a guest, and D. Leroy Dresser calls at nine in the evening.

headline: Archbishop Ryan and Pinchot to lunch
summary: Roosevelt talks with Archbishop Ryan about the friars' lands, then lunches with the Whitelaw Reids, the Elbridge Gerrys, the Archbishop and Gifford Pinchot, discussing Pinchot's planned trip to the Philippines. He urges Moody to give prizes for good gunnery on big naval guns.

headline: Off on the Sylph with Edith
summary: Late in the afternoon Roosevelt and Edith leave on the Sylph for Gardiner's Bay. He accepts Andrew White's resignation as ambassador, tells Hay that Charlemagne Tower will go to Berlin, and writes Philip Stewart about Colorado posts and his dislike of Senator Teller.

headline: Target practice on Edith's birthday
summary: On Edith's 41st birthday, she and Roosevelt watch Navy gunnery practice from the Mayflower in Gardiner's Bay.

headline: Cattle lands and congressmen
summary: Back home, Roosevelt receives Senator O. H. Platt and a group of congressmen and talks over Western cattle ranges with Philip Stewart. Architect Grant La Farge arrives that afternoon. He tells Hay he had promised Berlin to Storer but now wants Tower, and asks Albert Gleaves to sharpen the Mayflower's gunnery.

headline: Knox and the Pacific cable contract
summary: Roosevelt reviews the Pacific cable firm's government contract with Attorney General Knox, then lunches with Knox, his cousin Christine Roosevelt, McCullough and Lieutenant Dick.

headline: Letters on New York and an Army promotion
summary: Roosevelt writes Senator Platt about a New York political quarrel, and tells Senator Quay that promoting Hugh Scott all the way to general from captain is too much.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing further is recorded.

headline: Holmes named to the Supreme Court
summary: Roosevelt puts Oliver Wendell Holmes on the nation's highest court and writes Senator Hoar that he will announce it. Charles McKim calls to see Edith about the White House work, and Roosevelt lunches with China's Prince Tsai Chen and Senator Burrows.

headline: Thanks to Butler on the friar question
summary: Roosevelt lunches with William R. Grace; Bob Ferguson and Joseph Wilmer are guests. He thanks Nicholas Murray Butler for his help with the friars and writes him about the tariff.

headline: Ethel turns eleven
summary: It is Ethel's 11th birthday. Roosevelt confers in the morning with J. M. Bliss and Albert Washburn about the New York appraiser post, and in the afternoon Gifford Pinchot and Grant La Farge arrive to spend the night.

headline: Odell to lunch; Fuller approves of Holmes
summary: Roosevelt confers and lunches with Governor Odell while Grant La Farge and Pinchot are still guests. He defends his trust policy, along with Knox and Root, in a letter to Frederick Goddard, and writes Chief Justice Fuller, who likes the Holmes choice.

headline: Generals, a governor and Jacob Riis
summary: Generals Corbin and Young, Governor Francis, Jacob Riis and several others come for lunch, and Albert Shaw stays for dinner. Roosevelt asks Hay whether it is true that Vienna would balk at a Catholic ambassador such as Bellamy Storer.

headline: Bishop O'Gorman to dinner
summary: Bishop Thomas O'Gorman dines at Sagamore Hill.

headline: The Rixeys visit
summary: Roosevelt confers with Dr. Presley Rixey, the White House physician, who visits with his wife.

headline: Planning the fall congressional races
summary: Roosevelt has Major John Crane and F. C. Travers to lunch, then confers and dines with Congressmen Hull, Babcock and Overstreet on the state campaigns. He writes Senator Foraker, no friend of Storer, about the Berlin post.

headline: Assuring Holmes of easy confirmation
summary: Roosevelt tells Oliver Wendell Holmes he expects not one vote against him in the Senate. He also writes Governor Odell about Harriman and the trusts, and Massachusetts Governor Crane about campaign money.

headline: Setting the record straight on irrigation
summary: Albert Shaw and Frederick Holls call and stay for lunch with Lyon, and Grant La Farge is a guest. Roosevelt again tells Charles Lummis that Newlands had no part in getting the irrigation bill passed.

headline: Can Washington act on the coal strike?
summary: Roosevelt talks with Senator Pritchard about a vacancy on the Court of Claims and lunches with him and others. He asks Attorney General Knox whether the government can move against the coal operators to end the strike. Edith writes McKim proposing a gallery of First Ladies' portraits in the White House ground floor corridor.

headline: New England tour opens on the trusts
summary: Roosevelt takes the Sylph across to New Haven and starts a speaking swing to explain his case against the trusts. At Hartford he speaks on island policy and rides in a parade by automobile, which the record says made him the first president to ride in one. At Providence he gives a major speech on trusts, then speaks at three Connecticut towns and spends the night with the Winthrop Chanlers in Newport.

headline: Rolling through Massachusetts to Nahant
summary: Roosevelt's train carries him from Newport up to Boston, pausing at Myricks, Taunton and Fall River, and spends the night at Lodge's home in Nahant.

headline: Symphony Hall speech on trusts
summary: Roosevelt speaks at the Nahant library and Lynn City Hall, then takes on the trusts in a speech at Boston's Symphony Hall. He dines with Governor Crane, Lodge, Senator Hoar and others.

headline: Into New Hampshire and Maine
summary: Roosevelt praises former Puerto Rico governor Charles Allen at Lowell, speaks on the Philippines at Lawrence and on the Navy at Haverhill, then talks at Dover, New Hampshire, and at Old Orchard, Portland and Augusta in Maine, where he stays with Governor Hill.

headline: Governor's Day at the Maine State Fair
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Bangor on Governor's Day at the state fair, then at Ellsworth, and travels on to Waterville.

headline: New Hampshire stops end at the Hays'
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Nashua, Manchester, Concord, a soldiers' reunion at The Weirs, and Newbury, New Hampshire, where he spends the night at John Hay's summer home.

headline: A boar hunt in New Hampshire
summary: Near Newport, New Hampshire, Roosevelt goes boar hunting with Senator Proctor and Corbin.

headline: With novelist Winston Churchill to Vermont
summary: Roosevelt rides to Windsor, Vermont, in the company of novelist Winston Churchill, and passes the evening near Burlington, by Lake Champlain, at the home of L. M. Shaw.

headline: Kermit starts at Groton
summary: Near Burlington, Roosevelt dines at Dr. Webb's. Kermit begins his first term at Groton School.

headline: Whistle stops down Vermont
summary: Roosevelt stops at eight Vermont towns from Vergennes to Brattleboro and spends the evening with Navy Secretary Moody at Northfield, Massachusetts. He arranges to meet Senator Aldrich at Sagamore Hill on September 16.

headline: Alice waves from a passing train
summary: Roosevelt's train winds through the Berkshires. By chance Alice passes on a train heading the other way and waves wildly, but her father, mid-speech, never sees her. He speaks on trusts at Fitchburg and stops at Miller's Falls, Athol, Springfield, Worcester and Dalton.

headline: Trolley crash at Pittsfield
summary: In Pittsfield an electric streetcar slams into the open landau carrying Roosevelt, Governor Murray Crane and George Cortelyou. Secret Service agent William Craig is killed, and a horse dies. Roosevelt is hurled about 30 feet, hurting his left leg and bruising his face; Cortelyou suffers a deep scalp wound. Half an hour later Roosevelt goes on to speak at Lenox, and 30,000 people greet him at Bridgeport before he sails home.

headline: Recovering at home
summary: Back at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt has Joe Bishop as a guest.

headline: Leaving for Chattanooga
summary: Roosevelt sets out from Sagamore Hill for Chattanooga, Tennessee.

headline: Wheeling speech; thanks to the King
summary: Roosevelt speaks on the trusts at Wheeling, West Virginia. He thanks King Edward VII for asking after him, saying his injuries were minor, and compliments Martha Dunn on her article about Browning.

headline: Reviewing cavalry at Chattanooga
summary: In Chattanooga Roosevelt reviews the 7th Cavalry and tours the Civil War battlefield.

headline: Addressing the locomotive firemen
summary: Roosevelt addresses the locomotive firemen's union at its Chattanooga convention, then leaves for Knoxville.

headline: Speeches in North Carolina
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Asheville and Greensboro, North Carolina.

headline: Back to Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt returns home to Oyster Bay.

headline: Lucius Swift and civil service
summary: Lucius B. Swift visits and stays to lunch. Roosevelt writes James Garfield about civil service matters, including voluntary political donations from federal workers.

headline: Clarkson and McDonough to lunch
summary: Roosevelt lunches with J. S. Clarkson and J. T. McDonough, who stays on for dinner. The record also notes a statement by Navy Secretary Moody pledging that the United States will keep the isthmus neutral and transit across it open.

headline: Ted turns fifteen; an essay on trusts
summary: It is Ted's 15th birthday. Albert Shaw, Arthur Lee and Postmaster General Payne call and stay for lunch. Roosevelt writes an Outlook article, "Big Corporations Commonly Called Trusts." The piece also touches on citizenship.

headline: Sunday at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.

headline: A garden party for thousands
summary: The Roosevelts open Sagamore Hill to their Nassau County neighbors for an afternoon garden party. Thousands come, 60 New York City police stand guard, and guests take home 3,000 crystal punch cups engraved with the President's name and the year. He asks E. H. Harriman to talk tariff and trusts.

headline: Party leaders gather at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt brings Lodge, Spooner, Allison, Aldrich and Hanna to Oyster Bay to set strategy on the congressional campaign, tariff revision and the trusts.

headline: Fighting Joe Wheeler to lunch
summary: General Joseph Wheeler, Roosevelt's old commander from Cuba, visits and stays for lunch.

headline: Trusts with Jenks; a writing table Edith dislikes
summary: Lyman Abbott and Henry White call, and Roosevelt discusses trusts with economist J. W. Jenks before all three stay to lunch. Joe Bishop comes for dinner and the night. Roosevelt writes Hay about the Cuban treaty, while Edith tells McKim the new White House writing table is ugly and awkward to use.

headline: Starting west as the coal strike drags on
summary: Roosevelt leaves for a Western trip while Edith takes the Sylph into Manhattan, landing at East 23rd Street. He writes Senator Quay that John Mitchell refuses to call off the anthracite strike, which has run since May, and insists on a compromise.

headline: Cincinnati speech on tariff and trusts
summary: In Cincinnati Roosevelt speaks on the tariff and the trusts. The record also notes that the United States is guarding and guaranteeing passage across Panama.

headline: Lunch with General Alger in Detroit
summary: In Detroit Roosevelt lunches with General Russell Alger, McKinley's former Secretary of War.

headline: Detroit speech on Cuba and the Philippines
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Detroit on reciprocity with Cuba and on the Philippines.

headline: Surgery in Indianapolis ends the tour
summary: At Logansport Roosevelt tells Spanish-American War veterans he favors a tariff commission. In Indianapolis his leg, still swollen weeks after the Pittsfield crash, is found to hold an abscess; at St. Vincent's doctors numb it and draw off about two ounces of fluid. That evening he reads aboard his special train, leg propped up, headed for Washington.

headline: Ordered to rest on Jackson Place
summary: With the White House still under renovation, Roosevelt is carried to the house at 22 Jackson Place, where doctors insist on rest and quiet. Edith hurries down from New York to be with him.

headline: In a wheelchair, still receiving callers
summary: Roosevelt is in a wheelchair, his face still swollen three weeks after the crash, but he sees Japanese minister Takahira, Moody, Shaw, Wilson and Hitchcock. He congratulates Frank Higgins on his nomination for lieutenant governor and explains in a letter that the abscess forced him to give up the Western trip.

headline: Resting in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing more is recorded.

headline: A second operation and moves on the coal strike
summary: On Corinne's 41st birthday, Roosevelt sees Shaw and Wilson and explains to Hanna that his injury and the coal strike keep him from Ohio. When rest brings no relief, a doctor opens the abscess again and scrapes the shin bone; Alice helps care for him. Soon after, he twice gathers his advisers on what Washington can do in the strike and writes Lodge a key letter that sets up the talks.

headline: Summoning both sides of the coal strike
summary: Roosevelt wires John Mitchell asking to see him on October 3 about the failing coal supply, and invites railroad chief Alexander Cassatt and Senator Quay into the effort. He also sends condolences to Isabella Craig, whose son William, a Secret Service agent, died in the Pittsfield crash. Edith gets her first look at the rebuilt White House and plans an upstairs office for herself.

headline: Smaller spurs and a mending leg
summary: Roosevelt asks Root for smaller spurs for the cavalry, tells Senator O. H. Platt the rest has done him good and the doctors are done cutting, and writes Oswald Villard on the strike and the trusts.

headline: Operators and miners meet the President
summary: Still in a wheelchair, Roosevelt brings mine owners and union leaders face to face at his temporary home on Jackson Place, with Mitchell, Baer, Truesdale, Wilcox, Carroll Wright and Cortelyou among those present. He reports on the meeting to Hanna and Seth Low. In Panama, trains run under American protection.

headline: Strike talks with Knox and Wright
summary: Root calls in the morning, and Roosevelt confers with Knox and Carroll Wright on the strike.

headline: Exasperated with the operators
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday on the strike with Wright and four Cabinet members. He writes Grover Cleveland that the operators' language toward Mitchell seemed designed to make the miners refuse everything.

headline: Criticized from both sides; books from the Library
summary: Roosevelt confers with Frank Sargent on the strike and tells William Allen White that one camp calls him too friendly to the miners, the other too friendly to the companies. He asks Librarian of Congress Herbert Putnam for histories of the Mediterranean peoples and of Poland.

headline: Proposing an investigation of the strike
summary: Roosevelt publicly proposes an inquiry into the coal strike and meets Albert Shaw and Lyman Abbott. To Robert Bacon he likens his position to Lincoln's; to Lodge he describes his strike troubles.

headline: Reviewing the GAR parade
summary: Roosevelt confers with Root and Knox and reviews the parade of Union veterans of the Grand Army of the Republic. He thanks Herbert Putnam for books that let him set aside everything useful for a while.

headline: Could troops run the mines?
summary: Roosevelt holds more strike meetings with Root and Knox and sees Wilkins of the Washington Post. He writes Villard on whether sending soldiers to work the mines would be possible or lawful, and praises Silas McBee's strike column.

headline: Kermit's birthday; a commission takes shape
summary: On Kermit's 13th birthday, the Cabinet meets on the strike and Roosevelt receives the U.S. minister to Belgium. He tells Grover Cleveland his leg keeps him from Woodrow Wilson's Princeton installation and asks him to sit on a strike inquiry board, and writes Hanna about his plan for a settlement commission.

headline: A Siamese prince and more strike talks
summary: Roosevelt keeps up the strike meetings with his Cabinet, Wright and Sargent, sees Noyes of the Washington Star, and receives a prince of Siam. It is his niece Eleanor's 18th birthday. He praises Governor Odell's stand and answers John Kernan's request to serve on the commission.

headline: Up on crutches
summary: Strike meetings go on, with Root and Quay among the callers and Jenks at six. Cleveland agrees to serve on the commission. Roosevelt writes that he can now move about on crutches, and that while he is supposed to be minding Ethel, she will likely end up minding him.

headline: Morgan brings a plan to Jackson Place
summary: Roosevelt asks General Schofield about having the Army run the mines and receives the Chief Justice and the Supreme Court. That evening J. P. Morgan and Robert Bacon, fresh from talks with Root aboard Morgan's yacht Corsair, call on the President at his temporary quarters on Jackson Place. They agree to push the operators to accept a commission of Roosevelt's choosing, with the threat of Army control of the mines in the background.

headline: Settlement draws near
summary: Roosevelt confers with Wright and Wellman. He tells John Kernan the earlier commission plan must be dropped and writes Bishop that the strike is closer to ending. Back on Long Island, Sagamore Hill has Mrs. Clifford Richardson as a guest.

headline: Insisting on a free hand
summary: Roosevelt meets Mitchell, Wright and Sargent late in the morning, dines at John Hay's, and sees Bacon and George Perkins at night. He drafts but does not send a letter to Morgan saying he must pick the commission freely, because Mitchell is trusting him.

headline: Naming the Anthracite Coal Strike Commission
summary: Roosevelt names a seven-man commission to settle the coal strike: retired Army engineer General John M. Wilson; Labor Commissioner Carroll Wright; federal Judge George Gray of Delaware; E. E. Clark, head of the railway conductors' union, seated under the label of "eminent sociologist"; mining engineer Edward Parker; coal man Thomas Watkins; and Bishop John Spalding. He thanks Morgan and Hanna, explains to Cleveland that the operators would not accept him, and sends Mitchell the names.

headline: Getting a bishop onto the commission
summary: Roosevelt meets Wright, General Wilson and Parker of the new commission and lunches with Hay and Root. He tells Lodge how he got Bishop Spalding named and why Clark went on as a sociologist.

headline: An order on political contributions
summary: An executive order reminds federal officeholders to obey the laws on political donations. Roosevelt lunches with Regis Post; it is Bamie's son Sheffield's fourth birthday. He writes Bessie Van Vorst about wives, mothers and women's outlook.

headline: Edith and the baby trunk
summary: Roosevelt writes J. H. Woodard about the strike's end. At Sagamore Hill to gather the children, Edith writes her sister Emily that unpacking the baby clothes saddened her, and that she means to hold on to them in hope of another child.

headline: Nurse to two guinea pigs
summary: Root, Hitchcock, Knox and Japanese minister Takahira call; Roosevelt lunches with Judge Gray and dines at Hay's. He tells Elizabeth Stuart Phelps Ward he is nursing two tiny guinea pigs for Ethel, and tells Finley Peter Dunne the last strike conferences were funnier than anything Dunne ever wrote.

headline: The coal strike ends
summary: The anthracite strike is formally over. Roosevelt has John Kernan and M. E. Egan to lunch, and writes Taft that his Rome mission has failed and resentment of the Catholic church is growing in the Philippines.

headline: Telling Crane the strike story
summary: Roosevelt receives the Dutch minister and sends Massachusetts Governor Crane a long account of the strike from start to finish. He tells Payne he will hold off on Colorado appointments until after the election.

headline: Miners go back to work
summary: The anthracite miners return to the pits. Roosevelt lunches with Root, dines at Payne's, and formally charges the new commission to study the strike's causes and recommend remedies. Finley Peter Dunne writes that he found nothing funny about the strike.

headline: Commission meets; Yellowstone's bison and elk
summary: Roosevelt meets the strike commission, which chooses Judge Gray as chairman, and speaks briefly. He sees Booker T. Washington at noon and asks Yellowstone superintendent John Pitcher how the park protects its bison and elk, and how many rangers it has.
