headline: Wilson installed at Princeton without him
summary: Roosevelt misses Woodrow Wilson's inauguration at Princeton. In the Philippines, the new Independent Philippine Church is proclaimed and claims Catholic properties. Roosevelt confers with Knox on the Panama title and purchase and with two rear admirals, Bowles and Taylor, writes Mahan on ship size versus firepower, and tells Taft he would like to put him on the Supreme Court.

headline: Sunday in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Turning 44
summary: On Roosevelt's 44th birthday, a delegation from New York's Hungarian Club calls with good wishes. He writes Cuban President Tomás Estrada Palma, tells Quay the naval maneuvers will go ahead despite the strike, and asks to see Joe Bishop.

headline: Alaska and a Colombian complaint
summary: Roosevelt confers with Dudley Wooten on Alaska and takes no appointments after eleven. He writes Hay that Colombia has protested American meddling in its internal quarrel over the canal.

headline: Samuel Gompers at noon
summary: Roosevelt sees Benjamin Ide Wheeler in the morning and labor leader Samuel Gompers at noon, then dines with Father Doyle. He writes that the Kaiser likes Seth Low as mayor, that Taft is to remain in Manila, and replies to a bishop who wants him to condemn violence in the coal fields.

headline: "The Presidency" in Youth's Companion
summary: Roosevelt's essay "The Presidency" appears in Youth's Companion. The record adds a guest's sketch of a typical White House lunch that fall: bouillon, chicken and rice, salt fish and baked beans, with the President taking seconds of beans and fish, no cigar for him, and an American flag on his bread plate.

headline: At Manassas
summary: Roosevelt is at Manassas, Virginia; no details are recorded.

headline: Visiting Cedar Mountain battlefield
summary: From Manassas Roosevelt visits the Civil War battlefield at Cedar Mountain, then returns to Washington.

headline: Home to vote
summary: Roosevelt takes an afternoon train north to Oyster Bay by way of New York.

headline: Election Day walk with six dogs
summary: On Election Day in Oyster Bay, Roosevelt and Edith go for a walk with all six of their dogs.

headline: Moving into the rebuilt White House
summary: After a speech in Philadelphia, Roosevelt and Edith settle back into the rebuilt White House. The ground floor is unfinished, but the enlarged State Dining Room now holds 107 diners rather than 60. Edith places an order for a new presidential china service and begins hunting for old sets, the start of the White House china collection. The Navy's Caribbean squadron reaches Culebra.

headline: Election results and Tom Quartz the kitten
summary: Roosevelt meets Procter, Foulke and Garfield on civil service and sees Senator Beveridge at six. He writes cousin Emlen that the elections went well for Republicans, though Odell hears that New York went poorly. To Kermit he describes Archie carrying the kitten Tom Quartz on the train and Quentin falling asleep.

headline: Cabinet turns to the annual message
summary: Regular Cabinet meetings resume with a session on the annual message. Roosevelt discusses talks with Colombia with Hay and twice sees a Herald correspondent, Mr. Brown.

headline: Congratulating Hanna on Ohio
summary: Hay, Knox, Babcock and Lorimer call. Roosevelt congratulates Mark Hanna on the Republican win in Ohio.

headline: Drafting the annual message
summary: Roosevelt works on his annual message and sees Representative Babcock at three.

headline: The Isle of Pines and a rumor answered
summary: Roosevelt confers with Senator Cullom and others on the Isle of Pines and sees Leonard Wood, Garfield, J. M. McCormick and E. F. Ware before leaving that evening for New York. He firmly answers Robert Rhett about a rumor that his appointees include Black men of bad character.

headline: Chamber of Commerce and a call for preparedness
summary: In New York Roosevelt meets Nicholas Murray Butler for breakfast at the University Club, speaks at the dedication of the Chamber of Commerce building, and argues for military preparedness at a dinner at the Waldorf-Astoria. At midnight he leaves on a hunting trip.

headline: Southbound for Mississippi
summary: Roosevelt's train crosses Ohio, stopping along the way, bound for Smedes, Mississippi. He writes Jacob Riis about the dedication of Riis's new book and Root about keeping Army officers and men physically fit.

headline: Arriving at Smedes
summary: After a stop in Memphis, Roosevelt reaches Smedes, Mississippi.

headline: Bear hunting in the Mississippi canebrakes
summary: Near Smedes, Roosevelt goes after bear. In Washington, Edith writes her sister Emily that Dr. Rixey does not think her wish for another child is reasonable.

headline: Still on the bear trail
summary: The bear hunt continues near Smedes.

headline: Drawing the Line in Mississippi
summary: The hunt goes on near Smedes. Newspapers have picked up a story that Roosevelt refused to shoot a bear, a cub in some tellings and an old bear in others. Clifford Berryman's Washington Post cartoon "Drawing the Line in Mississippi" appears, toy makers soon turn out stuffed bears, and the teddy bear is born.

headline: In Mississippi
summary: Roosevelt is in Mississippi; no further detail is given.

headline: Leaving the hunting camp
summary: Roosevelt leaves Smedes for Memphis.

headline: Memphis speeches; Quentin turns five
summary: In Memphis Roosevelt speaks on the Philippines and joins a reception honoring General Luke Wright, then leaves for Washington that evening. It is Quentin's 5th birthday.

headline: Whistle stops on the way home
summary: On the way back to Washington, Roosevelt's train stops at Knoxville and Asheville.

headline: Cuba, the canal and the Pacific cable
summary: The Cabinet takes up Cuba, the Panama canal and the Pacific cable. Roosevelt lunches with Lodge, goes over tariff changes with Senators Scott, Burrows and Lodge, and sees Francis Leupp in the afternoon. The North Atlantic battle squadron reaches Culebra.

headline: Founder's Day at the Union League
summary: In Philadelphia Roosevelt gives the Union League's Founder's Day address, promising to tackle the problem of trusts and business combinations. He dedicates a school, lunches with C. E. Smith, and attends a reception at E. T. Stotesbury's home.

headline: Evening callers Sternberg and Knox
summary: Back in Washington, Roosevelt confers with Spooner and sees Baron Speck von Sternberg at 9 p.m. and Attorney General Knox half an hour later.

headline: Riding with St. Loe Strachey
summary: A long line of congressional leaders calls, including Speaker Henderson, Hanna, Cannon and Lodge. British editor John St. Loe Strachey is staying at the White House and rides with Roosevelt and Root, talking over Venezuela and the Alaska boundary. Sternberg comes to dinner.

headline: Germany and Britain move on Venezuela
summary: Germany and Britain formally announce they will force Venezuela to pay its debts. The Cabinet works on the annual message, and Roosevelt discusses the Philippines with Luke Wright, New York politics with George Dunn, and receives Senator Hale, the Italian ambassador and Chief Justice Fuller. It is Bamie's seventh wedding anniversary.

headline: Bringing Taft home for the Court
summary: On a crowded day, callers range from Clarence Darrow to Hay, Moody, Knox and several lawmakers. Roosevelt writes Taft that after a month of trying to arrange things his way, he will have to bring him home and seat him on the Supreme Court.

headline: Thanksgiving ride and a dance
summary: For Thanksgiving the family rides for three hours: Roosevelt on Renown, Ted on an Army horse, Edith on Jocko Root, Ethel on Yagenka and Archie on Algonquin, joined by Lodge, Douglas Robinson, cousin John Elliott, Bob Ferguson and Leonard Wood. Dinner follows in the enlarged State Dining Room with the riders, Corinne and her children and Brooks Adams, then a dance.

headline: Quentin gives the kitten a bath
summary: Senators T. C. Platt, Cullom and others call along with Leonard Wood; there is a Cabinet meeting and lunch with Judge Clarke. Roosevelt tells Kermit that Quentin gave the kitten Tom Quartz some special attention by setting him in the tub and turning on the tap.

headline: The fleet gathers in the Caribbean
summary: With the South Atlantic and European squadrons now at Trinidad, nearly the whole U.S. Navy is in the Caribbean. Roosevelt discusses the Venezuelan debt claims with Hanna, banker Isaac Seligman and Admiral Dewey, receives Salvador's new minister Rafael Lopez, meets congressional leaders, rides with Leonard Wood and dines with Root. He tells David Hill he will not commit himself on Venezuela before seeing Hay.

headline: Opening the new West Wing
summary: The new executive office wing is finished, with a staff of 38, and visitors stream through the new Cabinet Room from morning to early afternoon. A new tennis court sits just outside, on ground where the Oval Office was later built under Taft. Roosevelt confers with General Greene that night. The record also begins to describe his desk, made from a ship's oak timbers and presented to President Hayes.

headline: Trust legislation with Littauer
summary: Roosevelt confers with Lucius Littauer on trust bills and sees Quay, Millard, Beveridge, Gamble and Burke. H. H. Kohlsaat calls at ten and stays for lunch with New.

headline: Second annual message: 'Not a cloud on the horizon'
summary: Roosevelt sends his annual message to Congress, laying out his stand on the trusts. He meets congressmen on St. Louis vote fraud and naval bills, lunches with Jane Addams, George Kennan, Monsignor Kennedy and Eugene Philbin, and dines with Hanna, O. H. Platt and Payne. It is his and Edith's 16th anniversary. He asks Dean LeBaron Briggs when Ted should leave Groton for Harvard.

headline: Defending Dr. Crum's appointment
summary: Roosevelt receives the Persian minister, lunches with Lyman Abbott, Luke Wright and Albert Shaw, and sees Senator Beveridge and Chaplain Vattmann in the evening. He writes William Brawley about naming Dr. William Crum, a Black physician, to a federal post in South Carolina over local objections.

headline: Single-stick bouts with Wood
summary: On a busy day Roosevelt talks Cuban reciprocity with Senator Elkins and writes Quay about whether New Mexico and Arizona should become states. He tells Kermit that he and Leonard Wood often fence with padded wooden sticks, landing blows on each other.

headline: Ordering Knox to take a holiday
summary: The Cabinet meets on Cuban reciprocity and postal appointments, and Edith welcomes 150 members of a national Jewish women's organization. Roosevelt writes Butler about a Western trip next spring and orders Knox to take four weeks off.

headline: Planning the St. Louis fair
summary: Roosevelt meets Senators Carter and Thurston about the Louisiana Purchase Exposition, sees Addicks, and lunches with Von Briesen and Wilcox. He praises Woodrow Wilson's article on American ideals.

headline: Laurier at the White House
summary: Canadian Prime Minister Sir Wilfrid Laurier visits Roosevelt. Word comes that Thomas Nast, the cartoonist serving as U.S. consul general in Ecuador, has died there of yellow fever.

headline: Dewey takes the Caribbean fleet; praise for Edith
summary: Germany and Britain break relations with Venezuela, and Admiral Dewey, aboard the Mayflower, takes command of the fleet in the Caribbean. Roosevelt meets senators and German Ambassador Holleben. Writing Maria Storer, he calls Edith the best of wives and mothers and the ideal mistress of the White House.

headline: A dinner for Justice Harlan
summary: After a Cabinet meeting and talks with Senators Dryden and McCumber, Roosevelt speaks at an evening dinner for Justice John Marshall Harlan. He writes John Wilson about big business and labor.

headline: New York merchants call
summary: A delegation from the Merchants' Association of New York meets with Roosevelt.

headline: Venezuela talks and a plea for Turkey
summary: Roosevelt discusses Venezuela with Hay and Senator Cullom, sees Finley Peter Dunne, and has Regis Post, Evarts and Sprague to lunch. In the afternoon Morris Jesup leads a delegation seeking aid for Turkey. Edith hosts a hundred women from the National Indian Association, and Don Dickinson comes to dinner.

headline: Public lands and new states
summary: The Cabinet meets on Venezuela. Roosevelt confers with Representative Lacey about public lands and with Congressman Dick and others about statehood for the Southwest territories, and writes General Young about Army uniforms.

headline: Blockade and bombardment in Venezuela
summary: German and British ships blockade five Venezuelan ports and shell Puerto Cabello. Roosevelt had approved the Anglo-German-Italian blockade over Venezuela's unpaid bonds, though with serious doubts. He sees Senators Platt, Cullom, Frye and Spooner, Lieutenant Commander William Sims and the Russian ambassador, and hosts a large dinner. He tells Clement Griscom his son Lloyd will go to Japan as minister.

headline: Sunday callers Shaw and Spooner
summary: Treasury Secretary Shaw calls in the morning and Senator Spooner in the evening.

headline: Photographed, then back to work
summary: Mr. Ingersoll photographs Roosevelt in the morning. He confers with Hay and Cullom, goes over the Cuba treaty with Root, lunches with Sheffield, Boardman and Devereaux, and has a dinner at eight.

headline: Ships ordered toward the blockade
summary: After a Cabinet session on Cuba and Venezuela, Roosevelt decides to send American warships from Culebra into the blockade zone and hands reporters battle maps of the area. He works on the Militia Bill with Root, Proctor, Hull and Dick, and dines with a large party of congressional leaders.

headline: Tracey for the Philippine bench
summary: On a busy day Hanna, Dillingham, Tawney, Martin and Clarkson call, and Roosevelt has Joseph Barnes, Stranahan and Clarkson to lunch. He tells James Tracey he wants him on the Philippine Supreme Court.

headline: Britain asks Roosevelt to arbitrate
summary: Britain agrees the Venezuela dispute should be arbitrated and asks Roosevelt to serve as arbiter. Roosevelt later said he warned Germany of war if it refused arbitration. The Pacific fleet begins maneuvers, alarming German envoy Holleben. The day ends with the annual Cabinet dinner.

headline: Germany agrees to arbitrate
summary: Germany agrees to arbitration over Venezuela. The Cabinet meets on the crisis, and Roosevelt discusses currency with Lyman Gage and J. H. Rhoades.

headline: Mrs. Grant's funeral; off to the Rapidan
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts with Jacob Riis. Congress adjourns, Julia Dent Grant is buried, and after a meeting with Hay Roosevelt leaves for Rapidan, Virginia.

headline: Guest of Joseph Wilmer
summary: At Rapidan, Virginia, Roosevelt stays with Joseph Wilmer.

headline: Coal tariffs
summary: Back in Washington, Roosevelt meets Hay and writes Henry Higginson about duties on coal.

headline: Mabini in a Philippine jail
summary: After a Cabinet meeting on Venezuela and lunch with George Perkins, Roosevelt writes Senator Hoar about Apolinario Mabini, the insurgent leader held by the United States in the Philippines.

headline: Christmas Eve with Hay and the Sun
summary: Roosevelt confers with Hay on Venezuela, sees a Sun newspaperman named Matthews, and asks William Allen White whether Leonard Wood can stay at his club.

headline: Christmas at the White House
summary: The children are banging on the bedroom door by 6:45, and soon they are piled on the bed opening stockings; Archie has hidden a small gift-laden tree in a closet. After breakfast Archie gets a rifle and riding boots and Quentin an electric train. Roosevelt rides for three hours, lunches at Bamie's, fences single-stick with Wood and Ferguson, and ends with dinner and dancing in the East Room.

headline: Venezuela headed to The Hague
summary: After a Cabinet meeting, the government announces the Venezuela dispute will go to the Hague Tribunal. Roosevelt sends a Christmas letter to young James A. Garfield, and writes Shaw, Taft and Cleveland about upholding the Monroe Doctrine, Agassiz on the Philippines and Schurz on the arbitration.

headline: The Austrian ambassador calls
summary: Roosevelt receives the Austrian ambassador in the morning and writes Root and the Rev. William Rainsford, the latter on the trusts.

headline: Wayne MacVeagh calls
summary: Wayne MacVeagh is among Sunday's callers.

headline: Got what he wanted on Venezuela
summary: Wilson and Foulke call, Roosevelt lunches with psychologist Hugo Münsterberg, and Justice White visits in the evening. He writes George Hinman that he knew his aims in the Venezuela settlement and achieved them.

headline: Land Office business
summary: The Cabinet meets on General Land Office affairs. Roosevelt meets a Picayune editor, Mr. Robertson, and confers with Generals Young and Wood.

headline: Year's end with Rev. Billings
summary: Roosevelt dines with the Rev. Billings on the last day of 1902.

headline: New Year's reception in a renovated White House
summary: The freshly remodeled White House is formally unveiled, and Roosevelt greets the public at the New Year's reception from late morning into the early afternoon.

headline: Roller skates on the new East Room floor
summary: Roosevelt discovers his children and their friends have turned the East Room's new parquet into a skating rink. The Cabinet takes up the shuttered post office at Indianola, Mississippi, and he confers with Postmaster General Payne.

headline: German ambassador and a dinner at the Hays'
summary: Roosevelt opens the day with German Ambassador Holleben, talks Cuban reciprocity with H. T. Oxnard, and sees a string of senators and officials. He lunches with Holls, and that evening he and Edith dine with Secretary and Mrs. Hay.

headline: Talking battleships with House leaders
summary: On a Sunday, Roosevelt meets the House Naval Affairs Committee to work over the Navy's spending bill.

headline: Loomis named to the State Department
summary: Roosevelt makes F. B. Loomis an Assistant Secretary of State, lunches with Clarkson and others, and sees Mark Hanna late in the evening. He warns Postmaster General Payne he may release the papers on a Delaware postmastership. Admiral Dewey's squadron leaves the Caribbean.

headline: A call for trust laws, and a letter home
summary: Roosevelt urges Congress to pass antitrust laws without delay, and the Cabinet weighs Venezuela and the Cuban treaty. Writing Kermit at Groton, he says the house feels empty without the boys and reports that Tom Quartz the kitten pounced on Joe Cannon.

headline: Carnegie calls; a new public library opens
summary: Roosevelt sends the Philippine Commission's yearly report to Congress and fills his morning with appointments, from cartoonist Clifford Berryman to Andrew Carnegie and his wife. After lunch with Knox and Moody, he speaks at the dedication of Washington's public library.

headline: Diplomats, writers and a swollen wrist
summary: Roosevelt sits for photographer Tucker, then hosts the diplomatic reception, where guests include Richard Harding Davis, Finley Peter Dunne, Howard Pyle and Owen Wister. He tells Ted his wrist is puffed up from singlestick bouts with Frank McCoy and that Alice keeps very late hours.

headline: Wind Cave becomes a national park
summary: Wind Cave in South Dakota is made a national park. Roosevelt receives a delegation from the Pope and meets C. D. Wright, and the Cabinet again discusses Indianola. Papers report Holleben's quiet recall from Berlin and the choice of Roosevelt's friend Speck von Sternberg to replace him.

headline: Civil service talks and a Treasury dinner
summary: Roosevelt meets E. H. Goodwin and others about civil service reform and lunches with George W. Perkins. In the evening Secretary of the Treasury Shaw and his wife give a dinner for him and Edith.

headline: Late Sunday talk with Aldrich and Henderson
summary: Roosevelt holds a late-night Sunday meeting with Senator Aldrich and House Speaker Henderson.

headline: Government papers for the Library of Congress
summary: Roosevelt talks with D. J. Hill and Librarian Herbert Putnam about moving government records into the Library of Congress. He writes Henry Taft about his brother and the Court vacancy, consoles Nicholas Murray Butler on his wife's death, and answers Senator Hoar on Mabini.

headline: Trusts, and Root's tax bill
summary: Roosevelt meets the Littlefield subcommittee on trusts, holds Cabinet, and confers with a long list of congressmen and others. Theodore Noyes and Lawrence Abbott join him for lunch, and protests to Mayor Seth Low that New York is taxing Elihu Root far too heavily.

headline: Senators call; a note on Alaska
summary: Hanna, Hepburn, Quay and Foraker stop by, and Roosevelt lunches with Knox, Moody and three House members. He writes Secretary Hay about the disputed Alaska boundary.

headline: Romping with the boys, then a state dinner
summary: After meetings with Quay, Shaw and Hay, Roosevelt wrestles with Archie and Quentin before dinner and rumples his evening clothes. The Diplomatic Corps dinner follows, with Whitelaw Reid, Douglas Robinson and young Roosevelt cousins among the guests.

headline: Working the Cuban treaty
summary: Roosevelt huddles with Senators Aldrich, Lodge and Spooner over the Cuban reciprocity treaty, holds Cabinet, lunches with Guy Waring, and ends with a small dinner and music.

headline: Chopping trees with Garfield and Pinchot
summary: Luquillo National Forest is set aside in Puerto Rico, while German warships shell Fort San Carlos in Venezuela. Roosevelt confers on the Cuban treaty, trusts and statehood, has Joe Bishop to lunch, and tells Kermit he spent the afternoon felling trees with Garfield and Pinchot.

headline: Bamie turns 48
summary: It is the 48th birthday of Roosevelt's sister Bamie. That night he meets Attorney General Knox with Senators Spooner and Aldrich.

headline: A wireless greeting across the Atlantic
summary: Roosevelt sends King Edward VII the first wireless telegram to cross the ocean. George Bird Grinnell brings Blackfoot visitors at noon, and that night Roosevelt speaks at a YMCA dinner. He presses Senator Fairbanks to back Knox's trust program and writes Henry Taft again about his brother's future.

headline: A broken wrist from singlestick
summary: After Cabinet and visits from senators, Roosevelt receives delegates of a German society from New York. He tells Ted singlestick has left him with a broken wrist and a battered arm, so he walks daily with General Wood instead, and says Archie and Quentin insist he make up stories rather than read them.

headline: Militia Bill signed
summary: Roosevelt approves the Militia Bill and receives callers from the Japanese Legation, Congress and the Cabinet. Letters go to Edward Wolcott on Colorado politics, to Hay with thanks, and to General Francis V. Greene about New York's police commissioner.

headline: Hay-Herran canal treaty signed
summary: Colombia's envoy Tomás Herrán signs the Hay-Herrán treaty, leasing the United States a six-mile strip across Panama for a century at $10 million down plus $250,000 a year. Roosevelt lunches with the Woods and hosts the judicial reception; the Grant La Farges begin a four-day stay.

headline: Queen Liliuokalani at the White House
summary: Roosevelt and Edith receive Hawaii's former queen, Liliuokalani. Lunch brings in the Steinways, Tiffany and the painter Dewing. He tells Hanna the new department should leave 'Labor' out of its name and writes William Williams about Jewish complaints over Ellis Island.

headline: A portrait painter and a full calendar
summary: On a crowded day, Roosevelt sees Delaware's Addicks and Allee and economist J. W. Jenks on trusts, and meets portrait painter Théobald Chartran. He lunches with Hay, Bowen and Wood, and the Knoxes host him and Edith for dinner.

headline: Shaking hands left-handed
summary: Hanna, Foulke and Overstreet call in the evening. Roosevelt tells Kermit the singlestick injury has him greeting people with his left hand, that snow has turned his rides with Edith into walks, and that Grant La Farge is staying with them.

headline: Lunch with Lady Minto, then a train to Canton
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Lady Minto, Hay, Root and the Lodges, then boards a night train for Canton, Ohio. Edith writes Aunt Lizzie that McKim's renovation finally lets her make guests comfortable.

headline: Honoring McKinley in Canton
summary: In Canton, Roosevelt lunches at Judge William R. Day's home and marks McKinley Day, the late President's birthday, with a speech. Back in Washington, Alice confides to her diary that she believes her father cares far less for her than for the other children.

headline: Home from Canton
summary: Roosevelt travels from Canton back to Washington.

headline: Silver coinage and a Supreme Court dinner
summary: Roosevelt asks Congress to back Mexico and China in seeking a common coinage standard for silver-using nations. He lunches with Lord Charles Beresford, Admiral Dewey and other officers, hosts the Supreme Court dinner, and tells Taft he will stay in the Philippines while General Wood heads there soon.

headline: Turning down a Platt request
summary: Roosevelt meets Cannon and Speaker Henderson, holds Cabinet, sees Root and Quay, and dines with Lord Beresford before a musicale. He refuses Senator Platt's pick for a military attaché post for the Germans.

headline: Paying for state dinners himself
summary: Roosevelt meets Ambassador Speck von Sternberg and confers on the canal treaty, then dines with Secretary and Mrs. Moody. Alice heads off with Edith Root to Mardi Gras and on to Puerto Rico until April. Roosevelt covers the caterer's bills for official banquets from his own pocket.

headline: The Army gets a General Staff
summary: Congress passes the Army bill creating a General Staff. Roosevelt writes Kermit that a new dog, Bozzie, lives in the kitchen and Chartran is painting him, and tells Ted that Speck von Sternberg has turned up as Germany's ambassador.

headline: Mayor Low at the White House
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Postmaster General Payne and sees New York Mayor Seth Low in the early evening. He writes Philip Stewart again about Colorado.

headline: Trust-busting package nears passage
summary: Congress passes Roosevelt's three-part answer to the trusts: the Elkins Act, a Department of Commerce and Labor, and the Expedition Act. He also sees senators, the British envoy, Justice White and Arthur Street, editor of Collier's. Bill Sewall, his old Maine guide, arrives to stay.

headline: Thanking Fairbanks for a fast vote
summary: Roosevelt confers with Allison, George W. Perkins and Lodge, and thanks Senator Fairbanks for steering the bill to speed antitrust cases through the Senate.

headline: Bill Sewall's party at lunch
summary: Roosevelt's lunch table mixes General Booth, his old friend Bill Sewall with a party of seven, and Cabinet regulars. That night he hosts the congressional reception and asks Representative Hepburn to amend a bill before it passes.

headline: Clergy and a general at lunch
summary: Representative Vreeland calls at noon, and Roosevelt has Bishop Lawrence, Sheffield, Moody, General Duke and Rev. Peterson to lunch before seeing Leupp.

headline: Jusserand presents his credentials
summary: France's new ambassador, Jules Jusserand, presents his credentials, the start of a close friendship. On a packed day Roosevelt also sees three senators, lunches with Philip Stewart, and dines with the Paynes. He defends his Indianola stand to Richard Watson Gilder and praises Alice French's story about lynching.

headline: A dapper scholar from France
summary: Roosevelt writes Kermit about books and about meeting Jusserand, a diplomat he actually enjoyed talking with. Bill Sewall and his family have visited, and Edith walked to the Capitol with the dogs while Ethel skated and Archie biked along.

headline: Laid up with a cough
summary: Roosevelt confers with Beveridge and a bloc of House leaders and opens a hall for the canning industries. He tells Ted that he too was sick on Sunday and that Alice has behaved well lately, and refuses Grant La Farge's plea to drop Byrne's Delaware appointment.

headline: Antitrust bills with Senate leaders
summary: Roosevelt meets Littlefield, Spooner and Aldrich to push the antitrust bills along.

headline: Odell at lunch; a fan letter on Shakespeare
summary: New York Governor Benjamin Odell lunches with Roosevelt to talk state politics. Roosevelt writes Thomas Lounsbury that he loved his book on Shakespeare and Voltaire and wants him to meet Jusserand.

headline: Alice turns 19; Chief Joseph at the reception
summary: On Alice's 19th birthday, Roosevelt meets Platt, Odell and Littauer, rides with Edith, and hosts the Army and Navy reception, where the Nez Perce leader Chief Joseph and fellow chiefs appear. He tells Senator Knute Nelson that Cortelyou will lead the brand-new commerce and labor department.

headline: Commerce and Labor Department signed into law
summary: Roosevelt signs the law that creates a Cabinet department for commerce and labor, and sits for photographer Rockwood. Letters ask whether hounds may chase mountain lions in Yellowstone, salute a family of twelve, and sound out Taft about becoming Secretary of War in a year.

headline: Sargent paints the President
summary: Roosevelt confers with Hay and Senators O. H. Platt, Hanna and Aldrich, twice with Aldrich. He tells Ted that he is back at singlestick, rode with Austin Wadsworth, and is sitting for a portrait by John Singer Sargent.

headline: Cortelyou takes the new Cabinet seat
summary: Roosevelt names George B. Cortelyou the first Secretary of Commerce and Labor. He meets Beveridge, Cullom, Garfield and Cannon, and writes Root on Philippine currency and the tariff.

headline: Ellis Island and the trusts
summary: Roosevelt meets Speaker Henderson and Senators Perkins and Spooner and lunches with three guests. He writes Joe Bishop about corruption at Ellis Island and the antitrust fight.

headline: Planning a mountain lion hunt
summary: Roosevelt meets Senators Platt and Fairbanks, lunches with Saturday Evening Post editor George Horace Lorimer, and sees Ambassador Sternberg. He tells Major John Pitcher he hopes to go after cougars in the Yellowstone country, outside the park where hunting is barred.

headline: Pressing the Senate on Panama and Cuba
summary: Roosevelt publicly calls on the Senate to approve both the Cuban reciprocity pact and the Panama canal treaty at once. He greets Spanish-American War veterans, rides with Speck von Sternberg in good spirits over Venezuela, and sees William Allen White that evening.

headline: Elkins Act signed
summary: Roosevelt signs the Elkins Act, aimed at the railroads' long practice of secret rebates. He talks Iowa politics with Albert Cummins, holds a Cabinet session on the Navy, has the William Allen Whites to lunch, and hears the Washington Symphony under Reginald De Koven.

headline: Laying the Army War College cornerstone
summary: Roosevelt speaks as the cornerstone of the Army War College is set in place. He confers with Root, Beveridge, Judge Van Devanter and others, lunches with Philip Stewart and Admiral Evans, and dines with the Hitchcocks. A playful letter to Root pokes fun at the appointment game.

headline: A sharp answer to Platt
summary: Roosevelt sees Leupp and Crumpacker in the evening and fires off an angry reply to Senator Platt, who had protested one of his appointments.

headline: Coinage talks
summary: Roosevelt meets Treasury Secretary Shaw, R. B. Armstrong and Representative Boutell about a standard for coinage.

headline: Navy coaling stations in Cuba
summary: Roosevelt approves the agreement giving the U.S. Navy coaling stations in Cuba. He dines with the Aldriches, Pattersons, O. H. Platts and Jusserands and hosts a German singing society concert. Letters urge Lodge to hurry the Philippine tariff cut and explain his Southern appointments to editor Clark Howell.

headline: Feuding with Platt over New York jobs
summary: Callers include Cummins, Luke Wright and Foraker, and Roosevelt lunches with Sargent and others. He writes Platt over a disagreement on New York posts, and Aldrich and Cannon on the Philippine tariff and Cuban reciprocity.

headline: A Wesley bicentennial at Carnegie Hall
summary: After morning meetings, Roosevelt dashes to New York City to speak at Carnegie Hall on the 200th anniversary of John Wesley's birth, then returns to Washington. He asks Speaker Henderson whether the House can pass a resolution letting the amended Cuban treaty take effect once the Senate approves it.

headline: A thousand Daughters of the Revolution
summary: Roosevelt urges Congress to pass the Philippine tariff bill and holds Cabinet. In the afternoon his sister Bamie arrives with the Griscoms, and he receives a delegation of 1,000 women from the D.A.R.

headline: Seth Bullock comes to dinner
summary: Roosevelt hosts a lively dinner with Harriet Blaine Beale presiding because Edith is ill; guests include Root, Justice Holmes, Seth Bullock, Eugene Ware and William Allen White. He tells Platt he will name his judge despite Platt's objections. Chartran's painting of Edith becomes her official portrait.

headline: Retelling the big dinner
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Root, Lodge and Turner and dines with C. S. Mellen and the Woodruffs. He writes Ted all about the previous night's dinner party.

headline: Five dogs for Yellowstone
summary: Roosevelt confers with William Allen White, Leupp, Shaw and Cannon. He writes John Pitcher that he wants five dogs for his Yellowstone trip.

headline: Leupp and Burrows
summary: Roosevelt meets Francis Leupp and Senator Julius Burrows.

headline: One Congress ends, another begins
summary: The 57th Congress closes and the 58th opens with Republican majorities of 57 to 33 in the Senate and 208 to 178 in the House. Roosevelt spends the morning at the Capitol and dines with the Hays. He writes Hay on Romania's Jews, thanks Speaker Henderson, and tells Booker T. Washington he will resubmit Crum's name.

headline: Special session on the treaties
summary: Congress meets in special session, and Roosevelt asks it to ratify the Panama and Cuban treaties. Mrs. Taft and Seymour Edwards join him for lunch and receives the Argentine minister. He writes lumberman Frederick Weyerhaeuser hoping to talk forestry.

headline: Chief Joseph, and captains to sea
summary: Senators Hanna, Platt, Hale, Cullom and Lodge call, and Roosevelt discusses the Nez Perce leader Chief Joseph with Colonel Scott. He tells Navy Secretary Moody to send Captains Bradford and O'Neil to sea right away. Baseball's two big leagues agree on a joint rulebook.

headline: Howells takes aim; Burroughs invited west
summary: In Harper's Weekly, William Dean Howells criticizes Roosevelt's praise of big families. Roosevelt writes John Burroughs that he liked his piece on real and sham natural history, talks over the errors in animal stories, and invites him along to Yellowstone.

headline: A quiet Sunday
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; the record notes nothing else for the day.

headline: Exploring the Philippines
summary: Roosevelt meets Representatives Calderhead and Hill about coming finance bills and sees Hanna. He writes Charles Walcott about a broad plan to explore the Philippines and approves a new bankers' committee.

headline: Post Office scandal: Tyner asked to quit
summary: After Cabinet and lunch with Cannon, Roosevelt writes about the Post Office corruption probe, noting that Tyner has been told to resign. He also tells labor leader John Mitchell whom he has put in charge of the new commerce department and the Bureau of Corporations.

headline: General Funston calls
summary: Among the day's callers is General Frederick Funston.

headline: J. P. Morgan, and sweating over treaties
summary: Roosevelt names a committee under C. D. Walcott to study the executive departments and meets J. P. Morgan in the afternoon. He hosts a senators' dinner, and writes Hay that he is straining every nerve to get the Cuba and Panama treaties confirmed.

headline: No compromise on Alaska
summary: A commission led by Charles D. Walcott is named to look at the government's scientific work. Roosevelt sees Speck von Sternberg and sends Taft his sizing-up of Republican leaders in Congress. He tells Root there will be no compromise on principle over Alaska, and Hay that Americans will never let a European power control an American republic.

headline: Pelican Island: the first bird refuge
summary: Roosevelt sets aside Pelican Island in Florida as a federal bird reservation, the first of its kind, and five irrigation projects take shape in Montana, Arizona, Nevada, Nebraska, Wyoming and Colorado. He lunches with George Ward and Curtis Guild and is glad Burroughs will join him in Yellowstone.

headline: Charting the Caribbean coasts
summary: Roosevelt confers with Senators Spooner, Thomas Platt and Beveridge. He asks Root for information on the coastlines of the Caribbean nations.

headline: His favorite hymn
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Major Scott, and Secretary Shaw comes to dinner and stays the night. He tells Thomas Stewart his favorite hymn is 'How Firm a Foundation' and that he greatly admires 'The Battle Hymn of the Republic,' and asks Beveridge to talk trusts and tariff.

headline: Senate ratifies the canal treaty
summary: The Senate approves the Hay-Herrán treaty without amendment, opening the way for a canal across Panama. Roosevelt chooses Root, Lodge and George Turner as the American members of the Alaska boundary tribunal and writes each of them about his stance.

headline: Dinner for the coal strike commission
summary: Roosevelt confers with Hopkins and O. H. Platt and gives a dinner for the members of the coal strike commission. He writes Benjamin Ide Wheeler that he enjoyed his critique of Herodotus on the Battle of Salamis.

headline: Special session adjourns
summary: The special session of Congress ends. Joe Bishop and Grant La Farge come to dinner and stay over, and Roosevelt meets five senators late at night. He writes Taft about the Philippine friars and repeats that he wants him at the War Department when Root leaves.

headline: Niece Eleanor at dinner
summary: Roosevelt has George C. Lee Jr. and George Holls to breakfast and lunches with Lyman Abbott. At dinner his niece Eleanor joins the Winthrop Chanlers, the British ambassador and Lady Herbert, Lieutenant McCoy and Major Howze. He sends Ted family news.

headline: Coal miners get a raise
summary: The coal strike commission's report is published: miners win a 10 percent pay increase, but the United Mine Workers are not recognized. Roosevelt meets Archbishop Ireland and General Wood, and in the evening talks Indian policy with Commissioner Jones. Edith writes that she feels herself again and may ride.

headline: Caught in the Odell-Platt feud
summary: Roosevelt sees Stranahan and lunches with Haskell and Woodbury Kane. He drafts two letters to Governor Odell on the Odell-Platt fight over New York patronage, sending only one, tells David Thompson no one has asked him to seek an American cardinal, and defends the Byrne appointment to George Kennan.

headline: Admirals to inspect the canal route
summary: Roosevelt lunches with General and Mrs. Wood and Charles Francis. He names Admiral John Walker and two others to survey the Canal Zone in Panama, and thanks Judge George Gray for the coal strike commission's work.

headline: Riding at Fort Myer
summary: Roosevelt talks with J. M. Thurston about the Louisiana Purchase Exposition, then he and Edith go to the riding hall at Fort Myer.

headline: Speaking to the foresters at Pinchot's
summary: Roosevelt meets Hay and Root, Justice White and G. Minot Weld, then speaks that evening to the Society of American Foresters at Gifford Pinchot's home. He commends the National Economic League to Clarkson and urges William Crum, his Black appointee in Charleston, to run his office beyond reproach.

headline: Dewey's boast about the Kaiser
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Amory Gardner and Cushing. Admiral Dewey tells the New York Herald that the recent Venezuela episode taught the Kaiser a lesson.

headline: Dewey called on the carpet
summary: Roosevelt summons Admiral Dewey and reprimands him for his remarks about the Kaiser, and warns Admiral Taylor that such talk could harm the country. He tells Joe Bishop he means to stay clear of the quarrel between Platt and Odell, and writes John Clarke about Clarkson's plan for Republican clubs.

headline: Pinchot brings the lumbermen
summary: In the evening Secretary Cortelyou and Gifford Pinchot bring several lumbermen to see Roosevelt, followed by O. P. Austin and Frederick Holls.

headline: Too big a people to be careless
summary: Roosevelt lunches with James Barnes, Root, the Lodges, Harriet Blaine Beale, and the Holmeses. He writes Admiral Dewey that the nation cannot afford loose talk.

headline: Burroughs arrives; portraits finished
summary: John Burroughs comes to stay the night before the western trip. Sargent and Chartran finish their portraits of Roosevelt, who prefers Sargent's. He asks C. Hart Merriam about reports on western Indian tribes and writes Villard on the Philippine atrocity inquiry. Edith and three children set off on the Mayflower.

headline: The great western tour begins
summary: Roosevelt sets out at 9 a.m. on his long swing through the West, speaking in Baltimore and Harrisburg and stopping at Altoona. Leaving the White House, he writes Corinne that it feels odd without the children and hopes her hand is mending.

headline: Chicago: honorary degrees and the Monroe Doctrine
summary: In Chicago Roosevelt is made a Doctor of Laws by the University of Chicago and also honored at Northwestern. That evening he argues for a bigger navy and defends the Monroe Doctrine, crediting Germany and Britain for keeping their word in Venezuela.

headline: Wisconsin legislature and Milwaukee merchants
summary: Roosevelt addresses the Wisconsin legislature in Madison and speaks at a merchants' dinner in Milwaukee.

headline: Farmers and hired hands at trackside
summary: Roosevelt speaks at La Crosse and St. Paul, talking from the train to crowds he describes to Hay as sinewy farmers, townsfolk, veterans and children.

headline: Sunday in Sioux Falls
summary: In Sioux Falls, Roosevelt worships at a modest German Lutheran church and also attends a Dutch Reformed service. Afterward he covers 20 miles in the company of Dr. Rixey and Seth Bullock.

headline: Brass bands across South Dakota
summary: Roosevelt crisscrosses South Dakota, speaking at Sioux Falls, Yankton, Mitchell and Aberdeen, often from the back of the train. Local bands greeted him with 'Hail to the Chief' as if it were a fresh idea.

headline: Back in the Badlands
summary: At Fargo Roosevelt talks about the Army and the Philippine islands, and in Bismarck he attends a barbecue of a whole roasted ox. At Mandan, Sylvane and Joe Ferris climb aboard, and at Dickinson and Medora old neighbors remember the young 'four-eyed dude' of ranching days.

headline: Into Yellowstone
summary: Roosevelt finishes his Dakota visit and reaches Yellowstone National Park.

headline: Elk everywhere; a win in Northern Securities
summary: Entering the park from Gardiner, Montana, Roosevelt begins his camping trip and sees great numbers of elk. It is Archie's ninth birthday. In St. Paul, the federal circuit court rules for the government in the Northern Securities case.

headline: An 18-mile walk alone
summary: Still camping in Yellowstone, Roosevelt sets off by himself on an 18-mile hike.

headline: Camp moves to Cottonwood Creek
summary: The camping party shifts to a second camp at Cottonwood Creek. Edith writes Aunt Lizzie that the West is the sole corner of his domain where her husband can get away from reporters.

headline: Easter, Tower Falls and 3,000 elk
summary: On Easter Sunday the party moves camp to Tower Falls and sees a herd of some 3,000 elk. Edith writes her sister Emily that Alice has named her skinny green garter snake 'Emily Spinach' and carries it to fashionable parties.

headline: Algonquin rides the White House elevator
summary: Roosevelt is still camping in Yellowstone. In Washington Edith presides over the Easter Egg Roll, a custom she dislikes for what it does to the lawn. Archie is down with whooping cough and measles at once, and Quentin, with an usher's help, brings the pony Algonquin upstairs in the elevator to cheer him.

headline: Pygmy owl and mountain sheep
summary: In camp, Roosevelt and John Burroughs spot a pygmy owl, and the party watches mountain sheep while Roosevelt still has shaving lather on his face. The group naps on the rocks near Tower Falls canyon; others fish while he walks alone.

headline: Counting Yellowstone's elk
summary: Roosevelt has spent a week studying Yellowstone's elk. In a single day he counted 3,000 to 4,000 of the roughly 15,000 he estimates live in the park, where cougars are their only predator.

headline: Deer on the parade ground
summary: At Fort Yellowstone, Roosevelt writes Merriam that game is more abundant than on his visit twelve years before. He tells Ethel how tame the wild animals are, describing a dozen deer that wander onto the parade ground at the evening bugle.

headline: Among the geysers
summary: Roosevelt tours Yellowstone's geyser country; Burroughs later described him there.

headline: Norris and the Fountain Hotel
summary: Roosevelt and Burroughs stop at the Norris hotel, then ride on to the Fountain Hotel.

headline: A mouse for Merriam
summary: Roosevelt fishes in the afternoon and skins a mouse he trapped, saving it for naturalist C. Hart Merriam.

headline: Skiing near the Canyon Hotel
summary: From the Canyon Hotel, Roosevelt and Burroughs head out on skis across the snow.

headline: Tall tales with Hell Roaring Bill Jones
summary: Roosevelt trades stories with 'Hell Roaring' Bill Jones. Burroughs later recorded much of the President's campfire talk.

headline: Letters from Fort Yellowstone
summary: Back at Fort Yellowstone near Cinnabar, Roosevelt catches up on mail: praise for Taft and regret over the sugar beet bill, a note to Cleveland Dodge on trusts, more park observations for Merriam with a nudge to produce the standard work on the continent's mammals, and word to Hay on the Danish islands talks.

headline: Tyner dismissed
summary: Roosevelt is at Cinnabar, Montana, as Assistant Attorney General Tyner is dismissed amid the Post Office inquiry.

headline: Cornerstone of Yellowstone's arch
summary: At Gardiner, Roosevelt lays the cornerstone for a gateway to Yellowstone, then leaves for Livingston. He writes George Bird Grinnell about a Forest and Stream piece by 'Hermit' that attacked Burroughs's essay on fake nature stories.

headline: Pheasants and a smoky fireplace
summary: Roosevelt stops at towns in South Dakota and Wyoming and speaks across Nebraska. He writes Thomas Carter that grouse are declining and he likes the idea of bringing in pheasants, and tells Charles McKim the White House dining room fireplace must be fixed this summer because it will not draw.

headline: Sunday in Grand Island
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday at Grand Island, Nebraska.

headline: Good citizenship in Omaha
summary: Roosevelt speaks his way across Nebraska, from Hastings to Lincoln, and gives an evening address on good citizenship in Omaha. He writes Butler unhappily about the Odell-Platt feud, Bishop on the tariff, and Payne about the Post Office probe and how the press is covering it.

headline: Iowa, and a win on the franchise tax
summary: Traveling with Albert Cummins and Treasury Secretary Shaw, Roosevelt gives speeches in Des Moines, Ottumwa and other Iowa towns. He writes Knox that he is delighted the Supreme Court upheld New York's franchise tax, a law he forced through as governor.

headline: Good roads in St. Louis
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Hannibal, to a good-roads gathering in St. Louis, and in Quincy, Illinois. It is Corinne's 21st wedding anniversary.

headline: Dedicating the World's Fair
summary: Before 40,000 people in St. Louis, Roosevelt dedicates the Louisiana Purchase Exposition buildings, then leaves for Kansas City with Root and Butler. Gunton's Magazine comes out against his plan to lower tariffs.

headline: Through the two Kansas Citys to Topeka
summary: Roosevelt stops in Kansas City on both the Missouri and Kansas sides and in Lawrence, then speaks in Topeka that evening.

headline: Across the Kansas prairie
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Abilene, Salina, Ellsworth and other Kansas towns, and telegraphs Hay about the American fleet in French waters.

headline: A badger named Josiah
summary: At a packed church in tiny Sharon Springs, Kansas, a little girl offers Roosevelt a badger freshly trapped by her brother Josiah. His companions include Burton, Long, Butler, Warren and Foulke. In Washington, Edith dines at Henry Adams's farewell party before he sails for Europe.

headline: Supper off a chuck wagon in a top hat
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Denver and heads for Colorado Springs. Cowboys from a roundup ride in with their chuck wagon, and he sits on its tailboard eating range food in top hat and tails. He writes Hay about whether Grover Cleveland might seek a third term in 1904.

headline: Santa Fe and a Rough Rider reunion
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Santa Fe, which he calls a strange old desert civilization, and in Albuquerque, where old Rough Rider comrades, Captain William Llewellyn among them, climb aboard.

headline: Standing at the Grand Canyon
summary: Roosevelt sees the Grand Canyon and is overwhelmed, calling it beautiful, terrible and unearthly. He speaks, visits a miners' camp with Alexander Brodie, Butler and Dr. Rixey, then leaves for California.

headline: Irrigation talk in Redlands
summary: Crossing the Mojave Desert, Roosevelt stops at Barstow, speaks in Redlands about irrigation and forests, pauses at San Bernardino, and spends the night in Riverside.

headline: Flowers everywhere in Los Angeles
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Claremont and Pasadena and spends the night in Los Angeles, where flowers are everywhere he looks.

headline: Ventura and Santa Barbara
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Ventura and Santa Barbara.

headline: A beach ride at Del Monte
summary: At Del Monte, Roosevelt visits with Secretary Moody and Benjamin Ide Wheeler. He tells Ethel about a gallop along the beach among seals and seabirds, notes that western women ride astride, and writes Kermit about Josiah the badger, Archie about Bill the lizard, and Quentin about the trip.

headline: Santa Cruz, and irrigation politics
summary: Roosevelt stops at Pajaro and Watsonville, speaks in Santa Cruz, and heads for San Jose. He writes Pinchot that California's George Maxwell opposes the irrigation plans, and Payne about the postal inquiry.

headline: Forests at Stanford, a parade in San Francisco
summary: At Palo Alto, Roosevelt visits Stanford's president David Starr Jordan and speaks there on saving the forests. He lunches with H. T. Scott, rides in a San Francisco parade, and attends a citizens' committee dinner.

headline: Breaking ground for McKinley in Golden Gate Park
summary: In San Francisco, Roosevelt attends a reception and a military review and breaks ground in Golden Gate Park for a monument to McKinley, then speaks that evening. He writes Hay about trouble in Manchuria and Cuba, and Moody about Navy marksmanship awards.

headline: Honorary degree at Berkeley
summary: Roosevelt speaks in San Francisco, receives an honorary Doctor of Laws from the University of California, and speaks in Berkeley and Oakland.

headline: Camping with John Muir among the sequoias
summary: Roosevelt rides by way of Raymond, Berenda and Grub Gulch to meet John Muir at the Mariposa Grove in Yosemite, and the two camp beneath the giant sequoias.

headline: Snow among the silver firs
summary: In Yosemite, Roosevelt and Muir are caught in a snowstorm high among silver firs near the cliff edge.

headline: A night facing El Capitan
summary: Roosevelt sleeps out at Bridalveil Fall in Yosemite Valley, facing El Capitan with waterfalls roaring on both sides.

headline: Leaving Yosemite
summary: Roosevelt heads out through Wawona, Raymond and Berenda. The Government Printing Office drops William Miller from his post as assistant foreman. Roosevelt asks Hanna to meet him around the June 6 wedding of Hanna's daughter Ruth.

headline: Thanking Muir
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Carson City and Reno. He thanks John Muir for their days in Yosemite, asks Hitchcock to enlarge California's forest reserves, writes Allison about speaking on the tariff, and Root about wartime troop-transport blunders.

headline: Northern California toward Oregon
summary: Roosevelt speaks at stops across northern California on his way to Oregon.

headline: Lewis and Clark cornerstone in Portland
summary: Roosevelt arrives in Portland and lays the cornerstone of the Lewis and Clark monument. He asks Hay to check with Root and Cortelyou about whether he should give $100 toward relief for Russia's Jews, and writes William Richards about Oregon's forest reserves.

headline: Russian mendacity
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Olympia and Tacoma. He fumes to Hay about Russia's refusal to open Manchurian ports and says he might accept a German state in Brazil. He sends a farewell note to departing ambassador Holleben and writes Taft about money matters behind his choices.

headline: Puget Sound and Hanna's telegram
summary: In Seattle, Roosevelt cruises Puget Sound and inspects the Bremerton Navy Yard. Hanna wires that he has stopped Ohio Republicans from endorsing Roosevelt early for 1904. Roosevelt appoints William Byrne U.S. Attorney for Delaware and writes Payne about the postal probe and Hanna's move.

headline: Seattle's million
summary: Roosevelt predicts Seattle will one day be a city of a million people, and leaves that evening.

headline: Answering Hanna
summary: Heading east, Roosevelt speaks at Walla Walla, Wallula, Pasco, North Yakima, Ellensburg and Cle Elum. He replies to Hanna that he has asked no one for support, and invites Joe Cannon to join him through Illinois.

headline: Beef Trust ruling
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Spokane and at Harrison and Wallace, Idaho, and stops at Starbuck. Federal prosecutors win the Beef Trust suit.

headline: Butte, and the criminal rich
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Helena and Butte. He tells Clarkson the criminal rich are no better than the criminal poor, sends Bishop and Lodge copies of his telegrams with Hanna, and praises Alice for real service to the country on her Cuba visit.

headline: Admiring Boise
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Pocatello, Shoshone, Glenns Ferry and Mountain Home, and spends the evening in Boise, whose trees, library and homes impress him.

headline: Ranch stories with Seth Bullock
summary: Roosevelt visits Ogden and Salt Lake City with a Rough Rider escort and heads for Laramie, swapping ranching tales with Seth Bullock along the way. He writes Hanna explaining the telegrams and how Hanna's apparent coolness struck him.

headline: A 65-mile ride to Cheyenne
summary: Roosevelt speaks at the University of Wyoming, then rides horseback 65 miles from Laramie to Cheyenne, stopping at the Van Tassell ranch and changing horses five times.

headline: Decoration Day review in Wyoming
summary: On Decoration Day in Wyoming, Roosevelt reviews U.S. Army troops.

headline: Steer roping in Cheyenne
summary: At the Cheyenne fairgrounds Roosevelt watches top-notch steer roping and bronc riding, then heads for Iowa, speaking from the train at Osceola. He thanks Senator Hoar for kind words in Hoar's autobiography.

headline: Speaking about the flood at Denison
summary: At Denison, Iowa, Roosevelt speaks about the recent flood. Senators Allison and Dolliver and Treasury Secretary Shaw join his party.

headline: Nine Illinois speeches
summary: Roosevelt gives nine speeches across Illinois, among them Freeport, Aurora, Joliet, Lexington and Bloomington.

headline: At Lincoln's tomb
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Lincoln, at Lincoln's tomb in Springfield, and in Decatur and Danville, then leaves for Indianapolis.

headline: Home with a badger
summary: The western tour ends with stops at Pittsburgh and Altoona. Roosevelt brings Josiah the badger home for Archie, is greeted at Washington's station, visits John Hay, and is back in the White House by 9 p.m.

headline: The children cheer Josiah
summary: Back at his desk, Roosevelt holds Cabinet and goes over the postal investigation with Root and Payne, then sees the British ambassador and Leupp. He tells Lodge the children have given the young badger a wild welcome.

headline: Dedicating Grace Reformed Church
summary: Roosevelt speaks at the dedication of Grace Reformed Church, at the corner of 15th and O, then lunches with Ambassador Joseph H. Choate.

headline: Philippine talk over lunch
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Root, Henry Taft and Wayne MacVeagh, and the talk turns to the Philippines.

headline: Taft agrees to run the War Department
summary: Roosevelt leaves at 3 p.m. for Cleveland with Alice, the Cowleses and Loeb, stopping at Harrisburg and York. He writes Taft, who has agreed to succeed Root as Secretary of War, that he wants to live simply as President and will gladly return to plain living afterward.

headline: Ruth Hanna's wedding
summary: Roosevelt reaches Cleveland for the wedding of Ruth Hanna and Medill McCormick, then returns to Washington. In Morenci, Arizona, miners strike, and the territorial governor asks the President for help.

headline: Troops to Morenci; 'ridiculous' Rev. Long
summary: Roosevelt orders Regulars stationed in Colorado down to Arizona to keep order at the Morenci strike. He tells Henry Taft he wants Will in the Cabinet rather than as Vice President, writes Root about Taft's acceptance, and tells Burroughs that nature writer Rev. William J. Long is ridiculous.

headline: Kishinev with the Russian ambassador
summary: Roosevelt meets Russian Ambassador Cassini about the Kishinev massacre of Jews and talks trusts with Judge Grosscup. He and Edith are dinner guests of the Hays, and he orders Payne to investigate New York Postmaster Van Cott.

headline: Platt, Cromwell and the canal
summary: On a crowded day, Roosevelt breakfasts with Curtis Guild, lunches with Senator Platt on New York politics and a new county chairman, and talks Panama with William Nelson Cromwell. He tells Lowell he will be friendly toward Canada and writes Higginson on currency. Speaker-to-be Joe Cannon opposes his program.

headline: Moody and Hale call
summary: Navy Secretary Moody and Senator Eugene Hale visit the White House on Sunday.

headline: B'nai B'rith on Kishinev; song in Baltimore
summary: Roosevelt and Hay meet B'nai B'rith's executive council about the Kishinev massacre. After lunch with German and American guests and receptions for three ambassadors, he goes to the Baltimore Sängerfest with Speck von Sternberg and speaks about German immigrants. He writes Coubertin on physical education.

headline: Commencement at the University of Virginia
summary: At Charlottesville Roosevelt speaks at the University of Virginia's commencement on citizenship and a strong Navy, and visits Monticello before returning to Washington. He tells Leonard Wood the Senate is balking at his promotion to major general.

headline: Backing miner-operator agreements
summary: Roosevelt publicly endorses agreements between coal miners and mine owners. He lunches with Goddard, Moody, Governor Hunt and Captain Davis, dines with George Sheldon, and writes Root about General Wilson's speech attacking Wood and McKinley.

headline: Speeding up the postal fraud cases
summary: Roosevelt issues an executive order to hurry the postal fraud prosecutions. He meets Booker T. Washington at noon, sees Cecil Lyon, and lunches with Shaffer, Tracy and Ware.

headline: Defending the Post Office record
summary: After Cabinet and a midday meal with Hamilton Fish and Stranahan, Roosevelt has Byrnes and Mellen to dinner. Letters ask George Gray to speak for him on the Fourth in Wilkes-Barre, defend his policies to tariff leader Charles Moore, stand up for Payne, and tell John Wanamaker the postal corruption predates his administration.

headline: French and Chinese delegations
summary: Roosevelt hears from French and Chinese delegations and sees Payne.

headline: Thanking Perkins
summary: Attorney General Knox calls in the evening. Roosevelt thanks George W. Perkins for his help in the Ohio endorsement affair, which Mellen had told him about.

headline: Prosecute the postal offenders
summary: Roosevelt tells Knox the Post Office wrongdoers must be prosecuted and takes responsibility for Payne's actions amid heavy press criticism. He writes Lyman Abbott about peonage of Black workers in Georgia and Russia's stance in Manchuria, where Russia refuses to open the ports.

headline: No presidential name for a Jerusalem model
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Speyer and Knox and has John McCall to dinner and overnight, with Cortelyou joining them. He writes John Proctor about irregularities at the Washington post office and wires Joseph Burton that he refuses to endorse a for-profit model of Jerusalem planned for the 1904 fair.

headline: Leupp sent to Indian Territory
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Melville Stone and Ware and dines with Benjamin Ide Wheeler, the Hays, the Jusserands and Wayne MacVeagh; Wheeler stays the night. He asks Francis Leupp to serve as an impartial investigator of the Oklahoma Indian reservations.

headline: Supper at Great Falls
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Crane, Cooley, Proctor and Major Carson, then dines at Great Falls, Virginia, with Pinchot, Garfield and Proctor. Letters touch the postal probe, Ray Stannard Baker's articles, the press, and a false coal-strike story. Hanna will not give up the national chairmanship.

headline: Lunch for Sir Thomas Lipton
summary: Roosevelt hosts a lunch for yachtsman Sir Thomas Lipton with Moody, Andrew D. White, General Corbin, Hanna and others, and hears Perkins on Wall Street's view of his finance bills. He gives Perkins the pen that signed the Commerce and Labor act and spends the evening at Hay's with Douglas Robinson.

headline: Summer begins at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt travels to Oyster Bay and dedicates a cannon on the village green.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

headline: No delay on Alaska
summary: Lyman Abbott comes to lunch and Joe Bishop stays the night. Roosevelt tells Hay the Alaska boundary must be settled without delay, and writes Platt on New York appointments.

headline: Kermit off to hunt with Bullock
summary: Wilson Bissell, Governor Hunt and Senator Long come to lunch. Kermit leaves for the Black Hills to hunt with Seth Bullock.

headline: Angry at Russia over the Kishinev petition
summary: Sagamore Hill fills with guests, among them niece Eleanor, Gifford Pinchot and Beekman Winthrop, and Beveridge comes to dinner. Roosevelt writes Francis Loomis about a petition to Russia protesting the Kishinev massacre, and tells Hay he is angered by Russia's impertinence.

headline: How to handle the petition
summary: General Joseph Wheeler is among the callers. Roosevelt asks Loomis how the government should now proceed with the Kishinev petition.

headline: Quiet day at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Opening the Pacific cable
summary: On the Fourth of July Roosevelt speaks at Huntington, Long Island, to celebrate the newly completed cable across the Pacific, and sends a message across it to Governor Taft in Manila. He defends his irrigation policy to Ray Stannard Baker and tells George Holls he will act in the national interest whatever foreign powers think.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Badgers and nature fakers
summary: Roosevelt writes John Burroughs, setting a Friday meeting and musing on Josiah the badger, animal instinct, and writers who falsify nature.

headline: Hay at Sagamore Hill
summary: Secretary Hay, Winthrop Chanler and Grant La Farge are guests. Over lunch with Hanna, Fairbanks and others, Roosevelt and Hay take up Alaska, Manchuria and the petition to the Czar on behalf of Russia's Jews. He tells Seth Bullock that Ted and his cousin George will reach Deadwood on August 20 to hunt.

headline: Don't resign, take a holiday
summary: Winthrop Chanler, Grant La Farge and Massachusetts Governor Murray Crane are guests. Roosevelt urges Pension Commissioner Eugene Ware to take a vacation instead of resigning.

headline: Up the Hudson on the Sylph
summary: After dinner Roosevelt and Edith board the Sylph for a cruise up the Hudson. He thanks Rollo Ogden for the Evening Post's position on Black Americans and his Southern policy.

headline: Visiting Burroughs at Slabsides
summary: From the Hudson, Roosevelt calls on John Burroughs at his cabin, Slabsides, in West Park, New York, then returns to Oyster Bay.

headline: New York callers
summary: Roosevelt receives Hiscock, Hendricks, Philbin, Dryden and Kean at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Root on promotions and Alaska
summary: Secretary of War Root is a guest. He and Roosevelt discuss Army promotions, the Kishinev petition and the Alaska boundary.

headline: No union shop at the Printing Office
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Root, Archbishop Farley, Jacob Riis and others, and appoints Robert Shaw Oliver Assistant Secretary of War. In two letters to Cortelyou he refuses to let the Government Printing Office become a closed union shop.

headline: Miller to be reinstated
summary: Roosevelt meets Leo Levi, Simon Wolf and Oscar Straus about the Kishinev petition, sees Albert Shaw, and dines with Judge Sherman. He tells Cortelyou that W. A. Miller must be reinstated at the Printing Office even though he is not a union member, and sends Hay a cable for Russia.

headline: A family day aboard the Sylph
summary: Roosevelt spends the day on the Sylph with his family, Treasury Secretary Shaw and Jacob Riis, and sees Bonaparte, Ray Stannard Baker and Herman Kohlsaat. Bamie, Will and little Sheffield Cowles are guests. He tells Holls that Cassini never officially refused the petition.

headline: Not one man jack
summary: Lodge visits to discuss finance bills and Alaska, and Douglas and Corinne Robinson are guests. Roosevelt asks Hay to cable St. Petersburg, orders Payne to look into the letter carriers' convention, and warns Clarkson that Printing Office strikers would never work for the government again while he is President.

headline: A statement on currency reform
summary: Roosevelt releases a statement on currency reform legislation. Nicholas Murray Butler calls, and Roosevelt forwards to Root some praise Taft wrote about him.

headline: Irritated over Manchuria
summary: Seth Low, George Meyer and W. L. Ward call, and Butler and the Clifford Richardsons are guests. Roosevelt tells Hay he does not mind the Russians knowing how irritated he is over Manchuria, and writes Charles Emory Smith about his clash with Proctor.

headline: Congratulating Hamlin Garland on a baby
summary: Dr. Alexander Lambert and Nicholas Murray Butler visit and stay for lunch. Roosevelt congratulates Hamlin Garland on his new baby and lays out his belief in large families.

headline: Barry jumps the line
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Whitelaw Reid and his wife. He informs Colonel Thomas Barry that he now outranks more senior colonels as a newly made brigadier general.

headline: Bracing for a fight over Wood
summary: Titus Sheard calls. Roosevelt writes Ebenezer Hill on finance, warns Root that Wood's promotion may bring an ugly fight, and complains to Joe Bishop about Boston Herald falsehoods on the McSweeney case.

headline: Platt, Frick and a crowd of visitors
summary: A stream of visitors reaches Sagamore Hill, among them Senator Platt, Henry Clay Frick, Gifford Pinchot and Charlemagne Tower, and Roosevelt goes over finance bills with Cannon. He tells a congressman he listens to party bosses only selectively, and writes on Indian affairs and money matters.

headline: A 2 a.m. ride to Sayville
summary: At 2 in the morning Roosevelt sets out on horseback for Sayville, Long Island, to stay with his uncle, Robert B. Roosevelt, and lunches there with J. E. Roosevelt.

headline: Answering Bloomingdale on Kishinev
summary: Roosevelt returns to Oyster Bay and talks Navy growth with Secretary Moody. He replies to Emanuel Bloomingdale's letter on the persecution of Russian Jews and writes Whitelaw Reid on the Monroe Doctrine and Knox on lynching.

headline: No arbitration on Alaska
summary: Roosevelt discusses Puerto Rico with Samuel Lindsay. He tells Justice Holmes there will be no arbitration of the Alaska boundary, asks William Round not to publish an 18-year-old letter of his about Indians, and tells Oswald Villard he was advised against promoting Captain John J. Pershing.

headline: Clergy at lunch
summary: Miss Helen Buchanan is a guest, and Bishop McFaul and Father Belford come to lunch.

headline: A West Point appointment
summary: John Barrett calls at 10 a.m. Roosevelt writes S. Weir Mitchell about a West Point appointment for Mitchell's son.

headline: Kemeys for the World's Fair
summary: Roosevelt asks Augustus Saint-Gaudens to see that western sculptor Edward Kemeys has work shown at the 1904 fair in St. Louis.

headline: Missing Root
summary: Roosevelt talks finance with W. D. Washburn and lunches with Frank Higgins. He writes about friar land sales in the Philippines and tells Hay that Root will be missed, but that Hay is one man he could not do without.

headline: Postal frauds with Payne
summary: Roosevelt and Payne go over the postal fraud cases, and John R. Proctor is a guest. Letters cover the Port of New York, Father Hendrick's appointment as a bishop in the Philippines, the Panama Canal Commission, an article by Andrew D. White, and family life.

headline: Printing Office inquiry
summary: J. R. Proctor and Agriculture Secretary Wilson call; Roosevelt lunches with Woodbury Kane and reviews the Government Printing Office investigation with Proctor. Wilson stays the night, and nephew Stewart Douglas Robinson is a guest. He writes Archbishop Ireland about agitation for the friars in the Philippines.

headline: Night camping trip with the boys by rowboat
summary: Roosevelt heads out after dark to camp with Kermit, Archie and their cousins Philip, Oliver and Nicholas, the party filling two rowboats. His letters that day touch the Government Printing Office row, Leonard Wood's contested promotion and Seth Low's mayoral bid.

headline: Sunday visit from Bob Ferguson
summary: A quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill; the guest book records Bob Ferguson.

headline: Praise for Saint-Gaudens's Sherman statue
summary: Roosevelt writes Augustus Saint-Gaudens to admire his new equestrian statue of General Sherman, newly unveiled in Manhattan.

headline: Bareback ride leaves the President raw
summary: After a run of callers, among them Hamilton Fish and Melville Stone, Roosevelt and Ted ride bareback for an hour and a half, Ted on Renown and his father on Bleistein. The President comes home with the skin rubbed off the insides of his legs.

headline: Root confers on gloves and the General Staff
summary: Elihu Root comes out to talk over the new General Staff law and the Littauer-Lyon glove contract affair. Kermit and Philip set off to camp overnight but bad weather drives them home.

headline: Edith's birthday with cake and haybarn games
summary: Edith turns 42, and the appointment book is marked to keep visitors away. Ethel hemstitched handkerchiefs and wrapped the gifts, opened at breakfast; Kermit and Ethel carried in a cake at lunch, and the whole family spent the afternoon tumbling in the haybarn. Root also confers on the Alaska boundary.

headline: New German ambassador presents credentials
summary: Roosevelt receives Speck von Sternberg, who formally presents his papers as Germany's ambassador. Senator Heyburn, Millard, Howland and Regis Post also call, and Dr. Alexander Lambert is a guest.

headline: Miles retires as Alaska warning reaches London
summary: General Nelson Miles leaves the Army. In London, Colonial Secretary Chamberlain tells Prime Minister Balfour that Justice Holmes delivered a private letter from Roosevelt: the President agreed to arbitrate the Alaska boundary only to keep peace with Britain, and would occupy the American claim himself if the result fell short.

headline: Long letter to Hay recounting the Western tour
summary: Roosevelt sits down and writes John Hay a full account of his 1903 Western trip, stocked with stories from the road.

headline: Letters on the Cuban treaty session
summary: Roosevelt writes Senator Fairbanks about calling Congress back to act on the Cuban treaty, and Senator Hanna about the Outlook's Howland. Meanwhile his friend Jacob Riis is at work on a biography.

headline: Knox briefs him on glove and postal cases
summary: Attorney General Knox comes to discuss the glove contract case and the Post Office frauds. Bishop O'Gorman calls, and at three Howland arrives with a photographer.

headline: Colombia's senate rejects the canal treaty
summary: Roosevelt sees Jacob Riis, then spends the whole night with Senators Allison, Spooner, O. H. Platt and Aldrich hammering out a currency bill. Far away, Colombia's congress turns down the Hay-Herran Treaty, which would have paid $10 million in gold plus $250,000 a year for a canal zone in Panama.

headline: Ethel turns eleven; canal outlook murky
summary: Ethel's eleventh birthday. Roosevelt admits to Senator Morgan that he cannot see how the isthmus question will end, and presses Joe Cannon for congressional action on Cuban reciprocity. The Wall Street scare is easing.

headline: Crowded day of cabinet callers
summary: Treasury Secretary Shaw, Senator Cullom, Interior Secretary Hitchcock, John G. Carlisle, Lauterbach and Bishop Rooker all call. At noon a Mr. Hewitt photographs Ted, and Joseph Bucklin Bishop stays for dinner and the night.

headline: Mayflower officers call; Panama restless
summary: Captain Cowles settles in for the weekend and Monday's naval review. Roosevelt lunches with Robert Shaw Oliver, receives the Mayflower's officers at six, and hosts Captain Brownson overnight. From Bogota the American minister warns Hay that Panama's delegates now lean toward independence.

headline: "American Manhood" speech to Holy Name men
summary: Roosevelt speaks on American manhood to Holy Name Society members from Manhattan, Brooklyn and Long Island. Writing Emily Carow, he recounts a family ride and picnic at Jane's Hill with Speck von Sternberg and the children's backyard play, with Ted as George Washington and Quentin as Cupid. Everyone visits the battleship Kearsarge.

headline: Reviewing the fleet off Lloyd's Neck
summary: From the deck of the Kearsarge, Roosevelt reviews the North Atlantic Squadron's Caribbean ships off Lloyd's Neck with Sir Thomas Lipton, Navy Secretary Moody and Admirals Dewey and Taylor, then lunches aboard the Mayflower.

headline: A blank day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: "Jack rabbits" letter on the canal
summary: After callers Kearns and J. H. Sleicher, Roosevelt tells Hay to hold off on the canal for now, but floats building at Panama under the 1846 treaty and scorns the Bogota government as jack rabbits.

headline: Wilcox visits; no youth memoir, please
summary: Ansley Wilcox dines and spends the night. Roosevelt answers criticism for sending no commendation to the retiring General Miles, writes Senator Frye on the special session, and asks Richard Watson Gilder not to publish the story of his boyhood.

headline: Currency talks and a happy childhood
summary: Roosevelt talks currency legislation with Representatives Hill and Babcock, lunches with Governor Odell and dines with Babcock; Cortelyou stays the night. To Gilder he credits his parents for a happy childhood.

headline: Word of Taft's offer leaks
summary: Roosevelt sees G. W. Dunn and lunches with Carter. He writes Hanna that his offer of the War Department to Taft is now public, Platt about the Printing Office inquiry, and banker James Stillman with financial ideas.

headline: Rowing Edith to Lloyd's Neck
summary: Roosevelt rows Edith to the tip of Lloyd's Neck, where they picnic and read, explore a bit, and pull home under an odd, glimmering sunset.

headline: Taft says yes; Root steps down
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie that Taft has taken the War Department, and accepts Elihu Root's resignation with warm praise. He lunches with Hermann Kohlsaat, sees Senator Aldrich, and swipes at the Sun and the Journal.

headline: Wyoming proves too much horse
summary: Roosevelt writes Ted, away hunting, that Kermit has his hands full with the horse Wyoming and off limits to Edith; he rides Bleistein and she Yagenka. Senator Fulton hears about Oregon patronage and a fired Land Office man.

headline: Defending Wood and the currency system
summary: F. C. Travers drops by, as does Thomas Woodlock, a Wall Street Journal man. In letters he tells Bamie the nation's money system is sound overall, warns Cannon about pressure for inflation, and promises Leonard Wood he will keep fighting for his promotion.

headline: Fusionists call; false alarm from Beirut
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts with Jacob Riis, receives New York Fusion leaders and others, and lunches with Ansley Wilcox. The Mediterranean squadron sails for Beirut on reports, later proven false, that the American vice consul has been murdered. He offers Beekman Winthrop a Philippine commission seat.

headline: Hay comes to lunch
summary: John Hay confers with Roosevelt over lunch, and Treasury Secretary Shaw stays the night. Letters go to Bamie, to Joe Bishop on Taft and money, and to James Clarkson about next year's campaign and Herbert Parsons.

headline: Planning the Labor Day speech
summary: Mrs. Alexander Russell and Mrs. Ballington Booth visit. Roosevelt writes Nicholas Murray Butler about what he means to say on Labor Day.

headline: Quiet Sunday at Oyster Bay
summary: Nothing is recorded for the day beyond Roosevelt's presence at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Alice off with the Newport set
summary: After callers including McMackin, Roosevelt confirms Beekman Winthrop's Philippine appointment, tells Shaw he stands behind him and Hanna in Ohio, and writes Jacob Schurman on currency and Canadian trade. Alice is rarely home, spending her days with Newport society.

headline: On righteous and unrighteous war
summary: Roosevelt writes Theodore Brentano about condolences on Pope Leo XIII's passing, and tells Paul d'Estournelles de Constant his views on war and peace with Turkey and Beirut in mind.

headline: Lunch with Beveridge and Finley
summary: Senator Albert Beveridge, John H. Finley and Major Llewellyn come to lunch.

headline: Hunting tales for the little boys
summary: Roosevelt thanks Agriculture Secretary Wilson for advising silence on currency, writes Taft about the War Department and Miles, and tells Lodge about the Printing Office fight. He is reading hunting stories aloud to Archie and Quentin and calls Ethel a perfect little housewife.

headline: Turkey trouble and the fleet
