summary: Roosevelt breakfasts with editor Albert Shaw and sees Hitchcock and Colonel Bingham. He tells Lodge that the Cripple Creek miners' strike tops his worries, and comments on the platform and Taft's Harvard speech.

headline: Sympathy for Japan
summary: Roosevelt sees Civil Service Commissioner Black and others, lunches with Senator Proctor and Yerkes, and writes Richard Harding Davis that his sympathies lie with Japan in its war with Russia.

headline: Visiting Cortelyou's department
summary: Roosevelt drops in on Cortelyou at his Commerce and Labor offices on his final day as secretary. L. F. Payn visits, and Paul Morton stays the night.

headline: A reshuffled Cabinet takes its seats
summary: The Cabinet meets with its new lineup: Moody moves from the Navy to Attorney General in place of Knox, now Pennsylvania's senator; Paul Morton takes the Navy; and Victor Metcalf succeeds Cortelyou, who is running the campaign. Roosevelt talks Panama with John Barrett, and Metcalf stays the night.

headline: Fourth of July picnic by rowboat
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts with Lieutenant Moore and leaves for Oyster Bay. At Sagamore Hill, where William Hunt's Puerto Rico report reaches him, Independence Day guests include his niece Eleanor, Bob Ferguson and Alvord Cooley. He, Edith and Gifford Pinchot spend the whole day picnicking from a rowboat.

headline: Beveridge comes to lunch
summary: Senator Albert Beveridge visits Sagamore Hill and stays for lunch with W. N. Cohen. Gifford Pinchot is a house guest.

headline: Defeat would be a disaster
summary: Writing to Taft from Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt says he cannot predict the fall election, but a Republican loss would harm the country unless the winners adopted every one of his policies.

headline: Writing the acceptance speech
summary: Roosevelt spends the day at Sagamore Hill working on his speech accepting the nomination.

headline: Root picked for governor
summary: Governor Odell and William Barnes come to Sagamore Hill to plan the campaign and choose who should run for governor; they settle on Elihu Root. They stay for lunch, and Joseph Bishop dines and spends the night.

headline: Democrats pick Parker
summary: The Democrats choose New York judge Alton B. Parker as their presidential candidate with West Virginia's Henry G. Davis as his running mate. Roosevelt lunches with cartoonist Homer Davenport, tells Odell he is pleased with the July 8 meeting, and praises Hay's July 6 speech.

headline: Fairbanks visits
summary: His running mate, Charles W. Fairbanks, comes to Sagamore Hill.

headline: Campaign council at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt works over campaign issues with Fairbanks, Bliss and Cortelyou. He refuses Colonel J. F. Smith's resignation in the Philippines, tells Hay the Democrats will skip a currency plank, and vents to Taft about Mrs. Bellamy Storer.

headline: Portrait with the running mate
summary: Pach and Strohmeyer photograph Roosevelt and Fairbanks on the lawn outside his study. The two confer with Cortelyou, and Roosevelt lunches with Governor Hunt. In Chicago, the meat packers' butchers walk out.

headline: Camping down the Sound
summary: After a day on his acceptance speech, Roosevelt takes Kermit, Archie and two friends camping, rowing two boats some eight or ten miles along the Sound and frying steak, chicken and potatoes over a fire. He tells Garfield about a clothes-on point-to-point hike with six boys.

headline: Winning over Cleveland Democrats
summary: Roosevelt lunches with James Sheffield and receives Justin McCarthy. He tells Bliss that Oscar Straus and other Cleveland Democrats back him, hopes Joel Chandler Harris might help his standing in the South, and worries to Lodge about the strikes in Chicago and Colorado.

headline: Platt comes to Oyster Bay
summary: Senator Thomas Platt and Cortelyou confer with Roosevelt about New York politics, and Platt stays for lunch. Roosevelt warns Payne there must be no charge of postal workers meddling in Wisconsin's factional fights.

headline: Butler at Sagamore Hill
summary: Nicholas Murray Butler is a guest. Roosevelt writes Pinchot about filling an Agriculture Department post and answers Governor Odell on electors and his advice for the acceptance speech.

headline: Sunday callers
summary: Nicholas Murray Butler spends time with Roosevelt, and Howard Gould and E. D. Winslow drop in around midday.

headline: The speech goes to Cortelyou
summary: Roosevelt receives musicians' union leaders and confers with Knox and Root. Bamie, her son Sheffield Cowles and Bob Ferguson are guests. He mails Cortelyou the completed acceptance address for a final review.

headline: Colorado labor men call
summary: Roosevelt confers with Root and receives a Colorado labor delegation led by John B. Walsh, plus the Rev. John Chidwick of New York. He keeps at his acceptance speech.

headline: Reviewing the Puerto Rico report
summary: Gifford Pinchot calls. Roosevelt tells William Hunt he has gone over his report on conditions in Puerto Rico and thanks Herman Kohlsaat for advice on revising the speech.

headline: Birds around Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt receives Richard Murphy and Father Pitass of Buffalo's Polish church. He tells Admiral Evans he has read his report on naval wireless, and tells ornithologist Edward Forbush he has seen no decline of birds around Oyster Bay or Washington.

headline: George Bird Grinnell drops by
summary: Roosevelt confers with W. L. Ward and receives conservationist George Bird Grinnell, Mrs. Doubleday, C. F. Francis and J. A. Sleicher. Social secretary Belle Hagner is a guest. He tells Lodge, who is suffering with his teeth, that Republicans cannot break with La Follette in Wisconsin.

headline: Root says no to the governorship
summary: Roosevelt confers with Leslie Shaw and gives a speech at College Point on Long Island. Elihu Root asks not to be considered for governor of New York. Mr. and Mrs. Clifford Richardson are guests.

headline: A quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Nothing is recorded for this Sunday at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Crane spends the night
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Silas McBee and General Grenville Dodge, then meets with them and publisher M. H. de Young, Millard and Edward Brown. Former Governor Murray Crane dines and stays overnight. He writes Jacob Schurman about propaganda against him.

headline: Betting on Japan
summary: Senator Kean, Grant LaFarge, brother-in-law Douglas Robinson and Cortelyou are guests. Roosevelt tells Lyman Abbott about press falsehoods and the lily-white southern delegates, and tells Hay he expects Japan to win and that America may help keep it from being cheated of its victory.

headline: Accepting the nomination
summary: At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt receives the notification committee led by Speaker Cannon and delivers his speech accepting the Republican nomination. Russia seizes the ship Arabia, flying a German flag, calling her flour cargo contraband.

headline: Back to Washington
summary: Roosevelt leaves Sagamore Hill for Washington. He writes Root about his speech poking at the age of Henry Davis, the Democratic vice-presidential nominee, who was born during James Monroe's presidency.

headline: A Rock Creek scramble
summary: The Cabinet takes up national finances. Roosevelt confers with Senator Proctor, then leads Admiral Converse and Secretary Metcalf on a scramble down Rock Creek. He tells Hay he feels none too kindly toward Russia and asks Captain Pillsbury whether the Russian fleet could be bottled up at Vladivostok.

headline: Meat strike conference
summary: Roosevelt meets Cabinet members and congressional leaders on the Chicago butchers' strike. He tells Bamie he enjoyed her visit and that by next March he will have nearly seven years of public work since joining the Rough Riders, and asks the Canal Commission about a coal bid to an English firm.

headline: A ride to Burnt Mills
summary: Roosevelt and Edith ride out to Burnt Mills. He asks Charles Mellen whether the attacks on Lodge in Massachusetts can be stopped.

headline: Naval base talk and a pile of letters
summary: Roosevelt confers with Agriculture Secretary Wilson and labor statistician Carroll Wright, lunches with the big-game hunter St. George Littledale and Moody, and fires off letters on a Philippine naval base, religious tolerance, the press, and who should fill the open Agriculture post.

headline: Pressing Root to run for governor
summary: After a Cabinet meeting, Roosevelt urges Elihu Root to seek the New York governorship, thanks editor Ervin Wardman for his paper's backing, sends Justice Holmes a lighthearted note, and writes Booker T. Washington about rallying Black Republicans.

headline: Answering the campaign's slanders
summary: Roosevelt meets Taft and Postmaster General Payne, talks over the beef strike with Moody, and writes Speaker Cannon a defense against the charges flying at him, among them that his Benton biography slighted Quakers and that he has trampled the Constitution.

headline: Campaign planning with Cortelyou
summary: Roosevelt maps out the campaign with party chairman George Cortelyou and sees labor leader Samuel Gompers among other callers. He sends Carroll Wright his thoughts on the Colorado miners' strike report and thanks allies stumping for him.

headline: Trouble with Turkey over missionaries
summary: The Cabinet takes up Turkey, which has broken its treaty promise of equal treatment by mistreating American missionaries and teachers. Roosevelt also talks West Virginia politics, tells Carroll Wright he will not send troops to Colorado's mines, and dines with Hay, Taft and others.

headline: Warships ordered toward Smyrna
summary: On Edith's 43rd birthday, Admiral Jewell takes a strong U.S. squadron toward Smyrna while a second force at Gibraltar is told to stand ready. Roosevelt confers with Cortelyou and Moody, and warns Butler that Standard Oil is pouring money into Parker's campaign.

headline: A quiet Sunday in Washington
summary: No activities are recorded for this Sunday; Roosevelt is in Washington.

headline: No intention of making war
summary: Roosevelt meets Hay, receives Speaker Cannon and others, and refuses to spare John W. Burley from execution. To Daniel Sickles he explains the Smyrna deployment, insisting he has no power to start a war and no wish to.

headline: Steffens and Speck von Sternberg visit
summary: After a Cabinet meeting on Turkey, Roosevelt sees Garfield and Senator Foraker. Lincoln Steffens and German Ambassador Speck von Sternberg come for dinner and stay the night, and Roosevelt tells Moody federal judgeships must never be party rewards.

headline: A railroad president stays the night
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Patrick Egan, Treasury Secretary Shaw and Payne, then confers and dines with Hay, Moody, Morton, Loeb and railroad man Charles S. Mellen, who sleeps at the White House. At Sagamore Hill, the guest book lists George Martin plus Helen and Mallory Church.

headline: Proud of the Northern Securities case
summary: Roosevelt mocks Parker's promise of no change in a letter to Bamie, tells Lodge the Democrat's speech was poor, and reminds Cortelyou that the Northern Securities suit is among his proudest achievements, proof that the most powerful men answer to the law.

headline: The Sun endorses him; Turkey backs down
summary: Roosevelt picks up the endorsement of the New York Sun. Once the Cabinet has discussed Turkey and East Asia, he wires Minister Leishman that Turkey's statement satisfies the U.S. and the fleet will withdraw for now, and writes John Burroughs about Yellowstone bears with tin cans stuck on their paws.

headline: Ethel turns 13
summary: On Ethel's birthday, Roosevelt receives Loomis and Shaw. He writes Carroll Wright again about Colorado's strike and labor relations, and tells Cortelyou the news from New York is good, though he frets over how Methodists will vote.

headline: A honeymoon week with Edith
summary: Roosevelt dines with Switzerland's minister and John Hay. Writing to his ailing sister Corinne, he says Edith has come back to Washington to spend a week with him, a real honeymoon, and confesses his worry about Corinne's health.

headline: Wary of Britain in Manchuria
summary: Roosevelt talks campaign with Shaw and receives Japanese Minister Takahira. In a busy round of letters he suggests a Puerto Rico governor, tells Speck von Sternberg he distrusts British aims in Manchuria, and thanks Emperor Franz Joseph for books.

headline: Panama Railroad talks
summary: Roosevelt discusses the Panama Railroad contract with Governor Davis of the Canal Zone, sits through a Cabinet meeting, and lunches with John McCook.

headline: Taft at the table
summary: Roosevelt confers with Taft, sees Metcalf, Long and Jay, and has Taft and Garfield to dinner.

headline: Working on the acceptance letter
summary: Roosevelt goes over his letter accepting the nomination with Hay and Taft, sees Takahira, and hears from Robb about the Paper Trust inquiry. Silas McBee and Medill McCormick join him for lunch, and writes Moody about suing International Paper.

headline: Japan seizes a Russian ship at Shanghai
summary: Roosevelt has editor Albert Shaw for breakfast and lunch. The Cabinet weighs the Panama Railroad contract and Japan's capture of a Russian vessel at Shanghai, which endangers China's neutrality. He tells Moody the paper trust facts are not yet ready for action.

headline: Off to Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt leaves Washington for Oyster Bay.

headline: Quentin's new sailboat
summary: Home at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt writes Bamie a long letter about his election worries, adds a thank-you to her husband for a cheese scoop, and reports that Quentin now walks to Aunt Lizzie's on his own, has a toy sailboat, and swims quite well.

headline: Picnic, Lodge, and Chinese neutrality
summary: The family heads out on a picnic and Lodge arrives to spend the night. Roosevelt writes on tariffs, possible governors, Colorado's militia at Cripple Creek, and China's neutrality, and warns the State Department not to suggest the Navy will intervene.

headline: Ted is headed for Harvard
summary: Roosevelt and Lodge talk over Canadian reciprocity and the acceptance letter, and he lunches with Hinckley and Lucius Swift. He tells the State Department the U.S. won't guarantee China's neutrality and writes Endicott Peabody that Ted, now teaching Sunday school, will enter Harvard a year from this fall.

headline: Hunting for a New York governor
summary: Woodruff, Root, Cortelyou and Schurman gather at Sagamore Hill to sort out the New York governorship. Roosevelt writes Moody on antitrust suits, Morton on an admiral's promotion, and Hay that the U.S. won't step in if Japan hits Russian ships sheltering in a Chinese harbor.

headline: Urging Butler to run
summary: Joe Bishop is a guest and Congressman McCleary calls. Roosevelt presses Nicholas Murray Butler to seek New York's governorship, though Butler would rather stay at Columbia, and asks Moody to look into the Colorado strike while doubting Washington can intervene.

headline: Fairbanks is saying the right things
summary: Congressman Lucius Littauer and Mrs. Clifford Richardson visit Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt writes Schurman on Philippine independence as a campaign issue, praises running mate Charles Fairbanks's speeches, thanks Root, and promises to help Bluford Wilson's son into the cavalry.

headline: A square deal for everyone
summary: Representative Landis stays for lunch and a German Roosevelt League delegation calls. Roosevelt writes journalist Ray Stannard Baker that his labor record must be weighed alongside his dealings with capital, both summed up in his favorite formula: a square deal for everyone.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Betting on Japan
summary: Roosevelt agrees with Butler's decision to stay out of the governor's race, chides a government employee over a letter, and tells Hay he expects Japan to beat Russia soundly, adding that a victorious Russia would be unbearable.

headline: Polishing the acceptance letter
summary: Roosevelt puts the finishing touches on his letter accepting the Republican nomination. He tells Hay that Venezuela's President Castro is seizing American property, but any U.S. response will wait until after the election.

headline: Callers from the Brooklyn Eagle
summary: Judge Hansbrouck stays to lunch, and two Brooklyn Eagle men, Justin McCarthy and Robert Evans, stop by along with Edward Riggs. Nicholas Murray Butler signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.

headline: No rest ahead
summary: Roosevelt tells Robert Grant that a restful visit is out of the question this year. He also writes, plainly angry, about a letter he received from a man who opposes marriage.

headline: Call me Mr. President
summary: Roosevelt confers and lunches with Senator Albert Beveridge. He instructs acting Secretary of State Adee that foreign diplomats should address him as "Mr. President," not "Your Excellency," and writes Hay about Panama's complaints over Canal Zone tariffs and postage.

headline: Evening callers
summary: Percy Chilton and F. C. Travers call at Sagamore Hill at six in the evening.

headline: Sunday at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Grinnell, Leupp and Indian affairs
summary: Cortelyou comes to confer and stays overnight, John Hay visits, and Francis Leupp briefs Roosevelt on Indian affairs. Over lunch with George Bird Grinnell and the Doubledays, he tells John Morley he never plays bridge, has hunted only once as President, and now rides sedately.

headline: Vermont and Maine campaigns
summary: Attorney General Moody comes to Sagamore Hill to talk about the campaigns in Vermont and Maine and stays for lunch with George Smith. John Gaffney calls in the afternoon.

headline: Not satisfied with Venezuela
summary: Roosevelt sees Francis Loomis, lunches with Governor Odell and Captain Cuppers, and has Cortelyou as a guest. He tells Fairbanks the outlook is brightening and that Democrats want Parker out on the stump, and writes Charles Tweed of his dissatisfaction with Venezuela.

headline: Chicago butchers' strike collapses
summary: The Chicago meatpacking strike falls apart as most skilled workers return to their jobs. Roosevelt writes Edward Butler that victory is theirs unless Republicans throw it away.

headline: Hungarian visitors
summary: Count Albert Apponyi and the Austro-Hungarian Ambassador Hengelmüller call on Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Could a Catholic be President?
summary: A crowd of callers arrives at six, and Mrs. Clifford Richardson is a guest. Roosevelt writes Taft about the Philippine display at the St. Louis world's fair, muses to Eugene Philbin that a Catholic may one day be President, and tells Carroll Wright his letter on Chicago unions was very interesting.

headline: Acceptance letter goes public
summary: Roosevelt's letter accepting the Republican nomination is published. Late that night he confers with running mate Fairbanks, and Clifford Richardson and Alvord Cooley sign the guest book.

headline: Accepting the nomination formally
summary: Roosevelt confers with Senator McCumber, and Senator Fairbanks and Dr. Alexander Lambert are guests. His formal acceptance of the nomination, addressed to Speaker Cannon, lays out at length what his administration has done and what it means to do.

headline: Ted's birthday and the Russian ship Lena
summary: On Ted's 17th birthday, Roosevelt meets Platt and Governor Odell. When the Russian ship Lena limps into San Francisco and Japan demands action, he orders it dismantled; it stays in U.S. hands until the war ends. He also asks Cortelyou to send Fairbanks to Wisconsin.

headline: Higgins nominated for governor
summary: Bellamy Storer and Joe Bishop are guests and the Baroness von Münchhausen calls. The New York Republican convention names Frank W. Higgins for governor, the man Roosevelt and Odell finally settled on after Root and others said no.

headline: The Constitution Club
summary: Father Power and Father Rosa call in the afternoon. Roosevelt writes Hay about Democratic charges that he has broken the Constitution, charges that have even spawned a 'Constitution Club', and about the state Republican convention.

headline: Harriman may give
summary: Roosevelt sends news to the British editor John St. Loe Strachey and tells Whitelaw Reid that E. H. Harriman might make a large gift to the campaign.

headline: George Ade and the Stimsons at lunch
summary: Roosevelt's lunch table includes humorist George Ade, Delavan Smith, Taber, and Henry L. Stimson and his wife. He writes Ervin Wardman about Republican chances in New York and New Jersey.

headline: Quiet Sunday
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

headline: An unhung traitor
summary: Roosevelt receives several callers, including Nevada Stranahan. He tells Hay that, unlike most observers, he does not think Russia will win, and answers George Harvey about his past statements on Jefferson Davis, standing by his blunt verdict.

headline: Cigars and the political outlook
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge about the state of the race and the quarrel between Cuban and American cigar makers.

headline: Reading his letter between the preserves
summary: Frank Higgins, the new nominee for governor, and Jacob Riis come to lunch. Roosevelt sends a warm note to Mrs. C. H. Brown, whose letter Edith read aloud to him, picturing her reading his acceptance letter while putting up preserves.

headline: Back to Washington
summary: Roosevelt leaves Sagamore Hill for the capital. He writes Governor Odell about the fight against Democratic gubernatorial nominee D. Cady Herrick, a judge thought by Republicans to be corrupt.

headline: A short story and its heroine
summary: Back at work after a Cabinet meeting, Roosevelt sees Garfield, Knox and Senator Proctor. He brushes off E. H. Harriman's offer to meet, and tells his young friend Martha Selmes he liked her short story but not how its heroine behaved.

headline: Addressing the Interparliamentary Union
summary: Roosevelt speaks to delegates of the Interparliamentary Union and gives a dinner honoring Canterbury's archbishop. He writes Hay about U.S. demands concerning Russian Jews and heaps praise on Lieutenant Commander William Sims and his gunnery ideas.

headline: Sunday with Apponyi and the Tafts
summary: Count Apponyi and Bishop Charles Brent join Roosevelt for lunch, Ambassador Speck von Sternberg calls in the afternoon, and the President dines with William H. Taft and his brother Henry.

headline: Pastor Wagner stays the night
summary: A crowded day: Roosevelt confers with Hemenway and Eugene Ware, hosts a big lunch that includes Benjamin Ide Wheeler and the Tafts, and receives Italy's ambassador along with the Marquis di San Giuliano. French pastor Charles Wagner dines and spends the night.

headline: Scientists in the East Room
summary: On his sister Corinne's 43rd birthday, Roosevelt holds a Cabinet meeting, plots the campaign with Cortelyou, and lunches with Taft, Moody and others. In the East Room, Professors Newcomb and Münsterberg present 75 members of the International Congress of Arts and Sciences.

headline: Proposing Hague talks over Armenia
summary: Roosevelt sees Taft, Moody, General Corbin and others, and Albert Pulitzer calls in the evening. He writes Oscar Straus urging a Hague conference about Armenia, and answers charges that import stamps help sell Cuban cigars.

headline: Attack Parker
summary: Roosevelt meets Admiral H. A. Taylor and receives Gompers among other callers. Tired of playing defense, he tells Cortelyou in two letters to change the campaign's focus and go after Parker, and orders Taft to make no defensive speeches.

headline: James Bryce at the White House
summary: Senator George Frisbie Hoar dies. After a Cabinet meeting Roosevelt calls on the ailing Postmaster General Payne, then hosts British scholar James Bryce, who is staying at the White House, at a dinner with the Rockhills, the Italian Ambassador, and Justice and Mrs. Brown.

headline: The charge of Cortelyouism
summary: Roosevelt backs Frank Higgins for governor in letters to Platt and Bishop, complains to Moody that the Panama Canal Commission is inefficient, and writes Cortelyou about Democratic claims he is squeezing corporations for cash. Edith confides to Emily Carow that her nerves grow as the election nears.

headline: Payne is gravely ill
summary: Roosevelt is slated for morning service at Mt. Pleasant Congregational Church, then goes to see Postmaster General Payne. He dines with William Dudley Foulke and writes Lodge that Payne is near death, and that Samuel McCall's Atlantic article has upset him.

headline: Posing for a photographer
summary: Mr. Ives photographs Roosevelt at nine in the morning. He meets Agriculture Secretary Wilson, has Lord Hamilton, Crozier, Forwood and Greene to lunch, goes to the theater in the evening, and answers rumors of a votes-for-a-Senator bargain with the Mormons.

headline: Breton Island becomes a bird refuge
summary: Roosevelt creates the Breton Island Reservation in Louisiana for birds. He also discusses Alaska with W. A. Day, replies to accusations that he is hostile to Catholics, and learns that Postmaster General Henry Clay Payne has died.

headline: Who will run the Post Office?
summary: Roosevelt asks Cortelyou whether to fill the Post Office temporarily through Election Day or have Cortelyou quit the party chairmanship and take the job now. He also writes Bishop about Representative Heflin's remark that a bomb killing the President would be no loss.

headline: The campaign livens up
summary: Roosevelt confers with Senators Foraker and McComas and lunches with Julius Meyer. He writes Cortelyou about Wisconsin and the La Follette faction, recommends standard guns for the battleship New Hampshire, and tells Leonard Wood the dull campaign is finally getting lively.

headline: Payne's funeral
summary: Roosevelt attends the funeral of Postmaster General Henry C. Payne, holds a campaign session with Cortelyou and Woodruff, and lunches with publisher Frank Munsey and others. He thanks Lyman Abbott for an editorial defending Cortelyou.

headline: Ted bags a moose
summary: Roosevelt sees Gifford Pinchot and others and lunches with Henry Clay Frick and John Hay. He proudly tells writer Stewart Edward White that Ted, hunting in Canada with Dr. Lambert, killed a moose at night with 56-inch antlers, and names White a special inspector of California forest reserves.

headline: Sunday evening with Sternberg
summary: Ambassador Speck von Sternberg calls at 8:30 in the evening. Roosevelt writes Nathan Scott about the speeches Scott has been giving for the Republican ticket.

headline: Wynne takes over the Post Office
summary: Kermit turns 15, and Robert J. Wynne succeeds the late Henry Payne as Postmaster General. Roosevelt lunches with Egan, Sheffield Cowles and Wynne, writes Taft about Andrew Rowan of 'Message to Garcia' fame, and invites E. H. Harriman to Washington.

headline: Eleanor gets a ring; Taft offers to quit
summary: On his niece Eleanor's 20th birthday, Franklin Roosevelt gives her an engagement ring. Roosevelt dines with Root, Hay and Morton, and assures Taft, who offered to resign after their public split on the tariff, that no such step is needed.

headline: Admirals on warship building
summary: After a hectic morning, Roosevelt meets Navy Secretary Morton and Admirals Dewey, Converse and Evans about new warships and receives the Isthmian Canal Commission. He removes three New York steamboat inspectors over the General Slocum disaster.

headline: Penrose in the morning
summary: Roosevelt confers with Senator Boies Penrose at ten, sees Secretary Taft, and lunches with Barrett and Springer.

headline: Potomac scramble and a night at the theater
summary: As Russia's Baltic Fleet sets out on its 18,000-mile voyage to fight Japan, Roosevelt takes the afternoon off for a rough scramble near the Potomac with Ted and tutor Matthew Hale, then brings Edith, Ted and Ethel to see The Yankee Consul, which he found very funny.

headline: A wedding at Valley Forge
summary: Roosevelt and Edith ride the train to Valley Forge to see Senator Knox's daughter married, returning that night. En route he dictates a letter to Kermit with news of Ted studying with tutor Matthew Hale, the governess Mademoiselle, and Archie staying at Dr. Rixey's.

headline: A drive to Burnt Mills
summary: Roosevelt, Edith and Ethel take a Sunday drive out to Burnt Mills. The official report on the General Slocum disaster is made public, and in the evening Rev. Vattmann, Secretary Taft, Maurice Egan and James Jeffrey Roche call.

headline: Panama talk with Cromwell
summary: Roosevelt receives Moody, Morton, Ambassador Jusserand and others, and lunches with John Hay. At nine that night he goes over Panama business with the canal lawyer William Nelson Cromwell, then reports on the talks to Taft.

headline: Sending Taft to inspect the Canal Zone
summary: On nephew Sheffield Cowles's sixth birthday, the Cabinet takes up Panama and Roosevelt orders Taft to go see the Canal Zone himself. He tells Bamie he breakfasts daily with Edith, Archie and Quentin, and tells Corinne the election looks rather favorable.

headline: Harvard's Eliot comes aboard
summary: After a busy morning of meetings with Metcalf and Moody, Roosevelt hosts a dinner for Taft, Storer, Garfield, Morton and Ambassador Jusserand. He writes Harvard President Charles W. Eliot to thank him for backing his reelection.

headline: Writing a Quaker peace leader
summary: Roosevelt has Gifford Pinchot, Woodruff and Charles Dawes to lunch and meets immigration chief Frank Sargent. He writes Benjamin Trueblood, the Quaker who heads the American Peace Society, about the Hague conferences.

headline: Thanking Thomas Lawson
summary: The Cabinet discusses the campaign and the proposed Hague Conference. Roosevelt writes Cortelyou, thanks writer Thomas Lawson for his support, and sends Justice Holmes some thoughts on history.

headline: Lunch with Marconi
summary: Wireless pioneer Guglielmo Marconi, Viscountess Falmouth and her son, Hay, Moody and McCormick join Roosevelt for lunch. He writes Lodge on Panama and the race, and tells Robert Collier he is staying out of Missouri's governor fight between Folk and Walbridge.

headline: Sunday in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing else is recorded.

headline: A Grant comes calling
summary: Among Roosevelt's visitors are Ulysses Grant and H. T. Scott.

headline: A mind steeled for the outcome
summary: Roosevelt confers with Hay, holds a Cabinet meeting, and lunches with Knox and Sheffield Cowles. He tells brother-in-law Douglas Robinson that things look favorable but he is braced for any result, and asks John Morley to be his houseguest in November.

headline: Send back Standard Oil's money
summary: Roosevelt orders Cortelyou to give back the $100,000 Standard Oil donated to the campaign. He sends Kermit $5 to celebrate a win or soothe a loss, declaring that his record is what he must "stand or fall" by.

headline: A 46th birthday, and no third term
summary: Roosevelt turns 46 with a celebration and good wishes from New York's Hungarian Republican Club. He writes a memo on the Standard Oil money, twice more tells Cortelyou to give it back, and declares to Arthur von Briesen that he will not seek a third term.

headline: Joe Bishop spends the night
summary: After a Cabinet meeting and lunch with Moody, Roosevelt has Joe Bishop to dinner and to stay over. He writes Boies Penrose about the Jacob Bunn civil service case and Augustus Gardner about postmaster appointments.

headline: British steelmen at the White House
summary: Roosevelt welcomes a visiting party from Britain's Iron and Steel Institute and lunches with John Hay. He writes Collier about rumors of his support in Missouri and twice more presses Cortelyou on returning Standard Oil's $100,000, a request Cortelyou is thought to have ignored.

headline: Root in the evening
summary: Elihu Root calls on Roosevelt at nine on Sunday evening.

headline: A tumble the papers missed
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts with Albert Shaw and writes Collier again about Missouri, where Democrat Folk is widely said to have his quiet favor. He confides to Lodge that a week ago his horse put a foot through a rotten bridge plank and somersaulted, landing him on his head.

headline: Arbitration treaty with France
summary: The United States and France sign an arbitration treaty. Roosevelt has the Sternbergs to lunch, writes Lodge about Moody and Admiral Davis, confesses to publisher Frank Doubleday that he wishes the election were behind him, and thanks Rudyard Kipling for a book.

headline: Lunch with the Dartmouths
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Navy Secretary Morton, the Earl and Countess of Dartmouth, and international lawyer John Bassett Moore. He writes Cortelyou about a statement he intends to give the press.

headline: Reading Dickens before the vote
summary: Roosevelt receives Cuban minister Quesada and Ambassador Sternberg and thanks illustrator Howard Pyle for his support. To Kermit he praises a volume of Edwin Arlington Robinson's poems and lists his reading: Macaulay's essays, Martin Chuzzlewit, Bleak House and Arlo Bates on literature.

headline: Firing back at Parker
summary: After a Cabinet meeting, Roosevelt answers in the newspapers Parker's charge that his campaign has squeezed money out of corporations. His forceful rebuttal and Parker's feeble response are thought to have swayed the race. He also wires Root thanks for a stirring New York speech.

headline: An unfinished note
summary: Roosevelt writes William Loeb a campaign note that he never finishes; Edith sends news to her sister Emily.

headline: Heading home to vote
summary: Roosevelt confers with Hay, sees Morton and Dalzell, and leaves that evening for Oyster Bay to cast his vote. He writes about a New York City postmaster, newspapers, and thanks Don Dickinson for praising his November 4 statement.

headline: Elected in a landslide
summary: Election Day. Roosevelt votes at Oyster Bay, hears early returns with only Francis Leupp for company, and heads back to Washington. He and Fairbanks sweep the country but for the Deep South, carrying 336 electoral votes and the largest popular majority yet, and he pledges never again to seek or accept a nomination.

headline: Lunch with Taft and Fortescue
summary: The day after the election, Roosevelt lunches with Taft and Fortescue.

headline: Victory letters and a dinner for Morley
summary: Roosevelt hosts a dinner for English writer John Morley, who stays the night with Joe Bishop. A flood of victory letters goes out: he tells Kermit no candidate has ever won such majorities, admits to Anna Lodge he cannot explain the scale of it, and promises Tawney he will visit the St. Louis fair.

headline: Eight to ten thousand congratulations
summary: The Cabinet takes up Philippine tariff revision and Roosevelt discusses Panama with Representatives Hepburn and Mann. He tells Corinne he has received eight to ten thousand messages of congratulation, and writes John Goff that he'd like to hunt bear out West, though the party should claim to be after mountain lion.

headline: Pushing Canadian reciprocity
summary: After a hectic morning, Roosevelt invites Douglas and Corinne Robinson to the St. Louis fair with him and asks Vice President-elect Fairbanks to open talks on a reciprocity treaty with Canada. He also writes about Southern sectionalism and the Newfoundland treaty.

headline: Sunday in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing else is recorded.

headline: A morning of callers
summary: Roosevelt spends a busy morning receiving visitors, among them naturalist George Bird Grinnell, Admiral Davis, Charles E. Smith and Keep, and has Taft, Philbin and Wynne at his table.

headline: Prince Fushimi and new boxing gloves
summary: Roosevelt receives Japan's Prince Fushimi, returns the call at the Arlington Hotel, and gives a dinner in his honor. He asks his old sparring partner Michael Donovan of the New York Athletic Club to ship him boxing gloves and to suggest opponents in Washington.

headline: Evans over Davis
summary: Roosevelt talks New York politics with Governor Odell and tariff revision with Representative McCleary. Oscar Straus and Lyman Abbott and his son dine and stay the night. He offers Senator Cockrell a seat on the Interstate Commerce Commission and, against Lodge's wishes, chooses Robley Evans over Harry Davis for top naval command.

headline: Can Kermit come to the Inauguration?
summary: Roosevelt works with Taft on his annual message to Congress and lunches with Crane and Metcalf. He consoles John Hay on his brother's death, writes Tawney about a special session on the tariff, and asks Endicott Peabody to let Kermit leave Groton for the March 4 Inauguration.

headline: Dislikes sitting for photographs
summary: After a Cabinet meeting, Roosevelt lunches with Root and writer Alfred Henry Lewis, then dines with the Sternbergs and visiting German officers. He tells Richard Watson Gilder that people don't realize how little he enjoys posing for photographs.

headline: Frederick the Great unveiled
summary: On Quentin's seventh birthday, Roosevelt attends the unveiling of the War College's new statue of Prussia's Frederick the Great. Butler and Treasury Secretary Shaw dine and spend the night, Archbishop Ireland and Booker T. Washington call late, and he writes sculptor Frederick MacMonnies about a Rough Rider statue of himself.

headline: Speaking at a parish school dedication
summary: Roosevelt sees Governors Van Sant and Cummins, then speaks at St. Patrick's Catholic Church as Father Stafford's new school is dedicated. He has supper with Robert Bacon and, at nine, talks over the New York City postmastership with Governor Odell.

headline: Tariff talks; Lodge stays over
summary: Roosevelt confers on tariff revision with Governor Cummins, Senators Foraker and McCumber, and Representative Gillett. Lodge spends the night.

headline: Arbitration treaty with Germany
summary: The U.S. and Germany sign an arbitration pact. Roosevelt addresses the YMCA, lunches with Archbishop Ireland, Congressman Littauer and Ward, and heads to the Lafayette Opera House for a talk by Pastor Charles Wagner. He warns Senator Orville Platt he may call Congress back to revise the tariff.

headline: Whitelaw Reid to London; praise for Mr. Dooley
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Stranahan, Rosewater, Lauterbach and others. He tells Joe Bishop he has named Whitelaw Reid ambassador to Britain to succeed Choate, and writes humorist Finley Peter Dunne that his philosophy truly influences the country, having taken a Dooley piece on England and ancestry to heart.

headline: Thanksgiving, and a train to St. Louis
summary: On Thanksgiving Roosevelt sprains a leg when his horse Rusty takes a jump. At midnight he boards a train for St. Louis with Edith and Alice, Douglas and Corinne Robinson, the Loebs and Dr. Rixey. He writes George Otto Trevelyan a lengthy letter about the vote, Parker and third terms, likening Martin Chuzzlewit characters to modern politicians.

headline: A whistle-stop in Richmond, Indiana
summary: On the way to St. Louis, Roosevelt's train stops at Richmond, Indiana, where he gives a speech. It is also the ninth wedding anniversary of his sister Bamie.

headline: A whirlwind day at the World's Fair
summary: Roosevelt tours the Louisiana Purchase Exposition at a near run and gives a dinner speech there. He later recalls the day as a perfect whirl, with Edith keeping right up behind him, and thought the fair beautiful, above all when the buildings lit up at night.

headline: Dinner with David Francis
summary: Still in St. Louis, Roosevelt attends a dinner hosted by David R. Francis, president of the exposition.

headline: Leaving St. Louis
summary: Roosevelt leaves St. Louis for Washington.

headline: Proud of his Confederate kin
summary: Back at 7 a.m., Roosevelt goes straight to a Cabinet meeting and tariff talk with Lodge. He tells historian James Ford Rhodes he is half Southern and proud of his mother's Confederate kin, though their cause was wrong, and warmly congratulates Franklin Roosevelt on his engagement to Eleanor.

headline: A tariff plan for the Speaker
summary: Roosevelt receives Senators Hale, Cockrell and McComas and lunches with British journalist Valentine Chirol and others. He lays out a tariff revision plan for Speaker Cannon, writes Harriman on rail rates, and asks Populist Tom Watson to talk over Georgia politics.

headline: A place for Black Americans at Jamestown
summary: On a busy day, Roosevelt lunches with the Pattersons and Cohen. He thanks Sterling Edmunds for his St. Louis Chronicle's campaign support and tells Fitzhugh Lee that Black Americans should have an exhibit at the Jamestown Exposition.

headline: Tariff reform without splitting the party
summary: On his 18th wedding anniversary with Edith, Roosevelt works over the New York City postmastership with Platt and Littauer. He tells Butler he will push for tariff changes but will not split the party over them, and urges Charles Dawes toward a stronger Interstate Commerce Commission.

headline: Musicale night; Big Jim White again
summary: Roosevelt confers on tariff revision with Senator Smoot and Representative Dixon and lunches with Charles Bonaparte, Frank Polk, Fox and Harvey. The White House holds a musicale, and he tells Kermit he has seen Big Jim White again.

headline: Sunday evening appointments
summary: Architect Charles McKim calls in the afternoon, followed in the evening by Chauncey Depew, Senator Aldrich and Vice President-elect Fairbanks.

headline: Congress returns
summary: Congress convenes. Roosevelt meets Senator Kean and Representative Burton and sees Ambassador Sternberg. He writes Justice Holmes about Harvard President Eliot's new book, about history, and about Shelley's poem 'Ozymandias'.

headline: Annual Message: give the ICC teeth
summary: Roosevelt's annual message reaches Congress. He wants the Interstate Commerce Commission empowered to set reasonable railroad rates, presses for the Santo Domingo treaty and an employers' liability law for federal workers, and backs admitting Arizona, New Mexico and Oklahoma as states, plus two new battleships.

headline: Owen Wister comes to stay
summary: Roosevelt meets the House Interstate Commerce Committee and Senator Dietrich, and novelist Owen Wister is his houseguest. He writes Philip Stewart on Colorado politics and Beveridge on the liquor ban in Oklahoma's Indian Territory.

headline: Pershing, Dunne and Holmes at dinner
summary: Roosevelt meets Representative Watson on the tariff and the House Military Affairs Committee, and lunches with publisher G. H. Putnam and Hay. His dinner table holds Justice Holmes, Thomas Nelson Page, Brander Matthews, Finley Peter Dunne, Brooks Adams and Captain John J. Pershing, followed by a musicale.

headline: Farewell to Carroll Wright
summary: A parade of senators calls after the Cabinet meeting, and Roosevelt lunches with Frick, Gilder, Dunne and others. He accepts the resignation of labor commissioner Carroll Wright with praise for twenty years of service, and writes Butler about congressional resistance to his tariff aims.

headline: Shutting out the Boston Herald
summary: Roosevelt confers with Cortelyou and Speaker Cannon and lunches with Morton, Greene, Bacon and Ripley. Angered by a false Boston Herald story that his children ran after a turkey through the mansion on the holiday, he cuts the paper and its reporter off from official news until it retracts.

headline: J. P. Morgan on a Sunday night
summary: Roosevelt holds evening meetings with Treasury Secretary Shaw, J. P. Morgan, and then Senators Allison, Cockrell and Cullom with Commissioner Cooley.

headline: Ready for Eleanor's wedding
summary: Roosevelt confers with Judge Grosscup and cabinet members, sees J. P. Morgan again, meets Samuel Gompers in the evening and dines with Root. He tells Bamie to let Eleanor know he can attend her wedding to Franklin if it is before March 17, and writes Sheffield about New York's Senate seat.

headline: A sparring blow to the eye
summary: Roosevelt confers on Arizona statehood and Canadian reciprocity and lunches with Seth Low and Pinchot. He tells boxing coach Mike Donovan that sparring with Ted's friends and young officers wrenched his thigh and broke a blood vessel in one eye. The injury was worse than he knew: by 1908 the left eye was blind.

headline: Arbitration treaty with Italy
summary: The United States signs an arbitration treaty with Italy. Roosevelt receives Sereno Payne and Fairbanks, sees George W. Perkins late at night, declines Gompers's invitation to a National Civic Federation dinner, and writes MIT's Henry Pritchett about the moral egotist in politics and about Black Americans in public life.

headline: Southern bitterness over his appointments
summary: Roosevelt confers with Taft, with Beveridge on statehood, and with Representative Cooper on the Cooper-Quarles rail bill. He lunches with Andrew D. White and Bamie, speaks that evening at Grace Reformed Church, and writes James Ford Rhodes about Southern anger at his appointments of Black officials.

headline: A wall of congressmen
summary: After a Cabinet meeting, a long line of senators and representatives calls, along with Pennsylvania Railroad president A. J. Cassatt. Roosevelt lunches with Roche and Rose.

headline: Reading The Deerslayer to the boys
summary: Roosevelt confers with Admiral Walker and Representatives Humphrey and Jones on the canal and lunches with novelist Booth Tarkington and others. He tells Kermit of a cold, snowy week, rides at dusk and after dark, reading Cooper's Leatherstocking tales to Archie and Quentin, and Ethel singing on stage.

headline: Spooner on Sunday night
summary: Senator John C. Spooner calls on Roosevelt at nine in the evening.

headline: Lunch with Baron Kaneko
summary: Roosevelt receives Depew, Fairbanks and other senators, and lunches with Commander Takeshita and Japan's Baron Kentaro Kaneko. He writes Knox, who opposes him on railroad rates, about investigating the Interstate Commerce Commission, and Edith asks the Robinsons to come for the March Inauguration.

headline: Charles Lummis at lunch
summary: After a Cabinet meeting, Roosevelt lunches with Western writer Charles Lummis and receives Puerto Rico's Governor Winthrop, Cortelyou, Garfield and Senator Knox.

headline: Railroad rate control
summary: Roosevelt confers with Moody, Morton and shipper E. P. Bacon about controlling railroad rates, and with Speaker Cannon. Congress adjourns for the holidays. He recommends William Hall Harris to Senator McComas as Baltimore's postmaster.

headline: Planning the Forest Congress
summary: Roosevelt and Gifford Pinchot plan the upcoming forestry congress. F. N. Goddard, Morton and Taft call, and he lunches with George Cortelyou and his wife. He writes Platt about New York appointments.

headline: Pershing at lunch; the Newfoundland treaty
summary: Roosevelt confers with Garfield on antitrust laws and with Cannon, and lunches with Captain Pershing, General Crozier and other officers. That night Lodge, Hale and Moody talk over the Newfoundland treaty and Joe Bishop stays over. He presses Cannon to lower duties on Philippine goods.

headline: A Viking saga from John Hay
summary: John Hay gives Roosevelt a Viking saga for Christmas. He confers with Hepburn on the ICC, presses Sereno Payne on cutting the Philippine tariff, and accepts the resignation of Joseph Choate, his longtime ambassador in London.

headline: Christmas with Bob Ferguson
summary: Roosevelt's old Badlands friend Bob Ferguson spends Christmas at the White House. The Dawes Commission's report on the Indian Territory is published.

headline: Speak softly, act decidedly
summary: Roosevelt confers with Hay and Loomis on foreign affairs. He writes George von Lengerke Meyer, ambassador to Italy, that he wants to avoid bluster yet act firmly when American interests are threatened, and that he hopes to move Meyer to St. Petersburg.

headline: Warning Germany off
summary: Roosevelt talks freight rates with Moody. He tells Cecil Spring Rice he warned Germany away early in the Russo-Japanese War and urges 'Springy' to come over from St. Petersburg, asks Shaw for handsomer coins, plans a hunting trip with Philip Stewart, and names Henry White ambassador to Italy.

headline: An East Room lecture
summary: Roosevelt confers with Foraker on federal judgeships and attends an evening talk given by a Mr. Walstein in the East Room. He writes Knox about antitrust suits against anthracite coal, tobacco and International Harvester, while Edith offers to hold Eleanor's wedding at the White House.

headline: Philippine tariff with Taft
summary: Roosevelt confers with Taft on reducing the Philippine tariff, lunches with Lodge and others, and sees Gifford Pinchot at nine that evening.

headline: A light schedule
summary: After the Cabinet meeting, Roosevelt confers with Hay and Cooley; few other appointments are on the books.

headline: Oregon land fraud indictments
summary: Senator John H. Mitchell and Congressman Binger Hermann are indicted in the Oregon land fraud cases. Roosevelt confers with Moody, Wilson, Morton and Hay, and writes Senator Gallinger about William Crum, the Black customs collector at Charleston whose confirmation Senator Tillman and others have stalled.

headline: New Year's night caller
summary: Mrs. Paul Thorndike calls at nine on New Year's evening.

headline: New Year's reception; Port Arthur falls
summary: Roosevelt greets the public at the White House New Year's reception from late morning into the afternoon. Far away, Russia surrenders Port Arthur to Japan.

headline: Offering to mediate the war
summary: Roosevelt announces he is willing to mediate between Russia and Japan. The Cabinet weighs a special session on tariff cuts, and he sees Beveridge, Platt and George Perkins. He writes Richard Harding Davis about good and bad ambassadors, the bad ones being 'pink tea men'.

headline: Climbing Rock Creek with the boys
summary: Congress returns. Roosevelt sees Pinchot, Garfield, Fairbanks and others. He tells Emlen Roosevelt and his wife of a recent clamber along Rock Creek with Ted, Kermit, Archie and Archie's friends, writes Taft about Army weapons, and refuses to carve land out of Yosemite National Park.

headline: Speaking to the American Forest Congress
summary: Roosevelt speaks to the American Forest Congress, meeting at the National Theatre. He talks freight rates with Senator Elkins, meets Senator Dick, and hosts a Cabinet dinner; illustrator Howard Pyle, the Whitridges and their wives stay the night.

headline: Arbitration treaties go to the Senate
summary: Seven general arbitration treaties, with Spain, Italy, Portugal, Switzerland, Germany, France and Britain, go to the Senate. Roosevelt hosts a dinner on Southern questions and complains to Spooner that senators want to curb presidential power by calling every agreement a treaty.

headline: Senate leaders on arbitration and tariff
summary: Roosevelt meets congressional leaders including Aldrich, Spooner, Cannon and Payne on the arbitration treaties, tariff bills and a possible special session. The Senate tacks a special-agreement amendment onto the treaties. He lunches with Munro Ferguson and dines with Dr. Lambert.

headline: Higgins and Stranahan to dinner
summary: Judge Thomas Jones calls at midday, and Roosevelt dines with New York's Governor Frank Higgins and Nevada Stranahan.

headline: A raise for Dr. Gorgas
summary: Roosevelt confers on railroad rates, naval appropriations and more, then attends a dinner given by Fairbanks. He tells Taft that canal sanitation chief Dr. Gorgas should be paid $10,000 a year, rebuffs Maria Storer's lobbying, and notes the Beef Trust case has reached the Supreme Court.

headline: No halt in building the Navy
summary: Roosevelt issues a statement calling for immediate tariff revision, holds a Cabinet meeting, and dines at John Hay's. He tells Representative George Foss he earnestly hopes naval building will not pause, and writes Sternberg about German policy in China.

headline: Ratify the treaties as written
summary: Roosevelt publicly urges the Senate to ratify the arbitration treaties without amendment. He hosts a big dinner with Bob Ferguson, Justices Harlan and Brewer, Pinchot and others, drops in on the architects' dinner at the Arlington, and tells Lyman Abbott he treats the tariff as a matter of expediency.

headline: Henry James at the White House
summary: Roosevelt's lunch table gathers Henry Adams, painter John La Farge, sculptor Augustus Saint-Gaudens and novelist Henry James, who stays the night after the diplomatic reception. Roosevelt also confers with Cullom on the treaties and writes Hay and Sternberg about China.

headline: Canal commission report to Congress
summary: The Isthmian Canal Commission's report goes to Congress. Roosevelt confers on the treaties, discusses making Joseph Bristow a special Panama Railroad commissioner, sees Owen Wister and goes to the National Theatre. He flatly refuses Representative Foss's idea of pausing naval building for a year.

headline: Talking railroads with James J. Hill
summary: Roosevelt goes over railroad rate changes with Hepburn and Taft and with Morton and railroad magnate James J. Hill. Oscar Straus and Jusserand are among his callers, and he writes Dr. William Sturgis Bigelow about a letter the Japanese envoy's son sent Archie.

headline: Treaty talk on Sunday night
summary: Roosevelt confers with Senators Daniel, Foster and McCreary about the arbitration pacts at nine, then sees W. W. Rockhill. Edith writes Emily that she liked Henry James, and that her husband changed his mind and liked him too.

headline: Saint-Gaudens for the coinage
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Costello, Nelson and Page. He directs Hay to write both Japan and Russia urging them not to violate China's neutrality, and tells Treasury Secretary Shaw he wants Augustus Saint-Gaudens to design new American coins.

headline: Steamboat inspection and naval spending
summary: After a Cabinet meeting, Roosevelt discusses the steamboat inspection probe with George Uhler and naval appropriations with Morton and Taft. Treasury Secretary Shaw gives a dinner, and Roosevelt writes Robert Underwood Johnson about Yosemite and Yellowstone.

headline: Bamie turns fifty
summary: On his sister Bamie's 50th birthday, Roosevelt goes over the Beef Trust investigation with Moody and Solomon Bethea. He tells Benjamin Ide Wheeler he wants a strong ICC and wires Sternberg that Britain, Italy, Germany and the U.S. stand behind China's territorial integrity.

headline: Diplomatic dinner and a houseful of girls
summary: Roosevelt confers with Knox and hosts a diplomatic dinner at the White House. Three young guests, Eleanor Whitridge, Isabella Selmes and Lorraine Roosevelt, stay the night.

headline: Old friends from the West
summary: Roosevelt confers with Representative Dayton on naval spending and lunches with Bishop William Lawrence and a crowd that includes his old ranch partner Frank Merrifield, Pinchot, Leupp, Philip Stewart and the Swiss Minister. He dines with J. S. Elliott.

headline: A new room for Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt receives William Jennings Bryan and lunches with Charles Emory Smith. He hires architect Grant La Farge to add a large north room to Sagamore Hill for $16,000, nearly what the whole house cost in 1884, with work to run from March to June.

headline: Sunday supper
summary: Roosevelt has supper with J. S. Elliott.

headline: Boxing with a wrestler
summary: Roosevelt writes Kermit about presidential electors in town, among them Frank Merrifield from Montana. He and Ted keep boxing with Grant, a wrestler and so-so boxer; young Corinne and her friends visited for the diplomats' dinner; Archie and Quentin have the grippe; and he has finished reading The Deerslayer to them.

headline: Wichita game preserve created
summary: A new law creates the Wichita Game Preserve. Roosevelt attends a Peabody trustees' meeting at the Arlington Hotel, lunches with Shaw, Governor Francis and Saint-Gaudens, receives the Japanese and British envoys, and he and Edith dine with the Tafts.

headline: Corporate law in the capital
summary: Roosevelt confers with Speaker Cannon and lunches with Bamie, Perkins, Berry and Hasbrouck. He tells Moody that the District of Columbia's laws governing corporations fall short.

headline: Pressing the Roosevelt Corollary
summary: Roosevelt attends Mrs. Warren's wedding at noon, addresses a church conference on marriage and divorce, and hosts the judiciary dinner. He tells Elbert Baldwin he wants authority to act on his Caribbean policy and writes Hay about running Santo Domingo's customshouses.

headline: Cutting corners on the North Room?
summary: After the Cabinet meeting Roosevelt sees Senators Aldrich, Bard and Dietrich and Representative Crumpacker, and lunches with Joe Bishop. He asks Grant La Farge whether Sagamore Hill's new North Room could be built for less by using cheaper woods.

headline: Sketched by Ellen Day Hale
summary: Artist Ellen Day Hale sketches Roosevelt at nine in the morning. A packed day follows: treaty and Alaska talks, lunch with journalist Ray Stannard Baker, calls from Booker T. Washington and Bishop Satterlee, and the Gridiron Club dinner. He vents to Lyman Abbott about the stalled treaties.

headline: Spring Rice's secret visit
summary: Cecil Spring Rice arrives quietly in Washington, sent by the British government to talk with Roosevelt, who does not get on with Ambassador Durand. Staying with Henry Adams and dining with the President, he warns of Russia's sweeping Asian ambitions and harsh crackdown at home. The press never learns of the visit.

headline: Annapolis graduation and a Philadelphia speech
summary: Roosevelt addresses the graduating class at the Naval Academy in Annapolis, then speaks that evening at a Union League Club banquet in Philadelphia, calling for a stronger Interstate Commerce Commission able to enforce fair railroad rates. He also sends Congress a message about corporations operating in the capital.

headline: Taking over Dominican customs
summary: Roosevelt urges the Senate to ratify the arbitration treaties at once. The Beef Trust ruling is affirmed by the Supreme Court, and over congressional objections the U.S., at the Dominican government's invitation, takes charge of its customshouses. That evening he and Edith dine with Attorney General Moody.

headline: Forest reserves move to Agriculture
summary: The nation's forest reserves pass from Interior to Agriculture, where Gifford Pinchot's Forest Service takes charge. Roosevelt confers with senators on Alaska, arbitration and forests, lunches with General Young and dines with Cecil Spring-Rice.

headline: Justices dine at the White House
summary: Roosevelt talks with James Garfield about the Supreme Court ruling against the Beef Trust, lunches with General Chaffee and Colonel Schuyler, and hosts the justices for dinner that evening. C. Grant LaFarge and Robert Grant sleep over.

headline: Railroad rates and the Santa Fe charges
summary: The Cabinet takes up railroad rates and Alaska. Roosevelt meets Paul Morton and William Moody about Interstate Commerce Commission charges against the Santa Fe line, sees Senator Cullom on arbitration, lunches with the Robert Grants and receives the German ambassador.

headline: Boone and Crockett Club dinner
summary: After meetings with Paul Morton and Treasury Secretary Leslie Shaw and lunch with railroad chief A. J. Cassatt, Roosevelt joins the Boone and Crockett Club for dinner at the New Willard, where Dr. William Smith lectures. He writes Taft about Senate stalling on the Canal Commission.

headline: Sunday talks with two diplomats
summary: On Sunday evening Roosevelt confers with his friend Cecil Spring-Rice and British Ambassador Mortimer Durand, and also sees Secretary of War Taft.

headline: Senate balks on arbitration treaties
summary: Roosevelt meets Taft, Morton, Depew and Lodge, then writes a stack of letters: civil service exams for Agriculture hires, Senate trouble over the arbitration treaties, Russia and Japan, and Andrew Carnegie's acceptance of the Senate amendments.

headline: A scientific survey for the Philippines
summary: Roosevelt asks Congress for a scientific survey of the Philippines. He also holds Cabinet, meets Senators Allison and O. H. Platt, talks Indiana politics with Charles Fairbanks, and dines with Edith at Postmaster General Wynne's. He writes Taft about floating mines.

headline: Wanting an earlier Inauguration Day
summary: After lunch with editor Albert Shaw, Roosevelt tells Andrew Carnegie he opposes the Senate's treaty amendments and writes Congressman John Sharp Williams that a new President and new Congress ought to start work in January, not March.

headline: House passes the Esch-Townsend bill
summary: A packed day of talks on statehood, railroad rates and the Russo-Japanese War ends with the House passing the Esch-Townsend rate bill and the Congressional dinner at the White House. Booker T. Washington calls, and Roosevelt asks Taft to study Japanese labor in Hawaii on his trip east.

headline: No amendments, Roosevelt tells Cullom
summary: Following Cabinet, Roosevelt meets Booker T. Washington, French Ambassador Jusserand and the Japanese minister, and writes Senator Cullom that he wants the arbitration treaties left unamended.

headline: Senate ratifies amended arbitration treaties
summary: The Senate ratifies seven arbitration treaties, but with the amendment Roosevelt opposed. Gifford Pinchot hands in the Public Lands Commission report, and in the afternoon Roosevelt takes in an afternoon Keller show at the Lafayette Opera House.

headline: Alice turns 21
summary: Alice celebrates her twenty-first birthday. Roosevelt writes Lyman Abbott about Indian mission schools and charges that federal money for them was mishandled; the letter later runs in The Outlook.

headline: Lincoln Day speech in New York
summary: Roosevelt heads to New York, speaks briefly at a Press Club dinner at the Hotel Astor, and addresses the Republican Club's Lincoln Day dinner on the South and the shortage of federal posts for Black Americans. He declines to put the weakened arbitration treaties into effect.

headline: University Club lunch in New York
summary: At 422 Madison Avenue Roosevelt receives Seth Low, Oscar Straus and George Perkins, then joins Root, Taft, Joseph Bishop, Nicholas Murray Butler and others for lunch at the University Club. He speaks to the Hungarian Republican Club and takes a midnight train south.

headline: Dominican treaty goes to the Senate
summary: Roosevelt sends the Dominican treaty to the Senate with a message applying the Monroe Doctrine to Santo Domingo. He also meets Moody and Representative Charles Curtis about the Osage Indian bill, lunches with a group of guests, and dines with Edith at Secretary Morton's.

headline: Army and Navy dinner
summary: Roosevelt confers on the rate bill, sees Senator Platt and the German ambassador, and hosts the Army and Navy dinner. In letters he blasts the Senate's treaty amendments and tells Charlemagne Tower he doubts Britain wants a share of China.

headline: Naval appropriations and Alaska
summary: After a Cabinet session on appointments, Roosevelt works over the naval appropriation bill with Cannon, Allison, Wadsworth and Tawney, then talks Alaska legislation with Senator Beveridge.

headline: Planning for a second Hague conference
summary: Roosevelt discusses the naval bill with Morton and Rep. Dayton, talks with Richard Bartholdt about a second Hague peace conference, receives the Chinese minister and writes Moody on railroad legislation.

headline: Sunday evening callers
summary: Alvord Cooley and Ambassador Jusserand call on Roosevelt Sunday evening.

headline: Looking into Standard Oil in Kansas
summary: Roosevelt meets Garfield and Rep. Campbell about investigating Standard Oil's Kansas operations and confers with the authors of the rate bill. Letters go to historian James Ford Rhodes, Colombian President Rafael Reyes and Navy Secretary Morton.

headline: Indian land leases before the Cabinet
summary: The Cabinet takes up leasing of Indian lands. Roosevelt sees James B. Reynolds, lunches with John Hay and journalist Maurice Low, and dines with Edith at Interior Secretary Hitchcock's.

headline: Honorary degree in Philadelphia
summary: On Washington's Birthday Roosevelt travels to Philadelphia, gives a talk at the University of Pennsylvania, which awards him an honorary Doctor of Laws, then lunches with the First City Troop.

headline: Jiu-jitsu beats wrestling
summary: Roosevelt meets Hitchcock, Moody and prosecutor Francis Heney on the land-fraud cases and calls the Senate into special session for March 4. At five, he and General Mills watch his sparring partner Grant wrestle his jiu-jitsu teacher Professor Yamashita, who wins.

headline: Fatherly advice for Kermit
summary: After Cabinet and talks on the Santa Fe rebate inquiry, Roosevelt tells Kermit his grades might rise if he pined less for home. He also boxes with Grant, the national middleweight wrestling champion, and urges Senator Spooner to move on the Dominican protocol after a plot against that country's president.

headline: Mosby and Kaneko call
summary: Former Confederate raider John Mosby calls in the morning, and Japan's Baron Kaneko comes in the evening.

headline: Evening visit from Commissioner Leupp
summary: Indian Affairs Commissioner Francis Leupp calls on Roosevelt Sunday evening.

headline: A royal letter about the Kaiser
summary: Roosevelt receives Taft, Rep. Hepburn, General Francis Greene and others. He writes John Hay about a letter from King Edward VII concerning the Kaiser, and Cecil Spring-Rice about the naval fighting between Russia and Japan.

headline: Canal contracts and a farewell dinner
summary: The Cabinet discusses Panama Canal contracts. Roosevelt sees Congressmen Sulzer and Grosvenor and Senator McComas, lunches with Archbishop Ireland, Pinchot, Taft and others, meets Herbert Knox Smith, and is honored at a dinner given by Agriculture Secretary James Wilson at the New Willard.

headline: Philippine tariff clears the Senate
summary: The Philippine Tariff Bill clears the Senate. Roosevelt talks Alaska with Senator O. H. Platt and lunches with old friend Seth Bullock and his wife, General Otis, Moody and Metcalf. He tells Alice Gitterman which bills are stuck and writes about schools in the capital.

headline: Rough Riders come to town
summary: A delegation of his old Rough Riders calls on Roosevelt ahead of the inauguration, along with Senator O. H. Platt. Late in the evening he takes up consular appointments with Francis Loomis, and he writes about the Panama Canal Commission.

headline: A ring with Lincoln's hair
summary: On the eve of the inauguration John Hay gives Roosevelt a ring holding a lock of Abraham Lincoln's hair, and Roosevelt thanks him for three years of counsel. Garfield's meat-industry report goes to Congress, governors and their staffs arrive, a Columbus glee club sings in the East Room and neighbors from Oyster Bay call.

headline: Inaugurated President in his own right
summary: Roosevelt takes the oath before a record crowd of about half a million, with his whole family looking on, and tells the nation, "Much has been given us, and much will rightfully be expected from us." Cowboys, miners and Rough Riders march in a parade of three and a half hours, and that night he talks it all over with Corinne and Douglas in his room.

headline: Edith writes home about the big day
summary: A quiet Sunday after the inauguration. Edith sends her sister Emily the news of the ceremonies.

headline: The Kaiser's worries about Morocco
summary: Speck von Sternberg brings Roosevelt a message from the Kaiser, who suspects France and Spain of lining up against Germany in Morocco. Roosevelt sends Congress a second message on Santo Domingo, goes to the Columbia Theatre, and thanks Uncle Rob for standing in for his late father at the inauguration.

headline: Dinner at the Metcalfs'
summary: Roosevelt confers with Cortelyou and Robert Wynne, and he and Edith dine at the home of Commerce and Labor Secretary Victor Metcalf.

headline: The Supreme Court pays a call
summary: The justices of the Supreme Court call on the newly inaugurated President. Roosevelt lunches with the Danas and Lafayette Young, sees the German ambassador, and in the evening welcomes Seth Bullock and some two dozen companions.

headline: Life is a long campaign
summary: Roosevelt creates the Stump Lake bird reservation in North Dakota. In a long letter to George Otto Trevelyan he reflects on Lincoln and the plain people, on reining in big corporations without crippling business, and on the Monroe Doctrine's obligations. He also praises Booth Tarkington's stories and writes King Edward VII.

headline: Engineers favor a lock canal
summary: Roosevelt confers with Speaker Cannon and Illinois Senators Hopkins and Cullom over federal judgeships in their state, holds Cabinet on appointments, and writes Taft about the Bates survey report, which recommends a canal with locks at Panama.

headline: Congressional callers
summary: Vice President Fairbanks, Senator Elkins and Representatives Hepburn, Bartholdt and Townsend are among Roosevelt's callers.

headline: Tract Society meeting on Sunday
summary: Roosevelt goes to a meeting of the American Tract Society held at the Presbyterian church.

headline: Speaking to the Congress of Mothers
summary: Roosevelt addresses the National Congress of Mothers, worrying aloud about the falling birthrate and calling for the same divorce laws in every state. He lunches with Alfred Thayer Mahan and General Crozier and writes Taft twice about the canal and the Army. Spring-Rice opens a private correspondence with him by way of Edith.

headline: Against easy divorce
summary: An Italian cruiser appears off Santo Domingo to press money claims. Roosevelt breakfasts with Albert Shaw, holds Cabinet, and in letters tells Robert Grant he firmly opposes easy divorce and explains how honest American collectors would run the Dominican customs houses.

headline: The Dominican treaty again
summary: Roosevelt works over the Santo Domingo treaty with John Hay and Taft and receives Ambassador Jusserand in the afternoon.

headline: Visiting a sick John Hay
summary: Roosevelt calls on his ailing Secretary of State, John Hay. He also meets senators, lunches with Governor Crane, and writes about saving Civil War flags, Japan and the Philippines, and a possible wolf hunt.

headline: Giving Eleanor away
summary: Roosevelt spends St. Patrick's Day in New York, addressing a Friendly Sons of St. Patrick gathering, reviewing the parade and speaking at a Sons of the American Revolution dinner. In the afternoon he gives his niece Eleanor in marriage to Franklin D. Roosevelt, with Alice as a bridesmaid, and the guests trail him to the dining room.

headline: Coal miners' delegation with John Mitchell
summary: The Senate adjourns its special session. Roosevelt receives anthracite coal miners led by union chief John Mitchell, along with Lyman Gage and others, lunches with Judge and Mrs. Francis Lowell, Moody and Senator Crane, and sees both the German and British ambassadors.

headline: Boys in the White House trees
summary: Archie and Quentin have friends over and the boys spend the day climbing trees on the White House grounds. Frank Travers dies. Senator Beveridge calls in the evening.

headline: Riding with Edith, tennis with Ted
summary: Roosevelt sits for a photograph by Mr. Prince, sees senators and lunches with Baron Kaneko. Writing Kermit, he reports John Hay ill and describes a ride with Edith and tennis with Ted and Matt. He also writes Taft about Dr. Charles Reed's article on health in Panama.

headline: A false treaty with Santo Domingo
summary: The Cabinet discusses canal business. Roosevelt lunches with the Lodges and with Admirals Evans and Davis, and writes Robert Bridges about a bogus Dominican treaty and about a stenographer who helped with The Rough Riders.

headline: Army appropriations
summary: Roosevelt meets Generals Crozier and Oliver on Army funding, lunches with Senator Knox, Buxton, Hollander and Generals Crozier and Butt, and sees Taft in the evening.

headline: Fearing the ultraconservatives
summary: Roosevelt talks Virginia politics with John S. Wise and Dominican affairs with Admiral Dewey and three senators, then sees Booker T. Washington at night. To Joseph Bishop he confides a worry that stubborn financiers will push moderates into radical railroad measures, and touches on his pledge not to seek a third term.

headline: Reshaping the Canal Commission
summary: The Cabinet weighs Venezuela, Santo Domingo and a reorganized Isthmian Canal Commission. Roosevelt sees Baron Kaneko at midday and lunches with Taft, Curtis Guild Jr. and a Mr. Neland.

headline: Diplomas for Navy doctors
summary: Congressman Nicholas Longworth stops by in the morning. With White House physician Dr. Rixey, Roosevelt hands out diplomas at the Naval Medical School's graduation at the National Museum, then talks with Depew about the Dominican treaty and sees Senator Foraker at night.

headline: Spooner on Sunday night
summary: Senator John Spooner calls on Roosevelt Sunday evening.

headline: A fan letter to a struggling poet
summary: The Boise reclamation project in Idaho and Oregon gets under way. Roosevelt sees Taft, Senator Dick and Philippe Bunau-Varilla, and writes the little-known poet Edwin Arlington Robinson to praise The Children of the Night and ask how he is getting by.

headline: Holding the line in Santo Domingo
summary: After Cabinet and talks with Senators Spooner and Foraker, Roosevelt orders Minister Dawson to keep things as they are in Santo Domingo until the treaty is ratified. He attends the Mexican ambassador's funeral and writes Alvey Adee on the stopgap modus vivendi for running Dominican customs.

headline: Morning walks with Edith and Jack
summary: Roosevelt meets Moody, sees Dalzell and Fairbanks, and lunches with Taft, Bunau-Varilla and others. He sends a picture letter to his little nephew Sheffield Cowles, who is ill. Each morning after breakfast he and Edith stroll the garden with their dog Jack.

headline: Russia and Japan look toward peace
summary: Roosevelt receives Senators Kean and Lodge, Vespasian Warner and the German and British ambassadors. Writing to the ailing John Hay, he reports that Dominican President Morales has asked the U.S. to run the customs houses and that both Russia and Japan want to begin peace talks.

headline: The Kaiser lands in Morocco
summary: Kaiser Wilhelm visits Tangier and backs the Sultan of Morocco against France and Britain, alarming Europe. In Washington Roosevelt sees Jane Addams among other callers and writes about Edwin Arlington Robinson and Russo-Japanese peace talks, while Edith takes the children, minus Quentin, cruising on the Sylph in Florida.

headline: A new Panama Canal Commission
summary: Roosevelt's reorganized Panama Canal Commission takes over, with Theodore Shonts as chairman, Charles Magoon governing the Canal Zone and John Findley Wallace as chief engineer. He also talks Nebraska patronage with Rep. Hinshaw and lunches with Shonts and journalists.

headline: Wrapping up before a long trip
summary: On the eve of a six-week trip west, Roosevelt meets Francis Loomis, sees Clement Griscom and the Spanish ambassador, dines at Lodge's, and sends John Hay a survey of affairs at home and abroad, defending action in Santo Domingo.

headline: Off to hunt in the Southwest
summary: At nine in the morning Roosevelt leaves Washington to hunt in the Southwest, leaving Taft in charge at home. He writes Theodore Shonts about sanitation in Panama.

headline: Speaking in Louisville
summary: Roosevelt's train heads west, with a speech in Louisville and stops in five states from Kentucky to Missouri.

headline: Through Indian Territory to Dallas
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Parsons, Kansas, and at Muskogee, South McAlester and Durant in Indian Territory, then arrives in Dallas in the evening for another speech. Sternberg writes that Germany wants French ambitions in North Africa checked.

headline: Texas legislature and San Antonio
summary: Roosevelt stops at Taylor, addresses the Texas Legislature in Austin and reaches San Antonio. His diary jots notes on the men he will hunt with, including wolf catcher Abernathy, who lifts a coyote by the jaw on horseback, and Burk Burnett.

headline: Rough Riders reunion in San Antonio
summary: Roosevelt joins a reunion of his Rough Riders in San Antonio, where the regiment had trained in 1898, and says how much he admires Texans. His diary sketches Abernathy, who takes wolves with his bare hands, Texas Ranger Captain McDonald, and the cattlemen of the Four Sixes brand.

headline: Coyote hunt begins near Frederick
summary: After speeches in Fort Worth and Wichita, Roosevelt reaches Frederick, Oklahoma, and starts hunting at Cecil Lyon's ranch. Dogs catch the first coyote in a creek, and Alec Lambert rides well. He tells Taft he is handling Russia, Japan, Santo Domingo and Morocco just right.

headline: Headlong gallops after coyotes
summary: On Archie's eleventh birthday Roosevelt rides hard after coyotes from a camp in a bend of the Red River, on a Kiowa pony in the morning and a cow pony later. His hosts are old-style Texas cattlemen including Burk Burnett and Cecil Lyon. He writes Bamie about little Sheffield's ear trouble.

headline: A ten-mile chase
summary: Out with greyhounds and staghounds, Roosevelt's party takes a coyote after a three-mile run. In the afternoon comes an extraordinary ten-mile chase, and Abernathy captures the coyote alive with his hands, with Roosevelt one of the few riders there at the finish.

headline: Bobcats elude the hounds
summary: Camped on Deep Red Creek, Roosevelt is up before dawn for a morning hunt after bobcats that turns up nothing, and he rests in the afternoon.

headline: Six coyotes in a day
summary: With the chuck wagon along, the party rides southwest toward the Red River and kills six coyotes, losing only one after a seven-mile chase. A cowpuncher with nothing but a rope chases that one back for miles.

headline: Last day of the coyote hunt
summary: Roosevelt is in at the death of two more coyotes, then rides back to Frederick, where he speaks before leaving for Colorado. His diary tallies the party's total. Sternberg reports that the Kaiser is pressing for an international meeting on Morocco.

headline: Colorado speeches, and tales of Abernathy
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Trinidad, Pueblo and Colorado Springs and spends the night at Newcastle. He tells Kermit the hunting party took 47 wolves plus raccoons and rattlesnakes, and describes how Abernathy takes wolves alive. He also writes Garfield about the probes into Standard Oil and the Beef Trust.

headline: Into the Colorado high country
summary: Roosevelt rides about 20 miles from Newcastle with Philip Stewart, Dr. Alexander Lambert and guides John Goff and Jake Borah to Camp Roosevelt on East Divide Creek, with three horses, a Springfield rifle and some thirty hounds and terriers. Snow lies in drifts.

headline: Shorty and the bobcat
