summary: Roosevelt spends eleven hours in the saddle over rough ground. The dogs tree a bobcat, the bull terrier Shorty climbs nearly to it, and when it jumps the pack seizes it. A big glossy black bear is spotted.

headline: A 330-pound black bear
summary: With 26 hounds and four terriers Roosevelt follows a black bear through snowy canyons for nearly two hours. The bear refuses to tree and fights off the dogs, killing a terrier; Roosevelt breaks its hips at 60 yards and finishes it at 30. It weighs 330 pounds.

headline: Skip and Shorty, the fighting dogs
summary: Six hours in the snowdrifts turn up nothing. Roosevelt's diary praises the little terrier Skip, who loves to ride on horseback, and Shorty, the bull terrier mauled by the bear, who staggers back wagging his tail. He notes cranes, eagles, ravens and the first songbirds.

headline: Loeb visits camp
summary: Secretary William Loeb spends the night in camp. Roosevelt rides all day in the high mountains without seeing game, and records local talk about wolves, cougars and a trapper who took dozens.

headline: Snowbound, writing on Morocco
summary: Snow keeps the party in camp, and Roosevelt fills his diary with birds and small mammals. In letters he tells Ted about his guides, tells Taft the government should stay out of Morocco, wires Loomis that the U.S. will remain friendly with both France and Germany, and writes Lodge on Newfoundland fisheries.

headline: Skip bites a bobcat's tail
summary: More than ten hours in the saddle and on foot through belly-deep drifts end with the hounds treeing a bobcat. Stewart photographs it, Lambert shoots it with a revolver, and the little terrier Skip climbs thirty feet up the tree to bite its tail.

headline: Fever and a move to West Divide
summary: Roosevelt feels his old Cuban fever. The party moves camp to where Clear Creek meets West Divide, though the late cold season may have kept the bears denned up.

headline: A rest day in camp
summary: Roosevelt stays in camp and records guide Jake Borah's story of a 115-pound wolf his pack once held at bay before he shot it.

headline: A she-bear shot through the heart
summary: In an eleven-hour, forty-mile ride, four of them bucking snow, the pack jumps a yearling and its glossy dark mother. Lambert shoots the yearling in an aspen; Roosevelt drops the she-bear from a spruce with a shot through the heart.

headline: Another bear after twelve hours
summary: After twelve hours and more than thirty miles, Lambert shoots two yearlings with his revolver and the hounds tree their mother high in a spruce, where Roosevelt kills her. He notes what the bears had eaten. Sternberg writes that the Kaiser wants Roosevelt to nudge Britain toward harmony with Germany over Morocco.

headline: Ranchmen come to watch
summary: A touch of fever keeps Roosevelt in camp while some twenty hard-riding ranchmen turn out hoping to see the President kill a bear. He writes Ethel about prairie girls and admits he is homesick for the family.

headline: Cutting the trip short for peace
summary: Still feverish, Roosevelt stays in camp while Lambert has a big day of bear hunting. Sensing that Russia and Japan may reach an honorable settlement, he wires Taft that he will end his trip a week early.

headline: Watching a tame kingbird
summary: Another feverish day in camp. Roosevelt describes a tame bee martin that stays near the buildings with a plaintive note, and a big field mouse in the ranch house.

headline: Fever in camp again
summary: Roosevelt spends another day in camp with fever. It is his sister Corinne's 23rd wedding anniversary.

headline: Church in a schoolhouse; Edith finds Pine Knot
summary: Roosevelt goes to church in a little blue schoolhouse and wires Taft that he backs Japan's call for direct peace talks with Russia. In Virginia, Edith buys a small timbered house and five acres in Albemarle County for $195, calling it Pine Knot, a hideaway for the two of them.

headline: Eight hours and no game
summary: Hunting along Divide Creek, Roosevelt rides for eight hours without seeing anything. His secretary William Loeb stays over in camp.

headline: Ten bears so far
summary: Storms roll through camp and Philip Stewart rides out to join the party. Roosevelt tells Kermit he has taken ten bears and three bobcats, and has been fighting his Cuban fever for a week.

headline: Wet spring snow
summary: A heavy, wet snowstorm hits the camp on Divide Creek.

headline: Owls and a tame lark
summary: Through snow Roosevelt rides six hours without seeing game, but notes an owl on its nest, a great owl and a very tame lark, and adds to his running list of birds.

headline: A bobcat in the snow
summary: Another snowy six-hour ride ends with a bobcat taken. Roosevelt keeps up his bird list.

headline: Out of the mountains to Glenwood Springs
summary: Roosevelt rides down to Glenwood Springs and speaks there. He writes John Hay, glad to hear he is better and urging a summer of rest, and tells George Kennan about California's push to segregate schools amid fear of a yellow peril.

headline: Sunday in Glenwood Springs
summary: Roosevelt spends the day at Glenwood Springs, still noting the birds he sees.

headline: Denver speech on corporations
summary: Heading east, Roosevelt stops at Pueblo and Colorado Springs and in Denver argues for federal control of corporations. His diary ends with house finches singing in Denver and spring wildflowers, though he misses the blue columbine, Colorado's state flower.

headline: Across Nebraska to Omaha
summary: Roosevelt's train crosses Nebraska stopping at Fremont, Grand Island and North Platte, and he speaks in Omaha and in Council Bluffs, Iowa.

headline: Chicago and the teamsters' strike
summary: After speeches in Cedar Rapids and Clinton, Iowa, Roosevelt lunches and speaks at Chicago's Merchants Club. A labor delegation objects to any plan to send federal soldiers into the teamsters' strike, and he ends the day at the Iroquois Club banquet.

headline: Home by midnight
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Alliance and Canton, Ohio, and in Pittsburgh, then reaches Washington at midnight.

headline: Back with Skip the terrier
summary: Roosevelt is back at work, having cut his trip short over Morocco and the chance of Russo-Japanese talks. He has brought home Skip, the little hunting dog who attached himself to him in Colorado. Cabinet meets, and he confers with Fairbanks, Taft and Cortelyou.

headline: The Kaiser presses for a conference
summary: Sternberg hands Roosevelt the Kaiser's memo demanding a general conference on Morocco and blaming Britain for blocking it. Roosevelt and Herbert Knox Smith win at tennis, and he writes a batch of letters, telling Spring-Rice how he handles the Kaiser and Root about his three bears.

headline: Catching up on the work
summary: Taft and Moody call in the evening. Roosevelt tells Kermit that work piled up while he was away, that he went riding with Edith, and that Kermit's Groton marks delight him.

headline: Idaho forests and Chicago labor trouble
summary: Roosevelt talks over Chicago's labor troubles with Foraker, Grosvenor and Herbert Bowen and goes over Idaho's forest reserves with Gifford Pinchot. He lunches with the new canal leadership and tells Lodge the crowds in Texas and Kentucky were wildly enthusiastic.

headline: Buying canal supplies abroad
summary: The press reports that the Isthmian Canal Commission will buy construction supplies in foreign markets wherever they are cheapest, and Roosevelt takes full responsibility for the policy. He also holds Cabinet, sees Senator Elkins and receives Baron Kaneko.

headline: All forest reserves to Pinchot
summary: Roosevelt tells Interior Secretary Hitchcock that the nation's forest reserves will be consolidated under Pinchot's Forest Service. He discusses tariffs and rebates with Rep. Davis and Santo Domingo with Jacob Hollander, and informs the Japanese minister that the Kaiser denies calling Japan the yellow peril.

headline: Writing to Chief No Shirt
summary: Roosevelt discusses reciprocity with Speaker Cannon, Hemenway, Dolliver and Rep. Foss, and twice receives Baron Kaneko. He writes William Rockhill about China and Japan, and writes the Indian chief No Shirt about reservation land and relations between whites and Indians.

headline: Reversing the foreign-purchase order
summary: Having put tariff adjustment before Congress, Roosevelt has Taft cancel the May 16 order to buy canal supplies abroad. He meets Cortelyou and Morton after Cabinet, lunches with Cannon, Bonaparte and others, and praises Bishop Charles Brent's defense of American missionaries in the Philippines.

headline: Nicholas Murray Butler comes to stay
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Oscar Straus, Senator Warner and a Mr. Cowan, and dines with the Jusserands. Columbia's Nicholas Murray Butler arrives for a two-night White House visit.

headline: Senator Orville Platt dies
summary: Word comes that Connecticut Senator Orville H. Platt has died. Sportswriter Caspar Whitney calls at one, and Interior Secretary Hitchcock in the evening.

headline: Hopeless to reconcile England and Germany
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Taft, the Duke of Sutherland and naturalist George Bird Grinnell. He tells Ambassador Meyer he has given up trying to improve relations between England and Germany, and warns Senator Thomas Platt he will remove an appointee regardless.

headline: The Loomis-Bowen quarrel
summary: After Cabinet, Roosevelt and Taft take up the feud between diplomats Francis Loomis and Herbert Bowen. He lunches with Lyman Abbott, Moody, Taft and Richard Harding Davis.

headline: Rate bill or government ownership
summary: Roosevelt sees senators, the Brazilian ambassador, Sternberg, and in the evening Garfield and Pinchot. To Lodge he argues that killing the railroad rate bill would only feed the drive for government ownership of the railroads. He lets Hay know the Kaiser hopes to meet him, and admits he has no liking for Bowen.

headline: A government job for a poet
summary: Roosevelt confers with Joseph Bristow about the Panama Railroad and lunches with psychologist Hugo Münsterberg and others. He tells Kermit that Edwin Arlington Robinson, Kermit's favorite poet, is now at work in New York in the government post Roosevelt arranged for him.

headline: Dinner with Justice White
summary: After Cabinet, Roosevelt sees Senators Dolliver, Cullom and Dillingham, and dines with Justice Edward White and his wife. Joseph Bishop stays the night. He writes Spring-Rice about the Kaiser, the war and reports of a Russian-German alliance aimed at England and Japan.

headline: Japan sinks the Russian fleet at Tsushima
summary: Admiral Togo's Japanese fleet destroys the Russian fleet of Admiral Rozhestvensky in the Tsushima Strait. In Washington Roosevelt discusses a possible extra session of Congress with Senators Cullom and Elkins, sees Baron Kaneko, and asks Senator Thomas Platt to have management give a little in the Chicago strike.

headline: A blank Sunday
summary: The record for this Sunday in Washington is empty.

headline: Burroughs and the nature fakers
summary: Roosevelt sees naturalist C. Hart Merriam early, then Puerto Rico's Tulio Larrinaga and others, and lunches with the Sternbergs, the Mortons and Father Zahm. He writes John Burroughs about Rev. William Long's attacks and about protective coloration in animals, gets a new Morocco memo from the Kaiser, and leaves for Brooklyn at midnight.

headline: Memorial Day in Brooklyn
summary: In Brooklyn Roosevelt breakfasts at the Union League Club, reviews the Memorial Day parade and speaks at the unveiling of a monument to General Henry W. Slocum, then heads back to Washington.

headline: The Kaiser threatens war over Morocco
summary: A new message from the Kaiser, sent through Sternberg, warns that Germany may fight France over Morocco. Roosevelt confers on the Russo-Japanese War, congratulates Baron Kaneko on Japan's naval victory, and asks Taft to stress Subic Bay as a naval base on his Philippine trip. Around this time the Trophy Room is added at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Opening the Lewis and Clark Exposition
summary: At four o'clock Roosevelt presses a button that lights and opens the Lewis and Clark Exposition in Portland, Oregon. He sees the British, German and Japanese envoys during the day and tells Andrew White he will test whether an offer to mediate between Japan and Russia can work.

headline: The Keep Commission is born
summary: Roosevelt names a Commission on Departmental Methods, led by Charles Keep with Frank Hitchcock, Lawrence Murray, James Garfield and Gifford Pinchot, to root out waste and modernize executive departments. The Wichita Forest game preserve is set up in Oklahoma, and he meets Russia's Ambassador Cassini.

headline: Russian ships near the Philippines
summary: Roosevelt meets Moody, Morton and Taft about Russian warships moving off the Philippines, lunches with Ambassador Jusserand, and sees Japan's minister Takahira at night.

headline: The Kaiser urges mediation
summary: Sternberg brings Roosevelt a note in which the Kaiser says the President should mediate between Russia and Japan. Dr. Merriam also calls in the evening.

headline: An audience with the Czar
summary: Roosevelt wires Ambassador Meyer to seek an audience with the Czar, and briefs Lodge on his steps to end the war. Japanese admirals from Port Arthur visit, he lunches with the Bonapartes and Deweys, and Ted and a friend beat him and Alvord Cooley at tennis, four sets to three. He thanks Frederick MacMonnies for a statuette of him at San Juan.

headline: British fleet to visit New York
summary: Roosevelt confers with the British and French ambassadors on the war, sees Rep. Sulzer, and lunches with the Keep Commission members and others. He writes Arthur Lee on friendship among English-speaking peoples as Prince Louis of Battenberg's British squadron prepares to call at New York.

headline: A day of ambassadors
summary: Roosevelt confers with the envoys of Russia, Germany, France and Britain, along with Hugh O'Beirne, as peace efforts gather pace. Thomas Dawson, Dr. Rixey and the Italian ambassador call, and he lunches with Baron Kaneko.

headline: Proposing peace talks to Russia and Japan
summary: Roosevelt sends formal notes to Russia and Japan proposing a peace conference, after a run of afternoon and evening meetings with Durand, Kaneko, Takahira and Sternberg. Edith goes ahead to Pine Knot to ready it for his first visit.

headline: First trip to Pine Knot
summary: After seeing Francis Loomis, Roosevelt takes the train to Rapidan, Virginia, and goes on to Pine Knot, the little cabin Edith has just bought. He visits Joseph Wilmer and they dine at Plain Dealing. Edith is thrilled with the place.

headline: Alone at Pine Knot; both sides agree to talk
summary: Roosevelt and Edith have Pine Knot to themselves. He cooks breakfast and chops firewood while she rests in a hammock, and they fry chickens for supper with biscuits, cornbread, cherries and wild strawberries. Word comes that Japan accepts his call for peace talks; Russia will follow two days later.

headline: Beefsteak, church and the train home
summary: Roosevelt fries beefsteak for Edith's breakfast, they go to church together, and he takes the train back to Washington for talks with Taft and Loeb. He writes Kermit that Russia and Japan have agreed to meet. Another Kaiser memo on Morocco arrives.

headline: Regretting an old sharp reply
summary: Roosevelt sees Cassini and Takahira, decides not to prosecute Santa Fe railroad officers individually in the rebate case, and clears Paul Morton, who has left the Cabinet for Equitable Life. He urges Clara Hay to make John rest, and tells Clark Howell his 1885 retort to Jefferson Davis no longer seems clever.

headline: Chinese exclusion
summary: After Cabinet, Roosevelt discusses Chinese exclusion with Commerce Secretary Metcalf, lunches with Root, Robert Bridges and Baroness von Sternberg, and writes Senator Heyburn about forest reserves.

headline: Jusserand, Cassini and Kaneko
summary: Roosevelt receives Jusserand in the morning and Cassini before lunch, lunches with Shaw and Speyer, sees John Barrett and Edwin Denby, and meets Baron Kaneko in the afternoon.

headline: Trying for The Hague
summary: Roosevelt talks over the Panama Railroad with Shonts and Maxwell Evarts and receives Cassini, Takahira and Durand in turn. He tells Oscar Straus he hopes to bring the two warring powers to The Hague and writes Cassini about his talk with Takahira.

headline: Sizing up a peace settlement
summary: Roosevelt meets Booker T. Washington and Jusserand, then writes a flurry of letters on the war. To Spring-Rice in St. Petersburg he sketches a peace in which Russia gives up Sakhalin and pays an indemnity but keeps most of its East Asian holdings, and he sends Lodge a long, important letter on the negotiations.

headline: Asking Grover Cleveland a favor
summary: Roosevelt takes up the Santa Fe rebate case with Moody and Morton and Army appointments with Taft, and Cardinal Gibbons calls. He writes former President Cleveland asking him to chair the Jamestown Exposition committee and touches on the Equitable Life scandal.

headline: Thanks from Sternberg
summary: German Ambassador Speck von Sternberg praises Roosevelt for his work in easing the Morocco crisis.

headline: Dinner with the Hays
summary: Roosevelt talks with Moody about the Santa Fe case, lunches with Rep. Augustus Peabody Gardner, and dines with John and Clara Hay. He writes about Chinese labor, Russia, and prejudice against the Japanese.

headline: Overnight to Worcester
summary: The Cabinet takes up the Loomis-Bowen case and Roosevelt goes over postal appointments with Cortelyou. At nine that night he leaves for Worcester, Massachusetts.

headline: Bringing John Paul Jones home
summary: Roosevelt gives the Clark University commencement address in Worcester and leaves for Williamstown. He sends Taft a long letter on the Bowen-Loomis affair and directs Francis Loomis to go to France and bring home the remains of naval hero John Paul Jones.

headline: Williams College commencement
summary: Roosevelt speaks at the Williams College commencement in Williamstown and heads back to Washington.

headline: France agrees to a Morocco conference
summary: Roosevelt tells Speck von Sternberg that France has quietly dropped its objection to an international conference on Morocco, calling it a diplomatic triumph. The Cabinet discusses Chinese exclusion, and he sees Jusserand and Takahira.

headline: A mission to Japan for Calhoun
summary: Roosevelt confers with Penfield and Metcalf about Chinese exclusion and dines with the Jusserands. He asks William Calhoun to travel to Japan and report back, and responds to Lincoln Steffens's McClure's article on Ohio politics, McKinley and Hanna.

headline: Mediating between France and Germany
summary: The Jusserands come at midday and Sternberg in the evening, and Roosevelt writes the German ambassador about smoothing matters between France and Germany.

headline: Off to Harvard
summary: Roosevelt talks railroad rebates with Moody and sees Takahira, Durand and Jusserand before leaving for Cambridge at 5:30. He sends Russia a note about mediation. Edith goes ahead to open Sagamore Hill, getting her first look at the newly built North Room.

headline: Twenty-fifth Harvard reunion
summary: Roosevelt attends the 25th reunion of his Harvard class of 1880 at the Hotel Somerset, staying with George B. Lee Jr. and Bishop William Lawrence.

headline: Harvard Commencement
summary: Roosevelt attends Harvard's commencement and speaks at the Harvard Union and the alumni dinner. Sternberg writes to Sagamore Hill that the Kaiser is delighted with his work toward a Morocco conference.

headline: By the Sylph to Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Bridgeport, Connecticut, and takes the Sylph home across the Sound to Oyster Bay, where Sagamore Hill opens for the summer with Bob Ferguson as a guest. Puck runs a color cartoon, "Peace," showing a battleship fleet with Roosevelt's face on the lead ship.

headline: Nearly mad over Russia and Japan
summary: At Sagamore Hill Roosevelt sees immigration official Marcus Braun and Judge William Calhoun, who stays to dinner. He vents to Whitelaw Reid about Russia's muddle, asks Alice to join Taft's goodwill trip to Japan as his representative, and names John Stevens to replace John Wallace as chief canal engineer. Bob Ferguson marries Isabella Selmes.

headline: John Hay dies
summary: Secretary of State John Hay dies at his New Hampshire home. Roosevelt writes his widow Clara of the Sunday hours after church he spent with them. Charles Bonaparte succeeds Paul Morton as Navy Secretary, and Dan Moore and James Tracey of Albany visit Sagamore Hill.

headline: Peace talks set for August
summary: Word goes out that Russian and Japanese envoys will meet on August 5, with Oyster Bay named as the place. Roosevelt tells Taft he will make Elihu Root Secretary of State, adding that he had done most of the State Department's work himself. Alice and the Taft party reach Chicago on their way to Japan.

headline: Family and friends at Sagamore
summary: Guests at Sagamore Hill include brother-in-law Douglas Robinson, Bob Ferguson, Elliott Cowdin and E. C. Hammer Jr. Roosevelt writes Lyman Abbott about John Hay's death.

headline: Leaving for Hay's funeral
summary: Sternberg visits and stays for lunch, and that afternoon Roosevelt sets out for Cleveland with members of the Cabinet to bury John Hay. Out west, Alice sets off fireworks and shoots a revolver off the back of the Taft party's train, the men take in the Hart-Root prizefight at Reno, and the group reaches San Francisco.

headline: Burying John Hay
summary: Roosevelt attends John Hay's funeral in Cleveland and returns to Oyster Bay.

headline: Root named Secretary of State
summary: Roosevelt names Elihu Root to succeed John Hay at the State Department. Winthrop Chanler comes to dinner and stays over, with the E. D. Morgans also at the table. He sends Taft word of Root's acceptance and his love to Alice.

headline: Speech to the teachers at Ocean Grove
summary: Roosevelt travels to Ocean Grove, New Jersey, to address the National Education Association and returns home, where Teresa and Clifford Richardson and Baron Kaneko are guests. He tells Senator Spooner the Dominican treaty needs no amendment.

headline: Lunch with the poet Robinson
summary: After meeting Baron Kaneko, Roosevelt lunches with Robert Bridges, Alvord Cooley and the poet Edwin Arlington Robinson, while Douglas and Monroe Robinson, Senator Knox and others fill the guest book. Alice sails from San Francisco on the Manchuria with Taft's party of 80. He praises Augustus Saint-Gaudens's inaugural medals.

headline: Morocco settled without war
summary: In Paris, Germany and France sign an agreement on Morocco, a settlement Roosevelt helped broker and one that likely headed off war. At Sagamore Hill he lunches with Bishop Knight and the Washburns and has James Garfield and Gifford Pinchot to tea in the evening.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: The record for this day at Sagamore Hill is empty.

headline: Robert Bacon to the State Department
summary: Senator Philander Knox spends the night at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt writes Lodge about Hay's death, Hay's deep dislike of the Kaiser and the choice of Root, tells Root that Robert Bacon will be his first assistant, and sends Jusserand a letter on the Mongol campaigns of the 1200s.

headline: Gompers, Duncan and Mitchell visit
summary: John Mitchell, James Duncan and Samuel Gompers, who lead the American Federation of Labor, meet Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill. William Calhoun leaves on a special mission to Venezuela, and Roosevelt tells Moody that an Agriculture statistician, Edwin Holmes, was fired for using government data for private gain.

headline: Russia's new ambassador comes to lunch
summary: Baron Roman Rosen, Russia's new ambassador, lunches at Sagamore Hill and presents his credentials. Jacob Riis is a guest. Alice and Taft's group land in Honolulu.

headline: Ted wants to work on railroads
summary: Roosevelt and Japan's minister Takahira discuss Count Witte's naming as a Russian envoy to the coming peace talks. He lunches with Harriman, Takahira, Shonts, John Stevens and Hynes, and Root and others sign the guest book. To Harvard's Byron Hurlbut he explains that Ted hopes for a railroad career and a scientific school.

headline: No sympathy for anti-Japanese agitation
summary: An explosion of the gunboat Bennington's boilers kills more than 50 men. Roosevelt confers with Takahira, has Bamie among his guests, and tells Ambassador Lloyd Griscom to assure Japan that Americans reject the anti-Japanese agitation on the Pacific coast and that there will be no discrimination while he is President.

headline: A blank Sunday at Sagamore
summary: The record for this Sunday at Sagamore Hill is empty.

headline: Rowing around Lloyd Neck with Edith
summary: Roosevelt and Edith row fifteen miles around Lloyd Neck with a picnic lunch and a few books, carrying the boat overland at one point. He writes London editor John St. Loe Strachey that he has no great hopes for the peace conference, and tells John Sleicher he doubts Congress will cut spending.

headline: Camping out with the boys
summary: Roosevelt takes the boys out by rowboat to sleep under the stars, frying chicken or steak in bacon fat that the youngsters swear tastes like nothing else. He asks animal trainer Frank Bostock to compare the big cats, writes Morgan about a Chinese railroad concession, and tells Lodge that Ted passed his Harvard entrance exams with points to spare.

headline: Simply a good out-of-doors man
summary: Elihu Root takes office as Secretary of State. Roosevelt rows home from his overnight camp with the boys and writes Henry Needham a modest self-portrait: no athlete, not good at games, but a decent walker, rider and rifle shot.

headline: Nothing recorded
summary: The record for this day at Sagamore Hill is empty.

headline: A picture letter for Alice
summary: Roosevelt confers with Secretary Root, and Dr. Alexander Lambert and Lyman Abbott visit. He sends Alice, far off in Asia, one of his cartoon-filled picture letters, assuring her it is no posterity letter.

headline: Root, Morton and Lambert
summary: Roosevelt confers again with Root, and Paul Morton and Dr. Lambert spend the evening at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Alice reaches Tokyo
summary: Dr. Alexander Lambert is a guest at Sagamore Hill. Across the Pacific, Alice and Taft's group reach Tokyo, where she stays at the American embassy with the Griscoms.

headline: The Monroe Doctrine must grow
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Hawaii's George R. Carter. He tells Spring-Rice that the Monroe Doctrine cannot stand still while the nation grows, urges Shonts to improve living conditions for canal workers, and writes Governor Higgins about the Equitable Life troubles.

headline: Writing Jusserand on Morocco
summary: Roosevelt writes Ambassador Jusserand about France, Germany and Morocco.

headline: Praise for Little Citizens
summary: Roosevelt confers with Takahira about the peace talks and writes author Myra Kelly that he enjoyed her book Little Citizens.

headline: Japan's envoys aboard the Mayflower
summary: Roosevelt meets Japan's chief envoy Baron Komura, with Kaneko and Takahira, aboard the presidential yacht Mayflower. He writes Commander William Sims that Japan's eight-inch guns badly mauled the Russian ships at Tsushima.

headline: To Coney Island with Jacob Riis
summary: Senator Murray Crane is a guest at Sagamore Hill, and Roosevelt goes with his old friend Jacob Riis to see the Coney Island hospital.

headline: Thanking the Kaiser
summary: Roosevelt wires the Kaiser his thanks for help in settling where the Russo-Japanese peace talks will meet, and writes Taft, Whitelaw Reid and Baron Kaneko on Santo Domingo, Panama, Root and the preliminaries to peace.

headline: Nothing on the record
summary: The record for this Sunday at Sagamore Hill is empty.

headline: Approving the Taft-Katsura understanding
summary: Roosevelt wires Taft confirming the agreement he has reached in Japan, under which Washington accepts Japan's stake in Korea while Tokyo accepts America's position in the Philippines. He also lunches with Baron Rosen, Secretary Wilson and others, and discusses the Agriculture Department investigation with Wilson.

headline: Moody's overnight visit to Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt talks with William Moody about the probe into the Department of Agriculture, and Moody stays for dinner and the night. In a letter, TR admits that after two car rides as President, the fuss in the papers over his safety has kept him out of automobiles.

headline: A visit from Dr. Rixey
summary: The White House physician, Dr. Presley Rixey, calls on Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Lunch with diplomats and a Western maxim
summary: Roosevelt hosts a crowded lunch table that includes British Ambassador Sir Henry Durand and Commander William Sims. Writing to Whitelaw Reid, he sums up his approach to power with a frontier rule about never drawing a gun without intent to fire.

headline: Count Witte comes to Sagamore Hill
summary: Russia's chief peace envoy, Count Sergei Witte, visits Roosevelt along with Ambassador Roman Rosen. TR also edits Treasury Secretary Shaw's tariff speech with a blue pencil and writes about yellow fever in New Orleans.

headline: Russian and Japanese envoys meet aboard the Mayflower
summary: On the presidential yacht Mayflower in Oyster Bay, Roosevelt formally greets the delegations of Russia and Japan and raises a glass to a fair and durable peace. The envoys then head for Portsmouth, New Hampshire. Edith takes the children on a picnic to Cooper's Bluff.

headline: Edith turns 44
summary: Edith celebrates her 44th birthday at Sagamore Hill, with William Wilmer on hand as a guest.

headline: Morgan and a Chinese railroad deal
summary: Roosevelt meets Treasury Secretary Shaw, then sits down to lunch with Judge Ingram and the financier J. P. Morgan over the Hankow railroad concession in China. In the afternoon Japan's Baron Kaneko comes to talk.

headline: Lunch with Loomis and Hollander
summary: Roosevelt has lunch with Assistant Secretary of State Francis Loomis and Jacob Hollander, then holds a separate talk with Hollander.

headline: Peace talks open at Portsmouth
summary: Russian and Japanese negotiators sit down at Portsmouth, New Hampshire, while Roosevelt follows from Sagamore Hill. Ambassador Jusserand passes along French thanks for TR's work toward calm over Morocco.

headline: Speaking to the coal miners at Wilkes-Barre
summary: Roosevelt leaves Oyster Bay for Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, to address the United Mine Workers convention. Cameras catch him there alongside Cardinal Gibbons.

headline: Monroe Doctrine talk at Chautauqua
summary: At Chautauqua, New York, Roosevelt speaks on the Monroe Doctrine and U.S. policy toward Santo Domingo and Venezuela, then heads back to Sagamore Hill.

headline: TR praises a little-known poet
summary: The Outlook runs Roosevelt's review of Edwin Arlington Robinson's The Children of the Night, singling out the young poet as a rare bright spot in American verse. Senator Lodge is staying at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Ethel's 13th birthday
summary: Ethel turns 13 at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Kaneko calls again
summary: Baron Kaneko is among the day's visitors. Roosevelt writes Interior Secretary Hitchcock about naming a federal district judge for Oregon.

headline: Backing Gorgas on mosquitoes
summary: Writing to canal chief Theodore Shonts, Roosevelt takes up Shonts's criticism of conditions in Panama and Dr. William Gorgas's then-mocked idea that mosquitoes carry yellow fever. TR takes Gorgas seriously.

headline: Insurance oversight and a nod to Kermit
summary: Roosevelt confers with Charles Keep about his inquiry into the Government Printing Office and with James Beck and Representative John Dryden about federal oversight of insurance companies. He credits Kermit, in a letter, with first steering him to Robinson's poetry.

headline: No special session on the tariff
summary: George Cortelyou joins Roosevelt for lunch. TR tells journalist Walter Wellman he won't call Congress back early to take up the tariff, and writes Morgan about the Chinese railroad question.

headline: Portsmouth stalls over an indemnity
summary: Roosevelt meets Kaneko as the Portsmouth talks freeze on Japan's demand that Russia pay an indemnity. Dr. Alexander Lambert arrives for a stay through August 21.

headline: Siding with Canada on the fisheries
summary: After meeting Ambassador Rosen, Roosevelt writes Lodge that in the Newfoundland fisheries quarrel the Gloucester fishermen have the weaker case and Canada has the better case. He refuses Massachusetts calls to send warships.

headline: Quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: No events are recorded; Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.

headline: A message to the Czar through Berlin
summary: After a morning session with Kaneko and dinner with Shonts, Roosevelt cables Ambassador Speck von Sternberg to relay word on the peace talks to the Czar by way of Germany. He also briefs Jusserand on how negotiations stand.

headline: Pressing Japan to settle
summary: Roosevelt warns Baron Kaneko that the world will not look kindly on Japan if it drags out the war just to win an indemnity. Philip Stewart visits and stays the night.

headline: TR proposes splitting Sakhalin
summary: With Portsmouth still deadlocked, Roosevelt floats a compromise: Russia gives Japan half of Sakhalin Island, Japan gains Port Arthur, the Kwantung Peninsula, Manchuria and Korea, and no indemnity is paid. He sends a flurry of letters and cables to push it.

headline: Story time and roughhousing
summary: Edith reads The Lances of Lynwood aloud to Archie and Quentin, and their father wrestles boisterously with the boys. At Portsmouth, Sakhalin and the indemnity still block a deal.

headline: Fifty minutes under Oyster Bay in a submarine
summary: Roosevelt climbs into the submarine Plunger and spends 50 minutes beneath Oyster Bay, even taking the controls for a stretch; no President had done anything like it. That evening he reads poems to Archie and Quentin after prayers and tosses them around on the bed.

headline: Telling Kermit about the submarine
summary: Roosevelt writes Kermit about his 50-minute plunge beneath Oyster Bay the day before. He also passes along a family joke: asked by a reporter about his father, young Quentin claimed to see him now and then but to know nothing of his home life.

headline: Peace talks near collapse
summary: The Portsmouth negotiations come close to breaking apart. Roosevelt sees Melville Stone of the Associated Press in the evening, dines with Shonts, and cables the Kaiser a proposed formula built around Sakhalin and no indemnity.

headline: Bishop named to the Canal Commission
summary: Roosevelt lunches with J. P. Morgan over China's Hankow railroad rights and puts Joseph Bishop on the Panama Canal Commission. He tells the Civil Service Commission its rules can't work in Panama.

headline: Russia and Japan agree to peace
summary: Word comes from Portsmouth that Witte and Komura have settled terms to end the Russo-Japanese War. Roosevelt wires his delight to Herbert Peirce.

headline: Lunch with Aldrich
summary: Roosevelt hosts Senator Nelson Aldrich, Arthur von Briesen and Elbert Baldwin for lunch.

headline: Congratulating the Czar; Ted heads to Harvard
summary: Roosevelt wires Czar Nicholas II his congratulations on the peace and tells Douglas Robinson he is pleased. Far away, riots erupt in Japan over the treaty, China boycotts American goods over exclusion, Alice's party with Taft turns for home, and Ted begins at Harvard.

headline: Armistice signed
summary: Russia and Japan sign an armistice. At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt meets Francis Loomis and Senator Henry Burnham, and John St. Loe Strachey introduces the Evening Post's London man, Dibblee. TR tells Bamie the British squadron will skip New York.

headline: Rainy-day house party and a tired President
summary: The children play in the old barn on a wet afternoon during a house party for Ted and Ethel. Roosevelt writes Alice in China that Portsmouth made the peace possible, invites Kaneko to collect a bearskin, and confides to Lodge that the summer has worn him out.

headline: Holding Santo Domingo steady
summary: With J. W. Wadsworth as a house guest, Roosevelt sees Cortelyou, Beveridge and Penfield and talks Panama civil service with Cooley. He tells Bonaparte he will keep Santo Domingo as it is until the Senate acts on the treaty, and will put down any revolt.

headline: Treaty of Portsmouth signed
summary: The Treaty of Portsmouth is signed, formally ending the Russo-Japanese War. Roosevelt names Robert Bacon Assistant Secretary of State and explains to General Francis Greene that he got peace by going around old-style diplomacy and dealing directly with heads of state.

headline: Notes to two emperors
summary: Roosevelt writes Czar Nicholas II and Japan's Emperor Mutsuhito about the new peace. He tells Lodge he plans to oust Public Printer Frank Palmer and sends Speck von Sternberg a mixed letter touching on an old Roman fort and submarines.

headline: No entry
summary: Nothing is recorded for the day beyond Roosevelt's presence at Sagamore Hill.

headline: The Fairbankses and Bunau-Varilla
summary: Vice President Charles Fairbanks and his wife come for lunch, and Philippe Bunau-Varilla and his wife for dinner. Roosevelt writes Carl Schurz at Lake George making the case against disarmament.

headline: Lunch with Komura, dinner with Witte
summary: Roosevelt hosts Japan's negotiators Komura and Takahira at lunch and Russia's Witte and Rosen at dinner, with cousin Emlen Roosevelt and his wife at the table. He also writes China's Guangxu Emperor about the peace.

headline: Edith on stirring times
summary: Baron Kaneko lunches at Sagamore Hill. Edith writes Spring-Rice that the times feel so exciting she can barely wait for what comes next, and TR assures Rockhill that China will respect the treaty's terms.

headline: Canal engineers come to lunch
summary: Roosevelt lunches with the Panama Canal's board of consulting engineers. He credits the Kaiser, in a letter to Whitelaw Reid, for his help as a go-between, and writes Senator Fulton about an Oregon judgeship.

headline: Sizing up Witte for Trevelyan
summary: In a long letter to George Otto Trevelyan, Roosevelt reviews the peace conference, gives an unflattering portrait of Count Witte, mentions Tolstoy, and says he is reading William Morris. He hopes to visit England someday as a private citizen.

headline: Ted turns 18
summary: Ted celebrates his 18th birthday. Baron Rosen lunches with Roosevelt, who writes Ray Stannard Baker about his McClure's series on the railroads.

headline: Letting the Czar take credit
summary: Roosevelt tells Root that Rosen brought word the Czar wants to revive the Hague Conference. Although the idea was originally TR's, he is content to let the world think it came from the Czar.

headline: Tariff talks with Germany
summary: Roosevelt writes Shaw and Senators Aldrich and Allison about the tariff deal under discussion with Germany.

headline: A forest reserve in the White Mountains
summary: Roosevelt writes William Harvey about possibly buying White Mountains land for a forest reserve. He also accepts Archibald Sampson's resignation as Minister to Ecuador and writes Shaw and Reid.

headline: No entry
summary: Nothing is recorded beyond Roosevelt's presence at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Chinese diplomats on the boycott
summary: Roosevelt meets members of the Chinese legation about China's boycott of American goods. Charles and Ellen Bonaparte dine, and Nicholas Murray Butler stays overnight.

headline: Liking Plunkitt of Tammany Hall
summary: Roosevelt tells Whitelaw Reid he sees little he can do to warm relations between England and Germany. He writes William Riordon that he enjoyed Plunkitt of Tammany Hall.

headline: Root, Lodge and Choate stay over
summary: Clarence Mackay and his wife call in the afternoon with the Duchess of Marlborough. Root, Lodge and Choate come to confer and stay for dinner and the night.

headline: A newsy letter to Arthur Lee
summary: Roosevelt sends his English friend Arthur Lee a letter of news from Sagamore Hill.

headline: No entry
summary: Nothing is recorded beyond Roosevelt's presence at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Archie, "a little trump"
summary: Roosevelt writes Wayne MacVeagh about the uproar over big corporations' gifts to the 1904 Republican campaign. To Edith's sister Emily Carow he explains why Ted quit Groton one year ahead of schedule to be tutored for Harvard, and he praises Archie warmly.

headline: No entry
summary: Nothing is recorded beyond Roosevelt's presence at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Pushing back on Steffens
summary: Roosevelt tells Lincoln Steffens he is annoyed by the idea of handing back every campaign gift from big money. He recommends Alexander Sutherland's book on the moral instinct to Florence LaFarge, touching on the U.S. birth rate, and writes Richard Bartholdt about the Navy's size.

headline: Peabody, Porter and Dodge call
summary: Groton headmaster Endicott Peabody, General Horace Porter, canal chief Theodore Shonts and Cleveland Dodge are among the day's visitors.

headline: Taking aim at a nature faker
summary: On Corinne's 44th birthday, Roosevelt writes George Locke objecting to the animal myths in the Rev. William J. Long's Northern Trails. He tells Senator Allison the Germans want tariff talks held in Berlin.

headline: A tailor's visit
summary: A fitter from Brooks Brothers comes to Sagamore Hill in the evening.

headline: Shielding Ted from the press
summary: Roosevelt writes Harvard President Charles Eliot of his worry over newspapermen hounding Ted, who has just started his freshman year. Reporters and photographers trail the boy around Harvard Yard.

headline: Back to Washington
summary: Roosevelt and Edith leave Sagamore Hill in the morning and return to Washington. Senator Thomas Platt calls at 9 that night.

headline: Dinner with Jusserand
summary: Back in Washington, Roosevelt dines with French Ambassador Jules Jusserand.

headline: Railroad rebates and fatherly advice
summary: Roosevelt confers on the Keep Commission's work, railroad rebates and rate legislation. He writes Ted about coping with reporters, admits Pinchot beat him at tennis three sets to one, and describes Archie hauling a long garden hose toward the sandbox.

headline: Cabinet takes up the boycott and the Beef Trust
summary: The Cabinet discusses China's boycott and the Beef Trust case. Roosevelt also confers on postal jobs, rate legislation and coal with John Mitchell, and shares lunch with muckraker Lincoln Steffens, Robert Bacon and William Moody.

headline: A word to McClure on muckraking
summary: Roosevelt spends the day on rate legislation, consular posts, naval bills and the Ohio campaign. He writes Samuel McClure about the exposé articles his magazine favors.

headline: The Vatican and Alice's archbishop
summary: Roosevelt meets Townsend on rates and confers with Moody and Taft, then shares lunch with Japan's Minister Takahira and two doctors, Rixey and Stokes. He writes Taft about Vatican displeasure that Alice reportedly made much of an out-of-favor archbishop during the Far East trip.

headline: Calling a summit on football injuries
summary: The Cabinet works through Chinese exclusion, meatpacking, a second Hague Conference and canal administration. Roosevelt invites George Gray to a White House meeting on college football injuries set for October 9.

headline: Taft-Katsura and the ancient Greeks
summary: Roosevelt talks with Bartholdt about the coming Interparliamentary gathering in Brussels and with Virginia's Representative Slemp about his state's politics, and dines with Bacon and Garfield. He writes Taft about the Taft-Katsura agreement and Trevelyan about the ancient Greeks.

headline: Hughes for mayor?
summary: Roosevelt asks Root whether Charles Evans Hughes might be talked into running for mayor of New York; Hughes later says no. He tells MacVeagh the clamor over returning corporate campaign money is mostly hysteria with a little dishonesty.

headline: Saving college football
summary: Roosevelt and Root meet with representatives of Yale, Harvard and Princeton about making college football less brutal. That evening the justices of the Supreme Court are honored at a White House reception.

headline: Three new bird reservations
summary: On Kermit's 16th birthday, Roosevelt creates bird reservations at the Siskiwit and Huron Islands in Michigan and Passage Key in Florida. The Cabinet debates members campaigning locally, and he confers on tariffs, rates and Venezuela.

headline: Eleanor comes of age
summary: Niece Eleanor Roosevelt turns 21. Roosevelt confers on the Philippines, receives a lumbermen's delegation, and writes Frederic Delano on why railroad legislation matters. Edith writes Kermit praising his growth and tells Aunt Lizzie that Quentin is scaling the trees outside her window.

headline: Planning the Annual Message
summary: Roosevelt works with Metcalf and Garfield on his Annual Message, confers on rates and the Philippines, and lunches with Knox and Root. Senator Proctor calls.

headline: Alice sails from Yokohama
summary: The Cabinet takes up Venezuela, and Boutell, Cooley and Jusserand call. Across the Pacific, Alice boards the Siberia at Yokohama to come home.

headline: Investigating Hitchcock's charges
summary: Roosevelt directs the Keep Commission to look into Interior Secretary Hitchcock's statements about his own employees. He also meets Root, Bacon and Taft and writes Lyman Abbott about an Outlook piece alleging misuse of government privilege.

headline: Setting Kennan straight
summary: Roosevelt writes George Kennan a long letter correcting a misleading article about the Portsmouth peace, rich with background on how the settlement came about.

headline: Preparing for the Southern trip
summary: Roosevelt meets Grosvenor on finance bills and sees callers including Baron Rosen and John McIlhenny, who will join the coming Southern tour. Oscar Straus and Root come to lunch.

headline: Department heads get firing power
summary: An executive order lets Cabinet department heads remove employees. Roosevelt talks Philippines business with Sereno Payne and writes William Murphy that he wants no part of the so-called Roosevelt Home Club.

headline: Off on a Southern tour
summary: Roosevelt sets out with Edith, Dr. Rixey, J. C. Greenaway, Maurice Latta and others on a speaking swing through the South. He speaks at Fredericksburg, Ashland and Richmond, Virginia, then rolls on overnight toward Raleigh. Nephew Sheffield Cowles turns 7.

headline: Railroads and forests in North Carolina
summary: At Raleigh, Roosevelt speaks on railroad regulation and forestry, then stops at Greensboro, Durham, Salisbury and High Point. In Charlotte, Edith is welcomed by local women, among them Stonewall Jackson's widow.

headline: Visiting his mother's girlhood home
summary: Roosevelt and Edith visit Bulloch Hall in Roswell, Georgia, where his mother Mittie grew up. He meets Mam Grace and Daddy William, once enslaved on the plantation, and finds the house familiar from Mittie's stories though he had never seen it. He speaks in Atlanta; Edith heads back to Washington.

headline: Canal talk in Jacksonville
summary: In Jacksonville, Roosevelt speaks about the Panama Canal. That evening in St. Augustine he sits through a banquet with a string of six short speeches he found tiresome. Edith writes Kermit about her part of the trip.

headline: A swim in the Florida surf
summary: After church and a drive around St. Augustine with the mayor, Roosevelt takes a launch out to the island with Dr. Rixey, William Loeb and two Rough Riders and swims in the surf. He writes Ethel about the day and leaves that evening for Mobile.

headline: Telling Harriman to slow Alice's train
summary: Roosevelt is in Mobile. Alice lands in San Francisco from Yokohama and boards a special train east that E. H. Harriman hopes will set a coast-to-coast record. TR wires Harriman to ease off; the train breaks the record anyway.

headline: Speaking at Tuskegee
summary: Roosevelt addresses Tuskegee Institute on citizenship, then speaks in Montgomery and Birmingham.

headline: Denouncing lynching in Little Rock
summary: In Little Rock, Arkansas, Roosevelt gives a speech condemning lynching.

headline: New Orleans, then home by sea
summary: Roosevelt speaks and holds a reception in New Orleans, then boards the cruiser West Virginia that afternoon for the voyage back to Washington.

headline: A 47th birthday at sea
summary: Roosevelt marks his 47th birthday aboard the West Virginia. Alice gets back to Washington from four months in Asia, 20 pounds lighter, with the homeward leg from Yokohama done in a record 13 days. In New York, his birthplace on East 20th Street opens as a private museum.

headline: Steaming north
summary: Roosevelt is still at sea on the West Virginia, bound for Washington.

headline: Another day at sea
summary: The West Virginia continues north with Roosevelt aboard.

headline: Something troubling Alice
summary: Roosevelt is still aboard the West Virginia. In Washington, Edith tells Kermit that Alice seems careworn and worried but won't say why.

headline: Alice is engaged to Nick Longworth
summary: Roosevelt lands back in Washington and confers with Jusserand. Scribner's runs his "Wolf Hunt in Oklahoma." Around this time Alice finally tells Edith she is engaged to Congressman Nicholas Longworth, breaking the news while Edith brushes her teeth, as Nick asks TR for her hand downstairs. Both parents are delighted.

headline: Back from the South, catching up
summary: Roosevelt meets Root, Minister Takahira and Representative Tawney, then lunches with Jusserand and Joseph Bishop. He tells Kermit he enjoyed the Southern trip, has heard Alice's travel tales, rides and walks with Edith and the dog Skip, and admires the boys' pumpkin giant.

headline: Birthday wishes from Hungarian Republicans
summary: Roosevelt talks rate legislation with Senators Cullom and Dolliver. Hungarian-American Republicans from New York stop by with late birthday greetings, and the poet Madison Cawein is among his lunch guests.

headline: Prince Louis of Battenberg arrives
summary: After a Cabinet meeting and a rates conference with Vice President Fairbanks, Roosevelt receives Britain's Prince Louis of Battenberg. He lunches with Speck von Sternberg and Root.

headline: State dinner for Battenberg
summary: Roosevelt sees Admiral Dewey and Senator Depew, lunches with Speck von Sternberg, and gives a formal state dinner in honor of Prince Louis of Battenberg. He thanks William Ripley for articles including one on his railway policy in The Atlantic Monthly.

headline: The Equitable inquiry
summary: At 9 p.m., Roosevelt confers with Paul Morton about the investigation of the Equitable Life Assurance Society.

headline: Greek-style coins and a trip to vote
summary: Roosevelt discusses Cuban sanitation with Cullom and the atrocities in Russia with Oscar Straus and Root, and lunches with Prince Louis of Battenberg. He sends Augustus Saint-Gaudens ideas for the new U.S. coins and leaves at midnight for Oyster Bay to vote.

headline: Election Day in Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt casts his vote in Oyster Bay and heads back to Washington.

headline: Cheered by the election results
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge and Senator Beveridge of his pleasure at Republican wins, and sends George Otto Trevelyan three books he admires. He also takes up Oklahoma statehood and Panama conditions.

headline: Delaware politics and the tariff
summary: Roosevelt confers on Delaware politics with Senator Allee and lunches with Nevada Stranahan and Root. He writes Senator Allison about revising the tariff.

headline: No fan of Jerome
summary: Roosevelt talks Southern politics with John McLaurin and Judge Emory Speer. Writing to Nicholas Murray Butler about the New York district attorney's office, he makes clear he dislikes William Travers Jerome.

headline: Booker T. Washington at noon
summary: Booker T. Washington calls on Roosevelt at midday. TR tells editor Robert Bridges how much he enjoyed Ellen Velvin's new book about wild animals, and writes Paul Morton about Shonts and the Canal Zone.

headline: Selous comes to stay
summary: The famed African hunter Frederick Selous dines with Roosevelt and spends the night. TR writes Ted about playing football and about social life at Harvard.

headline: Scrambling through the woods with Selous
summary: Roosevelt takes Selous on one of his cross-country scrambles joined by Pinchot, Garfield, Bob Bacon and Ambassador Meyer. The hunter entertains Ethel, Archie and Quentin with lion and hyena stories and stays for dinner, while Edith is away in New York.

headline: Coins like ancient Greece
summary: After a Cabinet meeting and lunch with Shonts, Roosevelt dines at Secretary Root's. He writes Augustus Saint-Gaudens again, urging that the new coins look like those of ancient Greece.

headline: Susan B. Anthony calls
summary: Susan B. Anthony visits Roosevelt late in the morning. He also confers with Senator Platt and William Barnes on New York patronage and hears Massachusetts shoe manufacturers on the tariff. Philip Stewart and his family settle in at the White House.

headline: Pure food and insurance
summary: In a packed day, Roosevelt confers on railroads with Charles Mellen, on pure food legislation with Senator McCumber, and on the life insurance inquiry with John Dryden. Historian James Ford Rhodes dines with Root and Taft and stays on, as do the Stewarts.

headline: Calling for Odell's ouster
summary: After Cabinet and talks on the tariff and railroads, Roosevelt hosts a White House dinner and musicale with Baron Rosen, Commander Sims and Justice Brewer. He tells Nevada Stranahan that Benjamin Odell should lose his post as New York Republican leader.

headline: Correcting a misquote
summary: Representatives Hepburn and Hopkins, Senator Cullom and Speaker Cannon call. Roosevelt writes Paul Morton about Shonts, John Allison about economic manipulation, and Henry Whitney to say he was misquoted on reciprocity.

headline: A pig for Quentin's birthday
summary: Quentin turns 8 and is given a live pig by Oscar Straus. Roosevelt writes Kermit about racing and playing hide-and-seek with Archie's football team, his frequent tennis with Jusserand, and Nicholas Nickleby. He congratulates Ted on his first Harvard game and hopes his grades rise.

headline: Mapping the rate bill
summary: Roosevelt gathers Cabinet officers Root, Knox and Moody with Cullom, Hepburn, Mann and Prouty to plan railroad rate legislation, then talks Pennsylvania and New York politics, the latter over dinner with Governor Frank Higgins. He writes Baker on the rate bill and Senator Fulton on Oregon land frauds.

headline: At the Sims wedding
summary: At noon Roosevelt attends the wedding of Lieutenant Commander William Sims and Anne Hitchcock. He names Charles Wolverton a district judge in Oregon and sends Brander Matthews a playful letter about his review of Edwin Arlington Robinson.

headline: What the rate bill must do
summary: Roosevelt sets out for Ray Stannard Baker his views on rail rate regulation and the goals the coming bill must meet. He confers with Senator Heyburn on Idaho appointments and lunches with Henry Taft and Moody.

headline: Osage affairs and Chinese exclusion
summary: Roosevelt confers with Frantz and Commissioner Leupp on Osage Indian affairs. He writes T. C. Friedlander about the exclusion of Chinese immigrants and bias against them, Secretary Shaw on German tariff changes, and Senator Platt about Olcott.

headline: Ted breaks his nose against Yale
summary: Roosevelt assures Yale coach Walter Camp that Ted came through the Yale game without serious harm, though Ted in fact broke his nose. The day also brings a Cabinet meeting, a diplomatic reception, and letters on coinage, insurance law and the Republican chairmanship.

headline: Letting the Dominicans fight it out
summary: Roosevelt has the Navy told not to stop arms moving by sea between Dominican ports; he will let the factions fight as long as foreign lives and property are left alone. He writes Platt on picking a fair New York chairman and Root on Japan's protectorate over Korea. It is Bamie's 10th wedding anniversary.

headline: No entry
summary: Nothing is recorded beyond Roosevelt's presence in Washington.

headline: Lunch with Mark Twain
summary: Mark Twain joins Roosevelt at lunch with Speck von Sternberg, Moody and Bonaparte. TR works New York party politics with Root and Olcott, writes Pinchot on the open-range grazing problem, and holds a late conference. Edith tells Aunt Lizzie that Alice is truly in love.

headline: Neither demagogue nor corruptionist
summary: After a Cabinet meeting and a talk with Senator Dolliver on railroad legislation, Roosevelt writes Ray Stannard Baker that he despises demagogues as much as the corrupt and wants a rate law that will stand up in court.

headline: Lunch with Beveridge
summary: Senators Beveridge and Foraker, Representative Lacey, Root and Bonaparte call. Roosevelt lunches with Beveridge, his old Buffalo friend Ansley Wilcox, and a Mr. Winsor.

headline: Thanksgiving at Pine Knot
summary: Roosevelt leaves in the morning for Albemarle County, Virginia, to spend Thanksgiving with the family at Pine Knot, near Plain Dealing. Unable to attend Mark Twain's 70th birthday dinner at Delmonico's, he sends regrets. He asks Root to find a capable Black candidate for the Freetown, Sierra Leone post.

headline: Leaving Pine Knot
summary: After the Thanksgiving holiday at Pine Knot in Albemarle County, Virginia, Roosevelt heads back to Washington in the evening.

headline: Army-Navy game and three water projects
summary: On his and Edith's 19th wedding anniversary, Roosevelt watches Army play Navy at Princeton. The same day brings three new federal reclamation projects: Rio Grande and Carlsbad in New Mexico and Okanogan in Washington.

headline: Sunday evening callers
summary: At 9 p.m. Roosevelt receives Robert Bacon, William Willcox, Elbert Baldwin, Mrs. John Van Voorst and a Mr. Quellenec.

headline: The 59th Congress opens
summary: The 59th Congress gathers. Roosevelt talks New York politics with Olcott and that evening sees Chief Justice Fuller, Justice Holmes and Alexander Graham Bell. The Umatilla project in Oregon is approved, and TR tells Moody wood pulp should carry no tariff.

headline: A tougher Annual Message
summary: Roosevelt sends Congress his fifth Annual Message, a more forceful document pressing for railroad rate regulation and pure food laws. He also holds Cabinet, lunches with Brooks Adams, and sees Minister Takahira at night; Nicholas Murray Butler is a White House guest.

headline: A gift of Sully's Memoirs
summary: Roosevelt thanks Paul d'Estournelles de Constant for an early printing of the Duke of Sully's memoirs, a gift from the French government in gratitude for his help keeping peace with Germany. He also confers on Brooklyn patronage and on health in the Philippines with Dr. Gorgas, and dines with Lodge, Nick Longworth and others.

headline: Saving the golden trout
summary: Roosevelt writes David Starr Jordan about the golden trout named for him, a fish he had worked to protect. He tells Selous how much the family enjoyed his visit and demands that Charles McClelland account for his insurance dealings.

headline: A marshal's badge for a Rough Rider
summary: After Cabinet and a tariff talk, Roosevelt writes Senator Clarence Clark about naming Ben Daniels, a former Rough Rider and Western lawman, as a U.S. marshal. A musicale fills the evening.

headline: Seth Bullock comes to lunch
summary: Roosevelt confers with Beveridge on statehood, then sits down to lunch with two old Western friends, Seth Bullock and William Llewellyn, plus General Thomas and Nick Longworth. Booker T. Washington calls at 9 p.m., followed by Moody, Brownlow and Hale.

headline: William Barnes calls
summary: Sunday evening callers at the White House include New York Republican William Barnes.

headline: Ultimatum to the Storers
summary: In separate letters to Bellamy and Maria Storer, Roosevelt ends their meddling in Vatican affairs: they must stop writing Rome on Catholic matters and misrepresenting U.S. policy, or Bellamy loses his post as ambassador in Vienna. TR also meets labor leaders Mitchell and Gompers on Chinese exclusion.

headline: Carnegie and the Yakima project
summary: The Yakima reclamation project in Washington is approved. After Cabinet, Roosevelt discusses insurance legislation with Representative Landis and meets William Sulzer and immigration inspector Marcus Braun; Andrew Carnegie is among his callers.

headline: Dinner with Charles Freer
summary: Roosevelt discusses irrigation with Senators Smoot and Sutherland and canal business with Joseph Bishop. Nick's mother, Mrs. Longworth, comes to lunch, and art collector Charles Freer dines with the Lodges, the Holmeses and Mrs. Gardner.

headline: Alice's engagement made public
summary: The White House announces that Alice will marry Congressman Nicholas Longworth of Cincinnati on February 17, 1906. Roosevelt also writes Lyman Abbott about how party politics is tangling both the rate bill and the Dominican treaty, and Jacob Schiff about Russian Jews.

headline: A customs post for Bill Sewall
summary: Roosevelt proposes his old Maine guide Bill Sewall for a customs collectorship, thanks the Provençal poet Frédéric Mistral for a copy of Mirèio, and writes Moody denying any shielding of Paul Morton in the Equitable affair. The Strawberry Valley project in Utah is approved.

headline: Snowball fights behind the White House
summary: Snow falls, and Archie, Quentin, cousin Sheffield Cowles and Helen Elliott go sledding and pelt each other with snowballs behind the White House. Roosevelt's article "Federal Social Legislation" appears in Charities and the Commons, and he confers on Santo Domingo and the canal.

headline: Sunday supper with Major Wadsworth
summary: At 7:30 Roosevelt sups with Major W. A. Wadsworth, and later sees Senators Allison and Hale, Theodore Shonts and Joseph Bishop.

headline: Urging Selous to write
summary: Roosevelt meets Senator Kittredge, Shonts, Moody and Taft about pay for canal workers, and lunches with editor Richard Watson Gilder. He urges Frederick Selous to put his big-game knowledge into a book.

headline: A gift for his childhood nurse
summary: Roosevelt sends a $20 check, by way of Corinne, to Dora "Dolly" Watkins, his nurse as a boy. Joseph Bishop is named to the Canal Commission, and TR writes a stack of letters, thanking Admiral Togo for a revolver and denying he called Argentines superior to other South Americans.

headline: A win over Odell
summary: Roosevelt tells Herbert Parsons that Wadsworth has been picked over Merritt for New York Assembly Speaker, a setback for Odell. He asks Bonaparte to circulate an article on the Russo-Japanese naval fighting so it can shape U.S. ship design.

headline: Cabinet dinner as Congress recesses
summary: Congress breaks for the holidays, and Roosevelt hosts a Cabinet dinner; Eliot Gregory and Paul Morton stay the night. He tells Shonts a Mr. Sullivan is wrong to think William Cromwell ever had his confidence, and writes Secretary Wilson on saving Western grazing lands.

headline: Hide-and-seek with the children
summary: Roosevelt and the children chase one another through the mansion in a game of hide-and-seek. He talks Wyoming forest reserves with Senator Warren, sees Whitelaw Reid, and goes with Edith to a dinner in their honor given by Vice President Fairbanks.

headline: Dinner with the Hoosier poet
summary: Roosevelt confers on Brooklyn patronage and canal business, lunches with the Fairbankses and two Japanese visitors, Commander Takeshita and Mr. Kitagaki, and dines with James Whitcomb Riley and the Vice President.

headline: Christmas Eve callers
summary: On Christmas Eve, Roosevelt discusses New York politics with James Wadsworth Jr. and Commissioner Cooley, then sees Ambassador Jusserand and later Francis Leupp.

headline: Christmas at the White House
summary: The Roosevelts spend Christmas Day in Washington.

headline: Overruling Lucius Swift
summary: Roosevelt meets Root, Taft and Bonaparte in the afternoon. He tells Indiana reformer Lucius Swift that he will name Rothschild, Senator Beveridge's choice, surveyor of customs despite Swift's objections.

headline: Off to Pine Knot for the holidays
summary: Roosevelt receives Peru's new minister at 10 a.m., then leaves with the family for Pine Knot, their cabin in Albemarle County, Virginia.

headline: At Pine Knot
summary: The Roosevelts are at Pine Knot in the Virginia countryside; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Another day at Pine Knot
summary: The family remains at Pine Knot; no events are noted.

headline: Steunenberg assassinated in Idaho
summary: While Roosevelt is at Pine Knot, Harry Orchard, a Western Federation of Miners man, kills former Idaho Governor Frank Steunenberg.

headline: Home to Washington
summary: Roosevelt returns to Washington and sees Senator Eugene Hale at 10 p.m.

headline: New Year's reception
summary: Roosevelt greets the public at the White House New Year's reception from late morning into early afternoon, and sees British Ambassador Durand that night. He praises Charles Larned's article on the Army, which called for better pay.

headline: Wadsworth wins the Speakership
summary: Roosevelt wires Herbert Parsons to stand firm for James Wadsworth against Hamilton Fish's man, Wainwright. Wadsworth becomes Speaker of the New York Assembly, a clear victory for TR. The day also brings Cabinet and a stream of senators.

headline: Advice to a new Speaker
summary: Roosevelt talks statehood with Beveridge and confers with Grosvenor, then attends a Cabinet dinner at Secretary Root's. He sends counsel to James Wadsworth on his new job and writes Governor Higgins about Odell.

headline: The Hepburn rate bill goes in
summary: Congress returns, and Representative Hepburn's railroad rate bill is put before the House. Roosevelt's lunch table includes Herbert Parsons, Lloyd Griscom, Butler, Reid and Speck von Sternberg, and hosts the diplomatic reception that night.

headline: Lunch with Mr. Dooley's creator
summary: Humorist Finley Peter Dunne joins Roosevelt for lunch with Taft, Root, Jusserand and others. That evening TR takes up the Naval Personnel Bill with four Cabinet members; Butler stays over.

headline: The coinage is his pet project
summary: Roosevelt tells Augustus Saint-Gaudens that the new coinage is a project close to his heart and that he dislikes the Mint's objections to the designs. He also discusses canal labor with Shonts and J. B. Harris, Black appointments with Charles Anderson, and sees Alexander Graham Bell.

headline: Stimson for the trust cases
summary: Roosevelt writes Senator Platt that he wants Henry L. Stimson named district attorney to prosecute the American Sugar Refining Company and the New York Central Railroad under the Elkins Act.

headline: A special message on the canal
summary: Roosevelt sends Congress a special message on the Panama Canal and receives the American Bar Association's commission. He writes Leonard Wood with concern over a head wound, asks John Pitcher whether John Goff was mauled by a lion, and tells Luke Wright he wants him as Minister to Japan.

headline: No third term
summary: Roosevelt gives Lincoln Steffens free rein to investigate the executive branch. Writing Jeter Pritchard, he denies any shift toward a whites-only Republican policy in the South and flatly rules out a third term.

headline: A Medal of Honor at the White House
summary: Roosevelt pins the Medal of Honor on James Robb Church, the first such award handed out at the White House under the formal ceremony TR had ordered. He also makes Henry Stimson the federal prosecutor in Manhattan and addresses the American Medical Association.

headline: Diplomatic dinner
summary: Roosevelt hears Dominican property holders on the Santo Domingo treaty and discusses the Philippine tariff bill with E. J. Hill. The White House hosts a diplomatic dinner, and he writes Root on Venezuela and Taft on Army camps and the Chinese boycott.

headline: Schiff hurt, not helped
summary: After Cabinet and a talk with Watson about tariffs on Philippine goods, Roosevelt writes Butler again about Jacob Schiff's January 4 speech attacking U.S. finance policy, which he thinks did harm.

headline: A lock canal, and gifts for Alice
summary: Roosevelt writes Kermit that he favors a lock canal over a sea-level one at Panama, that he often rides and walks with Edith, and that wedding gifts for Alice are starting to come in. He sends along a pin given him by Oklahoma ranchmen.

headline: Meeting New York's postmaster
summary: Roosevelt confers with William Willcox, postmaster of New York.

headline: Jane Addams and Steffens drop in
summary: Roosevelt discusses New York politics with Herbert Parsons and the canal inquiry with Senator Kittredge. Among a crowd of visitors are reformers Jane Addams and Lincoln Steffens.

headline: Algeciras opens; Perdicaris visits
summary: The Algeciras Conference on the Franco-German quarrel over Morocco opens in Spain, a meeting Roosevelt helped arrange, with Henry White there to guide it. That afternoon Ion Perdicaris, the kidnap victim of 1904, calls with his wife. The House passes the Philippine tariff bill.

headline: Sevier National Forest created
summary: Roosevelt establishes the Sevier National Forest in Utah. In a packed day he confers on Alaska, railroad rates and the Hague Conference and lunches with Taft and Herbert Parsons.

headline: Arizona and New Mexico as one
summary: On Bamie's 51st birthday, Roosevelt tells Benjamin Ide Wheeler he hopes to bring the Arizona and New Mexico territories in together as a single state, since separate admission would take years. He meets Spooner on the Dominican treaty and a Puerto Rico delegation, and hosts the judiciary reception.

headline: Luke Wright to Tokyo
summary: Roosevelt appoints Luke E. Wright U.S. ambassador to Japan after a Cabinet meeting. His brother-in-law Douglas Robinson is staying at the White House.

headline: Dewey and the senators
summary: Roosevelt confers with Senator Elkins on rate legislation, and separately with Admiral Dewey, Senators Frye and Spooner and Representative McCall. Root, Hitchcock and Alger also call.

headline: Brooklyn patronage and Steffens
summary: On a Sunday, Roosevelt talks Brooklyn appointments with Timothy Woodruff, and Lincoln Steffens stops by.

headline: The comfort of books
summary: Roosevelt asks the Army's General Staff whether a war plan against Venezuela should be drafted and urges Leonard Wood to think about fortifying Hawaii given Japan's ambitions. To Trevelyan he writes that liking every sort of book is a great comfort and that reading rests him from work.

headline: Against coolie labor
summary: After Cabinet and a meeting with Speaker Cannon and Representative Humphrey, Roosevelt writes Whitelaw Reid that he opposes bringing Chinese coolie labor into the United States. Attorney General Moody gives a dinner for TR and Edith.

headline: Praise for Jane Addams
summary: Roosevelt receives China's imperial commissioners and talks Far Eastern matters with Paul Morton. He tells Jane Addams he admires her kind of reformer, writes Leupp about coal lands on Choctaw and Chickasaw reservations, and defends the Hague Conference to Ian Hamilton.

headline: Dinner for the Supreme Court
summary: Roosevelt works the statehood bill with a number of congressmen, lunches with Bowdoin president William DeWitt Hyde, and gives the justices of the Supreme Court an evening dinner.

headline: Bribes in the Beef Trust case
summary: Roosevelt writes Moody about bribes the meatpackers used to try to influence the government's Beef Trust prosecution and Senator Aldrich about tribal funds going to church-run Indian schools. He meets on trade with Asia and hosts a 32-guest dinner; Hugo Münsterberg calls.

headline: A Gridiron Club evening
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Dryden and Governor Stokes, sees C. E. Smith and Overstreet, and goes to the Gridiron Club's dinner at the Willard Hotel. He tells Ted he is glad his Harvard work has improved.

headline: Explaining the muck-rake speech to Steffens
summary: With canal money, the Hepburn rate bill, the Philippine tariff, the Dominican treaty and joint statehood all pending in Congress, Roosevelt sees Senator La Follette at 9:30 p.m. and then Lincoln Steffens, to whom he explains the thinking behind his Gridiron remarks.

headline: Fighting Joe Wheeler's funeral
summary: Roosevelt goes to General Joseph Wheeler's funeral, confers with Representative Keifer, and hosts an evening musicale.

headline: Riis comes to stay
summary: Roosevelt confers with Governor Charles Magoon on Panama and sees Lincoln Steffens again. Jacob Riis is a White House guest, and Secretary Cortelyou gives a dinner for TR and Edith. He tells French Chadwick a new President and Congress ought to take office together at New Year's.

headline: Pearls, tapestries and popcorn
summary: Gifts pour in for Alice and Nick: a Gobelin tapestry from France's president, embroidered gold cloth from Japan's emperor, a $25,000 pearl necklace from Cuba, a Saint-Gaudens bronze, an Italian mosaic table and a hogshead of popcorn. Alice turns nothing down. The Senate begins to move on the Hepburn bill.

headline: Reinstating a midshipman
summary: Roosevelt tells Representative George Foss he is letting Midshipman John Paul Miller return to the Naval Academy, though hazing ordinarily meant automatic dismissal. He also writes Meyer about French jitters over German demands at Algeciras and confers on rate legislation and Wisconsin patronage.

headline: A ride with Edith
summary: Roosevelt and Edith go riding. He discusses Government Printing Office business with Representative Landis, and Douglas and Corinne Robinson stay at the White House for a dinner and musicale.

headline: Harvard '80 at the White House
summary: Roosevelt hosts a dinner for his Harvard Class of 1880. Ted arrives from college and rides with his father, who writes Kermit about David Copperfield and his fondness for Thackeray. He presses the Storers for answers to his December letters.

headline: Kermit's amber beads
summary: Edith writes Kermit that Alice wears the amber beads he sent as a wedding present constantly; he had paid $50 for them at Fisher's.

headline: A report on the Pennsylvania Railroad
summary: The Interstate Commerce Commission's report on alleged antitrust violations by the Pennsylvania Railroad goes to the House. Taft, Speaker Cannon and three senators call on Roosevelt.

headline: Lunch with John Burroughs
summary: Roosevelt lunches with naturalists John Burroughs and C. Hart Merriam and Major John Pitcher. A letter of his to Congress on Annapolis hazing is made public, and he complains to Steffens that the Senate killed the Santo Domingo treaty along party lines.

headline: Artillery and the rate bill
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Dr. Alexander Lambert and Secretary Metcalf and dines with Robert Wynne. He writes Senator Knox backing better training for coast and field artillery and urging that the rate bill become law.

headline: The House passes the Hepburn bill
summary: The House of Representatives approves the Hepburn railroad rate bill, a key piece of Roosevelt's program. He also meets House naval committee members about hazing at Annapolis, hosts the Army-Navy reception, and writes Francis Heney about corruption in San Francisco.

headline: Ray Stannard Baker at lunchtime
summary: Roosevelt sees journalist Ray Stannard Baker at 12:45, confers with Senators Depew and Platt and editor Edward Butler on Buffalo jobs and on rates with Elkins, and gives a dinner for the Republican National Executive Committee.

headline: Indian Key bird reservation
summary: Roosevelt creates the Indian Key bird reservation in Florida. He meets a National Businessmen's League delegation, sees Jusserand, and warns Bonaparte and Taft that ammunition stocks would fall short in a war.

headline: Sunday night senators
summary: Senators John Spooner and George Nixon call on Roosevelt at 9 p.m.

headline: Alice turns 22; Bill Sewall at lunch
summary: On Alice's 22nd birthday, Roosevelt lunches with his old Maine guide Bill Sewall, Guy Murchie and Taft, and the White House throws a dinner and musicale in her honor. In a lengthy letter to John St. Loe Strachey he covers presidential power and free trade and describes Nick as a fine fellow and Harvard's best violinist.

headline: Relief for famine-struck Japan
summary: Roosevelt calls on Americans to help the people of Japan, then suffering a famine. He spends part of the day lunching and walking with John Burroughs, and tells Dr. Lambert he cannot write Wadsworth and Higgins about legislation.

headline: A treaty to protect Niagara Falls
summary: Roosevelt writes Root about a treaty with Canada to preserve Niagara Falls. He meets Bonaparte, receives members of the Dawes Commission among many callers, and writes Nevada Stranahan about Higgins and Odell.

headline: A dinner for the groom
summary: Two days before the wedding, the White House gives a dinner for Nick Longworth. Booker T. Washington is among the day's visitors, and Roosevelt lunches with Moody and Crane.

headline: Short on smokeless powder
summary: On the eve of Alice's wedding, Roosevelt warns Bonaparte that the Army and Navy lack enough smokeless powder and writes John Hull about funding military training. He hears a Massachusetts group on pure food legislation and dines with Endicott and Fannie Peabody.

headline: Alice marries Nick Longworth
summary: At noon on a clear, mild day, Alice Roosevelt, 22, marries Congressman Nicholas Longworth, 36, in the East Room before roughly 700 guests, with no bridesmaids. Her Lee grandparents are there, as are Sara Delano Roosevelt and young Franklin. Afterward Alice hugs Edith, and the couple leave to honeymoon in Cuba.

headline: Quiet after the wedding
summary: The day after the wedding, Roosevelt confers in the evening with Charles Stillings and Gifford Pinchot. Douglas and Corinne Robinson are staying at the White House.

headline: A lock canal, not sea level
summary: Roosevelt tells Congress he favors building a lock canal at Panama rather than a sea-level one. He meets railroad men and regulators on the rate bill, writes Speaker Cannon on the Knapp amendments, and Root sends Germany TR's specific proposals for Algeciras.

headline: Dinner at the Willard
summary: After Cabinet and a railroad session with Knox and Spooner, Roosevelt and Edith go to a dinner in their honor given by Agriculture Secretary James Wilson at the Willard. He writes William Ripley and Representative Edmund Hinshaw about the rate bill.

headline: Admiral Togo's words for U.S. sailors
summary: Roosevelt has the speech Admiral Togo gave his Japanese sailors reprinted for American sailors to read. He holds a string of rate-bill meetings, lunches with Bishop William Doane and Mrs. Doane, and writes Archbishop John Ireland about the Storers' indiscretions.

headline: Hold the Hepburn bill as written
