summary: Roosevelt sees Lincoln Steffens in the morning and Speck von Sternberg at 6, and dines with Lodge. He tells Pennsylvania Railroad president Alexander Cassatt he wants the Hepburn bill passed unamended, and presses for stricter medical screening of immigrants arriving at Ellis Island. In Chicago, Taft argues for a standing army.

headline: Ted on probation
summary: Roosevelt learns Ted has been put on academic probation at Harvard and writes him to buckle down, confident he can do it. He also defends Lodge to Lyman Abbott after The Outlook branded the senator a Massachusetts boss.

headline: Probing the immigration bureau
summary: Roosevelt names Ralph Easley, Jeremiah Jenks and James Reynolds to investigate the immigration bureau, and asks Francis Robbins to help prevent a coal strike. He also works on the German tariff and a ship subsidy bill.

headline: The Times takes aim
summary: Roosevelt writes John Sleicher that the Hepburn bill has moved to the Senate and that the New York Times is mocking him over it.

headline: Sun River project in Montana
summary: The Sun River reclamation project in Montana is created. Roosevelt meets Senator Elkins about rail regulation and with Lodge on the Philippine tariff and statehood. He also tears into Carl Schurz's ideas in a letter to Oscar Straus on Morocco and Germany.

headline: Thanking King Edward
summary: Roosevelt writes King Edward VII to thank him for his gift to Alice, adding words about Nick and the Russo-Japanese War. He asks Speaker Cannon for a new canal commission law and meets a long list of callers, among them England's Count Gleichen.

headline: Writing on factory laws
summary: The Ladies' Home Journal prints a Roosevelt article on factory laws protecting working women and children.

headline: Rail bill talks and a dinner for diplomats
summary: Roosevelt opens the day with Senator Clapp, then huddles with Crane and Spooner over the railroad rate bill and sees Ambassador Jusserand. That night he dines with Choate, Porter, Root, Bacon and Captain Sperry, and writes Whitelaw Reid that France and Germany are deadlocked at Algeciras.

headline: A quiet round with senators
summary: Roosevelt confers with Senator Spooner, receives Flint, Fulton and Warner, and in the afternoon meets Interstate Commerce chairman Knapp and James Garfield.

headline: A christening for the Loeb baby
summary: After a morning of meetings with Lodge, Allison, Cannon, Taft and others, Roosevelt and his wife Edith go to Bishop Satterlee's home for the christening of William Loeb's son. His essay holding up Washington as a model city appears in Charities and the Commons.

headline: Standard Oil report goes public
summary: Roosevelt releases the Bureau of Corporations' findings on Standard Oil and sees Secretary Taft in the morning. Edith writes Kermit that Ted's slipping grades at Harvard have come at a bad time for his father.

headline: Storer is asked to resign
summary: Roosevelt formally asks Bellamy Storer to step down as ambassador in Vienna after Storer leaves his letters unanswered. He also asks Congress for more Army and Navy ammunition, sits for artist Helen Todd Hammond with Edith, and spends the evening at the Belasco Theatre.

headline: Lunch talk on the Chinese indemnity
summary: After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt lunches with Root, Taft, Elkins, Lawrence Abbott and the missionary Arthur Smith, among others.

headline: Mourning General Schofield
summary: Roosevelt goes to St. John's Church for General John Schofield's funeral after a busy morning on Puerto Rico and the railroad bill. In letters he weighs Harvard football and talk that he might one day lead the university, and admits he does not care for Mahan's latest history of the 1812 conflict.

headline: Speaking to the lumber dealers
summary: Roosevelt addresses a delegation of the National Lumber Dealers Association, receives the justices of the Supreme Court and sees Jusserand. In the evening he and Loeb take up the Tillman-Gillespie resolution, and Root and Archbold call late.

headline: Archie stands by a hurt classmate
summary: At school Archie stays to help a boy struck in the eye by a baseball after the others flee. Roosevelt meets his Cabinet, Knox and Hopkins on the canal, and writes Edward Bacon about changes to the Hepburn bill. In Idaho, Haywood, Moyer and Pettibone are indicted in the Steunenberg murder.

headline: A short telegram to Gordon Johnson
summary: Roosevelt goes over Panama Canal progress with Senators Dryden and Ankeny and talks statehood with Beveridge. He wires Gordon Johnson, wounded in the Philippines, a short question.

headline: Letters about the boys in the sandbox
summary: Gordon Johnson wires back that he is well. Roosevelt sends Nannie Lodge a playful note about dinner talk and writes Kermit about how unlike Quentin and Archie are, the baseball episode, and the hours both boys spend in the sandbox.

headline: Weighing a Supreme Court pick
summary: Roosevelt talks over a Supreme Court appointment with Root and Taft, takes up statehood with Cannon and Watson, and receives the Chinese minister. He writes Agriculture Secretary Wilson about investigating the meatpackers in the wake of Upton Sinclair's The Jungle.

headline: Boston Symphony at the National
summary: After the Cabinet meeting and a talk with Spooner about the Tillman-Gillespie measure, Roosevelt and Edith go to the National Theatre to hear the visiting Boston orchestra. He backs New Mexico governor Hagerman for ousting dishonest officials.

headline: Talking consular reform at the White House
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Alice and Nick Longworth and a table of diplomats and friends, then speaks at the White House to delegates of the Consular Reform Convention. He writes Baron Kaneko about the Portsmouth treaty and Count Witte's careless handling of documents.

headline: A moral standard for the very rich
summary: With Edith away at Groton for Kermit's confirmation, Roosevelt dines at the Longworths' and writes a flood of letters: to Taft on his choice between the Chief Justiceship and the presidency, to Root naming Charles Francis to replace Storer in Vienna, and to Upton Sinclair on Zola, Tolstoy and The Jungle.

headline: Statehood and supper at the Lodges
summary: Roosevelt meets the Cabinet, presses Speaker Cannon on statehood, and hosts a lunch that includes Will and Bamie Cowles. He takes dinner with the Lodges.

headline: The muck-rake, first told at the Gridiron
summary: Roosevelt meets Admiral Dewey, talks canal matters with Hepburn, and sees the German and French ambassadors. After dining with Speaker Cannon he goes on to the Gridiron Club's dinner at the New Willard, where he first compares a certain breed of journalist to the man with the muck-rake in Pilgrim's Progress. Dr. Rixey calls near midnight.

headline: A blank Sunday
summary: The record shows Roosevelt in Washington with no recorded activity.

headline: Dogs, novels and the Kaiser
summary: Roosevelt meets Dryden, Elkins and Representative Garner on the canal and lunches with the Sternbergs and the Cowleses. He tells Kermit how the dogs Skip and Jack greeted Edith's return and that he has sent for Phineas Finn and De Quincey, and he fumes to Moody over a Debs article on the Haywood case.

headline: Evening with the Keep Commission
summary: After the Cabinet meeting and talks with Elkins and Jusserand, Roosevelt goes to Gifford Pinchot's home at night to meet the Keep Commission, then sees Ambassador Sternberg.

headline: A gift from the King of Italy
summary: The Italian chargé d'affaires delivers a present from King Victor Emmanuel, and Roosevelt then sits down with Samuel Gompers over labor bills. He dines with the Endicotts and Henry Adams.

headline: Pushing the eight-hour law
summary: Roosevelt meets Moody, Taft and Garfield, takes up Smithsonian business with Henderson, and goes to the opera. He thanks Charles Morrison for help on the meatpacking inquiry, tells Frank Morrison he will hold government contractors to the eight-hour day, and urges Moody to move on the alien contract labor question.

headline: Oklahoma lands and evening with Bishop
summary: After Cabinet and a railroad rate session, Roosevelt discusses Oklahoma public lands with Taft, Leupp and Lacey, lunches with Shiras and Holt, and sees both ambassadors. Joseph Bishop calls that night.

headline: The Bristol case
summary: Roosevelt confers with Moody and prosecutor Francis Heney on the Bristol case, receives Olcott, Lacey, Campbell and A. W. Dunn of the Associated Press, and meets Moody, Metcalf and Garfield late in the evening.

headline: Sunday evening callers
summary: Journalist Henry Needham and Postmaster General Cortelyou call on Roosevelt in the evening.

headline: Federal troops and the Idaho trial
summary: Roosevelt hears Charles Neill on breaches of the eight-hour law and writes Moody about using federal soldiers to keep the peace in Idaho during the Haywood trial. Other letters cover Kansas ranchers and the range laws, and charges over Cornelius Bliss's 1904 campaign fundraising.

headline: Settling the Bristol appointment
summary: Roosevelt meets the Cabinet, then gathers Taft, Moody, Knox and others to settle the Bristol appointment. He also discusses Puerto Rico with Representative Cooper and writes Bishop O'Gorman about Storer's removal.

headline: Talk of a giant battleship
summary: Roosevelt receives Spooner, Bartholdt and Foss. He praises Lindsay Denison's Everybody's article on the canal, welcomes Andrew Carnegie's support on the rate bill, and writes Representative Foss about his bill for an enormous battleship.

headline: Lunch with Root and Bacon
summary: Roosevelt hosts Root, Bacon, Governor Hoggatt and others at lunch, and has Senator Beveridge to dinner. He writes Thomas O'Brien about insurance bills.

headline: Upton Sinclair at lunch
summary: The Cabinet meets on the threatened coal strike. Roosevelt talks railroad legislation with Dolliver, has Upton Sinclair to lunch along with Neill and Leupp, and dines with the Longworths.

headline: A coal operator crosses him
summary: Roosevelt holds a big railroad conference with senators and commissioners, takes up New York appointments with Wadsworth and the Five Civilized Tribes bill with La Follette. He writes Theodore Shonts about a coal commission and rebukes John Winder, a coal company president who opposed miners' raises and tried to undercut his conference.

headline: Home alone with Skip and the kittens
summary: With Edith and the younger children in Cuba, Roosevelt writes each of them: Kermit hears he is through volume one of Trollope's Phineas Finn and that the rate fight is heating up; Archie that Skip misses the family and Jack has run off; Quentin that the kittens will be ready to pet when he returns. He also names a new Washington postmaster over Senator Platt's friend.

headline: No expedition to China
summary: Roosevelt confers with Elkins on the Hepburn bill amendment about judicial review and with Winthrop on Puerto Rico, then dines at Henry Adams's. He writes General Wood that he is pleased Wood is well and that no force will go to China.

headline: Earl Grey spends the night
summary: Roosevelt hosts a dinner for Canada's Governor General, Earl Grey, who stays overnight at the White House with Lady Grey and their daughter. He also approves missionary Arthur Smith's idea of putting part of the Boxer indemnity toward scholarships for Chinese students in America.

headline: Railroads for Alaska
summary: Roosevelt works the rate bill with Hepburn and takes up Alaskan railroads with Burnham, Piles, Kinkaid, Ankeny and Tawney. He dines at the Lodges'.

headline: Owen Wister arrives for a visit
summary: Roosevelt receives a group of city mayors led by Chicago's Edward Dunne. In the evening his old friend Owen Wister arrives to stay through Saturday, and they dine with the Bacons and David Gray.

headline: Seth Bullock comes to lunch
summary: Roosevelt meets senators on the rate bill and lunches with Captain Seth Bullock among others. At dinner the table holds the Jusserands, the Longworths, Owen Wister and the Bay Lodges. He tells Lodge the Philippine tariff can wait until the railroad vote.

headline: Boone and Crockett Club dinner
summary: Roosevelt confers with Lacey on public lands, lunches with Moody, Spooner, Wister and others, and meets the Russian envoy Rosen. That night he joins the Boone and Crockett Club at the New Willard.

headline: Sunday with the Danas and the Lodges
summary: Roosevelt shares a midday meal with Richard Henry Dana and Mrs. Dana, sees Ambassador Sternberg, and dines with Dr. Bigelow and the Lodge and Gardner families.

headline: Archie turns twelve; Bat Masterson at lunch
summary: On Archie's twelfth birthday Roosevelt lunches with Taft, the Cowleses, Colonel Sanger and the old lawman Bat Masterson. He signs a bill easing hazing penalties at Annapolis, writes Ray Stannard Baker about his muckrake speech, and asks Gilder to set a date for H. G. Wells to come to lunch.

headline: Saving Niagara Falls
summary: After the Cabinet meeting and a railroad session with Clapp, Nelson and Spooner, Roosevelt talks with Representative Burton about protecting Niagara Falls. He writes Oscar Straus about the plight of Russian Jews.

headline: First ride on Roswell
summary: Roosevelt romps at "tickley" with Archie and Quentin and, with Captain Lee along, tries out his new horse Roswell for the first time. He reassures a jittery Upton Sinclair that the meatpacking abuses will not be swept under the rug.

headline: A St. Bernard puppy for Archie
summary: Roosevelt sees Taft, Cannon, Ambassador Sternberg and others. He writes Kermit about Archie's new St. Bernard puppy, just seven weeks old and the morning walks he and Edith take around the White House grounds.

headline: Railroad bill in every meeting
summary: After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt works the rate bill with Crane, Overman and Nelson and goes over Interior Department matters with Fulton. He writes John Kernan on the same railroad bill.

headline: The muck-rake speech goes public
summary: Roosevelt lays the cornerstone of the new House Office Building and repeats in public his warning against writers who see only the muck. He calls for federal oversight of interstate corporations, presses Congress to pass the Hepburn bill, and backs a progressive inheritance tax. He also talks Indiana politics with Hemenway and ship subsidies with Taft and Humphrey.

headline: Easter Sunday
summary: Roosevelt spends Easter Sunday in Washington; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Easter Egg Roll for children only
summary: The annual Easter Egg Roll fills the White House lawn until one o'clock, and Roosevelt keeps the adults out. He meets Moody and Taft, and his brother-in-law Douglas Robinson calls that night.

headline: Breakfast with cousin Emlen
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts with his cousin Emlen Roosevelt, meets the Cabinet, and takes up the rate bill with Spooner and Simmons. Francis Vinton Greene and James Garfield are among the afternoon callers.

headline: San Francisco shakes and burns
summary: A great earthquake strikes San Francisco before dawn, and fire follows, leveling hundreds of blocks and killing hundreds. In Washington Roosevelt carries on with rate bill meetings, sends Congress a special message on the beef packers' trial, wires California's governor about the disaster, and tells Taft he will send troops to Idaho.

headline: Appealing for San Francisco
summary: Roosevelt calls on the nation to help San Francisco, sees a long list of senators and the German ambassador, and holds a reception for the DAR. On the Senate floor, newcomer Robert La Follette breaks custom by speaking on the Hepburn bill, and many senators walk out.

headline: Cabinet takes up the disaster
summary: The Cabinet devotes its meeting to the San Francisco disaster. Roosevelt confers with Spooner and writes Edgar Wells about Ted at Harvard and Moody about the rate bill.

headline: Muckrake speech reaches print
summary: The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's muckrake address. He spends the morning on the rate bill with four senators, Allison among them, sees Jusserand in the afternoon, and receives Booker T. Washington that evening.

headline: Apple blossoms and a healed eye
summary: Edwin Emerson walks back from the Dutch Reformed Church with Roosevelt. He tells Kermit that Ted is over his eye surgery, the apple trees are in bloom, and Quentin is writing poetry, and writes Mabel Boardman about Red Cross relief for San Francisco.

headline: He will not see Gorky
summary: Roosevelt declines to receive the Russian writer Maxim Gorky. He welcomes Admiral Campion and a party of French naval officers to a reception and dinner, and writes William Potter and Lyman Abbott about his proposed inheritance tax and taxes generally.

headline: Honoring John Paul Jones at Annapolis
summary: Roosevelt leaves Washington for the Naval Academy at Annapolis, where he speaks at the ceremonies for John Paul Jones.

headline: Crediting Jusserand with keeping the peace
summary: Roosevelt takes up San Francisco relief with Senator Flint and sees August Belmont. He writes Mayor Schmitz about the city's recovery, tells Jusserand he believes the ambassador kept France and Germany from war, and introduces F. W. Whitridge to King Edward VII ahead of the Spanish royal wedding.

headline: Answering labor and its critics
summary: Roosevelt meets the Interstate Commerce commissioners Knapp and Prouty on the rate bill, sees Archbishop Messmer and Jusserand, and answers two opposite complaints: one that he is too tough on labor, the other that he favors it and attacks great fortunes.

headline: Long critique of Lady Baltimore
summary: Roosevelt confers with Allison and Cullom and sits for a group photograph by Wiles with Root, Alger and two others. He writes Owen Wister a long letter on his new novel Lady Baltimore, which Edith loved and he found much to fault in, and on Black Americans and the Indianola post office.

headline: Off down the Potomac on the Sylph
summary: Roosevelt talks with Allison about court review in the Hepburn bill, then he and Edith set off for an afternoon cruise on the Sylph. He sends Whitelaw Reid a very long history of the road to the Algeciras conference, sharply doubting British ambassador Durand.

headline: A lonely spot tied to Washington
summary: Aboard the Sylph, Roosevelt and Edith visit a lonely spot linked to George Washington, then in ruins. At home it is his sister Corinne's 24th wedding anniversary.

headline: Archie soaked by the hose
summary: Back in Washington, Roosevelt tells Kermit the White House flowers are blooming and Archie is drenching himself with a hose. He writes Lodge on Egypt, Wood, the anti-imperialists, Cuba and Santo Domingo, and thanks Henry White for his Algeciras work. Congress gives the War Secretary control of water diversion at Niagara Falls.

headline: A power permit in California
summary: After the Cabinet meets, an act lets the Edison Electric company use certain southern California power sites for 40 years, paying rent each year. Roosevelt confers with Moody and Cannon.

headline: Presentation Day at Gallaudet
summary: Roosevelt sees Beveridge, Hopkins, Moody and the Associated Press man A. W. Dunn, then goes to Gallaudet College for its spring ceremonies. He dines with the Cowleses.

headline: A step forward, not a leap
summary: Franklin and Eleanor Roosevelt's daughter Anna is born. Roosevelt receives Japan's new ambassador, Aoki, and writes Brooks Adams that the Hepburn bill moves reform ahead in measured steps that will disappoint the extremists.

headline: Troops quietly sent to Idaho
summary: Roosevelt decides to back the Allison amendment to the rate bill and, without fanfare, sends federal troops into Idaho ahead of the Haywood trial. Columbia's Nicholas Murray Butler and Dr. Bigelow are staying at the White House, and a bootmaker fits the President for new shoes.

headline: Cape May warbler and Mount Vernon
summary: Roosevelt publicly endorses the Hepburn bill with the Allison amendment, then takes Butler aboard the Sylph for a trip to Mount Vernon. He talks New York politics over dinner with Governor Higgins, and tells John Burroughs about a Cape May warbler he has just seen.

headline: A telegram to the Grange
summary: Roosevelt wires the Pennsylvania State Grange at Harrisburg explaining why he supports the Hepburn bill.

headline: Uncle Joe turns seventy
summary: Roosevelt spends the day lobbying a long line of senators on the rate bill and lunches with Albert Shaw. In the evening he joins the crowd at the Arlington Hotel celebrating Uncle Joe Cannon's seventieth. He assures Hannah Schoff, who leads the national mothers' congress, that Mormons have given up polygamy.

headline: Colonel Mosby calls
summary: The Cabinet discusses the California disaster and Secretary Metcalf's trip west. Roosevelt meets Kansas Attorney General Davidson on the Standard Oil cases, receives the old Confederate raider John Mosby, and lunches with James Speyer.

headline: H. G. Wells comes to lunch
summary: Roosevelt meets Upton Sinclair in the morning and lunches with H. G. Wells, then touring America for a newspaper series. The two disagree, but Roosevelt tells Wells that even if nations must decline, he chooses to live as if America will not, and that the effort is worth it.

headline: Permission to punish Quentin
summary: Roosevelt talks New York politics and lunches with Taft. He tells Isaac MacVeagh he will follow his inheritance tax proposal with a graduated income tax, presses Allison on the Philippine tariff, and gives Quentin's teacher at the Force School leave to discipline him.

headline: Too many pension bills
summary: Roosevelt meets the Cabinet and goes over Indian policy with Hitchcock and Leupp. Meanwhile the Senate adopts four Allison amendments to the rate bill, and he grumbles to Senator McCumber about the flood of pension bills in Congress.

headline: Women and children at work
summary: Roosevelt meets labor leaders Gompers and Frank Morrison about breaches of the eight-hour law and a bill to curb injunctions. He asks Commerce and Labor Secretary Metcalf to investigate the labor of women and children, and writes George Horace Lorimer at length about David Graham Phillips's novel The Plum Tree.

headline: Evening call at a servicemen's club
summary: Roosevelt dines with the Lodges, the Lowells and the Luces, confers with Root, Taft and Lodge, and looks in on a club for soldiers, sailors and Marines that evening.

headline: Carl Schurz dies
summary: Carl Schurz, the reformer and former senator, dies. Roosevelt works the rate bill with Allison, Moody and two other senators and writes Allison about Senator Tillman's opposition.

headline: Civil service reformers at the White House
summary: After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt welcomes delegates to the convention of the civil service reformers' league. Garfield and James Reynolds see him at night.

headline: Naval affairs and a stream of senators
summary: Roosevelt goes over naval matters with Representatives Sherman and Cocks, meets Moody and Cortelyou, and receives a run of senators and congressmen.

headline: A wedding in the Harlan family
summary: Roosevelt sees Justice Harlan's granddaughter married and urges the Interstate Commerce Commission to value railroad property, an idea not carried out until 1912.

headline: Hepburn Act clears the Senate
summary: The Senate passes the Hepburn Act, Roosevelt's hard-won railroad rate law, giving the Interstate Commerce Commission power to set railroad and express rates and reach over pipelines and sleeping cars. He meets the Cabinet and sends Gilder a note about a piece on old Irish sagas for The Century.

headline: Waste in the Printing Office
summary: Roosevelt sees Cannon, Hepburn and others. He writes Lodge about the flap involving Chandler, Bailey and Tillman and the rate bill, Charles Keep on inefficiency at Interior and the printing office, and William Curtis on western irrigation.

headline: A samurai suit of armor
summary: Roosevelt writes his sister Bamie that the rate bill passed in fine shape and that Japan's new ambassador, Aoki, has given him a suit of old armor. He writes Ted about Dickens.

headline: Canal news and the Y.M.C.A.
summary: Senator Carter confers with Roosevelt on the Panama Canal among a run of callers. He has Egan, Hyde and Joseph Dunn to lunch and tells canal engineer John Stevens the Y.M.C.A. has sent A. Bruce Minear to Panama.

headline: Cabinet day and callers
summary: Roosevelt meets the Cabinet and receives Shonts, Cannon, Taft, General Wilson, the AP reporter A. W. Dunn and others.

headline: Not behind Beveridge's speech
summary: Roosevelt confers with Senator Aldrich and a long list of callers, and writes Beveridge about press stories claiming the President inspired his speech on meat inspection.

headline: Dinner for Ambassador Aoki
summary: Roosevelt confers on Delaware politics and the Chicago stockyards, lunches with his friend Philip Stewart, and gives a dinner for Japan's Ambassador Aoki with the Forakers, Hales, Lodges and Pellews.

headline: Beveridge offers a meat inspection amendment
summary: Senator Beveridge attaches a meat inspection amendment to the agriculture appropriations bill. Roosevelt meets the Cabinet and confers with Allison, Knox and Hepburn on Panama and the railroads.

headline: Rounding up votes for meat inspection
summary: Roosevelt spends the day in meetings with Cannon, Cullom, Neill and others on the Beveridge plan to inspect meat, lunches with Root, Taft, Nick Longworth and Crane, and writes James Wadsworth about the amendment.

headline: Pushing the immigration bill
summary: Moody and Hitchcock call in the evening. Roosevelt writes Hitchcock about charges against Oklahoma's governor Frantz and Commissioner Cade, and urges Speaker Cannon to pass the immigration bill, which did not pass.

headline: Grieving Carl Schurz
summary: Roosevelt keeps at the beef inspection fight with Beveridge, Neill and Carter. He writes Harry Rubens, once Schurz's secretary, of his sorrow at Carl Schurz's death.

headline: Wichita forest and a trip to Norfolk
summary: Oklahoma gains the new Wichita National Forest, with added land for its game preserve. Roosevelt sails for Norfolk on the Mayflower that afternoon after writing Sinclair, Beveridge, naturalist Henry Bigelow, and Hepburn, whom he wants to be sure the new act can reach Standard Oil and the coal-carrying railroads.

headline: Monument in Portsmouth, speech at Hampton
summary: On Memorial Day in Portsmouth, Virginia, Roosevelt speaks at the dedication of a veterans' monument, then addresses Hampton Institute on the education of Black Americans.

headline: Dinner for Justice Brown
summary: Back in Washington, Roosevelt meets Beveridge, Cannon and two others on beef inspection, lunches with the Sternbergs, and attends a dinner for Justice Henry Brown at the New Willard. He writes Garfield about Standard Oil and the railroad monopolies.

headline: Commencement talk for Howard graduates
summary: Roosevelt meets the Cabinet and works on the meat inspection amendment with Wadsworth, Crumpacker and Reynolds. That evening at the Congregational Church he addresses Howard University's graduating class.

headline: The stockyards report arrives
summary: Roosevelt receives the report of Charles Neill and James Reynolds on conditions in the Chicago stockyards. He sees congressmen and Moody, meets Dr. Egan and Father Zahm in the afternoon, and Senator Penrose at night.

headline: A blank Sunday
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Packinghouse message, and a sprained ankle
summary: Roosevelt sends Congress a special message calling for federal meat inspection, with the Neill-Reynolds findings attached. He breakfasts with Albert Shaw, lunches with Dr. Egan and Father Zahm, and turns his ankle at tennis but keeps playing a couple more sets.

headline: Room to grow for Yosemite
summary: Roosevelt meets the Cabinet, receives the railway special agents' association, and dines with the Lodges. He writes Senator Perkins about enlarging Yosemite National Park and General Wood about Grover Cleveland's vote on the immigration bill.

headline: Schoolgirls in the morning, cadets at night
summary: Roosevelt speaks to the graduating girls of the National Cathedral School in the morning, and in the early evening watches Washington's High School Cadets drill at the American League ball grounds.

headline: Cooper Union visitors
summary: Roosevelt confers with Speaker Cannon, receives a Cooper Union delegation and a run of senators, and in the evening meets Reynolds and Neill again on the packinghouse findings.

headline: The Antiquities Act becomes law
summary: The Antiquities Act passes, giving the President power to proclaim landmarks, ancient ruins and other places of historic or scientific value on federal land as national monuments. Roosevelt meets the Cabinet and Neill on the beef trust, and the Agriculture Department's packinghouse report goes to Congress.

headline: Opening the house at Sagamore Hill
summary: Edith goes ahead to ready Sagamore Hill for summer. Roosevelt tells Kermit his ankle has gotten much worse since Monday's tennis, that Dr. Sturgis Bigelow is visiting amid days of rain, and that he is glad Kermit will stay another year at Groton.

headline: Sunday evening with Lodge
summary: Lodge, Gardner and Metcalf call on Roosevelt late in the evening.

headline: Missing Edith and Sagamore Hill
summary: All national forest land is opened to farm settlement. Roosevelt meets Knox on the canal and Cannon, Beveridge and others on meat inspection, hosts a large lunch with the Tafts, Fairbanks, Garfield and Pinchot, and writes Ethel that he already misses her mother and their Long Island home.

headline: Rebuilding San Francisco
summary: After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt confers with a California delegation about rebuilding San Francisco and with Missourians about packinghouse conditions. He wires Treasury Secretary Shaw, annoyed by Shaw's protectionist speeches in Iowa.

headline: Cartoonist Homer Davenport visits
summary: Roosevelt takes up canal matters with Hepburn, sees several congressmen and Taft, and receives cartoonist Homer Davenport in the morning and Joseph Bishop in the afternoon.

headline: Commencement at Georgetown
summary: Roosevelt discusses Delaware politics with Allee, meets members of the Immigration Protective League, and gives the morning commencement address at Georgetown University.

headline: Beveridge does not speak for him
summary: Roosevelt confers with Cannon, Hopkins and Reynolds and with three congressmen on the meat inspection bill. He writes Wadsworth on the bill and warns Beveridge that nothing he says should be taken as the administration's official view.

headline: Statehood bill approved
summary: Roosevelt signs the Statehood Bill and spends the day on the canal, San Francisco's rebuilding and the Chicago stockyards. He praises Idaho Governor Gooding to Calvin Cobb for pursuing Steunenberg's killers, and explains to Minnie Kimberly why he missed his Uncle Robert's funeral.

headline: Attics and telepathy
summary: Roosevelt writes Ethel about how they both love poking through attics and wonder about mental telepathy, and notes she will teach Sunday school this summer. He writes Tawney about a travel allowance for the President and Platt about a New York appointment he opposes, and confers with Cannon that evening.

headline: A note to Mr. Dooley
summary: Roosevelt meets Allison and Representative Humphrey on beef legislation and lunches with Grant La Farge. He writes Finley Peter Dunne about Mr. Dooley, wires Russell Alger about a lock canal, and writes Platt again on the New York appointment.

headline: Yosemite grows
summary: Roosevelt signs a joint resolution enlarging Yosemite National Park. He also talks the meat bill over with Beveridge and Judge Cowan and with Bonaparte on Maryland patronage.

headline: Hearing of massacres in Russia
summary: Simon Wolf meets Roosevelt about massacres of Jews in Russia. He also takes up South Dakota appointments, Oklahoma politics, and a stream of callers, and warns a North Carolina revenue collector to keep honest or lose his job.

headline: Senate picks a lock canal
summary: The Senate approves a lock canal for Panama. Roosevelt confers with Representative Boutell about a training ship for the Great Lakes, and writes George Carter on island sugar interests and Owen Wister a postscript on the Indianola post office.

headline: Cabinet on Standard Oil
summary: The Cabinet takes up the Standard Oil prosecutions. Roosevelt receives senators and congressmen and tells Hitchcock what he thinks of La Follette's complaints about the Indian bill.

headline: No fan of Wister's new book
summary: Roosevelt discusses South Dakota patronage and Standard Oil proceedings, and at night meets Flint, Hitchcock, Pinchot and Walcott. He tells Winthrop Chanler he dislikes Owen Wister's new book.

headline: Saving a kitten on the way to church
summary: Walking to church, Roosevelt rescues a kitten from two dogs and hands it to a Black girl, he tells Ethel, who is looking after her two youngest brothers on Long Island while Edith stays with him. He signs himself the Tyrant, adds a sketch, and urges the newlywed Longworths to visit Budapest on their honeymoon to learn about Austria-Hungary.

headline: Stanford White is shot
summary: Roosevelt meets Cannon and Hepburn, plans his Panama trip with Taft, and receives the British and French ambassadors among many callers. In New York, Harry Thaw shoots and kills the architect Stanford White in Madison Square Garden in a jealous rage over his wife, Evelyn Nesbit.

headline: Put the date on the can
summary: Roosevelt confers on Montana appointments and dines with Lodge. He tells Gilder that Taft is not the man to speak on the tariff, urges Cannon to require packing dates on canned meat, and complains to Senator Cullom that the Senate is stalling the Algeciras treaty.

headline: A pile of letters on canal and treaty
summary: Roosevelt takes up Indian appropriations, lunches with Robert Bacon and has Gardner, Scott and his brother-in-law Will Cowles to dinner. His letters range over German-American relations and Venezuela, the Algeciras treaty, the type of canal for Panama, Poultney Bigelow's charges against the canal commission, Arizona statehood and an immigration inquiry.

headline: Reviewing the National Guard
summary: Roosevelt reviews the National Guard parade, receives senators and officials including F. B. Kellogg, and dines with Taft, Moody and Bacon. He writes Neill about the immigration investigation.

headline: Hepburn Act signed; Mesa Verde created
summary: A landmark day: Roosevelt signs the Hepburn railroad rate act. A Grand Canyon game preserve of nearly 1.5 million acres is authorized, and Platt and Mesa Verde national parks are created. He dines with Will Cowles, Root and Bacon.

headline: Pure food and meat inspection become law
summary: As Congress adjourns, Roosevelt signs the Pure Food and Drug Act and the agricultural appropriation that carries the new meat inspection law, and sends Beveridge the pen used on the meat bill. He also approves a law on shooting in the District that makes three-quarters of it a wildlife refuge, and leaves at midnight for Oyster Bay. Alice and Nick head to Cincinnati before sailing for Europe.

headline: Corporations, unions and the trusts
summary: On his first day home at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt writes Lyman Abbott about business combinations and organized labor out in the Rockies, setting his trust policy beside Cleveland's, which he finds close to his own, and Bryan's, which he sees as its opposite.

headline: Kind words from the World
summary: The New York World, usually hostile to Roosevelt, runs an editorial applauding him for enforcing the laws already on the books.

headline: Thanks to the World's editorial writer
summary: Roosevelt thanks Frank Cobb for his World editorial on law enforcement and writes Benjamin Ide Wheeler about the rate law and Taft. Guests at Sagamore Hill include Cecilia May and a Roosevelt cousin.

headline: Fourth of July in Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt gives the Independence Day address in Oyster Bay. Secretary of State Root sets off on a goodwill tour of South America that will last until late September, and Alice and Nick drop in at the American embassy in London.

headline: A note on Root's journey
summary: Roosevelt writes Navy Secretary Bonaparte about Root's goodwill voyage to South America.

headline: Lunch with New Zealand's premier
summary: Sir Joseph Ward, premier of New Zealand, comes to Sagamore Hill for lunch.

headline: Better shooting in the Navy
summary: Taft visits to discuss Army business. Roosevelt wires Whitelaw Reid about canned meat and tells Commander William Sims he is heartened by the Navy's improved gunnery.

headline: Quiet Sunday at home
summary: No activity is recorded at Sagamore Hill.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: No activity is recorded at Sagamore Hill.

headline: John Heard visits
summary: John Heard Jr. signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.

headline: Nothing recorded
summary: The record places Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill with no further detail.

headline: Dr. Lambert comes by
summary: Roosevelt's physician and friend Alexander Lambert visits, and Barclay Farr is a guest.

headline: Nothing recorded
summary: The record places Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill with no further detail.

headline: Trouble between Guatemala and Salvador
summary: Roosevelt wires Robert Bacon about the danger of war between Guatemala and El Salvador. E. Du Pont Irving and Elisha Gilbert are among the house guests.

headline: Nothing recorded
summary: The record places Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill with no further detail.

headline: Seal poachers shot in Alaska
summary: Roosevelt confers with Taft and Bacon on Latin American affairs and gathers them with Whitridge, Finley Peter Dunne, police commissioner Bingham and Dr. Lambert. Far off in Alaska, on St. Paul Island, seal poachers are fired on as trespassers; five die and two are wounded.

headline: Dinner with cousin West's family
summary: Roosevelt dines at the home of Mrs. J. West Roosevelt.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: No activity is recorded at Sagamore Hill.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: No activity is recorded at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Peace made aboard the Marblehead
summary: Guatemala and El Salvador settle their quarrel at a Central American conference held on the U.S. cruiser Marblehead.

headline: Bishop Ireland and the Storers
summary: Roosevelt writes Senator Knute Nelson about the Bureau of Corporations and Henry White about Archbishop Ireland, the Storers and Root's South American trip.

headline: A quiet Sunday
summary: No activity is recorded at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Planning the fall campaign
summary: Speaker Cannon, Senator Penrose and three other party men lunch at Sagamore Hill and talk strategy for the congressional elections.

headline: Mortimer Schiff calls
summary: The banker Mortimer Schiff visits Roosevelt in the evening.

headline: Writing the party's campaign case
summary: Roosevelt writes James Watson about drafting the main Republican campaign statement for the 1906 elections himself.

headline: A refuge for Russia's Jews
summary: Roosevelt writes Jacob Schiff about America as a haven for Jews fleeing Russia.

headline: Lunch with Gordon Johnston, and thoughts on Bryan
summary: Roosevelt confers with E. E. Clark on the Interstate Commerce Commission and lunches with Lieutenant and Mrs. Gordon Johnston, General Barry, Bacon and others. He writes Taft about Chinese labor on the canal, and praises Whitelaw Reid for defending American meat inspection in England and for handling the visiting Bryan, about whom he has strong feelings.

headline: Pennsylvania politics over lunch
summary: Charles Emory Smith lunches with Roosevelt to talk about Pennsylvania politics.

headline: Sunday sermon on home missions
summary: Roosevelt goes to services at the Oyster Bay Presbyterian Church, where the Rev. Charles Thompson of the Home Missions Board preaches. Thompson, the Washburns and the Russells join him for lunch.

headline: No tariff revision soon
summary: Roosevelt tells Representative Edgar Crumpacker that revising the tariff is not possible in the near term.

headline: Revolt in Cuba begins
summary: Senator Dick and Elmer Dover lunch with Roosevelt to talk Ohio and Midwest politics, and Admiral Mahan and Grant La Farge are guests. He writes William Allen White about his book Stratagems and Spoils, Bryan, the meat law and the rate law. In Cuba, rebels rise against President Estrada Palma.

headline: Wealth and democracy at college
summary: Roosevelt tells Yale president Arthur Hadley he liked his Harper's essay on how wealth and democracy play out on American campuses.

headline: A new governor for the Philippines
summary: Roosevelt writes Taft that Henry Ide will step down from the top post in Manila and that James Smith should succeed him, and comments on Taft's views on the islands and Panama.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: No activity is recorded at Sagamore Hill.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: No activity is recorded at Sagamore Hill.

headline: A quiet Sunday at home
summary: No activity is recorded at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Edith turns 45; a picnic in the boats
summary: On Edith's 45th birthday Roosevelt hosts neighbors and Henry Stimson at lunch, meets Senator Penrose, and ends the day with a picnic out in the boats. He tells Lodge he is truly resting this summer, muses to Lyman Abbott about joining The Outlook after the presidency, and plans the September fleet review. Archie is off for a week's sail with Captain Joshua Slocum.

headline: The Hague and the Spanish claims
summary: Roosevelt writes Moody about the Spanish Treaty Claims Commission and tells Whitelaw Reid that English thinking on the Hague Conference matches America's.

headline: Rowing home by starlight
summary: Roosevelt and Kermit row Edith over to Lloyd's Neck, where they share a picnic supper with about twenty people, and they pull back home under the stars.

headline: Hamilton, Jefferson and the midterms
summary: Roosevelt meets former Senator Jones and Barnsdall about the Standard Oil investigation. He praises Frederick Oliver's Alexander Hamilton and weighs Hamilton against Jefferson, and tells Lodge he is a bit more hopeful about the November congressional races but would not wager on them.

headline: Worry over Japan and the seals
summary: Roosevelt writes Bonaparte about the coming naval review and his concern that July's seal poaching killings could stir trouble with Japan.

headline: Alice and Nick home from Europe
summary: Alice and Nick come back from Europe and the whole family gathers at Sagamore Hill before the couple goes on to Rookwood, the Longworths' house in Ohio. Roosevelt writes John Sleicher on the tariff and William Allen White on Taft's chances for 1908.

headline: Arthur Woods visits
summary: Arthur Woods signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.

headline: Ethel turns fourteen
summary: On Ethel's 14th birthday Roosevelt talks congressional campaign strategy with Sherman and Nick Longworth and canal matters with Shonts and Joseph Bishop. Willard Straight, Henry Taft and Robert Bridges are guests.

headline: Shots fired in Brownsville
summary: At night in Brownsville, Texas, gunfire kills a white bartender and wounds two policemen; men of three Black Army companies at Fort Brown are blamed, and none will confess or name others. Roosevelt writes Henry White about the Kaiser and the 1902 Venezuela ultimatum, tells Robert Bridges of Ted's poem in Scribner's under a pen name, and writes Taft on Panama.

headline: Keeping immigration out of the Watson letter
summary: Roosevelt answers Speaker Cannon's objections to his tariff statement and tells Lodge he will leave immigration out of the campaign letter he is writing for James Watson.

headline: Should Old Ironsides be scrapped?
summary: Moody and Bacon confer with Roosevelt and stay the night. He writes Bonaparte about the possibility of scrapping the frigate Constitution.

headline: Harlan named to the ICC
summary: James S. Harlan gets a seat on the ICC. Roosevelt has Cleveland Dodge and General John Wilson to lunch and writes Cortelyou on railroad rates for mail and Taft on Bigelow's attacks on the canal commission.

headline: Quentin the pagan philosopher
summary: Roosevelt congratulates Root on his South American tour, and tells Kermit that Quentin is a pagan philosopher who swims and rides well while Archie dotes on his sailboat Why. He sums up his presidency for Trevelyan, fearing the pendulum may swing against him, sends James Watson his statement of Republican aims, and praises Winston Churchill's novel Coniston.

headline: Richardsons and Will Cowles visit
summary: Teresa and Clifford Richardson and William Sheffield Cowles are guests at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Backing simplified spelling
summary: After lunch with Admiral Robley Evans, Roosevelt tells the public printer, Charles Stillings, that he favors spelling reform and wants government publications to use simplified spellings. He also forces Senator Spooner's brother out as superintendent of the Indian warehouse.

headline: Printers and the eight-hour day
summary: Father York and two other priests call at 11 a.m. Roosevelt tells Neill he has read his eight-hour law report and wires Stillings with concern over a threatened walkout by government printers seeking an eight-hour day.

headline: Needham visits
summary: Journalist Henry Beach Needham calls on Roosevelt.

headline: Briefed on Brownsville
summary: Roosevelt talks campaign plans with Cortelyou, hears from General J. F. Bell about the Brownsville shooting, and confers with Gifford Pinchot.

headline: Hold the accused soldiers
summary: Roosevelt writes Pinchot about reclaiming and irrigating western lands as an irrigation conference meets in Boise. He wires acting War Secretary Ainsworth to have the battalion bring the accused Brownsville soldiers to San Antonio and hold them under guard.

headline: Talking Chile
summary: Robert Bacon and Dr. Hollander confer with Roosevelt about Chile.

headline: A quiet Sunday
summary: No activity is recorded at Sagamore Hill.

headline: His first spelling reform letter
summary: Roosevelt directs the government printer to adopt simplified spelling in all public documents from now on, and adds a gleeful postscript to Taft calling it his first letter in the new style. He also chides Hitchcock about the Interior Department's poor treatment of Indians.

headline: Spelling aims, and Moody may go
summary: Roosevelt explains his goals for simplified spelling to Charles Scott of the Simplified Spelling Board and writes Moody, who is weighing leaving the Cabinet for private life.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: No activity is recorded at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Cortelyou in the morning
summary: Postmaster General Cortelyou meets Roosevelt in the morning.

headline: Tho, thru and catalog
summary: Roosevelt pushes his simplified spelling plan, first urged on him by Brander Matthews of Columbia, which respells some 300 words like thru, tho and catalog. The government will not adopt it, but he keeps the spellings the rest of his life. He talks New York politics with Parsons, and riots erupt in Atlanta.

headline: Wary of sending troops to Cuba
summary: Roosevelt tells Army Chief of Staff Bell he is reluctant to send soldiers to put down the Cuban insurrection. He backs Charles Evans Hughes for New York governor in a letter to Jacob Schurman and tells Taft that Edith and Taft, not Loeb, will go with him to Panama. The Sternbergs and the La Farges are among the guests.

headline: A houseful of guests
summary: Ambassador Sternberg, Dr. and Mrs. Rixey, the writer James B. Connolly and Grant and Florence La Farge are staying at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Reviewing the fleet from the Mayflower
summary: From the deck of the Mayflower, Roosevelt reviews the ships of the North Atlantic Squadron with a party that includes the Dunnes, the Bacons, the Bonapartes, the La Farges and Commander Sims, and has the Dunnes and Bacons to dinner aboard.

headline: Hughes for governor
summary: Roosevelt writes Gardner on immigration limits, asks Vice President Fairbanks to speak in Chicago, sends Root a long letter on his tour, the naval review, the elections, Bryan and Hughes for governor, and writes Lodge about the Supreme Court choice.

headline: An evening at the Masonic lodge
summary: Roosevelt hears tariff reformers H. E. Miles and Lyman Bass, talks New York politics over lunch with Cortelyou and Littauer, and spends time at his Masonic lodge in town. He defends Joe Cannon to Edgar Clark and writes Florence La Farge about the Greek play Electra.

headline: The Longworths come to stay
summary: Alice and Nick are staying at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt lunches with W. H. H. Llewellyn and writes Andrew Carnegie about limits on battleship size and the Hague Conference.

headline: Bamie and Will visit
summary: Roosevelt's sister Bamie and her husband Will Cowles are guests, and he confers with A. R. Page.

headline: Two warships for Cuba
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Christ Church in Oyster Bay for its 200th anniversary and confers with Bacon and Reynolds. He wires Bonaparte to send two warships to Cuba to protect American interests, and tells James Bede that his Watson letter will be his only endorsement of Republican candidates.

headline: Balfour, Newfoundland and Cuba
summary: Roosevelt writes Sir George Otto Trevelyan about Arthur Balfour and British distrust of him, and about unrest in Cuba and the Newfoundland dispute.

headline: Lunch with Homer Saint-Gaudens
summary: Roosevelt goes over state politics with Governor Higgins of New York and lunches with Homer Saint-Gaudens. He writes Admiral Converse about naval armament and Bacon about the Cuban insurrection.

headline: New coins by Saint-Gaudens
summary: Roosevelt writes Wilson on meatpacking and the elections, Treasury Secretary Shaw on the tariff and Augustus Saint-Gaudens's new coin designs, and Strachey that he liked his piece on spelling reform.

headline: More ships to Havana
summary: Roosevelt works on his Annual Message. He writes Samuel Harper about Aaron Burr, tells Lodge of his dislike of Winston Churchill, and wires Bacon, and Bonaparte, to send more ships to Havana.

headline: Marines landed without orders
summary: On Ted's 19th birthday, Roosevelt learns that 125 Marines have gone ashore in Cuba without his authority and wires Bacon to pull them back to the ships. He writes Moody on the Washington ice trust, Standard Oil and spelling, and Harvard's President Eliot about honoring Walter Reed.

headline: Ready to send troops to Cuba
summary: Roosevelt meets Taft, Bacon and Bonaparte about the revolt in Cuba, lunches on the Mayflower and greets a yacht race delegation. He tells Bacon that if President Palma resigns he will send troops, and explains to Cuban Minister Quesada why that is necessary.

headline: The Knoxes come to Sagamore Hill
summary: Senator and Mrs. Knox are guests, and Woodruff, Sherman and Albert Shaw call. Roosevelt tells Pinchot he wants Taft to campaign in Idaho.

headline: A quiet Sunday
summary: No activity is recorded at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Army readiness for Cuba
summary: Roosevelt writes Cannon about the party's election preparations and Taft about readying the Army for possible intervention in Cuba, a lock canal, and the outlook in Colorado and Idaho.

headline: Indian office inquiries
summary: Roosevelt writes Indian Commissioner Leupp about Flynn, Frantz and investigations in the Indian service.

headline: Eight-hour day for government work
summary: Father Power calls in the morning. A proclamation opens Oklahoma land to homesteaders, and an order extends the eight-hour day to government work.

headline: Who is funding the rebels?
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Jacob Riis, William Allen White and others, hosts Senator and Mrs. Knox overnight, and dines with Archbishop Ireland and Bishop O'Gorman. He wires Taft asking whether Americans are financing the Cuban revolutionists and demands an honest count in Arizona's statehood vote.

headline: Taft and Bacon sent to Havana
summary: Roosevelt wires Taft about landing troops in Havana, concluding that Washington cannot keep President Palma in power, and sends Taft and Assistant Secretary of State Bacon to Cuba.

headline: Approving Taft's steps in Cuba
summary: Roosevelt presses Senator Knox to campaign, tells Harvard's Eliot that few Americans have funded the Cuban rebels and that Leonard Wood is needed in Cuba again, and wires Taft twice approving his moves to restore order.

headline: Rowing, tennis and chopping trees
summary: Roosevelt writes Kermit that he and Edith are off for a row, that he plays tennis daily and is cutting trees to keep the view open. Quentin hopes to join his friend Mike Landon at the Fay School, which pains Edith; Archie is sailing with Emlen; and the family went to church, where Ethel met them after Sunday school.

headline: Devils Tower, the first national monument
summary: Roosevelt proclaims Devils Tower in Wyoming the first national monument under the new Antiquities Act.

headline: Asking Palma to step down
summary: With Taft in Cuba, Roosevelt wires that President Palma should resign and that U.S. troops will go in if needed; he wants order restored without a drawn-out guerrilla war. He also writes Whitelaw Reid about Bryan.

headline: Three telegrams on the rebels
summary: Ralph Peters calls at noon among other visitors, and Roosevelt wires Taft three times about the rebels in Cuba.

headline: Corinne's birthday; big guns for battleships
summary: On his sister Corinne's 45th birthday, Roosevelt vents to Lodge about congressional critics of his Cuba moves, especially Foraker, and praises Commander Sims's answer to Mahan: both favor battleships armed only with big guns.

headline: Off to Provincetown; land the troops
summary: Roosevelt sails on the Mayflower for Provincetown and a review of the Atlantic fleet, with Grant La Farge along. He explains his Cuba policy to Senator Foraker and wires Taft three times, agreeing to a provisional government and telling him to land troops.

headline: Target practice on the Missouri
summary: Roosevelt boards the battleship Missouri in Buzzards Bay for target practice and lunch, then heads back to Oyster Bay on the Mayflower. Wireless telegrams relayed to Taft order the Marines ashore at once.

headline: Six thousand troops for Cuba
summary: Roosevelt wires Taft that 6,000 American soldiers are bound for Cuba. Secretary Root finishes his South American tour, reporting a remarkable journey and an enthusiastic welcome across the continent.

headline: Summer ends; back to Washington
summary: The Roosevelts shut up Sagamore Hill for the season and Roosevelt heads south, talking New York politics with Charles Evans Hughes aboard the train. That evening he meets Moody and Root in Washington.

headline: Cabinet takes up Cuba
summary: The Cabinet meets on the crisis in Cuba, and a stream of callers follows, Knox and Foraker among them. Roosevelt wires Secretary Taft on how the Army should keep order on the island and writes Hughes about his odds in the governor's race.

headline: Magoon named to govern Cuba
summary: Roosevelt puts Charles E. Magoon in charge of Cuba as its interim governor, then has dinner with both the Magoon and Root families. He tells Root he is unhappy with the American minister in Havana.

headline: Speeches at Harrisburg and York
summary: Roosevelt makes a day trip into Pennsylvania with Knox, Penrose and Dr. Rixey, speaking at the dedication of the new capitol in Harrisburg and then at the York fair before heading home. He writes Hughes about Catholic voters as Hughes trails William Randolph Hearst.

headline: Robb to the appeals bench
summary: After a Cabinet session, Roosevelt names C. H. Robb an associate justice of the District's Court of Appeals. He sends Hughes more encouragement and answers Senator Beveridge about congressional pushback on his Cuba policy.

headline: Warren fencing case strains Interior
summary: Roosevelt confers on Cuba with Magoon and General Bell and later sees Ambassador Speck von Sternberg. To Interior Secretary Hitchcock he writes about findings that Senator Warren took part in fencing off public land, findings Roosevelt set aside, opening a rift that ended with Hitchcock's resignation.

headline: Sunday politics with Sherman
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday on politics with James S. Sherman and Senator Penrose, then has Sherman to dinner. He wires Taft about the so-called horse order, which let Cuban rebels keep the horses they had seized.

headline: Canal talk and a court reception
summary: Roosevelt works through New York and Indiana politics with Sherman and Overstreet, discusses the canal with Theodore Shonts, and hosts a White House reception for the Supreme Court. He tells Lodge that E. H. Harriman will give nothing to Hughes because of the administration's stand on corporations.

headline: Antitrust plans with Root and Bonaparte
summary: Between a Cabinet meeting and talks on Illinois politics with Hopkins and with Tawney, Roosevelt sits down with Root and Bonaparte on antitrust law. He asks Oscar Straus to help swing Jewish voters to Hughes.

headline: Kermit turns seventeen
summary: Kermit's seventeenth birthday. Roosevelt receives Cabinet members, Father A. P. Doyle, Major J. M. Burke and others, holds a reception for Spanish War veterans, and wires Taft on Cuba.

headline: San Francisco bars Japanese pupils
summary: San Francisco's school board orders Japanese children out of the city's regular schools, and that afternoon Roosevelt sees Japanese Ambassador Aoki. Earlier he talks Cuba with Spooner and New York politics with W. J. Youngs; Arthur Lee arrives to stay at the White House. It is also his niece Eleanor's 22nd birthday.

headline: Lunch with Arthur Lee; a night at the theater
summary: Roosevelt talks New York politics with Ward and Wainwright, shares lunch with Admiral Cowles, Paul Morton and Arthur Lee, and takes Edith to the theater. He tells James S. Sherman that Cortelyou and Bliss oppose Hyde for an ambassadorship.

headline: Magoon takes charge in Havana
summary: Charles E. Magoon replaces Taft as Cuba's provisional governor. Roosevelt discusses Cuban annexation and his annual message with Beveridge, sits for photographer Mrs. DeWentworth, and in the evening speaks to about 45 members of the Aztec Club.

headline: Wishing an old Assembly friend well
summary: Roosevelt meets Cannon and Watson at dinnertime. He sends good wishes to William O'Neil, a friend from his Albany Assembly days now running for the state senate, and writes Woodruff again on the New York races.

headline: Thanking Arthur Lee for crossing the Atlantic
summary: Roosevelt goes over Delaware politics with Allee, DuPont and Ball and Ohio politics with Grosvenor. He thanks Arthur Lee for coming from England at his request to talk over Anglo-American problems, a sign of his low regard for British Ambassador Durand.

headline: Called a Socialist on the stump
summary: After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt confers with Root and Cortelyou and lunches with Governor Montague, McBee and Allison. He writes Lodge about the New York contest and about charges that he is a dangerous radical and a Socialist.

headline: Dentist at noon, Indian agents at night
summary: Roosevelt helps Root shape a campaign speech for Hughes, sees Cortelyou, and visits the dentist at noon. He lunches with Knox over Pennsylvania politics and that night meets the government's Indian agents.

headline: Kohlsaat to dinner and overnight
summary: Nephew Sheffield Cowles turns eight. Roosevelt reviews the annual message with Knox, sees Colonel McCook, and dines with Robert Bacon, the Tafts, General Greene and Kohlsaat; Kohlsaat stays the night.

headline: Moody on trust cases
summary: A Cabinet meeting, then a session with Attorney General Moody about prosecuting the trusts.

headline: Filling a Supreme Court seat
summary: Roosevelt meets Justices Harlan, White and Day about the coming Supreme Court vacancy, then goes over bids for canal work with Ropes, Bishop, Root and Taft. He explains to Lodge why he will not write Gussie Gardner a personal endorsement.

headline: Shaw on the nation's finances
summary: Treasury Secretary Shaw comes by at night to discuss federal finances. Roosevelt asks Woodruff to keep his planned Cabinet shuffle quiet until October 23.

headline: Photographed signing Thanksgiving proclamation
summary: A photographer named Dunn catches Roosevelt signing the Thanksgiving proclamation. He confers on canal contracts, on the campaign trips of Taft and Root, and on the Standard Oil case, and writes Sir Edward Grey on the Hague Conference and disarmament.

headline: Roosevelt unveils a new Cabinet
summary: Roosevelt announces the Cabinet that will serve from March 4, 1907: Root at State, Cortelyou at Treasury, Taft at War, Bonaparte as Attorney General, Meyer as Postmaster General, Metcalf at Navy, Garfield at Interior, Wilson at Agriculture and Straus at Commerce and Labor. He writes Kermit about Archie racing the dog Skip.

headline: Ellis Island under review
summary: Roosevelt and Metcalf review conditions at Ellis Island. Cabinet members, Henry Lee Higginson and Herman Ridder come by, and he urges Republicans to stand together in the elections.

headline: Lunch with Jusserand
summary: Roosevelt confers with Secretary Wilson, shares lunch with Cowles, Taft, Root and Jusserand, and takes up Cuban finances with J. D. Terrill. To John St. Loe Strachey he writes about Hearst, Bryan and Hughes.

headline: Taking the school fight to court
summary: Roosevelt names A. W. Cooley an assistant attorney general and goes riding with Speck von Sternberg while Edith, Ethel and Archie head down the Potomac by boat. He assures Baron Kaneko that the Justice Department is moving against San Francisco's segregation of Japanese pupils.

headline: A 48th birthday at work
summary: Roosevelt turns 48. A New York club of Hungarian-American Republicans stops by to wish him well, and he spends much of the day on California's treatment of Japanese schoolchildren, conferring with Metcalf and writing Senator Hale. Hugo Munsterberg joins Root and Metcalf for lunch.

headline: Outdoor service on Cathedral Heights
summary: Edith, Ethel and Archie come home from their river trip. In the afternoon Roosevelt and Quentin attend an open-air service on Cathedral Heights led by the old Rough Rider chaplain.

headline: Troops ready to protect the Japanese
summary: With his Panama trip ahead, Roosevelt gives Root authority to call out federal forces to shield Japanese residents if needed. He also asks Moody to look into a Wisconsin court order against the iron molders' union.

headline: Booker T. Washington after dark
summary: Another round on New York politics with Root and Cortelyou, then lunch with Admiral Cowles and a Mr. Kitigaki. Booker T. Washington calls at nine that evening.

headline: Off to Pine Knot with Edith
summary: Roosevelt hears from Hawaii's acting governor, Atkinson, about labor conditions in the islands, then leaves in the afternoon with Edith for their Virginia retreat, Pine Knot.

headline: Root stumps for Hughes
summary: Roosevelt is at Pine Knot. In New York, Elihu Root gives a forceful speech at Utica on behalf of Charles Evans Hughes.

headline: Quiet day at Pine Knot
summary: Roosevelt is at Pine Knot. The source records nothing more.

headline: In Richmond
summary: The source places Roosevelt in Richmond, Virginia, with no further detail.

headline: Turkey hunting, then home
summary: Roosevelt leaves Pine Knot for Washington and writes Kermit that he and Edith had a fine stay, with some turkey hunting for him.

headline: The Brownsville discharges
summary: Roosevelt orders the soldiers of three Black infantry companies tied to the Brownsville, Texas, shooting dismissed from the Army, a decision that will dog him for years. He lunches with Arthur Lee and leaves at midnight for Oyster Bay to vote.

headline: Election day: Hughes wins New York
summary: Roosevelt casts his ballot at Oyster Bay and returns to Washington. Hughes wins the New York governorship, Nick Longworth keeps his House seat, and Gooding is chosen governor of Idaho. Lolo National Forest in Montana is created.

headline: Labor leaders on the anti-injunction bill
summary: Samuel Gompers and other labor men press Roosevelt about the anti-injunction measure sponsored by Pearre. He congratulates Hughes on his win and tells Alice he admired the campaign she and Nick ran in Ohio.

headline: Setting sail for Panama
summary: Roosevelt and Edith take the yacht Mayflower down the river to Chesapeake Bay and transfer to the new 16,000-ton battleship Louisiana to start their voyage to Panama. Before leaving he thanks Taft for a speech that helped the party in Idaho.

headline: Rounding Cape Hatteras
summary: Aboard the Louisiana, the presidential party passes Cape Hatteras.

headline: Steaming past Georgia
summary: The Louisiana runs south along the coast, off Savannah, Georgia.

headline: Big guns named Tedd and the Big Stick
summary: Off Jacksonville, Roosevelt writes Quentin about the pets on board and tells Archie that the Tennessee and Washington are escorting them and that two of the ship's guns carry the nicknames Tedd and The Big Stick. Meanwhile Edith watches the crew's inspection and writes Aunt Lizzie that she has studied canal maps closely.

headline: Cuba and Haiti on the horizon
summary: With both Cuba and Haiti in view, Roosevelt and Edith talk over the islands' past. He writes Navy Secretary Bonaparte full of praise for the Louisiana and her men, with a few suggestions.

headline: Reading Milton and Tacitus at sea
summary: Nearing Colón, Roosevelt admits to Kermit he is "a little bored" while Edith is loving the voyage. He passes time with Milton, Tacitus and the German novel Jörn Uhl, walks the deck, inspects the ship, and recalls the troopships that carried him to Cuba eight years before.

headline: Arrival at Colón
summary: The Louisiana drops anchor at Colón. After a big reception on board, Roosevelt and Edith sleep on the ship. He writes Ted that the clean, well-run battleship shows America at its best and muses on Panama's history as the coast comes into view.

headline: By train across the isthmus
summary: In a steady downpour, Roosevelt and Edith ride the railroad from Colón across to Panama City with Theodore Shonts, John Stevens and President Amador. Film records the trip, and they stay over at the Hotel Tivoli.

headline: At the controls of a steam shovel
summary: Roosevelt spends eighteen hours in the field, from before six in the morning until nearly midnight, looking at workers and their living conditions. At Culebra he gives a speech, watches steam shovels bite into the cut and takes the controls of one, a moment caught on film. Heavy rain has turned the villages to mud.

headline: Gatun, Colón and a ball
summary: Roosevelt views the future Gatun Dam site and wishes he could linger to collect specimens. He speaks at Colón, dines with General Manager Biers at Cristobal, attends a reception and ball, and sails that night for Puerto Rico.

headline: Sailing for Puerto Rico
summary: The Louisiana heads for Puerto Rico. Edith writes Kermit of Panamanian children who waved American flags and sang "America" for the visitors.

headline: Quentin turns nine
summary: At sea on the way to Puerto Rico. Back home, it is Quentin's ninth birthday.

headline: Jungle memories near Ponce
summary: Off Ponce, Roosevelt writes Kermit about his hectic days on the isthmus and tells Ted about the stiff trade winds and how the jungle's flowers and animals captivated him. Edith, he reports, enjoyed every minute.

headline: Across Puerto Rico by automobile
summary: Roosevelt and Edith come ashore at Ponce, where Governor Winthrop greets them and Roosevelt speaks at City Hall. They motor some 80 miles over the mountains to San Juan, stopping at Cayey and Río Piedras, then dine, attend the governor's reception and sleep in the old Spanish governors' palace. Mr. Grahame turns up in his kilt.

headline: Picnic lunch and shipboard boxing
summary: The Roosevelts drive back to Ponce by another route, through Arecibo, and stop for an outdoor meal of chicken and eggs with bread and wine. Back on the Louisiana that afternoon, the crew puts on skits and three boxing bouts for them.

headline: Letters home from the Louisiana
summary: Heading north, Roosevelt writes Kermit a full account of Puerto Rico and describes both islands to George Otto Trevelyan. He is reading Milton and Samuel Dill's study of Rome in the age of Nero and Marcus Aurelius.

headline: Passing Hatteras again
summary: The Louisiana rounds Cape Hatteras on the way home.

headline: Last day at sea; Nobel news
summary: Roosevelt's last day aboard the Louisiana falls on Bamie's eleventh wedding anniversary. The source also logs here that he has won the Nobel Peace Prize, formally awarded December 10, and lists Quentin's "White House Gang" of boyhood friends.

headline: Back at the desk: railroads, child labor, Peary
summary: Home from the tropics, Roosevelt goes straight to work: interstate commerce law with Hepburn, a child labor bill with Beveridge, and the Army budget with Warren and Hull. Robert E. Peary is among the day's many visitors, and Joseph Bucklin Bishop comes by at nine that night.

headline: Twentieth anniversary, quietly
summary: Roosevelt and Edith reach their twentieth wedding anniversary and let it pass without fuss, though the Washington Post salutes them as ideal keepers of the White House's social traditions. E. H. Harriman calls at one o'clock.

headline: Congress returns
summary: Congress opens its new session and members stream into Roosevelt's office. At lunch he hosts a naturalists' table: William T. Hornaday, C. Hart Merriam and John Phillips, with Robert Collier and others.

headline: A bold annual message, in simplified spelling
summary: Roosevelt's annual message is read to Congress. It argues that big business, being interstate, belongs under federal oversight, rattling Wall Street, and draws more comment for being printed in simplified spelling. He receives Mabel Boardman and about 100 Red Cross delegates and later hears the Boston Symphony with Edith.

headline: Canal labor and the I stories
summary: Roosevelt hears from Moffett and Neill about labor on the Canal Zone and sees Ambassador Aoki. He writes Kermit about the first-person hunting tales, his "I" stories, that he tells Archie and Quentin, and about winning the Nobel Prize.

headline: A day of callers
summary: A long line of senators, congressmen and politicians files through, including La Follette, Spooner and New York's William Barnes Jr., along with Russia's Baron Rosen. Hemenway comes at 2:30.

headline: Rivers and harbors speech; Ted joins Porcellian
summary: Roosevelt addresses delegates to the Rivers and Harbors Congress and dines at Lodge's. He presses Senator Hale for more battleships, praises Treasury Secretary Shaw's record, and learns that Ted has been taken into Harvard's Porcellian Club.

headline: Mark Twain to lunch; three new monuments
summary: Roosevelt proclaims El Morro, Montezuma Castle and Petrified Forest as national monuments. Mark Twain, John Philip Sousa and Admiral Dewey are among the day's callers, and Twain stays for lunch. Harriman calls at six, and Roosevelt finishes the night at the Gridiron Dinner.

headline: The Storer letters go public
summary: Bellamy and Maria Storer publish their private correspondence with Roosevelt.

headline: Nobel Peace Prize awarded
summary: In Christiania, Norway, Roosevelt is formally awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for ending the Russo-Japanese War, the first American so honored. He wires thanks to the Nobel committee, pledging the prize money to a permanent body for industrial peace. That night he and Edith go to the Columbia Theater.

headline: Twain again; campaign committee dinner
summary: Roosevelt talks New York politics with Governor-elect Hughes and sees Mark Twain once more among the callers. He lunches with Cleveland Dodge and hosts the Republican campaign committee for dinner with Hughes, Taft, Lodge, Cannon and others.

headline: Foraker turns on Brownsville
summary: A full lunch table includes Pinchot, Garfield, Taft, Bacon, Stevens and Kellogg. Roosevelt writes Senator Matthew Butler about his growing quarrel with Senator Foraker, who has become a sharp critic of the Brownsville discharges.

headline: Retreat on simplified spelling
summary: Under heavy pressure, Roosevelt withdraws his order telling the Public Printer to use simplified spelling. Two houseguests, Beekman Winthrop and Paul Morton, are staying at the White House, and the Cabinet comes to dinner. He writes Hitchcock about illegal fences on public land and federal coal lands.

headline: Inviting Uncle Joe to Lincoln Day
summary: After the Cabinet meets and senators call, Roosevelt lunches with Ambassador and Mrs. Jusserand. He asks Speaker Cannon to give a speech at New York's Lincoln Day dinner in February.

headline: Buffalo Bill and a medal for Peary
summary: Buffalo Bill Cody talks western irrigation with Roosevelt, and Representative Townsend raises the shortage of freight cars. After dinner at Vice President Fairbanks's, Roosevelt goes to the National Geographic Society banquet at the New Willard and gives Commander Robert Peary a medal. His brother-in-law Douglas Robinson is a houseguest.

headline: Conceding on spelling
summary: Root calls on Sunday evening. Roosevelt tells Brander Matthews he could not have saved the reformed spelling by fighting for it, and thanks Moody for his years in the Cabinet.

headline: Moody to the Supreme Court; a Cabinet shuffle
summary: Roosevelt puts Moody on the Supreme Court, moves Bonaparte from Navy to Attorney General, shifts Metcalf to Navy and names Oscar Straus to Commerce and Labor. He sends Congress special messages on naval personnel and public land laws, and one on the canal illustrated with Canal Zone photographs.

headline: Message on Japanese immigration
summary: Roosevelt sends Congress a message on the Japanese immigration question. He takes up government pay, the freight car shortage, Indian affairs and a proposed loan to the Jamestown Exposition, and dines with Horace Plunkett. To Sir Edward Grey he urges tact over the Newfoundland fisheries.

headline: Freight cars and battleships
summary: Iowa's Governor Cummins and senators from the northern plains meet Roosevelt about the shortage of freight cars. Hamilton Fish is among a long list of visitors, and Roosevelt writes Representative Foss about battleships.

headline: The Colorado River breaks loose
summary: Roosevelt meets Walcott, Newell and Flint on the breach of the Colorado River and wires Harriman about who should pay to fix it. He discusses child labor law with Neill, writes Seth Low about turning his Nobel money into a peace commission, and dines at the Roots'. Nicholas Murray Butler stays the night.

headline: Lunch with the departing Durands
summary: After a Cabinet meeting, Roosevelt shares lunch with Whitelaw Reid, the Durands and other guests. To John St. Loe Strachey he writes about the Storer letters, Japan and William Jennings Bryan.

headline: The Harlans' golden wedding
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Belmont and Foulke, sees Speck von Sternberg, and attends Justice and Mrs. Harlan's fiftieth-anniversary reception. He offers Philip B. Stewart a Land Office job; Stewart will say no.

headline: Sunday night with Taft
summary: Secretary Taft and a Mr. Barrow call at nine in the evening.

headline: Christmas Eve at work; radio's first voice
summary: Roosevelt spends Christmas Eve on immigration with Sargent, the canal with Taft, and Brownsville with Senators Warren, Long and Cullom, then lunches with canal engineer John Stevens. Near Plymouth, Massachusetts, Reginald Fessenden makes the first radio broadcast of a human voice.

headline: Christmas at the White House
summary: At six in the morning the children's footsteps in the hall wake Roosevelt and Edith, and the family launches into one of its traditional Roosevelt Christmases.

headline: Back to Pine Knot
summary: After talks with Taft and Walcott and lunch with Bacon, Speyer and Root, Roosevelt and Edith leave for Pine Knot. He writes Corinne that Ted no longer gets as worked up about Christmas as he did as a boy.

headline: Turkeys and a life of Morton
summary: At Pine Knot, Roosevelt hunts turkey and reads William Dudley Foulke's biography of Indiana's Civil War governor, Oliver P. Morton.

headline: At Pine Knot
summary: Roosevelt is at Pine Knot. The source records nothing more.

headline: At Pine Knot
summary: Another quiet day at the Virginia retreat; no details recorded.

headline: At Pine Knot
summary: The Roosevelts remain at Pine Knot; the source adds nothing else.

headline: Home from Pine Knot
summary: Roosevelt and Edith return to Washington from Pine Knot to close out the year.

headline: 8,150 handshakes on New Year's Day
summary: Roosevelt opens 1907 by meeting sociologist Edward A. Ross, then comes down to trumpets for the New Year's reception: diplomats first, then the public, 8,150 hands in all, a record that stood for decades. Afterward he washes up, takes the family for a country drive and goes to Bamie's N Street house for chocolate, whipped cream and champagne. He ends the day reading Gissing on Dickens and Lowes Dickinson's The Greek View of Life.

headline: Calming railroad jitters
summary: Roosevelt meets Speaker Cannon and son-in-law Nick Longworth. He writes Paul Morton that railroad men, rattled by the Hepburn Act, are talking themselves toward a panic, and that he is trying to settle nerves on Wall Street.

headline: Taming the Colorado; diplomatic reception
summary: Roosevelt works with Walcott and Newell on controlling floods on the Colorado River, receives the Italian and Hungarian ambassadors, and hosts the evening diplomatic reception. He writes Lyman Abbott about tolerance toward Armenians, Japanese and Mormons.

headline: Dinner for the Cannons; young MacArthur attends
summary: After the Cabinet and more Colorado River talk with Walcott, Roosevelt sees Andrew Carnegie. He gives a dinner and musicale for Speaker and Mrs. Cannon; the guests include a young Lieutenant Douglas MacArthur. To Foulke he writes about Mrs. Storer's effort to oust MacNutt from his Vatican post.

headline: San Francisco's school order in focus
summary: Roosevelt meets Senator Perkins and U.S. Attorney Devlin about San Francisco's exclusion of Japanese pupils, then lunches with Philip Stewart, Garfield and Pinchot. He writes William Allen White about La Follette and the progressive wing.

headline: Sunday evening callers
summary: Taft comes at six. Later Rashid Bey, Senators Piles and Nelson, and Commander Sims stop by.

headline: Senators on Brownsville
summary: Senators Hemenway, Hopkins, Burkett and Hansbrough confer with Roosevelt on Brownsville. Lodge, Joseph Bishop and Governor Hoggatt are among the callers, and the Shaws give a dinner for Roosevelt and Edith.

headline: The Nobel medal arrives
