summary: Roosevelt confirms that his Nobel Prize medal has reached him. He talks legislation with Lodge, Knox and Nelson, writes Harrison Gray Otis about Japanese exclusion, seal poachers and the Navy, and sends the Kaiser assurances of trust.

headline: Fan mail for Mr. Dooley
summary: After a day of callers, Roosevelt dines with Justice Harlan and attends a Senate reception for Vice President Fairbanks. He writes Finley Peter Dunne to praise his Mr. Dooley.

headline: Carnegie upsets the Kaiser
summary: Roosevelt goes over the rivers and harbors bill with Representative Burton and hosts the diplomatic dinner. He tells Whitelaw Reid that Andrew Carnegie, repeating gossip from British ministers, has rattled the Kaiser by talking up strains between Germany and America.

headline: Ballinger tapped for the Land Office
summary: Roosevelt confers with M. D. Purdy on Brownsville and dines with Straus, Oliver, Longworth and author Robert Grant before an evening musicale. He asks Foss for two new battleships, returns Nannie Lodge's books, and tells Pinchot he will offer the Land Commissioner's job to Judge Richard Ballinger of Seattle.

headline: Asking Congress to fix the Colorado
summary: Roosevelt sends Congress a special message asking for money to close the Colorado River breaks. He presses Cannon for a commission on Japanese immigration and assures Captain Mahan that he has no plan to split the fleet.

headline: New York politics on a Sunday
summary: In the evening Roosevelt talks New York politics with James W. Wadsworth, and at nine he meets Garfield and Clement.

headline: Brownsville message to Congress
summary: Roosevelt sends Congress a special message defending his Brownsville decision and confers with Littauer on ship subsidies. He asks Louis Brandeis for his views on regulating insurance, and W. S. Simpson is an overnight guest.

headline: Caribou National Forest created
summary: On a rainy day Roosevelt discusses Judge Wickersham's case with Bonaparte, receives the Republican Clubs' executive committee and dines at the Tafts'. Caribou National Forest in Idaho and Wyoming is established.

headline: Praise for Robert E. Lee
summary: Rain again. Roosevelt takes up Wyoming land fraud and the ship subsidy bill, sees Jusserand, and lunches with Root, Bliss and Cortelyou. He writes Hilary Herbert praising Robert E. Lee on his centennial, wires Ballinger about taking the Land Office, and late at night drops in at a foreign commerce banquet at the Arlington.

headline: Judges at the White House
summary: In the rain, Roosevelt confers on railroads with Clements, Clark, Harlan and Knapp, and that evening hosts the reception for the judiciary. His cousin Emlen Roosevelt is a houseguest.

headline: Bamie turns 52
summary: Bamie's birthday. Roosevelt takes up the child labor bill with Beveridge and working conditions in Panama with G. W. Dunn, lunches with Bacon, Bonaparte and Taft, and writes Straus about contract labor and immigration.

headline: Cotton mills and child labor
summary: North Carolina's Governor Glenn talks cotton mills with Roosevelt as rain keeps falling. A long string of senators and officials calls, and he writes Cannon on immigration, Bartholdt on child labor, and Kermit about Brownsville.

headline: Strategy session at Lodge's
summary: Roosevelt meets at Lodge's home to plan for the Brownsville fight, sees Beveridge at one and Paul Morton in the evening, and writes Charles Fowler about currency law.

headline: Fighting the Foraker resolution
summary: Roosevelt spends the day lining up senators against Foraker's Brownsville resolution. He also covers finance with Tawney, ship subsidies with Grosvenor, reclamation with Lacey, and the Swettenham affair with Bacon and Taft, then dines at Henry Adams's. Sloan Simpson stays the night.

headline: Shonts quits the canal
summary: Roosevelt reviews the Swettenham and Brownsville matters with Lodge, and the Cabinet takes up canal contracts. He confers on coal land fraud and on La Follette's bill to lease coal and oil lands, then dines with the Bonapartes. He tells Bamie the British have behaved well over Durand's recall, and acknowledges Shonts's resignation as canal chairman.

headline: Pushing for ship subsidies
summary: Roosevelt sends Congress a message backing ship subsidy legislation. Independent makers of smokeless powder send a delegation, talks government pay with Representative Davis, and writes Ted about keeping his Harvard spending down.

headline: Supreme Court to dinner
summary: Roosevelt talks canal with Senator Millard and Yellowstone with Garfield, then gives the annual dinner for the Supreme Court. Letters go out on John Stevens and the canal, federal pay, railroad inquiries, Senator Warren, the personnel bill and freight car shortages.

headline: Canal contract on the Cabinet table
summary: The Cabinet weighs the canal construction contract. Roosevelt discusses Oregon appointments with Fulton, canal legislation with Hopkins, and the smokeless powder makers' accusations with du Pont, and wires Stevens that he will await his word.

headline: Clash with Foraker at the Gridiron
summary: Roosevelt attends Senator Alger's funeral in the afternoon. At the Gridiron Club dinner that night, Senator Foraker attacks his handling of Brownsville in a bitter, personal speech; Roosevelt answers just as hotly and storms out.

headline: The morning after
summary: Beveridge calls, and Roosevelt writes him about the previous night's clash with Foraker. He also writes Navy Secretary Metcalf on the personnel and naval bills.

headline: Novelist Churchill on New Hampshire
summary: Roosevelt discusses New Hampshire with Winston Churchill, the American novelist, land law with Heyburn, and stock-growers' meetings in Salt Lake City and Denver with Pinchot. The Metcalfs give a dinner for him and Edith, and he writes Taft that the William J. Oliver Company is in the running for canal work.

headline: Shonts, Mondell and civic plans
summary: Roosevelt confers on the canal with Shonts, on Wyoming with Mondell, and on improving Washington with Ralph Easley. He writes William Brownell about his Scribner's essay on Lowell.

headline: Californians on the school question
summary: California's congressional delegation meets Roosevelt about the Japanese school dispute. Metcalf and Underwood also call.

headline: Toward a Gentlemen's Agreement
summary: Roosevelt holds the congressional reception and works toward an informal understanding with Japan, later called the Gentlemen's Agreement, under which Japan would curb emigration. He writes William Dodd about rich men who want him gone and suggests to Mrs. E. H. Merrill an article on good husbands.

headline: Indian lands and Oklahoma railroads
summary: Roosevelt confers with Bird McGuire on Oklahoma's railroad laws and with western lawmakers on appointments, lunches with Root and Bacon, and hosts a White House musicale. He writes Hitchcock about Indian lands and the rights of Indian peoples.

headline: Rallying the Audubon societies
summary: Roosevelt receives the Mexican ambassador and tells Senator Elkins he has not yet chosen successors for Stevens and Shonts in Panama. Learning that Congressman Wadsworth has cut a bird-protection clause from a bill, he asks Florence LaFarge to rouse the Audubon societies to win it back.

headline: Sunday guests
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Mr. Matsukata, and that evening Robert Collier and Finley Peter Dunne come by.

headline: San Francisco howls
summary: Roosevelt sees naturalist C. Hart Merriam, reviews the Standard Oil cases with Bonaparte, Garfield and U.S. Attorney Sims, and holds a late session on withdrawing coal lands from entry. He tells Kermit that San Francisco is making the Japanese school fight as hard for him as it can, and writes Trevelyan about Jamaica's Governor Swettenham insulting the American sailors sent after the earthquake.

headline: Thomas Fortune Ryan on the canal
summary: Roosevelt talks canal construction with Thomas Fortune Ryan, meets the Cabinet, and goes over rivers and harbors legislation with Taft and Burton before dining at Secretary Hitchcock's.

headline: An evening at the Corcoran
summary: Roosevelt confers with Representative Perkins on the Chinese exclusion laws, then visits the Corcoran Gallery of Art with Edith. Letters go to Bishop William Lawrence on immigration, Cyrus Sulloway on pensions, and Cannon on railroad workers' hours.

headline: Army-Navy reception; the Lowells stay over
summary: Roosevelt reviews canal bids with Taft and public land law with Heyburn, and talks Ohio appointments with Senator Dick and two congressmen. After the Army and Navy reception, Harvard's A. Lawrence Lowell and his wife spend the night.

headline: Navy short of ammunition
summary: Roosevelt discusses Cuba with Taft and appropriations with Payne, lunches with editor Albert Shaw, and warns Senator Hale that the Navy's ammunition reserve is too low.

headline: Mayor Schmitz comes to Washington
summary: With Root at his side, Roosevelt meets San Francisco's Mayor Eugene Schmitz, Representatives Kahn and Hayes, and the city's school board about the Japanese pupils. He has two Howard University men, Kirkfield and Thompson, to lunch, and grumbles to Kermit that Japan is being cocky and not keeping to its understanding.

headline: A blank Sunday
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; the source records nothing for the day.

headline: Schmitz again; coal and range lands
summary: Roosevelt holds a second meeting with Mayor Schmitz, works on coal land and western land leasing with lawmakers, Garfield and Pinchot, and talks immigration law with Representative Bennet. He writes Senator Warren about federal oversight of grazing land and unlawful fences.

headline: Alice turns 23; Stevens fires off a letter
summary: On Alice's birthday the Cabinet takes up the Japanese school question, and the Roosevelts dine at Secretary Wilson's. Roosevelt writes Taft about John Stevens's angry letter attacking the canal commission's setup and offering to quit.

headline: Message on leasing western coal
summary: Roosevelt meets Root, Cannon, Taft and Mayor Schmitz on the school question and Sargent on immigration, and asks Congress to allow leasing of western coal lands. He also takes up canal contracts with R. S. Oliver.

headline: Accepting Stevens's resignation
summary: Roosevelt meets Representatives Bartholdt and Williams about the second Hague conference. He formally accepts John Stevens's resignation from the canal commission, thanking him for excellent work on the isthmus.

headline: Time for a treaty with Japan
summary: After meeting Root and Mayor Schmitz and the Cabinet, Roosevelt lunches with Straus, Seth Low and his old friend Seth Bullock. He urges Root to open treaty talks with Japan on immigration right away.

headline: Harvard '80 at the White House
summary: Roosevelt hosts his Harvard Class of 1880 for dinner. Earlier he confers on selling Indian lands and rides with Ethel and Seth Bullock. He writes the District commissioner that Quentin and Archie are upset by a proposal for longer school days, and tells Kermit he does not care for A Connecticut Yankee or for Browning's poetry.

headline: Alice and Nick's first anniversary
summary: Alice and Nick mark a year of marriage. Roosevelt and Edith go with the Lodges to the Corcoran to see its new painting, The Summit. He writes Carnegie about Japan and the rising tension between Nicaragua and Honduras.

headline: First meeting with Goethals
summary: Roosevelt takes up the school question with Senator Flint and an Idaho judgeship with Heyburn, and confers with Major George W. Goethals. He writes that a bill giving the government appeal rights in criminal cases is weaker than he wanted but will help in railroad cases.

headline: Breakfast with Dr. Lambert
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts with his friend Dr. Alexander Lambert, confers on ship subsidies and canal contracts, and names W. C. Bristol U.S. attorney for Oregon. Nicaragua invades Honduras, and the Strauses host the Roosevelts at dinner.

headline: Signing the immigration bill
summary: On a crowded day Roosevelt sees Richard Ballinger, discusses railroad law with Representative Wanger, and approves the Immigration Bill. He asks Straus about the investigation into the labor of women and children.

headline: Naval strength with Dewey
summary: Roosevelt goes over the Colorado River break with Flint and the Navy's strength with Admiral Dewey and Metcalf. Fairbanks, Longworth and Jusserand are among the callers.

headline: Off to Boston with the family
summary: After working through state judgeships and lunching with Francis Millet, Root and Admiral Cowles, Roosevelt sets out for Boston with Ethel, Nick, Alice and Edith. He writes Strachey on Germany and England, Japan and the Navy.

headline: Defending rough sports at Harvard
summary: In Boston, Roosevelt breakfasts at Dr. William Sturgis Bigelow's with Arlo Bates, Dean Briggs and the Rev. Samuel Crothers, goes to the Porcellian, visits the Lees at Chestnut Hill and stops at Houghton Mifflin. At the Harvard Union he pairs ideals with practical sense and pushes back against President Eliot's dislike of rough sports. In Washington, Senator Fulton moves to strip the President of power to create forest reserves.

headline: Groton visit with Kermit
summary: After breakfast with Austin Wadsworth, G. H. Lyman and Governor Guild, Roosevelt goes out to Groton to see Kermit at school and visit the Gardners, then returns to Boston and leaves for Washington.

headline: Bryce arrives as British ambassador
summary: Congress passes the agriculture bill carrying the Fulton amendment, which strips the President of authority to set aside new forest reserves. James Bryce presents his credentials as Britain's new ambassador in place of Durand, and that evening Roosevelt, Edith and the Lodges go to the Belasco Theater.

headline: Goethals takes over the canal
summary: Roosevelt announces that John Stevens is leaving and that Army Major George W. Goethals will run canal construction. He tells Shonts to reject all the construction bids and asks Senator Allison for a law letting the government investigate railroad accidents.

headline: Coal leases and the Columbia Theater
summary: Another busy day: Alabama appointments with Pettus and Clayton, labor law with Representative Sherman, and coal leases with the federal board that oversees Indian affairs. In the evening Roosevelt and Edith go to the Columbia Theater.

headline: An Immigration Commission named
summary: Roosevelt names an Immigration Commission led by Senator William P. Dillingham, with Jeremiah Jenks, Charles P. Neill and William R. Wheeler. He tells Sir Edward Grey he welcomes Bryce, cared nothing for Swettenham's letter, and has won some things and lost others from the departing Congress. The Senate has also approved the treaty with Santo Domingo.

headline: Hitchcock and Shaw step down
summary: Interior Secretary Hitchcock and Treasury Secretary Shaw leave the Cabinet. Roosevelt discusses ship subsidies with Watson, meets Lodge, and talks with Representative Hull about raising Army officers' pay.

headline: The midnight forests
summary: Racing the Fulton amendment, Roosevelt signs an order that adds or expands 32 forest reserves across the West, from Olympic and Rainier in Washington to San Juan in Colorado. He explains that waiting would have let vital reserves be lost. He also sees Harriman and confers on Indiana appointments, postal affairs, Utah coal lands and the canal.

headline: Archie has diphtheria
summary: Roosevelt writes Kermit that Archie is sick with diphtheria and the whole family is anxious. Quentin has been isolated with the policemen and ushers, Ethel is in Philadelphia, and the end of the congressional session keeps Roosevelt busy. He writes Washington's Governor Mead about the forest reserves, Pinchot and Ballinger.

headline: New Cabinet, new Congress
summary: The Cabinet changes take effect: Cortelyou moves to Treasury, Meyer becomes Postmaster General, and Garfield takes Interior. Joseph Bucklin Bishop takes Shonts's seat on the canal board, Chalmette National Monument in Louisiana is created, and the 59th Congress gives way to the 60th with Republican majorities in both houses.

headline: Lunch with George Sheldon
summary: After the Cabinet meets and Grosvenor, Post, Gamble and Dillingham call, Roosevelt lunches with George Sheldon.

headline: Signing the bill he outflanked
summary: Roosevelt signs the agriculture appropriation, whose rider forbids presidents to set aside forest land in six western states. His March 2 proclamations had already added some 16 million acres. He confers on immigration, Indiana patronage, ship subsidies and an Idaho judgeship, and sees Root and Speck von Sternberg that night.

headline: Archie near death
summary: Archie's diphtheria takes a dangerous turn, and anxious people collect at the White House gates. Roosevelt still meets Hepburn and Neill on railroads and sees Dolliver, Allison and Hemenway.

headline: Archie pulls through the worst
summary: The Cabinet takes up Japanese immigration, and Roosevelt goes to a big luncheon at Pinchot's. He writes his cousin William E. Roosevelt that Archie came very close to dying the day before and that Edith's trip south is off.

headline: Naval personnel bill with Foss
summary: Roosevelt discusses the naval personnel bill with Representative Foss and receives a string of senators and congressmen. He writes California's Governor Gillett about the Japanese question.

headline: San Francisco backs down; nature fakers
summary: Roosevelt presses Root and Governor Gillett to block California bills excluding Japanese children, and later wires San Francisco's mayor congratulations when the school order is withdrawn. Chaco Canyon becomes a national monument, J. P. Morgan briefs him on shaky markets, and he tells John Burroughs he has finally sailed into Long, Jack London and the other nature fakers.

headline: Enforcing the eight-hour day
summary: Roosevelt talks with Taft about enforcing the eight-hour law and talks immigration with Beveridge, Lodge, Dixon and Flint. Lacey and Gamble also call.

headline: Inland Waterways Commission; panic on Wall Street
summary: Roosevelt creates the Inland Waterways Commission, chaired by Theodore Burton, to study the nation's rivers for power, flood control and reclamation; its members include Pinchot, Newell, W J McGee and Senator Newlands. The same day panic hits the New York Stock Exchange. He talks federal railroad control with A. B. Stickney and sends Burton the commission's charge.

headline: Cabinet confronts the market panic
summary: The Cabinet meets on the Wall Street panic, and Roosevelt confers with Cortelyou about it. He also sits down with mine union chief John Mitchell and the mine owners, and asks the Interstate Commerce Commission to value every railroad as a basis for fair rates.

headline: Harriman and the Illinois Central
summary: Roosevelt meets James Speyer and several senators on the financial situation, and Illinois Governor Deneen and his attorney general, Stead, about Harriman and the Illinois railroad. He writes Secretary Wilson on labeling blended whiskey.

headline: Waterways appointments made public
summary: The names on the Inland Waterways Commission are published. Cousin Emlen Roosevelt calls that evening.

headline: Opening an exposition by telegraph
summary: At 3:30 Roosevelt presses a button that opens the Louisville exposition. He discusses South Dakota patronage with Gamble and tells Thomas Page he is less and less willing to talk with railroad men.

headline: Railroads with C. S. Mellen
summary: Roosevelt confers on politics with Hansbrough and on railroads with New Haven president Charles S. Mellen, and meets Franklin K. Lane. He thanks Ernest Pollard and the other congressmen who backed the ship subsidy bill.

headline: A crowded lunch table with Bryce
summary: Roosevelt hosts a large lunch that includes Ambassador Bryce and much of the Cabinet. He confers with Taft and Major Scott about West Street buildings, and with Hitchcock and Ballinger.

headline: A visitor from Groton
summary: Roosevelt confers with Senator Overman and receives Jusserand, Root and George Marvin of Groton School.

headline: Waterways commission meets the President
summary: Roosevelt meets the new waterways commission and its chairman, Burton and lunches with Jusserand, Meyer and Brooks Adams. He asks Richard Bowker to report on conditions in Panama in light of Stevens's complaints and departure.

headline: Tobacco trust and new coins
summary: Roosevelt takes up Indian matters with Garfield and Leupp, the tobacco trust with F. H. Levy, the canal commission with Joseph Blackburn, and the new coinage with Roberts. He writes Illinois Attorney General Stead, who is probing Harriman's railroad stock transfers.

headline: Speck von Sternberg on Sunday
summary: Ambassador Speck von Sternberg calls at 2:30.

headline: Bat Masterson drops by
summary: Roosevelt and Beveridge discuss making New Mexico and Arizona states, and frontier lawman Bat Masterson is among the callers. Roosevelt tells Taft he opposes printing complete government records of every American war, and tells Jacob Schiff that Wall Street sees him as a wild-eyed revolutionary.

headline: Henry Adams sees him hesitate
summary: Henry Adams writes that everyone, even the President, is tired, and that Roosevelt seems unsure for once about the financial strain. Roosevelt meets Cortelyou, Root, Lane and Clark on railroads, lunches at Dr. Rixey's, and holds an immigration meeting with members of the new commission.

headline: Carnegie to lunch; another dental visit
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Andrew Carnegie, two Navy captains and several officials, meets the Interstate Commerce Commission, and goes to the dentist.

headline: Toothache, boils and an unbending course
summary: Roosevelt's tooth aches, Ted is suffering from boils, and Archie is still mending. He writes Jacob Schiff about Wall Street's view of him and tells Henry Higginson, amid the market turmoil, that he will not budge from his chosen path.

headline: More railroad talks
summary: After the Cabinet, Roosevelt meets Neill, Knapp and Cullom on railroads. Wisconsin's Governor Davidson and James W. Gerard are among the callers.

headline: Down over Brownsville
summary: Roosevelt confers on the canal with Representative Marshall and on railroads with August Belmont, J. M. Levy and Frank Kellogg. He praises Ray Stannard Baker's article on the Atlanta riot and race, admitting the Brownsville affair has left him depressed.

headline: Easter: everyone mending
summary: On a cold, rainy Easter, Roosevelt writes Kermit that Archie has recovered, Quentin is fine and, in his father's words, 'as quaint and funny as ever,' and Ted has spent the past three days ill. He adds that he dislikes seeming to speak only to move the stock market.

headline: Dentist chair and an Easter egg roll
summary: Roosevelt spends another late morning at the dentist, then sees Senator Burrows, McCall and Bishop. The reorganized Panama Canal Commission takes charge, and children roll Easter eggs across the White House lawn.

headline: The Harriman letter goes public
summary: The New York World prints a private Harriman letter claiming Roosevelt had offered Chauncey Depew the Paris embassy in return for 1904 campaign money. Roosevelt flatly denies it, sees Franklin K. Lane and Senator Flint, and holds a Cabinet meeting.

headline: Stung by an article on schoolchildren
summary: Roosevelt receives Justice Harlan, Senators Cullom and Flint, Bishop Satterlee and Representative Kennedy. He writes Albert Shaw that a Review of Reviews piece by Dr. John J. Cronin, favoring a handful of ideal pupils over many neglected ones, has troubled him.

headline: Lunch with James Gerard
summary: A steady line of callers comes through, among them Hale, Burrows, Foss, Hull, Metcalf and Garfield. Roosevelt lunches with James Gerard and writes John St. Loe Strachey about the gloomy state of affairs at home.

headline: Taking stock of a record on peace
summary: Roosevelt sits early for A. Benzinger and holds a Cabinet meeting. He tells Andrew Carnegie that Root will speak to Carnegie's National Arbitration and Peace Conference, and lays out what his administration has done for peace.

headline: Senators Bourne and Hansbrough confer
summary: Roosevelt meets with Senators Jonathan Bourne and Henry Hansbrough, and with Hopkins. In the evening he dines with Dr. Jordan.

headline: Sunday with Sternberg and Riis
summary: An afternoon call from German Ambassador Speck von Sternberg, and an evening dinner with Roosevelt's old friend Jacob Riis.

headline: A French baron spends the night
summary: A full day: canal talk with Speaker Cannon, Honduras with Representative Smith, another dentist visit, and a dinner for Baron d'Estournelles de Constant with Jusserand, Pinchot and others. Roosevelt writes Arthur Lee about Archie's illness and Senator Patterson about the Harriman letter.

headline: Archie turns thirteen
summary: Archie celebrates his thirteenth birthday. His father spends part of the afternoon in the dentist's chair yet again.

headline: Whisky labels and Oklahoma jobs
summary: After breakfast with Albert Shaw, Roosevelt talks Oklahoma appointments with Dennis Flynn, visits the dentist and discusses the canal with Senator Curtis. Letters go to Secretary Wilson on whisky labeling, to Trevelyan on books, and to Lodge about the fleet's commanders, Admiral Evans among them.

headline: A new poem and a failed photo
summary: Roosevelt sits for his portrait, confers on the canal with Tawney and Olcott, and returns to the dentist. He writes Nick about backing Taft for 1908, and tells Kermit about a new Edwin Arlington Robinson poem, blurry jumping photos of himself and Ted, and a planned ride with Edith.

headline: Rough Riders monument at Arlington
summary: After a Cabinet meeting and talks with Root, Cortelyou and Senator Gamble, Roosevelt goes to the dentist and then to Arlington Cemetery for the unveiling of a memorial to his Rough Riders. He also writes Whitridge on valuing railroads.

headline: Archbishop Ireland calls
summary: A quiet Saturday of visitors: Speaker Cannon, Archbishop John Ireland and Representative Humphrey.

headline: Dinner for Harvard's President Eliot
summary: Ambassador Jusserand calls in the afternoon. That evening Roosevelt hosts Harvard president Charles W. Eliot at a dinner with Justice Holmes, Meyer, Garfield, Bonaparte, Moody, Leupp and Pinchot.

headline: An Arbor Day plea to America's children
summary: On Arbor Day Roosevelt sends a message to the nation's schoolchildren warning that their generation will pay for forests wasted now. He greets Harvard's lacrosse team, talks New York politics, and opens the Masonic Fair with the press of a button. He also writes that Cuba must one day govern itself.

headline: Wall Street rumors and veterans' squabbles
summary: A Cabinet meeting takes up the indictment of Senator Borah. Roosevelt lunches with Tower and McIlhenny, sees the dentist, and writes a stack of letters: on railroad valuation, a Memorial Day quarrel among veterans, ousting New Mexico's governor, and Wall Street gossip that he drinks too much.

headline: Taft looks like the man
summary: Former Iowa governor William Larrabee talks railroads with Roosevelt. In a letter to Charles Washburn, Roosevelt says plainly that Taft appears the best choice to rally behind as his successor.

headline: Ethel plans a dinner party
summary: Roosevelt receives S. H. Cowan, Hull, Elkins, Mondell, Clark and Admiral Evans, while Ethel prepares to host her friends at dinner. Senator Beveridge drops by late in the evening.

headline: Foraker among the callers
summary: After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt sees Allee, Bartholdt, Meyer, Senator Foraker and W. J. Coombs.

headline: Fit officers and Ohio's feud
summary: Roosevelt talks canal business with John Stevens and meets L. M. Shaw. He writes General Bell that Army officers must be physically fit, and tells Nick Longworth about the Ohio rift pitting Foraker and Dick against Taft and Boss Cox.

headline: Edith on reading and schoolwork
summary: A quiet Sunday. Edith tells Kermit that as a schoolgirl she kept poetry and novels for weekends, since they swallowed her attention too completely.

headline: Defending the 'undesirable citizens' remark
summary: New Mexico governor Hagerman resigns. Roosevelt poses for photographer Harris, talks New York politics with Representative Parsons, and sees Ambassador Bryce. Answering Honoré Jaxon, he stands by calling Harriman, Moyer, Haywood and Debs undesirable citizens, denying any intent to sway the jury.

headline: Kermit on the football team
summary: After Cabinet and a talk with Senator Borah, Roosevelt hosts a White House musicale. He writes Kermit, who has made Groton's second eleven and also rows and runs, that Archie takes the attacks on his father to heart.

headline: Borah's indictment on the table
summary: Roosevelt confers on New York politics with Vreeland, Sherman and Littauer, and again with Borah about his indictment. Dinner guests include the Cowleses, Meyer, Garfield, Jusserand, Justice Day, General Crozier, Herbert Wadsworth and Captain McCoy.

headline: Sailing for Jamestown on the Mayflower
summary: After meetings with Senators Penrose and Bourne, Harry New, and Representative Burton on the new Inland Waterways Commission, Roosevelt boards the Mayflower bound for the Jamestown Exposition, taking along Edith, the children Ethel, Archie and Quentin, the Bacons and Justice Moody. Manti National Forest in Utah is established.

headline: Opening the Jamestown Exposition
summary: Roosevelt formally opens the Jamestown Exposition marking 300 years since the English landing, after reviewing sixteen American battleships and cruisers alongside visiting foreign warships. He shrugs off the speechmaking and receptions as routine; Edith accidentally sits on his top hat. The family dines in Norfolk with St. George Tucker.

headline: Up the James past the old plantations
summary: The party cruises up the James River aboard the Sylph, taking in the colonial plantation houses at Shirley, Westover and Brandon, before switching back to the Mayflower for the return to Washington.

headline: Congratulations to Ambassador Takahira
summary: Roosevelt congratulates Kogoro Takahira on being named Japan's ambassador to Italy, and takes up the troubles facing Japanese residents of San Francisco.

headline: No third run, he tells Cummins
summary: On Corinne's silver wedding anniversary, Roosevelt receives Foraker, Cannon, former governor Durbin and a New York Central vice president, and sees Pinchot late. He tells Kermit spring has come, with an hour under an apple tree with Edith and a ride with Lodge, and assures Albert Cummins he will not run again.

headline: Dinner for the visiting foreign officers
summary: Roosevelt confers on Navy business with Meyer and Representative Foss, then hosts a dinner for officers of the foreign warships in port for Jamestown.

headline: Spying on torpedo works abroad
summary: Roosevelt meets Knox, Taft and Hemenway, and talks railroads with C. S. Mellen. He presses Governor Hagerman again on why he must resign, and asks Ambassador Whitelaw Reid and other envoys to help Commander Albert Gleaves inspect foreign torpedo plants.

headline: A statue for General McClellan
summary: Roosevelt confers with James B. Reynolds about the Idaho case against Moyer and Haywood and attends the afternoon unveiling of the General George B. McClellan statue on Connecticut Avenue. His cousin West Roosevelt is staying at the White House.

headline: Owen Wister comes to stay
summary: After the Cabinet meets, novelist Owen Wister arrives to spend the night, invited to stay as long as he likes. Roosevelt praises Senator Beveridge's speeches and articles in his running debate with William Jennings Bryan.

headline: Pure food and the Gatun Dam
summary: Roosevelt goes over the food and drug law with Lodge, Secretary Wilson and Representative Gill, and the Gatun Dam with Taft. Lunch brings together Governor Deneen of Illinois, Inland Waterways commissioners, Garfield and Charles MacVeagh.

headline: Evening caller Dr. Pritchett
summary: A quiet Sunday with one late visitor, Dr. Pritchett.

headline: Two new national monuments in California
summary: On a crowded day, Lassen Peak and Cinder Cone become national monuments. Roosevelt talks New York politics with Representative Parsons and, by pressing telegraph keys, opens the Actors' Fund Fair at New York's Metropolitan Opera House and a Schützenfest in Charleston.

headline: Doctors at the White House
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts with Dr. Alexander Lambert, holds Cabinet, meets Bonaparte, and lunches with Riis, Lawrence Abbott, Lambert, Merriam and Harg. He receives the American Medical Congress and ends the night on Internal Revenue appointments with Senator Elkins.

headline: A bureau of health and a broken mailbag
summary: Roosevelt talks Oklahoma statehood with Dennis Flynn and lunches with General Young. In Venezuela, the American legation's official mail pouch is illegally opened. Letters go to Irving Fisher on a national health bureau, to Sir Ian Hamilton on a Russo-Japanese War book, and to William Allen White about Borah.

headline: Planning the Mississippi trip
summary: Roosevelt keeps only morning appointments, going over the coming Mississippi River trip with Gifford Pinchot and seeing Bonaparte, Ballinger and Warner. He tells Senator Beveridge the railroads need to be valued.

headline: Lunch with the Duke of the Abruzzi
summary: The Italian explorer-prince the Duke of the Abruzzi lunches at the White House with the Bonapartes, Silas McBee and Italy's ambassador. In the afternoon Roosevelt receives the delegations that came for the Jamestown celebration.

headline: Horses, then a state dinner for Kuroki
summary: After Cabinet and a talk on Ohio politics with the Taft brothers, Roosevelt takes Lodge, Root, Meyer and Jusserand out jumping horses. That night a formal White House dinner honors Japan's General Kuroki and the Duke of the Abruzzi.

headline: Turtles in the bathtub
summary: General Arthur MacArthur calls in the evening. Roosevelt writes Kermit that General Kuroki is their houseguest and that friendly ties with Japan matter, and tells Ted about Archie's menagerie of tadpoles, tiny turtles and a little alligator.

headline: Defending his choice of judges
summary: Roosevelt reviews New York patronage with Cortelyou and Loeb, sees Post cartoonist Kirk Russell, and lunches with Knox. He writes Mark Sullivan reviewing his judicial picks, from Holmes, Day and Moody on the Supreme Court down to the lower benches.

headline: The Butlers stay the night
summary: Roosevelt receives Gaines, Hull and Knox. Columbia's Nicholas Murray Butler and his wife come for dinner and stay over. A letter to Nick covers the Taft-Foraker fight over patronage and Taft's endorsement.

headline: No third term, he tells Kermit
summary: After Cabinet, Roosevelt discusses Kansas and Oklahoma politics with Senator Curtis and canal business with Commissioner Smith, then lunches with Taft. He writes Kermit that he will not seek a third term.

headline: A children's matinee, then the dentist
summary: Roosevelt confers with Senators Burrows and Cullom, Burton and Martin, and lunches with Root, John Barrett, Admiral Brownson, Metcalf and Lt. Boyd. He goes to a children's matinee in the afternoon and to the dentist after.

headline: Off to Pine Knot
summary: Roosevelt leaves Washington for Pine Knot, the family's simple country retreat in Virginia.

headline: At Pine Knot
summary: Roosevelt is at Pine Knot. The record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: A Sunday at Pine Knot
summary: Another day at the Virginia cabin, with no events recorded.

headline: Mob violence in San Francisco
summary: While Roosevelt is at Pine Knot, a mob in San Francisco begins a string of attacks on Japanese residents and their property.

headline: A flock of passenger pigeons
summary: At Pine Knot Roosevelt spots a flock of passenger pigeons, making him one of the last people known to have seen the birds in the wild. Within seven years the species was gone, the final bird dying in a zoo in 1914.

headline: Back from Pine Knot
summary: Roosevelt returns to Washington. He writes Lodge about fanciful newspaper talk of splitting the fleet, and Edith tells Kermit about their stay at Pine Knot.

headline: Keep laborers home on both sides
summary: Roosevelt meets William Cocks on New York politics and Speaker Cannon, lunches with Taft, Cannon, canal man Jackson Smith and Judge Tracey, and dines with Sheldon, Warburton and naturalist C. Hart Merriam. To Baron Kaneko he suggests barring laborers from migrating between Japan and America for a generation.

headline: Commencement at Sidwell Friends
summary: After Cabinet, a talk with Senator Pettus about the Military Affairs Committee, visits from John Barrett and Pennsylvania Railroad president McCrea, and another trip to the dentist, Roosevelt attends the evening graduation at Sidwell Friends School.

headline: A foreword for Selous
summary: Roosevelt plans the postal inspection trip with Frank Hitchcock and sees a crowd of visitors, including Ambassador Bryce, writer Edwin Lefèvre and the Japanese, Hungarian and Panamanian envoys. After lunch with Root he finishes a foreword for a book by the African hunter Frederick Selous and mails it to him.

headline: Land fraud and Oklahoma's constitution
summary: Roosevelt writes Attorney General Bonaparte about land fraud and corruption in New Mexico and about whether Oklahoma's proposed constitution is lawful.

headline: A soaking ride to Mount Vernon
summary: After a morning meeting with William McAdoo, Roosevelt rides to Mount Vernon with Edith, Ethel, Meyer and Captain Fitzhugh Lee through showers that never let up. He also writes William Emlen Roosevelt about the nation's crops.

headline: Overnight train to Canton
summary: Roosevelt discusses Japanese exclusion with Bonaparte and meets Hemenway, Hitchcock, Bourne and Bartholdt. That night he boards a B&O train for Canton, Ohio, traveling with Secretary Wilson, Garfield and Root.

headline: Mrs. McKinley's funeral
summary: In Canton Roosevelt attends the funeral of Ida McKinley, the late President's widow, and dines at Justice Day's. Stopping at Akron that evening, he and Vice President Fairbanks walk out to nearby farms, chatting with families and drinking fresh milk.

headline: Memorial Day in Indianapolis
summary: Stopping at Sidney, Union City and Muncie on the way, Roosevelt reaches Indianapolis, lunches with Fairbanks, Beveridge, poet James Whitcomb Riley and others, and dedicates the Lawton statue. His Decoration Day address calls for federal oversight of railroads and their securities, federal incorporation, and valuation of their property. The Manhattans Fairbanks serves at lunch make headlines.

headline: Speeches in Lansing and an old cowboy
summary: At Lansing Roosevelt speaks at the Michigan capitol and that evening at the Michigan Agricultural College, visits Benjamin Ide Wheeler, and greets his old Badlands cowboy friend Bob McClellan. His article on railroad investments appears in the Review of Reviews, and Everybody's runs Edward Clark's attack on the 'nature fakers.' Alice and Nick head west for Yellowstone and Hawaii.

headline: Home by way of Pittsburgh
summary: Riding back to Washington through Pittsburgh with University of California president Benjamin Ide Wheeler, Roosevelt writes Kermit about the Mount Vernon ride, his memories of Mrs. McKinley, his annoyance that the funeral crowd fussed over him instead of her family, and his Midwest swing.

headline: Pigeons and nature fakers, to Burroughs
summary: Roosevelt writes John Burroughs about the passenger pigeons he saw at Pine Knot and about the quarrel over the Rev. William J. Long's animal stories. A second letter tells Clarence Clark why a Mr. Camplin will not get a Wyoming appointment.

headline: Navy talk with Metcalf and Brownson
summary: Roosevelt confers with Navy Secretary Metcalf and Admiral Brownson, and sees Senator Cullom and Smithsonian scientist Charles D. Walcott.

headline: Lunch with French officers
summary: After Cabinet, Roosevelt meets Root, Metcalf and Admiral Brownson, sees Representative Calder, Charles Lummis and Senator Elkins, and lunches with Ambassador Jusserand and a party of French officers.

headline: The Harriman case with Lane
summary: Roosevelt takes up mine railroads with Bonaparte and the Harriman investigation with Interstate Commerce Commissioner Franklin K. Lane. Root, Taft, Ambassador Bryce and Frank B. Kellogg also call.

headline: Thanks to a favorite author
summary: Roosevelt sees George Shiras and lunches with Jacob Riis's newly married daughter and her husband, the Owres. He writes author Mary Wilkins Freeman that he and Edith love her books and simply wanted to thank her.

headline: Western anger over land withdrawals
summary: Roosevelt confers on trusts with Milton Purdy and on the Inland Waterways Commission with Burton, holds Cabinet, and meets late into the evening with Root, Taft, Bonaparte, Garfield and the Interstate Commerce commissioners. He warns Secretary Wilson that the Denver Public Lands Convention will voice Western opposition to his timber and coal land withdrawals.

headline: A sculptor for Commodore Barry
summary: Roosevelt reviews land laws with Bonaparte and Ballinger, sees a long list of callers including Ambassador Bryce and James S. Sherman, and lunches with Taft. He recommends sculptor John Boyle to Senator Wetmore for the planned Barry statue honoring the Revolutionary naval hero. Sheffield Cowles signs the guest book.

headline: Back down to Jamestown
summary: Roosevelt sails for Jamestown on the Mayflower. He writes Bonaparte about Charles Mellen's push for a railroad monopoly and Taft about the Army Quartermaster Corps, where James Aleshire would be named Quartermaster General.

headline: Georgia Day and a copy of Bulloch Hall
summary: At the Jamestown Exposition Roosevelt dedicates the Georgia Building, a replica of his mother's girlhood home, Bulloch Hall in Roswell. Bamie and Will Cowles and Corinne and Douglas Robinson are with him. He speaks to the National Educational Association, returns to Washington, and names George Goethals to a federal fuels and materials board.

headline: Fuel for the Northwest's winter
summary: After Cabinet, Roosevelt discusses federal land policy with Senator Carter and the Harriman case with Lane, and lunches with George Shiras. He tells Postmaster General Meyer the Northwest must lay in fuel before winter.

headline: Summer begins: off to Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt leaves Washington for Oyster Bay and the summer White House at Sagamore Hill. His sister Bamie is recorded among the guests.

headline: Settling in at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt congratulates Kermit on a good year at Groton and a footrace win, and reports that he, Edith and Ethel are shelving books and unpacking for the summer. He also writes Senator Redfield Proctor about naming a Vermonter to the Second Circuit bench.

headline: A blank day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

headline: John Temple Graves visits
summary: Georgia journalist John Temple Graves calls at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Beveridge late on a Sunday
summary: Senator Albert Beveridge visits Sagamore Hill in the evening.

headline: Brownsville was not about race, he insists
summary: Roosevelt writes Senator James Hemenway, who sits on the committee investigating Brownsville, that discharging the Black soldiers had nothing to do with racial prejudice. He also writes Lodge about Massachusetts railroad mergers.

headline: Nothing recorded
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record is empty for the day.

headline: Burroughs arrives by automobile
summary: Burroughs and ex-Senator Childs motor in from Floral City in the morning, and Allison Swan calls in the afternoon. Edith tells Kermit that skipping geometry was one perk of being a girl.

headline: The Jusserands come for the weekend
summary: Ambassador Jules Jusserand and his wife Elise arrive for a stay through Saturday. Roosevelt praises Kenneth Grahame's books for children, writes Bonaparte about an Oklahoma census, his receivership plan for dissolving illegal corporations and the New Haven merger, and sends Trevelyan more talk of books.

headline: Against splitting the fleet
summary: Roosevelt hosts Root, Judge Ward, Bridges, Alvord Cooley and Herbert Knox Smith at lunch, and explains to Benjamin Ide Wheeler why he opposes dividing the battle fleet.

headline: A playful note to Burroughs
summary: Roosevelt sends John Burroughs a lighthearted letter about his recent visit and the birds around Sagamore Hill. The Jusserands' stay ends.

headline: Quiet Sunday
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Looking back on his Harvard grades
summary: The Dominican customs treaty is approved. Roosevelt thanks classmate Frederick Ranlett for a Harvard Graduates' Magazine piece on his college standing and studies, and reflects on his own years at Harvard.

headline: Songs on the piazza
summary: Taft comes to lunch. That evening Roosevelt and Ethel sit out on the piazza listening to the Black household staff sing. Edith is away seeing Ted and Kermit at New London, Connecticut.

headline: Declining the Medal of Honor Club
summary: Roosevelt declines to join the club for Medal of Honor nominees, telling Alexander Scott that although he was nominated, he does not think he earned the medal for San Juan Hill. He also writes Nick that Foraker is still making trouble and that he will see the Fleischmann brothers, Taft men.

headline: A big lunch and the Cove School
summary: After calls from Metcalf, Captain Wainwright and naturalist Ernest Ingersoll, Roosevelt hosts a large lunch with the Norwegian and Chinese ministers among the guests. He and Edith attend commencement at the Cove School. To Lodge he writes that Taft means to take on Foraker over the Brownsville affair, and mentions Martin Luther and young Trevelyan's book on Garibaldi.

headline: Captain McCoy settles in
summary: Captain Frank McCoy arrives for a stay lasting until July 1. Britain's envoy in Abyssinia, Harrington, joins him for lunch, and editor Paul Dana calls in the afternoon.

headline: Cosgrave calls; a word for Taft
summary: Editor John O'Hara Cosgrave visits in the morning, and Captain Long lunches. Roosevelt writes Ohio Democrat Allen Thurman about support for Taft.

headline: Haywood acquitted in Idaho
summary: In Boise, a jury acquits 'Big Bill' Haywood of the murder of former Idaho governor Frank Steunenberg. At Sagamore Hill Captain Winslow lunches, Frank McCoy and Grace Pollin sign the guest book, and Ethel keeps busy with parties in town and weekend riding at country houses.

headline: Russia, Japan and Carnegie's peace talk
summary: Roosevelt writes Taft about the Quartermaster General post and the canal, and sends Cecil Spring Rice his views on American diplomats in Russia, trouble with Japan, and Andrew Carnegie's peace conference.

headline: Fresh trouble brewing in San Francisco
summary: Ambassador Thomas O'Brien comes to lunch. Roosevelt writes Root about Aleshire's appointment, renewed strife in San Francisco, a German-American tariff deal, and the Hague and Carnegie peace meetings.

headline: Taking on the nature faker
summary: Roosevelt writes The Outlook a letter intended for publication that demolishes the Rev. William J. Long's credibility as a nature writer. Guests include Barclay Farr, Alexander Grant, his nephew Monroe Douglas Robinson and Phineas Chrystie.

headline: Fourth of July at the desk
summary: Roosevelt writes Paul Dana about a New York postmastership, Lodge on insurance probes and the New Haven line, and Taft about the Quartermaster department, Brownsville, and Major Samuel Reber's report that the Japanese public bears America little ill will.

headline: Callers from near and far
summary: A string of visitors comes to Sagamore Hill, including Edward B. Clark, Frank Hitchcock, Sir Jocelyn Booth, Admiral Brownson and General Aleshire.

headline: Thanking a cattleman ally
summary: Roosevelt thanks Murdo MacKenzie, the Texas cattleman, for backing his Western conservation policies, and protests to Herbert Satterlee about Navy Magazine articles faulting American warship designs. Henry Holt Jr. visits, and Robert Bacon stops by.

headline: Quiet Sunday
summary: No entries for the day at Sagamore Hill.

headline: A warbler, and a hard rule for Presidents
summary: Roosevelt collects a yellow-throated warbler. Writing Lawrence Abbott, he admits a President should stick to his job yet insists he may still speak out against Rev. Long's invented animal tales.

headline: Regrets for the Whittier centennial
summary: Lunch guests are Willcox and Herbert Knox Smith, and Moffatt of Collier's Weekly calls. Roosevelt tells Emily B. Smith he cannot attend the celebration of John Greenleaf Whittier's 100th birthday.

headline: The fleet will sail around the world
summary: With William Hepburn staying over, Roosevelt confides to Lodge that the whole battle fleet will be sent around the world, amid rumors it is already in the Pacific. Other letters cover federal control of railroad securities, Southern support for Taft, pictures, and the ICC railroad report.

headline: O'Brien goes to Tokyo
summary: Guests at the house are Hepburn, Cochran and Caspar Whitney. Roosevelt informs Thomas O'Brien of his appointment as minister to Japan and trades bird notes with John Burroughs.

headline: Admiral Yamamoto comes to lunch
summary: Japan's Admiral Yamamoto and Ambassador Aoki lunch at Sagamore Hill alongside the Fleischmann brothers, E. D. Morgan and Robert Bacon. Hall Roosevelt, Henry Holt Jr. and others sign the guest book, and Roosevelt writes Taft about Senator Borah's troubles.

headline: Why the fleet should go to the Pacific
summary: Roosevelt tells Root that sending the battle fleet to the Pacific should have a calming effect, and that the Navy must test in peacetime whether it can be done. He meets telephone company delegates with Charles Neill, confers with Bonaparte, and writes on the Newfoundland fisheries, Army fitness, the judiciary and rising Japanese immigration.

headline: Quiet Sunday
summary: Nothing is recorded at Sagamore Hill today.

headline: Vorys runs Taft's campaign
summary: Roosevelt writes Taft about Arthur Vorys, who is managing Taft's political campaign.

headline: A night out camping with the boys
summary: Roosevelt takes the boys on an overnight camping trip and spots two foxes. He writes Ambassador Sternberg explaining the Japanese troubles and peace advocates, and tells Melville Stone he hopes no European prince will tour the United States.

headline: Tariff talk over lunch
summary: The Persian minister calls in the morning. At lunch with Henry L. Stimson, Albert Shaw, Senator Hopkins and H. E. Miles, the conversation turns to revising the tariff.

headline: A shrew on the tennis court
summary: Playing tennis, Roosevelt finds a shrew by the court. He writes Senator Hopkins, annoyed that newspapers have reported Wednesday's lunch talk on the tariff. John McIlhenny and Harper Sibley are guests.

headline: Burroughs in the clover field
summary: Roosevelt writes John Burroughs about the day Burroughs helped him cut a clover field, and about the birds and small animals that dash across the tennis court mid-rally.

headline: Haywood, Borah and a Matthews article
summary: Roosevelt writes reporter Oscar King Davis about the Haywood trial in Idaho and the land-fraud charges against Senator Borah, and sends Brander Matthews a short note on one of his articles.

headline: Quiet Sunday
summary: No entries today at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Ships to Provincetown, not Boston
summary: Cortelyou comes to lunch. Roosevelt writes Lodge about false press stories and tells him the naval vessels will anchor off Provincetown instead of Boston for the holiday.

headline: War scare with Japan
summary: William Willcox calls. Roosevelt asks Lawrence Murray for Keep Commission material for his Annual Message and writes Root about the war scare, as talk spreads that Japan might fight over school segregation and immigration limits.

headline: Is Admiral Manney a lunatic?
summary: Over lunch with Willcox, Swift, Swan and Warner, Roosevelt fumes about Admiral Manney's notions on Japan and the Pacific, mocking them to Will Cowles and dismissing them to Truman Newberry. He tells Sternberg he doubts Japan wants to drag Mexico into a war.

headline: Quiet Thursday
summary: No events recorded at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Swollen heads in Japan
summary: Roosevelt complains to Root that Japanese pride has swelled remarkably and comments on Root's Yale lectures. Other letters go to Taft on fighting Foraker, Melville Stone on Japanese tensions, and Admiral Brownson on readying battleships in case of war.

headline: Tennis with Mr. Sears
summary: Mr. Sears drops by for a game of tennis. Roosevelt writes Alfred Henry Lewis about Hagerman, the former New Mexico governor.

headline: Quiet Sunday
summary: Nothing is recorded at Sagamore Hill.

headline: A miscarriage of justice in Idaho
summary: Governor Curtis Guild and Truman Newberry lunch at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt writes Llewellyn about removing Hagerman, Herbert Miles about a tariff commission, and Whitelaw Reid about foreign affairs and The Hague, calling Haywood's acquittal a gross miscarriage of justice.

headline: Books, printing and the Naval Academy
summary: Roosevelt talks naval business with Truman Newberry. He writes Edith Wendell about books and fine printing, Newberry about the Naval Academy, and William Allen White on why he favors Taft and on the charges against Senator Borah.

headline: Archie and Skip on the bay
summary: Roosevelt tells Root that Senator Hale is leading the opposition to sending the fleet around the world, and writes Ormsby McHarg about New Mexico politics. Joseph Bishop and others are guests, while Archie spends nearly every day out in his dory on Oyster Bay, his dog Skip aboard.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing more is recorded for the day.

headline: Trimming the Provincetown speech
summary: Bob Bacon, Alford Cooley and Peter Jay call. Roosevelt sends Attorney General Bonaparte the text of his August 20 Provincetown address, from which he has cut mention of his receivership plan, and notes North Carolina's Governor Glenn is at odds with the railroads.

headline: Father York comes calling
summary: Father York is among the guests, and Gardner Perry and Edward Venable Jr. sign the guest book. Roosevelt writes Taft about Foraker and where Taft stands politically.

headline: Saint-Gaudens dies
summary: Sculptor Augustus Saint-Gaudens dies. At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt lunches with his cousin John Ellis Roosevelt.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing more is recorded for the day.

headline: Edith turns 46; lessons from Russia's navy
summary: On Edith's 46th birthday, Roosevelt writes Truman Newberry that the Russo-Japanese War teaches one thing above all: keep the battleships together, the mistake Russia made being to divide them. He also discusses the coming voyage around the world.

headline: Cortelyou and Ambassador Francis
summary: Roosevelt confers with Cortelyou, then lunches with Ernest Abbott and Ambassador David R. Francis.

headline: A refuge for Louisiana's birds
summary: The Tern Islands Bird Reservation is established off the Louisiana coast.

headline: Lunch with William Allen White
summary: Loeb, John Yerkes, writer C. P. Connolly, William Allen White and Bonaparte lunch at Sagamore Hill. In the afternoon Roosevelt receives José de Diego, Speaker of Puerto Rico's House of Delegates.

headline: The Sternbergs arrive for the weekend
summary: The German ambassador and Baroness von Sternberg come in on the evening train to stay until Monday. Roosevelt writes Ralph Easley about Miss Beek's report on conditions in Panama and sends Truman Newberry details on the fleet's sailing.

headline: Sternbergs in the guest book
summary: Baron and Baroness von Sternberg spend Sunday at Sagamore Hill and sign the guest book.

headline: Not my fault, he tells Higginson
summary: Callers include William Barnes, Judge Hunt and Fleischmann. As critics blame his attacks on big business for the gathering financial trouble, Roosevelt writes Boston banker Henry Higginson rejecting any responsibility, and tells Bonaparte he believes Senator Borah innocent.

headline: Ethel turns 15
summary: It is Ethel's fifteenth birthday. Taft, Root and Meyer call; McBee, Taft, Meyer and Loeb stay for lunch, and the Roots spend the night.

headline: Provincetown draft goes to Lodge
summary: With the Roots as houseguests, Roosevelt lunches with McHay and Morgan. He sends Lodge a rough draft of the Provincetown speech along with thoughts on finance, praises Benjamin Wiggins's address, and writes Newberry on building torpedo boats.

headline: A family photograph
summary: The family gathers for a group photograph in the morning. Roosevelt explains to Higginson why civil suits against corporations are easier to win than criminal cases against individuals, and writes Bonaparte on that letter, finance, New Mexico, Borah and the railroads.

headline: Picnic, and fears of a world panic
summary: The family goes on a picnic. Roosevelt writes David Scull about the chance of a worldwide financial panic, and Root about Colombia recognizing Panama in exchange for a land settlement.

headline: Standard Oil rebates and a new bird refuge
summary: Roosevelt discusses the rebate prosecution of Indiana Standard Oil with Edwin Sims, and meets Cortelyou and Wilkinson. Shell Keys in Louisiana becomes a bird reservation. Letters cover the fleet's sailing, continued probes in New Mexico, and possible railroad prosecutions.

headline: Ethel's guest-book verse
summary: Dr. Alexander Lambert and Arthur Woods sign the guest book, along with a teasing rhyme about Ethel begging the doctor and the policeman for verses.

headline: Sailing for Provincetown
summary: Right at ten, Roosevelt sets out aboard the Mayflower for Cape Cod, with Ethel, Ted and Cornelia Landon. In Columbus, Ohio, Taft defends trust-busting and Roosevelt's economic course before the Buckeye Republican Club.

headline: 'Malefactors of great wealth'
summary: Speaking at the Pilgrim Monument in Provincetown, Roosevelt charges that some very rich men are deliberately worsening the financial strain to discredit his policies and force them reversed. He also meets 500 fishermen from Gloucester.

headline: Back home, writing Kermit
summary: Home again, Roosevelt tells Kermit about the Provincetown trip. Three letters to Taft cover the Panama-Colombia agreement, Army fire-control equipment, and the Philippines and Cuba. Cecilia May and Father Simpkins sign the guest book.

headline: A 'good' trust: International Harvester
summary: George W. Perkins calls in the morning, and Taft speaks in Lexington, Kentucky. Roosevelt writes Bonaparte twice: he counts International Harvester a good trust that should not be prosecuted, and adds notes on Borah and the panic.

headline: Admirals and a muckraker
summary: Truman Newberry, Admirals Evans and Brownson, Lincoln Steffens and Francis Leupp call. Roosevelt assures Governor George Curry that he has no plans to remove him in New Mexico.

headline: Backing arbitration in Central America
summary: Roosevelt writes Bonaparte about the Union Pacific and Standard Oil prosecutions and Ruick's removal from the Borah prosecution. By telegram he tells Alvey Adee he supports Mexico's idea of arbitrating the war between Nicaragua and El Salvador. He also writes Lawrence Abbott about heads of corporations.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing more is recorded for the day.

headline: Lunch with Smith and Kellogg
summary: Herbert Knox Smith and Frank B. Kellogg join Roosevelt for lunch.

headline: Answering Bishop Brent on the Philippines
summary: Responding through Silas McBee to Bishop Charles Brent's criticism of American policy in the Philippines, Roosevelt insists Americans have no wish to keep colonies and do favor self-rule for them.

headline: Zoologists from abroad
summary: Roosevelt hosts a large afternoon lunch and reception for forty overseas zoologists attending the International Zoological Congress. Isabella Hagner and C. Grant LaFarge sign the guest book, and Alford Cooley stays for dinner.

headline: Goethals breaks records in Panama
summary: Roosevelt writes Joseph Bishop, now in Panama, about Colonel Goethals's record pace of digging, praises Frank Sargent's report on the Japanese, and tells Lawrence Abbott about press opposition to the fleet's world cruise.

headline: Burton runs for mayor of Cleveland
summary: Garfield, McEnery and Foster call. Roosevelt writes Theodore Burton, who is running against Tom Johnson for mayor of Cleveland, and James Speyer on finances.

headline: 'The Nature Fakers' in print
summary: Roosevelt's article 'The Nature Fakers' appears in Everybody's Magazine. He writes on Arizona-New Mexico joint statehood and a Judge Noyes appointment. The boys scatter: Kermit rides with the cavalry and hunts in the West, Ted sees Jack Greenway about a job, Archie heads to Groton. In Tokyo, Taft speaks on Japanese-American relations.

headline: Sunday lunch with Rev. Washburn
summary: The Rev. James Washburn comes to lunch, and Bishop and Mrs. Johnson pay a call.

headline: Save Old Ironsides
summary: John M. Parker of Louisiana and Dr. Lambert lunch at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt tells Lodge the frigate Constitution will not be gotten rid of, and suggests the old ship go to Annapolis.

headline: Sizing up the 1908 field
summary: Roosevelt writes Albert Shaw about the battle fleet and asks Bonaparte not to prosecute the Chicago and Alton railroad. To Taft he surveys the race: Cortelyou is interested but will defer to Roosevelt, Hughes is curious, Root too ill, and Roosevelt himself is out of the race no matter what.

headline: Edith's century-old madeira
summary: Roosevelt tells author Arthur Train he enjoys his books. He writes Lodge that an expert has just recorked some of Edith's grandfather's 1816 madeira and judged her cellar one of the finest in the country.

headline: Lunch with Judge Landis
summary: Judge Kenesaw Mountain Landis comes to lunch, and Roosevelt advises him against prosecuting the Chicago and Alton railroad. He also writes Taft about the campaign.

headline: Swinburne and Goethals
summary: Roosevelt sends Joseph Bishop more praise for Goethals, writes Bonaparte on the Oklahoma gerrymander, the census, and Judge Landis's role in the Standard Oil case, and trades thoughts with Whitelaw Reid on Swinburne's poetry and Root's health.

headline: Anti-Japanese riots in Vancouver
summary: Rioters attack Japanese residents in Vancouver, British Columbia. Dr. and Mrs. Presley Rixey are guests at Sagamore Hill, and Roosevelt writes Caspar Whitney about his 'Nature Fakers' article.

headline: Socialism's rise, to Strachey
summary: Roosevelt writes John St. Loe Strachey about the growth of socialism in England and the threat he sees in it for America.

headline: The American rifle team
summary: Roosevelt welcomes the American Rifle Team to Sagamore Hill.

headline: A crowded guest book
summary: Lunch guests are Oscar Straus, Lawrence and Ernest Abbott, Charles Neill and Gordon Russell. Fitzhugh Lee, Harper Sibley, Georgiana Farr and others sign the guest book.

headline: Vancouver and the Newfoundland fisheries
summary: Roosevelt writes Benjamin Ide Wheeler about naming Clarence Merrill postmaster of Berkeley, Joseph Bishop about Goethals and the canal, and Lodge about a school for mounted troops, the Vancouver riots and the Newfoundland fisheries.

headline: Picnic on Jayne's Hill
summary: The family picnics on Jayne's Hill, Long Island's highest point. Roosevelt advises Taft to pay his own travel costs from now on so no one can accuse him of spending public money on his campaign.

headline: Ted turns 20; the fleet's real purpose
summary: On Ted's twentieth birthday Roosevelt lunches with Frederick Weeks, Mrs. Young, Commander Long and George Kennan. He asks Emily Carow to bring Ferrero's history of Rome when she visits, and tells Lawrence Abbott about the 1904 Harriman letters, campaign money, and the battle fleet, meant for offensive use while monitors, torpedo boats and forts guard the coasts.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing more is recorded for the day.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing more is recorded for the day.

headline: Muir pleads for Hetch Hetchy
summary: Roosevelt replies to John Muir, who is pressing him to save Yosemite's neighbor, the Hetch Hetchy Valley. He also writes Joseph Bishop about who should govern the Canal Zone.

headline: Kermit and Archie leave for Groton
summary: Kermit and Archie head off to Groton. John Sleicher and Robert Porter call, Judge Noyes and Luke Wright stay for lunch, and cousin Robert B. Roosevelt Jr. comes by with his wife in the afternoon. Roosevelt writes Lawrence Abbott about gifts to his 1904 campaign.

headline: Two priests come calling
summary: Percy Thomas calls, and in the afternoon Father York and Father Belford visit.

headline: New York papers line up against him
summary: Roosevelt writes sociologist Edward A. Ross twice about Ross's book Social Control. To Taft he discusses the campaign and Hughes's appeal, complaining that every New York paper opposes his Wall Street policy and the fleet's world voyage.

headline: A family report to Nannie Lodge
summary: Roosevelt tells Nicholas Murray Butler that the copper trade and New York transit show American business at its worst. To Nannie Lodge he sketches the family: Quentin adores his French-Canadian governess, Ted hopes to graduate from Harvard a year early, Kermit loves horses and poetry, Ethel teaches Sunday school, and Archie, who loves sailing, might go to Annapolis.

headline: Skip is killed
summary: Roosevelt writes Archie at Groton that Skip, his beloved dog, was killed by a car, the house is shut for winter, and Quentin is left with Secret Service men for company. He writes Justice Moody about Jefferson, Marshall, the idle rich and his St. Louis speech, and Lodge about charges over 1904 Standard Oil money and his drinking.

headline: Rowing to Lloyd's Neck
summary: Roosevelt and Edith take a rowboat to Lloyd's Neck, carry the boat across the narrow isthmus, and row home.

headline: Chopping through a gale
summary: With a gale blowing, Roosevelt spends two hours chopping wood. He asks Archie to be kind to the stepson of Leonard Opdycke, a Harvard classmate.

headline: A two-hour ride with Edith
summary: On a fine day Roosevelt and Edith ride for two hours. He writes Butler on world finance, the tariff and what makes a good President, asks William Youngs to help make Loeb a convention delegate, and tells Kermit, who is keeping an eye on Archie, to think about life after Groton.

headline: Back to Washington for the fall
summary: Roosevelt and Edith return to Washington with Ethel and Quentin.

headline: Back at work in Washington
summary: Roosevelt confers on trusts with Bonaparte, the Navy with Metcalf, and the presidential nomination with Senators McCumber and Curtis. He lunches with W. L. Ward and Loeb, sees Garfield, Bacon and others, and is glad to tell Root, who is feeling better, about Chinese envoy Wu.

headline: Lunch with Admiral Dewey
summary: On Corinne's 46th birthday, Roosevelt lunches with Admiral George Dewey and F. W. Vanderbilt, and sees Cullom, Cooley, Warner and Hyatt. He writes David Thompson about Oklahoma's new constitution and Senator Elmer Burkett on why national law overrides state law.

headline: Quentin shows his snakes
summary: Roosevelt confers on railroad mail rates with Meyer and on Pacific coaling stations with Metcalf and Admirals Cowles and Brownson, then lunches with the Bishop of London. He tells Archie how Quentin burst into a meeting with Bonaparte carrying snakes, and was sent to show four waiting congressmen too.

headline: Off on a three-week tour
summary: Roosevelt leaves Washington in the evening on a three-week speaking trip through the West and South. He writes Lodge about the coal shortage on the West Coast facing the battle fleet.

headline: Dedicating the McKinley Memorial
summary: In Canton, Ohio, Roosevelt joins the parade and dedicates the McKinley Memorial with an afternoon address, as the business slump turns into a crisis. Scribner's publishes his 'Small Country Neighbors.' Overseas, Taft opens the Philippine Assembly and speaks in Shanghai on China policy.

headline: Paddling down the Mississippi
summary: After speeches at Meredosia, Illinois, and Keokuk, Iowa, Roosevelt boards the stern-wheeler Mississippi. It is his first trip on the great river, and he writes the children about its history passing by. He tells Archie this will likely be his last major trip as President, and defends a story with an automobile as hero, likening it to Cooper's tales of boats.

headline: Speaking in St. Louis
summary: At St. Louis Roosevelt speaks on the Navy and on putting corporations and railroads under national oversight, then steams down the river toward Cairo, Illinois, with his old friend Seth Bullock.

headline: Cairo, then on to Memphis
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Cairo, Illinois, and continues toward Memphis. He writes Judson Clements of the Interstate Commerce Commission about the case over Alabama's state rate laws.

headline: Steamboat race and a jolt on deck
summary: With Governors Frantz and Curry and Gifford Pinchot aboard, the Mississippi leads a dozen steamers downriver, some racing. At Memphis Roosevelt speaks for a deep waterway commission. When the Fred Hartweg bumps his boat and knocks him to the deck, he wires for its license to be pulled. He also tells Beveridge joint statehood for Arizona and New Mexico cannot work.

headline: Into Louisiana bear country
summary: Roosevelt reaches Lake Providence and Stamboul, Louisiana, gateway to his bear hunt. Back in Washington the Orland Reclamation Project in California is approved.

headline: Camp on the bayou
summary: From camp near Stamboul, Roosevelt writes Ethel about Ben Lilly, the hunter who lives by a fierce religious code, a bear chase, the canvas fly rigged for the horses, and the steady rain.

headline: Hunting the Tensas canebrakes
summary: Roosevelt spends the day hunting bear in the Tensas Bayou country.

headline: Still after bear
summary: Another day of bear hunting in the Louisiana canebrakes along the Tensas.

headline: A third day in the canebrakes
summary: Roosevelt keeps hunting bear in the Tensas Bayou country.

headline: A deer but no bear yet
summary: Still hunting on the Tensas, Roosevelt marks Kermit's 18th birthday. He sends Archie a picture letter reporting a deer but no bear, and tells Edith he reads her letters over and over before he can bring himself to destroy them.

headline: Eleanor's birthday, far from camp
summary: The bear hunt goes on. Back east, Roosevelt's niece Eleanor turns 23.

headline: Edith asks for prayers for Archie
summary: Roosevelt hunts bear on the Tensas. At home, Edith asks her sister Emily to pray for Archie as he heads out into the wider world.

headline: Owls, a cat and a morning swim
summary: From a shack beside a lake, Roosevelt writes Quentin about a cat he feeds that the dogs leave alone, a morning swim, an evening row and the many owls calling at night. He thanks John Burroughs for Camping and Tramping with Roosevelt, reports a deer but still no bear, and describes the bayou's trees, flowers and animals.

headline: Three Arch Rocks protected
summary: Hunting continues on the Tensas. Off the Oregon coast, Three Arch Rocks becomes a federal bird reservation.

headline: Only lucky shots, he says
summary: The hunt goes on. Edith writes her Aunt Lizzie, teasing that her husband credits every good shot to luck and likes to call himself an old, broken man.

headline: Venison for dinner, still no bear
summary: Roosevelt tells Archie there is still no bear; the camp is living on deer meat.

headline: At last, a bear
summary: After twelve days of hunting in the Louisiana canebrakes, Roosevelt finally kills a bear.

headline: Sheffield Cowles turns nine
summary: Bear hunting continues. Bamie's son Sheffield Cowles has his ninth birthday.

headline: Last full day on the bayou
summary: Roosevelt hunts bear on the Tensas once more.

headline: Breaking camp
summary: After a final day's hunt, Roosevelt heads back out to Stamboul.

headline: Vicksburg welcome
summary: Roosevelt leaves Stamboul for Vicksburg, Mississippi, where he speaks and holds a reception.

headline: Panic on Wall Street; Treasury steps in
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Nashville and Chattanooga. To head off panic, Treasury Secretary Cortelyou rushes to New York to confer with Morgan and fellow financiers, pledging $25 million of federal surplus to New York banks while Morgan, Harriman and Rockefeller put up still more. Roosevelt writes Ted about the trip.

headline: Home to a financial storm
summary: After stops at Roanoke and Lynchburg, Roosevelt reaches Washington and confers that evening with Bacon, Beveridge, Ryan and Charles Magoon. Three Washington State sea rocks, Flattery Rocks, Copalis Rock and Quillayute Needles, become bird reservations. He congratulates Commander William Sims on record naval gunnery.

headline: Crisis meetings at the White House
summary: Roosevelt holds financial talks with Root, Knox, Metcalf, Garfield, Senator McCumber and Assistant Treasury Secretary Edwards, and sees Captain McCoy and Justice Harlan. He tells Governor Curry he doubts Arizona and New Mexico will win statehood this year.

headline: A run on the Trust Company
summary: Anxious depositors line up to pull their money from a Wall Street trust company. Roosevelt holds Cabinet on naval matters and a finance meeting with Senator Elkins, lunches with Ambassador Aoki and actress Maude Adams, and twice thanks Cortelyou for helping halt the panic. He approves wider locks for the canal.

headline: Tennis amid the panic
summary: Roosevelt meets Metcalf and Admirals Evans and Brownson on the Navy and receives a stream of callers, including Straus, Garfield and Delegate Andrews. At 3:30 he plays tennis with Ambassador Jusserand, Cooley and Bacon.

headline: Turning 49, with a newfangled wallet
summary: Roosevelt turns 49. A Hungarian Republican club from New York City calls late in the evening with birthday greetings. Edith tells Kermit she gave him a modern wallet for bills and calling cards; he was sweet about it, but she could see he was let down.

headline: Oklahoma and canal posts; Taft to skip Berlin
summary: Roosevelt discusses canal appointments with Tawney and the Oklahoma constitution with Governor Frantz, Representative McGuire and Senators McCumber, Long and Carter. He lunches with Booth, Cortelyou and Macfarland, and warns Taft to skip Berlin on his travels so France will not feel slighted.

headline: No war with Japan coming
summary: A Cabinet session and a talk with Cortelyou focus on money. Roosevelt meets Governor Frantz and Senator Warner, receives Spanish-American War veterans, and sees Nelson of the Biological Survey. He assures Ted that war with Japan is not close, and recommends Patterson's The Man-Eaters of Tsavo.

headline: Lyman Abbott overnight
summary: Roosevelt meets Representatives Hepburn and Mann, lunches with Jusserand and Bacon, and has Lyman Abbott to dinner and overnight. He writes Seth Low about the Chicago trust conference and its resolutions.

headline: Roosevelt in his own words
summary: Roosevelt talks politics with Senator Scott and hosts lunch for the Johnsons, Captains McCoy and Lee, and Governor and Mrs. Frantz. After seeing John McIlhenny he plays tennis with Jusserand and Winthrop. Cosmopolitan runs 'Roosevelt, By Himself.'

headline: Meeting Roald Amundsen
summary: After Cabinet and a talk with Paul Morton, Roosevelt receives the Norwegian minister and polar explorer Roald Amundsen, then goes riding. He meets Leupp and Garfield about the Utes' reservation lands, writes H. A. Dobson about whether chipmunks hibernate, and tells Dr. Lambert he knows he will be blamed for the panic.

headline: Warning Puerto Rico's governor
summary: Roosevelt goes over Oklahoma appointments with Garfield, Bonaparte and Governor Frantz, lunches with Murray and Cortelyou, walks, and sees Ambassador Sternberg. He warns Regis Post that loose talk threatens his post as governor of Puerto Rico, and writes Richard Henry Dana about removing Rochester revenue collector Archie Sanders.

headline: Sunday in Washington
summary: No events are recorded in Washington for the day.

headline: U.S. Steel takes over Tennessee Coal and Iron
summary: With the brokerage Moore and Schley near collapse, Gary and Frick propose that U.S. Steel buy the firm's Tennessee Coal and Iron holdings. To steady the economy, Roosevelt agrees not to sue under the Sherman Act, though the deal lifts U.S. Steel's market share from about half to 60 percent. He also confers on grain-moving credit, plays tennis, and leaves at midnight to vote in Oyster Bay.

headline: Voting in Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt casts his ballot in Oyster Bay and heads back to Washington. He writes Robert Bridges of Scribner's about his article on hunting in Louisiana.

headline: 'Checkered' election results
summary: Roosevelt talks with C. S. Mellen about the New Haven railroad investigation and with Bonaparte, Garfield, Governor Frantz and C. H. Hunter about Oklahoma jobs, and sees Moody, Root and others. He tells Lodge the election went both ways, and that Standard Oil may get behind Hughes for President.

headline: Spreading money to keep banks open
summary: Senators Gallinger and Heyburn, Herbert Parsons, Root and Ambassador Bryce call. After tennis with Pinchot, Garfield and Jusserand, Roosevelt sees Sternberg. He tells Richard Knott that he and Cortelyou are scattering federal deposits nationwide to prop up shaky banks.

headline: The Fisk Jubilee Singers perform
summary: After Cabinet and a meeting with J. A. Stewart and James Reynolds about the state's politics, Roosevelt lunches with Seth Low and Reynolds. In the afternoon the Fisk Jubilee Singers perform for him. He writes Ansley Wilcox about falsehoods in the press regarding him and big business.

headline: Immigration Commission and labor leaders
summary: Roosevelt meets Senator Dillingham, Jeremiah Jenks and W. R. Wheeler about the Immigration Commission, and AFL leaders including Samuel Gompers and Frank Morrison. After tennis, he tells cousin Emlen he will not run for President again, and writes Lucius Swift about banks.

headline: A letter to Alice
summary: Roosevelt writes Alice, who has been ill and is on the mend, about politics and the risk that a depression could hurt Taft's chances.

headline: Why 'In God We Trust' came off the coins
summary: Roosevelt discusses liquor prohibition with Joseph Babcock and lunches with Bacon, Jusserand, Garfield, Pinchot and others.
