He defends dropping 'In God We Trust' from the new coins, tells Nick Alice is recovering from appendicitis, invites Alabama's governor to a White House conference on natural resources, and discusses Cornwallis and Tarleton with Trevelyan.

headline: No secret deals with financiers
summary: After Cabinet and a talk with Representative Vreeland about oil leases on Indian lands and Empire State politics, Roosevelt sees Baron Rosen, Albert Shaw, cartoonist Homer Davenport and others, then rides. He tells Thomas Watson he will strike no secret bargain with financiers.

headline: Central American peace delegates
summary: Roosevelt discusses postal savings banks with Meyer, hosts a lunch with Root and Bacon for the envoys at the Central American peace talks, and plays tennis. He writes Willis Johnson about plans for a forestry school at Cornell.

headline: Ray Stannard Baker at lunch
summary: Roosevelt meets Meyer and Representative Campbell on federal help for banks, and lunches with journalist Ray Stannard Baker, J. R. Sheffield, Herbert Parsons and Arthur Train. Edith tells Kermit that dates and battles slipped from her memory at school.

headline: Carnegie and Archbishop Ireland
summary: After Cabinet, Roosevelt lunches with Philbin, Root and Andrew Carnegie, and visits with Archbishop John Ireland.

headline: Oklahoma becomes the 46th state
summary: On an extremely busy day, Roosevelt proclaims Oklahoma the 46th state and establishes Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument in New Mexico. Llewellyn, Foraker and McCumber call. He writes Douglas Robinson, William Dudley Foulke and Thomas Watson about restoring confidence after the panic, politics, Taft and Hughes.

headline: Treasury floods the banks with bonds
summary: The Treasury offers $100 million in certificates and $50 million in low-rate canal bonds, sold to banks on credit that may back new currency. Roosevelt sees Ray Stannard Baker in the morning, Root at six and Cortelyou late, and writes Cortelyou about the money shortage and the bond issue.

headline: Dinner with Joel Chandler Harris
summary: Roosevelt meets Representative Bartholdt about the waterways commission and dines with Joel Chandler Harris, creator of Uncle Remus. He answers Adolphus Busch's complaints that Cortelyou always favors New York interests.

headline: Paderewski plays the White House
summary: On Quentin's tenth birthday, Roosevelt holds Cabinet, meets Alaska's Delegate Cale over lunch, and attends a concert by pianist Ignace Paderewski. He tells Carnegie he will push for more battleships, Cortelyou that he does not want the nomination, and others about Japan, college football and the government's thin funds.

headline: The Brazilian ambassador calls
summary: Roosevelt discusses finances with Lodge, sees Meyer, Garfield, Hemenway, Leishman and others, and receives the Brazilian ambassador. He sends Cortelyou a financial proposal.

headline: Canal talk with Representative Taylor
summary: Roosevelt discusses the canal with Representative Taylor and receives Thomas Nelson Page, Helen St. George Tucker, William Sulzer, Charles Neill, Frank Lowden and others.

headline: Late-night meeting with Morgan on the money crisis
summary: After Cabinet and lunch with Henry Taft, Loeb, Justice Harlan, Root and Lodge, Roosevelt meets J. P. Morgan, George F. Baker, Bacon and Cortelyou late into the night on the money crisis. Talks with Tokyo over limiting Japanese immigration, which became the Gentlemen's Agreement, are under way.

headline: Bryan comes to call
summary: Roosevelt discusses the tariff with Payne and Dalzell and Puerto Rico with Governor Regis Post and Beekman Winthrop. William Jennings Bryan calls. After a walk with Pinchot, Garfield and Jusserand he sees Sternberg, and tells Emlen that Morgan and Baker approve his financial policies.

headline: Sunday in Washington
summary: No events are recorded for the day in Washington.

headline: Lunch with David Starr Jordan
summary: On Bamie's twelfth wedding anniversary, Roosevelt discusses South Dakota appointments with Senators Gamble and Kittredge and the tariff with Representative Hull. Carroll Wright and Charles Walcott call, Stanford's David Starr Jordan comes to lunch, and he plays tennis with Garfield, Cooley and Jusserand.

headline: A ride and the YMCA
summary: After Cabinet, Roosevelt discusses South Dakota jobs with Gamble and the Republican Congressional Committee with Loudenslager. He receives the International YMCA and the Belgian minister, rides in the afternoon, and sees Speaker Cannon at nine. He writes William Allen White about the uproar against his policies.

headline: Edith Root marries Ulysses Grant III
summary: Senators Borah, Gore and others call before Roosevelt attends the wedding of Root's daughter Edith to Ulysses S. Grant III. Jack Greenway and the Longworths are White House houseguests, and Roosevelt rides three hours with Greenway and Fitzhugh Lee. Letters go to Henry White on the panic abroad, Bishop on a House visit to the Canal Zone, Root on Japan, and Lawrence Abbott on corporations.

headline: Thanksgiving trip to Montpelier
summary: On Thanksgiving morning Roosevelt, Edith, Quentin, the Longworths, the Rixeys and the Cooleys travel to Montpelier, James Madison's Virginia home as restored by the du Ponts. They spend under two hours there and are back in Washington by four for Thanksgiving dinner.

headline: Dinner for Panama's President Amador
summary: After Cabinet and calls from Senators Dillingham, Latimer and Curtis, Roosevelt confers with Panama's President Manuel Amador and plays tennis with Nick Longworth, Meyer and Jusserand. That night he gives Amador a dinner with Root, Admiral Evans, General Bell, Commander Sims, Pinchot and others; Colonel and Mrs. Howze stay over.

headline: Ted battered, Archie ill, Alice's operation
summary: A crowded day of callers includes Gompers, Senators Allison, Depew and Beveridge, and the envoys of France and Russia. Ted arrives from Harvard, banged up from football and a three-story fall in a broken elevator. Archie, unhappy at Groton and looking very ill, is withdrawn for the year and operated on to ease his headaches. Alice's appendix is removed at the White House. Roosevelt chides Quentin about his weight.

headline: A Sunday letter about the panic
summary: On a quiet Sunday Roosevelt writes his friend and physician Dr. Alexander Lambert about the financial panic gripping the country.

headline: Anniversary gift as Congress convenes
summary: On their 21st wedding anniversary Edith gives Roosevelt Izaak Walton's The Compleat Angler, a gift he treasures. The 60th Congress opens, and he spends the day on currency and railroad law with senators, plays tennis with Jusserand and Pinchot, then laughs his way through the comedy Brewster's Millions.

headline: Annual Message calls for income tax
summary: Roosevelt's Annual Message goes to Congress, pressing for reform and proposing both an inheritance tax and an income tax. A congressional committee calls to report the session open, the Cabinet meets, and he walks with Jusserand and Winthrop before an evening on finance bills with Aldrich and Crane.

headline: A rebuke for Puerto Rico's governor
summary: Roosevelt sees Lodge and a line of other callers, receives German Ambassador von Sternberg at five, and takes an afternoon walk. By letter he scolds Puerto Rico's governor, Regis Post, for careless public remarks.

headline: Brander Matthews comes to stay
summary: Governor Cummins, naturalist C. Hart Merriam and Dr. Rixey join Roosevelt for lunch, and more lawmakers call. After a ride he dines with Columbia professor Brander Matthews and Yale's Thomas Lounsbury, who both spend the night at the White House.

headline: Federal troops ordered to Nevada
summary: With Nevada's gold camps sliding toward lawlessness, Governor John Sparks asks for help and Roosevelt sends Army troops under General Funston. He also tours the Corcoran with Brander Matthews, plays tennis, and dines with friends from his Louisiana bear hunt.

headline: A bird refuge for Louisiana
summary: Roosevelt sets aside East Timbalier Island in Louisiana as a bird reservation. He greets the ambassadors of Mexico, Italy and Britain, lunches with Captains Lee and McCoy and a Mr. Sargent, and rides. Mrs. J. West Roosevelt is staying at the White House.

headline: Evening callers on a Sunday
summary: A quiet Sunday ends with two evening visitors: Representative Fassett at nine, then diplomat William Rockhill half an hour later.

headline: A loving cup for Trevelyan
summary: Roosevelt meets a long list of lawmakers along with labor leader Samuel Gompers, and lunches with Thomas Watson, Cortelyou and Straus. He tells historian George Otto Trevelyan that he, Lodge and Root are sending a silver loving cup to honor his books on the American Revolution.

headline: Lunch with Ambassador Bryce
summary: After the Cabinet meets and a few congressmen call, Roosevelt lunches with British Ambassador James Bryce and Secretary Root, plays tennis with Garfield, Cooley and Jusserand, and dines at Lodge's.

headline: Conservation allies at day's end
summary: Roosevelt sees John Sharp Williams, Bonaparte and Meyer among the day's callers, lunches with his son-in-law Nick Longworth and others, rides, and closes the afternoon with Garfield, Pinchot and Beveridge.

headline: No third term, Roosevelt declares
summary: Roosevelt makes it public: he will not seek a third term as President, and he writes Taft about the statement. Between meetings on California appointments and lunch with Hoke Smith and Frank Kellogg, he still finds time for tennis with Garfield, Jusserand and Cooley.

headline: Cortelyou's panic report
summary: After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt sees senators and congressmen, lunches with Elliott and Assistant Navy Secretary Newberry, rides, and writes Treasury Secretary Cortelyou about his report on the panic.

headline: Postal business and a walk
summary: A light Saturday: Roosevelt goes over postal matters with Postmaster General Meyer, confers with Vice President Fairbanks, and takes a walk.

headline: Aboard the Mayflower for Hampton Roads
summary: Roosevelt boards the presidential yacht Mayflower bound for the Virginia coast. Along are Edith, Ethel, Bamie and her husband Will Cowles, cabinet and navy families, his niece Corinne Robinson and Belle Hagner. Before sailing he writes Senator Warren about bullet evidence in the Brownsville affair, pushing back on Senator Foraker.

headline: The Great White Fleet sails
summary: From the deck of the Mayflower at Hampton Roads, Roosevelt speaks and then watches sixteen battleships under Rear Admiral Robley Evans steam out on a voyage around the world. The cruise is meant to show Japan the nation's resolve, build support in Congress for the Navy, and prove a whole battle fleet can circle the globe. He returns to Washington.

headline: Bring the troops home from Nevada
summary: With Nevada calm since the soldiers arrived, Roosevelt wires Governor Sparks that he means to pull them out soon. He also meets the Cabinet, talks Missouri appointments with Representative Bartholdt, and plays tennis.

headline: Why not a third term
summary: Roosevelt sees Lodge and other lawmakers and goes riding. To English writer Frederic Harrison he lays out his reasons for stepping aside after this term, and mentions the introduction he wrote for Jeremiah Curtin's The Mongols: A History.

headline: Tonto National Monument proclaimed
summary: Roosevelt protects the cliff dwellings of Tonto in Arizona as a national monument. He sees Senators Warren, Cullom and Hale and Governor Hoggatt, plays tennis with Jusserand, Meyer and Nick Longworth, and hosts the Cabinet dinner.

headline: Troops coming out of Nevada
summary: Hearing nothing back from Governor Sparks, Roosevelt wires that he has decided to withdraw federal troops from Nevada. He also lunches with canal chief George Goethals, rides, and spends the evening with Root, Bacon and Taft.

headline: Central American peace delegates welcomed
summary: Roosevelt hosts the delegates to the Central American Peace Conference and talks New York politics with Herbert Parsons. He writes a long letter to Cecil Spring-Rice touching on his friend's frustration with diplomatic life, Australia, population and the panic, and tells Thomas Watson why printing greenbacks is no cure.

headline: Taft versus Foraker in Ohio
summary: On Sunday evening Postmaster General Meyer and Secretary Root call. Roosevelt writes Arizona's Governor Kibbey about maneuvering ahead of the Republican convention, where Taft's backers are battling Foraker's.

headline: A grandnephew is born to Franklin and Eleanor
summary: James Roosevelt, son of Franklin and Eleanor, is born. Roosevelt sits for photographer Frederick Hyde, discusses Pacific Coast defenses with Flint and Humphrey, and lunches with Leo Rowe and Kitagaki. He tells Charles Magoon the pitcher and basin Magoon sent will be Edith's Christmas present, and asks Bonaparte about stopping union boycotts.

headline: Christmas tree at the German Embassy
summary: On Christmas Eve Roosevelt meets the Cabinet, talks finance with Senator Hansbrough, and stops by the German Embassy to admire its Christmas tree before tennis with Pinchot and Jusserand. He tells Root that Panama has no say at all over the waters approaching the Canal Zone.

headline: Christmas at the White House
summary: At seven in the morning the children, Alice and Nick included, pile onto the bed to open stockings, then everyone heads to the library for presents. Roosevelt rides three hours with Root, Lodge, Fitz Lee, Ted, Kermit and Ethel, admires Archie's tree, and plays an hour and a half of tennis, while Quentin's three friends roughhouse all evening.

headline: Off to Pine Knot for the holidays
summary: Roosevelt heads for the family's Virginia cabin, Pine Knot, stopping in Charlottesville. He protests a New York Tribune editorial claiming Admiral Brownson quit over the order putting naval doctors in command of hospital ships, and tells Arthur Lee why he won't run again and about Philip de László's wish to paint him.

headline: At Pine Knot
summary: Roosevelt is at Pine Knot, the family's retreat in the Virginia woods. Nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Nevada must call its legislature
summary: From Pine Knot Roosevelt wires Governor Sparks that Nevada's legislature must be summoned at once. Keeping order is the state's job, he says, and if the call does not go out within five days the federal troops will leave.

headline: Report on the panic arrives
summary: Roosevelt remains at Pine Knot as Treasury Secretary Cortelyou turns in his account of the autumn's financial panic.

headline: Back to Washington from Pine Knot
summary: Roosevelt leaves Pine Knot in the afternoon and has appointments that evening in Washington. He writes Alabama judge John C. Anderson to praise him for enjoining state railroad regulation laws.

headline: Year ends as the panic eases
summary: Roosevelt closes 1907 with tennis and letters: to Taft on Ohio politics and Foraker, to Leo Rowe on ties with South America, and to Owen Wister on scholarship in America. With the economy recovering, the panic is over. Scribner's publishes his "In the Louisiana Canebrakes."

headline: Six thousand at the New Year's reception
summary: Roosevelt opens 1908 with breakfast with Captain Greenaway, then greets some 6,000 people at the New Year's reception. That afternoon he takes a hard two-hour ride with his children and their cousins and friends, and writes Trevelyan about the inscribed loving cup and the Revolution.

headline: Howard Pyle comes to lunch
summary: Roosevelt names J. E. Pillsbury to head the Bureau of Navigation, tours the Corcoran early, and lunches with Taft, illustrator Howard Pyle and Eugene Philbin. He writes Archie at Groton about Edith's fondness for the little dog Scamp, and congratulates Bonaparte on a Chicago speech on the misdeeds of the rich.

headline: A musicale after dinner
summary: After the Cabinet meeting and a few callers, Roosevelt plays tennis and hosts Goethals, Rockhill, Whitelaw Reid and Beveridge at dinner, followed by music.

headline: Doctors to command hospital ships
summary: Roosevelt hears from Charles Neill on labor conditions in Nevada and from Representative Humphrey on Puget Sound defenses, and sees Jacob Riis and Seth Bullock. He orders that medical officers will now command Navy hospital ships, and grumbles to Senator Warren about how badly many Army officers ride.

headline: Seth Bullock stays over
summary: Roosevelt's old Dakota friend Seth Bullock and his wife spend Sunday night at the White House.

headline: More power for Goethals
summary: As Congress returns, Roosevelt widens the authority of Colonel Goethals as chairman of the Isthmian Canal Commission. He poses for Mr. Hyde on the South Portico, plays tennis, and writes Taft about removing federal officeholders.

headline: Aldrich offers an emergency currency bill
summary: Senator Aldrich introduces a bill allowing $500 million in emergency currency when credit tightens. Roosevelt meets the Cabinet, lunches with Taft, Longworth and Seth Bullock, walks, and he and Edith dine with Vice President Fairbanks.

headline: George Ade at the table
summary: Roosevelt confers with Payne and Dalzell, the House's tariff men, and lunches with humorist George Ade, Robert Porter and Sloan Simpson, who stays the night. After a ride he dines with Captain Lee.

headline: Muir Woods saved
summary: Roosevelt proclaims Muir Woods in California a national monument, protecting its redwoods. Taft and La Follette are among the day's callers, he rides at three, and that night hosts the diplomatic reception. He sends George Meredith congratulations on the novelist's 80th birthday.

headline: A dinner for Speaker Cannon
summary: Roosevelt sorts out Nebraska postal jobs with Senators Burkett and Brown and later hosts a dinner and musicale honoring Speaker Joe Cannon. In New York, Taft speaks at Cooper Union on the origins of property. Roosevelt thanks his brother-in-law Douglas Robinson for managing his money.

headline: Grand Canyon becomes a national monument
summary: Roosevelt proclaims the Grand Canyon a national monument. He discusses fortifying Pearl Harbor, the tariff and an employers' liability bill, lunches and walks with Jusserand, and writes about saving Appalachian forests, better language teaching at West Point, and his record for working people.

headline: Senators on a Sunday
summary: Senators Warner and Warren call in the afternoon, and Roosevelt writes Cortelyou about the currency bill.

headline: Pursuing land fraud
summary: Roosevelt goes over land fraud prosecutions with Garfield and Ballinger and sees Bonaparte and Nebraska's Senator Burkett. Tennis is called off, so there is no exercise; he and Edith spend the evening at the National Theater. Letters go to Taft on returning Cuba to self-rule and to George Lee, his first wife's brother, on corporations.

headline: Standard Oil cases reviewed
summary: Roosevelt meets the Cabinet, goes over the Standard Oil prosecutions with District Attorney Sims, plays tennis, sees Louis Payn at six, and he and Edith dine at Secretary Root's.

headline: A growling teddy bear from the Black Forest
summary: Roosevelt hosts a late reception for both houses of Congress. To Archie he reports that Ted hopes to finish college in three years and earn his own way, that Quentin is playing with the Turkish minister's son, and that a walking, growling black teddy bear has made Ethel jealous.

headline: Pinnacles protected; a pure food inquiry
summary: Roosevelt sets aside the Pinnacles in California as a national monument. After tennis he hosts the diplomatic corps at dinner, and asks Johns Hopkins president Ira Remsen to lead a board looking into how the pure food law is being abused.

headline: An unsent rebuke to The Outlook
summary: After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt sees Senators Smoot and Brown and the Mexican ambassador, then rides. He drafts a protest to Lyman Abbott over an Outlook editorial on Admiral Brownson's resignation but holds it back, and writes about Pearl Harbor's defenses and a counterfeiter he has kept behind bars.

headline: Bamie turns 53
summary: It is his sister Bamie's 53rd birthday. Roosevelt meets again with Nebraska Senators Burkett and Brown, sees C. H. Treat, and rides.

headline: Patronage and Taft
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday writing to William Dudley Foulke about patronage and Taft's nomination.

headline: Quentin the philosopher
summary: Roosevelt lunches with C. A. Congdon and Herbert Smith, plays tennis, and takes Edith to the National Theater. He tells Archie about a letter from Mrs. Peabody at Groton and about Quentin, the family "philosopher," who is making regular use of the YMCA gym and pool.

headline: Booker T. Washington at six
summary: After the Cabinet meeting and a lunch with Kellogg, Fox and Witherbee, Roosevelt rides, sees Booker T. Washington at six, and dines with Edith at Secretary Cortelyou's.

headline: Talk of Hughes for President
summary: Roosevelt meets Representatives Bennet and Fassett about the push to nominate New York's Governor Charles Evans Hughes for President. Morris K. Jesup dies. Tennis fills the afternoon and Senator Beveridge calls late in the evening.

headline: Judges at the White House
summary: Roosevelt talks Army business with Senator McLaurin, rides in the afternoon, and hosts the annual reception for the judiciary that evening.

headline: Platt calls; a crowded lunch table
summary: Senator Thomas Platt calls at ten, and the Cabinet takes up postal appointments. Roosevelt's lunch guests include the Jusserands, the Strauses, the Meyers and the Cooleys, and after a walk he gives a dinner for lawmakers including Chauncey Depew, followed by music.

headline: Gridiron Club dinner
summary: Roosevelt discusses New York politics with Herbert Parsons and lunches with steel man Elbert Gary and Mackenzie King, Canada's deputy labor minister. Aldrich calls in the afternoon, and that evening Roosevelt goes to the Gridiron Club dinner.

headline: A Sunday night caller
summary: Journalist John Callan O'Laughlin calls on Roosevelt Sunday evening.

headline: Taft's campaign is going well
summary: Roosevelt greets a group of newspaper editors from around the country and lunches with historian Brooks Adams and William Phillips. He writes Kermit that Taft's campaign is moving along and that Hughes, he thinks, envies him, and tells Archie about Scamp and the kitchen cat.

headline: Low and Gompers on trust law
summary: Roosevelt meets Seth Low and labor leader Samuel Gompers on trust legislation and talks with Representative Campbell about Taft's candidacy. After a ride, he and Edith dine with Attorney General Bonaparte. He writes Henry Thompson on illuminated manuscripts.

headline: Kentucky jobs; Taft in Cleveland
summary: Roosevelt sorts through Kentucky appointments with a delegation led by Representative Langley and receives senators and congressmen before riding. In Cleveland, Taft argues against American isolationism.

headline: Dinner for the Supreme Court
summary: Roosevelt sees Governor Floyd, Senator Dolliver and others, rides at half past three, and hosts the Supreme Court justices at dinner.

headline: The most radical message of his presidency
summary: Roosevelt sends Congress a special message unlike any before it: he calls for a new employers' liability law, limits on injunctions in labor disputes, federal control of stock gambling, and tighter rules for railroads and big combinations. He blames Standard Oil, the railroad combines and the panic on the trusts, and faults the courts for siding with big business. That afternoon he plays tennis on a frozen court.

headline: Snow, and a letter to Laurier
summary: Snow falls on Washington. Roosevelt discusses the Government Printing Office with Representatives Landis and Overstreet, lunches with Bryce, Foulke and Mackenzie King, and walks. He writes Canadian Prime Minister Wilfrid Laurier about relations between the two countries, Japanese immigration and the deliberate overissue of passports.

headline: Three hours over the frozen snow
summary: From 4:30 to 7:30 Roosevelt tramps with Meyer and Winthrop over crusted snow to Chevy Chase and home by way of Rock Creek. He writes Arthur Lee about Maurice Low's attacks on him in the English papers and the de László portrait Lee suggested, and sends Kermit his thoughts on the January 31 message.

headline: Robert Peary calls
summary: Arctic explorer Robert Peary is among Roosevelt's callers, along with Vice President Fairbanks and Senator La Follette. After a walk he discusses New York politics with Woodruff and Barnes.

headline: Writing Bryan about the courts
summary: After the Cabinet meets, Silas McBee joins him for lunch, and following a walk Roosevelt and Edith dine at Postmaster General Meyer's. He wires Governor Sparks that the troops must leave Nevada no later than February 15, and writes William Jennings Bryan about his message and court rulings hostile to labor.

headline: The Public Printer suspended
summary: Public Printer Stillings is suspended, and Roosevelt writes Representative Landis about the inquiry into his office. He meets Taft and General Bell, hears manufacturers argue for a permanent tariff commission, and lunches with William Barnes. There is no time for exercise.

headline: Butler out of sympathy
summary: Roosevelt meets the House Naval Affairs Committee, lunches with Taft, and has supper with his old friend Jacob Riis, an overnight guest, before the congressional reception. He writes Nicholas Murray Butler, who has criticized his messages, and Seth Low about the Hughes boom.

headline: Jewel Cave protected
summary: Roosevelt creates Jewel Cave National Monument in South Dakota. He reviews Cuban affairs with Taft, Root and Magoon, sets March 7 for pulling troops out of Nevada, and stops Hawaii's governor from discussing more Japanese laborers with Japan. Groton's Endicott Peabody and Jacob Riis are house guests.

headline: No round-the-world trip for now
summary: The children play the banjo for Roosevelt in the afternoon, and that evening he visits the YMCA. He turns down Richard Watson Gilder's ideas of a memoir and world travels after the presidency, and writes Thomas Coolidge about backing Taft.

headline: A funeral at St. John's
summary: Roosevelt and Edith attend a funeral at St. John's Church in the afternoon.

headline: Balloons and Ohio politics
summary: Roosevelt hears Representative Hull on balloon experiments and talks Ohio politics with son-in-law Nick Longworth; there is no outdoor exercise. Taft speaks to young Republicans in Kansas City. A memo records how Roosevelt sees his ties to Lodge and George Lyman and Lyman's requests for jobs.

headline: Bases for the Pacific
summary: After the Cabinet meeting and lunch with Cecil Lyon, Roosevelt walks, then dines with Edith at Secretary Metcalf's. He writes Metcalf about naval bases and defenses at Pearl Harbor and in the Philippines, and praises Senator Knox for his Columbia speeches on big business.

headline: Alice turns 24
summary: It is Alice's 24th birthday. Roosevelt confers with Aldrich and rides. He writes Charlemagne Tower about Japanese advisers in Mexico and South America, and tells King Edward VII about the battle fleet's cruise and its planned stops in Australia.

headline: No patience for Jane Addams's book
summary: Roosevelt talks with Frank Hitchcock about Taft's campaign in the South and with Bonaparte about a miners' strike in Alaska, then rides. To Florence La Farge he pans Jane Addams's Newer Ideals of Peace, likening it to Tolstoy, whom he does not admire.

headline: Never lightweight champion
summary: Roosevelt lunches with William Allen White and Lyman Abbott, rides, and attends an evening reception given by a fine arts society. He congratulates Ted on his midyear grades and tells Thornton Simmons he was never Harvard's lightweight boxing champion.

headline: Battleships for Brazil?
summary: After lunch with Coolidge and a walk, Roosevelt tells Root he suspects the battleships England is building for Brazil may really be meant for Japan; they were in fact for Brazil. He writes Philip Stewart that he cannot think Ethan Hitchcock a bad man, though he had lost faith in his judgment.

headline: William Allen White in the evening
summary: Roosevelt meets census expert W. S. Rossiter, and Kansas editor William Allen White calls at half past nine.

headline: A young cousin's Badlands poem
summary: On Alice and Nick's second anniversary, Roosevelt dines with Ambassador Whitelaw Reid, and Douglas and Corinne Robinson come to stay. He writes Root about China and Japan, and tells young cousin Philip J. Roosevelt at St. Mark's how much he enjoyed Philip's poem about the Badlands.

headline: Against wage cuts on the railroads
summary: The Cabinet takes up immigration. Roosevelt rides and dines at Garfield's with Lodge, Jusserand, Justice Day and others. He writes the Interstate Commerce Commission objecting to railroad rebates and wage cuts, and urges the government to mediate.

headline: Antitrust talk and a recitation
summary: Roosevelt discusses the antitrust laws with Sherman and Knox and postal jobs with Meyer, sees Ambassador von Sternberg, and gives a dinner for Lodge, Governor Fort, Bourke Cockran, Nicholas Murray Butler and others, capped by a recitation. He writes about railroad pay cuts and a laborer disabled on the Panama works.

headline: Army and Navy reception
summary: Roosevelt talks battleship funding with Representative Hobson and meets financier James Speyer and Senator Smoot. Taft and Goethals come in at 2:30, Japanese Ambassador Aoki at 2:45, and that night he hosts the Army and Navy reception.

headline: Pacific defenses can't wait
summary: A day of meetings: Judge Wilfley's possible impeachment, an industrial school bill, finances with Aldrich, and Panama labor with Taft and Goethals. After a ride Roosevelt dines at Lodge's. He presses Vice President Fairbanks, and Speaker Cannon in a similar letter, for quick action to fortify the Pacific.

headline: Dinner with the Jusserands
summary: On Washington's Birthday Roosevelt fields congressmen on a Southern Pacific claim for Colorado River repairs, the military budget, Massachusetts politics and an alleged submarine lobby. He lunches with Judge Lowell and cousin Emlen Roosevelt, rides, and dines with the Jusserands and Justice Moody.

headline: Dickens, Bunyan and Thackeray
summary: Roosevelt dines with his sister Bamie. He writes Kermit his views on Dickens, Bunyan and Thackeray, and writes Senator Bourne about the Standard Oil case.

headline: Canal talk with Goethals
summary: Roosevelt hears from Senator McCumber and Representative Gronna about La Follette's campaign, goes over the canal with Goethals, and lunches with Taft, Root, Garfield and others. A National Educational Association delegation calls, Mackenzie King comes at three, and he dines with the Longworths.

headline: Opening the Hudson tubes by telegraph
summary: From Washington Roosevelt presses a button that starts the first trains running through the Hudson tunnels between Hoboken and Sixth Avenue at 19th Street in New York. He goes to Bishop Satterlee's funeral, rides, and he and Edith dine with Agriculture Secretary James Wilson and his wife.

headline: Waterways report goes to Congress
summary: The Inland Waterways Commission's report goes to Congress, and Roosevelt sends a message opposing bills that would free power companies from federal control and fees. He sees senators, walks, and gives a dinner for Japanese Ambassador Takahira.

headline: Indian commissioners at the White House
summary: Roosevelt meets the Board of Indian Commissioners, confers with Taft, and talks with Representative Langley about naming a new Public Printer. Judge Wilfley calls, and after a ride Roosevelt writes Grafton Cushing about the country and the French Revolution of 1789.

headline: Trying on riding clothes for a portrait
summary: Painter Gari Melchers and Taft come to lunch; Melchers is to paint Roosevelt in riding clothes for Charles Freer. Afterward Roosevelt models several outfits for Edith and Alice until they approve one. The Cabinet discusses the Wilfley case, and in the evening he and Edith go to the Columbia Theater.

headline: Two portraits finished; Dickens judged
summary: Philip de László finishes a portrait of Roosevelt in riding clothes and a pastel of Edith, which both admire, and Gari Melchers completes his portrait too. Roosevelt writes Kermit a scathing verdict on Dickens after reading Martin Chuzzlewit, and urges Cannon to back a stronger navy. At Harvard, Ted lands on probation again for skipping lectures.

headline: Advice to a future President
summary: Representative Denby calls at one and there are meetings in the evening. Roosevelt writes Taft about appointments made out of sympathy, hoping Taft will make fewer of them as President than he himself has.

headline: Dinner with Henry Adams
summary: Roosevelt meets Hepburn and Crane and rides, then he and Edith dine with Henry Adams. He tells G. H. Davis he backs child labor and employers' liability laws whatever big business thinks.

headline: Hornaday at the lunch table
summary: After the Cabinet meeting Roosevelt lunches with Kohlsaat, Seth Low, Senator Brandegee, zoologist William Hornaday and others, rides, and dines with Edith at Secretary Straus's.

headline: Dickens for pacifists
summary: Senator Redfield Proctor of Vermont dies. Roosevelt rides and meets Kohlsaat in the evening. He sends Kermit a passage of Dickens against pacifism, and tells Taft the Army's tests for chaplains are too hard, though they ought to include math.

headline: Writing Balfour on decadence
summary: Roosevelt meets Senator Burkett and Representative Hinshaw and rides. He writes Arthur Balfour about his essay on decadence, weighing examples from history and biology, and writes Charles Knoblauch about Wall Street bills stuck in committee.

headline: Dewey on warships; Beveridge for chairman
summary: The Cabinet takes up mail agreements with Italy and France, and Admiral Dewey talks warship building with Roosevelt. Lodge and Aldrich call. He suggests to Republican chairman Harry New that Senator Beveridge preside over the convention.

headline: Quentin's ball team on the White House lawn
summary: Quentin's ball club from the Force School holds practice on the White House grounds. New York Republicans endorse Governor Hughes for President. Roosevelt discusses the tariff commission bill with Beveridge, rides, and writes Arthur Lee on Balfour and Japan, Corinne about a sorrow in her daughter's life, and James Creelman in praise of his article on Mexico's President Díaz.

headline: Ethel's new bull terrier
summary: Admiral Will Cowles calls at lunchtime. Roosevelt tells Archie that Ethel has a new white bull terrier named Mike, and passes on to Kermit the Kaiser's view of the American navy.

headline: A trip to the dentist
summary: After naval talks with Representatives Hobson and Foss, Roosevelt visits his dentist, Dr. Bryant, walks, and dines with Edith at Miss Tuckerman's. He writes Henry Adams that, like John Quincy Adams in his diary, he finds parts of the presidency tedious.

headline: Speaking to the Congress of Mothers
summary: Roosevelt addresses and receives the National Congress of Mothers, meets the Cabinet and Aldrich, sits for painter Philip de László at three, and rides.

headline: Brownsville message to Congress
summary: In a special message Roosevelt endorses the Brownsville findings of most of the Senate's military committee. He talks Taft's campaign with Senator Long, hears Montanans on the Northern Pacific's allegedly illegal land holdings, and in the evening discusses restitution for the Colorado River break with Garfield and Maxwell Evarts.

headline: No signature for the Foraker bill
summary: Roosevelt discusses Oklahoma politics with Governor Frantz, lunches with railroad man Stuyvesant Fish, Leslie Shaw and Alexander, rides, and takes Edith to the Columbia Theater. He tells Ernest Abbott he will not sign Foraker's Brownsville bill.

headline: An Outlook article on Taft
summary: After the Cabinet meeting and talks with Parsons and Langley, Roosevelt plays tennis with Bacon, Cooley and Jusserand. He compliments Lawrence Abbott on his Outlook piece about Taft and writes Eugene Philbin about Bishop Hendrick in the Philippines.

headline: Quentin's team routs P Street
summary: Roosevelt tells reporters the battle fleet, already at sea, will go all the way around the world. On the White House grounds Quentin's Force School team trounces the P Street School 22 to 5. He also confers on Taft's campaign, the third-term question and Brownsville, and warns Metcalf that Japanese ships outclass American ones.

headline: Mike the dog must go
summary: Edith and Emily Carow leave for New York, Emily soon to sail back to Italy, and Roosevelt dines at Bamie's. He tells Archie that Mike attacked Ethel's horse and must be given away, asks C. Hart Merriam about an air gun to shoot English sparrows at Sagamore Hill without hurting other birds, and complains to Kermit that Ted has cut 38 lectures since New Year's.

headline: Lincoln Steffens at lunchtime
summary: Roosevelt goes over legislation with Aldrich, discusses Tennessee politics with Representative Hale, sees muckraker Lincoln Steffens at one, and plays tennis with Garfield, Pinchot and Jusserand. Taft speaks on the rights of Black Americans at Plymouth Church in Brooklyn.

headline: Lunch with Andrew Carnegie
summary: Roosevelt meets and lunches with Andrew Carnegie after the Cabinet meeting, sees Cullom and Representative McKinley, and rides. He urges James Miller that Washington help pay to fix the broken Colorado River dam, a plea Congress ignored; the Southern Pacific paid instead.

headline: Water rights and Philippine policy
summary: Roosevelt confers on a Tennessee judgeship, the ship subsidy bill and Aldrich's currency bill, then lunches with Nick Longworth and William Barnes, plays tennis, and dines with the Longworths. He sends Senator Frye a statement on federal water rights and writes Spokane publisher William Cowles about railroad pay cuts.

headline: Spanish War veterans call
summary: Roosevelt discusses the Philippines with Taft and Eugene Philbin, receives Representative Cockran and a group of Spanish War veterans, rides, and sees Booker T. Washington at six.

headline: First letters about an African safari
summary: Roosevelt starts planning life after the White House: he asks hunter Frederick Selous when and where to go in Africa, and puts the same question to John Patterson. He also tries to stop La Questione Sociale, an anarchist paper out of Paterson, N.J., or failing that to bar it from the mails, and talks tariff revision with Western businessmen.

headline: Careful with shore leave in Japan
summary: Roosevelt meets Aldrich, Payne and Dalzell on legislation and Crane and Beveridge on the tariff, lunches with Leigh Hunt, and rides. He warns Admiral Charles Sperry to be cautious about sailors' shore leave when the fleet reaches Japan. Lincoln Steffens calls in the evening.

headline: Late Sunday callers
summary: Japanese Ambassador Aoki calls at 9:30 Sunday night, followed by Representative Hepburn and Seth Low.

headline: Four battleships, and Evans retires
summary: Roosevelt talks New York politics with Woodruff, lunches with Low, Merriam and the British ambassador, and walks. He accepts Admiral Robley Evans's resignation with regret and presses Speaker Cannon to authorize four new battleships and fortify Hawaii, mentioning the tariff along the way.

headline: Postal pay and battleship money
summary: The Cabinet weighs a raise for postal workers. Roosevelt talks battleship funding with Hobson, Brownsville with Senator Borah, and the fleet's cruise with Senator Flint, then rides.

headline: Another special message; Sundays off
summary: Roosevelt sends Congress a special message on antitrust, interstate commerce, finance and child labor laws. He meets Nebraska cattlemen on federal land grants and the Pure Food advisory board, and asks every cabinet officer to avoid Sunday work in their departments wherever possible.

headline: No new indictment for Borah
summary: Roosevelt discusses antitrust law with Hepburn, sees Beveridge, Purdy and others, and rides. He tells Bonaparte there will be no reindictment of Senator Borah, and writes Albert Key on improving the Navy.

headline: Alaska strikes and Venezuela
summary: The Cabinet discusses strikes in Alaska and the quarrel with Venezuela. Roosevelt meets Senator Frazier and Tennesseans about a judgeship, plays tennis at 4:30, and spends the evening at Lodge's.

headline: Boone and Crockett dinner
summary: Roosevelt weighs rival employers' liability bills with Senators Borah and Knox and currency with Representative Weeks, plays tennis, and dines with the Boone and Crockett Club at the Metropolitan Club. He writes Root about how many Japanese laborers are being let in.

headline: Castro refuses arbitration
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Taft, Yale's Arthur Hadley and Silas McBee and dines with Bamie. He writes Root that Venezuela's President Castro will not accept arbitration.

headline: Yellow fever quarantine in Cuba
summary: Roosevelt discusses Venezuela with Root and a yellow fever quarantine in Cuba with Taft, lunches with Alice, and meets Interstate Commerce Commissioners. After tennis he spends the evening with the German ambassador, Bacon and Root, and writes Whitelaw Reid about Japan and the fleet.

headline: Hill named to Berlin
summary: Roosevelt nominates David Jayne Hill as ambassador to Germany and picks S. F. Eddy to represent the country in Argentina, and sends the Senate the diplomatic papers on Venezuela. Former Treasury Secretary John G. Carlisle calls. He dines with the Austro-Hungarian ambassador, the Meyers, Alice and Nick, and Mrs. Beale, and writes Beveridge about curbing child labor in the capital.

headline: Henry Adams in the evening
summary: Roosevelt confers on the Massachusetts primaries, Indian affairs and battleships, sees Speaker Cannon, and hosts a big lunch for Alice, Bamie and her husband, and G. C. Ward. After a ride he sees von Sternberg and then Henry Adams. He writes Seth Low on executive control of corporations.

headline: Equal accommodations on trains
summary: Roosevelt writes Booker T. Washington about equality for Black Americans and instructs the Justice Department that train accommodations for Black passengers must equal those for whites. He tells Cecil Lyon he will turn down the party's nomination, and dines at Ambassador von Sternberg's.

headline: Drill at Fort Myer
summary: Roosevelt meets mine workers' leader John Mitchell about an inquiry into labor conditions on the isthmus, sees Senator Curtis, and watches troops drill at Fort Myer before tennis with Winthrop. He drafts, but does not send, a letter to Charlemagne Tower about opposition to Hill's appointment in Berlin.

headline: Dinner with the Holmeses and Henry Adams
summary: Roosevelt names J. S. Leech Public Printer, talks Indiana politics with Beveridge and battleships with Hobson, and sees editor Henry Watterson. After tennis he dines with the Roots, the Lodges, Henry Adams, and Justice Holmes and his wife. He writes the Kaiser about Hill and the fleet, and Magoon on Cuba's government after the American withdrawal.

headline: Three Sunday visitors
summary: Ambassador von Sternberg calls at 12:30, Herbert Smith at 2:30, and Speaker Cannon at 9:30 that night.

headline: Bird refuge in the Dry Tortugas
summary: Roosevelt creates the Tortugas Keys Bird Reservation in Florida. He meets Representatives Hill and Weeks, sees von Sternberg, and rides.

headline: The paper trust again
summary: After the Cabinet meeting Roosevelt hears Herman Ridder on the paper trust, sees Senator Heyburn, receives Booker T. Washington at three, and rides.

headline: A waterway from Boston to Key West
summary: Roosevelt talks with Heyburn about a Snake River irrigation dam and with a group of congressmen about an inland waterway from Boston to Key West, then walks with Captain Fournier and William Phillips. He tells Arthur Lee he enjoyed sitting for de László, and writes Edward Curtis about Custer's final fight.

headline: Archie turns 14; medicine ball
summary: On Archie's 14th birthday Roosevelt asks Congress for laws against anarchism, discusses New York politics with Fassett and Cocks, and tosses the medicine ball with Pinchot, Garfield and Jusserand. He writes Metcalf about the very high desertion rate among Navy engine-room crews.

headline: Spitballs on the portraits
summary: On a rainy day Quentin and three friends decorate the White House hallway portraits with spitballs. Roosevelt defends his Brownsville decision to Herbert Parsons and objects to New York Republican resolutions on Southern representation and on Brownsville. He rejects Albert Key's plan to reorganize Navy command and wants a Pacific drydock in two or three years, not five or six.

headline: Mad at Quentin over the spitballs
summary: Roosevelt meets Senator Cullom and Puerto Rico's Larrinaga, rides, and dines with the Bacons, Longworths, Cowleses, novelist Mrs. Humphry Ward and her husband, and others. He tells Archie that Ethel has a bulldog pup on trial and that he is angry with Quentin over the spitballs, and writes Kermit about books, politics and next year's African hunt.

headline: Sunday dinner at Henry Adams's
summary: Roosevelt rides, and he and Edith dine with Henry Adams. Gardner, Pinchot and Jusserand call in the evening.

headline: Alaska coal lands
summary: Roosevelt confers on New York politics and with Garfield on Alaska's coal lands, plays tennis, and he and Edith dine at Justice Moody's. He tells Representative Humphrey he wants a Pacific drydock built in two years.

headline: Foraker speaks for the Brownsville soldiers
summary: On the Senate floor Joseph Foraker speaks in defense of the Brownsville troops. Roosevelt meets the Cabinet, talks currency with Representative Vreeland, plays tennis, and discusses adjournment with James Watson in the evening.

headline: A strong call for four battleships
summary: On a very full day Roosevelt has Ambassador James Bryce to lunch (he once called Bryce, fondly, a prodigious memory with hair on it) and sends Congress a forceful message asking for four new battleships. He rides at 4:45.

headline: Natural Bridges and a new national forest
summary: Roosevelt proclaims Natural Bridge National Monument in Utah and Manzano National Forest in New Mexico. He meets bankers on currency, the National Gallery's advisory committee, and Taft, and plays tennis. Ted arrives home from college nursing a sore throat.

headline: Thinking about Japan and war
summary: After the Cabinet meeting Roosevelt discusses Japanese immigration with Representative McKinley and plays tennis with Hallowell, Winthrop and Phillips. He writes Root about Japan and the chance of war, and Bonaparte about an employers' liability bill.

headline: Springtime ride with Edith
summary: Roosevelt and Edith ride in the late afternoon, and he notices the season's wildflowers along Rock Creek. He hears Ralph Easley on amending the Sherman Act, and writes Kermit and Senator Warren about his fight for four battleships, Frank Munsey with thanks for his articles, and Pearl Wight about sending a Black Louisianan to the convention.

headline: Move the gold to Denver
summary: Roosevelt suggests to Treasury Secretary Cortelyou that the gold reserve be moved inland from San Francisco to Denver should war come.

headline: Game preserves for Alaska
summary: Roosevelt talks currency with Representative Hill and Alaska game preserves with writer Emerson Hough and C. Hart Merriam, and plays tennis with Ted, Cooley and Hallowell. In New York, Taft addresses a laymen's missionary gathering at Carnegie Hall.

headline: A Minnesota judgeship
summary: After the Cabinet meeting Roosevelt discusses a Minnesota judgeship with Senator Clapp, lunches with Bonaparte, Kellogg and others, rides, and dines with Winthrop, Phillips and the Longworths.

headline: Cleveland and the coal strike
summary: The Outlook runs Roosevelt's article on how Grover Cleveland handled the coal strike. He meets West Coast senators about the battleships, rides, and plays tennis. He thanks Senator Piles for leading the Senate fight for four battleships and asks Lodge to stand strong, or at least appear to, for them.

headline: Pressing Flint on battleships
summary: Roosevelt sees Cooley, Charles Pepper and Senator Overman, plays tennis, and dines with the Lodges. He presses Senator Frank Flint to hold out for all four battleships.

headline: Liability law for federal workers
summary: Roosevelt signs the employers' liability bill covering government workers. He also writes Senator William Smith, restating his conviction that Black soldiers carried out the Brownsville shooting.

headline: A Tennessee judgeship
summary: Roosevelt talks with Representative Gaines about a Tennessee judgeship and plays tennis with Meyer and Winthrop.

headline: Edith wary of the Africa plan
summary: Senators Clay, Overman and Dixon call late Sunday evening. Edith writes Kermit that she dislikes the idea of Roosevelt's planned hunting trip to Africa.

headline: Congress agrees to two battleships
summary: Roosevelt works senators on the battleship issue and sends Congress a special message on injunctions and national control of corporations. He rides with Ambassador von Sternberg and writes Henry White that he likes Asquith, Britain's new prime minister. Congress agrees to two new battleships.

headline: Cabinet and tennis
summary: A short record: the Cabinet meets, and Roosevelt plays tennis at 4:30 with Jusserand, Garfield and Cooley.

headline: Indian land claims
summary: On Corinne's 26th wedding anniversary Roosevelt discusses Indian land claims with Senators Ankeny and Piles, receives a long list of callers, and rides. He writes Speaker Cannon about the civil bill, lifting wage limits in Panama, and the child labor bill.

headline: Funding the Hepburn Act
summary: Roosevelt talks Western politics with Representative Hull and the Snake River dam with Piles and Jones, and meets four congressmen on money to enforce the Hepburn Act. After tennis, Edith goes to a lecture. He writes Cannon about the ICC section of the sundry civil bill.

headline: Ethel's friends to dinner
summary: After the Cabinet meeting Roosevelt sees Parsons, Piles and Long and rides. Edith invites some of Ethel's friends to dinner.

headline: General Wood to watch European maneuvers
summary: Senators Elkins and Rayner call, then von Sternberg, and Roosevelt plays tennis. Grant La Farge and his wife and Miss C. Roosevelt arrive as house guests. He writes General Bell about Leonard Wood attending German and French army maneuvers, and Charles Littlefield about injunctions.

headline: Guests stay through Sunday
summary: The La Farges and Miss C. Roosevelt remain at the White House.

headline: A thousand Japanese in April
summary: Roosevelt talks Taft's campaign with Frank Hitchcock and currency with two congressmen, plays tennis with Grant La Farge and others, and takes Edith to the National Theater. He warns Root that more than 1,000 Japanese arrived in April and an exclusion law may follow, and writes Emerson Hough on socialism and Marx.

headline: Postal savings and Brownsville
summary: Roosevelt discusses a postal savings bank bill with Senator Carter, Brownsville with Borah, and pending legislation with Speaker Cannon, then rides. The La Farges and Miss C. Roosevelt are still visiting.

headline: Cardinal Gibbons to lunch; Burroughs arrives
summary: Roosevelt confers on a Tennessee judgeship, Oklahoma patronage, an Alaska game preserve bill and Utah forest reserves, and lunches with Cardinal Gibbons. John Burroughs joins the house guests. He writes the Kaiser hoping for an arbitration treaty with Germany, and C. Hart Merriam about Mendel's law.

headline: Off to Pine Knot with Edith
summary: Roosevelt and Edith leave late in the morning for Pine Knot. He writes Senator John Stewart about discharging the Brownsville soldiers, remarking that he is often accused of breaking the Constitution.

headline: Archie Butt joins the White House
summary: While Roosevelt is at Pine Knot, Captain Archibald Willingham Butt takes up duties as a military aide at the White House in place of Charlie McCauley. By September Butt will be chief aide, succeeding Frank McCoy.

headline: A brisk bird walk with Burroughs
summary: John Burroughs comes out to Pine Knot, and Roosevelt marches him four quick miles to the cabin while the two name the birds they pass. Edith scolds her husband for the punishing pace he set for the old naturalist. She tells Kermit her husband is now pretending the African trip holds no appeal for him.

headline: Squirrels evicted, then let back in
summary: Roosevelt swats a mosquito so hard Burroughs likens it to a lion-killing blow, and says he needn't fear assassins because he carries a gun; he doesn't know Edith has two plainclothesmen in the woods at night. After a bird walk they head back to Washington. He tells Archie that Burroughs evicted some squirrels from the cabin and the Roosevelts moved them back.

headline: Cornerstone for the Pan American building
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Kerens, Root, Archbishop Ireland and Andrew Carnegie, then helps lay the cornerstone of the Bureau of American Republics building. He proclaims Lewis and Clark National Monument in Montana and loses at tennis to Pinchot. By telegram he agrees to Taft's request for U.S. oversight of Panama's elections.

headline: Governors gather for conservation
summary: Governors from across the states and territories, Supreme Court justices, the Cabinet, scientists and public figures including William Jennings Bryan come in Washington for the conservation conference. Roosevelt hosts a dinner for seventy. He writes Ted about Rabelais and other writers, Quentin learning baseball from the butler James, and Archie losing his head and steering into the other boat at Groton.

headline: The Governors' Conference opens
summary: The Governors' Conference on conserving the nation's resources opens in the East Room, and Roosevelt sits in from 10:30 to 2:30 before turning to appointments. Archie Butt attends his first White House luncheon, with Yale's President Hadley, the Cowleses and the Lodges. Roosevelt asks Speaker Cannon to pass a bill making the Inland Waterways Commission permanent; it fails.

headline: Second day with the governors
summary: Roosevelt again spends 10:30 to 2:30 at the conservation conference, then discusses the anti-injunction bill and a Norfolk Navy Yard contract. After tennis with Winthrop, Cooley and Meyer, he thanks the Kaiser for a letter and gift and tells him about the fleet. Edith goes to the National Theater.

headline: Governors declare for conservation
summary: The Governors' Conference closes with a declaration in favor of conservation; 38 states go on to form conservation commissions, and the meeting gives rise to the annual governors' conferences. Pinchot will call it the first national gathering anywhere to treat resource protection as a single problem. Roosevelt creates Kansas National Forest, lunches with historian James Ford Rhodes, and holds a reception; rain turns the planned garden party into a White House tea.

headline: Peary's next Arctic push
summary: Roosevelt discusses the Rainy River dam bill, sees John Mitchell, Borah and others, and talks with Robert Peary about his coming Arctic expedition. He speaks at the Methodist gathering at American University near Tenleytown, opens a St. Louis charity bazaar by pressing a button, and plays tennis.

headline: Roswell gets kicked
summary: Archie Butt is called to the White House because Roosevelt's horse Roswell has been kicked, and finds the President calmer than he expected. Timothy Woodruff comes in the evening to talk New York politics. Roosevelt tells Archie that Quentin is wrapped up in baseball and the grounds are in full bloom.

headline: Checking on the fleet's progress
summary: Roosevelt discusses Kentucky patronage, plays tennis, dines with the Cowleses and the Italian ambassador, and meets Taft late on canal business. He writes Captain Cone of the torpedo flotilla traveling with the fleet about what the cruise has done so far.

headline: Election fraud in Panama
summary: The Cabinet discusses election fraud in Panama. Roosevelt meets congressmen on the Inland Waterways bill, sees Newberry and Pinchot, and dines with Metcalf. Miss Potter and Mr. and Mrs. Harvier are house guests.

headline: Ship subsidies and the Sherman Act
summary: Roosevelt meets Speaker Cannon at ten, then discusses anti-injunction legislation, Sherman Act amendments and the ship subsidy in the postal bill. After tennis with Garfield and Jusserand he dines with Bacon. David Gray and Miss Potter are staying.

headline: Clarence Darrow calls late
summary: Roosevelt discusses Venezuela with Cullom and the Rainy River dam with Bede, Hepburn, Garfield and Stevens, and hears a delegation pushing battleship work at the Norfolk yard. He lunches with Root, General Young and his wife, and others, rides, and at ten that night receives Clarence Darrow and Lincoln Steffens.

headline: Admiral Evans calls
summary: After the Cabinet meeting, Admiral Robley Evans, Senator Sutherland and Representative Langley call. Roosevelt discusses New York politics with Wadsworth, plays tennis, and writes Albert Shaw about the coming convention.

headline: A range for the bison; the little bear leaves
summary: A new law creates the National Bison Range in Montana, starting with 18,000 acres and 80 bison, and Roosevelt declares the Minnesota National Forest. He writes Edward Buxton about planning next year's African trip, and tells Ted, who is deciding what to do in the fall, that it pains him to see "the little bear" heading out into the world.

headline: Nothing recorded
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; the record lists nothing for this Sunday.

headline: Envoys from Liberia
summary: Roosevelt meets Senators Beveridge and Kean, grants Austrian Ambassador Hengelmüller a private audience, and with Root receives three envoys from Liberia. After tennis he discusses Indian Territory with Garfield. He tells Whitelaw Reid he dislikes the custom of presentation at court. Archie Butt escorts Edith to the theater.

headline: A noon wedding on N Street
summary: Roosevelt goes to a noon wedding at 1753 N Street, where Francis R. Stevens marries Elizabeth Oliver. Between conferences with his cabinet, he talks with Depew about the government liability bill and with Fassett about James S. Sherman for Vice President, lunches with Colonel Hugh Scott, and rides.

headline: Spanish War veterans and Taft
summary: Senator Bourne calls in the morning and Walter Hale, representing veterans of the war with Spain, at 11:30. Roosevelt confers with Taft and Root in the afternoon and plays tennis at 4:30.

headline: The New Haven merger will stand
summary: Father Doyle brings twelve student priests to call, along with the District commissioners, and Roosevelt rides at five. He writes Alston Dayton about West Virginia delegates for Taft, John Hull on revising Army promotions, and Lodge that the New Haven railroad combination will not be broken up.

headline: Seven sets and mint juleps
summary: Roosevelt plays seven sets of tennis with Archie Butt, Garfield and Captain McCoy, after which they all have mint juleps, joined by the Longworths, Pinchot and others. He gives Fitzhugh Lee a pistol. He tells Alston Dayton he will not let his name go on the ballot, and Lyman Abbott that he will not be renominated.

headline: Congress adjourns; Quentin's beehive
summary: The Aldrich-Vreeland currency bill passes and Congress adjourns; Roosevelt signs the last bills at the Capitol that evening. He rides with Archie Butt, lunches with Ranger Bill McDonald and Admiral Cowles, and plays tennis. To Kermit he describes summery evenings under the apple tree with Edith and La Follette's filibuster; to Archie, Quentin's new beehive and a foul tip to the eye.

headline: Ted graduates from Harvard
summary: Roosevelt calls on J. J. Gaff at 1520 20th Street to see a painting of a farmer, and dines with the Jusserands. "The Successful Mother" by Roosevelt appears in the Ladies' Home Journal, and Ted finishes at Harvard. Archie Butt has become Edith's regular escort on solo outings, long walks and antique hunts. On June 18 the Republicans will nominate Taft.

headline: Campaign strategy session with Taft
summary: Roosevelt talks labor and paper-trust legislation with House members, plays tennis in the afternoon, and spends the evening plotting the fall campaign with Taft and party leaders. He also tells the Republican chairman flatly that he will not seek a third term.

headline: Cabinet day and a stream of callers
summary: After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt receives a busy line of senators, congressmen and the journalist James Creelman, then gets out for a ride. He writes to Elmer Youngman about the currency bill.

headline: Writing Ray Stannard Baker on race
summary: Roosevelt sees Taft, Cortelyou and Jacob Schiff among other callers and plays afternoon tennis with Ambassador Jusserand. In letters he discusses New York politics with Chauncey Depew and responds to Ray Stannard Baker's magazine series on Black Americans in the South.

headline: Tariff talk with Senator Cullom
summary: Roosevelt confers with Senator Cullom on what the Republican platform should say about the tariff, talks campaign matters with Senator Long, and meets Agriculture Secretary Wilson with food-safety chemist Dr. Harvey Wiley. Ambassador Bryce calls, and Roosevelt rides.

headline: Waterways letters and a note to Steffens
summary: Roosevelt holds a Cabinet meeting, discusses an executive order on hiring extra federal workers, and plays tennis. He writes about the Inland Waterways Commission and sends Lincoln Steffens a lengthy defense of his battle against corruption.

headline: Hunting advice for Kermit
summary: Roosevelt goes over Canal Zone business with Taft, rides, and holds an evening campaign meeting with Taft, Root and Burkett. Looking ahead to Africa, he tells Kermit that big-game hunters must cover for one another.

headline: Thrown into a brook on a ride
summary: A Sunday ride ends with Roosevelt's horse spilling him into a stream. He also meets with Taft and writes to ornithologist Frank Chapman about bird photography.

headline: National Conservation Commission created
summary: Roosevelt names the National Conservation Commission, chaired by Gifford Pinchot, to take stock of America's natural resources. Between naval talks and tennis, he dines that night with Edith at the home of Alice and Nick Longworth.

headline: Tennis win over Archie Butt
summary: Roosevelt beats his military aide Archie Butt at tennis on a day of Cabinet business, currency talks with Cortelyou, and lunch with Massachusetts Governor Curtis Guild Jr. He weighs a new Army Chief of Engineers and wires about rival Louisiana delegations.

headline: Liberian delegation and Booker T. Washington
summary: Roosevelt receives a delegation from Liberia late in the evening, accompanied by Booker T. Washington. Earlier he sees Taft, Root and others, plays tennis, and dines with Postmaster General Meyer, and he assures his brother-in-law Will Cowles about his future.

headline: Praise for a corporate annual report
summary: Roosevelt talks with Francis Loomis about the planned Tokyo exposition and receives several callers before riding. He writes George W. Perkins about International Harvester's annual report, an early experiment in a company courting public goodwill.

headline: A senator declines the Conservation Commission
summary: Roosevelt plays tennis, meets the Spanish Treaty Claims Commission and the Japanese ambassador, and sees George Perkins and Ray Stannard Baker that night. John Sharp Williams wires that he is refusing his seat on the new commission, arguing only Congress can create such bodies.

headline: Talk of a national anthem on horseback
summary: Out on his new mount Georgia, joined by Fitzhugh Lee and Archie Butt, Roosevelt muses about a national anthem; both he and Butt favor Julia Ward Howe's Civil War battle hymn. That afternoon the 150 voices of the Arion Chorus sing at the White House for about fifty guests.

headline: Another ride on Georgia
summary: Roosevelt takes his new horse Georgia out for a second ride.

headline: Uncle Remus and patriotic songs
summary: Roosevelt meets Taft, discusses prison reform with Commissioner Macfarland, and plays tennis with Archie Butt. He writes Joel Chandler Harris about Uncle Remus and patriotic songs, and wires Lodge about planks in the Republican platform.

headline: Republican convention opens in Chicago
summary: As the Republican National Convention gets under way in Chicago with Alice in attendance, Roosevelt fires off telegrams opposing a proposed plank on court injunctions and again turning down a third term. At home he plays tennis in the rain and greets delegates bound for a scientific congress in Chile.

headline: Roosevelt on Tolstoy and socialists
summary: With the Chicago convention still in session, Roosevelt rides and writes letters. To Lyman Abbott he takes on Christian Socialists, Eugene Debs and Big Bill Haywood, and condemns Tolstoy's Kreutzer Sonata as the work of "a sexual degenerate."

headline: Taft nominated after a Roosevelt stampede
summary: The convention erupts in a 45-minute demonstration for Roosevelt before Lodge heads off any move to draft him, and Taft wins the nomination on the first ballot. Progressives balk at the adopted platform. In Washington Roosevelt confers with Root and Taft, plays tennis with Bacon, and wires Lodge his thanks.

headline: Quentin dreads leaving the White House
summary: New York's James S. Sherman takes the vice presidential nomination in Chicago. Roosevelt holds Cabinet, meets Taft and Ambassador Aoki, and writes Nannie Lodge praising her husband and passing along Quentin's lament about leaving home.

headline: Summer begins at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt leaves Washington for Oyster Bay, and the guest book notes that Sagamore Hill has been opened for the season. He writes Charles Walcott about plans and routes for his coming African expedition.

headline: Quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Eyes turning toward Africa
summary: Writing to his sister Bamie, Roosevelt says his mind has already left politics for Africa and that Ted has finished Harvard and begun working. He tells Benjamin Ide Wheeler he would have preferred Dolliver or Cummins to Sherman.

headline: A snake expert visits; Grand Canyon preserve set aside
summary: Harris Dickson of Vicksburg comes to lunch, invited to bring a specimen of a so-called stinging snake. That day a game preserve is established at the Grand Canyon. Roosevelt tells his sister Corinne he is delighted with the convention and calls Lodge's management of it masterly.

headline: Grover Cleveland dies
summary: Former President Grover Cleveland dies at Princeton, New Jersey. At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt writes Lodge about the convention, Taft's chances and the African trip, and answers charges that immigration laws are going unenforced.

headline: Selous on Africa, and no sun helmets
summary: Roosevelt writes to the famed hunter Frederick Selous about plans for his African hunting trip, adding that he does not care for sun helmets.

headline: At Grover Cleveland's funeral
summary: Roosevelt travels to Princeton, New Jersey, to attend the funeral of former President Grover Cleveland. Along the Texas border, Mexican rebels raid Las Vacas in a short-lived uprising. He writes Corinne explaining why he is giving up the presidency.

headline: Taft, Stimson and Steffens to lunch
summary: Roosevelt goes over War Department business with Taft and Luke Wright and talks politics with Frank Kellogg and W. L. Ward. Robert Bridges and Lincoln Steffens also come, and the whole group, Henry Stimson included, stays for lunch.

headline: Quentin's sunburn
summary: Quentin comes in with legs badly burned by the sun and jokes that they resemble one of Turner's sunsets, then adds a line from Poe.

headline: Standard Oil seeks a settlement
summary: Senator Bourne and Standard Oil's John D. Archbold come to Sagamore Hill hoping to settle the government's case out of court. Roosevelt also plans the African trip with Caspar Whitney, entertains a Mexican senator at lunch, and wires about the border incident.

headline: Taft steps down from the War Department
summary: Taft's resignation as Secretary of War takes effect so he can run his campaign full time, and four troops of cavalry head for the Mexican border. At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt sits for the sculptor Victor D. Brenner and writes Navy Secretary Metcalf about flaws in American ship design. Half a world away, an enormous blast flattens the forest near the Tunguska River in Siberia.

headline: Ninety-four National Forests created
summary: Ninety-four National Forests are established on this day. Luke E. Wright, once ambassador to Japan, succeeds Taft as Secretary of War. Roosevelt hosts S. S. McClure and Caspar Whitney for lunch and writes about San Juan Hill, warships and an unhappy H. C. Frick.

headline: An honor for Edith from the Sultan
summary: With calm returning along the Mexican frontier, Roosevelt writes Meyer again about Frick's discontent and asks Root about an award the Sultan of Turkey wishes to give Edith. He also tells Taft about Hitchcock as party chairman and discusses African trip articles with Robert Bridges.

headline: Joel Chandler Harris dies
summary: Joel Chandler Harris, the Uncle Remus author Roosevelt admired, dies. Roosevelt writes Truman Newberry about warship building and Senator Bourne about Standard Oil.

headline: Independence Day guests at Sagamore
summary: The Sagamore Hill guest book fills with Fourth of July visitors, among them Beatrice Flagg, nephew Monroe Douglas Robinson and Elizabeth Hoyt.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Condolences to Joel Chandler Harris's son
summary: Roosevelt sends two letters of sympathy to Julian Harris on the death of his father, Joel Chandler Harris. He also agrees to speak at the Naval War College on July 22 and writes Meyer about Post Office removals.

headline: Peary sails the Roosevelt into Oyster Bay
summary: Robert Peary brings his ship, named the Roosevelt, into Oyster Bay on the way north to try for the Pole, and he and his wife come to lunch. Roosevelt tells the explorer he believes in him and in his success. He also meets Robert Bridges about Africa and the Public Printer about the Government Printing Office.

headline: Lunch with Lyman Abbott
summary: Lyman Abbott comes to lunch, and Fortescue, Needham and Sullivan call. Roosevelt writes Admiral Chadwick about Spain and history's great navies, and tells Senator Bourne he wants a federal incorporation law passed next session.

headline: Dr. Lambert arrives for a long weekend
summary: Dr. Alexander Lambert, Roosevelt's physician and friend, comes to Sagamore Hill to stay through Monday. Roosevelt writes Robert Collier about his African articles and assures Richmond Hobson he never called war with Japan likely.

headline: Weighing a return to his frontier history
summary: Dr. H. H. Washburn calls. Roosevelt writes Taft about a friendly New York Times editorial, asks George Putnam about completing The Winning of the West, and writes Harvard's President Eliot about two students disciplined for stealing books.

headline: Speech at the John Underhill monument
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Matinecock, Long Island, as a monument to the colonial captain John Underhill is unveiled. Dr. Lambert is staying at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt writes Taft about campaign money and Harry Johnston about a planned book on Black Americans.

headline: Root and family at Sunday lunch
summary: Elihu Root, Dr. Lambert, Arthur Woods, and Douglas and Corinne Robinson with their son Monroe are among the Sunday guests, and Roosevelt lunches with Root and Bacon.

headline: A forest named for Cleveland
summary: Roosevelt writes Frances Cleveland proposing that the San Jacinto National Forest be renamed for her late husband. Father York calls at noon, and Roosevelt advises Taft on how to take on Bryan and the Democrats.

headline: Two new Oregon forests
summary: The Deschutes and Fremont National Forests in Oregon are created. Roosevelt writes Medill McCormick about the Democratic platform's call to drop tariffs on lumber, timber and pulp, which Republicans firmly resist.

headline: A lunch table of writers and publishers
summary: Henry Fairfield Osborn, the painter F. D. Millet, publisher Charles Scribner and George W. Perkins are among Roosevelt's lunch guests. He writes Frank Hitchcock about labor leaders and party funds.

headline: No to Prohibition, thanks to a riding mentor
summary: Roosevelt thanks David Gray for helping Kermit become a better horseman and tells Taft he objects to any national prohibition law.

headline: Osborns and Munns at Sagamore
summary: Henry Fairfield and Josephine Osborn, Frederic Burnham and the Munns sign the guest book. Roosevelt writes Taft about campaign issues, including a postal savings bank.

headline: A Texas postmaster's last chance
summary: Roosevelt meets Attorney General Bonaparte and talks Central American affairs with Robert Bacon. He tells Senator Culberson that the Abilene postmaster, Mrs. Morrow, a descendant of Sam Houston, has already been given two chances.

headline: A strong President, plainly put
summary: In a letter to Lodge, Roosevelt says he has no wish to cling to power and lays out his belief that the presidency should be a mighty office held by a forceful man. Guests at lunch are Creel, Buchanan, and an assistant attorney general named Bacon with his wife.

headline: Cuba on his mind
summary: Roosevelt writes Secretary of State Root about affairs in Cuba.

headline: Off to Newport on the Mayflower
summary: Roosevelt boards the presidential yacht Mayflower in the evening, bound for Newport. He tells George Putnam he cannot commit to finishing his frontier history now, writes Spring-Rice about soft living among English-speaking peoples, and wires Taft a critique of his acceptance speech.

headline: A big-navy speech at the War College
summary: Speaking to the Navy's War College gathering in Newport, Roosevelt makes his case once more for a powerful fleet, warning that the Monroe Doctrine means little without warships behind it.

headline: Taft spends the night
summary: Roosevelt brings the Mayflower back to Oyster Bay. Taft stays the whole day and overnight, and Root is also a guest. Letters go to Perkins on railroad rates and Bonaparte on the Indiana Standard Oil case.

headline: Archie Butt arrives for a Sagamore stay
summary: Military aide Archie Butt and Beekman Winthrop arrive at Sagamore Hill, swim, and sit down at eight to fried chicken in white gravy and corn on the cob. Butt records Edith's remark that the house has no rules at all. Earlier Roosevelt meets Taft and the sculptor Brenner.

headline: Swimming in the rain, and a cut toe
summary: William Phillips arrives in time for a breakfast of peaches and cream, liver, bacon and grits. Despite rain the household swims and plays tennis; when Archie Butt gashes himself while swimming, Roosevelt teases Phillips about his toenails. Over lunch he talks at length about Africa, and Butt senses Edith's worry.

headline: Church, then the West Roosevelts
summary: Archie Butt goes to church with the family; Roosevelt keeps Sundays free of work and games. Afterward they visit the West Roosevelts, where Roosevelt spins stories after dinner and talks about Africa.

headline: Tennis and talk of Bryan
summary: Roosevelt and Archie Butt play tennis and talk over William Jennings Bryan's campaign.

headline: Taft accepts the nomination
summary: In Cincinnati, William Howard Taft formally accepts the Republican nomination for president.

headline: A placeholder entry with forward notes
summary: The record for this date holds only forward-looking notes: Ambassador Speck von Sternberg's death and the creation of the Country Life Commission, both of which belong to later August dates.

headline: Visiting Squadron C's camp
summary: After breakfast with Bacon, Roosevelt takes up West Point dismissals with Luke Wright and canal business with Joseph Bishop. In the afternoon he visits the Squadron C camp at Huntington, and he tells naturalist Edgar Mearns the African passage is booked for March 23, 1909.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the day passes without other recorded activity.

headline: Bamie and Sheffield visit
summary: His sister Bamie and her son Sheffield Cowles come to Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt tells Taft that Hitchcock needs reining in, asks Root to chair the New York Republican convention, and writes Bryce about Tibet and India and Jusserand about books and leaving office.

headline: Lunch with Collier's editors and Cortelyou
summary: Roosevelt's lunch guests include publisher Robert Collier, journalist Mark Sullivan, Norman Hapgood and Treasury Secretary Cortelyou.

headline: Word of Senator Allison's death
summary: News arrives that Iowa's Senator William B. Allison died the day before. Architect C. Grant LaFarge stays the night, and Roosevelt asks Henry Fairfield Osborn for a standard natural history reference so he can study up on African wildlife.

headline: Edith turns 47
summary: Edith celebrates her 47th birthday, and Jacob Riis comes to dinner. Roosevelt writes Lyman Abbott about the 1902 coal strike and his offer to place Grover Cleveland on the arbitration board.

headline: A painting from Arthur Lee
summary: Roosevelt plans the campaign with Frank Hitchcock and takes up the cadet dismissals again with Secretary Wright. Henry Lee Higginson and Frank Chapman call. He thanks his English friend Arthur Lee for the gift of a painting and discusses Quebec's tercentenary.

headline: Bird refuges at Key West and Klamath Lake
summary: Federal bird reservations are established at Florida's Key West and at Klamath Lake on the Oregon-California line. Roosevelt tells John Hammond the Brownsville decision was his alone, not Taft's, and writes Lodge that Edith is pleased his African trophies will go to a museum.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing further is noted.

headline: Country Life Commission launched
summary: Worried that farm life is fading as cities grow, Roosevelt creates the Country Life Commission and asks Cornell's Liberty Hyde Bailey to lead it. He also tells Truman Newberry a naval lieutenant should not be dismissed and writes William Allen White about Ohio's Senate seat.

headline: A quiet Tuesday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no activity is recorded.

headline: A report on the Kaiser from Oscar King Davis
summary: Times correspondent William Bayard Hale calls, and Oscar King Davis brings Roosevelt an account of the Kaiser, later describing the visit in his memoir. Roosevelt writes Taft about disclosing campaign donations and praises James B. Reynolds's Panama report.
