headline: Ethel's sweet sixteen
summary: Ethel turns 16. The Clifford Richardsons and William Appleton visit, and Roosevelt lunches with New York Republicans William Barnes, Francis Hendricks and Herbert Parsons along with Gifford Pinchot. He writes Commander Sims about a commission to reorganize the Navy.

headline: Keep the safari quiet
summary: John Donovan and Representative Barchfeld call. Roosevelt asks Robert Bridges to keep publicity about the African trip to a minimum, and advises Taft to back Governor Hughes privately without issuing a statement.

headline: No pardons for two bankers
summary: Roosevelt tells Robert Thompson he will not pardon Curtis and Morse, the two indicted top officers of a New York bank. He also asks Newberry for the Newport conference's battleship findings and writes Bonaparte about rising railroad rates.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.

headline: Manuel Quezon to lunch
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Cortelyou, Fassett, the Filipino leader Manuel Quezon, Escamillo and Olin. Former New York police chief John McCullagh and Lindsay Denison call, and Charles Sheldon and Truman Newberry stay for dinner and the night.

headline: Invited to give Oxford's Romanes Lecture
summary: Roosevelt accepts Lord Curzon's invitation to deliver the Romanes Lecture at Oxford, which he will give in 1910. Malheur Lake in Oregon becomes a bird reservation. He tells Taft that Bryan is attacking his Unitarian faith, and sends Lodge a clipping about a Texas statue of himself that amuses him.

headline: Pruning the safari grocery list
summary: Roosevelt goes through Selous's list of supplies for Africa, keeping tinned beans, peaches and tomatoes, cutting back the liquor, dropping pepper and mustard, and swapping cocoa for coffee. Secretary Meyer comes to dinner and stays the night.

headline: Hughes renomination talks; a colonel's uniform for Europe
summary: Roosevelt huddles with Sherman, Hitchcock, Bacon and New York party men over renominating Governor Hughes. He writes Whitelaw Reid about African game licenses and royal visits, saying he wants to wear his cavalry colonel's uniform at European courts.

headline: Backing Hughes despite his flaws
summary: Roosevelt writes William Barnes Jr. that Governor Hughes ought to be renominated, shortcomings and all, and discusses the race with Lyman Abbott. He also sends thanks to the authors of the Panama report.

headline: Saturday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events are recorded.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events are recorded.

headline: Grief for Speck von Sternberg
summary: Roosevelt's old friend Baron Speck von Sternberg, the German ambassador, dies of cancer in Germany, and Roosevelt wires his sorrow. Alice and Nick Longworth visit, and he writes William Barnes Jr. about Hughes and New York politics.

headline: Evening train to see Corinne
summary: After lunch with Governor Charles Magoon of Cuba, Roosevelt leaves in the evening for Jordanville, New York, to visit Corinne and Douglas Robinson. He asks Hitchcock to have an expert review Taft's labor rulings for the campaign.

headline: Dedicating Douglas Robinson's library gift
summary: In Jordanville, Roosevelt dedicates the public library his brother-in-law Douglas Robinson has given to the town. Clifford and Teresa Richardson sign the guest book.

headline: Home, with Vanderbilt to lunch
summary: Back at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt lunches with Cornelius Vanderbilt and sends Herbert Parsons his thoughts on the governor's race.

headline: Chase Lake refuge in North Dakota
summary: A bird reservation is set aside at Chase Lake, North Dakota. Roosevelt thanks Douglas and Corinne for their hospitality, concedes to Newberry on the Newport battleship plans, and cites history in defending Taft against attacks on his religion.

headline: Missionaries in China
summary: Baron Takahira and Dr. Iglehart call. Roosevelt writes Lyman Abbott about missionaries in China and Taft about bank deposits and postal savings.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Olympians at Sagamore; the children scatter
summary: Roosevelt welcomes members of the American Olympic team. The children head off to new chapters: Ted starts at a Connecticut carpet mill for $7 a week, Kermit begins college at Harvard, Archie returns to Groton, and Quentin enrolls at Episcopal High School across the Potomac in Alexandria.

headline: Telling Taft to go on offense
summary: Roosevelt meets Cortelyou and W. L. Ward and lunches with publisher George Haven Putnam, Francis Leupp, Colonel Brodie and William Travers Jerome. The architect Grant LaFarge and his wife Florence arrive for a stay. His advice to Taft is blunt: don't reply to Bryan, go after him.

headline: Public endorsement of Governor Hughes
summary: Roosevelt issues a press statement backing Charles Evans Hughes for another term as New York governor, then spends the evening at Matinecock Lodge. He tells Arthur Lee that the gift painting hangs in the North Room for lack of a better place.

headline: Fisheries and Africa in a letter to Reid
summary: The LaFarges are still Sagamore Hill guests. Roosevelt writes Whitelaw Reid about the Newfoundland fisheries dispute and his coming African trip.

headline: Bishop Brent and the press at lunch
summary: Immigration commissioner Frank P. Sargent dies. John Sleicher and Henry Wise call, and Roosevelt's lunch table includes Bishop Charles Brent, correspondent Richard Oulahan and Hamilton Fish; Major Wadsworth stays overnight.

headline: Bryan's jab at DuPont
summary: With Major Wadsworth still at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt warns Taft that Bryan is using DuPont's role to paint Republicans as the party of trusts. He also writes Sherman about labor and Root about the campaigns and extraditing Russian Jews.

headline: Hearing Dr. Fox preach
summary: Roosevelt attends the Presbyterian church to hear a sermon by Dr. Fox.

headline: The Dalai Lama and the fleet in Australia
summary: Frank Kellogg comes to lunch. Roosevelt tells Ambassador Bryce about Tibet and the splendid welcome the American fleet received in Australia, and writes William Rockhill about his meeting with the Dalai Lama.

headline: Better housing for Washington's alleys
summary: Roosevelt receives a string of local and political visitors and writes Charles Welles about improving housing in Washington's overlooked neighborhoods.

headline: Taft and he share the same views
summary: In a letter meant for the record, Roosevelt tells Conrad Kohrs that Taft and he see eye to eye on the national interest. He also lists his accomplishments for William B. McKinley, discusses Jack London and animal intelligence with Mark Sullivan, and writes Lodge about canal supply ships.

headline: Choosing a shotgun for Africa
summary: After a big lunch whose guests include William Loeb, Paul Morton, Bonaparte and Medill McCormick, Roosevelt tells gunmaker A. H. Fox he will bring a 12-bore to Africa. Other letters touch on farm schools, Speck von Sternberg's death and lies told about Grover Cleveland.

headline: Hit them hard, old man
summary: Roosevelt urges Taft to go after Bryan's record and keep smiling while he does it. He also writes Henry Needham about endorsing Republican congressmen for reelection.

headline: Stagecoach holdups in Yellowstone
summary: A Pall Mall Gazette writer named Dawbarn calls. Roosevelt tells Selous he hopes to see him on safari, and writes General Samuel Young about a string of stagecoach robberies in Yellowstone; he will later propose civilian park rangers.

headline: Ted turns 21
summary: Ted reaches his 21st birthday. Working as a mill hand in Connecticut and eager to make money quickly before entering politics, he had declined to join the African trip. His father gives him $1,000.

headline: Winchesters arrive for the safari
summary: Roosevelt meets Root and Cocks and wires Root at the Saratoga convention as he works to quiet resistance to Hughes. He tells Kermit the Winchester rifles have come and he will try them tomorrow, and describes Ted's birthday picnic on Jayne's Hill.

headline: Hughes renominated; Tumacacori protected
summary: Tumacacori National Monument in Arizona is proclaimed and Florida's Pine Island becomes a bird reservation, while New York Republicans renominate Governor Hughes. Roosevelt writes Metcalf about battleships carrying 14-inch guns and tells General Young that Yellowstone needs civilian rangers.

headline: McBee calls
summary: Silas McBee pays a call at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Oyster Bay neighbors and German singers
summary: Roosevelt hosts his Oyster Bay neighbors at a reception, hears a German singing society from Hicksville, and lunches with Collier's editors Mark Sullivan and Norman Hapgood. He teases Spring-Rice for fretting about his safety in Africa, admits he would have liked to stay President, and praises Root's work at Saratoga.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Foraker's Standard Oil letters surface
summary: Roosevelt's essay on Taft's candidacy appears in The Outlook. He lunches with Lord Bryce and Mrs. Brown, and wires Taft twice after Hearst publishes letters showing Standard Oil payments to Senator Foraker, which ended Foraker's career.

headline: Archie Butt back from Europe
summary: After two months of European leave, Archie Butt is back in Washington.

headline: Wishing Taft would hit harder
summary: Roosevelt meets Woodruff and Congressman Augustus Gardner, cuts Foraker loose, and confides to Bamie that he wishes Taft would smash into Bryan. He insists campaign money must not come from the trusts and compliments Nick Longworth on a speech.

headline: Back to Washington for the season
summary: Roosevelt reaches Washington at 6 p.m., ending his summer at Sagamore Hill. He writes Lyman and Lawrence Abbott about Foraker.

headline: Answering Bryan in the papers
summary: Roosevelt has no time for Archie Butt while he drafts a reply to a Bryan telegram published in the newspapers, tying Governor Haskell and Foraker to shady money. He demands DuPont's resignation from the campaign, sees Ballinger, Bonaparte and others, and receives the International Fisheries Congress.

headline: An old trolley injury still aches
summary: Roosevelt talks West Virginia and Ohio politics and sees Archie Butt at five, mentioning that his leg still hurts from the 1902 trolley crash. He and Edith go to the National Theater. A letter from Quentin reveals he is being hazed at boarding school.

headline: DuPont steps down
summary: Coleman du Pont resigns from the campaign. Roosevelt holds Cabinet, discusses Illinois politics, and welcomes Gifford Pinchot and the members of the farm-life commission. He asks Selous to make sure only he and Kermit will be shooting on the expedition.

headline: New coins and two Florida bird refuges
summary: Roosevelt talks New York politics, immigration and the design of new coins, and sees Admiral Dewey. Matlacha Pass and Palma Sola in Florida become bird reservations. He wires Lawrence Abbott to come to Washington about evidence against Oklahoma Governor Haskell, while Edith fixes up Quentin's school room in Alexandria.

headline: Drafting the reply to Bryan
summary: On Corinne's 47th birthday, Lawrence Abbott meets Roosevelt in the morning; Abbott later wrote of how Roosevelt composed his Bryan letter and talked of Cabinet choices. Roosevelt sends Bryan his published answer.

headline: Quentin comes home from boarding school
summary: Quentin, hazed without mercy at boarding school, is sent home sick. Roosevelt talks tariff with Senator Burrows and impresses Archie Butt with his deft handling of Ambassador Aoki. His public exchange with Bryan comes to an end.

headline: Standard Oil before the Cabinet
summary: The Cabinet takes up the Standard Oil cases. Roosevelt sits for a photograph by Ward, dines with Mrs. Taft, Bacon, and the Corbins, and goes with Edith to the Columbia Theater. Quentin writes Archie that the older boys forced cigarettes on him and made him box a much bigger boy.

headline: Missing Fitzhugh Lee
summary: Callers include John Hays Hammond, Fletcher Maddox and the portrait painter C. A. Whipple. Roosevelt writes Sherman about grumbling from state committees and tells Fitzhugh Lee how much the family misses him, with news of the four boys.

headline: Taking on the Democratic platform
summary: The surviving fragment for this date covers the campaign's issues: Democrats want federally guaranteed bank deposits, caps on corporate size and Philippine independence. Roosevelt calls the size limits unworkable and independence premature.

headline: Quentin becomes a day boy
summary: After his rough start as a boarder, Quentin returns to Episcopal High School as a day student and happily lives at the White House. Roosevelt confers with Ray Stannard Baker on race and Goethals on the canal, wins three sets of tennis, and has Alice to tea. Ted starts at the carpet company.

headline: Speech to the Tuberculosis Congress
summary: Roosevelt addresses the International Congress on Tuberculosis and talks labor with railroad union leaders Patrick Morrissey and Warren Stone. He writes Kermit about his Harvard courses and reading Greek.

headline: Sunday in Washington
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; nothing else is recorded.

headline: An evening at The Melting Pot
summary: Roosevelt and Edith see Israel Zangwill's play The Melting Pot. Earlier he meets Bonaparte and Governor Comer about railroad injunctions, and in letters he discusses Taft's candidacy, a poorly run government sanitarium, early popular Senate elections, and socialism in Denmark.

headline: Refusing to send Pouren to Russia
summary: Roosevelt tells Root he wants the extradition of Jan Pouren to Russia denied, and writes Lawrence Abbott about Black appointments and Taft's attitude. After Cabinet and lunch with George Sheldon, he spends the evening with Root, Cortelyou and others mapping the New York fight.

headline: A heated lunch with Israel Zangwill
summary: Roosevelt hosts a White House luncheon for Israel Zangwill, author of The Melting Pot, and the two argue long and hard. Later he meets the Austro-Hungarian ambassador, Prince Hatzfeldt and Dr. Koch, plays tennis, takes tea with the Jusserands and dines at the Straus home.

headline: Tea-table talk of Alice in Wonderland
summary: Roosevelt invites himself to lunch at Archie Butt's next Tuesday. George Hamlin sings at the White House. On the court, Jusserand and Meyer beat Roosevelt and Phillips, and over tea the group talks about Alice in Wonderland.

headline: The labor vote and the fleet
summary: The Cabinet discusses the fleet's voyage and Army appointments, and James B. Reynolds briefs Roosevelt on the labor vote. He lunches with Silas McBee and John Mott. In Newfoundland, voters reject British policy on the fisheries.

headline: Falling into Rock Creek
summary: On Kermit's birthday Roosevelt takes Archie Butt on a hard afternoon scramble in Rock Creek Park, tumbling into the creek along the way. They swim, climb and talk of George Washington, and Roosevelt names Poe the best American writer. He writes Sherman about religious bigotry aimed at Taft.

headline: Eleanor Roosevelt turns 24
summary: It is the 24th birthday of Roosevelt's niece Eleanor. Nothing else is recorded.

headline: A message to Russia's young men
summary: Roosevelt sees his tailor, receives the Supreme Court, and dines with Bacon; Justice Moody and Dr. Lambert are overnight guests. He sends John Mott a message for young Russian men and praises Taft while condemning anti-Catholic attacks on him.

headline: Lunch at Archie Butt's house
summary: Roosevelt pays Archie Butt the rare compliment of lunching at his home, with Edith, Belle Hagner, McCoy, Cheney and Phillips, while detectives ring the house. The meal runs from cantaloupe to peach ice cream, and Phillips finds spurs in his soup with a mock knighthood. Roosevelt stays past three and has a fine time.

headline: Northcliffe at the White House
summary: Lord and Lady Northcliffe join a large lunch at the White House. Roosevelt goes over the New York race with Mark Sullivan and writes Governor Hughes praising his campaign.

headline: Zangwill trims the lines he disliked
summary: Roosevelt thanks Israel Zangwill for cutting the divorce lines in The Melting Pot that had offended him. He confers with Garfield, Pinchot and Straus, lunches with Lord Northcliffe and rides. Edith tells Archie Butt she is uneasy about his attending the open-air play on the White House grounds.

headline: Players on the White House lawn
summary: Edith's children's playground charity opens the White House grounds to the Ben Greet Players, and Roosevelt watches part of the open-air show. Garfield, Spreckels and Greet join him for lunch. He lashes Governor Haskell in a letter and accepts General Young's resignation as Yellowstone superintendent.

headline: Welcoming the players on a hot day
summary: In unseasonable heat the Ben Greet company performs "Pandora's Box" and "Midas" on the White House grounds, and Roosevelt gives a short welcome. He writes Kermit that Quentin has sold one of his pigs to an animal dealer, and discusses the Kaiser's insulting remarks about England with Henry White and Arthur Lee.

headline: Taft back from the South
summary: Taft returns from a Southern campaign swing unsure of the region's vote, and spends the day with Roosevelt over breakfast, lunch and a working dinner. Root, Knox, Moody and Loeb join the lunch, and Roosevelt goes to All Souls' Church. It is nephew Sheffield Cowles's 10th birthday.

headline: Dutch nursery rhymes for a diplomat
summary: On a hot day Roosevelt receives the Dutch and Honduran envoys, singing the Dutch envoy nursery rhymes he learned as a child. He also greets survivors of a Vermont Civil War regiment, plays tennis, and goes to the National Theater with Edith.

headline: Portrait and lecture at once
summary: While Joseph DeCamp paints his portrait, Roosevelt dictates his Oxford Romanes Lecture at the same sitting. He hosts a Cabinet dinner with the Meyers, Lord and Lady Rodd, Root and the Bacons, and tells Kermit about a quiet campaign against Taft's Unitarian faith.

headline: Morning walk in the garden with Edith
summary: After his 8 a.m. breakfast Roosevelt strolls the garden with Edith until a quarter to ten, then talks safari preparations with Archie Butt. Charles Freer and Root are among the lunch guests. He writes Senator Knox, in a letter soon published, comparing Taft's and Bryan's records on labor.

headline: A note to Kenneth Grahame
summary: Roosevelt discusses Indiana politics with Lieutenant Governor Miller, lunches with R. P. Perkins and rides. He tells Kenneth Grahame he will enjoy his book.

headline: Cheering the fleet's welcome in Australia
summary: The Cabinet takes up Ohio politics, and a new Florida bird reservation is created. Roosevelt congratulates Admiral John Pillsbury on how well the fleet's cruise is going and on its Australian welcome.

headline: The election is absolutely assured
summary: Roosevelt plans the African trip with J. C. Hartsell and C. Hart Merriam, and his Outlook article on American attitudes toward the Philippines appears. He tells Kermit the campaign is improving and assures Taft that victory is certain.

headline: A Sunday with Winthrop Chanler
summary: Roosevelt spends the day with his friend Winthrop Chanler.

headline: Army machine guns and a Wyoming refuge
summary: Roosevelt discusses New Jersey politics with Representative Parker and the Army's machine gun service with General Bell. Evangelist Gipsy Smith and Ambassador Aoki call. Loch Katrine in Wyoming becomes a bird reservation.

headline: Fifty, and over every jump
summary: Roosevelt marks his 50th birthday by riding his horse Roswell over every jump in Rock Creek Park. The Hungarian Republican Club calls with birthday wishes, and he urges Taft to speak out on labor.

headline: Not slowing down at 50
summary: The Great White Fleet reaches Japan. Roosevelt walks for exercise, tells Frederic Remington he has no plans to slow down at 50, and thanks Alice for her birthday wishes.

headline: Memorial for Speck von Sternberg
summary: Roosevelt attends memorial services for his late friend, Ambassador Speck von Sternberg. Earlier he discusses Ohio politics with Meyer and meets with Bonaparte, Representative Dwight and the painter DeCamp, among others.

headline: Confident of Taft's election
summary: After Cabinet and a meeting with Jusserand, Roosevelt assures John Pringle he expects Taft to win. He writes William Dudley Foulke about newspaper falsehoods claiming he took tainted money in 1904 and abetted corruption in Panama.

headline: Art store, oil cases, and talks with Japan
summary: Roosevelt stops at Fisher's art store after breakfast and goes over the Standard Oil prosecutions with Frank Kellogg. Talks go on toward what becomes the Root-Takahira Agreement, under which the United States and Japan pledge to respect each other's Pacific holdings.

headline: No to the Catholic Encyclopedia
summary: Frank Kellogg calls. Archie Butt is back in the capital, having buried his mother. Roosevelt declines Charles Bodkin's offer of a Catholic Encyclopedia subscription.

headline: Night train home to vote
summary: Roosevelt works on his Annual Message and plays tennis with Jusserand, while Edith and Archie Butt cruise the Potomac on the Sylph and take a launch to Pohick Church. At 10:30 that night he and Edith board a train for Oyster Bay to vote.

headline: Taft wins: beaten to a frazzle
summary: Roosevelt casts his ballot in Oyster Bay as Taft defeats Bryan, 321 electoral votes to 162, to become the 27th President. Back at the White House by six, he lets an election-night party run until 12:30 while he reads upstairs. Alice and Nick spend the evening at Taft's side in Cincinnati.

headline: A medal for the Cuban occupation
summary: Roosevelt authorizes a campaign medal for service in the occupation of Cuba. Luke Wright calls. He writes Taft about Catholic missionaries to Native Americans, backs a pension for Frances Cleveland, and sends J. C. Martin a letter on religious tolerance.

headline: Radiant over Taft's victory
summary: Archie Butt finds Roosevelt glowing over Taft's win. After talking trusts with Bonaparte, he rides with Butt, Roosevelt on Audrey and Butt on Georgia, then plays tennis at 3:30.

headline: No President has enjoyed it more
summary: Roosevelt tells E. S. Martin that no President has had a better time in office, though he will miss the levers of power a little. He compares British and American elections with Bryce, sees Aldrich on the tariff and Goethals on the canal, and talks Africa that evening with Sir Harry Johnston, his overnight guest.

headline: Signing on with The Outlook
summary: It is announced that Roosevelt will join The Outlook as a contributing editor from March 5, 1909. He confers with Payne on the tariff and Cameron Forbes on the Philippines, walks in Rock Creek Park, and watches Archie Butt stumble through the introductions at a diplomatic tea.

headline: A purposeful tumble into Rock Creek
summary: Ambassador Bryce calls, and Liberty Hyde Bailey, Gifford Pinchot, Beekman Winthrop and John Graham Brooks come to dinner. Roosevelt writes Archie that Quentin is thriving at school and recounts a spill into Rock Creek during a climb; Butt believed the fall was deliberate, to make the out-of-shape officers follow.

headline: Arizona returns and a farm-life letter
summary: Roosevelt's callers range from Representatives Dalzell and Hull to former Interior Secretary Ethan Hitchcock and the Cuban minister Quesada. After afternoon tennis he writes about Arizona's election, Grover Cleveland, and the Country Life Commission.

headline: Congratulating President-elect Taft
summary: Roosevelt writes Taft his congratulations, along with thoughts on the House revolt against Speaker Cannon and Thomas Platt's exit from the Senate. He also writes Harriet Taylor Upton on votes for women, talks tariff with Senator Cullom, and sees Wanamaker and Bourke Cockran.

headline: Howard Pyle sketches the lunch table
summary: At a big White House luncheon with the incoming Vice President, James Sherman, plus the Bryces, Seth Low and others, the illustrator Howard Pyle draws the guests and gives the sketches to Alice. Mrs. Bryce takes Roosevelt to task over his religious tolerance letter. He writes Kermit comparing the American and Japanese navies.

headline: Tariff talk with Representative Weeks
summary: Roosevelt discusses the tariff with Representative Weeks and receives Justice McKenna, diplomat Henry White, editor Albert Shaw and other callers before riding.

headline: Writing on race and the Indianola affair
summary: After Cabinet, Admiral Evans calls and Roosevelt plays tennis. He writes John Brooks about the rights of Black Southerners, appointments and the Indianola post office case, and John O'Laughlin about relations with Japan.

headline: Speaking at Quentin's school
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Episcopal High School in Alexandria, Quentin's school, and later hosts a big dinner with Major Edgar Mearns and Percy Madeira to discuss Africa. Truman Newberry is named Secretary of the Navy as of December 1, and Taft spends the night.

headline: Sunday with Root and Taft
summary: Roosevelt meets and lunches with Root while Taft remains a White House guest. He takes a walk and writes Alvin Sanders about revising the tariff.

headline: Hearst at 9:30; China's rulers dead
summary: William Randolph Hearst and Chauncey Depew call, and word arrives that China's Emperor and Empress Dowager have died; Roosevelt sends condolences. Preoccupied with Congress, he plays tennis in silence. Letters defend Black appointments, praise Cleveland and discuss H. G. Wells.

headline: Dinner for labor leaders
summary: Roosevelt hosts a dinner for labor leaders including Terence Powderly, P. H. Morrissey and Warren Stone, joined by Justice Holmes, Straus, Pinchot, General Wood and the Abbotts. He also discusses the tariff with Senator McCumber and rides.

headline: Ethel in grown-up clothes
summary: Roosevelt lunches with the Abbotts and Robert Bridges of The Outlook, which he will join under contract next March. Ethel appears in grown-up dress and Archie Butt finds her charming. Roosevelt discusses postal savings with Senator Carter and spends the evening on safari plans with Cecil Lyon.

headline: Quentin turns 11
summary: On Quentin's 11th birthday, Roosevelt jokes with Root and Archie Butt about special yellow Army underwear as a jab at timid leadership in the Army's upper ranks. He and Edith laugh over the Reichstag's rebuke of the Kaiser. He writes Gilder proposing Howe's battle hymn as national anthem.

headline: Carl Akeley on Africa; Leech asked to resign
summary: Roosevelt plans the safari with naturalist Carl Akeley, talks Ellis Island with Straus, and takes Edith to hear a concert at the National. He asks Public Printer John Leech to resign and writes Ted about the Kaiser and women's suffrage.

headline: A damaged Gilbert Stuart Washington
summary: As Edith oversees a top-to-bottom cleaning of the White House, serious damage turns up on Gilbert Stuart's famous Washington portrait, and she sends it out for restoration. Roosevelt lunches with Akeley, Merriam and Pinchot, plays tennis, and confers with Lodge that evening.

headline: A rose for his buttonhole
summary: Edith pins a rose in Roosevelt's buttonhole before their morning walk. He writes Archie that Quentin's leg is in a cast, and tells Kermit he has sought safari advice from Carl Akeley and Colonel Patterson and has written both his Romanes Lecture and a Sorbonne address the French government requested for 1910.

headline: Tribute to Eliot of Harvard
summary: Roosevelt writes Harvard's Charles W. Eliot on his retirement after forty years as president. He discusses the tariff with Representative Tawney, sees Vice President Fairbanks and Lodge, plays tennis, and writes about Panama supply ships and civil service reform.

headline: National Forests in Florida and North Dakota
summary: The Ocala National Forest in Florida and the Dakota National Forest in North Dakota are created. Lincoln Steffens calls at 12:45. Roosevelt writes John Loomis about the books he wants to take to Africa.

headline: Borglum's Sheridan statue unveiled
summary: Roosevelt lunches with sculptor Gutzon Borglum on the day Borglum's statue of General Sheridan is unveiled. Booker T. Washington calls, Speaker Cannon and Senator Aldrich stop in, and Roosevelt writes Bryce about charges of American misbehavior at the Olympics. It is Bamie's 13th wedding anniversary.

headline: Thanksgiving: a 25-pound turkey and a new YMCA
summary: With Archie Butt and William Loeb, Roosevelt helps dedicate a new YMCA building for young Black men. Quentin, out of his cast, roller-skates and plays football with friends, and the family sits down to a 25-pound turkey and roast pig with the Longworths and Willard Straight. Judge Kenesaw Mountain Landis and Ambassador Bryce call.

headline: Receiving the diplomatic corps
summary: Choctawhatchee National Forest is created in Florida, and Roosevelt holds the White House reception for the diplomatic corps. Between tariff talks and tennis, he writes Franklin K. Lane on railroad rates and Leonard Wood with praise for his work in Cuba.

headline: The Awakening of China in The Outlook
summary: Roosevelt's article on the awakening of China appears in The Outlook. He discusses with Lucius Littauer the New York Senate seat Platt is leaving, and sees Charles P. Taft and Senator Penrose.

headline: Panama supply ships
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday on letters, writing Taft and Luke Wright about the two canal supply vessels and Chauncey Depew about Satterlee for Assistant Secretary of the Navy.

headline: Quentin bags three rabbits
summary: Out hunting with Dr. Rixey, Quentin brings down three rabbits. Roosevelt confers with Root and several senators, and his essay "Christmas Dinner on a Ranch" appears in Everybody's Magazine. Taft's plan to replace the White House ushers with liveried servants dismays Edith.

headline: A Navy shake-up and an embassy from China
summary: Roosevelt's Cabinet names Truman Newberry to lead the Navy in place of Victor Metcalf. Roosevelt attends a jubilee high mass for Austria's emperor at St. Patrick's, tours the Corcoran, shares lunch with Mark Sullivan and Minot Weld, then greets a special Chinese embassy, bristling once more at the title "excellency."

headline: Twenty-two years married
summary: Roosevelt and Edith mark their 22nd wedding anniversary. He confers with Hepburn, Root and Woodruff, rides in the afternoon, and tells the Associated Press's Melville Stone he will have no reporters trailing him in Africa.

headline: Wolf-catching film at the White House
summary: Roosevelt screens kinetoscope film of Oklahoma marshal John Abernathy seizing a live wolf barehanded, a show Edith skips and disapproves of. The Chinese ambassador gives Alice jade bracelets from the Empress, and Roosevelt hears from Bryce and from his lawyers on the Anaconda Copper case.

headline: Congressional dinner with family at the table
summary: After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt lunches with Caspar Whitney and rides. About 80 sit down to a congressional dinner, Bamie and Corinne among them, where one hostile congressman is heard wishing the African lions luck.

headline: Hashing out the Anaconda smelter dispute
summary: Roosevelt gathers Hoyt, Pinchot, Lodge and Montana men to sort out the Anaconda Copper quarrel, then receives Lord Northcote, Bryce and a string of senators. In letters he forgives William Garrott Brown and asks Admiral Sperry about keeping the fleet in battle gray.

headline: A Sunday evening caller
summary: Roosevelt's one recorded appointment is a 6 p.m. visit from New York Republican leader William Barnes Jr.

headline: Congress returns and the President is cross
summary: As the 60th Congress opens its second session, Roosevelt is out of sorts, sees Dr. Lambert, and fumes at the press, the New York Sun above all. He confers on Oklahoma land frauds, proclaims Wheeler National Monument in Colorado, and ends the night at the Saint-Gaudens show.

headline: A fighting last annual message
summary: Roosevelt's final annual message lands on Capitol Hill, restating his ignored proposals more sharply and scolding Congress for curbing the Secret Service, a blow that ends what goodwill was left. He addresses a conservation meeting, is stung by a New York World editorial on Panama, and hosts a dinner capped by the wolf pictures.

headline: Deciding to sue Pulitzer for libel
summary: Roosevelt tells Henry Stimson he will take the New York World and its owner, Joseph Pulitzer, to court for libel. He and Taft attend the governors' meeting at the Belasco, and he gets in a tennis match with Meyer, Winthrop and Jusserand, while Archie Butt persuades the Tafts to keep Edith's favorite ushers.

headline: A quiet lunch for the President-elect
summary: Roosevelt confers on the canal with H. W. Farnham and on appointments with Scott and Elkins, then gives Taft a small informal luncheon. He sends Taft his views on who deserves federal posts.

headline: Opera night with Edith
summary: After the Cabinet session and a walk, Roosevelt dines with the Earl of Warwick, takes Edith to the opera at the Belasco, and talks with Taft late in the evening.

headline: Eye exam, then two club dinners
summary: Roosevelt works through appointments with a parade of senators and lunches with Taft and Root. Dr. Rixey checks his eyes, and that night he goes to the Gridiron Club's dinner as well as the Boone and Crockett Club's.

headline: Sending Taft to inspect the Gatun Dam
summary: Roosevelt receives the Chinese ambassador and stops by the Corcoran. He writes Colonel Goethals that Taft and a team of engineers will go to Panama to inspect the Gatun Dam and answer the canal's critics.

headline: Brownsville report goes to Congress
summary: Congress receives the Brownsville report. Roosevelt spends the afternoon on the tennis court with Garfield, Pinchot and his son Ted.

headline: Answering the Panama critics, then tennis
summary: Roosevelt sends Congress a message rebutting newspaper lies about the Panama Canal contracts. He and Meyer beat Jusserand and Archie Butt three sets of four, Taft barges into tea with whisky distillers, and he speaks that night at the Saint-Gaudens memorial meeting.

headline: Planning the safari with Walcott
summary: Roosevelt talks over the African expedition with the Smithsonian's Charles D. Walcott, goes over patronage with three congressmen, and rides. He writes Ted advising him against joining the governor's staff.

headline: A state dinner he would rather skip
summary: Roosevelt sends Congress a message on governing the District of Columbia and talks with Wright about Foraker's push to investigate the Secret Service. He lunches with both Taft brothers, walks, and endures a Cabinet dinner, the kind of formal state affair he heartily disliked.

headline: Bison, not lions, for the mantel
summary: The Cabinet takes up the Foraker resolution, and Roosevelt lunches with illustrator Howard Pyle and Pinchot. His essay "Lessons From China" appears in Science, and he asks architect William Kendall to swap the State Dining Room's lion heads for American bison carved in stone.

headline: Protecting the restored White House
summary: Roosevelt gets in tennis with Pinchot, Garfield and Jusserand and dines with the Vice President and his wife. He writes Cass Gilbert asking that the newly restored White House be guarded against change.

headline: Looking back on the presidency
summary: On a Sunday, Roosevelt meets newsman Oscar King Davis and writes his friend Arthur Lee that he has largely accomplished what he set out to do in office.

headline: Introducing Taft to Horace Plunkett
summary: Roosevelt receives Irish farm reformer Sir Horace Plunkett, plus China's envoy and Representative Bates. He thanks Henry Fairfield Osborn for his review of the Oxford Romanes Lecture, and asks Taft to meet Plunkett and to send biographical notes for a sketch TR is writing for the inaugural book.

headline: Lunch with Plunkett and Pinchot
summary: Roosevelt shares lunch with Sir Horace Plunkett and Gifford Pinchot, and sits down with Senator Lodge at 9 p.m.

headline: Country Life Commission meets
summary: The Country Life Commission convenes at the White House, and Roosevelt confers with Knox and sees Heney. At lunch are his sister Bamie with her husband Will, Whitelaw Reid, Newberry, Bacon and the Harringtons.

headline: Safari talk with Major Mearns
summary: On Christmas Eve Roosevelt goes over the African expedition with Army surgeon and naturalist Edgar Mearns. At lunch are Knox, Joseph Alsop, and the Heney, Garfield and Cowles couples, and he invites Canada's Wilfrid Laurier to the coming conservation conference.

headline: Last White House Christmas
summary: Photographers Harris and Ewing pose the Roosevelts on the South Portico, and more than 50 relatives and friends, Lodges and Longworths included, gather for Roosevelt's final Christmas dinner as President. Afterward everyone heads downstairs to the tree in the crypt to swap presents.

headline: Selous will join the safari
summary: Roosevelt confers on Indian land frauds and immigration work and greets a run of callers. He cheers the news that hunter Frederick Selous will go to East Africa, sends the Kaiser New Year greetings, and asks Root to vet his speech on British rule in India.

headline: Sunday with nothing recorded
summary: The chronology lists Roosevelt in Washington with no events noted for the day.

headline: Ethel's debut in the White House
summary: Ethel makes her debut before 440 guests on the White House ground floor. Earlier Roosevelt confers on Alaska with Governor Hoggatt and greets New York musicians. Alice, back from Boston, mourns the coming end of the Roosevelt years, and Ted meets Eleanor Alexander socially for a second time.

headline: Big guns and Indian rights
summary: After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt lunches with Ambassador Bryce, Justice Holmes and Lodge, then rides. His letters range from a government job for his secretary William Loeb to naval gun sizes, battleship design and the rights of American Indians.

headline: Germany's new ambassador presented
summary: Count von Bernstorff presents his credentials as Germany's new ambassador. Roosevelt confers on the savings bank bill, sees Underwood and Jusserand, stops in at the Navy Department, and dines with humorist Finley Peter Dunne.

headline: Testing rifles for Africa
summary: Roosevelt spends the last morning of 1908 trying out rifles for the safari, then heads out to his physician Rixey's farm by Cherrydale in Virginia. He writes Taft that Taft never wrote the Serbian women the press claims he did.

headline: Shaking 6,665 hands on New Year's Day
summary: Roosevelt greets 6,665 people at his final New Year's reception, and the receiving line runs so long that he, Edith, Archie Butt and Bromwell miss lunch until 3 p.m. He writes Taft about his maneuvering to send Burton, not Foraker, to the Senate from Ohio.

headline: Planning help for quake-stricken Italy
summary: Roosevelt gathers Cabinet officers and congressmen to arrange American relief after the Messina earthquake. Major Mearns and a stream of officials call, and he writes the Kaiser on Speck von Sternberg, a possible Berlin speech, the fleet and China.

headline: Sunday with nothing recorded
summary: The chronology places Roosevelt in Washington but notes no events.

headline: Messages on the Secret Service and Italian relief
summary: Roosevelt sends Congress a special message defending the Secret Service and another seeking aid for earthquake-stricken Italy, then receives a long line of lawmakers. Taft agrees to put William Loeb in charge of the New York customs house as collector.

headline: A luncheon full of Ethel's friends
summary: After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt hosts some 30 at lunch, among them Owen Wister and his family and a daughter of J. P. Morgan, most of them Ethel's society friends. That evening he and Edith dine at the Roots'.

headline: Praising Churchill's book, not the man
summary: Roosevelt sends Congress a message on the Tennessee Coal and Iron Company. China's ambassador, now out of favor at home, dines with him alongside Mrs. Beale and the Lodges, and Roosevelt writes Winston Churchill to praise My African Journey, though he heartily disliked its author.

headline: Franklin and Eleanor at the White House
summary: Land fraud charges against Senator Tillman go public. Roosevelt holds a reception for 350, Bamie regales Archie Butt with stories of their mother Mittie and Georgia, and Franklin and Eleanor Roosevelt are house guests.

headline: Dancing at Ethel's ball
summary: Roosevelt works through a Cabinet meeting and visits from senators and Speaker Cannon. That night a ball is given for Ethel, and he and Edith take the floor, his dancing marked by lively little hops.

headline: A day of callers
summary: Roosevelt receives a string of visitors, Cabinet members Meyer and Straus, Senator Lodge, his old Buffalo friend Ansley Wilcox and reformer William Dudley Foulke among them.

headline: Quentin earns a whipping
summary: Roosevelt writes Kermit about Ethel's ball and the safari rifles. To Archie he reports that Quentin came home with a cough after crashing through ice, slipping away from school and lying about it, and so got the first real whipping TR ever gave a child.

headline: Conservation Commission report arrives
summary: The National Conservation Commission hands Roosevelt its three-volume report, and he urges Congress to improve the capital's civic life. He attends a reception for senators at Fairbanks' home and writes Lyman Abbott on Governor Hughes's plan to change how candidates are nominated.

headline: Douglas Robinson to testify
summary: Roosevelt holds a Cabinet meeting and sees senators and congressmen, then is honored at a dinner given by Secretary Wright. He writes his brother-in-law Douglas Robinson, who will be a witness in the libel suits against the World and the Indianapolis News.

headline: The ninety-mile ride to Warrenton
summary: To prove his three-day, 90-mile riding test for officers is fair, Roosevelt leaves at 3 a.m. with his aide Butt, Dr. Rixey and naval surgeon Cary Grayson for Warrenton, Virginia, and back in one day. They push through sleet and reach Washington near 8 p.m., some 17 hours later; the distance was first put at 98 miles and later at 104.

headline: Labor leaders at the White House
summary: Roosevelt confers with Newberry on the Navy, meets the American Federation of Labor's executive council, and sees Senator Knox. After a diplomatic dinner he writes Kermit about his long ride and his battles with Congress.

headline: Admirals talk Navy reform
summary: Roosevelt hosts a working lunch on reorganizing the Navy Department with Admirals Mahan, Luce and Evans, Captain Sims and others. He also writes a letter of praise for Archie Butt's service record.

headline: Fighting California's anti-Japanese bills
summary: Roosevelt confers on the Navy with Senator Hale and receives a stream of callers. He fires off two telegrams to California Governor James Gillett, determined to stop anti-Japanese bills in the legislature, while Archie Butt quietly sorts out an awkward affair involving one diplomat's wife and another envoy.

headline: Sunday with nothing recorded
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; the chronology lists no events for the day.

headline: Praising British India to missionaries
summary: On Bamie's 54th birthday, Roosevelt addresses Methodist missionaries in the evening and commends Britain's rule in India. He tells painter Gari Melchers he loves the new portrait, which shows him dressed as he was for his long ride.

headline: Cabinet dinner at Bonaparte's
summary: Roosevelt holds a Cabinet meeting, sees Congressman Davidson and W. H. Phipps, and attends a Cabinet dinner at Attorney General Bonaparte's.

headline: A Council of Fine Arts and a Nevada forest
summary: By executive order Roosevelt sets up a national arts council, and Humboldt National Forest in Nevada is established. Knox, Senator Curtis and Mark Sullivan are among his visitors.

headline: The Japanese school question
summary: Roosevelt confers with Senators Flint and Fulton on California's treatment of Japanese schoolchildren, and Moapa National Forest in Nevada is created. He hosts the judicial reception and hears from Bryce that his India speech was well received.

headline: Conservation report goes to Congress
summary: Roosevelt sends Congress the National Conservation Commission's report with a special message, as the House passes the Navy bill. He enlists Andrew Carnegie and William Kent against California's anti-Japanese bill, seeks backing for ballad collector John Lomax, and stays for the dance after a 30-plus dinner.

headline: Teeth checked before Africa
summary: Roosevelt meets a California delegation on the Japanese school question, and his essay on national statesmen appears in The Outlook. He tells Kermit he is having his teeth seen to before the safari and asks Bay Lodge to critique his European address.

headline: Sunday with nothing recorded
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; no events are noted for the day.

headline: Edith rules out prize fights at dinner
summary: Roosevelt sees Fairbanks, Root, Bonaparte and others, plus a group of state dairy and food officials, and takes up the care of orphans in Washington. When boxing comes up at a formal dinner, Edith shuts the topic down, which she thought unfit for the table.

headline: Root resigns; Pelican Island grows
summary: Roosevelt accepts Elihu Root's resignation as Secretary of State, enlarges the Pelican Island bird reservation in Florida, and renames Cleveland National Forest. He sends Governor Gillett legal arguments against California's anti-Japanese bills and speaks at a dinner on the care of dependent children.

headline: Bacon takes over at State
summary: Robert Bacon replaces Elihu Root at the State Department; Root heads to the Senate in Platt's seat, and John Callan O'Laughlin becomes assistant secretary. Roosevelt names a commission to reorganize the Navy, Mahan among its members, and writes Taft denying he ever demanded the Cabinet be kept intact.

headline: Cuba handed back to Cubans
summary: Government of Cuba returns to Cuban hands, and Pecos National Forest in New Mexico is created. Roosevelt lunches with the Meyers, Alice and Mrs. Frederick Vanderbilt, dines with the Supreme Court, and writes Lodge disputing much in the newly published Letters of John Hay.

headline: Callers from La Follette to Hoggatt
summary: After the Cabinet meets, Roosevelt receives Senators La Follette and Borah, editor Albert Shaw and Alaska Governor Hoggatt, among others.

headline: Gridiron dinner, poker at Butt's
summary: Roosevelt sees Woodruff, Cortelyou, Pinchot and others and lunches with family, the Douglas Robinsons and George Sheldon. He spends the evening at the Gridiron Club dinner while Archie Butt hosts Alice and 18 others for poker.

headline: Packing up the White House
summary: As the household packs and Roosevelt hands out souvenirs, he writes Ted that he has worked to avoid an outright break with Congress and wires the AP that no reporters go to Africa. His essay "A Tribute to Lincoln" appears in the Review of Reviews, and Edith drops her wish to keep a White House sofa after a leaked request stirs a press outcry.

headline: Stopping by Holy Cross Academy
summary: Roosevelt sees Bacon, Pinchot, Beveridge and other callers, stops in at Holy Cross Academy, and Prescott National Forest in Arizona is created. He and Edith dine with the Lodges, and he writes Lawrence Abbott about Africa.

headline: Dinner at the Newberrys'
summary: Roosevelt and Edith dine at Navy Secretary Newberry's. He writes Senator Aldrich on the Brownsville resolution and Albert Shaw about a postmastership in Fremont.

headline: Hawaiian Islands bird refuge created
summary: Roosevelt sets aside the Hawaiian Islands Bird Reservation, a vast refuge for seabirds. A crowd of senators, editors and officials call, and he is troubled by the Nevada legislature's stance on a measure the record leaves unnamed.

headline: Up to his ears in work
summary: Roosevelt tells Selous he is buried in the last of his presidential work, wires Governor Gillett that California's anti-Japanese school bill must fail, and informs cousin William Roosevelt that on March 4 he will ride public transit like any private citizen.

headline: Vetoing the census bill
summary: Roosevelt vetoes the census bill. Indian Commissioner Leupp, Pinchot and Representative Sulzer are among the day's visitors, and he later meets with Bacon, Cummins and others.

headline: Alice slips off from Ethel's dance
summary: At a White House dance, Alice sneaks away to Archie Butt's house and throws a dinner party of her own. Roosevelt defends his census veto, praises Governor Gillett's handling of the Japanese school fight while grumbling about Senator Perkins, and wires California's assembly speaker.

headline: Selous gets a second white hunter
summary: Roosevelt writes Selous that he has cabled R. J. Cunninghame, the safari's professional hunter, to engage a second man. Other letters go to Secretary Wright about the Brownsville bill and Arthur Lee on his closing weeks in office.

headline: Lunch with Henry Adams
summary: Roosevelt confers with Bacon, O'Laughlin, Franklin Lane and two California lawmakers on the Japanese school question, and Calaveras Bigtree National Forest is declared to protect California's giant sequoias. He lunches with Henry Adams and writes Knox, Taft's coming Secretary of State, on foreign policy.

headline: Country Life report to Congress
summary: Roosevelt sends Congress the Country Life Commission's report on rural America, sees Speaker Cannon, Pinchot and Lodge, and dines with Edith at Secretary Garfield's.

headline: California backs down; four forests added
summary: Roosevelt congratulates Governor Gillett after the California Assembly defeats its anti-Japanese bill. Tonto, Marquette, Nevada and Dixie National Forests are created, and he tells George Turner the fleet he built now ranks behind only Britain's.

headline: Off to Kentucky for Lincoln
summary: After talking New Mexico statehood with Governor Curry and creating Michigan National Forest, Roosevelt leaves Washington at 11 a.m. for Kentucky with Edith, Ethel, Secretary Wright, Loeb and Dr. Rixey. He reads the whole way, with stops at Baltimore, Harrisburg and Altoona.

headline: Lincoln's centennial in Kentucky
summary: On the 100th anniversary of Abraham Lincoln's birth, Roosevelt speaks in Kentucky and sets the cornerstone for a memorial on the farm where Lincoln was born. Alice celebrates turning 25 far away in Grand Rapids, Michigan, where Nick is giving a speech.

headline: Back to Washington; Edith a little sad
summary: Roosevelt returns to Washington as Klamath and a Minnesota national forest are created. He writes Ted about the California school fight and his Lincoln speech, and Stimson about indicting Pulitzer, while Edith confides to Aunt Lizzie that she is a bit sad to leave the White House.

headline: Sunday with nothing recorded
summary: Roosevelt is in Washington; the chronology lists no events.

headline: Burning the "mewing cat" portrait
summary: Roosevelt sees Bacon, Knox, Aldrich and others, and several national forests in New Mexico and the Dakotas are created, Black Hills among them. Edith has Archie Butt burn a portrait the family mocked as the "mewing cat" and smash all the chipped presidential china, and TR goes to a church reception at Grace Reformed.

headline: Tafts back from Panama; lunch with the safari team
summary: The Tafts return from Panama, and Roosevelt confers with the President-elect. He lunches with members of his African expedition, sees Justice Holmes and Hamlin Garland, an Alaska forest is created, and he praises Garfield and Pinchot for their conservation work in letters meant as a foreword to their book.

headline: Taft's Panama report goes to Congress
summary: On Alice and Nick's third wedding anniversary, Roosevelt meets Taft and sends Capitol Hill Taft's findings from his canal inspection. Colonel Goethals is among his callers.

headline: North American Conservation Conference opens
summary: Roosevelt addresses the North American Conservation Conference, gathered at the White House to weigh the continent's natural resources, with Pinchot, Bacon and Garfield as the U.S. commissioners. The evening brings a reception and the Army and Navy dinner, and General Wood stays the night.

headline: Corinne's gift: the Pigskin Library
summary: As the conservation conference goes on, Secretary Bacon invites 45 nations to a world conservation meeting at The Hague, a plan that died after Roosevelt left office. TR thanks Corinne for the Pigskin Library, a set of his favorite books bound in tough pigskin for the safari, and trades thoughts on Jefferson and Hamilton with William Allen White.

headline: Starting work an hour earlier
summary: With the conservation conference still meeting, Roosevelt begins reaching his desk at 9 a.m., an hour earlier than before, and drops his morning walk. Toiyabe National Forest in Nevada is created; he lunches with Wright and Newberry and ends the day at a reception at Senator Depew's.

headline: Corinne's son Stewart dies
summary: Corinne's youngest boy, 21-year-old Stewart Robinson, falls to his death from a Harvard window, and Corinne is shattered. Roosevelt wires condolences to her and Douglas, then boards the Mayflower with Edith and Alice for Hampton Roads.

headline: The Great White Fleet comes home
summary: Sixteen months after it sailed, the Great White Fleet steams back into Hampton Roads, and Roosevelt reviews it from the Mayflower's deck as some 2,000 small boats look on. He later judged the voyage his greatest service to peace. In Washington the conservation conference closes with a call for an international meeting.

headline: Lining up the Outlook job
summary: After the Cabinet meets, Datil and Chugach National Forests are created and Roosevelt leaves that evening for New York. He writes Lawrence Abbott about the Outlook editorship he takes up March 5, and Taft about a push to keep Fowler as port collector, a job Taft had promised Loeb.

headline: Burying young Stewart Robinson
summary: In New York, Roosevelt, Edith, Ted and Kermit attend the funeral of Corinne's son Stewart Robinson, and TR heads back to Washington. He writes Pinchot in praise of Interior Secretary Garfield.

headline: Seventeen bird refuges in one day
summary: Roosevelt creates 17 bird reservations across the West, most of them on new irrigation reservoirs, plus Modoc, Ozark and California National Forests. The Naval Commission's report goes to Congress, and he writes Jusserand about John Lomax's cowboy ballads and denies the stories about his drinking.

headline: Maxim demonstrates a silent rifle
summary: Roosevelt sends Congress the North American Conservation Conference report. At a lunch for Admiral Sperry, inventor Hiram Percy Maxim shows off his new noiseless rifle. Edith writes Kermit that Corinne's grief is her own.

headline: Where to shoot an elephant
summary: Seth Bullock, Garfield and Pinchot are among a crowd of callers. Roosevelt proclaims Arkansas National Forest, the Fire Island game preserve in Alaska and seven bird reservations from the Bering Sea to Puerto Rico, and asks Carl Akeley where to aim at an elephant's head.

headline: The White House emptied
summary: Every Roosevelt belonging is now out of the White House, and Edith makes sure the rooms are spotless. Roosevelt makes plain he means to step aside fully, with no wish to cling to past power.

headline: Farewell lunch for the Tennis Cabinet
summary: Fortified by his usual eggs and rolls, with saccharin in the coffee, Roosevelt gives a farewell luncheon for 31 friends of his "tennis cabinet," some of them in tears, who present him with a bronze cougar by Alexander Phimister Proctor. He bids Congress goodbye, and he and Edith go on to teas and a dinner at Secretary Bacon's.

headline: Final Cabinet meeting and a burst of forests
summary: Roosevelt holds his last Cabinet meeting and greets Haiti's new minister at a full diplomatic reception. In a final sweep he proclaims Mount Olympus National Monument, thirteen national forests from Shasta to Sequoia, and the Bogoslof bird refuge in Alaska, then hosts 50 close friends and dines at the Strauses'.

headline: Last night in the White House
summary: The Tafts dine and stay overnight at the White House, a meal Taft later called "that funeral"; only Roosevelt seemed cheerful. He leaves Taft a parting warning never to split the battleship fleet between the oceans before the canal is done, and writes final notes of praise for Archie Butt, Garfield and Pinchot.

headline: Taft sworn in; home to Sagamore Hill
summary: A winter storm drives the inauguration indoors, and William Howard Taft takes the oath as the 27th President in the Senate Chamber. Skipping the customary ride back to the White House, Roosevelt and Edith head straight to Union Station with New York Republicans, bands playing "Auld Lang Syne," and return to Sagamore Hill. The National Bison Range is created.

headline: Contributing editor at The Outlook
summary: His first full day as a private citizen, Roosevelt officially joins The Outlook as an editor, contracted for twelve articles a year at $1,000 each.

headline: Why he backs The Outlook
summary: Roosevelt's essay explaining why he believes in the kind of journalism The Outlook stands for appears in the magazine.

headline: Not missing the presidency
summary: Writing to Archie, Roosevelt guesses Washington was sorry to see the family leave. He does not miss the White House or the office.

headline: Woodland walks with Edith
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge about rumors that Taft may remove Henry White as ambassador in Paris, and about the African trip ahead. He and Edith enjoy walks together in the Sagamore woods.

headline: Snow and a blazing fire
summary: Dictating by a roaring fire in the North Room with snow outside, Roosevelt tells Bamie his homecoming was a happy one and that Edith has recovered from readying the White House for the Tafts.

headline: First day at the Outlook office
summary: Roosevelt reports to The Outlook at 287 Fourth Avenue in New York, sets up his office, and at an editorial meeting proposes a piece on the government's case against the Sugar Trust. He writes Cecil Spring-Rice that he has had a great time as President.

headline: Henry Adams writes Edith
summary: Henry Adams writes Edith explaining why he could not bid her goodbye in person.

headline: Oyster Bay welcomes them home
summary: The people of Oyster Bay hold a reception for Roosevelt and Edith.

headline: Breakfast with Robert Collier
summary: Roosevelt goes into New York for a breakfast Robert Collier gives in his honor. Robert La Follette praises him in his weekly magazine, and an Outlook piece by TR drawing on judicial experience appears.

headline: A guest named Von Steiner
summary: The Sagamore Hill guest book records a visit from Von Steiner.

headline: Carrie Louise Munn signs the guest book
summary: Carrie Louise Munn is recorded as a guest at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Mail to Nairobi, then Khartoum
summary: Roosevelt writes Arthur Lee that he looks forward to seeing him in England in 1910, and gives his forwarding addresses for the long trip: Nairobi until November, then Khartoum.

headline: At Matinecock Lodge
summary: Roosevelt attends a meeting of Matinecock Lodge, his Masonic lodge in Oyster Bay.

headline: A new Roosevelt baby
summary: Franklin and Eleanor's son Franklin Jr. is born. Roosevelt receives the Nassau County delegation that attended the inauguration and writes Charles Amidor about flaws in the courts.

headline: At home, nothing recorded
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events are noted.

headline: Where he parts ways with socialists
summary: Alice visits Sagamore Hill, and The Outlook prints Roosevelt's essay on the points where he cannot work with socialists.

headline: Family gathering
summary: The family gathers at Sagamore Hill for a reunion before Roosevelt leaves for Africa.

headline: Inspecting the Hamburg
summary: In New York, Roosevelt visits Mame Ledwith, his children's old nurse, and the Theodore Douglas Robinsons, then crosses to Hoboken to look over the S.S. Hamburg, the ship that will carry him to Europe.

headline: Sailing for Africa
summary: At 11 a.m. Roosevelt and Kermit sail from Hoboken on the Hamburg amid a crush of well-wishers. He has signed with Scribner's for African articles at $50,000, thanks Taft for his farewell gift, and notes in his diary that he sailed. Edith, who thinks him too old for the venture, spends the rest of the day walking the Sagamore woods.

headline: At sea
summary: Roosevelt is aboard the Hamburg bound for Europe; nothing more is recorded.

headline: Shipboard company
summary: On the crossing, Roosevelt spends time with fellow passengers Emily Putnam and Ruth Dana Draper.

headline: Homesick for Edith
summary: Roosevelt thanks Corinne for the note she handed him at the pier, says he was touched by how many acquaintances came to see him off, and admits he is homesick for Edith.

headline: Two Outlook pieces in print
summary: The Outlook runs two Roosevelt essays, one on where he can work with socialists and one on his scientific expedition. He writes Bamie that he and Kermit are well apart from one queasy day, and that every American aboard has come to talk with him.

headline: At sea
summary: The Hamburg continues east; nothing else is recorded.

headline: At sea
summary: Another day on the Atlantic with no events noted.

headline: Ashore in the Azores
summary: The Hamburg stops at São Miguel in the Azores, and Roosevelt goes ashore at Ponta Delgada and Horta.

headline: Outfitting the safari
summary: As Roosevelt steams on, the record details his safari: about $75,000 in costs borne mainly by the Smithsonian, with Carnegie and other friends contributing; naturalists Mearns, Heller and Loring; hunters Cunninghame and Tarlton; and his khaki kit, rifles and Pigskin Library. At home Edith writes Kermit that only the children give her strength to bear the separation.

headline: At sea
summary: Roosevelt is still aboard the Hamburg; no events recorded.

headline: Landing at Gibraltar
summary: The ship puts in at Gibraltar, where Roosevelt calls on the governor, General Forestier-Walker.

headline: At sea
summary: The voyage continues; Cornelia Landon appears again in the Sagamore Hill guest book.

headline: At sea
summary: Another day at sea; cousin Nicholas Roosevelt is recorded as a guest at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Naples, and a new ship for Mombasa
summary: Edith's sister Emily Carow and cousin's wife Laura Roosevelt greet Roosevelt in Naples, and he visits the Aosta ducal couple at the Capodimonte Palace. He and Kermit then board the S.S. Admiral for Mombasa.

headline: Among Messina's ruins
summary: At Messina, Roosevelt meets King Victor Emmanuel III aboard an Italian battleship and walks through the wreckage of the great earthquake, a scene he calls terrible beyond words. Far to the north, Robert Peary's party arrives at the Pole that same day.

headline: At sea
summary: Roosevelt is aboard the Admiral; Edith sends Kermit a newsy letter.

headline: At sea
summary: The Admiral steams on; Roberto Centaro is recorded in the Sagamore Hill guest book.

headline: Welcomed at Port Said
summary: F. K. Watson greets Roosevelt at Port Said, and he dines with officials of the Suez Canal. Back home, Archie turns 15.

headline: Through the Suez Canal
summary: The Admiral passes through the Suez Canal while The Outlook prints Roosevelt's essay mocking political snake-oil remedies.

headline: Easter treats for Quentin
summary: On Easter, with Roosevelt at sea, Alice, Belle Hagner and Archie Butt motor out to Quentin's school in Alexandria with presents from Edith. Alice slips him two dollars despite family rules against extra gifts.

headline: Selous on board
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie that the Kaiser sent him flowers and that Frederick Selous is traveling on the same ship.

headline: Proud of Kermit at sea
summary: Roosevelt tells Corinne neither he nor Kermit enjoys sea voyages and that writer Francis Dawson will tag along. To Ethel he paints passengers straight out of Kipling and praises Kermit, who plays poker and bridge with young Englishmen and strums his mandolin.

headline: Port call at Aden
summary: The Admiral stops at Aden, which Roosevelt notes in his diary.

headline: At sea
summary: The voyage down the African coast continues; the Osborns and Evelyn Irving are recorded at Sagamore Hill.

headline: At sea
summary: Roosevelt is aboard the Admiral headed for Mombasa; no events recorded.

headline: At sea
summary: Roosevelt is aboard the Admiral headed for Mombasa; no events recorded.

headline: At sea
summary: Still at sea; Barclay H. Farr and Martha R. Phillips begin a stay at Sagamore Hill lasting through the 22nd.

headline: At sea
summary: Roosevelt is aboard the Admiral headed for Mombasa; no events recorded.

headline: Arrival in Mombasa
summary: The Admiral reaches Mombasa, where Lieutenant Governor Frederick Jackson welcomes Roosevelt and Kermit to Government House. After dinner at the Mombasa Club, TR notes a downpour in his diary.

headline: Riding the cowcatcher
summary: Roosevelt takes the train inland toward Kapiti Plains, riding with Selous on a seat rigged on the engine's cowcatcher. He takes in the tidy stations and the dress and ornament of the people along the line.

headline: A living zoological garden
summary: Riding the cowcatcher again through game country, Roosevelt and Selous see giraffes, waterbuck, hartebeest, zebras, impala and ostriches. At Kapiti Plains station the safari waits with its supplies and some 200 porters.

headline: First hunt in Africa
summary: Roosevelt and Kermit move from Kapiti Plains to Sir Alfred Pease's ranch as guests, and TR hunts in the afternoon and lists his bag. The camp sits on a bare, dry plain where all water must be boiled and ticks are a nuisance.

headline: A hartebeest bull
summary: Roosevelt rides to Pease Ranch and shoots a hartebeest bull, sketching each animal with the spot where his bullet struck. Riding out with Kermit, Sir Alfred and Hill, the party sets up camp and takes a Thomson's gazelle and three tick-covered wildebeest.

headline: Into the Kitanga hills
summary: A 16-mile ride brings the party into the Kitanga hills, country that reminds Roosevelt of Montana and Wyoming. He marvels at herdsmen with filed teeth and finds the Boers he meets know a Dutch nursery song from his boyhood.

headline: Kermit runs down a hyena
summary: Roosevelt calls it a blank day for himself, but Kermit, after a ten-mile chase on horseback, rides down and shoots a hyena.

headline: Field notes on hartebeest
summary: At Pease Ranch Roosevelt fills his diary with long descriptions and drawings of hartebeest and other game.

headline: Twelve hours afield with the Peases
summary: Roosevelt spends twelve hours out with Sir Alfred, Lady Pease and Miss Pease, and writes up a lion kill with drawings. At home it is Corinne's 27th wedding anniversary.

headline: Lunch with the McMillans and Selous
summary: The McMillans and Selous come to lunch at Pease Ranch, and Roosevelt spends time writing. In America a comic animated cartoon of his African arrival appears, and Alice's "night riders" are dropping in on Washington hosts at all hours demanding refreshments.

headline: Lion country in the Mua Hills
summary: Out after lions with Selous in the Mua Hills, Roosevelt drops a very old hartebeest bull for the camp pot but scolds himself for poor shooting, ten cartridges for four hits. He rides over to tea with Mrs. McMillan, and Sydney Brooks's essay on his record as President is published.

headline: Three lions in a day
summary: After a 13-hour hunt that ends in camp at Potha on the plain, Roosevelt records killing three lions, while Kermit shoots five cheetahs.

headline: A safari on the march
summary: Roosevelt shifts camp in the afternoon to a small pond at Bondini, shooting a warthog sow on the way, and delights in the safari's march with chanting, horns, whistles and drums.

headline: A blank day
summary: Roosevelt's hunt comes up empty; he watches the beaters knock over rabbits with throwing sticks and notes the wildlife.

headline: Missing everything at Kilimakiu
summary: On the march to Kilimakiu, Roosevelt misses a steenbok, an impala and a Grant's gazelle and calls it awful; Kermit does better, taking a hartebeest and a Grant's.

headline: Charged by a rhino
summary: Riding all day with Captain Slatter, Roosevelt kills an eland cow after long shots, then walks up on a rhino bull, hits it at 35 yards with his .450 Holland, and drops it at 14 paces as it charges. He later goes out with Heller and porters to the carcasses.

headline: A Chanler's reedbuck at last
summary: Out with Clifford and Harold Hill, Roosevelt misses a galloping giraffe at long range but, after poor shooting, kills a good male Chanler's reedbuck.

headline: A lion kills Slatter's horse
summary: Roosevelt misses a waterbuck bull and a wild dog, and records how a lion killed Captain Slatter's horse. His article on the Japanese question appears in The Outlook.

headline: Two giraffes
summary: Roosevelt kills two giraffes, one a medium bull dropped by a spine shot at 350 yards, and Kermit takes another.

headline: Skinning the giraffe
summary: The day goes to skinning the giraffes for the museum collection.

headline: Safari on the move
summary: The safari moves on toward Potha.

headline: First article for Scribner's
summary: Roosevelt heads to Machakos and spends the night at Sir Alfred Pease's. He writes Robert Bridges at Scribner's with his first African article and a plan for the series, though the letter waits until May 23 to go out.

headline: Visiting the American mission
summary: At Machakos, Roosevelt stops at the American mission, then rides to Juja Farm.

headline: Guest of William McMillan
summary: Roosevelt settles in at Juja Farm, William McMillan's home, and writes Quentin with safari news.

headline: Kermit's leopard mauls a bearer
summary: Roosevelt is out for hours before dawn; Kermit shoots a leopard that charges and mauls a gun bearer. TR's letter to Lodge covers the tariff fight, the Turkish uprising and the hunt so far, adding a note about the next day's rhino and Kermit's leopard.

headline: A charging cow rhino
summary: Off by 5:30, Roosevelt is charged by a cow rhino and has to shoot her, and writes up a rhino story with a drawing of the kill.

headline: Proud of Kermit
summary: Roosevelt records a waterbuck and another buck with weights and distances. He tells Ted he is proud of Kermit, the once-timid boy now cool and daring, and writes Root about the trip and the tariff.

headline: An impala and a python
summary: Roosevelt shoots an impala buck at 300 yards and records a python and its weight.

headline: Homesick, and a bad shooting day
summary: Roosevelt misses everything while Kermit gets two waterbuck, and they see the Nairobi falls. He tells Bamie he misses Edith but the hunt is going well and the three naturalists are splendid.

headline: The expedition splits up
summary: Roosevelt, Kermit and taxidermist Heller move on to Kamiti Ranch, owned by Hill and Heatley, while Mearns and Loring head down the Nairobi River to collect specimens. Roosevelt shoots two wild pigs on the way.

headline: Buffalo in the swamp
summary: While moving camp, Roosevelt kills two buffalo bulls, finishing one Kermit probably hit first, then gets a third bull in a swamp.

headline: Meat for the camp
summary: In an afternoon shoot Roosevelt kills two zebras and two hartebeest to feed the camp.

headline: East Africa's biggest dairy
summary: At Kamiti, Heatley's ranch and the largest dairy farm in East Africa, Roosevelt goes after buffalo in the morning without seeing any. His May 12 letter to Bridges finally goes out with the first two Scribner's articles.

headline: Nearly charged by a buffalo herd
summary: Roosevelt drops a buffalo and nearly has the entire herd come at him, in country laced with game trails, dusty and swampy by turns.

headline: At Heatley's house
summary: Roosevelt goes to Heatley's house and describes the farm and its plants and animals.

headline: Into Nairobi
summary: Roosevelt travels from Kamiti Ranch into Nairobi.

headline: Willard Straight in the guest book
summary: Roosevelt is at Kamiti Ranch; George Marcius and diplomat Willard Straight sign the Sagamore Hill guest book.

headline: To McMillan's town house
summary: Roosevelt moves to William McMillan's house in town.

headline: The French Catholic mission
summary: Roosevelt tours the French Catholic Mission near Nairobi, seeing its plantations and school, works through the day, and spends the evening at "Nairobi Hollies."

headline: Sunday at church and mission
summary: Roosevelt attends the Episcopal church and visits a Catholic mission.

headline: A new gun bearer, a memory trick
summary: Roosevelt notes a visit involving Loring and Dawson. A man named Gouvimali replaces Mahomet as his gun bearer, and when TR keeps forgetting the name, Kermit suggests he think of "Gouverneur Morris."

headline: Naturalists rejoin the party in Nairobi
summary: Edgar Mearns and J. Alden Loring come back from a specimen-gathering trip, and the whole party stays with Lieutenant Governor Frederick Jackson. Roosevelt writes Andrew Carnegie for more expedition money and sends Scribner's four more articles, floating a title for the eventual book.

headline: Tea at the governor's
summary: Roosevelt's diary for the day notes only an afternoon tea call at the governor's residence in Nairobi.

headline: Off to Kijabe
summary: Roosevelt leaves Nairobi for Kijabe, the jumping-off point for the next leg of the safari.

headline: Lunch at the American Mission
summary: At Kijabe, Roosevelt calls at the American mission station and stays for lunch.

headline: Setting out across the thirst
summary: With 196 porters and four ox wagons, the safari leaves Kijabe heading south toward the Sotik and the waterless stretch called the thirst. They reach it about midday, rest while the porters dance, water the animals and push on at dusk. The Outlook prints a Roosevelt piece on the South.

headline: Crossing the dry country
summary: The march goes on. Once the sun is high the party halts to rest and sleep, then sets off again at noon through hilly brush country, moving again at 9 p.m. in rain.

headline: A 3 a.m. start in the rain
summary: Roosevelt is in the saddle by 3 a.m., and the rain keeps falling as the safari keeps moving.

headline: The oxen finally drink
summary: A rest day in camp. The porters straggle in about 10:30, and the oxen get water for the first time in three days once the wagons arrive.

headline: On to the Nyarok
summary: The safari moves on to the Nyarok, and Roosevelt jots notes about a python.

headline: A running wildebeest at 300 yards
summary: Reaching the Guaso Nyero, Roosevelt drops a wildebeest bull on the run at long range, and Kermit takes topi. That night Masai herders swap hunting stories at the fire.

headline: Hunting the Sotik, reading by the tent
summary: In the Sotik, Roosevelt hunts with two gunbearers and a dozen porters, taking a Thomson's gazelle and two bull elands, and records weights, ranges and sketches. Later he settles at his tent door with a book from his Pigskin Library.

headline: Kermit bags two cheetahs
summary: Kermit kills a pair of cheetahs, and Roosevelt logs other kills with sketches. At home, the record notes friction over Nick Longworth turning up at the White House in casual dress, and warmth toward President Taft.

headline: Alone after impala
summary: Roosevelt goes out by himself for impala and Roberts' gazelle and brings in two impala and a Grant's gazelle.

headline: A lioness at sunset
summary: Hunting lion with Leslie Tarlton, Roosevelt kills a lioness near sundown, a pregnant animal topping 300 pounds that porters haul back to camp. Archie Butt calls on Edith at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Five days' tally, then camp moves
summary: The party breaks camp. Roosevelt's bag from five days of shooting includes a hyena, a warthog boar, two zebra, two eland, topi, two impala and gazelles.

headline: Giraffes for the museum
summary: Riding out under cool, cloudy skies to find rhino and giraffe for the museum, Roosevelt shoots giraffes while Kermit photographs. Edith writes Kermit of Butt's visit, Mrs. Taft's stroke and the President's wavering.

headline: Father and son both score
summary: Kermit takes a Roberts' gazelle and three topi; Roosevelt gets a topi bull and a wildebeest, adding notes and sketches.

headline: A galloping rhino
summary: Roosevelt's diary records a rhino taken at a gallop and a wildebeest bull.

headline: Kermit runs down an eland
summary: Kermit rides an eland to a standstill while Roosevelt hunts on his own and brings back a Grant's buck, a hartebeest and a Thomson's gazelle. The Outlook carries his essay on names.

headline: Rhino cow and calf
summary: Roosevelt and Kermit go shooting together and come upon a rhino cow with her calf.

headline: No newspapers in the Sotik
summary: A lion turns up close to camp in the morning. Writing to Bamie, Roosevelt says he has stayed clear of the news, frets that Kermit takes risks, praises his shooting and likens him to Bob Ferguson. He tells Corinne he is busy on his Scribner's pieces.

headline: Zebra and an old wildebeest
summary: Roosevelt shoots a Roberts' buck, zebra and an old wildebeest bull. Archie Butt writes Edith with good wishes for her coming trip to Europe.

headline: Lion at point-blank range
summary: Roosevelt's terse diary line records a lion shot at just eight and four yards.

headline: New camp beside the Masai
summary: Camp moves to a pool near a Masai settlement under a line of tall hills. Roosevelt gets a Thomson's buck; Kermit kills a lioness and an impala.

headline: A charging maned lion
summary: Roosevelt stops a maned lion in mid-charge with a shot to the chest at a hundred yards.

headline: A day in camp
summary: Roosevelt stays put in camp.

headline: Edith and the children sail for Europe
summary: Roosevelt shifts camp and shoots a zebra. Across the Atlantic, Edith boards the S.S. Crete with Ethel, Archie and Quentin, carrying $10,000 for five months of travel in Europe.

headline: Long shots at topi
summary: Roosevelt drops two topi at 350 and 400 yards, plus a Thomson's gazelle, a boar and an impala.

headline: Rhino, zebra and bustards
summary: A full day's bag: a rhino at 60 yards, zebra on the run, a steinbuck and two kinds of bustard.

headline: Alice watches the Wrights fly
summary: Roosevelt shoots an impala doe. In Virginia, Alice is in the crowd at Fort Myer for the Wright brothers' test flights.

headline: Mail reaches the Sotik
summary: A mail delivery catches up with the safari in the Sotik.

headline: A dik-dik on the run
summary: Roosevelt shoots a dik-dik buck as it runs at fifty yards.
