summary: Delegates defy the state committee's choice of Vice President Sherman and elect Roosevelt temporary chairman, 568 to 443. In his keynote he praises President Taft. It is also Corinne's 49th birthday.

headline: Stimson for governor
summary: Roosevelt speaks again, and the convention nominates his close friend Henry L. Stimson for governor of New York.

headline: Dutchess County Fair
summary: Roosevelt speaks at the fair in Poughkeepsie and returns to Oyster Bay.

headline: Rallying the Republican clubs
summary: Roosevelt meets progressive Republicans, sees Griscom and Longworth at The Outlook, and speaks to the state's league of Republican clubs. Alice and Nick are guests at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Lunch with Nassau County delegates
summary: Roosevelt hosts the Nassau County delegation to the state Republican convention for lunch at Sagamore Hill. He writes Lodge about speaking in New England and admits his voice is wearing thin.

headline: Family and friends at Sagamore
summary: A quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill, where the guest book records Richard Derby, Nick Longworth and Willard Straight.

headline: Strategy talks with Stimson and Longworth
summary: Roosevelt meets at home with Henry Stimson, the Republican pick for governor, and his son-in-law Nick Longworth. Novelist Stewart Edward White and his wife Elizabeth are among the guests.

headline: Addressing volunteer firemen in Freeport
summary: Roosevelt travels to Freeport, Long Island, to address the state's volunteer firemen, and lunches with Kansas City editor William Rockhill Nelson and journalist Ray Stannard Baker.

headline: Citizenship speech in Brooklyn
summary: In Manhattan, Roosevelt confers with Lloyd Griscom, the county Republican chairman, and sees Senator Albert Cummins at The Outlook before heading to Brooklyn to talk about citizenship.

headline: Busy office day, then off south
summary: A steady stream of visitors reaches Roosevelt at The Outlook, labor leader John Mitchell and canal builder George Goethals among them. After lunch with Herbert Croly, he boards a train for a southern speaking tour with Harper and the Howlands.

headline: Whistle-stops across East Tennessee
summary: Roosevelt speaks his way across East Tennessee, from Bristol to Knoxville. In a letter to Lucius Swift he defends his role at the state convention despite its tariff plank, noting the West stands firmly against the tariff.

headline: Visiting his mother's girlhood home
summary: In Georgia, Roosevelt tours the Berry School at Rome, gives speeches in Atlanta, and goes to Roswell to see Bulloch Hall, where his mother Mittie grew up.

headline: Three states in one day
summary: The southern tour rolls on with talks across Tennessee, Alabama and Mississippi.

headline: Hot Springs, and a gift for Kermit
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Hot Springs, Arkansas. Back east, Kermit turns 21 and carries on at Harvard; his father marks the day with a $500 gift.

headline: First president to fly
summary: In St. Louis, Roosevelt climbs into a plane with aviator Arch Hoxsey and rides about four minutes at some 50 feet. Landing, he tells reporters it was the best thing he ever did. He also addresses audiences in Clayton and St. Louis. Niece Eleanor turns 26.

headline: Illinois stops at Springfield and Peoria
summary: Roosevelt addresses crowds in Springfield and Peoria, and makes a plea for religious tolerance in Africa.

headline: Stumping Indiana for Beveridge
summary: Roosevelt crosses Indiana, from Covington to Indianapolis, campaigning for Senator Albert Beveridge's re-election. Beveridge is a firm opponent of President Taft.

headline: Southern tier of New York
summary: Back in his home state, Roosevelt speaks at six stops along New York's southern tier, from Dunkirk to Elmira.

headline: Meeting the state committee
summary: In Manhattan, Roosevelt meets with Griscom and the state Republican committee. The Outlook runs his article on clean government and popular rule.

headline: Sunday lunch with Stimson
summary: Henry Stimson comes to Sagamore Hill for lunch.

headline: Up the Hudson by speech
summary: Roosevelt works up the Hudson and Mohawk valleys with speeches from Yonkers to Hudson. He writes Sydney Brooks a frank letter about American politics, prompted by Brooks's article on the subject.

headline: Nephew Sheffield turns twelve
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill on the 12th birthday of his nephew Sheffield Cowles.

headline: Dogs in the bathtub
summary: On a foggy day at home, Roosevelt writes Ted about his California political friends and reports that James is giving Scamp and Ace, the dogs, a bath in his own tub. He also writes Senator Bourne and thanks poet Edwin Arlington Robinson for a dedication.

headline: Answering a tax smear
summary: Roosevelt speaks in New York City and writes Annie Bissell to rebut false claims that he skipped paying his 1898 taxes.

headline: Boston rally for Lodge and Draper
summary: Roosevelt goes to Boston to speak for Senator Lodge and Governor Eben Draper. He tells Elihu Root he will not return to Ohio before the election, despite their wishes and Taft's.

headline: New Hampshire for Bass
summary: Roosevelt campaigns in Concord, Manchester and Nashua for Robert Bass, New Hampshire's progressive candidate for governor.

headline: Boston back to New York
summary: Roosevelt travels from Boston to New York City.

headline: Binghamton, Ithaca and Oswego
summary: The upstate campaign continues with stops at Binghamton, Ithaca and Oswego.

headline: Finger Lakes swing
summary: Roosevelt speaks through the Finger Lakes country, from Penn Yan and Canandaigua to Auburn and Syracuse.

headline: North to the St. Lawrence
summary: Roosevelt's train carries him north from Phoenix and Fulton through Oswego and Watertown to Ogdensburg on the St. Lawrence, with speeches at each.

headline: A 52nd birthday on the stump
summary: Roosevelt spends his 52nd birthday campaigning through the Mohawk Valley, from Fonda to Utica.

headline: Rome, Lyons and Rochester
summary: More upstate speeches, this time in Rome, Lyons and Rochester.

headline: Tribute to Senator Dolliver
summary: Roosevelt addresses audiences at Kingston, at Bronxville and in New York City. The Outlook carries his piece on the late Iowa Senator Jonathan Dolliver.

headline: Edith hopes for winter quiet
summary: Edith writes Kermit that she is glad winter will keep his father safely at Sagamore, and wishes Kermit will grow more like him over the years. Roosevelt speaks in New York City and dines with Henry Stimson.

headline: African Game Trails hits the shelves
summary: Scribner's publishes African Game Trails, Roosevelt's account of his safari, and it becomes a bestseller at once. Putnam's brings out his African and European Addresses the same day.

headline: Buffalo to Manhattan in a day
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Buffalo, Lockport and Albion, then in New York City, and dines with Buffalo publisher Edward H. Butler.

headline: Baltimore, and two pointed letters
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Baltimore. He writes Simeon Baldwin, Connecticut's Democratic nominee for governor, about remarks he made against him and about the courts. To Wall Street broker Alfred Borden he defends his record, including leaving the tariff alone as President.

headline: Through Ohio, Indiana and Illinois
summary: A long day on the rails brings talks across Ohio, Indiana and Illinois.

headline: Iowa for the progressives
summary: In Iowa, Roosevelt speaks at four Iowa stops, Davenport to Des Moines, on behalf of Grilk, Carroll and Senator Albert Cummins.

headline: Remembering Justice Moody
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Toledo and Cleveland. The Outlook publishes his tribute to William H. Moody, his former Attorney General and Supreme Court appointee.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Election eve in New York
summary: On the last night of the campaign, Roosevelt speaks in New York City and dines with the Hungarian Republican Club.

headline: Republicans routed at the polls
summary: Roosevelt casts his vote in Oyster Bay and watches the Republicans take a beating. Stimson, his choice for governor, loses. Democrats win the House for the first time since Cleveland, 26 governorships including Woodrow Wilson's, and ten Senate seats, among them Beveridge's. Franklin Roosevelt wins a state senate seat.

headline: Beaten, but enlisted for the duration
summary: The day after the defeat, Roosevelt writes General Francis Greene that he means to see the fight through.

headline: Setting Platt's record straight
summary: Roosevelt writes John Jacob Astor about the untruths he finds in Thomas Platt's autobiography.

headline: Cats own the nights
summary: Roosevelt sends a stack of post-election letters. He jokes to his sister Bamie about cats and dogs, tells Ted his hopes for 1912 and plans for California, and admits to Arthur Lee that the defeat was heavy, hoping he won't be a candidate in 1912 and judging Taft harshly.

headline: Riding over to see Stimson
summary: Roosevelt rides on horseback to call on Henry Stimson, the defeated candidate for governor.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Sizing up the defeat
summary: Roosevelt tells Seth Low that leaning harder or softer toward Taft would only have made the loss worse. He forwards Low's view of the situation to Henry Stimson and writes George Tait about the wallpaper trust and his tariff position.

headline: Too radical for New York
summary: In the city, Roosevelt confers with Lodge and receives callers at The Outlook, including Wisconsin's Charles Van Hise and Henry Pritchett. He tells William Allen White that New Yorkers found him too radical.

headline: Lecturing Washington on African wildlife
summary: In Washington, Roosevelt is received at the National Press Club and lectures the National Geographic Society on people and animals of Africa.

headline: Back in the President's chair
summary: With Taft away in Panama, Roosevelt revisits the White House, tours the staff quarters, inspects the new oval office and takes his old seat at the President's desk. Ike Hoover, the chief usher, weeps. He sees callers, dines with the Smithsonian, and speaks there to an overflow crowd. Quentin turns 13 at Groton.

headline: A full Sunday guest book
summary: Five Sunday guests, among them Richard Derby and Josephine Osborn, visit Sagamore Hill.

headline: Relieved of a 1912 decision
summary: Roosevelt tells Joseph Bucklin Bishop he is glad not to face choosing whether to accept the 1912 nomination. In a long letter to Benjamin Ide Wheeler he concedes he erred in letting himself be drawn into the fight and dissects what went wrong.

headline: Commuting to The Outlook
summary: Roosevelt is based at Sagamore Hill these weeks but often goes into Manhattan to his Outlook office on Fourth Avenue. Cornelia Landon is a guest.

headline: Too many speeches
summary: Roosevelt tells Henry Pritchett where he went wrong in the campaign, chiefly by giving too many speeches, and has words for crooked politicians. He thanks author Gouverneur Morris, a descendant of the founder whose biography he wrote, for three books.

headline: Thanksgiving at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt spends Thanksgiving Day at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Bamie's anniversary
summary: At Sagamore Hill on the 15th wedding anniversary of his sister Bamie and William Sheffield Cowles.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Declining Taft's invitation
summary: Roosevelt writes Congressman William Kent about Pinchot and Ballinger, Taft, and the Japanese in California. He tells President Taft he cannot come to the White House or the Gridiron Dinner, and passes on Kent's warning of new anti-Japanese bills in California.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: The New Nationalism in print
summary: The Outlook Company publishes The New Nationalism. The family is scattered: Alice in Washington with Nick, Ted selling carpets in San Francisco, Kermit a Harvard sophomore, Archie at school in Arizona, and Quentin suddenly thriving at Groton. Only Ethel is home.

headline: Bill Sewall comes to Sagamore
summary: Roosevelt is home with frequent trips to the city. Guests include his old Maine guide and Elkhorn foreman Bill Sewall, Oscar Straus and his wife, editor Albert Shaw and his wife, and Alice and Nick.

headline: Twenty-four years married
summary: Roosevelt and Edith mark their 24th wedding anniversary at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Guests from the city
summary: James L. Derby, Cornelia Landon and the Chadwicks sign the guest book.

headline: A long ride, then a blizzard
summary: Roosevelt and Edith ride together for three hours. That evening they settle by the fire in the North Room as snow outside builds into a blizzard.

headline: Content at home
summary: Roosevelt writes Ted about a warm note from Johnston, pokes fun at a know-it-all letter from William Kent, and discusses Taft, the Japanese question and the California trip. Ethel is back from Geneseo and Kermit heading there. He feels no itch to be elsewhere.

headline: Notes on Panama and Japan
summary: Roosevelt sends a short note to Ernest Harvier and writes Taft about Panama, thanks him for his kind words, and discusses the Japanese situation in California. He plans to see Secretary Knox.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Reviewing Taft's message
summary: Roosevelt sends Taft his comments on the President's annual message to Congress, along with thoughts on Japan and immigration.

headline: A book about beetles
summary: Roosevelt thanks Indiana State Geologist Willis Blatchley for sending his book on beetles.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Books, bronzes and wood fires
summary: Roosevelt explains to William Allen White why he should not run again, describing a happy life at home with Edith and only Ethel still under their roof. He backs the initiative, referendum and direct primaries and lays out his political creed, though many think him too radical.

headline: New Haven, with Baldwin absent
summary: Roosevelt speaks to New Haven's business leaders; Governor-elect Simeon Baldwin declines to come. He sends Ernest Harvier a brief note about an interesting comparison.

headline: Harvard lecture on applied ethics
summary: At Harvard, Roosevelt delivers the Noble Lecture on applied ethics, touching on conservation.

headline: Calling on Governor Draper
summary: In Boston, Roosevelt pays a call on Governor Eben Draper.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Nephew and friends visit
summary: Visitors include Roosevelt's nephew Monroe Douglas Robinson, along with Alice and Nick.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Objections to Platt's memoir
summary: Roosevelt writes Louis Lang, who helped Thomas Platt with his autobiography, listing what he disputes: Platt's story of the 1900 vice-presidential nomination, his claimed backing for the Navy post, and money in the 1898 governor's race.

headline: Forests for Oregon
summary: Roosevelt writes Oregon Congressman Abraham Lafferty about farm and forest lands, national forests in Oregon, and federal versus state control of forests.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Japan, Manchuria and the open door
summary: In a very long letter, Roosevelt reports to Taft on his talk with Knox and the Japanese question. He will not urge steps against Japanese moves in Manchuria, though Knox favors them, and discusses the open door.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Writing about miners' homes
summary: The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's account of his August visit to Pennsylvania coal country.

headline: Stockings for everyone
summary: Roosevelt and Edith share Christmas dinner with Alice, Nick, Kermit, Ethel and Quentin; Ted is in California and Archie in Arizona. The children fill their parents' stockings with joke gifts.

headline: A book he loves
summary: Dorothy Whitney comes to Sagamore with Robert Bacon Jr. Roosevelt thanks Ted and Eleanor for a book he treasures and notes Kermit has not yet made the Porcellian Club.

headline: Two holiday visitors
summary: Barclay H. Farr and Grafton H. Pyne sign the guest book.

headline: On John Brown and Homer Lea
summary: Roosevelt gives Lyman Draper his view of John Brown. He also writes General Ian Hamilton about Homer Lea's book imagining a Japanese invasion of the West Coast, which he dislikes.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Turning down LaFollette's league
summary: Roosevelt turns down membership in the new progressive Republican league organized by Senators Robert LaFollette and Jonathan Bourne. Its platform calls for direct election of senators, direct primaries, recall, initiative, referendum and laws against corrupt practices.

headline: A settee from the White House
summary: President Taft sends Edith, as a New Year's gift, the settee she loved in the White House. The Outlook runs Roosevelt's Christmas in Mid-Africa. Isabella Hagner visits.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: A zebra skin for Ted
summary: Lloyd Griscom lunches at Sagamore, seeming less buoyant than before. Roosevelt sends Ted a zebra skin and offers a rhinoceros-foot inkstand, calls LaFollette and Bourne extremists, and writes Robert Bacon's family that Quentin has stunned Groton by ranking high in his class.

headline: Corruption talk with Lodge
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge about bribery charges against Vardaman and Senator William Lorimer, sends him a zebra skin, and mentions a book on superstitions he is reading. He also writes LaFollette about the new progressive league.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Comparing notes with Ian Hamilton
summary: Roosevelt writes General Ian Hamilton about conscription in the British Army and about his own soldiering at Santiago with the Rough Riders.

headline: A promise to Harvier
summary: Splitting the day between home and the city, Roosevelt tells Ernest Harvier he will write him about Mitchell.

headline: Staying out of the Lorimer fight
summary: Roosevelt writes Taft that Beveridge is moving to expel Senator Lorimer and that both of them will keep out of the fight. He thanks Taft for the settee sent to Edith.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: The Greys visit
summary: Richard Derby, Evelyn Irving and a couple named Grey are guests at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Between Sagamore Hill and the city
summary: Roosevelt splits the day between home and Manhattan.

headline: Harvard Overseers meeting
summary: In Cambridge, Roosevelt sits with the Harvard Board of Overseers and dines with the Alumni Association's directors.

headline: Praise for Canadian reciprocity
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge about his re-election speech and the Lorimer case. He tells Taft that Knox's trade reciprocity pact with Canada is excellent and will help the party in the long run, and notes Lodge is cool on Beveridge's resolution.

headline: National Civic Federation
summary: Roosevelt addresses the National Civic Federation in New York.

headline: A grandchild on the way
summary: Ted and Eleanor share news that a baby is due in August, and Roosevelt answers with delight. The Outlook carries his article on international neighborliness.

headline: The Griscoms visit
summary: Lloyd Griscom and his wife come to Sagamore Hill. They later tell Archie Butt that Roosevelt and Edith seemed low in spirits.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Irish Home Rule, privately
summary: Roosevelt writes Cleveland Dodge about New Jersey progressives, answers Gifford Pinchot's complaint that he called Taft upright, tells Thomas Gill he favors Irish Home Rule but won't say so publicly, and writes Lodge about campaign lies and two Panama supply ships.

headline: Bamie turns 56
summary: Roosevelt speaks to the governing council of the Reform synagogue union. It is his sister Bamie's 56th birthday. He writes Edwin Van Valkenburg about the employers' liability law and the 1912 nomination.

headline: Reluctant vice president of historians
summary: Roosevelt writes Maurice Egan about Catholic missions and socialism. Told he has been elected a vice president of the American Historical Association, he tells John Jameson he doubts he would serve well and wants to decline. He writes John O'Laughlin on Lorimer.

headline: Ambassador Reid comes calling
summary: Whitelaw and Elizabeth Reid and Josephine Osborn are guests at Sagamore Hill.

headline: A progressive league is born
summary: LaFollette and Bourne launch the National Progressive Republican League to liberalize the party, with the unspoken aim of blocking Taft in 1912. Roosevelt holds back from formal support but praises it in The Outlook, where he also writes on popular rule. He attends Paul Morton's funeral.

headline: Grandchildren would complete the picture
summary: Roosevelt writes Ted that he and Edith think four, or five at most, is a fine number of children, and that grandchildren are the one thing their happiness lacked. He also discusses the California trip.

headline: Naturalist Alden Loring visits
summary: J. Alden Loring, the naturalist from the African safari, and Elizabeth S. Hoyt sign the guest book.

headline: Backing the league from outside
summary: Roosevelt tells William Allen White he will support the progressive league without joining, and that a 1912 nomination would be a mistake. To LaFollette he offers help through The Outlook but wants distance, recalling complaints about his political meddling in 1910.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Friday guests
summary: Roosevelt goes between home and the city; five guests sign the Sagamore Hill book.

headline: Answering Judge Baldwin
summary: The Outlook publishes two Roosevelt pieces: an open letter to Judge Simeon Baldwin and an essay on nationalism and special privilege.

headline: Cheering on Franklin
summary: Roosevelt sends a warm note to his cousin, State Senator Franklin D. Roosevelt, who heads a revolt of reform Democrats in Albany against Tammany.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Endorsing Frances Perkins's league
summary: Roosevelt endorses the Consumers' League of New York, where Frances Perkins is executive secretary, in its fight against sweatshops, child labor and overlong workdays. He also writes Lodge about Platt's autobiography, Canadian reciprocity and Lorimer.

headline: Commuting to Fourth Avenue
summary: Roosevelt is based at Sagamore Hill, often heading into Manhattan to his Outlook office. Former Massachusetts governor Curtis Guild Jr. is among the guests.

headline: Arguing about bird markings
summary: Roosevelt writes zoologist Charles Kofoid about a paper by Henry Chester Tracy on white markings in perching birds. He argues that protective coloration does not explain every case and rejects Abbott Thayer's theories.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Rebutting the Mormon smear
summary: Roosevelt writes Isaac Russell to refute a Pearson's Magazine charge that he traded leniency on plural marriage for Mormon electoral votes in the West. The Outlook runs his essay on nationalism and the working man. Cousins and safari naturalist Edmund Heller visit.

headline: Sunday with Heller
summary: Roosevelt spends time with Edmund Heller, the naturalist from his African safari.

headline: Finish the specimens first
summary: Roosevelt tells Smithsonian Secretary Charles Walcott that Heller should complete mounting the Roosevelt expedition's specimens before setting off on another trip.

headline: For popular election of senators
summary: Roosevelt writes John O'Laughlin about Senator Lorimer and says voters, not legislatures, should choose senators. He also writes historian William Roscoe Thayer about his article on great Italians and about the Catholic Church.

headline: Lords reform and the founders
summary: Roosevelt writes British author Frederick Oliver about a plan to reform the House of Lords, and compares Jefferson and Hamilton to today's progressives.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Blessing for Heller's next safari
summary: Roosevelt sends regrets to Boy Scout leader James West but voices strong belief in Scouting. He wishes Heller well as he joins Paul Rainey's African expedition, and writes Eben Martin about trusts and Will Cowles about reciprocity, Admiral Sperry's death and Lodge's stand on senators.

headline: Lincoln Day in Grand Rapids
summary: Roosevelt gives the Lincoln Day address in Grand Rapids, Michigan. The Outlook publishes his essay on nationalism and working women.

headline: Lincoln's birthday in New York
summary: Roosevelt attends the Republican Club's Lincoln dinner in New York and speaks. It is Alice's 27th birthday. In Illinois, President Taft privately compares Roosevelt and Lincoln.

headline: Touring Brooklyn's slums
summary: Roosevelt tours poor neighborhoods of Brooklyn and has lunch with his old friend Jacob Riis.

headline: A Hungarian count at Sagamore
summary: Hungarian statesman Count Albert Apponyi visits, along with General Francis Greene and E. Reeve Merritt.

headline: Home and the city
summary: Roosevelt splits the day between home and Manhattan.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Catholics on the YMCA board
summary: On Alice and Nick's fifth anniversary, Roosevelt presses Cleveland Dodge to let Catholics serve as YMCA directors; he later learns they may. He also welcomes Congressman Edmund Madison's support.

headline: Two pieces in The Outlook
summary: The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's essay on Greeley, Sumner and Morton and his article on a higher-education project.

headline: Thinking of Eleanor
summary: Roosevelt writes his daughter-in-law Eleanor, expecting her first child, that she and Ted fill his and Edith's thoughts.

headline: Overnight train to Chicago
summary: Roosevelt boards the Lake Shore Limited at Grand Central at 5:30 p.m., bound for Chicago. He writes Michigan's progressive governor Chase Osborn about electing senators by popular vote.

headline: Harvard men in Chicago
summary: In Chicago, Roosevelt addresses the Harvard Club's dinner.

headline: Union League dinner
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Chicago, including at a Union League Club dinner on Washington's Birthday.

headline: Home and the city
summary: Roosevelt splits the day between home and Manhattan.

headline: Finding a lost boy
summary: In Gramercy Park, Roosevelt comes to the aid of a little boy who has lost his way.

headline: The Richardsons visit
summary: Clifford and Teresa Richardson are guests at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Sunday callers
summary: Three guests, among them James L. Breese Jr., sign the Sagamore Hill book.

headline: Curriculum and postage
summary: Roosevelt writes Syracuse English professor Joseph Pennypacker about Amherst's curriculum plan, and Paul Collins about Canadian reciprocity and postal rates for periodicals.

headline: Nationalism and the judiciary
summary: Alice is among the guests at Sagamore Hill. The Outlook carries Roosevelt's piece on nationalism and the courts.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Proud of Quentin's marks
summary: Roosevelt tells Quentin he can't find a Springfield rifle for Quentin's friend James White, but bursts with pride over the boy's class standing and reports that the family car is worn from a hard winter.

headline: Against the Aldrich plan
summary: Roosevelt tells Elisha Garrison he opposes Senator Aldrich's banking reform plan, and writes Lodge about the pension bill both men oppose.

headline: Writing about San Juan
summary: The Outlook runs Roosevelt's account of the battle of San Juan along with his judiciary essay. Alice, Richard Derby and Dorothy Whitney are among the Sagamore guests.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Tepid on suffrage
summary: Taft accepts Interior Secretary Ballinger's resignation. Roosevelt writes General Greene about Washington, Frederick the Great and the 1905 Portsmouth peace, Frank Tracy about Francis Lowell's death, and anti-suffragist Mary Swift that he leans toward votes for women, though only mildly.

headline: Off on a 34-day tour
summary: Roosevelt sets out with Edith and Ethel on a speaking tour that will last 34 days, stopping first in Washington. He writes Lucius Swift about reciprocity and Indiana opinion.

headline: Southern Commercial Congress
summary: In Atlanta, Roosevelt addresses the Southern Commercial Congress.

headline: Child labor conference in Birmingham
summary: Roosevelt speaks to the National Child Labor Conference in Birmingham, Alabama.

headline: Mississippi to New Orleans
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Jackson and McComb, Mississippi, and in New Orleans. The Outlook carries his judiciary essay and a piece on the Third Avenue railway and its workers.

headline: Into Texas
summary: The tour reaches Texas with speeches in Houston and Beaumont.

headline: Five Texas cities
summary: Roosevelt speaks his way through San Antonio, Austin, Waco, Fort Worth and Dallas, and visits the Army post at Fort Sam Houston.

headline: Ready to raise a regiment
summary: With Mexico's Díaz government collapsing, Taft quietly sends troops to Texas for so-called maneuvers. From Dallas, Roosevelt writes Taft about the danger of war and says he would want to raise a regiment if serious fighting came.

headline: Edith rejoins in Albuquerque
summary: Roosevelt speaks in El Paso and Albuquerque. Edith joins him in Albuquerque after visiting their old friend Bob Ferguson, who is ill with tuberculosis, in Silver City.

headline: Archie meets the train
summary: After talks at Flagstaff and then Williams, Archie meets his parents, healthy but lean.

headline: Into the Grand Canyon
summary: With Governor Richard Sloan, Roosevelt and his son Archie descend into the Grand Canyon on horseback while Edith rests at the rim. Later that day the party heads to Phoenix and drive out toward Roosevelt Dam, which he has been asked to dedicate.

headline: Dedicating Roosevelt Dam
summary: Roosevelt speaks at the opening of the great reclamation dam on the Salt River that bears his name, then returns to Phoenix. The Outlook again runs his judiciary essay.

headline: Visiting Archie's school
summary: The Roosevelts drive from Phoenix to Mesa to see Archie's school.

headline: Lunch with old Rough Riders
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Phoenix, lunches with Rough Rider veterans, and visits the Territorial Normal School at Tempe.

headline: Los Angeles and Pasadena
summary: In Los Angeles, Roosevelt lunches with Earl and Francis Heney and gives a speech, then speaks at Throop Polytechnic Institute in Pasadena.

headline: Occidental College talk
summary: Roosevelt speaks to the City Club and at Occidental College in Los Angeles.

headline: "I took the Isthmus"
summary: After a speech in San Francisco, Roosevelt gives the University of California's Charter Day address at Berkeley, with his famous line about taking the Isthmus and letting Congress debate him while the canal got built.

headline: Earl Lectures begin
summary: Roosevelt opens his Earl Lecture series at Berkeley with a talk on realizable ideals and speaks at a student rally.

headline: Home and child; fire in New York
summary: Roosevelt's Earl Lecture at Berkeley is about home life and children. Back east in Manhattan, fire sweeps the Triangle Shirtwaist factory near Washington Square, killing 146 workers, mostly young women, trapped by poor safety measures and too few exits. The Outlook runs his essay on nationalism and democracy.

headline: The Bible and the people
summary: Roosevelt's Earl Lecture at Berkeley takes up the Bible and everyday life.

headline: Public servants and the Eighth Commandment
summary: In another Earl Lecture, Roosevelt discusses honesty in public life and the moral duties of both employers and workers.

headline: Staying with Ted and Eleanor
summary: Roosevelt's last Earl Lecture concerns the press and the Ninth Commandment; he then speaks in San Francisco. Quentin meets the family there, and the three of them lodge at Ted and Eleanor's home while Ethel lodges with friends.

headline: In San Francisco
summary: Roosevelt remains in San Francisco with his family; no specific activity is recorded.

headline: In San Francisco
summary: Roosevelt remains in San Francisco with his family; no specific activity is recorded.

headline: Lectures spoken, not written
summary: Roosevelt is in San Francisco. His Earl Lectures, which included a talk on money and wealthy men, were given without a text, taken down by stenographers, and later published as Realizable Ideals.

headline: His last speaking tour, he says
summary: From San Francisco, Roosevelt tells Taft this will be his final speaking tour and thanks him for explaining the Mexican situation. He had been asked to mediate in Mexico but thought it improper. The Outlook runs his essay on international relations.

headline: In San Francisco
summary: Roosevelt is in San Francisco; no specific activity is recorded.

headline: Taking on Reno's divorce trade
summary: In Reno, Nevada, Roosevelt speaks out against the city's reputation as a haven for quick divorces.

headline: Before the California Legislature
summary: Roosevelt addresses the California Legislature in Sacramento. In Washington, Congress meets in special session to take up Canadian reciprocity.

headline: Oregon, and Edith's proud letter
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Eugene, Albany and Portland, Oregon. Edith writes Cecil Spring-Rice that the welcome he receives everywhere is moving and funny, and that she is proud of both the country and its people.

headline: Puget Sound stops
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Tacoma and Seattle.

headline: In Spokane
summary: Roosevelt is in Spokane; no specific activity is recorded.

headline: Worrying about birthrates
summary: In Spokane. The Outlook publishes two Roosevelt essays, one on old and new education and one on falling birthrates among English-speaking peoples.

headline: Idaho, and Archie turns 17
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Moscow and Sandpoint, Idaho, on Archie's 17th birthday.

headline: In Spokane
summary: Roosevelt is in Spokane; no specific activity is recorded.

headline: Missoula, and a portrait of Quentin
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Missoula. Edith writes Spring-Rice that Quentin is a warm-hearted, oversized puppy of a boy, wrapped up in his wireless and anything mechanical, and now first in his class at Groton.

headline: In Helena
summary: Roosevelt is in Helena; no specific activity is recorded.

headline: In Helena
summary: Roosevelt is in Helena; no specific activity is recorded.

headline: Helena to Madison
summary: Roosevelt leaves Helena, Montana, heading for Madison, Wisconsin.

headline: Madison, then homeward
summary: After speeches in Madison, Roosevelt, Edith and Ethel turn back toward New York. The Outlook runs his piece on ethics in journalism, and Collier's prints his February letter rebutting the Mormon polygamy charges.

headline: Home to Oyster Bay
summary: The Roosevelts arrive back at Oyster Bay and Sagamore Hill after five weeks on the road.

headline: Border clash at Douglas
summary: Roosevelt is home again, with regular trips into the city. At Douglas, Arizona, Mexican rebels and federal troops fight, and several Americans are wounded.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Two guests at Sagamore
summary: Janetta Alexander and J. T. Coolidge visit Sagamore Hill.

headline: A guest at Sagamore
summary: Arnold Hunewell signs the guest book.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Writing about tenements
summary: The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's account of a tenement visit. The Richardsons and Cornelia Landon are guests.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: A guest at Sagamore
summary: R. May signs the guest book.

headline: For the Berry School
summary: Roosevelt speaks to the Berry School Association in New York and sends Annie Nathan Meyer his thoughts on her play The Dominant Sex.

headline: Governor Bass talks direct democracy
summary: New Hampshire Governor Robert Bass visits, and the two discuss initiative, referendum and recall. In Manhattan, Taft and Archie Butt attend an exposition for the blind at the Metropolitan Opera House, where Roosevelt's sister Corinne and her husband Douglas turn up too.

headline: The British ambassador visits
summary: Ambassador James Bryce and Mrs. Bryce come to Sagamore Hill, along with F. L. Derby.

headline: A fund for the Smithsonian
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Charles Walcott. He writes James Garfield about Ballinger's exit, Scouting and Taft's handling of Mexico; tries, unsuccessfully, to persuade Emma Kennedy to endow a Smithsonian publication fund; complains to Ida Tarbell about a magazine piece on James Gordon Bennett; and sends Charles Willard a long letter on direct democracy.

headline: Corinne's anniversary
summary: It is the 29th wedding anniversary of Roosevelt's sister Corinne. Old friends Winthrop and Margaret Chanler are among the Sagamore guests.

headline: Archie's sleeves, Ethel's proposal
summary: Archie comes home, his long arms poking out of his sleeves. Ethel is torn: Dr. Richard Derby, a 30-year-old surgeon, has proposed.

headline: Back to the Outlook routine
summary: Roosevelt is settled at Sagamore Hill again, often going in to his Manhattan office.

headline: Diplomat Henry White visits
summary: Veteran diplomat Henry White and Florence Lafarge visit. Roosevelt writes Oscar Hallam about a historical point in his essay on the judiciary.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Cornelia Landon visits
summary: Cornelia Landon is a guest at Sagamore Hill.

headline: No 1912 nomination, he insists
summary: Roosevelt writes Groton headmaster Endicott Peabody about his essay on falling birthrates, Constantine Howard about the Bayne Law he helped pass to protect small game, Ted about the warm reception in Wisconsin, and William F. Knox that he will not accept the 1912 nomination.

headline: Murder is murder
summary: The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's piece on the dynamite case. He tells Ida Tarbell what he thinks of the Herald, discusses The Outlook's format, and touches on free trade.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Lodge and Ian Hamilton visit
summary: Senator Lodge and General Ian Hamilton are guests. Roosevelt tells Henry Fairfield Osborn he is at work on an article about protective coloration in animals.

headline: Pressing for direct election
summary: Roosevelt writes Senator William Borah about Central American treaties and direct election of senators, and urges Senator Joseph Dixon to pass the constitutional amendment providing for it.

headline: Americans killed at the border
summary: Fighting across the Mexican border near El Paso, Texas, kills four Americans. Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Stimson to the War Department
summary: Henry Stimson and his wife spend the night at Sagamore Hill. Taft has named Stimson Secretary of War, and he talks the appointment over with Roosevelt.

headline: Taxing the childless
summary: Roosevelt addresses students at DeWitt Clinton High School in Manhattan. He tells John Greenaway he dislikes Taft's handling of the border fighting, and suggests to W. H. Wilmarth taxing unmarried and childless people to reverse a falling birthrate.

headline: On workers' compensation
summary: The Outlook carries Roosevelt's article on workmen's compensation. Clifford and Teresa Richardson visit.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Talking to the clergy
summary: In New York, Roosevelt speaks to a gathering of ministers from the church federation.

headline: A guest at Sagamore
summary: F. W. DeLaw signs the guest book.

headline: Seth Bullock calls
summary: Roosevelt's old Dakota friend Seth Bullock, the Deadwood sheriff and marshal, is among the day's callers.

headline: Welcoming new citizens
summary: In Brooklyn, Roosevelt speaks to immigrants seeking citizenship. He writes British envoy James Bryce about the arbitration pacts Taft proposes, Judge Ben Lindsey on the great money interests, and William Knox that he will not be the 1912 nominee.

headline: Against Taft's arbitration treaties
summary: The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's case against Taft's proposed arbitration treaties with Britain, France and Germany.

headline: Sunday visitors
summary: Four guests sign the Sagamore Hill book.

headline: Pinchot and Garfield come by
summary: Conservation allies Gifford Pinchot and James Garfield visit Sagamore Hill, with Evelyn Irving.

headline: Statehood for Arizona and New Mexico
summary: Roosevelt tells Owen Wister he enjoyed Members of the Family, and urges Lodge to back statehood for New Mexico and Arizona. The bill will pass, only for Taft to veto it.

headline: Concern for Fisk University
summary: Roosevelt writes Harvey Simmons that he is troubled to hear Fisk University, the historically Black school in Nashville, needs money.

headline: Court strikes down workers' comp
summary: The Outlook runs Roosevelt's article on the great moneyed interests. He writes Labor World editor Leon Sutton, upset that New York's highest court has voided the workmen's compensation law, and lays out his views on labor.

headline: Child labor and the Alaska boundary
summary: Roosevelt writes Judge Ben Lindsey about child labor laws. To John W. Foster, who has called his arbitration views inconsistent, he sends a rebuttal that also takes up the Alaska boundary dispute.

headline: Praising Wisconsin progressivism
summary: The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's essays on the Bible in everyday life and on Wisconsin as a model for the nation, praising that state's progressive government.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Answering critics at Grant's Tomb
summary: In Newark, Roosevelt speaks as a new statue of Lincoln is unveiled. At Grant's Tomb that Decoration Day, he criticizes Taft's policies and answers wealthy critics who claim his ideas invite revolution, saying true revolutionaries fear him most.

headline: Tutoring Archie for Harvard
summary: Roosevelt tells Oscar King Davis he has no intention of running in 1912 and notes Stimson's appointment as Secretary of War. He writes Lodge about the arbitration treaty and Lodge's Outlook article on American folk myths. Archie is home studying for Harvard exams, with Edith teaching him French and his father history and civics.

headline: June opens at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt spends June based at his Oyster Bay home, heading into Manhattan often for work.

headline: Writing about House probes and arbitration
summary: Roosevelt warns William Loeb that the new Democratic House means to use investigations of Panama, sugar and steel to embarrass Republicans, and writes James Bryce about warmer ties with Britain.

headline: Outlook essay on the Standard Oil ruling
summary: The Outlook carries Roosevelt's response to the Supreme Court's Standard Oil decision, laying out his updated thinking on how to regulate trusts. Douglas and Corinne Robinson are among the day's visitors.

headline: Sunday at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt spends a quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill; no events are recorded.

headline: An angry letter to John W. Foster
summary: Roosevelt sends John W. Foster a scorching reply to an article he wrote, objecting to several untruths in it, among them words Foster put in John Hay's mouth.

headline: Cardinal Gibbons's jubilee in Baltimore
summary: In Baltimore for Cardinal Gibbons's jubilee, Roosevelt speaks and meets President Taft along with Root, Lodge, Penrose, Sherman and Cannon. Archie Butt later recalled TR trading wisecracks with Taft while others spoke. He also writes Richard Knott on breaking up trusts.

headline: Speaking in White River Junction
summary: Roosevelt gives a speech in White River Junction, Vermont. He also answers Samuel Gompers, who had replied to TR's article condemning the 1910 dynamiting at the Los Angeles Times, and writes Ralph Easley on trusts.

headline: Thanking Mahan for public support
summary: Henry and Margaret White visit Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt writes Alfred Thayer Mahan, whose New York Times letter backed TR's position on arbitration, and touches on the Alaska boundary fight.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: James F. Curtis visits
summary: Roosevelt welcomes James F. Curtis to Sagamore Hill.

headline: Sunday at home
summary: A Sunday at Sagamore Hill with nothing on record.

headline: A batch of letters on arbitration
summary: Roosevelt fills the day with correspondence: to Hiram Collier on pacifists, to novelist Cora Older on her book and Jefferson, to Senator Coe Crawford on pending treaties, and to Lodge on arbitration and Mahan's Panama article.

headline: Calling John W. Foster a liar
summary: Roosevelt writes John W. Foster again, flatly denying that John Hay ever gave Foster a mocking nickname. He also writes historian John Bury about his Romanes Lecture.

headline: Denying a Taft endorsement story
summary: Roosevelt writes editor Edwin Van Valkenburg about an Associated Press report, issued June 7 and denied by TR the next day, claiming he had backed Taft for 1912.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Another day at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record is silent on the day's doings.

headline: Answering Gompers and Otis in print
summary: The Outlook runs Roosevelt's piece on the dynamite charges, taking on both Samuel Gompers and General Harrison Gray Otis. The same day Senator Robert La Follette formally enters the race for the 1912 Republican nomination.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt passes Sunday at home; no events are noted.

headline: Ready to testify on Tennessee Coal
summary: Roosevelt writes James Drain on pacifism, Thomas Warren on his poetry address, John Jackson on garbled reports of his Decoration Day speech, Lodge on Taft and the treaties, and Nick Longworth to say he will testify on Tennessee Coal and Iron if summoned.

headline: Ted and Eleanor's first anniversary
summary: As Ted and Eleanor mark a year of marriage, Roosevelt writes Ted that he likes La Follette but expects Taft to win the nomination, and reports on Archie's Harvard exams. Other letters go to Charles Willard, Gilson Gardner, Hiram Collier and Charles Walcott.

headline: Edward Filene among the callers
summary: A group of visitors comes to Sagamore Hill, including E. H. Madison, Harold Howland and Boston merchant Edward Filene.

headline: Tariff thoughts for Thomas Marvin
summary: Grace Potter visits, and Roosevelt sends Thomas Marvin his views on the tariff.

headline: The Bishops come to Oyster Bay
summary: Joseph Bucklin Bishop and his wife Harriet are among the guests at Sagamore Hill, along with R. Perkins, George Marvin and James Breese.

headline: Weighing in on recalling judges
summary: The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's article on Arizona and the recall of judges.

headline: Sunday at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill for a quiet Sunday.

headline: Archie Butt's prank at Alice's party
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. In Washington, Archie Butt writes of an evening at Alice's home where she sat reading the Bible amid the guests, and he livened things up by pouring mineral water from a White Rock bottle down a diplomat's collar before fleeing home to brace for revenge.

headline: A long family letter to Arthur Lee
summary: With Alice among the day's guests, Roosevelt writes Arthur Lee a wide-ranging letter about the children, Sagamore Hill, animal camouflage and British politics. He also writes Ben Lindsey on child labor, Mahan, James Drain, Henry Wallace and War Secretary Henry Stimson.

headline: Writing Maurice Egan on Europe
summary: Roosevelt writes Maurice Egan, the American minister in Copenhagen, about Denmark and Russia.

headline: Siding with suffrage against Bamie
summary: Roosevelt tells his sister Bamie he supports votes for women, a view she does not share. He also writes Melville Post about a letter printed without his consent and Frank Chapman about Abbott Thayer's angry defense of his camouflage theories.

headline: Last day of June at home
summary: Roosevelt closes out June at Sagamore Hill with no recorded events.

headline: An Outlook piece on Haggard
summary: July finds Roosevelt at Oyster Bay, making regular trips to his Fourth Avenue office in Manhattan. The Outlook prints his article on the novelist H. Rider Haggard and the work of the Salvation Army.

headline: Three young callers
summary: Arnold Hunnewell, E. Dick Jr. and Francis Gray visit Sagamore Hill.

headline: Turning down a Morristown invitation
summary: Hamilton Coolidge visits, and Roosevelt courteously declines Stephen Pierson's invitation to speak to a historical group in Morristown, New Jersey.

headline: A sweltering Fourth
summary: Independence Day at Sagamore Hill is scorchingly hot.

headline: Pushing for a seaside park
summary: Ogden and Helen Rogers Reid visit. Roosevelt urges New York City Comptroller William Prendergast to buy land for an oceanfront park; Rockaway Beach was later acquired.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Saccharin and his health
summary: Roosevelt tells John Queeny that years of using saccharin, which he took in large daily amounts, seem to have done his health no harm.

headline: Defending the canal's management
summary: Roosevelt's Outlook article on running the Panama Canal answers a critical piece by Hayden Talbot printed in the same issue.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt spends a quiet Sunday at home.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Midsummer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events are recorded.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Another quiet July day
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill with nothing on record.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Will Cowles visits; decency essay runs
summary: Roosevelt's brother-in-law Will Cowles is a guest, and The Outlook publishes TR's essay on decency.

headline: Sunday at home
summary: A quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Summer days at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home; the record notes nothing more.

headline: Praise for honest advertising
summary: Roosevelt commends Samuel Dobbs for his work to make advertising truthful.

headline: Why he joined The Outlook
summary: Josephine Osborn visits. Roosevelt writes John Rose a reflective letter about his record and why he took the Outlook job, noting he must provide for his sons. To James West he praises the Boy Scouts as training for citizenship.

headline: The Richardsons arrive
summary: Clifford and Teresa Richardson visit. Roosevelt writes Joseph Bucklin Bishop about Hayden Talbot's Outlook article on the canal.

headline: Taking on Taft over Alaska
summary: Two Roosevelt pieces run in The Outlook. In the one on Alaska he stands by his own administration's record and faults Taft's.

headline: Alice and Nick come to visit
summary: Alice and Nick Longworth are at Sagamore Hill, along with Austrian visitor Hans Gregor Wilczek.

headline: Struggling with a long letter to Trevelyan
summary: Hans Gregor Wilczek stays on. Roosevelt tells George Otto Trevelyan he is dictating an account of his 1910 trip from Khartoum to London but finds it hard to finish, worrying it sounds too self-centered. The letter finally went out October 1.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Taft defends his Alaska record
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill as President Taft sends Congress a message standing behind his Alaska policies.

headline: Championing Captain Charles Young's book
summary: Roosevelt suggests that Harry Judson publish Captain Charles Young's study of military morale. Young was then the only Black officer on active duty in the Army.

headline: Family news for Bamie
summary: Roosevelt thanks Will Cowles for peaches and sends Bamie a chatty letter: Edith wants a new paved road to the house, Teresa Richardson is visiting, Archie is cramming for Harvard and Quentin plays ball with the butler. He also writes Ernest Harvier, George Wickersham and Charles Bonaparte.

headline: Reviewing Houston Chamberlain
summary: Edward Kent visits. The Outlook prints Roosevelt's articles on the initiative and referendum and on Oxford and Kansas, plus his review of a much-discussed book by Houston Stewart Chamberlain.

headline: Memories of baby Ted
summary: Roosevelt writes his daughter-in-law Eleanor about Ted's infancy.

headline: A paved road; Kermit heads west
summary: Workers lay a hard-surfaced road at Sagamore Hill. Kermit goes to visit the Fergusons in Silver City and hunts in the Mexican desert, Ethel is with friends in Maine, and Archie and Quentin are home.

headline: Declining a New Hampshire speech
summary: Roosevelt tells Judge Edgar Aldrich he cannot speak in New Hampshire, and comments on the Post Office Department and the supposed attack on the courts.

headline: August begins quietly
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.

headline: Arbitration treaty goes to the Senate
summary: Secretary of State Philander Knox signs the general arbitration treaty, which is then sent to the Senate for approval. Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Testifying on U.S. Steel
summary: Roosevelt goes into New York City to testify before the congressional committee probing U.S. Steel. The Outlook carries his article on labor unions and class feeling, along with an editorial critical of Taft's Alaska course.

headline: Edith turns fifty
summary: For Edith's 50th birthday Roosevelt gives her a set of Punch drawings she had picked and a surprise thermos pitcher. In the afternoon the two row across to the Mathisons' on Lloyd's Neck.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Asking about air power abroad
summary: Roosevelt writes Richard Knott on price fixing, Albert Walker on his steel testimony, Bamie on Archie's studying and Quentin's new beehive, and General William Wotherspoon with questions about German and Japanese air power.

headline: Telling Ted about the birthday
summary: Roosevelt writes Ted about Edith's birthday and his U.S. Steel testimony, saying he thought it improper to have been called. He also writes Outlook writer William Hulbert about corruption in Alaska.

headline: Kermit in 140-degree heat
summary: While Roosevelt stays at Sagamore Hill, Kermit is in Wellton, Arizona, with Win and Ike Proebstel, where the thermometer reads 140 degrees.

headline: Kermit after desert sheep
summary: Kermit crosses the desert to Tinajas Altas hunting bighorn. At home, Roosevelt writes Congressman Edmond Madison, who with Asher Hinds had mocked George Earle's sugar trust charges, and Arthur Farquhar on breaking up Standard Oil.

headline: Another Alaska broadside
summary: The Outlook prints Roosevelt's second editorial on Alaska, again critical of Taft.

headline: Lunch with Admiral Togo
summary: On Ethel's 20th birthday, Roosevelt lunches with Japan's Admiral Togo, who presents him with small-scale samurai armor and cleans TR's samurai swords.

headline: Backing Lodge's treaty changes
summary: Roosevelt tells Lodge he likes Lodge's proposed amendments to the British arbitration treaty and is surprised the insurgents are dragging out the special session.

headline: Opposing Taft on Alaska lands
summary: Roosevelt writes William F. Knox in dismay at the opening of Alaska public lands to railroads tied to big corporations, a point on which he firmly opposes Taft.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: First grandchild, Grace, is born
summary: In San Francisco, Ted's wife Eleanor delivers a daughter, Grace, the first grandchild of Theodore and Edith. Edith plants pines at Sagamore Hill as a small grove for the baby to play in.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: His account of the 1907 panic
summary: In The Outlook Roosevelt sums up his U.S. Steel testimony about the 1907 panic and the takeover of Tennessee Coal and Iron, granting the steel men may have had mixed motives.

headline: Sunday at home
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday at Sagamore Hill; nothing is recorded.

headline: Admiring Corinne's poem
summary: Roosevelt praises a poem by his sister Corinne and asks Mahan to write The Outlook about the arbitration treaties, which Mahan never does.

headline: Sizing up Taft, Wilson and Pinchot
summary: As Congress's special session ends, Roosevelt writes Rider Haggard, Lodge, Arthur Lee, Spring-Rice and Ted. He confides disappointment in Taft, hopes to retire at 60, calls Pinchot a fanatic, and predicts Wilson could beat Taft.

headline: Rebutting Thayer on animal camouflage
summary: The American Museum of Natural History's Bulletin publishes Roosevelt's paper on concealing and revealing coloration in birds and mammals, a critique of Abbott H. Thayer's theories.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Late summer at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with nothing on record.

headline: Dante and the Bowery
summary: The Outlook runs Roosevelt's essay arguing that Dante wrote about the gritty everyday life of Florence with a frankness no 19th-century author brought to his own hometown.

headline: Lamberts, Bridges and Hapgood visit
summary: Dr. Alexander Lambert and his wife Ellen, editor Robert Bridges and Norman Hapgood spend the day at Sagamore Hill.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Praising Viereck's switch to English
summary: Roosevelt applauds George Viereck for turning his German-language paper into an English one, and writes William Hulbert about Alaska and public ownership of railroads and coal.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Alice and Nick head for Panama
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill as Alice and Nick Longworth set out for Panama.

headline: Open to government coal mining
summary: September opens with Roosevelt dividing his time between Oyster Bay and Manhattan. He tells Frank Knox he is open to the government working Alaska's coal fields itself.

headline: On getting self-government wrong
summary: Edward Kent visits, and The Outlook prints a Roosevelt article on how not to pursue self-government.

headline: Sunday at home
summary: A quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Lunch with a Benedictine abbot
summary: Isabella Hagner visits, and Roosevelt shares a midday meal with Abbot Charles H. Mohr of St. Leo Abbey in Florida, who teaches theology and commercial law.

headline: Nonpartisan city government
summary: Roosevelt writes Ernest Harvier in favor of nonpartisan city government, William Hulbert criticizing Taft's pick of Walter E. Clark as Alaska's governor, and Maurice Egan about notes on Russia and Father John Zahm.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: At home in early September
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the day goes unrecorded.

headline: Bryan calls; treaty attack in print
summary: At The Outlook office, Roosevelt's callers include William Jennings Bryan. His criticism of the arbitration treaty runs in the morning papers, and he writes James Bryce about Dante.

headline: Making the case on arbitration
summary: The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's article laying out his position on the arbitration treaty with Britain.

headline: Sunday guests
summary: Ellen Rogers, Chalmers Wood and Evelyn Irving visit Sagamore Hill.

headline: A long ride with Stimson and Wood
summary: Roosevelt lunches and takes a long ride with Henry Stimson and General Leonard Wood, both of whom share his views on the arbitration treaty. He also urges Frederick Selous, nearly 60, to go on safari again.

headline: Warning of war in Europe
summary: Roosevelt tells Lodge his Outlook colleagues want the arbitration treaty adopted at once while he and Lodge want better wording. He discusses German moves in Morocco and the Congo, possible German marches through Belgium or Switzerland, and the need for a strong French army.

headline: Ted turns 24
summary: Ted celebrates his 24th birthday in San Francisco while his father is at Sagamore Hill.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: A visit to the Children's Court
summary: Roosevelt goes into New York City and visits the Children's Court.

headline: Hunter-naturalist in print
summary: The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's piece on hunting and natural history across two continents.

headline: Sunday at home
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday at Sagamore Hill.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Inviting William Kent to talk
summary: Roosevelt writes Congressman William Kent, a fierce Taft opponent who wants a La Follette and Pinchot ticket, and invites him to Sagamore Hill to discuss politics.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Another day at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events are noted.

headline: Quentin off to Groton
summary: Roosevelt tells Ernest Harvier that Progressives try to do too much, writes Lodge on the treaty and Canada, and urges Ted not to back Wilson over Taft. Archie has finished another round of Harvard exams, and Quentin heads to Groton with a cheeky reply to his mother.

headline: Writing about the Pacific Coast
summary: The Outlook prints Roosevelt's article on West Coast Americans.

headline: Sunday at home
summary: A quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Laid up with rheumatism
summary: Teresa Richardson visits. Roosevelt writes Arthur Lee about Canadian trade and the treaty, mentioning that he is suffering from rheumatism.

headline: Pennsylvania Grangers drop by
summary: At The Outlook in New York, Roosevelt's callers include a party of 100 Pennsylvania Grange members.

headline: Corinne turns fifty
summary: Roosevelt's sister Corinne celebrates her 50th birthday.

headline: Belle Willard visits
summary: Belle Willard, later Kermit's wife, and Gertrude Evans are guests at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Enjoying La Follette's memoir
summary: Roosevelt writes Ernest Harvier about open primaries and tells Senator Robert La Follette he likes the autobiography running in the American Magazine.

headline: Edith badly hurt in a riding fall
summary: Riding at a gallop with Roosevelt and Archie, Edith is thrown from Pine Knot onto the paved road by Cove School and knocked unconscious. TR flags down a delivery wagon whose driver, Benny Vorhis, was an old schoolmate of Ted's, to carry her home; she lies insensible for 36 hours. The Outlook runs his review of Arthur Weigall's book on ancient Egypt.

headline: A fifty-page letter to Trevelyan
summary: Roosevelt finally sends George Otto Trevelyan his marathon letter: why he sent the battle fleet around the world, impressions of the Kaiser and Germany, and a country-by-country tour of his 1910 trip from Khartoum through Rome, Vienna, Paris and Scandinavia to London.

headline: Edith suffering after her fall
summary: Roosevelt writes Ted about Edith's riding accident; she is in severe pain from a headache.

headline: Dr. Rixey comes to treat Edith
summary: Dr. Presley Rixey arrives to care for Edith. Roosevelt writes Lodge about her accident, the Honduras and Nicaragua treaties and the Alaska committee.

headline: At home with Edith
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events are recorded.

headline: Kings squabbling at a funeral
summary: Roosevelt writes Herbert Parsons on Assembly nominations and Corinne in anger at the Barnes-run state party's treatment of her son Teddy. To David Gray he sends a comic sequel to his Trevelyan letter about royals feuding over rank at King Edward's funeral.

headline: Dr. Lambert tends Edith
summary: Dr. Alexander Lambert comes to Sagamore Hill, staying through October 8 to care for Edith.

headline: How the canal rights were won
summary: The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's account of how the United States gained the right to build the Panama Canal.

headline: Village improvement meeting
summary: Roosevelt attends a meeting of the local society working to improve Oyster Bay village.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Edith on the mend
summary: As Kermit turns 22 at Harvard, Edith is gaining ground but recalls nothing of her fall and has lost taste and smell; her headaches are agonizing. Roosevelt brings in a neurologist and a pair of nurses for round-the-clock care. Her ability to smell would never return.

headline: Niece Eleanor turns 27
summary: Roosevelt's niece Eleanor Roosevelt marks her 27th birthday.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Another quiet October day
summary: Roosevelt stays at Sagamore Hill; no events are noted.

headline: Arbitration with Russia, not abrogation
summary: Two Roosevelt articles run in The Outlook. One deals with the Chicago Vice Commission and the post office; the other urges arbitration rather than tearing up the U.S. treaty with Russia.

headline: Sunday at home
summary: Roosevelt spends a quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Progressives back La Follette
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill as the National Progressive Conference calls for direct primaries and endorses Robert La Follette for president in 1912.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Nephew Sheffield turns 13
summary: Bamie's son Sheffield Cowles celebrates his 13th birthday.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Carnegie Hall speech on women and children
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Carnegie Hall on protecting women and children. He thanks Bob Ferguson for career advice to Kermit and writes Lodge about Russia's exclusion of Jews and the treaty, reporting Edith is finally better.

headline: Play sports, don't just watch
summary: In an Outlook article on commercialism and hysteria, Roosevelt urges Americans to take part in sports rather than merely watch them.

headline: Sunday at home
summary: A quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Dodging nomination talk
summary: Roosevelt writes William Allen White about the novel White is working on, says he is steering clear of nomination talk, and sizes up La Follette.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Taft sues U.S. Steel
summary: The Justice Department sues U.S. Steel, implying that Elbert Gary and Henry Frick misled Roosevelt in 1907 when the company bought Tennessee Coal and Iron. Roosevelt is furious.

headline: Turning 53 and weighing a run
summary: On his 53rd birthday Roosevelt tells Marshall Stimson he won't accept the 1912 nomination, yet confides to California's Governor Hiram Johnson that he may be the best one to lead a lost cause. He also writes Charles McCarthy, Ray Stannard Baker and Will Cowles.

headline: Kermit joins the Porcellian
summary: Kermit is elected to Harvard's Porcellian Club, adding to his memberships in Hasty Pudding, DKE, the Sphinx and the Institute of 1770. Roosevelt writes Ernest Harvier and Charles Willard.

headline: Sunday at home
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Edith still weak
summary: Roosevelt tells Ted that Kermit made the Porcellian after one classmate stopped blackballing him, that Edith is better but still frail and headachy, and that the new road cost a lot. He also writes Everett Wheeler about the U.S. Steel suit.

headline: Taft playing politics with steel
summary: Roosevelt tells James R. Garfield he believes Taft is using the U.S. Steel suit for political advantage. The Republican Party is now divided between conservative Standpatters and progressive Insurgents.

headline: November between Oyster Bay and Manhattan
summary: Through November Roosevelt lives at Sagamore Hill and travels often to his New York City office.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Early November at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with nothing on record.

headline: Carl Akeley calls
summary: Naturalist Carl Akeley is among Roosevelt's visitors. The Outlook prints TR's piece contrasting real and sham arbitration, and he writes Henry Stimson about labor and how it is managed in government.

headline: Sunday at home
summary: A quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Voting; nephew Teddy elected
summary: Roosevelt casts his ballot in Oyster Bay on Election Day. His nephew Theodore Douglas Robinson, Corinne's son, wins a State Assembly seat representing Herkimer County.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Ted's letters comfort Edith
summary: Roosevelt tells Ted his letters have cheered Edith, who is walking a little but still cannot taste or smell. He celebrates nephew Teddy Robinson's win over the party bosses and discusses Woodrow Wilson. He also denies to Edwin Van Valkenburg that he endorsed Rudolph Blankenburg for mayor of Philadelphia.

headline: Owen Johnson's college stories
summary: Roosevelt writes Harvard president A. Lawrence Lowell about Owen Johnson's articles on college life.

headline: Kermit home from Harvard
summary: Kermit comes down from Harvard for a visit.

headline: Kermit at home, Ethel away
summary: Kermit spends Sunday at Sagamore Hill while Ethel is away.

headline: Kermit runs cross-country
summary: Roosevelt writes Ted that Edith keeps getting better, that Kermit is on Harvard's cross-country team, and about his forthcoming Outlook article on the trusts.

headline: Keeping religion out of politics
summary: Roosevelt tells Ernest Harvier he will always resist mixing religion with politics. He also writes William Llewellyn on New Mexico and Senate graft, and William Hulbert on Interior Secretary Walter Fisher's plans for Alaska.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Reading Ethan Frome
summary: Roosevelt writes Edith Wharton that Edith is recovering. His wife read Ethan Frome first and passed it to him; he found it powerful.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Good trusts and bad trusts
summary: In The Outlook Roosevelt answers the U.S. Steel suit and attacks the Taft administration's whole approach to trusts, arguing that some combinations are good and others bad.

headline: Quentin turns 14
summary: Quentin celebrates his 14th birthday at Groton.

headline: Writing Bryan on electing senators
summary: Olivia Cutting and the Richardsons visit. Roosevelt writes William Jennings Bryan about electing senators by popular vote and Abbot Charles Mohr about Catholic appointments and prejudice.

headline: Explaining his trust policy
summary: Roosevelt sets out his trust policy for Brooks Adams and writes New York state Senator T. Harvey Ferris about water power.

headline: Judge Learned Hand on recall
summary: Roosevelt explains his thinking on recalling judicial decisions to Judge Learned Hand.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Uneasy about an Ohio endorsement
summary: Roosevelt tells James R. Garfield he is uncomfortable that Toledo's Garfield Republican Club has endorsed him for the nomination.

headline: On lynching and the tobacco trust
summary: On Bamie's 16th wedding anniversary, The Outlook prints Roosevelt articles on the tobacco trust ruling and on lynching. He tells Alexander Moore he still does not want to run.

headline: Lady Gregory visits
summary: Irish playwright Lady Augusta Gregory and Mary Cadwalader Jones are Sunday guests.

headline: Correcting a history of the Cabinet
summary: Roosevelt writes Thomas Lounsbury about his essays, Browning and Kermit's writing, and sends Mary Hinsdale corrections for her Cabinet history, insisting Lodge was never his Senate mouthpiece.

headline: A night at Synge's Playboy
summary: In New York Roosevelt attends Synge's Playboy of the Western World as Lady Gregory's guest. He tells John Yeiser he won't speak but says nothing about withdrawing from Nebraska's primary.

headline: Speaking at Groton
summary: Roosevelt addresses Groton's students and spends time with Quentin. Alice and the Richardsons are with him.

headline: St. Mark's School address
summary: Roosevelt speaks to the boys of St. Mark's School in Southborough, Massachusetts.

headline: December, and no to the nomination
summary: Roosevelt starts December at home in Oyster Bay, often going in to his Manhattan office, and tells James R. Garfield he does not want the nomination.

headline: Silver wedding anniversary
summary: Theodore and Edith mark 25 years of marriage. The Outlook runs his essay on reverent inquiry, discussing books by Thomas Dwight and Émile Boutroux, and he writes George Sheldon, Dan Hanna and James Kennedy about 1904 donations, muckrakers and the nomination.

headline: Telling Sheffield to stick with school
summary: Roosevelt urges his nephew Sheffield Cowles not to quit school.

headline: A warning for Archie Butt
summary: Janetta Alexander visits as Congress reconvenes. In Washington, Alice passes Archie Butt a spoken message from Roosevelt: leave his White House post for his own sake, since the strain is showing.

headline: Nomination would be a calamity
summary: Roosevelt turns down Millard Bloomes's December 30 banquet and discusses treaties. He tells Ben Lindsey a 1912 nomination would be a disaster for him personally, though he would accept it.

headline: Defending a third term in principle
summary: Roosevelt tells Herbert Parsons he doesn't seek the nomination but insists he could rightly serve again after a gap.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: A brief note to Harvier
summary: Roosevelt dashes off a short note to Ernest Harvier.

headline: The American hunter-naturalist
summary: The Outlook publishes Roosevelt's piece on the American hunter-naturalist.

headline: Auchincloss visitors
summary: Priscilla and J. Howland Auchincloss and Cornelia Landon visit Sagamore Hill.

headline: California and the McNamara trial
