summary: Roosevelt writes Charles Willard about California politics, Taft, the Progressives, his possible nomination, and the McNamara brothers' trial for the Los Angeles Times bombing.

headline: Travelers Club in Boston
summary: In Boston Roosevelt attends a Travelers Club meeting. He tells Ray Stannard Baker, a La Follette man, he doesn't want the nomination, and warns Pinchot that George Record's extreme plans drive people away.

headline: Harvard Overseers and Progressive talks
summary: Still in Boston, Roosevelt attends a Harvard Overseers meeting and confers with Progressive Republicans, assuring Baker and Gilson Gardner he won't take the nomination from La Follette. He writes Lodge about his speech against direct democracy and Bishop about avoiding the nomination.

headline: Back at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.

headline: The Grenfells visit; dynamite essay
summary: Young guests and Labrador missionary Wilfred Grenfell and his wife Anna visit. The Outlook prints Roosevelt's 'Murder is Murder' piece on the dynamite case.

headline: Preaching at the Labor Temple
summary: In New York Roosevelt preaches a lay sermon on applied Christianity at the Labor Temple.

headline: Sunday at home
summary: A quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Joking about the nomination
summary: Julian Kerns visits. Roosevelt sends a playful letter to William Allen White about not wanting the nomination, repeats the point to Garfield, and writes George Sheldon about 1904 campaign money.

headline: Bannard briefs Taft
summary: Otto Bannard informs President Taft in Washington that Roosevelt would enter the race should Taft stand aside. TR writes Herbert Croly about his 1900 vice-presidential nomination for Croly's book on Mark Hanna.

headline: A photo for a namesake
summary: Roosevelt writes Benjamin Ide Wheeler on treaties, trusts, the nomination and the field; introduces Medill McCormick to Cecil Lyon; writes Franklin K. Lane; and sends his picture to young Kermit Roosevelt Nothstein, a boy named for his son.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Quentin, taller than his father
summary: The Outlook prints Roosevelt's Carnegie Hall speech on women and children. He writes Archie that Quentin has come home half an inch taller than his father, and tells William Howland he is not a candidate, though he'd accept a draft. Other letters go to Watts, Lodge, Hulbert and Archibald Gracie.

headline: Christmas Eve at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home on Christmas Eve; no events are recorded.

headline: Christmas with chopping and a long walk
summary: Kermit, Archie, Quentin, Alice and Nick, and Laura Roosevelt with her children Oliver and Nick spend Christmas at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt and Nick Longworth chop wood in the morning, and TR takes a walk of three or four hours in the afternoon.

headline: Outgrown by his youngest
summary: Roosevelt writes Ted that Christmas loses some edge when the youngest is taller than his father. He hopes to give Kermit advice and to talk politics with Ted.

headline: Only an overwhelming call
summary: Nick and Alice Longworth visit. Roosevelt tells William F. Knox he would accept the nomination only if public demand were overwhelming.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Remembering Komura
summary: Francis C. Gray visits. Roosevelt writes Japanese diplomat Kogoro Takahira on Jutaro Komura's death, the Portsmouth peace and China.

headline: Denouncing the Russian treaty's end
summary: The Outlook carries Roosevelt's attack on abrogating the treaty with Russia, which was dropped because Russia barred Jewish Americans from travel, and his denial concerning Republican campaign contributions.

headline: Year's end; Ted takes a banking job
summary: Roosevelt ends the year at Sagamore Hill. Around this time Ted joins the New York investment bank Bertron Griscom & Co. and moves with Eleanor and Grace to East 74th Street, and Kermit's article on desert sheep appears in Scribner's.

headline: New Year at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt begins 1912 at Oyster Bay, making regular trips to his Manhattan office.

headline: Staying on Nebraska's ballot
summary: Roosevelt tells George Norris he won't ask to be removed from Nebraska's primary, rebuts stories to Thomas Robins that he was pandering to labor, and writes Jacob Schiff about a remark on Oscar Straus and a 'Jew in the Cabinet' falsely pinned on him.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Lawrence Abbott on TR and Taft
summary: Lawrence Abbott publishes an article in a Cornwall, New York, paper about the relationship between Roosevelt and Taft.

headline: Garfield and Mike Donovan call
summary: At The Outlook, Roosevelt's callers include James R. Garfield and his old boxing teacher Mike Donovan. He writes Lodge about the arbitration treaties.

headline: New Mexico joins the Union
summary: New Mexico enters the Union as the 47th state. The Outlook runs Roosevelt's piece on judges, drawn from his Carnegie Hall speech, and he writes Bernardo San Severino about possible U.S. arbitration between Italy and Turkey, then at war.

headline: Conferring with Stimson
summary: Roosevelt meets with Henry L. Stimson at Sagamore Hill.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Speech at the Aldine Club
summary: Roosevelt speaks at an Aldine Club dinner in New York. He writes Florence Kelley that he could become a fierce suffragist if convinced women would fight sexual vice, and trades notes with William Ward, Herbert Parsons, a Taft man, and Henry Needham about the nomination.

headline: Lunch with McAneny and Prendergast
summary: In the city, Roosevelt lunches with George McAneny and William Prendergast, and urges Senator William Borah to oppose the arbitration treaties unless amended.

headline: Advice to David Goodrich
summary: Roosevelt suggests David Goodrich leave Wall Street for state government in New Mexico.

headline: Edith ill with erysipelas
summary: At The Outlook Roosevelt sees callers including Frankfurter. He tells Bamie he expects Taft to win renomination, ice covers the roads, and Edith, sick with erysipelas, is recovering in the sunny old nursery. He also writes Charles Brown recalling a long-ago Maine trip with Sewall and Dow.

headline: A Roosevelt committee forms in Chicago
summary: Alice and Cornelia Landon visit, and The Outlook prints four Roosevelt pieces. In Chicago, Tribune editor James Keeley, William Ward, Frank Knox and John C. O'Laughlin set up a Roosevelt National Committee against his wishes.

headline: Butt and Corinne talk of the feud
summary: At a luncheon at the Longworths' in Washington, Archie Butt and Corinne discuss the bitterness between Taft and Roosevelt.

headline: Birds' nests and Darwin
summary: Roosevelt praises Francis Herrick's pamphlet on how birds build nests, and discusses Darwin and his theories.

headline: Won't seek it, would accept it
summary: With Roosevelt headquarters now open in Chicago, he tells Frank Munsey he will not chase the nomination but would take it if offered, and recalls how Lincoln weathered press attacks. He writes Senator Elihu Root on the treaties.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is on record for the day.

headline: Planning the governors' letter
summary: On Bamie's 57th birthday, Roosevelt works with Michigan's Governor Chase Osborn to arrange a joint letter from seven Progressive governors urging him to run; his planned reply: he won't go after it, but he would serve if chosen.

headline: Who wrote the Sherman Act
summary: Roosevelt writes former Senator Joseph Foraker about who authored the Sherman Antitrust Act, and Henry Stimson about the U.S. Steel case.

headline: Telling the governors he'll serve
summary: Horace White and Everett Colby call at The Outlook, which runs Roosevelt's article on the George Junior Republic. He writes the Progressive governors that he would run if nominated.

headline: Sunday guests
summary: Eliot Cross, Joseph Burden and Cornelia Landon visit Sagamore Hill.

headline: The political pot boils
summary: Roosevelt dines in the city with social reformers Homer Folks and Edward Devine. He tells Chase Osborn the moment may have arrived to declare himself publicly and writes Will Cowles and William Allen White.

headline: More letters to the governors
summary: Roosevelt confers with the brother of New Hampshire's Governor Bass, a war correspondent, and writes Governors Hadley, Stubbs, Johnson and Bass about the nomination.

headline: Still on the Nebraska ballot
summary: Roosevelt sends a short note to Ernest Harvier and tells Franklin Shotwell his name will stay on Nebraska's primary ballot.

headline: Time to speak out?
summary: Roosevelt writes Kentucky's Governor Augustus Willson that Governor Bass agrees with Willson: the moment has come for TR to declare himself.

headline: Pushing for a children's bureau
summary: Roosevelt lunches in town with Governor Glasscock and Crothers; Norman Hudson and Arthur Hill are guests. He writes White that Governors Hadley and Aldrich advise silence, Perkins on the Palisades and Wilson, Root urging a federal children's bureau, and former Governor John Fort on the nomination.

headline: Lunch with Governor Stubbs
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Kansas Governor Walter Stubbs, Judge Nortoni and John C. O'Laughlin. The Outlook runs his article on the church and the people.

headline: Archie Butt at Sagamore Hill
summary: Archie Butt visits Sagamore Hill, joining a houseful that includes Ambassador Jusserand, Ethel, Ted and Eleanor, and little Grace. Roosevelt has been felling trees that fell across the telephone lines to the house.

headline: Touring a Brooklyn factory
summary: At The Outlook Roosevelt sees Governor Carey, Jacob Riis and Reynolds, then tours a Brooklyn factory with William Redfield. He tells Joseph Bucklin Bishop he doubts he could be elected again, and discusses the canal investigations.

headline: Two letters to Chase Osborn
summary: Roosevelt sends Governor Chase Osborn two letters as they consult about the nomination.

headline: Edith takes a city house
summary: Edith leases Laura Roosevelt's house on East 31st Street in Manhattan so she can enjoy plays, the opera and friends, and above all escape the political commotion at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Home base at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt opens February at Sagamore Hill, running into New York City often as talk of a 1912 candidacy builds.

headline: La Follette stumbles in Philadelphia
summary: A worn-out Senator Robert La Follette gives a rambling talk to publishers in Philadelphia that sinks his own presidential hopes, and many of his backers drift toward Roosevelt. At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt writes to Robert Schauffler about race and stereotypes.

headline: Quiet Saturday at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt spends the day at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further for the day.

headline: Talks with Pinchot and a leaked letter
summary: Roosevelt meets Gifford Pinchot and fires off letters, including an angry note to Hermann Kohlsaat after his January letter to Frank Munsey about the nomination turned up in print.

headline: The Goethals family drops by
summary: At The Outlook offices Roosevelt receives Colonel George Goethals, builder of the Panama Canal, and Mrs. Goethals, and asks William Allen White to come see him about the nomination.

headline: Holding off on an announcement
summary: Roosevelt tells Missouri Governor Herbert Hadley he will wait before declaring for the nomination, writes son-in-law Nick Longworth about his backing of Taft, and hears from Michigan Governor Chase Osborn about direct primaries.

headline: A premature report of his candidacy
summary: A Lincoln Steffens piece in the Washington Star wrongly says Roosevelt has entered the race. Roosevelt writes about his old 1904 pledge against a third term and about La Follette's collapse.

headline: Outlook callers, then home
summary: Roosevelt sees a caller named Hull at The Outlook before heading back to Sagamore Hill.

headline: Seven governors ask him to run
summary: Meeting in Chicago, seven progressive Republican governors, from West Virginia to Wyoming, sign a petition urging Roosevelt to declare for president. He writes William Sulzer about trust legislation.

headline: Speech to the Historical Society
summary: Roosevelt speaks at a New York Historical Society meeting. Edith writes Kermit that his father now feels he must join the fight since La Follette's collapse, and that politics fill her with dread.

headline: Taft goes on the attack
summary: On Alice's 28th birthday, President Taft publicly attacks Roosevelt in New York. Roosevelt writes John O'Laughlin about the race and the bogus report of his candidacy.

headline: Seth Bullock comes calling
summary: Old Dakota friend Seth Bullock and D. C. Collier visit The Outlook. Roosevelt tells Nick Longworth he has to speak out and declare, and notes that Loeb, now a Taft appointee, cannot help him.

headline: A war council at The Outlook
summary: Roosevelt huddles with Pinchot, Bullock, Oscar Straus, California Governor Hiram Johnson and others. Arizona becomes the 48th state. He answers Elihu Root's case against running with his own.

headline: Too tame or too wild?
summary: Amos Pinchot and his brother find Roosevelt's planned Columbus speech too mild; Roosevelt writes back that the Pinchots run a bit too radical. Senator Moses Clapp calls at The Outlook.

headline: Kansas City editor visits
summary: William Rockhill Nelson of the Kansas City Star calls on Roosevelt at The Outlook.

headline: An Outlook essay on industrial justice
summary: Alice and Nick mark six years of marriage, and Roosevelt's article "A Phase of Industrial Justice" runs in The Outlook.

headline: Sunday at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with nothing else recorded.

headline: Between Oyster Bay and Manhattan
summary: Roosevelt shuttles between Oyster Bay and Manhattan; no details survive.

headline: "Purely for a principle"
summary: Roosevelt heads west to Columbus, Ohio. In letters he denies abandoning La Follette and tells Truman Newberry he is in it for principle, though he privately expects Taft to win the nomination.

headline: "My hat is in the ring"
summary: Before the Ohio Legislature Roosevelt delivers "A Charter of Democracy," backing popular recall of judicial decisions, a stand that alarms conservatives and business. Chatting with reporters along the way, he lets it be known that his hat is in the ring. His formal answer to the governors who urged him to run comes three days later.

headline: Back east and denying rumors
summary: Roosevelt returns to New York and writes Edwin Earl to knock down claims that he drinks to excess.

headline: Lunch with city reformers
summary: Roosevelt sees Ward and Halpin at The Outlook and lunches with Prendergast, O'Meara and Curry, then writes Senator Joseph Dixon about organizing the campaign.

headline: Accepting the governors' call
summary: Roosevelt answers the seven governors that he will accept the nomination if it is offered, then dines at Harvard's Porcellian Club. Edith and Ethel set off for South America, and two of his essays appear in The Outlook.

headline: Judge Grant's house at the center
summary: In Boston Roosevelt stays with Judge Robert Grant, whose home suddenly becomes the focus of national attention as the reply to the governors is released. Dinner brings in William Allen White, Arthur Hill and William Thayer.

headline: Backing primaries in Massachusetts
summary: Roosevelt tells the Massachusetts legislature he supports direct nominations and primaries, then shifts his lodging to J. D. Cushing's house. New Hampshire Governor Robert Bass drops by.

headline: Dinner with Harvard's president
summary: Roosevelt confers with Robert Bass and Matthew Hale, dines with Harvard President A. Lawrence Lowell, and stays with W. S. Bigelow.

headline: Harvard Overseers, then home
summary: Roosevelt sits in on a Harvard Board of Overseers meeting in Cambridge, lunches with Arthur Hill, and returns to New York.

headline: Campaign staff takes shape
summary: Roosevelt's campaign team forms: Senator Joseph Dixon runs the New York office, Truman Newberry the Chicago money operation, and John O'Laughlin Washington. He writes Hadley that he is officially in, and tells Will Cowles judicial recall has split him from Lodge.

headline: "Warm personal affection" for Lodge
summary: Roosevelt assures Henry Cabot Lodge that their split over the campaign will not cool his affection, and hosts William Allen White, Regis Post, Judge Hand and others for dinner at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Archie Butt sails for Rome
summary: Torn in loyalty between Taft and Roosevelt, both of whom he served as aide, Major Archie Butt leaves for a rest in Italy. Roosevelt's "The Court of the Children" runs in The Outlook.

headline: Sunday visitors and family
summary: Senator Albert Beveridge and C. B. Landis call at Sagamore Hill, and the guest book records his sister Corinne, her husband Douglas Robinson, Benjamin Ide Wheeler and Frances Theodora Parsons.

headline: A candidate on jury duty
summary: Even mid-campaign, Roosevelt reports for jury service at Mineola. He asks Ormsby McHarg to assure him no Southern votes have been bought.

headline: Grief for Corinne, fire for the fight
summary: Roosevelt writes his sister Corinne in sorrow after her infant grandchild dies of whooping cough. He also tells Andrew Carnegie he has "not changed" and owes a duty to the people, and complains to Matthew Hale that party bosses oppose him.

headline: Alice stops by during jury week
summary: George Perkins calls at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt serves another day on the Mineola jury, and daughter Alice signs the guest book.

headline: Back in the jury box
summary: Roosevelt again sits as a juror at Mineola.

headline: Government "by the people"
summary: Roosevelt writes Senator Joseph Dixon that the progressive fight is about putting the people's will into effect, not prizes for individuals. Six states hold their first direct primaries this year.

headline: A Saturday at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing more is noted.

headline: Judge Lindsey to dinner
summary: Juvenile-court reformer Judge Ben Lindsey and McCormick dine at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Up against "a hard combination"
summary: After another day of jury service, Roosevelt writes Congressman Charles Lindbergh, the aviator's father, about North Dakota, and tells Governor Bass that officeholders, bosses, newspapers and money are stacked against them.

headline: War loans and the ICC
summary: Between jury sessions Roosevelt lunches with Stoddard and Duell, and writes about the North Dakota primary and about taking a stand against loans for international wars.

headline: A meeting with Ward
summary: Roosevelt confers with a man named Ward at Sagamore Hill.

headline: No bodyguard, thanks
summary: Roosevelt declines an offer from former Rough Rider John Rhoades to act as his bodyguard, and complains to Senator Moses Clapp that Massachusetts lacks seasoned leaders. William Draper Lewis and George Rublee visit.

headline: A full house at The Outlook
summary: A stream of supporters, including Amos Pinchot, Beveridge, Perkins, Frank Munsey and Governors Hadley and Glasscock, crowds into The Outlook to see Roosevelt.

headline: Bracing for North Dakota
summary: Expecting to lose North Dakota, Roosevelt tells Dixon to call a La Follette win a progressive triumph since it rebukes the administration. He bristles at Hermann Kohlsaat's plea to quit and notes Taft men purging his federal supporters.

headline: Pure-food crusader calls
summary: Dr. Harvey Wiley and Richmond Pearson visit Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Doubts about winning
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Father York in Huntington and confides to Joseph Bucklin Bishop that he sees no chance of taking the nomination.

headline: La Follette takes North Dakota
summary: Edith and Ethel return from Panama, Tobago and Costa Rica. In North Dakota's primary La Follette wins 34,123 votes to Roosevelt's 23,669, with Taft far behind at 1,876. A delegation of Black New Yorkers from Harlem visits The Outlook.

headline: Carnegie Hall case for popular rule
summary: At Carnegie Hall Roosevelt makes the case for popular government, calling for leaders who dream greatly, and clarifies that recall would never apply to judges or the Supreme Court.

headline: "Much alone here"
summary: Owen Wister signs the guest book. Roosevelt thanks North Dakota's campaign manager and writes Arthur Lee in England that he feels isolated, rates his chances very low, and is moved by Lee's loyalty.

headline: Off to Maine
summary: Roosevelt leaves Sagamore Hill for Portland, Maine.

headline: Speaking in Portland
summary: In Portland Roosevelt meets with Robert Bass, McCormick, F. Hale and Frank Dingley, then gives a speech.

headline: Friends across a political divide
summary: After meetings in Portland Roosevelt returns to New York, where he and Edith see Cabot and Nannie Lodge; the two men keep their friendship intact despite their split.

headline: Stumping on the East Side
summary: Roosevelt gives speeches on Manhattan's Lower East Side.

headline: Crushed in the New York primary
summary: In a deliberately confusing New York primary with a ballot 14 feet long, Taft routs Roosevelt, who wins just 13 delegates. Roosevelt sets out on a Western speaking tour and thanks John St. Loe Strachey for defending him in the British press.

headline: Fort Wayne and Chicago
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Fort Wayne, Indiana, and in Chicago.

headline: Rallying Missouri
summary: In St. Louis Roosevelt gives speeches and meets with his Missouri backers.

headline: Whistle-stops across Iowa and Minnesota
summary: Roosevelt speaks at ten stops in a single day, from Cedar Rapids and Waterloo in Iowa to the Twin Cities of Minnesota.

headline: Through Michigan to Milwaukee
summary: The tour crosses Michigan with six speeches, ending in Detroit, then pushes on to Milwaukee.

headline: Home to sad news
summary: Roosevelt returns to New York and Oyster Bay. Aunt Lizzie dies, and his old friend Henry Adams is disabled by a stroke.

headline: Catching breath at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill between campaign swings; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Heading south to campaign
summary: After seeing Duell and George Henry Payne at The Outlook, Roosevelt leaves on a speaking swing through the South.

headline: Fourteen stops in two states
summary: Roosevelt works his way by rail through southern West Virginia, from Ronceverte to Huntington, then across Kentucky, ending the day in Louisville.

headline: Along the Ohio River
summary: More rear-platform speeches carry Roosevelt from Point Pleasant and Parkersburg in West Virginia to Covington, Augusta and Maysville in Kentucky.

headline: Martinsburg, then west
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Martinsburg, West Virginia, and boards a train for Chicago.

headline: Ten Illinois towns in a day
summary: Roosevelt barnstorms Illinois from Rockford to Springfield. Back east, Collier's Weekly prints Kermit's hunting story "After Moose in New Brunswick."

headline: Easter at Lincoln's tomb
summary: On Easter Sunday in Springfield, Roosevelt lunches with Illinois Governor Charles Deneen and visits Abraham Lincoln's grave.

headline: Downstate Illinois and Indiana
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Danville, Decatur, Mattoon, Urbana and other Illinois towns, then in Peru and Fort Wayne, Indiana.

headline: First primary win: Illinois
summary: Roosevelt carries the Illinois primary two to one over Taft, his first victory, taking 56 of 58 delegates. New York's Republican convention goes for Taft. It is also Archie's 18th birthday, and Roosevelt speaks in Pittsburgh.

headline: Crossing Pennsylvania
summary: Roosevelt speaks his way east across Pennsylvania from Jeannette to Philadelphia. He wires Medill McCormick that Illinois was a win over bosses and money, and laments delegates lost in Michigan, Kentucky and Indiana conventions.

headline: Last Pennsylvania stops
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Easton, Reading and Allentown before returning to New York and Sagamore Hill.

headline: Into New England
summary: Roosevelt leaves Oyster Bay for New England and speaks in Springfield, Massachusetts.

headline: Pennsylvania delivers
summary: Roosevelt wins the Pennsylvania primary, taking 55 of 64 delegates, while he campaigns through Worcester and other Massachusetts towns and on to Nashua, Concord and Manchester in New Hampshire. Alice signs the guest book.

headline: The Titanic goes down with Archie Butt
summary: As Roosevelt returns home, the liner Titanic, bound for New York, collides with an iceberg and goes down in the North Atlantic. Among the dead is Major Archie Butt, his former military aide, coming home from his rest in Europe.

headline: Westward again
summary: Roosevelt leaves Sagamore Hill on another Western speaking trip.

headline: Talk of a third party
summary: Speaking across western Illinois and southern Iowa, Roosevelt writes Michigan Governor Chase Osborn that a third party is possible should party bosses steal the nomination, and blasts the Taft managers' tactics.

headline: Hastings and Omaha
summary: Roosevelt takes his campaign into Nebraska with speeches in Hastings and Omaha.

headline: No debate with Gardner
summary: Roosevelt crisscrosses southeastern Nebraska with ten speeches. By telegram he refuses Congressman Augustus Gardner's challenge to debate, and answers Gardner's claims that he went easy on Morgan-backed trusts.

headline: Sweeping Nebraska and Kansas
summary: Roosevelt wins all 16 Nebraska delegates, polling 46,795 votes to La Follette's 16,785 and Taft's 13,341, and takes most of Kansas. Edith tells Arthur Lee his hair is curling hard, which she jokingly credits to psychic electricity.

headline: His voice gives out
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Oklahoma and in three Arkansas towns, including Little Rock, then wires Oscar King Davis that his voice is failing and the rear-platform speeches must stop. "On Natural Resources" appears in The Outlook.

headline: Rolling toward North Carolina
summary: Roosevelt spends Sunday traveling to North Carolina.

headline: Greensboro and Salisbury
summary: Roosevelt campaigns in North Carolina with speeches in Greensboro and Salisbury.

headline: Taft takes New Hampshire
summary: Roosevelt heads home as Taft wins New Hampshire's primary by about two votes to one.

headline: Puzzled by "Gussy"
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge wondering why Lodge's son-in-law, Congressman Augustus Gardner, has attacked him personally, and discusses Lodge's letters about Senators Lorimer and Crane.

headline: Taft fights back, then weeps
summary: In Boston President Taft finally answers Roosevelt, charging him with breaking his no-third-term pledge, flip-flopping on Canadian reciprocity, and pushing recall; offstage Taft breaks down in tears. Roosevelt has already been calling Taft a "fathead" on the stump.

headline: Firing back in Worcester
summary: Roosevelt leaves for Massachusetts and, in Worcester, tosses aside his prepared text to tell a roaring crowd that Taft has deliberately twisted his record.

headline: Southeastern Massachusetts swing
summary: Roosevelt speaks in six towns between Brockton and Fall River, finishing the day in Boston.

headline: Strategy in Boston
summary: Roosevelt plans strategy with Baxter, Arthur Hill and Matthew Hale and stays with W. S. Bigelow. Edith writes Kermit that his reserved manner, like her own when young, can be mistaken for indifference.

headline: Mill towns to the Berkshires
summary: On Corinne's 30th wedding anniversary, Roosevelt speaks in Lowell, Lawrence, North Adams and Pittsfield, then returns to New York and Oyster Bay.

headline: "A fight of minutemen"
summary: Taft narrowly edges Roosevelt in the Massachusetts primary, 86,722 votes to 83,099, though eight at-large delegates pledge to Roosevelt. Roosevelt sweeps Oregon's 10 delegates, and Washington State's results are in dispute.

headline: Bowing to the Massachusetts vote
summary: Roosevelt says he will honor the Massachusetts preference vote and tells his at-large delegates to back Taft, though they later stay with him at the convention. Pennsylvania's state convention hands him all 12 at-large delegates on top of his 55 from the primary.

headline: Off to Maryland
summary: After callers Matthew Hale and C. H. Thompson, Roosevelt leaves for Maryland. He explains to Lodge why he held off criticizing Senator Crane before the Massachusetts vote.

headline: Eastern Shore to Baltimore
summary: Roosevelt campaigns in Salisbury and Havre de Grace and in Baltimore.

headline: Taft vows to hit hard
summary: While Roosevelt works western Maryland from Westminster to Cumberland, Taft tells a Hyattsville crowd that though he is a man of peace, he will hit hard when cornered.

headline: Home for Sunday
summary: Roosevelt travels back to New York and Sagamore Hill.

headline: Planning Ohio with Garfield
summary: At Sagamore Hill Roosevelt meets Walter F. Brown and James Garfield, both key to his Ohio effort.

headline: Thin support in New York
summary: Four callers, Amos Pinchot among them, visit The Outlook. Roosevelt writes Paul Murphy about his meager backing in New York State.

headline: Dinner with the Garfields
summary: Ward calls, and James and Helen Garfield and Grace Alexander are guests; the Roosevelts dine with the Garfields.

headline: Protecting Nick
summary: Roosevelt writes Nick Longworth about Ohio and instructs Walter Brown that nothing in the campaign should set him against his son-in-law.

headline: On Buddhism
summary: Roosevelt sends William Sturgis Bigelow his thoughts on Bigelow's Buddhism book.

headline: "I never drink whisky at all"
summary: Roosevelt refuses to be filmed with Boy Scouts, calling it cheap, and tells George Payne he drinks no whisky and no wine on the road. He bars his committee from buying liquor that critics could use against him.

headline: Quiet Sunday
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no further activity is recorded.

headline: "Egotist" and "demagogue"
summary: As Roosevelt leaves for Ohio, Taft brands him an egotist and a demagogue. Roosevelt writes Elon Hooker about the crooked New York primary of March 26.

headline: California comes through
summary: Roosevelt barnstorms a dozen eastern Ohio towns from Bellaire to Canton and wins California's primary and all 26 delegates, though Taft claims two from San Francisco. He tells Arthur Lee that Taft is "a good bit of a blackguard."

headline: Fourteen stops and an insult
summary: Roosevelt speaks in fourteen Ohio towns from Kenton to Dayton. In Chicago, real estate man R. M. Patterson tells the newspapers Roosevelt is insane.

headline: Northwest Ohio to Toledo
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Greenville, Piqua, Lima and Defiance before ending in Toledo.

headline: Southern Ohio to the capital
summary: From Ironton on the Ohio River, Roosevelt campaigns north through Chillicothe, Athens and Lancaster to Columbus.

headline: Marion to Cleveland
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Marion, Delaware, Mansfield and Akron and closes the day in Cleveland.

headline: Sunday with the Garfields
summary: Roosevelt rests at Mentor, Ohio, as a guest of James and Helen Garfield.

headline: Through the Muskingum valley
summary: Roosevelt's final Ohio swing runs from Marietta through Zanesville and Newark to New Philadelphia.

headline: Taft beaten in his home state
summary: Roosevelt wins Taft's own Ohio, 165,809 votes to 118,362, with La Follette at 15,570, taking 34 of 42 delegates. Alice backs her father while the Longworth family stands with Taft, leaving Nick caught in the middle.

headline: A day at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill between campaign trips.

headline: A dozen New Jersey towns
summary: Roosevelt speaks across northern New Jersey from Paterson to Jersey City. He writes about Little Missouri roundups, Denver elections, and convention plans, pushing Governor Hadley over Elihu Root for temporary chairman.

headline: South Jersey to Trenton
summary: Roosevelt campaigns from Burlington through Egg Harbor City and Atlantic City to Camden and Trenton, and writes T. R. McAnally about the contested Washington primaries.

headline: Shore towns and McGovern
summary: Roosevelt speaks in eleven central New Jersey towns from Trenton to Elizabeth and tells Senator Dixon he wants Wisconsin Governor Francis McGovern as the convention's permanent chairman.

headline: No strings attached
summary: At Sagamore Hill Roosevelt meets Senator Dixon and Medill McCormick, and writes Dixon that he welcomes industrialists like T. Coleman du Pont but will promise them nothing.

headline: Northern New Jersey, and a weary Edith
summary: Roosevelt campaigns from Hoboken and Bayonne west to Phillipsburg. At home, Edith apologizes in a note to Ethel for being stern, writing that she has much to bear.

headline: New Jersey goes for Roosevelt
summary: Roosevelt wins the New Jersey primary. He urges Senator Clapp to fund more battleships, discusses Trevelyan's new book, declines to pick a running mate, and seeks a convention alliance with La Follette's delegates.

headline: Bound for Gettysburg
summary: Roosevelt dines with Regis Post and Reynolds in New York, then leaves for Gettysburg.

headline: Decoration Day at Gettysburg
summary: Roosevelt gives a Memorial Day address on the Gettysburg battlefield and returns to New York.

headline: "Hold a separate convention"
summary: Roosevelt has now won primaries in nine states, from Illinois to Oregon. He accuses Taft of stealing delegates and wires Arizona allies to meet on their own if unseated.

headline: Illinois delegates come calling
summary: A delegation from Illinois visits Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill, along with McNinch, Revell, F. Hale and C. Dewey.

headline: A full Sunday guest book
summary: Ted and Eleanor visit Sagamore Hill along with Evelyn Irving, the Leigh Hunt family, Hapgood, Hand, Joseph Cutting and George Rublee.

headline: Rival conventions in Arizona
summary: Roosevelt confers with Perkins, Gifford Pinchot, Frank Kellogg, Senator Dixon and others. Arizona's Republican convention picks only Taft delegates, and Roosevelt's backers there meet on their own.

headline: Against Root as chairman
summary: Roosevelt tells William Kent he will fight Elihu Root's selection as temporary convention chairman, and explains his views on recall to Sydney Brooks.

headline: Planning with Pinchot
summary: Roosevelt plans with Hapgood, Judge Hand, McCormick and Gifford Pinchot at Sagamore Hill.

headline: National Committee convenes
summary: The Republican National Committee opens its sessions in Chicago. Roosevelt talks with Pittsburgh boss William Flinn, editor Van Valkenburg and publisher Alexander Moore, and writes Lorenzo Lake about federal help after the Mississippi floods.

headline: Hearst in the wings
summary: Roosevelt tells Oscar Straus that William Randolph Hearst will back him if the Democrats nominate Bryan or Wilson. Enrique Fernandez of Costa Rica signs the guest book.

headline: Platform ideas for Borah
summary: Roosevelt urges Senator William Borah to put conservation, government railroads and harbors for Alaska in the Republican platform; the Progressives later adopt them.

headline: Sunday strategy
summary: Roosevelt meets with Richmond Pearson and Truxtun Beale at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Masons on the lawn, a wire to Chicago
summary: Some 400 Masons from three North Shore towns gather on the lawn while Perkins, Munsey and Walter Brown talk platform inside, and two telegraphers in the Gun Room keep a direct line to Chicago. Roosevelt tells Lyman Abbott how much he enjoys working at The Outlook.

headline: "No longer a Republican"
summary: Roosevelt writes that Kermit has taken a job with the Brazil Railroad Company, asks that a Black delegate second his nomination, and tells James B. Reynolds he no longer considers himself a Republican.

headline: Judge Lindsey again
summary: Roosevelt meets Judge Ben Lindsey; a caller named Fort also stops in.

headline: A guest at Sagamore Hill
summary: Eleanor Greene signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.

headline: Called to Chicago
summary: Alarmed supporters summon Roosevelt after the National Committee hands Taft 238 of 254 contested seats, about a third of the convention. He and Edith leave for Chicago.

headline: Arriving with Roman history in hand
summary: Roosevelt and Edith reach Chicago with books of Roman history and a primary tally of 1,157,397 votes to Taft's 761,716. He speaks at the Congress Hotel and meets McCormick, Dixon, Pinchot, Garfield and Cecil Lyon.

headline: Seventy delegates short
summary: Roosevelt is 70 delegates shy of nomination. His daughter Alice with Nick, Kermit, and Ted and Eleanor join him in Chicago as he confers with allies.

headline: "We stand at Armageddon"
summary: After meetings with the seven progressive governors, Perkins, Dixon and Pinchot, Roosevelt gives a speech Edith and Alice helped review to a progressive rally at the Coliseum, closing with a call to battle for the Lord.

headline: Root takes the gavel
summary: The Republican National Convention opens, and Elihu Root, a Taft man, wins the temporary chairmanship and rules to seat the Taft delegates. Roosevelt keeps meeting with his allies.

headline: Hadley's motion fails
summary: The convention votes down, 564 to 510, Governor Hadley's motion to keep disputed delegates from voting on their own contests. Roosevelt confers with allies.

headline: Perkins and Munsey pledge their money
summary: As the Credentials Committee argues over seats, George Perkins and Frank Munsey meet Roosevelt late into the night and agree to fund an independent Progressive campaign. Perkins soon becomes his de facto manager. It is Ted and Eleanor's second anniversary.

headline: "Toot! Toot!"
summary: With ruling after ruling going to Taft, Roosevelt delegates scrape sandpaper and toot like a steamroller. Allies including Senator Borah, Perkins, Straus and Governors Johnson and Stubbs call on Roosevelt.

headline: "Thou shalt not steal!"
summary: The Republicans renominate Taft and Sherman; Taft gets 561 votes, Roosevelt 107, and 349 delegates sit out. Roosevelt brands the proceedings void, and his followers gather at the Chicago Opera House to call a new party convention.

headline: Organizing for the fight ahead
summary: Roosevelt sets up committees for the new campaign in Chicago, while Alice and Nick take the train back to Washington.

headline: Heading home
summary: After a last round of talks with progressive leaders, Roosevelt and Edith leave Chicago for Oyster Bay.

headline: Building a new party
summary: Roosevelt shares lunch with editor Albert Shaw, Father John Zahm, Dean George Kirchwey and others, and writes about organizing the Progressive Party. Alice and Nick travel to watch the Democratic convention in Baltimore.

headline: A talk with Prendergast
summary: Roosevelt confers with William Prendergast; Delano Andrews and Teresa Richardson sign the guest book.

headline: Brooklyn bolters
summary: Roosevelt meets George Perkins and a group of Brooklyn Republicans who have broken with the party, and writes about the fraudulent convention.

headline: "A fight that must be made"
summary: As the Democratic convention deadlocks, Roosevelt hopes Champ Clark wins. He tells Rider Haggard the fight is worth making, discusses protective coloration with Frank Chapman, and writes Hadley that the Republican Party is finished as a tool for reform.

headline: Opera House speech in print
summary: The Outlook publishes the speech Roosevelt gave at the Chicago Opera House on June 22.

headline: First film at Sagamore Hill
summary: Cameras record Roosevelt at home for the first time: riding his horse Sidar, romping with three dogs, and chopping down a tree with Archie's help. Kermit and Alice tour the African specimens at the Smithsonian, and Ted's wife Eleanor and their baby Grace are staying at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Wary of a progressive Democrat
summary: R. S. McCormick calls, and Roosevelt warns William Dudley Foulke that a progressive Democratic nominee would likely carry the election.

headline: Democrats choose Wilson
summary: On the 43rd ballot in Baltimore, the Democrats nominate New Jersey's reform governor Woodrow Wilson, with Alice and Kermit watching. Roosevelt lunches with Dixon, Munsey, Croly and Outlook editors and writes that Wilson's nomination makes his own path much harder.

headline: Settling on a run
summary: Roosevelt meets Perkins, Munsey and Flinn and writes Herbert Knox Smith about his decision to run for president.

headline: Independence Day meeting
summary: Roosevelt spends the Fourth at Sagamore Hill conferring with C. H. Thompson.

headline: Osborn defects to Wilson
summary: Roosevelt confers with McCormick, Dixon, Perkins and Stoddard, and writes Governor Chase Osborn, who has publicly backed Wilson, and Paul Ewart about false drinking stories.

headline: Dissecting Taft's majority
summary: Callers including Ransom, Heney and Merriam visit, and Roosevelt meets Perkins. His analysis of how Taft's convention majority was built runs in The Outlook.

headline: The call for a Progressive Party
summary: A general call goes out to form a Progressive Party. General Daniel Sickles, Curry and E. Colby visit Sagamore Hill.

headline: New York Progressives arrive
summary: A group of New York Progressives, with Chadbourne and W. M. Chandler, calls at Sagamore Hill.

headline: How far down the ticket?
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Hotchkiss and writes Will Cowles and others on whether Progressives should run for lesser offices or only the top of the ticket. He warns Madison Peters that backing Wilson means backing the bosses.

headline: "A forlorn hope"
summary: Herbert Knox Smith visits. Roosevelt thanks poet William Watson for a sonnet, admitting his cause this year is a forlorn hope, and writes about weak Iowa support and wavering insurgents.

headline: Pettigrew and Butler call
summary: Former Senator Richard Pettigrew and M. Butler visit Sagamore Hill.

headline: Delaware Progressives visit
summary: A Delaware Progressive delegation, Woodruff, A. P. Moore, Heard and Allee call. Roosevelt writes about the tariff and about presidential electors.

headline: "Thou Shalt Not Steal" in print
summary: Roosevelt's article "Thou Shalt Not Steal" appears in The Outlook, and he writes Herbert Knox Smith about flaws in the Democratic platform.

headline: Van Hise and Dr. Lambert
summary: Wisconsin's Charles Van Hise and Henry Cochems call, and Dr. Alexander Lambert, Helen Leigh Hunt and Henry Morgan are guests.

headline: Calling the nomination fraudulent
summary: Roosevelt writes Governor Hadley that he regards Taft's nomination as fraudulent.

headline: A Great Lakes-to-Gulf waterway
summary: Roosevelt admits to W. F. Cochran his odds are small, refuses shared Taft-Roosevelt electors, and tells LaVerne Noyes a navigable channel from the Great Lakes to the Gulf would rival the Panama Canal in importance.

headline: Strategy with O. K. Davis
summary: Roosevelt meets Dixon, Perkins and Oscar King Davis and writes Robert Bass about third-party tickets.

headline: Social reformers shape the platform
summary: Roosevelt brings social reformers to Sagamore Hill to draft the Progressive platform, among them Homer Folks, Raymond Robins, Walter Weyl, Henry Moskowitz, the Kellogg brothers and Samuel McCune Lindsay.

headline: Hadley stays Republican
summary: Roosevelt writes Albert Nortoni about Governor Hadley's decision to remain with the Republicans.

headline: "Men Who Live Softly"
summary: Progressive leaders including Charles McCarthy, George Record and Herbert Knox Smith gather at Sagamore Hill for strategy. Roosevelt's "Men Who Live Softly" appears in The Outlook.

headline: The Osborns visit
summary: Cochems calls, and Henry Fairfield Osborn and his wife Josephine, along with Hamilton Fish Jr., sign the guest book.

headline: Lithuanian voters in Chicago
summary: Roosevelt meets William Flinn and writes Medill McCormick about Lithuanian support in Chicago.

headline: Rallying New York's county leaders
summary: Roosevelt meets 48 Progressive county chairmen from across New York State at the Metropolitan Tower, and writes about New England support and Governor Deneen's backing of Taft.

headline: On Black equality
summary: Alice visits. Roosevelt writes O. J. Moore about Cummins and boss rule in the Republican Party, and Rev. Bradley Gilman on equality for Black Americans.

headline: Minnesota and local Progressives
summary: Roosevelt meets Progressives from Minnesota and Oyster Bay and writes F. A. Johnson about third-party tickets.

headline: A blank day
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Kermit sails for Brazil
summary: Roosevelt's first diary entry of the year notes Kermit sailing via England for a railroad job in Brazil. A Freeport delegation calls, and an Outlook article attacks the Democratic platform as insincere. Alice, kept from the convention, is home to see Kermit off.

headline: Sunday with Dixon
summary: Roosevelt talks politics with Dean George Kirchwey and Senator Dixon.

headline: At home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with no other details recorded.

headline: Race and the new party
summary: A delegation of Black voters from three states, Virginia among them, visits The Outlook. Roosevelt writes on Black voters and Booker T. Washington's support of Taft, jokes that Croly could write his biography, and clarifies he has no contract with The Outlook.

headline: Vermont Progressives visit
summary: A group of Vermont Progressives calls on Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill.

headline: The question of Southern delegates
summary: Roosevelt writes Julian Harris, whose father created Uncle Remus, about Black delegates to the coming Progressive convention, favoring the white Southern delegations. The stance leaves Southern delegations all white and alienates Black voters, many of whose leaders, including Booker T. Washington, back Taft.

headline: A note to Munsey
summary: Roosevelt writes Frank Munsey about the campaign.

headline: Deciding on Black delegates
summary: At Chicago's Congress Hotel, the party's provisional committee gathers to settle whether Black Southern delegates will be seated. Roosevelt writes Horace Plunkett his analysis of Wilson and the Democratic platform.

headline: To the Bull Moose convention
summary: Roosevelt and Edith board a train west for the new party's national convention in Chicago.

headline: The Progressive convention opens
summary: Just after 12:40 in the afternoon the new party's convention opens at the Coliseum before 10,000 people and 2,000 delegates from every state except South Carolina. Beveridge delivers the keynote. The committee votes not to seat the Black Southern delegates.

headline: A "Confession of Faith"
summary: On Edith's 51st birthday Roosevelt gives a 52-minute "Confession of Faith" laying out the New Nationalism: direct election of senators, unemployment insurance, an end to child labor, a minimum wage, and initiative, referendum and recall.

headline: Nominated by the Bull Moose party
summary: The Progressives nominate Roosevelt for president and California Governor Hiram Johnson for vice president. Jane Addams seconds Roosevelt, the first woman to address a major party convention.

headline: A platform for the people
summary: The convention adopts a platform calling for trust regulation, farm credit, direct primaries, woman suffrage, a tariff commission, safer factories, a minimum wage, an eight-hour workday and no child labor. Roosevelt thanks Jane Addams and heads home with Edith, who tells Kermit of red bandannas and the "Battle Hymn of the Republic."

headline: Back to Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt travels home through Manhattan to Oyster Bay.

headline: "Better contented"
summary: Roosevelt writes Cecil Spring-Rice that though he is probably losing, with the press and most cultivated opinion against him, he has never been more contented. Ted's wife Eleanor visits.

headline: A quiet Sunday
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing more is noted.

headline: Thanking Judge Lindsey
summary: Roosevelt wires Judge Ben Lindsey his thanks for a seconding speech at the convention.

headline: Ethel turns 21
summary: On Ethel's 21st birthday Roosevelt meets Perkins, Dixon, Bird, Judge Lindsey and O. K. Davis. The family picnics on Jayne's Hill, and Roosevelt walks there with Archie and young Nicholas Roosevelt.

headline: Tennis, and a forecast
summary: Roosevelt tells Arthur Lee that Wilson will win but he will outpoll Taft; he likes Wilson but doubts he is a true progressive. He also plays tennis with Ethel, joined by Archie, and talks late with Nicholas.

headline: Defending his Vatican stand
summary: Roosevelt answers charges that his 1910 Vatican episode alienated Catholics, plans how to win over Taft-pledged Republican electors, and explains again why he is running.

headline: Infantry Hall in Providence
summary: After meeting Dixon, Perkins and Prendergast at The Outlook, Roosevelt travels to Providence and speaks at Infantry Hall.

headline: Eighteen thousand on Boston Common
summary: Roosevelt addresses up to 10,000 people at the Point of Pines Hotel in Revere, speaks again to Progressives indoors, then draws 18,000 on Boston Common. It is granddaughter Grace's first birthday.

headline: Sunday at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no more is recorded.

headline: Ted visits
summary: Ted signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.

headline: Bird for governor
summary: Lindbergh, E. Colby and Heney call. Roosevelt asks Governor Robert Bass to urge Charles S. Bird, the governor's father-in-law, to seek the Massachusetts governorship.

headline: A priest's golden jubilee
summary: Roosevelt leaves for Wilkes-Barre to honor Father Curran's fiftieth jubilee. He writes Hermann Hagedorn about a poem to the Progressives and asks Gifford Pinchot for material against the Democrats, including his conservation pamphlet.

headline: The campaign officially begins
summary: Roosevelt formally opens his campaign with speeches in Wilkes-Barre. Edith asks Corinne to send him good books: history, science, or a novel where he can play the hero.

headline: Home again
summary: Roosevelt returns to New York and Sagamore Hill.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home; no further activity is recorded.

headline: The Loebs visit
summary: George Fred Williams and William Loeb with his family call at Sagamore Hill.

headline: A home day
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill with nothing else noted.

headline: Prendergast calls
summary: William Prendergast visits Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Answering the money charges
summary: Before leaving for Vermont, Roosevelt sends Senator Moses Clapp a long letter on Senate probes of 1904, 1908 and 1912 campaign gifts, including the Harriman money, Penrose's charges, and Perkins. He also praises a Catholic group fighting indecent plays and films.

headline: Western Vermont with Metzger
summary: With gubernatorial candidate Fraser Metzger beside him, Roosevelt speaks from Bennington north to Burlington.

headline: Suffrage in St. Johnsbury
summary: Roosevelt speaks across northern Vermont, and at St. Johnsbury he backs votes for women and rebuts Senator Boies Penrose's attacks.

headline: Southern Vermont swing
summary: Roosevelt finishes in Vermont with speeches in Barre, Randolph, Windsor, Bellows Falls and Brattleboro. A caller named Churchill visits.

headline: "Never was there a fight better worth making"
summary: Back home before heading west, Roosevelt tells his sister Corinne the campaign is a draining but worthy fight, and he looks to election day as the end of a battle.

headline: Connecticut kickoff
summary: Roosevelt launches his long campaign tour with four Connecticut speeches, from Stamford to Hartford.

headline: Three states in a day
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Mattoon, Illinois, Indianapolis, and St. Louis.

headline: Dawn in Keokuk
summary: Starting at 7 a.m. in Keokuk, Roosevelt speaks across Iowa to Des Moines, where he meets Senator Albert Cummins.

headline: Fifty thousand at the State Fair
summary: Roosevelt draws some 50,000 at the Minnesota State Fair grounds in St. Paul and rides in a Minneapolis parade. In Syracuse, New York Progressives nominate Oscar Straus for governor.

headline: Back in North Dakota
summary: Roosevelt campaigns in North Dakota, speaking at Grand Forks, Fargo and Jamestown.

headline: Across Montana
summary: Roosevelt speaks his way west through Miles City, Billings, Livingston and Bozeman to Helena, where he takes on Wilson.

headline: Straus over Prendergast
summary: Leaving Helena for Spokane, Roosevelt writes Oscar Straus that though he had wanted Prendergast for governor, Straus is the stronger candidate.

headline: Rallies with women voters
summary: In Spokane, where women already vote, Roosevelt speaks and attends two women's rallies.

headline: Seattle and Tacoma
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Seattle and Tacoma.

headline: Portland, Oregon
summary: Roosevelt gives speeches in Portland.

headline: Boise and Borah
summary: After more Oregon stops, Roosevelt speaks in Boise and confers with Senator William Borah.

headline: Ted turns 25
summary: On Ted's 25th birthday, Roosevelt speaks in Blackfoot and Pocatello, Idaho, and Ogden, Utah.

headline: Answering the New Freedom
summary: After stops in Reno, Sacramento and Oakland, Roosevelt delivers in San Francisco a full rebuttal of Wilson's "New Freedom," titled "Limitation of Governmental Powers."

headline: "What a fine fight it is"
summary: In San Francisco Roosevelt lunches with Benjamin Ide Wheeler and meets Heney, Pinchot and Pardee. He writes Corinne that the trip is wearing but the fight is fine, and writes Loeb, who will testify to the Senate about the 1904 Harriman gift.

headline: 200,000 in Los Angeles
summary: Crowds estimated at 200,000 line the Los Angeles streets, and Roosevelt speaks at the Shrine Auditorium before heading on.

headline: Phoenix
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Arizona, including Phoenix.

headline: Laguna and Albuquerque
summary: Roosevelt campaigns in New Mexico at Laguna and Albuquerque.

headline: Taking on the trusts in Colorado
summary: Roosevelt speaks from Trinidad through Pueblo and Colorado Springs to Denver, hammering the trusts.

headline: On film in Pueblo
summary: Motion pictures capture Roosevelt speaking in Pueblo, Colorado. He then campaigns in Nebraska at Hastings, Lincoln, Minden and Omaha.

headline: Kansas allies gather
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Ottawa and Topeka and confers with Senator Joseph Bristow, Victor Murdock, Governor Stubbs, W. R. Nelson and William Allen White.

headline: Sunday at William Allen White's
summary: Roosevelt spends the day in Kansas as the guest of editor William Allen White.

headline: Kansas into Missouri
summary: Roosevelt campaigns through southeastern Kansas towns such as Pittsburg, then crosses into Missouri for Lamar, Springfield, Aurora and Monett.

headline: Through Oklahoma
summary: Roosevelt campaigns in Tulsa, Chandler, Oklahoma City and McAlester.

headline: Waterways in Little Rock
summary: In Little Rock, Roosevelt speaks to a group promoting a Great Lakes-to-Gulf waterway.

headline: Memphis and Jackson
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Tennessee at Memphis and Jackson.

headline: A French Quarter parade
summary: On Corinne's 51st birthday, Roosevelt parades through New Orleans's French Quarter and gives a speech.

headline: Alabama and Atlanta
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Montgomery, Opelika and other Alabama towns and in Atlanta.

headline: Hecklers, then his mother's home
summary: Hecklers badly disrupt Roosevelt's Atlanta speech. He visits Roswell and Bulloch Hall, his mother's girlhood home.

headline: East Tennessee swing
summary: Roosevelt speaks at four East Tennessee stops, from Chattanooga to Knoxville. Funk publishes his collection "Conservation of Womanhood and Childhood."

headline: Bull Moose campaign crosses North Carolina
summary: Roosevelt carries the Progressive campaign through North Carolina, stopping at Raleigh, Durham, Burlington, Salisbury, Asheville and Hickory.

headline: Home to Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt heads back to Sagamore Hill after the southern swing.

headline: Strategy sessions at Sagamore Hill
summary: At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt meets a stream of Progressive allies and advisers, among them Senator Joseph Dixon, Frank Munsey, Oscar King Davis and his cousin George Roosevelt.

headline: Testifying on campaign money in Washington
summary: Roosevelt appears before a Senate committee probing campaign contributions, then tours the National Museum. He spends time with General and Mrs. Albert L. Mills, Senator Moses Clapp, John Callan O'Laughlin and John McIlhenny.

headline: Back to New York; thanks to Henry White
summary: Roosevelt returns through New York City to Sagamore Hill. He writes diplomat Henry White to thank him for a gift to the campaign.

headline: Praise for Corinne's first poems
summary: Roosevelt meets Oscar Straus, Governor Hiram Johnson, Frank Munsey, George Perkins and others at Sagamore Hill. He writes his sister Corinne admiring her first book of verse, The Call of Brotherhood, and admits the campaign has been costly to his friends.

headline: Off on a Great Lakes speaking tour
summary: Roosevelt leaves Sagamore Hill to begin a campaign tour through the Great Lakes states.

headline: Whistle-stops across Michigan
summary: The campaign train rolls through Michigan, with Roosevelt speaking at Detroit, Flint, Saginaw and Bay City.

headline: Upper Michigan campaign stops
summary: Roosevelt keeps campaigning in Michigan, reaching Marquette, Cheboygan and Houghton.

headline: Campaigning in Duluth
summary: The tour crosses into Minnesota, with Roosevelt speaking at Duluth. A family 23rd birthday falls on this day.

headline: Wisconsin stops, including Oshkosh
summary: Roosevelt campaigns in Wisconsin, including a stop at Oshkosh. A Roosevelt family member turns 28.

headline: Hoarse at the Chicago Coliseum
summary: After a parade, Roosevelt tears into Wilson and the New Freedom before more than 12,000 at the Chicago Coliseum, his voice worn ragged from weeks of speaking; Alice is in the hall. A Michigan paper, the Iron Ore, smears him as a liar, a curser and a drunk.

headline: Voice gone; speeches canceled
summary: With his voice spent, Roosevelt calls off planned appearances in Wisconsin, Indiana and Illinois. He dines with Alice and with Medill and Ruth McCormick, and the talk turns to the campaign.

headline: Shot in Milwaukee, he gives the speech anyway
summary: Leaving the Gilpatrick Hotel for an evening speech, Roosevelt is shot in the chest by John Schrank. He begs the crowd to spare the gunman, then delivers all 50 pages of his address with the bullet in him, holding up his bloodied shirt. The folded manuscript and his glasses case slowed the bullet, which cracked a rib and stopped short of his lung.

headline: Recovering at Mercy Hospital
summary: Roosevelt lies in Chicago's Mercy Hospital on Prairie Avenue. Alice arrives from Cincinnati while Edith is still on her way, and Father Vattman and Albert Beveridge stop in.

headline: Edith reaches his bedside
summary: Edith arrives in Chicago with Ethel, Ted and Dr. Alexander Lambert, met by Alice. Father Curran visits, and both Wilson and Taft halt their campaigns while Roosevelt is laid up. Edith writes Bamie that he is doing well but she fears infection.

headline: From his hospital bed: keep fighting
summary: Roosevelt issues a statement urging that the campaign go on without him. Jane Addams visits, and Beveridge carries a message from him to a Louisville audience. Edith tells her sister Emily the wound is no bigger than a dime and shows no infection.

headline: Bacon and Johnson at the bedside
summary: Robert Bacon and Governor Hiram Johnson call on Roosevelt at Mercy Hospital. His nephew Sheffield Cowles turns 14.

headline: A hospital stay he calls a spree
summary: Francis Heney reads reporters Roosevelt's answer to Wilson's charges. Visitors include Oscar King Davis and Governor Johnson. Roosevelt dictates a letter to Bamie from bed, saying the days with Edith and the children have been a treat; Edith adds that he tires easily.

headline: A quiet Sunday in the hospital
summary: Roosevelt spends the day mending at Mercy Hospital.

headline: Discharged and homeward bound
summary: Roosevelt and Edith leave Chicago by train for Sagamore Hill. Edith writes Kermit in South America that his father is improving and reading magazines in his berth.

headline: Home again, and a demand to Bryan
summary: Roosevelt and Edith reach New York and go on to Sagamore Hill. He writes William Jennings Bryan insisting he retract printed misstatements of Roosevelt's views on trusts and monopoly.

headline: Perkins and Lyman Abbott call
summary: At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt receives George Perkins and Lyman Abbott. Cecil Lyon signs the guest book.

headline: Journalists at Sagamore Hill
summary: Mark Sullivan, Finley Peter Dunne, Robert Collier and Cecil Lyon visit Roosevelt. He thanks Senator William Flinn for writing after the shooting.

headline: Campaign advisers return
summary: George Perkins, Frank Munsey and Frederick Hotchkiss call on Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill.

headline: On his feet too soon for Edith
summary: Barely a week and a half after the shooting, Roosevelt is out of bed and moving around Sagamore Hill, much to Edith's dismay.

headline: A 54th birthday with the family
summary: The family gathers at Sagamore Hill to celebrate Roosevelt turning 54. He writes Bamie that he loved her gift and feels strong, though the wound has not yet closed.

headline: First press meeting since Milwaukee
summary: For the first time since he was shot, Roosevelt is permitted to see reporters. Frederick Davenport calls, and Roosevelt tells Henry Cabot and Nannie Lodge he is on the mend.

headline: Accepting the risks of public life
summary: Roosevelt answers a worried letter from the historian George Otto Trevelyan, saying a man in public life must reckon with the chance of being shot.

headline: A 41-minute ovation at Madison Square Garden
summary: Still weak, Roosevelt speaks to 16,000 about what the Progressive Party stands for packed into Madison Square Garden. The crowd cheers for 41 minutes until he pounds a table and calls for quiet. Corinne and Douglas have to slip past the guards; Edith watches from a box with Ethel, Ted, Eleanor and Quentin.

headline: Dixon and Perkins visit
summary: Senator Joseph Dixon and George Perkins call at Sagamore Hill in the last days of the race.

headline: Rallying for Oscar Straus
summary: Roosevelt returns to Madison Square Garden to speak for Oscar Straus, the Progressive candidate for governor. He also writes Frederick Selous hoping he can bag a fine bull giant eland for the museum in Kensington.

headline: Lunch with Frances Kellor
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Frances Kellor at Sagamore Hill. A message from him runs in Collier's, and he sends Ernest Harvier a note about the race.

headline: Sunday lunch with Alice and Jacob Riis
summary: Alice Longworth and the reformer Jacob Riis join Roosevelt for lunch at Sagamore Hill two days before the election.

headline: Last speeches on Long Island
summary: On election eve Roosevelt speaks close to home in Oyster Bay and Mineola. He writes Beveridge, Straus and other Progressive candidates that the fight was worth making whatever the outcome.

headline: Election Day: Wilson wins, Roosevelt runs second
summary: Roosevelt casts his ballot in Oyster Bay. Woodrow Wilson takes the presidency with 435 electoral votes; Roosevelt, carrying six states and 88 electoral votes, finishes ahead of President Taft. In New York, Straus loses the governor's race, Franklin Roosevelt keeps his state Senate seat, and Nick Longworth loses his House seat by 97 votes.

headline: Taking stock with Progressive leaders
summary: The day after the defeat, Roosevelt meets George Perkins, Frank Munsey, Senator Dixon, Governor Johnson and Amos and Gifford Pinchot at Sagamore Hill. Edith writes Kermit that the outcome was no surprise.

headline: Retelling the Milwaukee shooting
summary: At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt walks a visitor, his young cousin Nicholas Roosevelt, through the attempt on his life in Milwaukee in close detail.

headline: We kept the faith, he tells Garfield
summary: Roosevelt goes to The Outlook, where Hotchkiss, Bainbridge Colby and Senator Dixon call. He writes James Garfield that the Progressives have nothing to regret, and writes Andrew Rahn on Minnesota, a state he carried while the party lost locally.

headline: A guest at Sagamore Hill
summary: A guest identified as S. Farr signs in at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Sunday at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more.

headline: The Progressives are here to stay
summary: Roosevelt tells the press the new party will endure. He answers Gifford Pinchot's ideas for its future, such as a Washington headquarters and a salary for Dixon, but rejects his doubts about William Flinn and George Perkins.

headline: Cheers for Spring-Rice; Schrank in court
summary: In Milwaukee, John Schrank is arraigned and plainly insane. Roosevelt congratulates his old friend Cecil Spring-Rice on becoming British ambassador to the United States, and writes Henry White, Henry Summers and Seth Bullock that the new party must keep its independence.

headline: Standing by Flinn and Perkins
summary: Roosevelt, dividing his time between Sagamore Hill and the city, again defends William Flinn and George Perkins, chairman of the party's executive committee, in a letter to Gifford Pinchot.

headline: Shoring up local Progressive groups
summary: Mark and Marie Sullivan visit. Roosevelt writes Charles Willard about keeping the Progressives going, with more praise for Perkins, and tells New Hampshire's Governor Robert Bass that local organizations need building up.

headline: Explaining Milwaukee to Edward Grey
summary: Roosevelt writes Britain's Foreign Secretary, Sir Edward Grey, summing up the election and describing the shooting, including why he gave his speech before going to the hospital.

headline: Ruth Draper visits; Quentin glad it's over
summary: Ruth Draper, Bill Bird and Alice Longworth are guests at Sagamore Hill. From Groton, Quentin writes his mother that school is gloomy and he is relieved the election is done. Roosevelt tells Ben Lindsey he regrets nothing and Perkins deserves support.

headline: Edith's worries about Ted
summary: Edith writes Kermit that Ted spends too much time at the Brook Club and that Eleanor may not see it.

headline: At home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded.

headline: Woman suffrage and a woman in the cabinet
summary: Roosevelt speaks to a gathering of party leaders at the Holland House on Quentin's 15th birthday. He tells British suffragist Millicent Fawcett he favors equal footing for women and would have named Jane Addams to his cabinet, and writes on antitrust policy, judicial recall and party feuds.

headline: Belle Willard visits
summary: Belle Willard is a guest at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt writes Benjamin Ide Wheeler about the Progressives and the incoming Wilson administration.

headline: At home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.

headline: Schrank ruled insane; a bird quarrel
summary: A Milwaukee court formally finds John Schrank insane. Roosevelt writes Witmer Stone objecting to an article in The Auk that disputes his views on protective coloration, and sends two letters on Maine politics.

headline: Writing on the Balkans
summary: Roosevelt's article on the Balkans appears in The Outlook. He writes Charles Merriam agreeing with his thoughts on the party and the income tax, and touches on Perkins.

headline: At home
summary: A quiet Sunday at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Bamie's wedding anniversary
summary: Roosevelt's sister Bamie marks 17 years of marriage.

headline: Looking ahead to a party convention
summary: Roosevelt sends Ernest Harvier a brief note and writes Governor Hiram Johnson about the coming Progressive convention.

headline: At home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events are recorded.

headline: Thanks to a supporter
summary: Roosevelt writes Richard Newton to thank him for standing with him.

headline: Visitors at The Outlook
summary: In New York, Gifford Pinchot, William Draper Lewis and Roosevelt's nephew Theodore Douglas Robinson call on him at The Outlook.

headline: Where the children are this fall
summary: Cecil Spring-Rice reaches Washington as Britain's ambassador. Ted is selling bonds for a New York firm and often brings Eleanor and baby Grace to Sagamore Hill; Archie is a student at Andover's Phillips Academy, and Quentin, at Groton, has a nose broken by a hockey stick.

headline: Edith on Alice's hard season
summary: Edith writes Kermit that Alice looks sick and exhausted and has struggled with Nick, who cannot accept losing his seat in Congress.

headline: Twenty-six years married
summary: Roosevelt and Edith mark their 26th wedding anniversary at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Worried for Edith, writing to Kermit
summary: Roosevelt meets William Prendergast and his nephew Theodore Douglas Robinson. He tells Kermit, traveling in South America, that Edith has not been well since a riding fall a year earlier. Other letters go to Selous, to Fanny Parsons about what a striving boy can achieve, and to two Maine correspondents.

headline: A note to Edna Ferber
summary: Roosevelt writes Edna Ferber about his campaign remark that one of her characters ought to have married. He also advises Ruth Hanna McCormick that her husband Medill ought to keep his Springfield seat rather than run for the Senate, and writes Mark Sullivan and Walter Emerson on party matters.

headline: A long letter to Amos Pinchot
summary: Oliver W. Roosevelt is a guest. Roosevelt writes Amos Pinchot at length on Perkins, trusts and antitrust policy, the party platform, race, and Lincoln's stand on slavery.

headline: Charles Duell visits
summary: Charles H. Duell signs the Sagamore Hill guest book.

headline: Fairman Dick visits
summary: Fairman Dick is a guest at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Special train to Chicago
summary: Roosevelt sets out for a Progressive conference in Chicago aboard a train chartered by party members from New York and New England.

headline: Speaking to Illinois Progressive lawmakers
summary: In Chicago, Roosevelt speaks to the state legislators who joined the Progressives.

headline: Opening the Progressive conference
summary: Roosevelt opens the Progressive conference at the La Salle Hotel before some 1,500 delegates and speaks again at a crowded evening dinner. He writes his old friend Bob Ferguson about the Balkan war and the Pinchots' attacks on the party's moderates.

headline: Keeping Perkins as chairman
summary: The Progressive National Committee debates moving headquarters to Washington and whether to keep George Perkins as chairman; Roosevelt has come to Chicago to block the push to remove him. He is a guest at a Progressive women's luncheon honoring Jane Addams and dines with her that night.

headline: Leaving Chicago
summary: Roosevelt starts home for New York and Sagamore Hill.

headline: Preparing the libel suit
summary: Back in New York, Roosevelt writes James Pound, his Detroit lawyer in the libel case against editor George Newett of the Ishpeming Iron Ore, about witnesses to his sobriety. He also defends Perkins to Francis Heney and writes George Record on the Sherman Act plank.

headline: At home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing more is recorded.

headline: Ambassador Whitelaw Reid dies
summary: Whitelaw Reid, the American ambassador to Great Britain, dies; Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.

headline: On the man who shot him
summary: Writing to the British editor John St. Loe Strachey, Roosevelt argues that Schrank was less a madman than a man of criminal temperament who knew where to strike, and says he bears him no ill will.

headline: At home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events noted.

headline: Few hopes for his own future
summary: Mark and Marie Sullivan visit again. Roosevelt writes Sir Henry Lucy that he expects little from his own political prospects.

headline: Lawrence Abbott visits
summary: Lawrence Abbott of The Outlook signs the guest book.

headline: Praise for a book of parodies
summary: Roosevelt compliments Franklin P. Adams on his new collection of parodies, In Other Words, and writes E. C. Bowler about Maine politics.

headline: Explaining his stand on Perkins
summary: Roosevelt meets with Joseph Alsop and Herbert Knox Smith, and lays out his position on Perkins to Gifford Pinchot. Both Pinchots object to Perkins as too wealthy and not radical enough.

headline: Sunday guests
summary: Edwin Mead, Chalmers Wood Jr., and Philip and Katherine Weld sign the Sagamore Hill guest book.

headline: Two bills, two opinions
summary: Roosevelt writes Senator Joseph Bristow about bills for an industrial commission and for electing postmasters; he favors the first and is cool toward the second.

headline: Snowbound Christmas Eve
summary: A blizzard sweeps over Sagamore Hill.

headline: Christmas stockings in Edith's drawing room
summary: The family opens stockings and gifts in Edith's drawing room, with Ted, Eleanor, Archie, Quentin and Grace Alexander on hand. Roosevelt is sorry that little Gracie must stay away because of the storm.

headline: Family in the guest book
summary: Esther Rowland, Ted, Eleanor and Alice Longworth are recorded as guests.

headline: Elected to lead the historians
summary: In Boston, Roosevelt is elected president of the American Historical Association and delivers his address 'History as Literature.' He stays with William Sturgis Bigelow and tells Ben Lindsey the party team is pulling together.

headline: Military historians in Boston
summary: Roosevelt addresses the Military Historical Society in Boston.

headline: Edith's low point with Ted
summary: Jack Wiley and Clifford Rochman are guests. Edith writes Kermit that Ted chose lunch at the Ritz with business contacts over a trip to Sagamore Hill, and calls it his low point.

headline: Answering the drinking rumors
summary: Nicholas Roosevelt is a guest. Roosevelt writes James Keeley about the 'Take me to Murphy at Mercy' rumor and claims that he drank heavily in Mercy Hospital.

headline: A trade risk, he tells Spring-Rice
summary: Roosevelt returns to Sagamore Hill and writes a stack of letters: telling Spring-Rice that being shot is simply a hazard of public life, discussing Panama Canal tolls, a white slavery bill and an industrial commission, and urging the defeat of Republican Edwin Burleigh for the Senate.

headline: New Year between home and the city
summary: Roosevelt begins 1913 at Sagamore Hill, making regular trips into New York City.

headline: At work on his autobiography
summary: Roosevelt has started writing his memoirs. Lawrence Abbott of The Outlook is a guest.

headline: Letters on electors and a mother's burden
summary: Roosevelt writes four senators about Progressive electors barred from the 1912 ballot. A woman writes him that raising a big family has held her back, a letter he later cites in his autobiography. He also wires a protest after Progressive newspapermen are jailed in Boise.

headline: A walk with Edith to Cooper's Bluff
summary: Roosevelt and Edith take a stroll to Cooper's Bluff. He thanks her sister Emily for two books of simple Italian stories and reports that Edith is mending but weak, with Ethel handling the mail, checkbook and household.

headline: No fusion in Connecticut
summary: Roosevelt meets Connecticut Progressives about whether to merge forces with the Republicans.

headline: Between home and the city
summary: Roosevelt splits the day between home and Manhattan; no details survive.

headline: Writing Brander Matthews on race
summary: Roosevelt writes about Progressive electors, the Industrial Commission bill, and, to his friend Brander Matthews, about race problems in America.

headline: At home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Senate races
summary: Roosevelt writes Senator Joseph Bristow about Senate elections.

headline: At home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

headline: A novel for a weary mother
summary: Roosevelt answers the woman who wrote on January 3 about her large family, sending her Kathleen Norris's novel Mother. He also writes James Bryce with news and Dan Hanna about the party.

headline: At home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

headline: At home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Resisting a merger with the Republicans
summary: Martha Wadsworth visits. Roosevelt tells Charles Bonaparte he opposes any fusion of Progressives and Republicans, and writes Bishop Charles Brent that Wilson could turn out a good President.

headline: At home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

headline: At home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

headline: At home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Garment strikers and a full guest book
summary: On Bamie's 58th birthday, Roosevelt talks with Miss Doty about striking garment workers. A crowd of guests, Father Zahm among them, signs in, and his Outlook article on white slavery appears.

headline: Hester Chanler visits
summary: Hester Chanler is a guest at Sagamore Hill.

headline: At home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Visiting the garment strikers
summary: Roosevelt goes into the city to see striking garment workers at St. Mark's Place and on Henry Street. The mother he wrote to sends her thanks, and he writes several letters about West Virginia politics.

headline: Witness in the U.S. Steel case
summary: At The Outlook, Roosevelt sees Henry Moskowitz, Bourke Cockran and John Purroy Mitchel. He testifies in a special examination in the government's U.S. Steel case, and lays out for Robert Vessey and other correspondents where he stands on the party.

headline: Prisons and Indiana greetings
summary: Roosevelt writes R. G. Anderson about American prisons and sends greetings to Indiana Progressives through A. W. Tracy.

headline: Siding with the garment workers
summary: Roosevelt has lunch with leaders of the garment strike. He writes Michael Schaap, Progressive floor leader in the state Assembly, that he stands firmly with the union, and reports on his visit to the strikers.

headline: A case for workmen's compensation
summary: Collier's publishes Roosevelt's 'Sara Knisley's Arm,' an argument for a workmen's compensation law.

headline: At home
