summary: Roosevelt is aboard the Aidan, heading home.

headline: At sea, bound for New York
summary: Roosevelt is aboard the Aidan, heading home.

headline: At sea, bound for New York
summary: Roosevelt is aboard the Aidan, heading home.

headline: A quiet, thin homecoming
summary: Roosevelt lands in New York 35 pounds lighter, on a cane, helped by two men, and jokes about his 'big stick.' His wife Edith and sons Ted and Archie are waiting; there are no crowds or parades. Edith and Dr. Lambert have the yacht Joyance carry him to Oyster Bay.

headline: Politics resumes at Sagamore Hill
summary: Home one day, Roosevelt meets with Perkins and Pinchot; Frances Kellor, Lillian Wald and Dr. Lambert call. He writes Ruth and Arthur Lee about his exploring, the skeptics, and his new grandson.

headline: Oyster Bay welcomes him home
summary: Roosevelt sees Robert Bacon at The Outlook, and Oyster Bay holds an official homecoming. He writes General Francis V. Greene that he would raise a cavalry regiment if war with Mexico came.

headline: A full house of Progressives
summary: Roosevelt meets with William Flinn, Pinchot, Wilkinson, Perkins, Oscar King Davis, Robert Bass and Knox. Stoddard, Mark Sullivan and Edmund Heller call. He writes Dan Hanna about the elections and Progressivism and thanks Charles Fairbanks.

headline: Planning the trip to Britain
summary: Roosevelt talks politics with his nephew Theodore Douglas Robinson, Garfield and Arthur Garford; Regis Post visits. He writes Ambassador Walter Hines Page about his coming British visit.

headline: A pound a year younger
summary: Roosevelt meets with V. K. Kellogg, Victor Murdock, Perkins, Bourke Cockran and William Loeb. Edith writes Kermit that her husband looks a year younger for each pound lost.

headline: Callers at Sagamore Hill
summary: Visitors include John Callan O'Laughlin, Albert Beveridge, Alsop, Schaffer, and Judge Ben Lindsey with Mrs. Lindsey.

headline: Brazil lecture in Washington
summary: In Washington Roosevelt tours the National Museum, attends a Lodge reception, and calls on President Wilson. He meets Progressive members of Congress including Garfield, Murdock, Clapp, Butler, Falconer and Pettigrew, then speaks about Brazil before the National Geographic Society.

headline: Testimony in a miners' case
summary: At The Outlook Roosevelt sees Felix Frankfurter and Walter Lippmann, then gives testimony to a special commission in a coal miners' lawsuit. Edith writes Ruth Lee.

headline: New York Progressives confer
summary: Roosevelt meets at home with Theodore Douglas Robinson, Perkins, Frank Munsey, Frederick Davenport, Hamlin, Bird and Ransom.

headline: More Progressive talks
summary: Robinson, Perkins, Davenport, Hamlin and Bird return for discussions, and Alexander P. Moore, Medill McCormick and Albert Shaw call.

headline: Sailing for Kermit's wedding
summary: After meeting Perkins, Moore and McCormick at Progressive headquarters, Roosevelt boards the Olympic with his daughter Alice and Philip Roosevelt, bound for Spain and Kermit's marriage to Belle Willard, daughter of the American minister there. Edith stays behind.

headline: Crossing the Atlantic
summary: Roosevelt is at sea on the Olympic, heading for Europe.

headline: Crossing to Europe
summary: Roosevelt is at sea aboard the Olympic on his way to Kermit's wedding.

headline: Standing by Perkins
summary: From shipboard Roosevelt writes George Perkins about demands that he leave the Progressive Party, saying that if Perkins is pushed out, he will go too.

headline: Still on the Atlantic
summary: Roosevelt remains at sea on the Olympic.

headline: Still on the Atlantic
summary: Roosevelt remains at sea on the Olympic.

headline: Landing at Cherbourg
summary: Roosevelt comes ashore in France at Cherbourg.

headline: A busy day in Paris
summary: Roosevelt sees the sights of Paris, lunches with Gabriel Hanotaux and calls on President Poincaré. Philippe Bunau-Varilla and T. P. O'Connor visit, and Ambassador Myron Herrick hosts him for dinner.

headline: Breakfast with Edith Wharton
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts with novelist Edith Wharton and receives Mrs. Cornelius Vanderbilt before he and Alice leave Paris for Madrid.

headline: Arriving in Madrid
summary: In Madrid the Roosevelts dine at the American embassy and lodge with the Willards, the family of Kermit's bride.

headline: Lunch with the King of Spain
summary: A couple of hours by motorcar take the Roosevelts to the country palace of Spain's King Alfonso XIII and his queen, Victoria Eugenie, for lunch; Alice recalls the royal pair as very cold. Roosevelt also talks with Spanish journalists.

headline: El Greco in Toledo
summary: Roosevelt tours the Prado and travels out to Toledo for its El Greco paintings, then dines at the American embassy.

headline: Kermit marries Belle Willard
summary: Roosevelt and Alice witness Kermit's civil wedding to Belle Willard in Madrid, with Philip Roosevelt as best man. Roosevelt writes Edith hopefully about the couple and tells Wolfgang Joerg about the Brazil expedition, then goes back to the Prado.

headline: Off to London
summary: Roosevelt sets out for London while Alice remains in Europe.

headline: Welcomed in London
summary: In London, Roosevelt is greeted by Ambassador Walter Hines Page, the Archbishop of Canterbury and his old friend Arthur Lee. He lunches with Page, and geographer J. Scott Keltie calls.

headline: A grandson named Theodore
summary: Roosevelt is Arthur Lee's guest at Chequers Court in Buckinghamshire. In America, Ted and Eleanor welcome a son, Theodore Roosevelt III.

headline: Films of Scott's Antarctic journey
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Sir Edward Grey and watches motion pictures of Scott's Antarctic expedition. James Bryce calls, and he dines with Lee and Lord Northcliffe.

headline: Brazil talk to the Royal Geographical Society
summary: After seeing Westminster Abbey and London's natural history museum, and lunching with Lee, Selous, Harry Johnston and Francis Younghusband, Roosevelt addresses the Royal Geographical Society on his Brazilian exploration and dines with the Geographical Club.

headline: The National Gallery and old friends
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts with the Bishop of London, sees the National Gallery, visits Dr. St. Clair Thomson, and lunches with Arthur Balfour, Gilbert Murray and J. B. Bury.

headline: Homeward on the Imperator
summary: Roosevelt leaves for America aboard the Imperator.

headline: At sea, homeward
summary: Roosevelt is crossing the Atlantic on the Imperator.

headline: Ted and Eleanor's anniversary
summary: Roosevelt remains at sea while Ted and Eleanor mark four years of marriage.

headline: Crossing the Atlantic
summary: Roosevelt is at sea on the Imperator.

headline: Crossing the Atlantic
summary: Roosevelt is at sea on the Imperator.

headline: Crossing the Atlantic
summary: Roosevelt is at sea on the Imperator.

headline: Back home to Sagamore Hill
summary: The Imperator reaches New York, and Roosevelt heads home to Oyster Bay.

headline: Urged to run for governor
summary: A large group of Progressives, including Perkins, Robinson, Hotchkiss, Hamlin, Childs, Davenport, John M. Parker and William Draper Lewis, gather at Sagamore Hill and press Roosevelt to seek the governorship of New York.

headline: Progressive strategy at home
summary: Roosevelt meets with Perkins, Medill McCormick, Albert Beveridge, John M. Parker and Holland Duell, and writes Dwight Heard about the Progressive Party.

headline: Doctor's orders: rest the voice
summary: After talks with Senator Moses Clapp, Wanamaker and Frank Munsey, Roosevelt hears from Dr. Lambert that his larynx cannot stand a speaking tour. He is told to rest for four months.

headline: Shots in Sarajevo
summary: At Sagamore Hill Roosevelt is at home as news breaks of Archduke Franz Ferdinand's assassination in Sarajevo. Alice, still in Europe, attends the Grand Prix race in France.

headline: Leaving The Outlook
summary: Roosevelt rows on the Sound, gives up his editorial post at The Outlook in a letter to Lyman Abbott, and tells Arthur Lee that politics swallowed him the moment he got home.

headline: Back on the stump in Pittsburgh
summary: After a Progressive League banquet, Roosevelt gives his first big speech since 1912 at Exposition Hall, blasting the Republican Old Guard and Wilson's economics. He returns home groggy with jungle fever; Edith and Lambert order months of rest. The family gathers, and Ted joins a Philadelphia investment firm.

headline: A throat specialist's verdict
summary: Roosevelt lunches at the natural history museum with its president, Henry Fairfield Osborn and has his throat examined by a Manhattan specialist, Dr. H. Holbrook Curtis, who links his slack vocal cords to malaria. Perkins and Governor Hadley call at headquarters. He writes Samuel McCall and Hiram Johnson.

headline: Guests at Sagamore Hill
summary: The Mitchels and Judge and Mrs. Ransom are guests at the house.

headline: A day at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.

headline: Rowing Edith 16 miles
summary: For a Fourth of July picnic at Lloyd Neck, Roosevelt rows Edith eight miles out and eight back, while the younger family members drive over.

headline: Quiet Sunday
summary: Roosevelt is at home; no events are recorded.

headline: Against state-run railroads and prohibition
summary: Roosevelt tells William Allen White he opposes government ownership of the railroads and a ban on liquor.

headline: Letters on Colombia, labor and Barnes
summary: Roosevelt writes Senator Moses Clapp of his anger over Bryan's Colombia treaty, Frank Gilbreth on labor, and Richard Harding Davis about naval promotions and boss William Barnes.

headline: Callers at headquarters
summary: At Progressive headquarters Roosevelt sees Dwight Heard, Cleveland Dodge, I. E. Vernon, Augustus Gardner, Wilkinson and Nettleton. Film shows him rowing at Oyster Bay and at his Outlook desk.

headline: At home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events are recorded.

headline: With Joe Bishop
summary: Roosevelt meets with Joseph Bucklin Bishop and writes William Draper Lewis about the party and his June 30 speech.

headline: Fighting the Colombia treaty
summary: Roosevelt writes Senator William Joel Stone that the treaty with Colombia insults the nation, opposes paying $25 million, and asks to testify before Congress. No hearing comes, but the Senate later rejects the treaty.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay with nothing further recorded.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay with nothing further recorded.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay with nothing further recorded.

headline: New York leaders at headquarters
summary: At Progressive headquarters Roosevelt meets Duell, Robinson, Perkins and other state leaders, and has lunch with representatives of the state's Progressive Service. His physician, Dr. Lambert, stays at Sagamore Hill.

headline: A quiet day at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events are noted.

headline: A quiet day at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events are noted.

headline: Oyster Bay meets Belle
summary: Roosevelt holds a reception so Oyster Bay can meet Kermit's new wife, Belle. He writes Ernest Harvier that Chautauqua opinion is running hard against him in the governor's race.

headline: Hinman and Robinson call
summary: Harvey Hinman and Theodore Douglas Robinson visit.

headline: Planning with Perkins
summary: Roosevelt confers with Robinson, Perkins and Frederick Davenport.

headline: At home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events are noted.

headline: Calling Barnes a crooked boss
summary: After meeting Perkins and Robinson, Roosevelt backs Harvey Hinman as a Progressive-Republican fusion candidate for governor and lashes out at Republican boss William Barnes Jr., calling him as crooked as Tammany's Murphy. Barnes will sue for libel.

headline: Barnes sues for libel
summary: Boss William Barnes takes Roosevelt to court for libel, and Austria-Hungary issues its ultimatum to Serbia. Roosevelt promises Franklin D. Roosevelt an article opposing splitting the fleet.

headline: No run for governor
summary: Roosevelt tells Chauncey Hamlin he will not seek the governorship of New York.

headline: Weighing candidates
summary: Roosevelt writes Royal W. France about possible candidates for governor.

headline: Johnson for President?
summary: Roosevelt writes California's Governor Hiram Johnson that he would make a good President, and covers New York politics and the Barnes suit.

headline: At home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is recorded.

headline: War begins in Europe
summary: While Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill, the Austro-Hungarian empire goes to war against Serbia.

headline: McHarg and Colby at headquarters
summary: At Progressive headquarters, McHarg and Everett Colby call on Roosevelt.

headline: The Progressive future, in a long letter
summary: Roosevelt sends Hiram Johnson a lengthy letter on California and New York politics, fusion, the party's future and the Barnes suit.

headline: Europe at war, Panama Canal open
summary: Roosevelt receives a Maine Progressive delegation as war spreads across Europe and Alice comes home. The source also records the Panama Canal opening at a cost of $223 million, apart from $40 million to the French company and $10 million to Panama.

headline: Germany at war with Russia
summary: As Germany declares war on Russia, The Outlook prints Roosevelt's piece on women and the state constitutional convention. To Arthur Lee he mocks Bryan and Wilson, reports Belle down with typhoid, and touches on Irish home rule and the spreading war.

headline: A day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.

headline: Germany declares war on France
summary: Germany goes to war with France, and the first vessel moves through the Panama Canal. Roosevelt writes Winfred Denison about the Philippines.

headline: Britain enters the war
summary: Herbert Croly and Felix Frankfurter lunch at Sagamore Hill on the day Germany invades neutral Belgium and Britain declares war on Germany.

headline: Wilson declares neutrality
summary: Russian troops cross into Germany and President Wilson proclaims American neutrality. Roosevelt tells Governor Martin Glynn he stands by his corruption charges against the state highway department.

headline: Edith turns 53
summary: On Edith's 53rd birthday, Roosevelt writes Walter Weyl about labor, civil disorder and the push for a minimum wage for women in New York.

headline: A day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.

headline: 'Cast down over the war'
summary: The Outlook carries Roosevelt's article on the people's right to review judge-made law. He writes Hugo Münsterberg that he won't rush to condemn Germany.

headline: A day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.

headline: A day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.

headline: A day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.

headline: 'A radical' in every fiber
summary: George Record laments Roosevelt's refusal to lead the Progressives. Roosevelt writes Raymond Robins about Perkins, radicalism, Barnes and fusion, and Frederick Davenport about Barnes, bossism and Hinman.

headline: Ethel's 23rd birthday
summary: On Ethel's birthday, Roosevelt explains his own stance and the Progressive Party's in a letter to Henry Wallace.

headline: A day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.

headline: Pinchot's wedding, then New England
summary: Roosevelt attends Gifford Pinchot's marriage to Cornelia Bryce in Roslyn, then leaves for New England and speaks in Hartford. He congratulates Edward Costigan on his Progressive nomination for Colorado governor.

headline: With Cherrie in Vermont
summary: Roosevelt stays in Newfane, Vermont, as the guest of his Brazil expedition companion George Cherrie.

headline: Campaigning in Boston
summary: In Boston Roosevelt meets Massachusetts Progressive leaders and speaks for Joseph Walker. Granddaughter Grace turns three, and Franklin and Eleanor Roosevelt have a son, Franklin Jr.

headline: Stumping in Maine
summary: Roosevelt gives speeches across Maine, including Lewiston and Portland, and spends the night in Massachusetts.

headline: Heading home
summary: Roosevelt leaves Massachusetts for Oyster Bay.

headline: A day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.

headline: Pulling support from Hinman
summary: Roosevelt meets New York Progressive leaders and withdraws his backing of Harvey Hinman, because Hinman will not commit to a Progressive candidacy should Republicans reject him in the primary.

headline: 'Giants' locked in a death struggle
summary: The Outlook runs Roosevelt's war article about the great powers locked in combat. He writes Arthur Lee that he would protest Germany's handling of Belgium, that Belle is well, and on Wilson, Bryan, Churchill, the fleet and the empires.

headline: A day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.

headline: A day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.

headline: William Sulzer visits
summary: Roosevelt confers with former New York governor William Sulzer.

headline: Childs at headquarters
summary: At Progressive headquarters, William H. Childs calls on Roosevelt.

headline: No White House bid in 1916
summary: Writing John Callan O'Laughlin, Roosevelt shifts his support for governor from Hinman to Frederick Davenport and rules out running for President in 1916. He also covers Wilson, Bryan and the Colorado strikes.

headline: General Wood visits
summary: Leonard Wood is a guest at Sagamore Hill.

headline: A day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.

headline: A day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.

headline: Dick Derby volunteers in France
summary: Ethel's husband, Dr. Richard Derby, joins six fellow American surgeons in volunteering at the American Ambulance Hospital in France; Ethel goes with him.

headline: Writing the Brazil book's preface
summary: Roosevelt writes the preface for Through the Brazilian Wilderness and sends Emily Carow family news about the war and each of his children.

headline: Headquarters callers
summary: Roosevelt sees William Sulzer, Theodore Douglas Robinson and Frederick Davenport at Progressive headquarters.

headline: A day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.

headline: Kitchener and the war
summary: Roosevelt writes Arthur Lee about the war, Lord Kitchener, and the errors of Wilson and Bryan.

headline: South to Louisiana
summary: Roosevelt sets out for Louisiana, with William Draper Lewis and editor E. A. Van Valkenburg of the Philadelphia North American riding with him to Philadelphia.

headline: Traveling south
summary: Roosevelt is on the way to Louisiana.

headline: Speaking in New Orleans
summary: Roosevelt campaigns in Louisiana, with speeches including one in New Orleans.

headline: Cane country stump speeches
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Franklin, Jeanerette and New Iberia, Louisiana.

headline: Back toward Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt travels home from Louisiana.

headline: Oscar Straus calls
summary: Oscar Straus visits Sagamore Hill.

headline: A day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.

headline: A day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; no events are recorded.

headline: Ted turns 27
summary: Roosevelt is at home on Ted's 27th birthday.

headline: Too many invitations
summary: Roosevelt visits the Cove School and tells William Allen White he can't speak everywhere he's wanted in the campaign.

headline: A grandson's baptism
summary: Oscar King Davis calls, and Roosevelt attends the christening of Theodore Roosevelt III.

headline: Strategy session at home
summary: Roosevelt confers with Perkins, Robinson, Bird, Davenport, Hamlin and a Dr. Katherine whose surname is lost.

headline: Off on a western tour
summary: After a meeting with Charles J. Bonaparte and fellow party leaders, Roosevelt leaves on a western speaking trip. He writes Hungary's Count Albert Apponyi about the war.

headline: Westbound
summary: Roosevelt travels west on his speaking tour.

headline: A close call with a train in Kansas
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Wichita, to some 6,000 people, and in Hutchinson. His car is nearly struck by a train.

headline: Guest of William Rockhill Nelson
summary: In the Kansas Citys of Kansas and Missouri, Roosevelt stays with editor W. R. Nelson.

headline: Suffrage appeal in Lincoln
summary: In Lincoln, Nebraska, Roosevelt speaks up for woman suffrage. He writes Henry Coonley about his policies and the war.

headline: Iowa stops and a war essay
summary: Roosevelt takes the stump in Iowa at Des Moines and Boone as The Outlook publishes his essay on the tragedies and lessons of the World War.

headline: Three Illinois cities
summary: Roosevelt addresses crowds at Peoria, Galesburg and Rock Island and is the guest of Illinois Governor Edward Dunne.

headline: Stumping for Raymond Robins
summary: Roosevelt takes the stump for Raymond Robins in two southern Illinois cities, Marion and East St. Louis.

headline: Indiana for Beveridge
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Indianapolis and Terre Haute on behalf of Albert Beveridge.

headline: Belgian commissioners call in Ohio
summary: In Ohio Roosevelt stays with James Garfield and receives members of the Belgian commission on atrocities. A war piece by him appears in a New York paper.

headline: Cleveland and Columbus
summary: Roosevelt campaigns in Cleveland and Columbus for Garfield.

headline: Toledo stop
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Toledo, Ohio.

headline: Michigan, and the Brazil book is out
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Bay City, Michigan, staying with Roy Woodruff. The Outlook runs his article on the causes of the war, and Scribners publishes Through the Brazilian Wilderness.

headline: Rallying 12,000 in Philadelphia for Pinchot
summary: Roosevelt campaigns in Philadelphia for Gifford Pinchot's Senate bid, addressing some 12,000 people packed into the First Regiment Armory, then heads back toward New York City.

headline: Declining a bed at Franklin's house
summary: Back at Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt writes Sara Delano Roosevelt that he had better not stay with her son Franklin, since his upcoming speeches will take aim at the Wilson administration.

headline: Letters on Germany and Belgium
summary: Roosevelt writes three letters about the European war: to Cecil Spring-Rice on German anger at his war article and the ultimatum he would have sent Berlin, to Hugo Münsterberg on Belgium, and to Rudyard Kipling on German atrocities.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Stumping up the Hudson Valley
summary: Roosevelt opens a campaign swing up the Hudson, speaking in Yonkers, Beacon, Cold Spring, Poughkeepsie and Wappingers Falls before spending the night at Hyde Park. He tells Elbert Baldwin the war leaves him deeply saddened.

headline: Six more stops up the river
summary: The campaign tour rolls on through Kingston, Saugerties, Catskill, Athens and Hudson, ending with a speech at the Music Hall in Troy.

headline: Speaking from Schenectady to Glens Falls
summary: Roosevelt carries the Progressive message north, with speeches at Schenectady, Saratoga, Ballston Spa, Glens Falls and Hudson Falls.

headline: Campaigning along Lake Champlain
summary: The tour reaches the Champlain country, where Roosevelt speaks at Ticonderoga, Fort Henry, Keeseville and Plattsburgh.

headline: North Country stops near the St. Lawrence
summary: Roosevelt works the far north of the state, speaking at Malone, Potsdam, Canton and Ogdensburg.

headline: Watertown and Utica on Kermit's birthday
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Gouverneur, Watertown and Utica. Back home it is his son Kermit's 25th birthday.

headline: Sunday with his nephew at Jordanville
summary: Roosevelt takes a break from the stump as the guest of his nephew Theodore Douglas Robinson in Jordanville. It is also his niece Eleanor Roosevelt's 30th birthday.

headline: Herkimer and Gloversville
summary: Back on the campaign trail, Roosevelt gives speeches in Herkimer and Gloversville.

headline: Through Cooperstown country
summary: Roosevelt's tour passes through Cobleskill, Cooperstown and Oneonta, with a speech at each.

headline: Campaigning in Syracuse
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Syracuse, among other stops on his New York tour.

headline: Speeches in Auburn
summary: The campaign brings Roosevelt to Auburn, where he speaks for the Progressive ticket.

headline: Speeches in Rochester
summary: Roosevelt addresses audiences in Rochester as the upstate tour continues.

headline: Off to Illinois
summary: Roosevelt leaves New York for a campaign side trip to Illinois.

headline: Dinner with Mercy Hospital doctors
summary: In Chicago, Roosevelt dines with physicians from Mercy Hospital. He wires Gifford Pinchot, troubled by Pinchot's plan for a breakneck speaking tour of Pennsylvania. His nephew Sheffield Cowles turns 16.

headline: Chicago, then Gary, Indiana
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Chicago and then crosses into Indiana for a speech in Gary.

headline: Back in New York at Chautauqua
summary: Returning to western New York, Roosevelt speaks at Westfield and Chautauqua.

headline: Another day of New York speeches
summary: Roosevelt keeps up his speaking schedule in New York State; the stops are not recorded.

headline: Ithaca and Binghamton
summary: The tour reaches the Southern Tier, with speeches in Ithaca and Binghamton.

headline: Into the Catskill foothills
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Liberty, Monticello and Middletown.

headline: Goshen and Newburgh
summary: The New York swing winds down with speeches at Goshen and Newburgh.

headline: Libel trial moved out of Albany
summary: Roosevelt leaves for Pennsylvania. His lawyers win a change of venue in William Barnes Jr.'s libel suit, moving the trial to Syracuse and away from Albany, the heart of Barnes's political machine.

headline: A windswept day on the stump with Pinchot
summary: Roosevelt and Gifford Pinchot share the platform on a gusty October day across Pennsylvania, from Williamsport and Pottsville through Johnstown, Altoona and Uniontown, with a hop into Morgantown, West Virginia.

headline: Turning 56 on the campaign trail
summary: Roosevelt spends his 56th birthday making speeches in Pennsylvania.

headline: Reading to Lancaster
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Reading, Wilkes-Barre, Hazleton and Lancaster.

headline: From Pennsylvania back to Manhattan
summary: Roosevelt gives speeches in Pennsylvania and in New York City.

headline: New Jersey stops and city rallies
summary: Roosevelt crosses into New Jersey to speak at Elizabeth, Princeton and Trenton, then returns for more speeches in New York City.

headline: His Brazil book comes out

summary: The Explorers Club gives a luncheon in Roosevelt's honor in New York, where club president Robert E. Peary talks about the Panama Canal. Roosevelt also answers George Viereck's charge that he has been unfair to the Kaiser, advising him to give up being an American and join Germany's army.

summary: The libel suit William Barnes Jr. brought against Roosevelt goes to trial in Syracuse. Justice William S. Andrews refuses the defense's motion to dismiss and the jury is seated. summary: Roosevelt hears the Rev. John F. Dobbs preach at First Reformed Church, motors into the countryside, and meets his lawyers. A Times cartoon shows him and Barnes hauling an elephant skeleton out of a closet.

summary: Syracuse lawyer William L. Barnum takes over the cross-examination and pins Roosevelt to yes-or-no answers. Letters Roosevelt wrote to Thomas Platt as Governor and as President are read into the record.

headline: Turning the tables in court
summary: Allowed at last to explain himself, Roosevelt lays out his real relationship with Platt and dismantles two days of cross-examination. Bowers resumes direct questioning; Roosevelt has now spent 35 hours on the stand.

summary: With the trial over, Roosevelt returns to Oyster Bay.

headline: Thanking Douglas and Corinne
summary: Roosevelt writes his sister Corinne and her husband Douglas Robinson to thank them for standing by him through the Barnes trial.

headline: No longer the people's choice
summary: Roosevelt tells John St. Loe Strachey that Americans will not look to him again as a leader. He also writes George Otto Trevelyan about the Dardanelles, Judge Charles Amidon about the Lusitania, Richard Child about Louisiana politics, and Lodge about the trial and dual citizenship.

headline: Writing Borglum about Wilson
summary: Roosevelt writes the sculptor Gutzon Borglum about Wilson and his pacifist pronouncements.

headline: A full house of grandchildren
summary: Roosevelt thanks his daughter-in-law Belle for all she has meant to Kermit. Ted and Eleanor are staying with their two babies; little Grace heads to the beach daily, and Roosevelt checks on Eleanor and young Ted each morning. Metropolitan also runs his article questioning divided American loyalties.

headline: Congratulating Lloyd George
summary: Roosevelt writes Gifford Pinchot about the Lusitania and the Progressives, congratulates David Lloyd George on Britain's new coalition government, and tells Albert Bushnell Hart that Wilson's passivity recalls Jefferson.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: A long letter to Raymond Robins
summary: In a sweeping letter to Raymond Robins, Roosevelt covers foreign policy, Germany, Japan and Russia, leading pacifists, the Barnes trial, prohibition, Catholics and his failed 1910 papal audience, and why he will not run in 1916. He also condemns pacifists in a letter to Hudson Maxim.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill

headline: Bird Island while Bryan quits

headline: On the Mississippi coast
summary: Roosevelt remains at Pass Christian; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Another day at Pass Christian
summary: Roosevelt is still at Pass Christian, with nothing more noted.

headline: Visiting Gulf bird sanctuaries
summary: Roosevelt starts for home, stopping at the Pelican Island and Breton Island bird sanctuaries.

headline: Speaking in Atlanta

headline: Grandson's first birthday
summary: Roosevelt is back at Sagamore Hill for his grandson Theodore Roosevelt III's first birthday.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Last name in the guest book
summary: Alice Longworth signs the Sagamore Hill guest register, the final entry in the book kept since 1887.

headline: Wishing for the trenches
summary: Roosevelt tells Arthur Lee he is sick at heart over America's course, and wishes he and his sons were in the trenches beside him. He mentions ribs broken when a horse threw him as he mounted, now nearly mended, and writes editor W. H. Cowles opposing the arbitration treaties.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.

summary: Edith writes Kermit that his father enjoys having the house crowded with all sorts of visitors.

headline: Ted and Eleanor's anniversary
summary: Ted and Eleanor celebrate five years of marriage; Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Never looking better
summary: Edith writes her sister Emily that Roosevelt looks better than she has ever seen him and is so full of energy she can barely keep up.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Sizing up 1916 hopefuls
summary: Roosevelt writes Charles Washburn that John W. Weeks is too standpat to be the Republican nominee and considers others. He writes Owen Wister about pacifists and Wilson, and Julian Street about historical parallels to Wilson.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Watching police drill at Gravesend
summary: Roosevelt goes to Gravesend Racetrack to watch mounted and foot police rehearse.

headline: Rowing Edith into a thunderstorm
summary: Roosevelt writes Belle about magic and magicians and reports his ribs are mending. He takes Edith rowing for the first time this summer, and a thunderstorm soaks them both. Ethel and Dick have come with the baby, and Archie is home with a Harvard friend.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: A visit from Ted

headline: Dreaming of cottages for the family
summary: Roosevelt writes Ted's wife Eleanor that Ethel is staying with her baby Richard, and that he would love to build small houses on the place for his children and grandchildren. He also writes E. A. Van Valkenburg about an international peace conference.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing more for the day.

headline: Summer opens at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt begins July based at his Oyster Bay home, making regular trips into Manhattan as the month goes on.

headline: Turning down a welcome for Jane Addams
summary: Roosevelt writes three letters from Oyster Bay: one to Langdon Warner about digs in China and the war, a refusal to help greet Jane Addams home from the Hague peace meeting, and corrections to William Roscoe Thayer's Panama article for Harper's Monthly.

headline: An empty page at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no activity is logged for the day.

headline: Fourth of July call for preparedness
summary: At Oyster Bay's Independence Day parade, where New York lawyer Frederick R. Coudert is the featured orator, Roosevelt is called on for a few remarks and uses them to argue that the country must get ready for war.

headline: Talks with Ambassador Spring-Rice
summary: Britain's envoy to Washington, Cecil Spring-Rice, sits down with Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Sympathy for J. P. Morgan
summary: Roosevelt writes to the financier J. P. Morgan Jr. after a pro-German assailant attacked him inside his own house.

headline: Writing Owen Wister about the war
summary: Roosevelt answers his friend Owen Wister about Wister's essay "The Pentecost of Calamity," and turns to the Lusitania sinking and Wilson's response.

headline: Explaining his quarrel with Wilson
summary: In a letter to writer Julian Street, Roosevelt lays out why he objects to Woodrow Wilson, drawing comparisons from history.

headline: Quiet Friday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home at Oyster Bay. The record notes nothing else.

headline: Planning a cavalry regiment
summary: Roosevelt sends William Roscoe Thayer more Panama material, tells Frank McCoy how he would organize the cavalry regiment he hopes to raise, and writes William Rainsford about savage newspaper attacks on him.

summary: San Francisco's Panama-Pacific International Exposition marks a day in Roosevelt's honor, and he uses the stage to press his case for national preparedness.

summary: Roosevelt takes in the Exposition grounds, then writes British author Frederick S. Oliver a long letter about Oliver's book on readiness, the division he hopes to lead, Edward Grey, Wilson and Taft, and his own record with Britain as President.

summary: Roosevelt spends a second day walking the grounds of San Francisco's world's fair.

summary: Roosevelt talks to young men enrolled in the War Department's student instruction camp at San Francisco.

summary: Roosevelt is in Los Angeles; the record gives no other details.

summary: Roosevelt is in San Diego. Nothing more is noted for the day.

summary: Roosevelt addresses the Panama-California Exposition and huddles with California Progressives. A film camera catches him and Edith pulling up by car and standing on a building's steps.

summary: Roosevelt starts the long trip back east toward New York and Oyster Bay.

summary: Roosevelt is traveling across the country on his way back to New York.

summary: The homeward journey continues, with Roosevelt en route to New York.

headline: Sons at Plattsburg's first camp
summary: Roosevelt is still traveling east. This summer the first Plattsburg camp trains civilians as soldiers, and his sons Archie, Ted and Quentin take part. He is also writing Metropolitan articles calling for preparedness and a harder line on Mexico and Germany.

headline: Nearing New York
summary: Roosevelt spends another day on the train heading back to New York.

headline: Back from the West, ready to fight
summary: Roosevelt gets home from his California trip. A New York Times reporter finds him in fine health and spirits.

headline: Settling back in at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home in Oyster Bay; the day carries no other entry.

summary: Roosevelt writes the American novelist Winston Churchill to applaud his book A Far Country, about capital and labor, and shares thoughts on the Socialists.

headline: Callers at the Metropolitan office
summary: Roosevelt goes into Manhattan, where Theodore Douglas Robinson and a Mr. McCormick stop by his Metropolitan magazine office, and he has lunch with Robert Bacon.

headline: Edith turns 54
summary: It is Edith's 54th birthday. Roosevelt writes his English friend Arthur Lee about readiness for war, his scorn for pacifists, and how the fighting is going.

headline: His imagined course for 1914
summary: Writing to Russian diplomat Baron Roman Rosen, Roosevelt sketches the course he would have taken in the summer the war began, had he been in the White House.

summary: Roosevelt is home at Oyster Bay; nothing more is noted.

summary: Roosevelt writes his old hunting friend Frederick Selous, now a lieutenant with the 25th Royal Fusiliers, about the war, and writes Arthur T. Warner about a possible Democratic-Progressive alliance in New York's upcoming election.

headline: A "rational Socialist" and a note to John L. Sullivan
summary: Roosevelt tells writer Reginald Kauffman he counts himself a "rational Socialist," and sends the old heavyweight champion John L. Sullivan good wishes for his lecture tour on temperance.

summary: Roosevelt sends his son Kermit news of the Plattsburg camp and his views on Wilson and his policies.

summary: Roosevelt writes Archie about the camp, the uproar over his speech, and Winchester rifles and cartridges. A long letter to Arthur Lee covers universal military service, Wilson, German agitation inside America, pacifism, his hoped-for division and Russia.

summary: Anna Cabot Mills "Nannie" Lodge, wife of Roosevelt's close friend Henry Cabot Lodge, dies of heart disease. Roosevelt comes back to New York with a pewter sardine box from Gaspé for Edith, who likes it.

summary: Roosevelt and Edith travel to Boston for the funeral of Nannie Lodge.

summary: Roosevelt and Edith stop at Harvard to see Archie and Quentin, who is reading The Anti-Jacobin, Layard's Nineveh and an English version of a Chinese biography of Genghis Khan, then return home. His essay on hyphenated Americanism appears in the Metropolitan.

headline: Worrying over Kermit in Brazil
summary: Roosevelt writes Kermit's wife Belle that Kermit is unhappy at his bank job in Brazil, and that he understands what his son longs for. Edith is in bed, worn out with nervous fatigue after Nannie Lodge's funeral.

summary: Roosevelt opens November at Sagamore Hill, often going into Manhattan. He tells Harry V. Osborne he won't take up the cause of the Armenians until he has spoken out for the Belgians.

summary: On Election Day Roosevelt goes down to the village of Oyster Bay to vote.

headline: Two days before Christmas
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.

headline: Christmas Eve on Long Island
summary: Roosevelt spends Christmas Eve at Sagamore Hill; the record has no details.

headline: Christmas at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt keeps Christmas at his Oyster Bay home.

headline: Day after Christmas
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing is recorded.

headline: Hiram Johnson over Knox
summary: Roosevelt tells George Miller he prefers California's Hiram Johnson to Philander Knox for the 1916 nomination, given Knox's stance on Mexico. He urges English novelist Mary Ward to explain Britain's view of the conflict.

headline: Writing Hiram Johnson directly
summary: Roosevelt writes Governor Hiram Johnson of California to say he backs him for the 1916 presidential nomination.

headline: Democrats divided on preparedness
summary: Roosevelt writes Medill McCormick about the rift among Democrats over Wilson's defense program.

headline: Last days of 1915
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the day has no entry.

headline: America First, a Metropolitan essay
summary: Roosevelt writes Charles J. Bonaparte about what Progressives should stress in 1916. His new Metropolitan article on putting America first attacks Wilson's neutrality and his handling of Mexico.

headline: A foreword for a book of travels
summary: Roosevelt starts the new year at Sagamore Hill, with regular trips to Manhattan, and writes the foreword for his coming collection of outdoor travel essays.

headline: First Sunday of 1916
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.

headline: Monday at home
summary: No events are recorded; Roosevelt is in Oyster Bay.

headline: Tuesday on Long Island
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. The day has no entry.

headline: Talking to the American Defense Society
summary: In Manhattan, Roosevelt addresses a joint meeting of the American Defense Society's trustees and advisory board.

headline: Lincoln, Root and Gussie Gardner
summary: George W. Perkins calls at the Metropolitan. Roosevelt writes Henry Cabot Lodge about a critic of his portrait of Lincoln in Hero Tales, weighs Root and Lodge as Secretary of State material, and commends both Lodge and Augustus "Gussie" Gardner for what they have done in Congress.

headline: Regulate arms makers, don't own them
summary: Roosevelt tells Gardner Harding the government should oversee private munitions plants rather than take them over, and commends Madeleine Doty for her prison reform work in New York State.

headline: Saturday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home; nothing is recorded.

headline: Sunday in Oyster Bay
summary: The record places Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill and is otherwise blank.

headline: Monday at home
summary: Roosevelt is on Long Island with no events listed.

headline: Progressives gather in Chicago
summary: While Roosevelt stays at Sagamore Hill, the Progressive Party's national committee convenes in Chicago.

headline: Wednesday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home; nothing else is noted.

headline: Urging Admiral Sims to testify
summary: Roosevelt presses Admiral William S. Sims to go before Congress and argue for a stronger navy. He tells Willard Straight that a New Republic piece guessing how he would have handled Germany in 1914 gets it right, though it also repeats tales of his cursing at Santiago.

headline: Friday at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. No events are recorded.

headline: Saturday on Long Island
summary: Nothing is logged for Roosevelt, who is in Oyster Bay.

headline: Sunday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home; the day has no entry.

headline: Monday at home
summary: The record places Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill and says nothing more.

headline: Bamie turns 61
summary: Roosevelt's older sister Bamie celebrates her 61st birthday.

headline: Federal oversight of munitions
summary: Roosevelt writes Fred P. Barnett that every private arms factory should be under federal supervision.

headline: Philadelphia speech on duty and loyalty
summary: Speaking in Philadelphia for the National Americanization Committee, Roosevelt calls for mandatory military readiness and condemns divided, hyphenated loyalties.

headline: Back at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is home after Philadelphia; nothing is recorded.

headline: A member of the Security League
summary: Roosevelt mentions in a letter to his sister Corinne that he belongs to the National Security League, a group campaigning for preparedness.

headline: Sunday at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; no events are entered.

headline: Visitors and the Boxer indemnity
summary: Roosevelt tells Corinne that Judge Albert Nortoni and Robert Bacon have come out to see him. He writes Lawrence Abbott about putting the Chinese indemnity money toward education.

headline: Tuesday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home; nothing else is noted.

headline: Political weather report to Lodge
summary: Roosevelt writes Henry Cabot Lodge about the political prospects, the National Security League, readiness for war, and what he sees as Wilson's poor policies.

headline: Planning a Caribbean voyage
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie that her son Sheffield hopes to go hunting over his vacation, and that he and Edith will sail for Barbados and Trinidad in February, a trip he thinks will do Edith good.

headline: Defending his preparedness record
summary: Roosevelt writes Franklin Hall to stand up for his record on military readiness.

headline: Telling Henry Ford where he stands
summary: Roosevelt writes Henry Ford to make plain his opposition to Ford's pacifism, and writes Isaac MacVeagh about the upcoming Republican nomination.

headline: Lecture in Brooklyn
summary: Roosevelt gives a talk in Brooklyn at the Academy of Music, sponsored by the borough's Institute of Arts and Sciences.

headline: A new book and a hospital dedication
summary: Roosevelt speaks as the city's Orthopedic Hospital and Dispensary opens its new building. Doran publishes his new book of preparedness writings, named for the Philadelphia speech, and National Geographic runs his essay "How Old Is Man?"
location_name: New York Orthopedic Hospital and Dispensary

headline: A luncheon and a YMCA dinner
summary: Roosevelt speaks twice in the city: at a National Americanization Committee luncheon and at a YMCA dinner.

headline: Wednesday at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home; nothing else is recorded.

headline: Hoping not to be nominated
summary: Roosevelt has lunch with Rear Admiral Bradley A. Fiske, and writes Bamie that he sincerely hopes the Republicans pass him over, along with a cutting verdict on Wilson.

headline: Four letters on Wilson and the war
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge that the papers are casting Root, Stimson and Lodge as supporters of Wilson's preparedness plans. He criticizes Wilson to Charles Bull, thanks Mary T. Bays for standing against pacifism, and writes the Rev. Gustavus Hiller about German-Americans.

headline: A girl raising money for a battleship
summary: Roosevelt writes 13-year-old Marjorie Sterrett of Brooklyn, who is collecting money so the Navy can build a battleship, and tells her about his four grandchildren.

headline: Sunday at home
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill; the day has no entry.

headline: Lunch with East Side neighbors
summary: In New York, Roosevelt is the lunch guest of a group of Jewish New Yorkers from the Lower East Side at the Little Hungary restaurant, and gives a speech.

headline: German-American Progressives and Münsterberg
summary: Roosevelt writes Gifford Pinchot about German-American Progressives who oppose his policies; lays out his views on readiness, the Alaska boundary and Panama to Harvard psychologist Hugo Münsterberg; and writes Willard Straight about a New Republic article on his Philadelphia speech.

headline: More navy, less pacifism
summary: Roosevelt writes John Graves about strengthening the Navy and tells Henry Ford again how much he dislikes pacifism.

headline: Packing for the islands
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill the day before sailing; nothing is recorded.

headline: Sailing for the West Indies
summary: Roosevelt and Edith board ship in New York Harbor for a Caribbean holiday, and he poses on deck for the cameras.

headline: Out to sea on Alice's birthday
summary: Roosevelt is at sea on his daughter Alice's 32nd birthday. Footage survives of the ship pulling away from the pier and passing under the Manhattan Bridge.

headline: Sunday on the Atlantic
summary: Roosevelt and Edith are at sea, bound for the Caribbean.

headline: Quentin's poems arrive
summary: At sea, Roosevelt receives a note from Edward Huntington, Quentin's Harvard math professor, enclosing some of Quentin's poetry.

headline: Root breaks with Wilson
summary: While Roosevelt is at sea, Elihu Root tells the New York Republican convention he opposes Wilson's preparedness policies, his first such stand, clearing the way for other moderate Republicans.

headline: A grandson born in Buenos Aires
summary: Kermit and Belle welcome a son, Kermit Roosevelt Jr., in Buenos Aires. His grandfather is at sea.

headline: Landfall in the Caribbean
summary: Roosevelt and Edith reach the West Indies. Back home, Alice and Nick Longworth mark ten years of marriage.

headline: No nomination, no embargo
summary: From the West Indies Roosevelt writes Arthur Lee about Lloyd George, says he will not be the nominee, and comments on the embargo question.

headline: Caribbean Saturday
summary: Roosevelt is in the West Indies; nothing else is noted.

headline: A midnight send-off in Guadeloupe
summary: Edith writes Kermit that the whole town in Guadeloupe came out at midnight to see them to their boat, cheering for Roosevelt.

headline: Arrival in Barbados
summary: Roosevelt and Edith are in Barbados; the record gives no details.

headline: Barbados, day two
summary: Roosevelt remains on Barbados. Nothing else is listed.

headline: Island days on Barbados
summary: The couple's Caribbean stay continues on Barbados, with no events recorded.

headline: Still on Barbados
summary: Roosevelt is in Barbados; the day has no entry.

headline: Friday in Barbados
summary: No activity is logged; Roosevelt is on the island.

headline: Saturday on Barbados
summary: Roosevelt and Edith are still in Barbados.

headline: Sunday in the islands
summary: The record places Roosevelt in Barbados and says nothing more.

headline: Late February on Barbados
summary: Roosevelt's holiday in Barbados goes on without a logged event.

headline: A preparedness film and a new book
summary: With Roosevelt in Barbados, the film Shall We Prepare? comes out, including shots of him at Sagamore Hill and at his Metropolitan desk. Scribner's also brings out his new book of outdoor travel essays.

headline: Caribbean holiday with Edith
summary: Roosevelt and his wife Edith are away on a winter holiday in the West Indies.

headline: Still in the West Indies
summary: Roosevelt's Caribbean holiday continues; the record notes only his location.

headline: At Port of Spain, Trinidad
summary: Roosevelt is in Port of Spain, Trinidad, during his West Indies holiday. No other activity is recorded.

headline: Says he does not seek the nomination
summary: From Trinidad, Roosevelt issues a statement to reporters saying he does not want the Republican nomination for President, and that choosing him would only make sense if the nation were in a heroic frame of mind.

headline: At Port of Spain, Trinidad
summary: Roosevelt remains in Port of Spain, Trinidad. The record lists no activity for the day.

summary: Roosevelt remains in Port of Spain, Trinidad. The record lists no activity for the day.

headline: At Port of Spain, Trinidad
summary: Roosevelt remains in Port of Spain, Trinidad. The record lists no activity for the day.

headline: A new Roosevelt baby for FDR and Eleanor
summary: While Roosevelt is in Trinidad, his niece Eleanor and her husband Franklin welcome a son, John Aspinwall Roosevelt.

headline: At Port of Spain, Trinidad
summary: Roosevelt remains in Port of Spain, Trinidad. The record lists no activity for the day.

summary: Roosevelt remains in Port of Spain, Trinidad. The record lists no activity for the day.

summary: Roosevelt remains in Port of Spain, Trinidad. The record lists no activity for the day.

headline: Sails home on the Matura
summary: Roosevelt boards the steamer Matura bound for New York, leaving his wife Edith behind to continue her stay in the West Indies.

headline: At sea, northbound
summary: Roosevelt is on the ocean, steaming north toward New York.

summary: Roosevelt is on the ocean, steaming north toward New York.

summary: Roosevelt is on the ocean, steaming north toward New York.

headline: Home from Trinidad
summary: Roosevelt arrives back in the United States after his Caribbean trip.

headline: Back to politics, and lunch with Ted
summary: Roosevelt spends the day in the city and at home on Oyster Bay, meeting with George W. Perkins and Horace Wilkinson and lunching with his son Ted.

headline: Nick Longworth stops by
summary: At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt receives visitors, among them his son-in-law Nicholas Longworth.

headline: Praise for a poet's new book
summary: Roosevelt talks politics at Sagamore Hill with Charles Sumner Bird and Augustus Gardner, sends news to his sister Corinne, and writes Edwin Arlington Robinson that he likes the poems in The Man Against the Sky.

headline: Talks with Perkins and Van Valkenburg
summary: Roosevelt meets at Sagamore Hill with George W. Perkins and the Philadelphia editor Van Valkenburg.

headline: Wary of a Wilson with whiskers
summary: Roosevelt meets again with Augustus Gardner and writes George von Lengerke Meyer about his Trinidad statement, Lodge's backing of Hughes, and his wish that Hughes say plainly where he stands.

headline: Speaks at a Jewish bazaar
summary: In New York, Roosevelt addresses a Jewish bazaar at Grand Central Palace, sees callers including Robert R. Moton at the Metropolitan, and confers with Perkins and Wilkinson.

headline: Midday meal with Root, Lodge and Wood
summary: Roosevelt lunches with Elihu Root, Henry Cabot Lodge and Leonard Wood at Robert Bacon's house, then meets Progressives at George W. Perkins's home. The Non Partisan League presses him to run for President.

headline: Visits from Bacon and Wise Wood
summary: At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt's callers include Robert Bacon and Henry A. Wise Wood.

headline: Lunch invitation for Corinne
summary: Roosevelt writes his sister Corinne asking her and some of her friends to lunch at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Standing by the Trinidad statement
summary: Joseph Alsop and Gifford Pinchot call at Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt tells Matthew Hale he will not be the nominee and holds to his March 9 statement, and writes Governor Hiram Johnson against dual citizenship and about the Progressives.

headline: Ethel and Dick's anniversary
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill on the third wedding anniversary of his daughter Ethel and Dr. Richard Derby.

headline: Strategy session at home
summary: Roosevelt meets with George W. Perkins, Horace Wilkinson, Henry L. Stoddard and John C. Shaffer at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Making the case for preparedness
summary: Roosevelt writes George W. Perkins explaining why he presses for military readiness, pointing to China as a warning, and discussing Germany, Mexico and the errors he believes Wilson made.

headline: Flower show, Burroughs, and a crowd of callers
summary: In New York, Roosevelt meets a long list of politicians, visits John Burroughs, and tours a flower show with General Wood and Ethel. Elihu Root declares for the presidency. Roosevelt writes Frederick S. Oliver praising his book.

headline: Lunch with the Abbotts, and memories of 1912
summary: Roosevelt hosts George Meyer and Charles G. Washburn, then shares a midday meal with the three Abbotts (Lyman, Ernest and Lawrence), the Regis Posts and W. A. Wadsworth, and talks over his 1912 split with Taft.

headline: Off to Boston on Archie's birthday
summary: On his son Archie's 22nd birthday, Roosevelt travels to Boston to stay with William Sturgis Bigelow and has dinner with the Robert Grants, the novelist Owen Wister, and the William Roscoe Thayers.

headline: Harvard overseers and tea with Lowell
summary: Roosevelt sits in on a meeting of Harvard's Board of Overseers, lunches with Archie and some of his classmates, and has tea with President A. Lawrence Lowell.

headline: With the Cowleses in Farmington
summary: Roosevelt goes from Boston to Farmington, Connecticut, staying with his sister Bamie and her husband, and dines with Joseph Alsop and Herbert K. Smith.

headline: Lunch with fellow naturalists
summary: Back in New York, Roosevelt sees Frederick Davenport and Regis Post at the Metropolitan and lunches with George Cherrie, Frank M. Chapman and Mark Sullivan.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.

headline: Weighing a Tribune editorial
summary: Roosevelt reads a New York Tribune line casting the coming convention as a choice of national direction, and likens the moment to the choices of the 1890s.

headline: Callers, then a funeral
summary: Roosevelt sees William Loeb, Raymond Robins and George W. Perkins at Sagamore Hill and goes to Cold Spring Harbor for F. Hall's funeral.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.

headline: Buried in mail
summary: Roosevelt writes Dwight Heard about the coming Progressive convention and tells James W. White that more than a thousand letters a week reach him.

headline: William Draper Lewis calls
summary: At Sagamore Hill, Roosevelt's callers include William Draper Lewis.

headline: Visitors at the Metropolitan
summary: Roosevelt goes into the city, where R. C. Morris and Everett Colby call on him at the Metropolitan.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.

headline: Calling off a Massachusetts boom
summary: Roosevelt writes Augustus Gardner asking him to halt the Massachusetts drive Gardner was leading to win Roosevelt the Republican nomination.

headline: A doctor for his throat
summary: In the city, Roosevelt sees Dr. Holbrook Curtis about his throat and meets Judge Albert Nortoni. He tells Julian Street he does not expect to be nominated.

headline: Back to the throat doctor
summary: Roosevelt again visits Dr. Holbrook Curtis in New York City.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.

headline: Dinner speech to the Methodists
summary: Roosevelt addresses a Methodist Social Union dinner in New York and writes his sister Bamie that Americans have yet to rouse themselves.

headline: Backs a federal suffrage amendment
summary: Roosevelt meets Alice Carpenter of the Women's Roosevelt League, then tells a Congressional Union for Woman Suffrage delegation he supports a constitutional amendment giving women the vote. He leaves that evening for Chicago.

headline: Speech to Illinois lawyers, visit to Jane Addams
summary: In Chicago, Roosevelt sees callers, lunches with McChesney, gives the Illinois Bar Association an address on America's duties at home and abroad, and calls on Jane Addams. It is his sister Corinne's 34th wedding anniversary.

headline: Lunch with Chicago Progressives
summary: Roosevelt lunches in Chicago with Harold Ickes, Walter L. Fisher, Merriam, John C. Shaffer, La Verne Noyes and Revell.

headline: Homeward by train with Perkins
summary: Roosevelt heads back to New York and Oyster Bay, talking politics on the way with George W. Perkins and Henry L. Stoddard.

headline: Where does Hughes stand?
summary: Roosevelt writes William Noble that nobody knows what Charles Evans Hughes thinks or where he stands.

headline: Teasing Brooks Adams about age
summary: Roosevelt jokes to Brooks Adams that the country has as little use for him as for Adams, and writes Henry Fairfield Osborn that William Beebe needs a Ford.

headline: Expecting Hughes, not himself
summary: After seeing callers at the Metropolitan, Roosevelt writes that Hughes will likely be the choice though his views are unknown, and that the Chicago convention will pass him over.

headline: Talk at the Cove School
summary: Roosevelt gives a talk at the Cove School near home.

headline: Letter on the convention
summary: Roosevelt writes Charles G. Washburn about the coming Republican national convention.

headline: Night at Ethel's
summary: Roosevelt goes into New York City and spends the night at his daughter Ethel's home.

headline: Edith comes home from Havana
summary: Roosevelt greets his wife Edith in New York as she returns from Havana, and they go home to Sagamore Hill.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.

headline: A crowded Progressive luncheon
summary: Roosevelt sees Bacon and Butler at the Metropolitan, hosts a big lunch of Progressive and Republican leaders, speaks at a memorial for Youngs, and writes Meyer, William Allen White and Foster Brown about the nomination.

headline: Laying out his principles
summary: Roosevelt writes Guy Emerson of the Roosevelt Non-Partisan League setting out the principles he stands for.

headline: His principles in the Times
summary: Roosevelt's letter to Guy Emerson laying out his principles runs in The New York Times.

headline: Edith marches for preparedness
summary: Roosevelt talks to the local Scouts and to a Methodist Bible class while Edith marches up Fifth Avenue in a Preparedness Parade. A four-page Saturday Evening Post ad urges his election, and he thanks Thomas Edison for a kind letter.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.

headline: Officers of his non-partisan backers
summary: Guy Emerson and Desmond, the Non-Partisan League's secretary and treasurer, call at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Lukewarm on direct democracy
summary: Roosevelt writes Guy Emerson again about his principles and tells Frederick Eldridge his support for initiative, referendum and recall is lukewarm, just as in 1912.

headline: Meyer and Wainwright call
summary: At the Metropolitan, Roosevelt sees George Meyer and J. Mayhew Wainwright.

headline: Off on a speaking tour
summary: Roosevelt leaves on a speaking trip, after writing William Moody about Root and Pinchot and praising Moody.

headline: Preparedness talk in Detroit
summary: In Detroit, Roosevelt speaks for military readiness and regrets the popularity Henry Ford has won with his antiwar views, then starts home.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.

headline: Callers, then a train to Washington
summary: Roosevelt receives George Meyer, Professor Hiram Bingham, J. Mayhew Wainwright, R. C. Morris and Alexander P. Moore at Sagamore Hill, then leaves for Washington.

headline: Character witness in Washington
summary: In Washington, Roosevelt testifies to the good character of a man named Glover, then returns home. He writes W. Cameron Forbes that the United States should keep the Philippines.

headline: Belmont among the callers
summary: At the Metropolitan, Roosevelt sees Robert Bacon, Lemuel Quigg and August Belmont Jr.

headline: Mary Roberts Rinehart visits
summary: The novelist Mary Roberts Rinehart is among Roosevelt's callers at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Correcting cousin Franklin
summary: Roosevelt hosts Regis Post and Nassau County Progressives, and writes Franklin D. Roosevelt that he is mistaken: shore staff were not cut to send the battle fleet around the world in 1908-09.

headline: Big rally on his lawn
summary: More than 2,000 people turn out for a rally at Sagamore Hill as Roosevelt addresses the Roosevelt Non-Partisan League. He urges Henry Reuterdahl to keep naval engineering strong and tells Brooks Adams he doubts he will be nominated.

headline: Heading west
summary: Roosevelt leaves New York on a western trip.

headline: Hinting at a third-party run
summary: In Chicago, Roosevelt meets Butz and other Progressives and writes Charles J. Bonaparte that he might run on a third ticket if the Republicans pass him by.

headline: Memorial Day in Kansas City
summary: Roosevelt gives a Memorial Day address in Kansas City and meets with Progressives, writing his sister Corinne beforehand that he hopes she will like the speech.

headline: No pussy-footer in St. Louis
summary: Roosevelt gives two speeches in St. Louis calling for universal military training and service, scorning "weasel words." The Metropolitan also prints his new article warning against national drift.

headline: Industrial exhibition in Newark
summary: Roosevelt speaks at an industrial exhibition in Newark and dines with two former New Jersey governors, John Franklin Fort and Franklin Murphy.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.

headline: A book for Maurice Egan
summary: Roosevelt sends Maurice Egan a copy of A Book-Lover's Holidays in the Open and writes him about the West Indies.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.

headline: Can't help Major Parker
summary: George Cortelyou calls. Roosevelt writes Major John Parker that he cannot win him the nomination, describing Parker as untested but ambitious.

headline: Praise for Pershing in Mexico
summary: Roosevelt lunches with General Wood and Simkhovitch, writes Carrie Chapman Catt on woman suffrage, and praises General Pershing's Mexico expedition. Lodge, while expecting Hughes, quietly works to get Roosevelt the Republican nod.

headline: Both conventions open in Chicago
summary: The Republican and Progressive conventions open in Chicago on the same day, with George W. Perkins on a private phone line to Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt writes Arthur Lee on politics and the war, and Thomas Warren on John Hay, books, and the Kaiser's bust of himself.

headline: Telegram on Republican-Progressive unity
summary: Roosevelt writes Frank C. Laughlin about Root and wires Senator William P. Jackson urging Republicans and Progressives to join in a shared cause.

headline: Asking Chicago to delay
summary: With nominations approaching in Chicago, Roosevelt asks his allies there to hold off.

headline: Hughes nominated; Roosevelt turns down the Progressives
summary: After a 3 a.m. call from Nicholas Murray Butler, Roosevelt backs Lodge and refuses the Republican nod for himself. Republicans choose Charles Evans Hughes; the Progressives nominate Roosevelt, and he wires them declining and recommending Lodge.

headline: Kermit's anniversary
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill on his son Kermit's second wedding anniversary.

headline: General Wood and old allies
summary: Leonard Wood comes out to Oyster Bay, and Roosevelt meets with William Loeb, Gifford Pinchot, James Garfield and William Draper Lewis.

headline: No reporters allowed
summary: Roosevelt bars reporters from Sagamore Hill, then meets Perkins, Hiram Johnson, Chester Rowell and Oscar Straus at his daughter Ethel's city home in the city.

headline: A tired Roosevelt at the Langdon
summary: Roosevelt, looking worn, confers at the Hotel Langdon with Raymond Robins, Harold Ickes and Governor Hiram Johnson. His grandson Theodore Roosevelt III turns two.

headline: Kermit and Belle come home
summary: Roosevelt meets his son Kermit and daughter-in-law Belle at a New York pier, where he needs a doctor's attention, and holds Progressive talks at the Hotel Langdon.

headline: Dry pleurisy, and a pledge to back Hughes
summary: Doctors find Roosevelt has dry pleurisy. Still meeting callers at the Langdon, he writes Bamie, Isaac Russell and William Roscoe Thayer that he will support Hughes, and writes Edgar Lee Masters about his poems.

headline: Thanks to Senator Fall
summary: Roosevelt meets Perkins and Hiram Johnson at the Langdon before going home, and thanks Senator Albert Fall for placing his name in nomination; the Roosevelt demonstration lasted 36 minutes, the convention's longest.

headline: Reporters sent away again
summary: Roosevelt once more asks the press to clear out of Sagamore Hill.

headline: Urging Progressives toward Hughes
summary: A crowd of Progressive and Republican leaders, Lodge among them, call at Sagamore Hill, and Roosevelt urges the Progressives to back Hughes. He writes Henry Stimson on the platform and James Bryce on Jutland and the Germans.

headline: Ted and Eleanor's anniversary
summary: Roosevelt meets George Meyer, Charles Bonaparte, Joseph Alsop and H. N. Jackson at Sagamore Hill on his son Ted and Eleanor's sixth wedding anniversary.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.

headline: Endorses Hughes, ending the Bull Moose era
summary: At the Hotel Langdon, Roosevelt formally backs Charles Evans Hughes. His letter to the Progressive National Committee marks the party's end and calls for defeating Wilson.

headline: Done with national politics
summary: Kermit and Belle visit. Roosevelt tells Corinne he is through with national politics, writes Whitmell Martin about Southern Progressives, and urges William Wadsworth to back Hughes.

headline: Callers and house guests
summary: Chester Rowell and Kirkwood are among callers at Sagamore Hill, Nicholas Longworth is a house guest, and Roosevelt writes T. H. Wanamaker about the Progressives' prospects in Southern states.

headline: At Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. The entry holds only a reading note on the 1916 Progressive convention.

headline: Progressives fall in behind Hughes
summary: The Progressive committee votes to support Hughes. Roosevelt agrees with Clement Brumbaugh that Harvard is a Democratic school.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.

headline: Three-hour peace dinner with Hughes
summary: Roosevelt and Charles Evans Hughes patch things up over a three-hour dinner at the Hotel Astor. He also writes Senator Joseph Foraker a warm letter.

headline: Hughes won over on suffrage
summary: Reporters finally leave Sagamore Hill at Roosevelt's repeated urging. He tells Alice Carpenter he has persuaded Hughes to back votes for women, and writes Lemuel Quigg on politics.

headline: Volunteers, a carpet mill, and a houseful of grandchildren
summary: Roosevelt sends Hughes campaign ammunition against Wilson. Offers to join a Roosevelt regiment pour in for Regis Post to handle. Archie has been at a Connecticut carpet mill; he, Quentin and Dick Derby head back to Plattsburg. Five grandchildren fill Sagamore Hill.

headline: Summer at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt settles in for the summer at Sagamore Hill, going into New York City often.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.

headline: Ready to raise a division for Mexico
summary: Roosevelt tells Julian Street he will raise a division if war comes with Mexico. He writes Dwight Heard that the Progressives have split, and tells Lodge about the Cape Cod Canal, his talk with Hughes, Wilson's weakness, and the problems of sending the Guard to Mexico.

headline: Fourth of July in Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt joins the Independence Day parade in Oyster Bay and gives a speech. Film of the day survives.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.

headline: Asks the War Department for a division
summary: Roosevelt writes Secretary of War Newton D. Baker describing the division he wants permission to raise and lead into Mexico should war break out.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; the record notes nothing further.

headline: Quiet day at Sagamore Hill

Roosevelt and Edith scrap a Caribbean holiday and an eight-month scientific expedition to Polynesia; he wants to lead a division against Germany. He also writes Elisabeth Cary about German-Americans.

summary: Roosevelt tells Ambassador Jusserand he hopes America will enter the war soon, because he cannot take up arms before his country does. To Wilfred Osgood he wishes C. Hart Merriam and Edward Nelson would publish more on nature.

headline: Hartford speech: hit Germany hard
summary: Roosevelt, dividing his time between Oyster Bay and New York, travels to Hartford and calls on the nation to strike Germany with full force.

summary: Roosevelt thanks Frederic Walcott for research on machine guns and aircraft for his planned division, and writes John C. O'Laughlin about the senators, led by La Follette, blocking the arming of merchant ships.

headline: Applauding military drill in California schools
summary: Roosevelt writes California state senator Will Sharkey to praise his push for military training in the state's high schools.

summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Dinner with Wood, Root and young Franklin
summary: In New York, Roosevelt dines with C. N. Bliss, Morgan, Elihu Root, Meyer, Mayor Mitchel, General Leonard Wood and his cousin Franklin D. Roosevelt.

headline: Revolution in Russia
summary: A provisional government takes power in Russia. Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.

headline: The Colombia treaty again
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge about the 1903 treaty with Colombia and the effort to renegotiate it.

headline: The Czar steps down
summary: Czar Nicholas II of Russia abdicates. Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Three American ships torpedoed
summary: German submarines send three American vessels to the bottom: the Vigilancia, the Illinois and the City of Memphis. Roosevelt tells Lodge he has held his tongue for weeks and is fed up with talk of standing behind the President.

headline: Protesting the sinkings
summary: Roosevelt speaks out in public against Germany's attack on the three U.S. vessels and wires Secretary Baker once more for leave to raise a division.

headline: At the Union League: a state of war exists
summary: Speaking at the Union League Club in New York, Roosevelt argues that Germany's renewed submarine campaign means the two nations are already at war. He talks things over with Choate, Root and Hughes, and writes letters on the Colombia treaty and on a 1914 episode with the German ambassador.

headline: Views on preparedness
summary: Roosevelt writes John Richeson setting out his thinking on military preparedness.

headline: Frustration with the War Department
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge about the obstacles he keeps hitting with Baker's War Department.

headline: Off to Florida to hunt devilfish
summary: Roosevelt leaves for Punta Gorda, Florida, to go after giant rays, called devilfish, with harpoon expert Russell J. Coles. Before going he writes Secretary Baker again about the division, citing his record as a soldier and former commander in chief.

headline: A speech in Jacksonville
summary: On his way south, Roosevelt makes a speech in Jacksonville, Florida.

headline: Devilfishing at Punta Gorda
summary: Roosevelt is at Punta Gorda on Florida's Gulf Coast for his devilfish hunt with Russell Coles.

headline: Devilfishing at Punta Gorda
