headline: Last day on the Florida waters; "Now We Must Fight"
summary: Roosevelt winds up his devilfish trip at Punta Gorda. His article "Now We Must Fight" runs in the Metropolitan, and Ted and Archie are ordered to Plattsburg for active duty as reserve officers.

headline: Heading home from Florida
summary: Roosevelt starts north, speaking at Punta Gorda and then at Lakeland as he goes.

headline: Wilson asks Congress for war
summary: As President Wilson goes before Congress to seek war against Germany, Roosevelt stops in Washington on his way north and calls at the White House to congratulate him, but Wilson is in a Cabinet meeting. Roosevelt issues a statement praising the President's step.

headline: Back in New York
summary: Roosevelt returns to New York City and goes on home to Sagamore Hill.

headline: Ethel and Dick's anniversary
summary: Ethel and her husband Dick Derby celebrate four years of marriage; Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Send troops to France now
summary: In a published statement, Roosevelt calls for American soldiers to be sent to France without delay. He also talks privately with reporters.

headline: America declares war
summary: Congress formally declares war against Germany. Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Archie turns 23
summary: It is Archie's 23rd birthday; Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Asking Wilson in person for a division
summary: Roosevelt and Edith go to Washington, where he has a long White House talk with Wilson and asks to lead a division in France. Wilson gives no firm answer, but Roosevelt will in the end be kept out of the fight. Staying with Alice and Nick, he lobbies Baker, Jusserand, Spring-Rice and others for his plan.

headline: Disbanding the division
summary: After breakfast with Brigadier General Joseph Kuhn in Washington, Roosevelt goes home and formally breaks up the volunteer division, a ceremony held in his Trophy Room at home. He also writes Don Marquis about writing.

headline: Asking Pershing to take his sons
summary: Roosevelt asks General Pershing to accept his sons as officers. He thanks Secretary Baker for the April 10 meeting and urges Senator George Chamberlain to pass the draft bill.

headline: To Boston for Archie's wedding
summary: Roosevelt and Edith set out for Boston. He sends John C. O'Laughlin a detailed account of his meeting with Wilson; Baker had courteously turned the division down.

headline: Archie marries Grace Lockwood
summary: Roosevelt and Edith watch Archie marry Grace Lockwood at Emmanuel Church in Boston. Quentin is best man, Ted, Kermit and Dick Derby serve as ushers, and Alice and Ethel are there too.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Turning down a Guard generalship
summary: Governor Charles Whitman offers to make Roosevelt a general in the state's National Guard, and he says no. He tells Cecil Spring-Rice that Quentin is starting flight training and asks whether Britain or France might take his volunteer division.

headline: Home Guard visit and a Mineola speech
summary: Roosevelt welcomes Oyster Bay's Home Guard to Sagamore Hill. At Mineola he addresses a Farmers Club gathering and speaks for the Reserve Battalion.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Long letter to Baker on the rejection
summary: Roosevelt writes Secretary Baker at length about the refusal of his division, the government's conscription plans and his own military career. He tells Frederick Allen he will not write to Lowell.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Explaining the Guard refusal
summary: Roosevelt writes Medill McCormick about why he refused a general's commission in the state Guard.

headline: Sidelined, while Quentin enlists
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie that he is sure the government will never give him a war role. Quentin, meanwhile, has signed up as a sergeant in the Army's flying service.

headline: Leaving for Chicago
summary: Roosevelt goes into New York City and leaves for Chicago.

headline: Stockyards speech in Chicago
summary: In Chicago Roosevelt speaks at the Stockyards Pavilion for the National Security League, and a parade is held. The same day the Army draft bill clears Congress.

headline: Train back east
summary: Roosevelt travels back toward New York. It is his sister Corinne's 35th wedding anniversary.

headline: Lunch with Count Ilya Tolstoy
summary: In New York Roosevelt lunches with Count Ilya Tolstoy, wires Warren G. Harding about the draft bill, and writes his old Maine friend Bill Sewall that all four of his sons now wear uniforms. The Metropolitan prints his piece "The Brotherly Court of Philadelphia."

headline: Gearing industry for war
summary: Living at Sagamore Hill and often in town, Roosevelt writes Alexander Moore that American industry must be mobilized for the war, and writes Ilya Tolstoy about the revolution in Russia.

summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.

summary: In New York Roosevelt joins Henry L. Stimson and Choate at a preparedness meeting held at the Harvard Club.

summary: Secretary of War Baker writes once more to explain why Roosevelt's division cannot be accepted.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Two thousand volunteers a day
summary: Roosevelt reports that applications to join his proposed division are pouring in at about 2,000 a day.

headline: Preparedness speech in Brooklyn
summary: At Brooklyn's Kismet Temple Roosevelt makes the case for preparedness and sends Secretary Baker another long appeal with details of his division, objecting to reliance on the National Guard.

headline: Meeting Marshal Joffre
summary: Roosevelt attends a dinner for the visiting French Mission at Henry Clay Frick's New York home and meets Marshal Joseph Joffre.

summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Waldorf dinner for the Allied missions
summary: At a Waldorf-Astoria dinner honoring the French and British Missions, Roosevelt talks again with Marshal Joffre. Baker's latest reply holds to the same refusal.

summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Four hours with Balfour
summary: Roosevelt spends four hours at Sagamore Hill with British statesman Arthur Balfour and Ian Malcolm, a Member of Parliament.

headline: Bat Masterson offers to help
summary: Bat Masterson writes Roosevelt about helping to organize the division for service in Europe.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Call on Governor Whitman in Albany
summary: Roosevelt travels by way of New York City to Albany and calls on Governor Charles Whitman.

headline: Wilson as Buchanan
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie he is getting four to five thousand letters a week, likens Wilson to James Buchanan, and says he cannot picture waging the Civil War under so weak a president.

headline: Wire to Wilson: let me raise two divisions
summary: Roosevelt telegraphs Wilson seeking leave to form two divisions and take them straight to the front; Wilson answers that volunteer divisions will not be used. He asks Pershing to take Ted and Archie to France with the first troops, and praises Lodge's Senate attack on Wilson. Quentin is having back trouble.

headline: Callers at the Metropolitan
summary: At the Metropolitan magazine office in New York, Roosevelt sees visitors including A. P. Moore.

headline: Congratulating Pershing
summary: Roosevelt writes General Pershing to congratulate him on being picked to lead the American army going to France.

headline: Statement to his would-be volunteers
summary: Roosevelt writes a message for the many men who had hoped to serve under him; it will be released on May 25.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Dancing to "Garry Owen"
summary: Roosevelt writes his daughter-in-law Belle that Ethel is visiting. Late in the afternoon in the North Room, he, Ethel, Dick and young Richard put "Garry Owen" on the Victrola and dance.

summary: Roosevelt formally releases and thanks the men who signed up for his division, which he says could have reached 200,000. He sends Charles J. Bonaparte the full exchange with Wilson from May 18.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Clemenceau urges him on
summary: In remarks carried by the press, French leader Georges Clemenceau urges Roosevelt to rethink giving up the volunteer division.

headline: Yale Club talk; a rebuke for White
summary: Roosevelt speaks at the Yale Club in New York and writes William Allen White that he is shocked by White's praise of Wilson.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Memorial Day in Mineola
summary: At Mineola Roosevelt reviews the Nassau County Sheriff's Reserve Corps and gives a Memorial Day speech. He writes Ted about his efforts to get the boys into the war, and delights in Ted's wife Eleanor and the children, who are staying at Sagamore Hill.

headline: "Liberal Russia" in print
summary: Quentin is accepted at Mineola. Roosevelt's article "Liberal Russia" runs in the Metropolitan, and his message to soldiers is printed in American Bible Society Bibles for the troops. Ted and Archie leave Plattsburg under confidential orders.

headline: Kept from France
summary: Roosevelt writes Captain de Rochambeau of the French 5th Infantry Regiment that the American government will not let him go to France.

headline: Speaking to the nation's doctors
summary: In New York, Roosevelt speaks to the American Medical Association's convention.

summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: Railroad men's memorial in Philadelphia
summary: In Philadelphia Roosevelt speaks at memorial services held by the Railroad Brotherhood and the Order of Railway Telegraphers.

headline: Kermit and Belle's anniversary
summary: Kermit and Belle mark three years of marriage; Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill.

summary: Roosevelt leaves Sagamore Hill for Nebraska.

headline: Nebraska's fiftieth birthday
summary: In Lincoln, Roosevelt speaks at the celebration of Nebraska's 50 years of statehood. Back east, grandson Theodore Roosevelt III turns three.

headline: Heading home
summary: Roosevelt travels back east from Nebraska.

summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.

headline: A granddaughter, Edith Derby
summary: Ethel and Dick Derby welcome a daughter, Edith Roosevelt Derby.

headline: Seeking a British post for Kermit
summary: Roosevelt asks Arthur Lee to use his influence to get Kermit into British service in Mesopotamia.

summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill, and no other activity is recorded for the day.

summary: On Ted's seventh wedding anniversary, he and Archie sail for France aboard the Chicago. headline: Wood's camps in the South
summary: Roosevelt writes General Leonard Wood about his choice of sites for training camps in the South. Since April 2 Roosevelt has refrained from criticizing Wilson.

summary: Roosevelt writes C. A. A. McGee objecting to the barring of people born in enemy countries from Red Cross service in France.

headline: Missing the grandchildren
summary: Roosevelt writes Ted's wife Eleanor that he misses her and the children. Quentin and Belle are expected to drive over later.

headline: Four sons headed to war
summary: His latest Metropolitan article, on the kind of peace worth fighting for, is published. Ted and Archie are now officers with Pershing in France; Kermit, now a British officer, is preparing to go to Mesopotamia by way of England; and Quentin has passed his flying exams despite poor eyes and a bad back. Quentin is quietly engaged to Flora Payne Whitney.

summary: Roosevelt writes to thank Marion Couthouy Smith for a poem about him, and sends Kermit a letter on getting ready to ship out, adding that he does not approve of wives following their husbands overseas.

headline: Independence Day speech at Forest Hills
summary: Roosevelt addresses an enormous Fourth of July crowd at Forest Hills, Queens, and reviews the local rifle club; cameras record the occasion. In France the same day, Pershing's American troops parade into Paris.

headline: A letter on German-American loyalty
summary: Roosevelt writes Ralph M. Easley about the behavior of certain German-Americans during the war.

headline: Clash with Gompers at Carnegie Hall
summary: At a Carnegie Hall rally held by American Friends of Russian Freedom, Roosevelt and labor leader Samuel Gompers spar openly on stage over the deadly race riots that had just torn through East St. Louis.

headline: Blessing for Eleanor; Northcliffe visits
summary: Roosevelt sets aside his objection to wives going overseas and gives his blessing to Ted's wife Eleanor, who is bound for France to work with the YMCA. Lord Northcliffe pays a call, and word comes that Kermit must be ready to go by Tuesday.

headline: Alice tracks Kermit down in Boston
summary: After hours on long-distance calls, Alice finally reaches her brother Kermit in Boston, where John Singer Sargent is drawing his portrait.

headline: Seeing Kermit in the city
summary: Kermit, his wife Belle and little Kim come into New York and share a hotel breakfast with Alice. Roosevelt goes into the city to see Kermit, and Alice heads back to Washington.

summary: Kermit, Belle and little Kim are about to leave for Mesopotamia. He telephones Alice, who hurries back to New York.

headline: Kermit sails on the Carpathia
summary: Roosevelt, his wife Edith and Alice go down to the pier to wave off Kermit, Belle and Kim, who board the Carpathia for England on the way to the war in Mesopotamia.

summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Writing a labor leader on lawlessness
summary: In a letter to Victor A. Olander, Roosevelt takes up labor, the East St. Louis race riots, the I.W.W. and lawlessness in general, and returns to the Brownsville affair.

headline: Reviewing Beveridge's John Marshall
summary: The Outlook carries Roosevelt's review of Albert Beveridge's two-volume life of Chief Justice John Marshall.

headline: Talking suffrage with Mrs. Baker
summary: Roosevelt meets with Mrs. Baker to discuss votes for women.

headline: Greetings to the new Russia
summary: As Alexander Kerensky takes over as Russia's prime minister, Roosevelt sends a salute to the Russian people through Prince Georgy Lvov, with a like message to Mikhail Tereshchenko.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Quentin's last night at home
summary: Edith tucks her youngest, Quentin, into bed one final time before he leaves for France the next morning.

headline: Quentin sails for France
summary: Roosevelt, Edith and Alice say goodbye to Quentin at the 14th Street pier as he boards the Orduna with his school and college friend Hamilton Coolidge. Edith writes Ethel that the house on the hill now stands empty of its boys, borrowing a line from Edwin Arlington Robinson.

headline: Eleanor sails on the Espagne
summary: Ted's wife Eleanor leaves for France aboard the Espagne to take up YMCA work.

headline: Off to Pittsburgh
summary: Roosevelt sets out for Pittsburgh. He writes Archibald Coolidge about the Celts, and a newsy letter arrives from Quentin for Edith.

headline: Addressing the Moose in Pittsburgh
summary: Roosevelt gives a speech in Pittsburgh to the Loyal Order of Moose at its convention.

headline: On air power and Japan
summary: Back home, Roosevelt writes Augustus Post in favor of air power, and tells George F. Miller that Japan is sending no soldiers to Europe while seizing whatever territory it can in China.

summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Sending William Allen White to France
summary: William Allen White is heading to France for the Red Cross, and Roosevelt supplies him with letters of introduction. In the same letter he judges the administration's war preparations harshly and finds fault with Wilson's character.

headline: Visit from Columbia summer students
summary: A party of some 120 students from the West, attending Columbia's summer session, comes calling at Sagamore Hill.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Edith turns 56; a letter on Ireland
summary: It is Edith's 56th birthday. Roosevelt writes the Irish poet George W. Russell that he favors home rule for Ireland, but warns that the Ulster counties cannot be split off from the rest of the island.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Proud of Ted's new command
summary: Roosevelt writes Ted that he is delighted his son now has a regular command with the 26th Infantry of the 1st Division. He passes along news of Archie, Quentin and Kermit, reports that grandson Richard Derby Jr. has had his appendix out, and notes that little Gracie is staying for two weeks.

headline: Calling for a ban on German-language papers
summary: Roosevelt issues a public statement urging that German-language newspapers be outlawed in the United States. Quentin, held up for a long spell at Halifax, is at last steaming across the Atlantic.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Quentin lands in England
summary: Quentin's ship docks at Liverpool, and a troop train rushes him and Ham Coolidge to Folkestone to catch a boat across the Channel.

headline: Ethel's birthday
summary: Daughter Ethel turns 26.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Welcoming Root home from Russia
summary: In New York, Roosevelt speaks at a reception honoring Elihu Root and the American mission just back from Russia, then talks about the war at the Harvard Club. He also writes Lodge about the conflict and what he sees as Wilson's failings.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Gracie turns six; letters on free speech
summary: Granddaughter Grace has her sixth birthday. Roosevelt writes the city's police commissioner denouncing antiwar protesters, objects to Thomas E. Watson about government censorship of The Jeffersonian, and sends his English friend Arthur Lee a sharp assessment of the President.

headline: Quentin reaches Paris
summary: Quentin is in Paris, lodging at 29 Rue Villejust.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Quentin posted to Issoudun
summary: Quentin takes up duties as supply officer at the American flying camp at Issoudun.

headline: Quentin's motorcycle spill
summary: Quentin has a motorcycle accident in France.

headline: Belgian Mission on the lawn
summary: The Belgian Mission comes to Sagamore Hill along with Coudert and O'Connor, and Roosevelt speaks to the crowd gathered on his lawn. He writes Ted of his pride in his sons. In France, Quentin wrecks a motorcycle for the second time.

headline: Dinner with Perkins; Quentin learns to fly
summary: Roosevelt dines with R. P. Perkins. He confides to Archie how much he dislikes giving rousing "bugle call" speeches, and tells daughter-in-law Eleanor in France about a picnic boat outing with Edith. Quentin is learning to fly at Issoudun, home of the American aviation school.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Quentin's French pays off
summary: Quentin explores Bourges, and his command of French makes it easy for him to obtain supplies for the Issoudun camp.

headline: A French officer to lunch
summary: Captain Bertrand Vigne of the Chasseurs Alpins comes to Sagamore Hill for lunch.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: At the Natural History museum
summary: Roosevelt tours the American Museum of Natural History in the company of Coles and Luther. He writes Senator Hiram Johnson about limiting war profits and tells Joel Spingarn which poems he enjoys.

headline: From Wilson to Hannibal
summary: Roosevelt writes William Greenough on two subjects: Woodrow Wilson and Hannibal.

headline: Benefit speech at the Comedy Theater
summary: Roosevelt speaks at New York's Comedy Theater to raise money for the Divisional Headquarters Fund.

headline: Four sons and a son-in-law in uniform
summary: From the Union League Club balcony, Roosevelt reviews a parade of the New York National Guard, and his essay "Must We Be Brayed in a Mortar Before Our Folly Depart From Us?" runs in The Metropolitan. By now Ted commands a battalion of the 26th Infantry in France, Kermit serves with British engineers in Mesopotamia, Archie leads a company in Ted's division, and Quentin handles supplies at Issoudun.

headline: A round of letters to the boys
summary: Roosevelt writes all three sons in France: praise for Ted, a promise to Quentin that he will help him and Archie get started once the war ends, and a note to Archie carrying Edith's first error-strewn try at typing. He adds how much he enjoys having little Gracie in the house.

headline: Camp Mills and a Garden City speech
summary: Roosevelt visits the troops at Camp Mills near Mineola and speaks on military preparedness at Garden City, with film cameras on hand.

headline: Into the city
summary: Roosevelt splits the day between home and Manhattan; no details are recorded.

headline: Reviewing the draftees
summary: In New York, Roosevelt joins Mayor John Purroy Mitchel, Charles Evans Hughes and others to review a parade of newly drafted men, and the scene is filmed. He writes Judge Emory Speer that while he rejects the views of Tom Watson's Jeffersonian, the government has no business barring it from circulation.

headline: Speaking at the Columbia County Fair
summary: Roosevelt is the speaker at Chatham's Columbia County Fair, New York. The Outlook prints his "The Children of the Crucible," a call for Americans to stand together against Germany, along with his tribute to Roger Allier, killed in France. Quentin, meanwhile, is hauling equipment across France through storms and floods.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Rowing with the grandchildren; officers to dinner
summary: Roosevelt and Edith take grandchildren Richard and Edith Derby out in the rowboat, while their mother Ethel remains with Dick. In the evening Major William Donovan comes to dinner with four of his 165th Infantry captains at the house.

headline: Opening the suffrage campaign; four stars
summary: Roosevelt speaks at the launch of New York's second state suffrage campaign. He tells Archie he has hung out a service flag with a star for each of his four sons overseas, and writes Senator Frank B. Kellogg for a graduated tax on war contractors' excess profits.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Asking Gorgas to send Dick to the front
summary: Roosevelt writes Surgeon General William Gorgas asking that his son-in-law Dick Derby be assigned to the front.

headline: A good word for Russell Coles
summary: In a letter to Judge Joseph Buffington, Roosevelt speaks warmly of Russell Coles.

headline: Roosevelt takes to the air
summary: On Ted's 30th birthday, Roosevelt goes to the Mineola flying field with the Hitchcocks and goes up in a Liberty-engine airplane, then writes Ted about his brief flight with the trainee pilots. In France, Quentin joins the 1st Aero Squadron and stays with Eleanor in Paris.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Edith writes Kermit
summary: Roosevelt writes Dr. George C. Dyer about the war. Edith tells Kermit that his absence is harder on his wife Belle than on herself.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: How to rise in the Army
summary: Roosevelt writes Archie about getting ahead as an Army officer.

headline: Heading west with Edith
summary: Roosevelt and Edith set off on a trip west. In France, Quentin is asked to remain with the supply unit at Issoudun.

headline: Through Chicago
summary: Roosevelt stops in Chicago on his way west.

headline: Signing on with the Kansas City Star
summary: At the Kansas City Star, Roosevelt signs a $25,000-a-year contract to write for the paper, while keeping his short monthly Metropolitan editorial at $5,000 a year. He and Edith stay with the Star's editor, Kirkwood.

headline: Sunday in Kansas City
summary: Roosevelt remains in Kansas City; nothing else is noted.

headline: Speeches and a talk with Wood
summary: Roosevelt makes speeches in Kansas City and meets with General Leonard Wood.

headline: Bound for Illinois
summary: Roosevelt leaves Kansas City and travels toward Illinois.

headline: Visiting Camp Grant
summary: Roosevelt tours Camp Grant at Rockford, Illinois, and speaks for the National Security League. Edith heads home, and writes Ruth Lee that she is well pleased with his Kansas City Star deal.

headline: Fort Sheridan, Great Lakes and Racine
summary: A full day of speaking: Roosevelt addresses audiences at Fort Sheridan, at the Navy's Great Lakes training station and in Racine, Wisconsin. It is his sister Corinne's 56th birthday.

headline: Speaking in the Twin Cities
summary: Roosevelt speaks in both St. Paul and Minneapolis, and writes Archie about the Kansas City visit and the training camps on his route.

headline: Eastbound via Chicago
summary: Roosevelt starts back toward New York, stopping in Chicago.

headline: Red Cross Sunday in Johnstown
summary: Roosevelt is the speaker for a Workingmen's Red Cross Sunday program in Johnstown, Pennsylvania. Back at Sagamore Hill, Flora Whitney pays a visit and writes Quentin how much she loves the place, while Edith keeps practicing her typing.

headline: The Foes of Our Own Household published
summary: Doran brings out Roosevelt's new book, The Foes of Our Own Household, its title an idea of Edith's. That evening he speaks in New York for John Purroy Mitchel, who is fighting to keep the mayor's office.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: The Japanese Mission calls
summary: Members of the Japanese Mission visit Roosevelt at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Praise for Hoover, complaints to Munsey
summary: Roosevelt addresses the Methodist Episcopal Church's Social Service Commission in New York. He complains to publisher Frank Munsey about the nation's unreadiness and commends Herbert Hoover for his handling of food supply and rationing.

headline: Madison Square Garden rally
summary: Roosevelt speaks to a patriotic gathering at Madison Square Garden. He tells his sister Corinne he plans a stay in Stamford to drop some weight, and explains why he is backing Mitchel.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Introducing Hagedorn to Bill Sewall
summary: Roosevelt writes his old Maine guide and Elkhorn partner Bill Sewall to introduce Hermann Hagedorn, who later interviewed Sewall for his books on Roosevelt's Badlands years.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Off to Jack Cooper's health farm
summary: Roosevelt heads to Jack Cooper's training camp in Stamford, Connecticut, for a course of diet and exercise meant to trim him down and restore his stamina. Kermit marks his 28th birthday with the British in Mesopotamia.

headline: At Stamford; niece Eleanor's birthday
summary: Roosevelt continues his stay at the Stamford health farm. His niece Eleanor Roosevelt turns 33.

headline: Still at the Stamford health farm
summary: Roosevelt remains at Jack Cooper's camp in Stamford working on his diet and exercise program; nothing else is noted.

headline: War on Germany's allies too
summary: Writing in the Kansas City Star, Roosevelt insists that the United States declare war on Germany's partners as well. Nephew Sheffield Cowles turns 19.

headline: Still at the Stamford health farm
summary: Roosevelt remains at Jack Cooper's camp in Stamford working on his diet and exercise program; nothing else is noted.

headline: Letters from Stamford
summary: From Stamford, Roosevelt writes Ted about his work for the war effort, and sends daughter-in-law Eleanor an account of life at Jack Cooper's and of romping with her children, telling her how dearly he loves them.

headline: Last day in Stamford
summary: Roosevelt's stay at the Stamford health farm continues; film footage exists for the day.

headline: Home from Stamford, fourteen pounds lighter
summary: Roosevelt comes home from Stamford having shed 14 pounds and three and a half inches around the waist, though Edith sees little real benefit. She writes Ethel that the stay wore on his nerves.

headline: Grandson Cornelius turns two
summary: Ted's son Cornelius V. S. Roosevelt turns two while staying with his grandparents at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Liberty Loan speech
summary: Roosevelt speaks on behalf of the Liberty Loan drive.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Furious over "Financial Imperialism"
summary: Roosevelt writes Ernest E. Smith in anger over Frederic C. Howe's article "Financial Imperialism."

headline: Turning 59 with a houseful of grandchildren
summary: On his 59th birthday Roosevelt writes Ted's wife Eleanor about her children, Gracie, Teddy and Cornelius, who are living with their grandparents while Ted and Eleanor serve in Europe.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Stumping for Mitchel
summary: Roosevelt goes into New York to give speeches for Mayor Mitchel's reelection campaign.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: The Kaiser in the Metropolitan
summary: The Metropolitan prints Roosevelt's "The German Kaiser and the German People." Corinne's son, Captain Monroe Robinson, is serving with the 77th Division's ammunition train at Camp Upton on Long Island.

headline: Campaigning for Mitchel; a job for Joe Murray
summary: Roosevelt makes speeches in New York for Mayor John Purroy Mitchel. He asks Grayson Murphy whether his old political friend Joe Murray might be taken on by the Red Cross in France. A letter arrives from Quentin describing French towns and the cathedral city of Chartres.

headline: A school visit and a Hartford rally
summary: Roosevelt inspects Public School 45 in New York, then travels to Hartford to address Connecticut war workers at the State Armory.

headline: Touring Bridgeport's munitions plants
summary: In Bridgeport, Connecticut, Roosevelt inspects munitions factories and gives a speech on behalf of S. Merritt.

headline: Dinner with King, Leary and Bridgeport police
summary: Roosevelt dines with John T. King, the reporter John J. Leary, six Bridgeport policemen and others before heading home. Ethel and Dick are staying at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Medals for Nassau County Scouts
summary: Roosevelt hands out medals to Boy Scouts of Nassau County and sends news to his sister Corinne.

headline: Election Day in Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt casts his ballot in Oyster Bay, and son-in-law Nick Longworth wins another term in Congress. He also writes George Dyer about his push for war declarations against Germany's allies.

headline: Revolution in Russia
summary: The Bolsheviks seize power in Russia. Roosevelt writes Ted that Ethel will soon see Dick off to France, and writes Representative Ernest Lundeen about his opposition to the war.

headline: Swapping Dakota stories over lunch
summary: At the Hotel Langdon in New York, Roosevelt lunches with Corinne and his old friend Patty Selmes, and they trade stories of the Dakota days and the Marquis de Mores.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Breakfast for all in New Rochelle
summary: On the drive back to New York from Bridgeport, Roosevelt stops at New Rochelle's Post Road Inn and picks up the breakfast bill for the whole party.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Dick Derby sails for France
summary: Son-in-law Dick Derby leaves for Europe to serve in the Army Medical Corps.

headline: Caution on embargoes
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge about embargoes on neutral nations that trade with Germany, advising a careful approach.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Princeton: strength and duty
summary: At Princeton, Roosevelt delivers "National Strength and International Duty," talks to the undergraduate battalion, dines with President John Grier Hibben and his wife, and stays for the student smoker.

headline: Still in love, 32 years on
summary: Still at Princeton, Roosevelt writes Quentin on the anniversary of his engagement to Edith, telling his son he is as much in love with her as ever.

headline: Speaking to the troops at Camp Upton
summary: Roosevelt addresses soldiers at Camp Upton in Yaphank, Long Island.

headline: Quentin turns 20
summary: Quentin marks his 20th birthday in France.

headline: Addressing the suffragists
summary: Roosevelt speaks in New York at the state convention of the Woman Suffrage Party.

summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Off to Canada
summary: Roosevelt sets off for a Canadian speaking tour with Edith, Ethel and Flora Whitney. He tells William Hornaday that teachers who will not sign the loyalty oath should lose their jobs. It is his sister Bamie's 22nd wedding anniversary.

headline: Speeches in Hamilton and Toronto
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Hamilton and Toronto, Ontario. He writes James Bryce about the conflict and the upheaval in Russia, and Thomas Nowlin on the Mooney bombing case in California.

headline: Back from Canada
summary: Roosevelt returns through New York City to Oyster Bay.

headline: Lunch with Smoot and Madden
summary: Roosevelt has Smoot and Madden to lunch at Sagamore Hill.

headline: Thanksgiving with a full house
summary: On Thanksgiving, Roosevelt writes Ted that Alice is visiting and Ethel and her children are at the house too, and fills him in on his war speeches. He also writes Kermit, who is now serving in Baghdad as an engineer captain.

headline: A Permanent Training Policy
summary: Roosevelt's "A Permanent Training Policy" runs in The Metropolitan, faulting the country for failing to prepare before the war.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: A 31st wedding anniversary
summary: Roosevelt and Edith mark 31 years of marriage.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Lunch with Jusserand
summary: French Ambassador Jean Jules Jusserand, an old friend, comes to lunch.

headline: At the Allied War Bazaar
summary: Roosevelt gives a talk for the Allied War Bazaar at New York's Grand Central Palace.

headline: War on Austria-Hungary
summary: The United States declares war on Austria-Hungary, a step Roosevelt had been urging for weeks.

headline: Pennsylvania Society dinner; Quentin takes command
summary: Roosevelt speaks at a Pennsylvania Society of New York dinner. At Issoudun, Quentin is put in charge of the headquarters detachment, some 600 cadets and 40 officers flying Nieuports; a couple of weeks earlier he had nearly been burned in one.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Wartime prohibition and the Mooney case
summary: Roosevelt tells Clarence True Wilson he favors prohibition while the war lasts, and writes Chester Rowell about the Mooney and Billings trials.

headline: Applauding Wadsworth
summary: Roosevelt commends Senator James Wadsworth for bringing to light the shortages in Army training camps.

headline: To Cincinnati
summary: Roosevelt travels to Cincinnati, Ohio, and attends a dinner at a businessmen's club.

headline: Camp Sherman lacks guns
summary: At Camp Sherman near Chillicothe, Ohio, Roosevelt sees for himself that the troops are short of machine guns and artillery.

headline: Red Cross talk; Quentin falls ill
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Hempstead for a Red Cross campaign. In France, pneumonia forces Quentin to stop training pilots.

headline: Two hours of sledding
summary: Snow covers Sagamore Hill, and Roosevelt spends two hours sledding with his grandson Richard.

headline: Backing Wadsworth in print
summary: In the Kansas City Star, Roosevelt stands behind Senator Wadsworth's charges of Army shortages. He writes Dick Derby about Ethel and the children. Quentin is hospitalized in France with pneumonia and will later be nursed by his sister-in-law Eleanor.

headline: Against recalling Judge Fickert
summary: Roosevelt writes Felix Frankfurter about the Mooney trial, arguing that the recall of District Attorney Charles Fickert was not justified.

headline: More on military shortages
summary: The Kansas City Star runs another Roosevelt editorial on the Army's shortages.

headline: Presents for Ted's children
summary: Roosevelt delivers presents to his son Ted's three youngsters, and writes George W. Perkins about William Randolph Hearst and about Japan.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Thanks for the soaps
summary: Roosevelt writes daughter-in-law Eleanor about the gifts he has given the grandchildren and tells her how much he loves the soaps she mailed him.

headline: Christmas Eve at Christ Church
summary: Alice and Nick join the family for Christmas Eve dinner. Everyone goes to sing carols at Christ Church, where Roosevelt speaks at the Christmas party, and he makes calls on neighbors; the day is captured on film. He also presses Quentin to keep up a steady correspondence with Flora.

headline: A wartime Christmas
summary: Alice and Nick, plus Ethel with her son Richard and infant daughter Edith, come for Christmas dinner while Eleanor spends the holiday with the YMCA in France. Roosevelt sends Christmas wishes to Grace, news to Ted, and tells Kermit how much he values Alice's political judgment.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Against "broomstick preparedness"
summary: In the Kansas City Star, Roosevelt ridicules troops drilling with broomsticks instead of real weapons. The thermometer stands at zero, with Nick and Cousin Laura staying as guests.

headline: Proud of Archie's promotion
summary: Roosevelt tells Archie's wife Grace he is delighted by Archie's promotion and offers money if she needs it. A letter from Quentin reports a joyless Christmas.

headline: A bird under the piazza roof
summary: On a bitter day, Roosevelt steps out the front door to read the thermometer and startles a small bird that had been sheltering on the piazza.

headline: A small Christmas, described
summary: Edith writes Archie about the family's sparse Christmas, with only the two daughters at home to share it.

headline: Year's end in the cold
summary: Roosevelt writes his sister Bamie about the fierce cold. Around this time London recalls its ambassador, Cecil Spring-Rice, John T. King serves as Roosevelt's spokesman in the Midwest and West, Eleanor sets up YMCA centers at Aix and Chambéry, and The Metropolitan prints "Put the War Through."

headline: New Year's Day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt begins 1918 at home at Sagamore Hill; nothing else is noted.

headline: Defense groups, suffrage and a doctor's bill
summary: Roosevelt explains to L. B. Hayes how the American Defense Society differs from the National Security League, presses William Willcox to act on woman suffrage, and tells Archie's wife Grace he will cover her doctor's bill.

headline: Manpower worries
summary: Roosevelt writes General John Biddle about shortfalls in manpower and training.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Edith writes Kermit about music
summary: Edith sends Kermit a letter about music.

headline: A fan of Heywood Broun
summary: Roosevelt writes Heywood Broun that he likes his articles about the Army.

headline: Wilson's Fourteen Points
summary: President Wilson lays out his Fourteen Points for peace in an address to Congress.

headline: Commencement at Peirce School
summary: Roosevelt speaks at commencement for the Peirce School in Philadelphia.

headline: Into the city
summary: Roosevelt divides the day between home and Manhattan; no details are recorded.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Ohio Society of New York
summary: In New York, Roosevelt speaks to the Ohio Society.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: No friend of the Bolsheviks
summary: Roosevelt writes Raymond Robins about Russia and makes plain his dislike of the Bolsheviks.

headline: Quentin back at Issoudun
summary: Recovered from pneumonia, Quentin returns from Paris to the Issoudun camp.

headline: East Side homes and a new grandson
summary: Roosevelt speaks at an American Defense Society trustees' lunch, then tours homes on the Lower East Side with the Community Clearing House to see child malnutrition firsthand. Kermit and Belle's son Joseph Willard Roosevelt is born, and Roosevelt praises Caspar Whitney's reporting on shortages at the front.

headline: Touring the city's child welfare work
summary: With the Community Clearing House, Roosevelt visits an infant welfare station, the Boy Food Scouts at P.S. 40, the neighborhood association at Bowling Green, and the Post Graduate Hospital.

headline: Bamie turns 63
summary: On his sister Bamie's 63rd birthday, Roosevelt writes Belle about her new baby.

headline: Two New York talks
summary: Roosevelt speaks to the League for Political Education and at the Society of the Genesee's dinner.

headline: Remembering Choate
summary: Roosevelt pays tribute to Joseph H. Choate at a memorial service and at a National Security League luncheon.

headline: Off to Washington
summary: Roosevelt and Edith leave for Washington, D.C.

headline: Holding court in Washington
summary: Staying with Alice and Nick, Roosevelt receives a stream of senators and congressmen, among them Chamberlain, Hale, Curtis, Wadsworth, Kahn, Lenroot, Madden and Gallivan. He lunches with Senator Hiram Johnson and dines with John T. King, R. K. Hynicka and a dozen lawmakers.

headline: Pinchot lunch and a bad night
summary: Roosevelt confers with politicians and lunches with Gifford Pinchot, then suffers a severe bout of indigestion; a doctor sees him and sends him to bed early. He writes Richard Hurd that Thorstein Veblen ought to be jailed for a book he wrote.

headline: Taking on the War Department
summary: After another round of meetings, a lunch with Senator James Phelan and dinner with Lodge, Roosevelt takes the podium at the National Press Club and lays into the War Department.

headline: Breakfast with New York's delegation
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts with New York's members of Congress, calls on Franklin D. Roosevelt, and with Edith and Alice dines with Henry Adams and McCormick before heading back to New York.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Snowed in, fires in the Library
summary: A heavy snowstorm hits; the North Room is shut and fires burn in the Library. Roosevelt writes Quentin that Edith is in Baltimore with Belle Hagner James while he stays home with Ethel. In France, Quentin is weary of camp life but flying more.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Edith writes Bamie
summary: Edith sends news to Bamie.

headline: Dedicating a hall at Camp Merritt
summary: Roosevelt helps dedicate a new hall at Camp Merritt, New Jersey. In France, Quentin receives a parcel of books from home.

headline: Ships too slow
summary: Roosevelt writes Albert Shaw about America's sluggish shipbuilding and Grace Macurdy about the war. The Metropolitan publishes his "The Countrymen of Muhlenberg and Custer."

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Kermit at Tekrit; shoes for Archie's men
summary: Roosevelt is thrilled to learn that Kermit helped capture Tekrit in Mesopotamia the previous November, and writes him and Belle about it, adding news of the children and his views on the Bolsheviks. He tells Archie he will personally pay to put 200 pairs of shoes on the feet of Archie's soldiers.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: A quiet day at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at home at Sagamore Hill; no other activity is recorded for this day.

headline: Who should run the Republican committee

summary: Roosevelt congratulates William Howard Taft on his Saratoga speech and tells Loren Palmer what livestock and crops he raises at Sagamore Hill.

summary: As Roosevelt dictates to his secretary Josephine Stricker, AP reporter Phil Thompson carries out a fragment of a cable telling reporters to watch Sagamore Hill. Roosevelt begins to fear that one of his sons has been hurt. In Russia, the Bolsheviks kill Nicholas II and his family.

summary: Phil Thompson returns with an unofficial dispatch: Quentin has been shot down. Roosevelt goes inside to talk with Edith, and together they release a statement to the press. Then he goes back to his desk and dictates until his work is done.

summary: Two days after the news, Roosevelt and Edith travel by way of New York to the unofficial Republican State Convention at Saratoga, where Corinne joins them. His speech rouses the crowd. summary: Roosevelt tells Congressman James Gallivan how he will divide his Nobel Prize fund into 28 gifts of varying size. The Red Cross gets the largest share, $6,900. Ted's wife Eleanor channels $5,000 to the YMCA, the Jewish Welfare Board gets $4,000, Emily Carow passes $1,000 to the Italian Red Cross, and many soldiers' families receive $500 apiece.

headline: Illinois turns 100
summary: In Springfield, Illinois, Roosevelt speaks at the centennial of Illinois statehood; film catches him speaking and stepping out of a car. He writes Taft about universal military training.

headline: Train back east
summary: Roosevelt is traveling back toward New York City.

headline: Shipyard workers call
summary: Visitors to Sagamore Hill include Desmond and a group of workers from the Newburgh shipyard.

headline: Capper for the Senate

headline: Stimson and soldiers from Camp Mills
summary: Henry L. Stimson calls at Sagamore Hill, as do twenty soldiers from Mineola's Camp Mills.

headline: Ted restless in Paris
summary: Roosevelt is at home. Across the Atlantic, a recuperating Ted is itching to return to the fighting.

headline: Launching the U.S.S. Newburgh
summary: Roosevelt goes up the Hudson to Newburgh to speak as the U.S.S. Newburgh slides down the ways. Ted, meanwhile, earns a promotion to lieutenant colonel.

headline: Stimson home from Europe
summary: Roosevelt writes General Leonard Wood about Henry L. Stimson, just back in the United States from Europe.

headline: Archie comes home
summary: Archie, discharged because of his wounds, lands in New York. His parents greet him at the Hotel Langdon, where Archie lays eyes on his baby son, now five months old, for the first time. Archie cannot yet move his left arm, and his leg faces more surgery. Roosevelt writes Lodge, now Republican leader in the Senate, about politics and the draft.

headline: Proud of Sheffield
summary: George W. Perkins calls. Roosevelt tells Bamie how proud he is of her son Sheffield.

headline: A League of Nations as supplement, not substitute
summary: At Lafayette Day and Marine Day observances in New York, Roosevelt argues that any League of Nations should add to American strength, never replace it. Film shows him waving from the City Hall steps. He writes Gifford Pinchot about Perkins's push for a progressive stand and tells John T. King he could never be named a peace commissioner.

headline: At home at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Writing Arthur Lee
summary: Roosevelt writes Arthur Lee about Quentin's death, his other sons' wounds, and Lee's decision to quit the British food agency.

headline: Douglas Robinson dies
summary: Corinne's husband, Douglas Robinson, dies without warning, and Roosevelt and Edith hurry to Henderson House, her place in the Mohawk Valley. He writes Richard Derby about Archie, wires Raymond Benjamin about California Republicans coming back together, and writes Robert Montgomery about poor aircraft materials.

headline: Ted's birthday at Henderson House
summary: Still at Henderson House, Roosevelt marks Ted's 31st birthday by congratulating him and Eleanor on Ted's fine service. He also backs Truman Newberry over Henry Ford for the Senate from Michigan.

headline: With Corinne in Mohawk
summary: Roosevelt stays on in Mohawk, New York, after Douglas Robinson's death. Nothing else is recorded.

headline: With Corinne in Mohawk

headline: A Jewish homeland and fair draft rules
summary: Back home, Roosevelt writes Julian Miller that it would be right to establish a Zionist state around Jerusalem, and tells James Bates that draftees will get no special favors.

headline: The Great Adventure
summary: Newspapers carry "The Great Adventure," Roosevelt's tribute to Quentin, with its lines on living fully and facing death without fear.

headline: Rallying women's war service
summary: In New York, Roosevelt helps launch a campaign by New York's National League for Women's Service, a wartime women's group.

headline: Archie's grave wounds
summary: Roosevelt writes Corinne about Archie's serious injuries and Elmer Peterson about Wilson's government and the farmers' Non-Partisan League.

headline: Get well, Franklin

headline: France honors Quentin
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie that President Raymond Poincaré has sent a French government certificate honoring Quentin.

headline: Women for the War Labor Board
summary: On Corinne's 57th birthday, Roosevelt urges Taft to see women named to the National War Labor Board, and thanks General Pershing for his condolence letter and enclosures.

headline: Fourth Liberty Loan opens in Baltimore
summary: At Oriole Park in Baltimore, Roosevelt speaks to launch the Fourth Liberty Loan and greets Cardinal James Gibbons.

headline: On the way to Ohio
summary: Roosevelt is traveling to Ohio.

headline: Liberty Loan in Columbus
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Columbus for the Liberty Loan. The Metropolitan carries an article of his arguing against birth control. He and Edith are enjoying the fall and often go rowing.

headline: Senate rejects woman suffrage
summary: Roosevelt is traveling toward Missouri as the Senate votes down the woman suffrage amendment.

headline: Still bound for Missouri
summary: Roosevelt continues his trip to Missouri.

headline: Seeing Wood in Kansas City
summary: In Kansas City, Roosevelt sees General Leonard Wood.

headline: Speech in Alliance, Nebraska
summary: Roosevelt gives a speech in Alliance, Nebraska.

headline: Liberty Loan in Billings
summary: Roosevelt speaks in Billings, Montana, on behalf of the Liberty Loan.

headline: Heading home; Edith's picnic
summary: Roosevelt starts back east. Edith writes Kermit about picnicking at Eel Beach under a beautiful sky and seeing an osprey.

headline: Rolling east by train
summary: Roosevelt is on the train back to New York City.

headline: Rolling east by train
summary: Roosevelt is on the train back to New York City.

headline: Back to Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt arrives in New York City and goes on to Sagamore Hill.

headline: No talks with Germany until victory
summary: On Kermit's 29th birthday, Roosevelt issues a statement that Wilson ought not to negotiate with Germany before the war is won.

headline: Niece Eleanor's birthday
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill on his niece Eleanor Roosevelt's 34th birthday.

headline: Another Liberty Loan speech
summary: Roosevelt makes a speech for the Liberty Loan.

headline: Worried about Bamie
summary: Roosevelt writes Corinne that he is pleased with her son Monroe Robinson, anxious about Bamie's illness, and against Wilson opening preliminary talks with Germany.

headline: At home at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Speaking to the Council of Jewish Women
summary: With Archie at his side, Roosevelt speaks for the Liberty Loan at Liederkranz Hall, addressing the Council of Jewish Women's New York section. He thanks Louise Imogen Guiney in England for her sympathy and endorses Selden Spencer for the Senate.

headline: Republican line on peace talks
summary: In New York, Roosevelt writes Will Hays about where Republicans should stand on negotiating peace with Germany.

headline: Rhode Island rallies; a nod to Coolidge
summary: Roosevelt speaks for the Liberty Loan in Providence and Newport, and writes the Massachusetts Republican committee backing Calvin Coolidge for governor.

headline: Sheffield turns 20
summary: On nephew Sheffield Cowles's 20th birthday, Roosevelt writes John Bartlett in support of New Hampshire's Republican candidates.

headline: Against the Non-Partisan League
summary: Roosevelt explains to Gifford Pinchot why he opposes the Non-Partisan League.

headline: A funny story about Mrs. Vanderbilt
summary: Roosevelt sends Ted and Eleanor an amusing account of Grace Vanderbilt at Newport.

summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.

summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Grandson Cornelius turns three
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill on grandson Cornelius's third birthday.

headline: Demand unconditional surrender
summary: Roosevelt wires Lodge that the Allies must insist on Germany's unconditional surrender.

headline: Leave Quentin where he fell
summary: Owen Wister and Alice visit. Roosevelt tells Lodge peace must come by force of arms, asks Peyton March that Quentin's body stay in France, and writes Winthrop Chanler about Quentin.

headline: Wilson asks for a Democratic Congress
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill as President Wilson openly appeals to voters to return a Democratic Congress.

headline: Turning sixty
summary: Roosevelt marks his 60th birthday with letters to Kermit and Corinne, joking that he is now officially as old as he feels and calling himself Methuselah's understudy.

headline: Two hours against Wilson
summary: At Carnegie Hall Roosevelt speaks for two hours, sharply attacking Wilson.

headline: Kermit joins the 1st Division artillery
summary: After training at Saumur, Kermit joins the 1st Division as an artillery officer. Roosevelt wires Senator Albert Fall his support for reelection. Edith tells Kermit his father thinks of Quentin constantly.

headline: Taking on the Fourteen Points
summary: The Kansas City Star runs Roosevelt's "What Are the Fourteen Points?", another broadside at Wilson. He wires Albert Fall again and sends Medill McCormick good wishes for the election.

headline: Nationalism before internationalism
summary: Roosevelt writes Albert Beveridge that nationalism must come ahead of internationalism. Scribner's brings out his new book, The Great Adventure, a collection of essays on American nationalism.

headline: Taft and Roosevelt call for a Republican Congress
summary: Roosevelt and William Howard Taft jointly appeal for a Republican mandate and Germany's unconditional surrender. With Archie, he speaks at a Boys' Victory Mobilization rally in New York, and wires Stitzel Way his backing for North Dakota's Republican ticket, with words on the I.W.W.

headline: Carnegie Hall for Negro War Relief
summary: Roosevelt speaks at Carnegie Hall to benefit Negro War Relief. He wires Henry Timken his support for Ohio Republicans, writes Charles Bird about John Weeks's Senate race, and tells Julian Street about the Republicans and his dealings with King.

headline: At home at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: A history textbook
summary: Roosevelt writes William Potter about a history text titled Medieval and Modern Times.

headline: Out of a sickbed to vote
summary: On Election Day Roosevelt is in bed with swollen joints and a fever of 102, but gets up to cast his ballot in Oyster Bay. Voters turn against Wilson and elect Republicans. Ted is back in battle with the 1st Division.

headline: The Badlands made him President
summary: Roosevelt tells A. T. Volwiler that he owes the presidency to his years in the Badlands.

headline: The Kaiser abdicates
summary: Kaiser Wilhelm II gives up his throne and flees to Holland.

headline: Flat on his back with gout
summary: Roosevelt sends Ted family news; Edith adds a note that he is laid up in bed with gout.

headline: Armistice Day, back in the hospital
summary: The war ends with the Armistice. Roosevelt, his left foot too swollen for a shoe, is taken back to Roosevelt Hospital with inflammatory rheumatism. Edith will sleep in a nearby corner room for 44 nights, seeing friends, going to plays, and reading him Shakespeare at night. Ted and Eleanor meet at the front, and General Francis Marshall writes TR praising Ted as a soldier.

headline: No Non-Partisan League pamphlets, thanks
summary: From his hospital bed Roosevelt tells Robert Pope he has no intention of reading the Non-Partisan League's pamphlets.

headline: Ted and Eleanor in Paris
summary: Roosevelt is in the hospital. In Paris, Ted and Eleanor have some time together.

headline: Letters on peace and Bolshevism
summary: Ted heads back to the front, not to see Eleanor for four months. From the hospital Roosevelt writes William Allen White about the peace commission and Lodge about the West's stand against Bolshevism and Weeks's loss, and wires William Davies agreeing with Australia's prime minister in opposing the Fourteen Points.

headline: Nine months of service for every young man
summary: Roosevelt writes Charles Van Hise about universal service and George Haven Putnam about closer ties with Britain, and sketches for Elmer Peterson a plan of nine months' military training for every man between 19 and 23.

headline: Against Wilson's League
summary: Roosevelt writes Senator Miles Poindexter that he opposes Wilson's League of Nations.

headline: Hailing the Republican win
summary: In the Kansas City Star, Roosevelt celebrates the Republican election victory.

headline: Taking stock of the war
summary: Roosevelt writes Arthur Lee a summing-up of the war's tragedy. To James Bryce he writes about the war's causes, his view that America should have fought Turkey, the black republics, Russia, and his three surviving sons.

headline: On freedom of the seas
summary: The Kansas City Star publishes Roosevelt's article on freedom of the seas. He tells William Allen White the government should regulate, not own, the merchant marine, and writes Lodge about the Bulgarians.

headline: Writing Kipling about Quentin's chapter
summary: Roosevelt tells Rudyard Kipling that the first chapter of The Great Adventure is about Quentin, and writes of his other sons, Wilson and the peace talks, Americanism and pacifism.

summary: Roosevelt is still in the hospital on his sister Bamie's 23rd wedding anniversary.

summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge about battle casualties and observes that Henry White is the lone Republican on Wilson's delegation to Versailles.

headline: Kipling and Anglo-American friendship
summary: Roosevelt writes Kipling again about The Great Adventure, his opposition to the Fourteen Points, the old rivalry and newer friendship between Britain and America, the Alaska boundary, the Royal Navy, and Wilson. He is also writing a steady run of pieces for the Kansas City Star.

headline: Thirty-two years married
summary: Roosevelt and Edith mark their 32nd wedding anniversary while he is in the hospital.

headline: A small stone for Quentin
summary: Roosevelt writes Ted how proud he is of his war record. Quentin will be left buried in France, and he and Edith hope to visit the grave and set a small stone there.

headline: Wilson sails for the peace conference
summary: President Wilson sets sail on the transport George Washington, bound for the peace conference in France, while Roosevelt is still hospitalized.

headline: Arbitration with Britain
summary: Roosevelt tells George Haven Putnam that America and Britain should draw up a universal arbitration treaty, and writes about the navy.

headline: No apology to Colombia
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge, who is to eulogize Senator Ben Tillman, about the revenue bill. He praises Philander Knox's resolution to keep the League of Nations apart from the German peace and opposes any treaty apologizing to Colombia over Panama. He tells H. Rider Haggard he doubts he will return to public life.

summary: Edith writes Kermit that she has just finished reading Macbeth aloud to Roosevelt. Rheumatism has spread to his left arm, and his wrist is bandaged and splinted. He writes John M. Clark about Wilson using a naval buildup to push Britain toward arms limits.

headline: Eleanor home from France
summary: Roosevelt tells Ted that Eleanor is home and came to the hospital first thing to see him, that Archie will stand in for him at the Cove School Christmas party, and writes about the Mexican oil business.

summary: Roosevelt writes D. H. Clark that trying to keep the Progressive Party going would be foolish.

headline: Christmas at home
summary: Dizzy from his inflamed ear, Roosevelt still refuses the doctor's help as he walks out of the hospital. At Sagamore Hill he has Christmas dinner with Edith, Archie, Alice, Gracie and Ethel, enjoys watching little Edie Derby dash about the drawing room, and is tired enough by afternoon to be put to bed.

headline: A sickroom routine
summary: Roosevelt eats breakfast in bed, joins the family downstairs at midday, and dictates while lying on the library sofa, the pattern of his next several days.

summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Rheumatism and the League
summary: Roosevelt writes Bamie, on paper from his Madison Avenue office, about his rheumatism and sciatica and why he is against the League of Nations. He also writes Henry West about Wilson and the League and Henry J. Haskell about Wilson.

headline: Hoping the family is home soon
summary: Roosevelt writes Ted that he wants them all back home as soon as they can manage.

headline: An hour's drive with Edith
summary: Edith takes Roosevelt out for a drive of an hour. He writes Madison Grant about where soldiers came from and Richard Derby about Ethel, Ted and Kermit.

headline: Another drive to end the year
summary: Edith again takes Roosevelt out for an hour-long drive.

headline: Upstairs in the old nursery
summary: On a rainy New Year's Day, Roosevelt's leg and hand hurt badly, and he now passes most of each day upstairs, resting on a sofa in what was once the nursery. He writes Russell Coles hoping for another devilfish hunt, consoles Alice Page on her husband's death, and objects to Ogden Reid about calling Wilson an idealist.

headline: At home at Sagamore Hill
summary: Roosevelt is at Sagamore Hill. Nothing else is recorded for the day.

headline: Dictating on the League of Nations
summary: Roosevelt dictates an article on the League of Nations for the Kansas City Star, to run January 13. He writes Richard Hurd about Americanism and sends an Iowa man, Carroll E. Armstrong, a sharp critique of Wilson.

headline: Recovery, but slowly
summary: Edith tells Ethel that Dr. Hartwell expects Roosevelt to get well, though not quickly.

headline: Last words: put out the light
summary: On a sunny day Flora Whitney visits. Roosevelt writes Kermit and jots a memo to Will Hays, his last written words. At 11 p.m. he sets down corrected proofs of a Kansas City Star editorial and asks his valet James Amos to turn out the light.

headline: Roosevelt dies at Sagamore Hill
summary: Around a quarter past four in the morning, Theodore Roosevelt dies in his sleep at Sagamore Hill of a coronary embolism. Archie wires his brothers Ted and Kermit in Europe that the old lion is dead. About a hundred dignitaries and Oyster Bay schoolchildren attend a plain funeral, with no music, and he is buried in Youngs Cemetery.
